**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 16:13 UTC

Reliability issues are mostly networking failures in Travis CI, which generally one solves by rerunning things that fail.  Since e.g. our provision process is idempotent, I think it would be worth exploring just rerunning provision if it fails the first time (we don't want to rerun it if it succeeds, since that would be slow and defeat the point).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 16:14 UTC

Performance issues with Travis CI are mostly a matter of profiling, which @Aditya Bansal nicely did in https://travis-ci.org/zulip/zulip/jobs/238791359

**Umair Khan** · 2017-06-02 16:15 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 16:16 UTC

My read from the Travis CI output is that:
(1) there's some apt optimization we could do by preventing things like `git` from being upgraded using `apt-mark hold`
(2) Our caching stopped working at some point in Travis CI, so we seem to be redoing `pip install` etc. every time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 16:17 UTC

So I think there's a pretty good project around Travis CI that could take days to weeks.  It's the kind of project that parallelizes well with other routine work (that's easy to switch branches to/from), since basically one ends up needing to wait for CI builds to test what you're doing

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 16:20 UTC

## topic model

*2016-08-08 to 2016-08-08 · 1 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/topic.20model/with/11618)*

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-08 18:00 UTC

I've been working on and off on creating a new Topic table so that we can deprecate message.subject.  There are basically two DB issues to work through:
* We need topic names to be case-insensitive, so we need to have our indexes/constraints deal with that, and our write code as well.  Also, we need to decide whether a name change that is casing-only updates the "official" casing of the name.  It may make sense to have two name fields in Topic, one for lookup that's always upper case, and then an attribute that's like display_name.  But that's a lot of extra disk space.
* We need to link Topic back to Message, and Message can be really huge for some installations, and adding columns, indexes, and backfilled data can be expensive.  It may make sense to have a third join table that links Message to Topic.  This is not how we'd do it if we were starting over, but it may make sense operationally.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2018-05-23 04:54 UTC

One caveat from my experience working on #P380 experimenting on applying this to the api repo previously,  which you can also see represented in Tim's benchmarks, is that the daemon needs to keep running, since (re)starting it can be similar or worse than running mypy normally with *no cache* (not in incremental mode).

Basically:
*  'incremental mode' (disk cache) mypy + subsequent runs, is slow and faster
* 'dmypy' (memory cache) + subsequent runs, is slow and *much* faster.

I experimented with loading the latter from disk, which improved the initial run of dmypy, but we're holding off from that for now, I understand.

Also, I've not experimented with the merged version including the updated git dmypy, but does it just run indefinitely in our current situation?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-23 05:40 UTC

Yeah, it just runs indefinitely in the background.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-23 05:40 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-17 05:23 UTC

So, I'm going to do the migration to have `tools/run-mypy` run as part of our linter suite.  This is what that means:
* What used to be `tools/run-mypy -d` (aka the ~100x faster daemon mode) will now be the default; `tools/run-mypy --no-daemon` is how you get the old default mode.  With modern mypy, there doesn't seem to be much advantage to running it not in daemon mode.
* `tools/lint` will now automatically run `tools/run-mypy` (aka in daemon mode), if any python files were changed.  Note that 
* You should no longer need to manually run `mypy` when doing Zulip server development.

Do we consider Stream to be a parent of Recipient, or vice versa?

Is there good terminology for describing these relationships?

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-11 15:59 UTC

I guess I would describe Recipient as a table containing all the things you can send a message to, which includes streams, users, and "huddles" aka group private message groups

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-11 16:01 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-11 16:01 UTC

I think Blog is still the parent, and article.blog is just looking at the parent pointer

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-08-11 16:01 UTC

rather than looking at a child pointer

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-11 16:02 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-11 16:04 UTC

So Article becomes the parent, or at least older sibling, in the Python parse tree, but it's still the child in the database model.

yeah.

In some upcoming release, probably 1.5, I have proposed that we should take a stab at some DB cleanup.  There are a few types of cleanup:
- structural changes (e.g. moving topic to its own table)
- field name changes (consistent naming on timestamp fields)
- semantic changes (don't have a good example here, but something where we change how a field is used)

It might be worth creating some sort of mega-ticket for DB changes, and then we should come up with a process to work though design issues.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-16 23:08 UTC

So here's what I'm thinking now.  You have a `server_plugins` directory.  It has subdirectories for different bot contributors.  Each directory has a bare __init__.py, some kind of config file, and then a bunch of Python files that each implement one server-side plugin.  Everything is ultimately controlled by the Zulip admin, but the config file in particular is controlled by the admin, and it locks down which messages the plugins can play with.  For simple sites, there's just a subdirectory called "general," and the admin collects plugins from users and configures them as needed.  For bigger sites, an admin might have a trusted org that writes a bunch of plugins, and that org will just publish an entire directory of plugins (including the config file) that the admin can copy into `server_plugins`.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-16 23:09 UTC

And then the config file, which might be JSON, but might be more like a lightweight Python module, will have easy ways to configure some bots by alert word, but it will have escape hatches for super-user bots or bots that are more regex-based than alert-word-based.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-08-16 23:10 UTC

And then for ease of development, we publish some kind of bot driver code that makes it natural for bot writers to structure their code in a way that the bot can run on their laptop, but once they get it polished, can submit the "real" bot code to Zulip admin for server-side inclusion.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2025-02-21 20:37 UTC

We have two Groonga APT repositories on Ubuntu, the Launchpad PPA (for postgresql-14-pgroonga) and the one on packages.groonga.org (for postgresql-14-pgdg-pgroonga, etc.). They both have a libgroonga0 package, but the PPA usually has it with a higher version number so that one gets used. But a new Groonga release might make its way to packages.groonga.org first, so during that window APT selects libgroonga0 from packages.groonga.org, which depends on libarrow and comes with all the pain we’ve had with the libarrow dependency on Debian (#**automated testing>libgroonga installation**).

## stream counts

*2016-10-11 to 2016-10-12 · 32 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/stream.20counts/with/36122)*

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-11 21:21 UTC

@Tim Abbott and I starting to dig deeper into displaying stream counts, particularly for streams that you've never subscribed to.  For larger realms we start to have some non-negligible scaling concerns (although still probably dwarfed by other bottlenecks in the near future).

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-11 21:22 UTC

by stream counts, we mean "counts of the number of subscribers on streams"

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-11 21:24 UTC

Currently our back end gives the browser subscriber lists for streams the user is subscribed to.  These are needed for other features like dimming out non-recipients in the right sidebar when you send to a stream.  But for a large site like RC we might not want to send subscriber lists for streams you're **not** subscribed to.  Except that if we did, it makes displaying counts kind of convenient.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-11 21:25 UTC

I think we eventually want a dual approach--make the UI super zippy for small realms where pushing out actual subscribers is cheap, and then make the UI scalable for large realms, where we might need counts to be more on-demand and where we might no longer be able to afford things like graying out users when you compose a stream message.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-11 21:26 UTC

And when I say "I think" I mean "Tim has persuaded me"--not putting words into your mouth too much, I hope, Tim.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-11 21:32 UTC

It occurs to me that instead of making the behavior different based on the size of the realm, we might want it to be based on the size of the stream (i.e. number of subscribers).  Maybe we have a tiered approach based on the stream size:
* < 10 users: always send actual subscribers to JS, so JS can show users on hover, gray out buddy list on compose, etc.
* 10-80 users: only send actual subscribers to users who currently have the stream active; everybody else gets counts;  UI is still zippy for scanning counts on undiscovered streams and buddy list still grays out when you compose to a stream
* 81+ users: only "push" counts to users; users who want a detailed list of subscribers have to "pull" that from stream settings; don't do buddy list graying for large streams

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-11 22:12 UTC

hmm, yeah, that's an interesting approach

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-11 22:18 UTC

The nice part of that approach is that I think it keeps the code a little cleaner not to have per-realm settings, and we just do the most appropriate thing for the size of the stream (of course, we'd still have to test three different code paths).  The downside is that it could potentially be confusing for a realm when streams jump tiers (although I think that's mostly manageable on a feature-by-feature basis).

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-11 22:20 UTC

yeah.  I think with either approach, we can for right now just implement the small-realm version, and plan to add the large-realm one later.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-11 22:25 UTC

sounds good

## peer_add/peer_remove

*2016-10-19 to 2016-10-20 · 70 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/peer_add.2Fpeer_remove/with/42960)*

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-19 20:47 UTC

So I'm digging into sending peer_remove messages to non-subscribers (public streams only).  I want to talk my approach through a bit, as this is some of our more complex code.  @Tim Abbott

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-19 20:48 UTC

cool!

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-19 20:49 UTC

So one bit of trickiness is that we have these pairs of functions to maintain--the single and the bulk.  Normally I wouldn't mind that too much, but the logic is getting kind of complex, and our test coverage isn't necessarily 100%.  (There's line coverage support, but we don't actually inspect the events, as I can comment out a send_event call and break only one test, which only checks for formatting, not business logic).

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-19 20:52 UTC

Another question I have is how much it optimizes things to send the same event to multiple users.  When you do a bulk remove, all current subscribers are going to receive different messages, since their peers always exclude themselves.  But the never-subscribed folks all get the same messages.  If bulking them is helpful, we could send peer_adds that include the user themselves, which is kind of ugly, but leads to consistency.  Or, the other extreme, which would simplify the code, is to send a single message for each stream/peer combo, and then there's less tricky logic slicing and dicing sets.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-19 20:53 UTC

And then another question is for due diligence, which is do we want to store some of this stuff in memory.  (It would speed things up, but I'm worried about race conditions and fragility.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-19 20:55 UTC

It's an important design consideration to avoid calling `send_event` in a loop, since that would effectively DoS our Tornado process

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-19 20:56 UTC

So the bulk events are important for that reason

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-19 20:58 UTC

If I add alice, bob, and cathy to a stream, I need to send alice, bob, and cathy each their own peer_add messages now, correct?  (bob,cathy) for alice; (alice, cathy) for bob; (alice, bob) for cathy

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-19 20:58 UTC

yeah, we do

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-19 20:59 UTC

That is probably problematic at best

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-19 21:00 UTC

Just read the `bulk_add_subscriptions` code -- it looks like that basically does call `send_event` in a loop

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-19 21:02 UTC

actually, for the new subscribers, it's not clear to me that we are sending them info about their peers, but they probably get subscribers in the "add" event (not to be confused with "peer_add")

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-19 21:02 UTC

gtg lunch but one strategy would be for Tornado to support auto-removing you from the list when it issues you your personal version of the event.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-19 21:02 UTC

That would move the cost in Tornado-land from "process 1 rabbitmq event per subscriber" to "modify a Python list per subscriber" which seems a lot better

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-19 21:03 UTC

oh, yeah, you're right

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-19 21:03 UTC

the `peer_add` event there is sending to the people who are already subscribed

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-19 21:03 UTC

Yeah, so that could easily be changed to just be a bulk operation

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-19 21:03 UTC

ok -> lunch

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-19 21:04 UTC

I think there's still complexity due to different streams having different users...but, yeah, go eat :)

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-19 21:40 UTC

So right now we send S*U events of size P.  For each stream+user-subscribed we bulk up the list of peers.  It seems easy enough to modify the code to send S messages of size U*P.  Sending just one event will be more difficult.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-19 21:50 UTC

yeah, that's good enough

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-19 21:50 UTC

`bulk_add_subscriptions` is rarely called with >1 stream

## recent topics query

*2016-10-27 to 2016-10-27 · 52 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/recent.20topics.20query/with/46584)*

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-27 03:38 UTC

@Tim Abbott We want to query recent topics for folks to populate '(more topics)' going back further than it does now.  The query would be over M messages on N topics for 1 user and 1 stream.

One of the tricky bits there is getting unread counts.  If we try to do the query in one pass, a naive approach would be to filter user_message rows that have the unread flag set, but then you omit topics that are completely read.  In order to get everything in one pass, you have a few options:
* do something fairly complex in SQL that might stretch Django's aggregation capabilities
* use raw SQL (like we still have in the analytics codebase)
* have Django's ORM return all the (message.subject, message.pub_date, um.flags) tuples to Python and let Python count stuff up and sort by recency

Other options:
* do one query to get unread counts for unread messages, and then do another query to find distinct topics [with max(pub_date)] in the same message range (filtering out topics you found in the first pass)
* tackle this in our analytics module so that the web server can do simpler queries
* create a denormalized table with (user_id, topic_date, last_touched, num_unread) that we backfill one time and then keep up to the date in the app

The only option that I'd rule out almost immediately is the last one, since I don't think this feature justifies a complicated backfill.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-27 14:01 UTC

I'm starting on this with a spike-style PR that will use a couple different queries that we can maybe kibitz on.

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-27 14:59 UTC

A non-optimized approach could basically use this query and then process the results a bit in Python.

```
    ums = UserMessage.objects.filter(
        user_profile_id=user_profile_id,
        message__recipient_id=recipient_id,
        ).values(
            'flags',
            'message__subject',
        ).order_by('-message_id')[:message_limit]
```

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-27 15:42 UTC

The summarizing code is simple enough, and probably fast enough, but it doesn't deal with the fact that we have an O(N*M) sql result coming over the wire:

``` .py
    def summarize(result):
        topic_counts = dict()
        topics = []
        for row in result:
            topic = row['topic']
            read = row['read']
            if topic not in topic_counts:
                topic_counts[topic] = 0
                topics.append(topic)
            if not read:
                topic_counts[topic] += 1

        history = [(topic, topic_counts[topic]) for topic in topics]
        return history
```

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-27 16:14 UTC

This is the gist of a subquery approach, which would be two rows per topic sent over the wire (except for topics that only had all-read or all-unread):

``` .sql
    SELECT topic, read, count(*), max(message_id)
    FROM (
        SELECT
            ("zerver_usermessage"."flags" & 1) as read,
            "zerver_message"."subject" as topic,
            "zerver_message"."id" as message_id
        FROM "zerver_usermessage"
        INNER JOIN "zerver_message" ON (
            "zerver_usermessage"."message_id" = "zerver_message"."id"
        ) WHERE (
            "zerver_usermessage"."user_profile_id" = %s AND
            "zerver_message"."recipient_id" = %s
        ) ORDER BY "zerver_usermessage"."message_id" DESC LIMIT %s
    ) messages_for_stream
    GROUP BY topic, read
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-27 16:14 UTC

So, I think we actually may not need to deal with unread counts in this code path, at least for now.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-27 16:15 UTC

The reason is that the the unread counts for any older topics will be 0

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-27 16:15 UTC

And the frontend will fetch messages from the server until it gets from the pointer (where it starts; all messages older than the pointer are already marked as read) all the way to current messages.

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-27 16:16 UTC

So, ignoring the fact that this makes life a little messy for the frontend, I think we don't actually need the unread count data to be returned by the new endpoint

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-27 16:16 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-27 16:16 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-27 16:17 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-27 16:18 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-27 16:18 UTC

Yeah, the point I'm making is that the frontend already has access to all the topics that have nonzero unread counts

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-27 16:18 UTC

So the only things we need a new query to fetch are the ones that are more than 1000 messages older than the pointer, and thus have 0 unread counts

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-27 16:19 UTC

So, as long as we're willing to generate the list by splicing data from 2 sources on the frontend (which is messy, but not the end of the world), the new query doesn't need to know about unread counts or muting

```
EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT topic, count(*)                       
    FROM (
        SELECT
                                                       
            "zerver_message"."subject" as topic,
            "zerver_message"."id" as message_id
        FROM "zerver_message"
        WHERE (                         
            "zerver_message"."recipient_id" = <ID>
        ) ORDER BY "zerver_message"."id" DESC
    ) messages_for_stream
    GROUP BY topic;
```

**Steve Howell** · 2016-10-27 18:25 UTC

Ok, I have to run soon, but we can finalize a few discussion points later today:
* do we do two passes to cut out UserMessage overhead for pre-pointer topics?
* do we really need 1500 old topics or should we limit them (the browser could plausibly use them in search, I suppose)
* once we get a final copy of a query that you've blessed with prod analysis, I'll resume the PR

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-10-27 18:40 UTC

* do we do two passes to cut out UserMessage overhead for pre-pointer topics?

It looks like it costs about 5-10ms to do the with-UserMessage sort of query over the last day or so, which is usually the pre-pointer cutoff.  So switching to the simpler Message query at that point would definitely be a useful optimization

* do we really need 1500 old topics?

We can probably cut it to 100 before sending to the frontend, though there's an argument for just sending everything in that it might simplify the frontend code (don't have to still display a "more topics" button).  But from a perf perspective, with this query structure, it doesn't matter.  I can imagine coming up with a query that would cause the database to stop scanning messages once it got to 100 topics, and I think that would actually be faster (I think what's going on in these traces is that the database is collecting all the topics and then limiting)

I think this query works to start, and we should ship with it:
```
    SELECT topic, read, count(*), max(message_id)
    FROM (
        SELECT
            ("zerver_usermessage"."flags" & 1) as read,
            "zerver_message"."subject" as topic,
            "zerver_message"."id" as message_id
        FROM "zerver_usermessage" 
       JOIN "zerver_message" ON (
            "zerver_usermessage"."message_id" = "zerver_message"."id"
        ) WHERE (
            "zerver_usermessage"."user_profile_id" = %s AND
            "zerver_message"."recipient_id" = %s
        ) ORDER BY "zerver_usermessage"."message_id" DESC
    ) messages_for_stream
    GROUP BY topic, read
```

If we find from the server log data that it's too expensive done that way, we can do the pointer-based optimization first (I think that will have the biggest impact) and then the "only the last year" optimization, which would force some extra UI work on the frontend to show that there are still more older topics (relevant primarily for very-low-traffic streams).

## unread counts

*2016-11-11 to 2018-03-09 · 60 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/unread.20counts/with/52183)*

**Steve Howell** · 2016-11-11 16:06 UTC

This is really a JS-backend thing, but when we start pulling old topics from the backend, we are going to have unread counts that aren't really backed by messages in the front end.  I am thinking we have the concept of a "provisional back end count", and then topic-unread counts are calculated as follow:
* if no provisional counts exist, we calculate as we do today, by counting the number of messages in unread.get_counts()
* provisional counts get populated from the back end
* if provisional counts do exist, we take the max of either the front-end-num-of-msgs count or the provisional counts
* as either "old" messages come in or downloaded get read, we continue to set/unset unread_topics[stream][topic][msg_id] as we do now
* for any activity on a particular message, we also incr/decr the provisional count if we can detect the status has flipped
* as an optimization, the moment that the front end count becomes >= the provisional count, we can dispense of the provisional count to cut down on bookkeeping

The above algorithm is certainly feasible, but I'm open to other suggestions on how to either figure out the counts more quickly/reliably or maybe tweak the UI somehow for the zoomed-in case.

## webhook code structure

*2016-11-27 to 2016-11-27 · 38 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/webhook.20code.20structure/with/58977)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-27 18:00 UTC

Hey folks!  We're working on trying to simplify the organization of the webhook code.  Currently, when you have a webhook integration like the one for Travis CI, you end up making changes in several places:
* zerver/lib/integrations.py (1 line in the registry of integrations; 200 LOC)
* zerver/views/webhooks/travis.py (the actual view code)
* zerver/tests/webhooks/test_travis.py (tests)
* zerver/fixtures/travis/travis_*.json (test fixtures)
* templates/zerver/integrations.html (a giant file with all the integrations in it)
* static/images/integrations/logos/travis.png (the integration's logo)
* static/images/integrations/travis/* (any screenshots for the integration)

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-27 18:03 UTC

We're looking at trying to reorganize the model to put more of the code inside a single directory tree, under the theory that it'd be easier to manage.  E.g. we might have:
* zerver/webhooks/travis/{views.py,tests.py} for the views and tests
* zerver/webhooks/travis/fixtures/*.json for the test fixtures
* Maybe zerver/webhooks/travis/docs.html (or .md?) for the documentation
* (not sure we'd want to move the images as well since we've historically kept all static assets in one place, but maybe!)

**Tim Abbott** · 2016-11-27 18:04 UTC

We're looking for feedback on this design!  Is the proposed new model better?  Should it be `zerver/webhooks/travis`, or `zerver/webhooks/views/travis`, or even `webhooks/travis`?

I'd also have an open mind about making the webhook Python files define their own tests and have some kind of custom test discovery engine. > Python's semantics for initializing parameters is that you are actually assigning an empty array to files, and this array will actually grow every time you call the function!

```python
def do_api_query(self, orig_request, url, files=[], method="POST", longpolling=False):
```

Doesn't `files` have a function-only scope here?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-10 19:25 UTC

The problem actually is **exactly** that `foo` is scoped to the function, and not the caller, although it's quite subtle.

~~~ py
def glitchy_append(x, foo = []):
    foo.append(x)
    print foo 

glitchy_append(4, [1,2,3])
glitchy_append('apple')
glitchy_append('banana')

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-10 19:28 UTC

The assignment statement there happens when Python's interpreter "evaluates" the "def" statement, not at call time.  The reasons are somewhat esoteric.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-12 14:29 UTC

Ok, I think I found an issue that probably needs to be addressed sooner.  When we look up streams by id, I think it's important to be defensive in our code and check that `stream.realm_id` matches `user_profile.realm_id`.  There's often another layer of defense behind our lookup--if the user's not subscribed to the stream, we'll complain too--but I want to avoid the situation of us accidentally publishing stream info to the wrong realm.  We can probably do this with a helper function like `get_stream_by_id(stream_id, user_profile)` that automatically does the validation and throws a JsonError if the stream doesn't match.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-12 14:33 UTC

Also,we would then raise `JsonError(_('Invalid stream id'))` in both the cases that a) the stream id doesn't exist at all or b) the stream id is invalid for the user's realm.

This makes it a little less convenient for a hacker to probe which stream ids outside of their realm might be valid.

```.py
# get_stream_backend takes either a realm id or a realm
@cache_with_key(get_stream_cache_key, timeout=3600*24*7)
def get_stream_backend(stream_name, realm):
    # type: (Text, Realm) -> Stream
    return Stream.objects.select_related("realm").get(
        name__iexact=stream_name.strip(), realm_id=realm.id)

def get_stream(stream_name, realm):
    # type: (Text, Realm) -> Optional[Stream]
    try:
        return get_stream_backend(stream_name, realm)
    except Stream.DoesNotExist:
        return None
```

## API beyond REST & webhooks

*2017-01-17 to 2017-01-26 · 54 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/API.20beyond.20REST.20.26.20webhooks/with/131289)*

**Sumana Harihareswara** · 2017-01-17 17:32 UTC

@Andrea  Longo has [a question](https://groups.google.com/d/msg/zulip-devel/wc6iTwxDJTo/f7sSf2CoAgAJ) @Steve Howell @Tim Abbott kind of related to my request for a [State Of The APIs](https://groups.google.com/forum/#!topic/zulip-devel/AV4PM9jP0HU) a while back.... I welcome an overview!

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-17 18:06 UTC

Every project of sufficient size has layers to its API.

I would say our lowest level API of note is our URL endpoints.  We can hit the URLs from basically any language that has an http library.

And then the thing that we actually brand as our "Python API" is a really just a thin layer--with some exceptions--on top of our URL scheme that allows you talk to Zulip making Python function calls without having to know that HTTP is our transport scheme.

The bot API is a really simple API--basically three functions--oriented toward bots that basically do request/response.

@Andrea  Longo also mentions the integrations API, which I'm not really an expert on.  In some sense our integrations scheme is more of a vertical slice than another layer on the pyramid.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-17 18:11 UTC

You can see some example usages of the Python API here: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/tools/lib/api_tests.py

We eventually want to come up with much better documentation of the Python API wrappers.  But, really, the most important layer to document is the layer that @Andrea  Longo is addressing--the low-level REST API.  If we can get that layer easy for folks to understand, it empowers folks to develop clients in multiple languages and package up higher level code that is more oriented to specific problems.  The REST API is at the bottom of the pyramid, so it's the most powerful interface to Zulip, but it's also the most broad and primitive layer, so it has a steeper learning curve, and it's tied to our current transport mechanisms.

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-01-17 18:12 UTC

The layers you mention are oriented towards external developers integrating in some way, how much are also used within the webapp itself? Like the URL endpoints.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-17 18:12 UTC

The URL endpoints are used very directly by the webapp.

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-01-17 18:12 UTC

So if they can also be used by external developers, in practice are they?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-17 18:13 UTC

If you do this `git grep channel.post -- '*.js'` and follow some of the results, you'll see what I mean.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-17 18:14 UTC

We don't have **tremendous** insight into how external developers interact with Zulip--since they don't always report back to us (nor are they obligated to)--but I've definitely seen examples in the wild of folks using the low level REST api.

**Alex Dehnert** · 2017-01-17 18:15 UTC

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-01-17 18:15 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-17 18:16 UTC

@Alex Dehnert I would hope that most Python folks do use the Python API. :smile: Let me go find my PHP example, though, haha...

**Alex Dehnert** · 2017-01-17 18:16 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-17 18:18 UTC

@Andrea  Longo Yes, bots are largely message-centric.  We may eventually add some helpers to the bot API for subscribing to streams, but we deliberately try to make the bot API a very small and understandable subset of the overall Zulip API.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-17 18:19 UTC

And the bot API also works on a higher layer--for example, `triage_message` doesn't really map to a REST call; instead it's a protocol between our bot driver and the implementation of a specific bot like giphy, thesarus, tictactoe, etc.

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-01-17 18:19 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-17 18:19 UTC

yes :)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-17 18:21 UTC

Maybe "complicated" isn't quite the right word--I would just say that it's "large".  The individual parts are simple enough.  It just has lots of stuff that most folks would never need for simple applications.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-17 18:22 UTC

Yeah, I agree that bots are kind of their own special case.  For bots the magic is not in the interaction with Zulip; the magic is in whatever the bot does that's cool, like call out to giphy or whatever.  So we try to keep the Zulip interface really basic.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-17 18:23 UTC

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-01-17 18:24 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-01-17 18:24 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-01-17 18:25 UTC

@Tim Abbott When we call Message.get_raw_db_rows to get messages (and cache them), we get several fields that are directly on UserProfile record for the sender:
* id
* email
* full_name
* short_name
* avatar_source
* is_mirror_dummy

We may soon be adding `avatar_version` to this.  I am wondering if we should consider taking some of those rows out of our message cache and instead hydrate those rows when we send them to the client using our user caches.  Pros: less work for DB, smaller cache, more current user data.  Cons: may be slower.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-02 17:43 UTC

The other issue to consider here is that our browser client really only needs sender_id, and it should hydrate everything client side.  But we probably need to send all the other stuff to our non-browser clients.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-02 18:06 UTC

The browser client needs more than sender_id for the unusual case of non-pre-declared cross-realm messages (e.g. the cross-realm support PMs we used to do), but that's about it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-02 18:08 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-02 18:09 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-02 18:09 UTC

And can't be easily invalidated

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-02 18:10 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-02 18:11 UTC

nope; but it'd be an easy application of generic_bulk_cached_fetch, I think

## deleting streams

*2017-02-15 to 2017-02-16 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/deleting.20streams/with/151779)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-15 03:09 UTC

So the performance problems for deleting streams basically date back to an extremely naive implementation of iterating through every use in the realm (not even the stream!) and remove their subscription.  It may be a pretty simple fix.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-15 04:07 UTC

@Tim Abbott The following fix greatly improves the performance for stream deactivations:

~~~
 def do_deactivate_stream(stream, log=True):
     # type: (Stream, bool) -> None
-    user_profiles = UserProfile.objects.filter(realm=stream.realm)
-    for user_profile in user_profiles:
-        bulk_remove_subscriptions([user_profile], [stream])
+    subscriptions = Subscription.objects.select_related('user_profile').filter(
+        recipient__type=Recipient.STREAM,
+        recipient__type_id=stream.id,
+        active=True)
+
+    user_profiles = [
+        sub.user_profile
+        for sub in subscriptions]
+
+    bulk_remove_subscriptions(user_profiles, [stream])

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-15 04:09 UTC

But I think we can go further.  We can probably avoid all the complexity inside of `bulk_remove_subscriptions` and just deactivate the subscriptions with a few simple lines of Django code.  And then, instead of sending events for each unsubscribe, we could send a deactivate-stream event to all the users who care about the stream and let the clients do what they need to do.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-15 04:10 UTC

(We actually already send a stream/delete event, so it's really just a matter of letting the JS code handle that in terms of doing a "deep" delete, if it doesn't already do that.)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-15 04:11 UTC

Currently the JS client ignores the stream/delete event, so we'd need to change that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-15 04:52 UTC

wow, that code is pretty terrible :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-15 04:53 UTC

That plan sounds good

**Alicja Raszkowska** · 2017-02-15 10:22 UTC

I think this would be a great live coding session to learn a lot from :)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-16 04:27 UTC

I didn't end up live coding delete-streams, just because there was a lot of context that would have been difficult to communicate over chat.

One question I have is what our policy should be in terms of deactivate default streams.  Two basic options:
* Don't allow somebody to deactivate a default stream.  Require them to make it non-default first.  This can possibly prevent accidental deactivations, and it simplifies live-updating a tiny bit.
* Just automatically remove the DefaultStream row if it exists.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-16 04:34 UTC

Hmm

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-02-16 04:35 UTC

I feel like probably people expect the second outcome more (under the assumption that people think of a default stream as more of a bit on the stream object than a separate concept)?  But I could go either way...

**Alicja Raszkowska** · 2017-02-16 09:21 UTC

do we want to prevent in any way not having default streams?

**Alicja Raszkowska** · 2017-02-16 09:23 UTC

I think it's not that probable, but we might want to make sure there is at least one default stream when a new user logs in - it can be confusing if there are none

**Steve Howell** · 2017-02-16 15:03 UTC

@Tim Abbott I am about to submit a PR that removes users from the buddy list if they haven't logged in for two weeks.   The goal, as we discussed over PMs, is to improve performance for large sites and probably make the buddy list more usable for many use cases (less noise from users who have long since disappeared).   I have a couple questions:
* Is two weeks too small an interval?  (My thought process is to go a little extreme on this, to get feedback, and then we can dial it back as needed before the next release.)
* We want to slim the list even during the initial page load, correct?
* The next iteration would be to allow more control over the interval.  Can we do this with a Django settings, or should we make it a field on Realm?  If we go with configuration options, how do we want to specify the interval?  Is weeks granular enough?

## Rate limiting

*2017-03-11 to 2017-03-13 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Rate.20limiting/with/166125)*

**Tommy Ip** · 2017-03-11 14:36 UTC

Is there a reason why we implement our own rate limiting? I have had a look at the `zerver/lib/rate_limiter.py` module and the logic is not terribly complex, couldn't we just use nginx's `limit_req_zone` directive?
I know our rate limiting is done per user bases and nginx's is per IP, but by removing the custom code we could also remove redis and lower the memory footprint of Zulip #34. (is there something I am missing?)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-03-11 15:08 UTC

Implementing rate limiting in the app gives us more control over rate-limiting specific users or specific realms, and we give nice error messages to API users who are not necessarily malicious.  Small installations who want low memory footprints already have the option to set RATE_LIMITING to False, although I don't think we actually disable redis itself for them, so that might be an optimization that is available now without having to totally change our philosophy here.

Another thing to consider here is that we may eventually find other uses for redis for the project.  I'm also curious how much memory redis actually consumes in a typical Zulip installation.  I imagine it has some memory overhead due its focus on speed (trade memory for speed), but I doubt it's huge.

**Tommy Ip** · 2017-03-11 15:51 UTC

Ok, also is #16 still active? or should that be closed

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-13 17:41 UTC

We use redis for a few other things

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-13 17:42 UTC

I think we actually want to be using nginx's `limit_req_zone` feature as well; I was just looking into that a few weeks ago

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-03-13 17:42 UTC

(specifically for the /events where a rate-limited request consumes about as much resources as a real one)

## webhook integrations

*2017-04-28 to 2024-12-27 · 26 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/webhook.20integrations/with/193992)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-28 18:17 UTC

@Eeshan Garg @Tomasz Kolek @Siddharth Mahapatra @Andrea  Longo I want to start a conversation about some further optimizations to our webhook integrations system.  Right now, we have a few auth decorators used, depending on the type of webhook.  By far the most common (used for almost all new ones) is `@api_key_only_webhook_view("WebhookName")`, which passes 3 positional arguments into the function: `request`, `user_profile`, and `client`.  `client` is used only to pass into `check_send_message()`.  

The problem is that our other auth decorators only pass 2 positional arguments, which has several times caused confusion when folks realized they had the wrong auth decorator (since they were copying from another integration), since they'd often end up basically passing an argument both positionally and via kwargs, which is super confusing to debug in Python is you haven't read the code for the decorators involved (I know I've had to help 2-3 people debug that precise problem already!).  

So my proposed solution is to make `api_key_only_webhook_view` just set `request.client` and pass just `request` and user_profile` as positional arguments, just like our other auth decorators; the result is that the `check_send_message` calls would need to have `request.client` passed to them rather than the `client` argument.  I think that this would be a relatively easy to do change that would save some time people spend debugging their webhook integrations.  Thoughts?

**Eeshan Garg** · 2017-04-28 18:25 UTC

I agree. Haven't had to explicitly deal with this particularly, but the auth decorators have confused me on occasion. I think it would be better if all of our auth decorators follow similar patterns wherever possible. Consistency is good (okay, maybe not always!) I'd love to help out with this once we hear from everyone else! :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-04-28 18:25 UTC

I guess the only downside I really see is that it's work to migrate the code, so probably that means we should err on the side of doing so :)

**Eeshan Garg** · 2017-04-28 18:29 UTC

Yeah its gonna be some work, but if we decide to do this, we might as well do it sooner rather than later. Because GSoC will bring in more integrations with it! And if you've already run into problems with this a couple of times, I'm sure we will again! :)

**Andrea  Longo** · 2017-04-28 18:49 UTC

I think anything furthering a goal of "least surprise" is good. Yeah, migration is a pain. But coming in new and doing a webhook is totally a copy-paste-edit kind of thing. It's what makes it approachable as an early contribution. Less pain sooner is better than subjecting folks to more cumulative pain long-term. When do we start? :)

## OStatus integration

*2017-05-12 to 2017-05-12 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/OStatus.20integration/with/201531)*

**Rein Zustand** · 2017-05-12 00:57 UTC

I wonder if this has been discussed in a topic somewhere (fulltext search is nil), but what are your thoughts on Zulip integration with the OStatus protocol? I am still going through the api/ to see how the former can be translated to the latter.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-05-12 01:00 UTC

Fulltext search is limited to either (1) your personal history or (2) the history of a stream you're narrowed to, so it's not currently easy to check if something was discussed long before you joined (basically for perf reasons; it's really expensive to search the entire organization's public history when that's rarely what folks want).  But in this case that's probably what you wanted, so a useful data point.

Anyway, it hasn't been discussed.  It seems like OStatus is an open twitter-like protocol?  What kind of integration did you have in mind?

**Rein Zustand** · 2017-05-12 16:40 UTC

(disclaimer: I apologize if there are flaws or ignorance in reasoning since I did
not write these protocols. There is a viewpoint that could be understood only
by the authors themselves. I am still a passerby)

> (basically for perf reasons; it's really expensive to search the entire
> organization's public history when that's rarely what folks want)

This can be fixed by adding more hardware, and the fulltext+fullhistory search
can be UI-guarded with several steps to perform.  Yes, it is my use case, in
that I often search for past discussions logs at IRC (via botbot.me) or mailing
list / public inbox archives (which is common in FLOSS projects). Unfortunately
I don't have access to any usage data to conclude if the majority of the users
are in corporate settings or in whatever situation where it is essential to not
disclose or retain the logs (which has been raised in
https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/106).

> It seems like OStatus is an open twitter-like protocol?

Yes, in that the content posted is public, but not necessarily permanent
(as in, has been replicated by a sufficient number of mirrors), if the server
is configured to be uncrawlable by bots and/or moated by account sign-in's and
CAPTCHA requirements.

> What kind of integration did you have in mind?

The usual integration routine. If Zulip could understand OStatus, then Zulip
would be able to integrate with several other OStatus-speaking ecosystems.
In addition, it enables federated intercommunications between realms.

It is best as a reference point to include in a spec design other than the
other few proprietary platforms. Could it be said that Zulip is in between
Solid and OStatus? What can be standardized first out of Zulip?


## infrastructure team

*2017-05-30 to 2017-06-09 · 71 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/infrastructure.20team/with/213991)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-05-30 16:42 UTC

Because we have so many folks working on Zulip this summer, we've been setting up "teams" with regular weekly group checkins to discuss priorities, coordinate work, and otherwise try to accelerate the project and avoid duplicating efforts.  We recent set these up for Mobile and Bots and Integrations.  I think it's probably worth doing a similar group for the tooling, backend and infrastructure projects, basically covering the "tooling", "test infrastructure", "provision", "dependencies", and "production" labels (plus maybe some other things like analytics and "documentation (production)", and some parts of refactoring that are closer to this than anything else).  These teams are not exclusive and folks who participate are welcome to work on whatever they want; the purpose here is just to coordinate work and make sure everything important is getting the attention it deserves.

@Aditya Bansal @Steve Howell @Greg Price @sinwar @Fahri Cihan Demirci @Archana @Moritz Neeb @Rein Zustand @Umair Khan @Sampriti Panda @Tommy Ip @Paul Weaver FYI.  Other folks are very welcome to participate as well; I'm just trying to make sure most of the folks who are excited about these sorts of things are notified with this batch of mentions :).

For now, I think the only thing we need to decide is a schedule for our first meeting.  For Zulip meetings in general, we've had good luck with mornings Pacific time (e.g. 9AM or 10AM) working across all time zones; does that work for everyone interested in participating?  If so I think maybe we could do our first one on Friday at 9AM Pacific and then schedule future ones at that meeting?

## process_visible

*2017-05-30 to 2017-05-31 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/process_visible/with/214247)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-30 19:10 UTC

I have been trying to track down why we call `unread.process_visible` in `stream_list.js` when we process the `narrow_activated.zulip` event.  Going back to last year (to rule our recent refactorings), the code looks like this:

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/f8bb7503e6dea707bca6a34dcba66d89d8c64839/static/js/stream_list.js#L626

~~~ js
        var op_stream = event.filter.operands('stream');
        if (op_stream.length !== 0 && stream_data.is_subscribed(op_stream[0])) {
            var stream_li = get_filter_li('stream', op_stream[0]);
            var op_subject = event.filter.operands('topic');
            var subject;
            if (op_subject.length !== 0) {
                subject = op_subject[0];
            } else {
                stream_li.addClass('active-filter');
            }
            rebuild_recent_subjects(op_stream[0], subject);
            unread.process_visible();
}
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-30 19:12 UTC

I am thinking there is a more appropriate place to call `unread.process_visible` that truly coincides with us re-rendering the message pane.  Probably Tim has the best history on this, but I'm thinking out loud hear for transparency sake and so as not to clutter my PM feed with Tim, haha.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-30 19:14 UTC

Moving this code somewhere else will also break the only dependency of `stream_list` needing `unread_ops`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-05-30 20:17 UTC

I think my best hypothesis is that we do want to call `unread_ops.process_visible` immediately after a narrow is activated, and it just happened to end up in this code path due to some series of refactors.  But more likely is that this is just a bug.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-30 20:24 UTC

It turns out that whenever we narrow, we effectively generate a `message_pane.scroll` event, so that the call there has been largely irrelevant.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-30 20:26 UTC

~~~ js
226     message_viewport.message_pane.scroll($.throttle(50, function () { 
227         unread_ops.process_visible();
228         scroll_finish();
229     }));
~~~

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-05-30 20:30 UTC

OK cool, so we should be able to delete it then

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-30 20:32 UTC

Ok, I'll go with deleting it for now.  Having it go through the scroll path to update visible counts is kinda hacky, but I don't think it's  urgent from a practical manner to address that.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-05-31 17:35 UTC

@Tim Abbott FYI this is yesterday's thread on process_visible.

I think one of the more important investments we can make is to optimize the no-op or incremental `./tools/provision` performance, since people run it all the time

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 16:35 UTC

That does sound good to fix

We use a ton of caching; without that it would take like 10-20m

I guess just tested, and it's 30s.

* We dump and rebuild the manual testing database from scratch every time

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 16:37 UTC

That's 15s of the total

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 16:37 UTC

And also is kinda annoying, because if you setup some cool test data, we toss it

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 16:38 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 18:57 UTC

@Aditya Bansal I'm going to write some notes about what I see

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 18:59 UTC

I guess first, structurally, there's 2 major sections of every Travis CI build:
* The setup job.  This is usually hidden (so you have to click to see it) and for `backend` runs provision.  Code in e.g. `tools/travis/setup-backend`
* The test job.  This actually runs the tests.  code in e.g. `tools/travis/backend`

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 18:59 UTC

You can get that pretty quickly reading `.travis.yml`, but the part that isn't intuitive is that the setup job is hidden, and is actually most of the time in most of our suites

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 19:00 UTC

Actually, I'm maybe going to stop doing this braindump and instead write a quick developer doc for this

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-06-02 19:01 UTC

yeah that will be useful later as well.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 19:02 UTC

So on the front of actual problems in the output, there are 2 that I noticed.  The small one is that in the production suite, we're upgrading a bunch of packages like `git-core`, which we can fix by using `apt-mark hold`.  We actually do this in a bunch of places in `tools/travis/production-helper` (aka the code that runs as the test job for production), but I think maybe we want to move that to the setup job, because for packages like `git-core`, `provision` will do an `apt-get install` for that package to make sure it's there, but we don't want to actually upgrade it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 19:03 UTC

The other one, which is major, is that we (used to) have Travis CI configured to cache the virtualenvs, npm caches, emoji caches, etc. generated by provisioning from build to build, yet the caches aren't being used.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 19:04 UTC

There are ~3 possible reasons that could be:
* the caches weren't uploaded at the end of a successful build
* the caches weren't downloaded at the start of a new build
* the caches didn't have the files or format we needed

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 19:07 UTC

So one just needs to be systematic about debugging how that happens.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 19:08 UTC

The upload happens in the "storing build cache" section around line 5369 of https://travis-ci.org/zulip/zulip/jobs/238791359.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-06-02 19:11 UTC

Caching here is a travis thing?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 19:11 UTC

So we actually use the caching in provision, and in production, too

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 19:12 UTC

As a simple example, `scripts/lib/node_cache.py` is a simple example

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-02 19:13 UTC

Basically, how it works in development is that it hashes `package.json` (and maybe a few other things like node/npm versions), then looks in the cache directory (by default `/srv/zulip-npm-cache/`, to see if that combination has already been downloaded before

@Tim Abbott So, the plot thickens a bit.  For huddles, the recipient links back to the sender's user_profile record, so all huddles include senders in display_recipient.

For PMs, consider that 1:1 conversations share the same recipient id.  For example, imagine sender:target of aaron:cordelia and hamlet:cordelia.  Both messages have the same recipient id, and the recipient id only points to cordelia.  So, it's understandable that the cache doesn't have sender for 1:1 PMs, because sender is not attached to recipients, it's attached to conversations.

For our unread counts PR, I think we need to be dealing with conversation, not recipients.  And we'll need to do the same hack-in-the-sender thing that we do with messages.

## docker

*2017-06-09 to 2020-01-31 · 95 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/docker/with/222927)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-09 17:30 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-09 17:32 UTC

I feel like there are 2 versions of what people want with Docker in production:
* A quick way to install an everything-in-one-container Docker setup that's simple to manage but not well isolated
* A quick way to install and manage a ~7-container Docker setup with each service in its own container

The first is somewhat easier to do, so maybe if we had just one, we should do that, but we should probably eventually support both.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-09 17:33 UTC

I think the big question with both of these models and Docker is how to do persistent storage of things like uploaded files, logs, and the postgres database in a way where users are unlikely to accidentally delete their content.

Anyways, to use this sort of inheritance without having to mess with the SQL tables, I was thinking in something like what we do with `json_success` and `json_error`:

~~~python
def json_response(res_type="success", msg="", data=None, status=200):
    # type: (Text, Text, Optional[Dict[str, Any]], int) -> HttpResponse
    content = {"result": res_type, "msg": msg}
    if data is not None:
        content.update(data)
    return HttpResponse(content=ujson.dumps(content) + "\n",
                        content_type='application/json', status=status)

def json_success(data=None):
    # type: (Optional[Dict[str, Any]]) -> HttpResponse
    return json_response(data=data)

def json_error(msg, data=None, status=400):
    # type: (str, Optional[Dict[str, Any]], int) -> HttpResponse
    return json_response(res_type="error", msg=msg, data=data, status=status)
~~~

**Harshit Bansal** · 2017-09-15 17:02 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-15 17:03 UTC

@Umair Khan I briefly looked at your PR related to the file locks, but I have to admit I haven't been tracking to that issue.  Can you give a bit of context?

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 17:04 UTC

Yeah. So it basically tries to solve the problem related to the Casper flake.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 17:05 UTC

After the password change test in Casper, the user gets logged out randomly.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 17:06 UTC

It's mainly because we have a race condition in the code path where we change the password. Whenever the password is changed in Django 1.7+, the user hash changes. This hash is used by Django to verify the authenticity of the user.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 17:06 UTC

The PR adds a lock around this critical section so that other threads/processes can't access it.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 17:07 UTC

But for the time being we have decided to just activate this code in Dev environment.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-15 17:08 UTC

Is it fair to call this a flaw with Django?  Or is Zulip doing something out of the ordinary here?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-15 17:08 UTC

@Steve Howell the problem is that our password change flow is within the logged-in app, I think

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-15 17:09 UTC

And so the browser gets logged out, and depending on a race between `get_events` and the next step in the casper script, may e.g. reload the browser or get some other weird error.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-15 17:09 UTC

So, it's a feature of Django we need to work around for our tests.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 17:09 UTC

No, I think it's just our distributed nature of the application.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-15 17:10 UTC

Possible solutions include disabling the Django feature somehow (at least for the tests, but maybe overall) and various other ideas.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-15 17:10 UTC

So I guess you're sort of implying that most apps log you out temporarily when you change a password, @Tim Abbott?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-15 17:10 UTC

Well, it's a recent change in Django.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 17:10 UTC

In Django 1.7+ you always log out on password change.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 17:10 UTC

We want to avoid that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-15 17:11 UTC

I think it's correct to say that many webapps log out other browser sessions on password change, under the theory that you may have been changing your password because the old one was compromised.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 17:11 UTC

Yeah.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-15 17:12 UTC

That actually seems like a reasonable policy to me.   Are we sure we don't want to take steps to abide by it somehow?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-15 17:13 UTC

Well, the problem is that we want to have a casper test for changing your password that isn't broken.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-15 17:13 UTC

I think it'd be reasonable to disable that Django feature for the Casper tests just to let the test run non-flakily.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 17:15 UTC

Perhaps we can just change the arrangement of tests? Or make the test expect that the user might log out and make it resilient?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-15 17:17 UTC

I like the idea of rearranging the tests somehow, like have 99_change_password.js with a huge comment at the top explaining our temporary hack.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 17:20 UTC

Actually there is another problem due to which just rearranging won't work. Our password change test checks for the "Settings updated" message and sometimes the user gets logged out before the frontend receives this event.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 17:21 UTC

I think we will have to remove this check as well. After doing the password change, we can just log out and then log in with new credentials.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-15 17:21 UTC

Huh, this is an interesting problem.  Kind of painful, too, haha.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 17:21 UTC

Yeah :)

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-15 17:25 UTC

I think this "I think we will have to remove this check as well. After doing the password change, we can just log out and then log in with new credentials." might just work If we are alright with not waiting for "Settings updated" message.

**James Rowan** · 2017-06-20 19:04 UTC

In `settings.py`we have two email addresses, defaulting to 

```
                     ("NOREPLY_EMAIL_ADDRESS", "Zulip <noreply@example.com>"),
                     ("DEFAULT_FROM_EMAIL", "Zulip <zulip@example.com>"),
```

## Filters

*2017-06-22 to 2017-06-27 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Filters/with/234211)*

**Harlan Lieberman-Berg** · 2017-06-22 02:50 UTC

So... I'm trying to understand this.  We're doing realm filters both on the client side in bugdown and on the server side using re?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-22 11:06 UTC

@Harlan Lieberman-Berg Our modified version of markdown is called bugdown.  We have parsers on both sides of the network to convert bugdown to HTML.  We have it on the JS side so that we can do "local echo" and render the message you just sent before the server round trip.  Then we re-parse on the Python side for a couple reasons:
* It avoids the need for JS to send HTML to us, which would consume bandwidth.
* Even if JS sent HTML to us, we couldn't trust it.
* There are some things in our bugdown that require info that only the server has.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-26 22:46 UTC

@Harlan Lieberman-Berg does that explanation make sense to you?

**Harlan Lieberman-Berg** · 2017-06-27 14:50 UTC

Yes... it makes things a bit more complicated, but not too much.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-27 15:01 UTC

One thing I should probably clarify from my earlier message is that there is some subset of messages that we can't render on the JS side, so we have to depend on the server for those to be rendered.  But most text-based messages get rendered identically by both engines.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-27 20:20 UTC

It's also worth noting that the JS renderer doesn't have the same security requirements as the backend one, since it's only used to render messages that you yourself send (so you can't attack someone else with it).

One thing I wanted to discuss is the order in which we run our test suites in Travis CI. Our current order is:
* Static analysis
* Production tests
* Frontend tests
* Backend tests

I think it would be better to run the production tests in the last since most of the PRs include changes only to backend/frontend and it is rare for them to break production test suite. * Static analysis
* Frontend tests

* Production tests

**Yago González** · 2017-06-26 21:39 UTC

~~~
type:stream
content:"iutf yukf tydyt"
to:"4"

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-26 22:06 UTC

Yep, my personal opinion is that one big JSON payload makes more sense than form data, and I agree with you on `check_string`.  In a form-encoding world, requiring quotes around strings just creates a new type of pitfall--instead of accidentally accepting non-strings, you accidentally strip quotes off of strings.  Of course, no encoding scheme works unless both sides agree to it, but JSON is more modern.

**Yago González** · 2017-06-26 22:13 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-26 22:32 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-26 22:33 UTC

I'll slightly rephrase what I said earlier--any encoding scheme is legit insofar as both sides agree to it.  And then the nice thing about `validator` REQ parameters is that we don't have custom parsers for them--they're all just using JSON, and the validators just do Python-level checks.

**Yago González** · 2017-06-26 22:40 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-26 23:05 UTC

**Yago González** · 2017-06-27 01:28 UTC

I noticed that an HTTP `DELETE` to `/streams/{stream_id}` calls `zerver.views.streams.deactivate_stream_backend`. However, after taking a quick look at the view's code, and seeing that the UI indicates that the stream will be permanently deleted, I wonder: why is it `deactivate` and not `delete`?

**Yago González** · 2017-06-27 01:29 UTC

I mean in the view's name (and also in some methods that it calls, like `do_deactivate_stream`).

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-27 01:36 UTC

We don't truly delete the stream, we just make it inactive, and we don't surface any way that I know of to reactivate the stream.   From the user's perspective the stream is deleted, but there are still messages attached to the stream in the database.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-27 01:38 UTC

It's more of an extreme deactivation than, say, user reactivations, where folks can still see inactive users in their old message streams, and where allow admins to reactivate users, I believe.

**Yago González** · 2017-06-27 01:40 UTC

Oh, I see. So it's a deactivation indeed. I got a bit confused by this message, especially the "the stream's content will not be recoverable" part:
[Message](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/6/EEeY3SQny8c0KxMBu3NaTSZy/pasted_image.png)

**Yago González** · 2017-06-27 01:41 UTC

Anyway, since there isn't any "official" way to reactivate the stream, it makes sense to describe this endpoint as "Deleting a stream", right?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-06-27 01:42 UTC

Yep, I think that's fair.  I'd rather err on the side of caution here--even though streams are recoverable in some sense, there's no documented way to do it without mucking around in the database.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-06-27 20:21 UTC

I think we do want to change this to some name like "archive stream" that's a bit clearer.

```
(zulip-py3-venv) tabbott@coset:~/zulip$ time ./tools/run-mypy --no-daemon

(zulip-py3-venv) tabbott@coset:~/zulip$ time ./tools/run-mypy --no-daemon
real	0m2.104s
```

to

```
(zulip-py3-venv) tabbott@coset:~/zulip$ time ./tools/run-mypy --no-daemon
real	0m11.855s
(zulip-py3-venv) tabbott@coset:~/zulip$ time ./tools/run-mypy --no-daemon
real	0m1.321s
```

With this updated version, even if the mypy daemon wasn't running, `tools/lint --verbose-timing` shows its only slightly slower than pyflakes.  And it's now one of our fastest linters to check the entire codebase if the daemon is running (at least on my laptop).

## ScheduledJob

*2017-07-02 to 2017-07-03 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/ScheduledJob/with/241815)*

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-07-02 05:34 UTC

ScheduledJob is used by send_future_email to send emails in the future. On a cursory skim, it looks like we use this for day1, day2, missed message, digest, and invitation_reminder (though for digest emails we could also use a queue processor). 

I want to propose a schema change, from 
```
class ScheduledJob(models.Model):
    scheduled_timestamp = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=False, null=False) # type: datetime.datetime
    type = models.PositiveSmallIntegerField() # type: int
    # For EMAIL, filter_string is recipient_email
    EMAIL = 1

    # JSON representation of the job's data. Be careful, as we are not relying on Django to do validation
    data = models.TextField() # type: Text
    # Kind of like a ForeignKey, but table is determined by type.
    filter_id = models.IntegerField(null=True) # type: Optional[int]
    filter_string = models.CharField(max_length=100) # type: Text
```
to 
```
class ScheduledEmail(models.Model):   [instead of ScheduledJob]
    scheduled_timestamp [same as before]
    to_user (A UserProfile object. Used for all emails but invitation_reminder.)
    to_email (Used for invitation_reminder)
    type (stores which type of email it is, e.g. ScheduledEmail.DIGEST)
    data [same as before]
```

Some thoughts:
* The original schema was written in 2013, and hasn't been changed since. It seems like it was written for much more generality than it ended up being used for.
* We might want to schedule other things, like onboarding zulips. However, I think it's likely that will be done by a bot of some sort in the end, rather than this, and I can't think of other things on the horizon that need scheduling of this sort. So I think it makes sense to optimize this table for email.
* Knowing the user is useful; it allows using send_email_to_user instead of send_email, and automatically takes care of things like users changing their email address. Using user instead of email as a primary key here will also help with the "email can be used on multiple realms" feature.
* Sometimes we need to pull certain emails from the queue, e.g. when people click on unsubscribe links. Having a "type" will make doing this easier (currently we just remove all emails to you whenever you click on any unsubscribe link, rather than just the type of email you unsubscribed from).

I guess this isn't a huge decision; this is used only a couple of places in the code. But wanted to check if I'm missing anything.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-02 12:02 UTC

Your new proposed model seems clearly superior to me.  I think it's generally a mistake to have overly abstracted DB models like the 2013 version.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-03 17:02 UTC

> We might want to schedule other things, like onboarding zulips. However, I think it's likely that will be done by a bot of some sort in the end

I think a ScheduledZulip/ScheduledJob implementation would likely be a lot more pleasant to manage than a "bot", if by bot you mean something deployed like a bot rather than a piece of code along these lines.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-03 17:04 UTC

I think a more specialized system would be reasonable, but I think there's a good chance we'd end up making a ScheduledZulip class that's very similar, and maybe other things, not too long after.  Unclear whether that'd be a problem really.  

For the actual problem of `send_email_to_user`, a smaller change would be to just include the user ID (where available) in the `data` object and look up the user ID to call `send_email_to_user`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-03 17:05 UTC

I'm not sure `ScheduledJob` is a particularly great interface for also adding a `ScheduledZulip` feature (or other things), but I would encourage being thoughtful about the amount of migration effort involved in specializing it to just do emails.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-07-03 17:33 UTC

The migration effort is small at this point, now that the hard work of getting everything into send_future_email has already been done :). It's the top commit at #5658. We're already clearing the ScheduledJob queue earlier in that PR, so the additional migration is not costly from that perspective. 

Putting user_id in the data object doesn't seem great to me. Almost all interactions with ScheduledJob use the user (e.g. do_deactivate_user, unsubscribe_from_digest_emails, etc). If the user is in the data, all those calls look something like 
```
for job in ScheduledJob.objects.all(): 
     data  = loads(job.data)
     if user_id in data and data['user_id'] = the user_id we care about:
            delete job, or add it to a list of jobs to be deleted in the next pass
```
instead of 
`ScheduledJob.objects.filter(user=user).delete()`

There is also a class of existing bugs that are solved by ScheduledEmail.type, which is that unsubscribing from something deletes your entire ScheduledJob queue, regardless of what you unsubscribed from.

(For scheduling Zulips, I should have said, I don't have a concrete use case for it in the near future, even for onboarding. And if we do end up doing it for onboarding, it feels different enough from email that I think a ScheduledZulip class would be totally reasonable.)

## unified confirmation

*2017-07-08 to 2017-07-09 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/unified.20confirmation/with/246567)*

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-07-08 21:38 UTC

Copying from github issue, since this is a better place for discussion:

Background: We currently have 5 confirmation paths and are adding 2 more, so we're doing a basic cleanup of our current confirmation paths before we add new ones. The next step is deciding how we want to do error handling for broken and expired links. 

Two options that come to mind are
* Raise exceptions (e.g. `ConfirmationKeyException('expired'))` in the link confirmation path, and then each of the callers catches the exception, and calls something like `render_confirmation_error(exception.error_type)`.
* Have all confirmation links pass through `confirmation.views.confirm` (so all confirmation links would have the same URL structure). That function would do all the error checking, and redirect to the appropriate place in `zerver/views`.

Cons of the first: lots of duplicated code. zerver code has to import/understand a bunch of confirmation logic.

Cons of the second: all the URLs look the same. A bunch of indirection for developers trying to understand how zerver URLs get called. Migration cost, in that all current unsubscribe (and email_change) links will break.

Thoughts?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-08 21:46 UTC

How much semi-duplicated code are we talking about here?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-08 21:47 UTC

It seems to me like the former may be better if it's not large.

something like

```
from confirmation.views import ConfirmationKeyException, render_confirmation_error

    try:
        obj = get_object_from_key(confirmation_key)
    except ConfirmationKeyException as e:
        return render_confirmation_error(request, e.error_type)
```

up to 7 times? Not sure if that is a lot or a little.
Or maybe there is a better way to say these four lines?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-08 23:40 UTC

That seems worthwhile to de-duplicate.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-09 15:37 UTC

It seems like that could be de-duplicated using a function, but if it can't be, I'd rather have that pattern appear in 7 places than have the code be really hard to understand

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-09 15:41 UTC

Yeah, we could add middleware next to JsonableError

Update on this:
* I have updated this #5782 with a test for private streams as well.
* I would like a bit of discussion upon digest emails here. For context Tim and I had a conversation in PM's regarding digest emails having a weird history because of this feature for the user. I agreed at that moment and concluded from a over view of code that adding simple conditionals would probably solve our problem there. I guess I was wrong and now I get the deeper problem Tim was trying to bring forward for me. Reading the code I see two options here we arguments both in favour and against.

* Option 1:
We leave the digest generation code as it is! So reading the digest code indicates we generate digest emails based upon publish date cut off i.e. messages greater than a particular publish date. Also we must be sending digest emails occasionally I guess some time period. Same kind of a time period will be used for marking users soft deactivated. Now what I am saying is that we leave digest code as it is so that user who has not being around for long time say 28 days will receive one last digest. After this since UserMessage rows have not been created user won't be receiving any digest emails. The digest code would look to generate email and conclude there is simply not enough traffic for such a email. A user who has not been around for long time probably won't even be interested to read the digest emails I guess. Since our notification emails work differently they continue to receive any PM, mention alert mail.
(PS: All this is based on assumption that long_term_idle users won't be interest in digest mails.)

* Option 2:
We modify the add_missing_messages code to optionally create usermessage rows and return all user message rows which would probably have been created. We also modify digest email code to compensate for this change and use this data to generate long term idle users digest emails.
