## python3 switcharoo

*2017-07-20 to 2017-07-20 · 1 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/python3.20switcharoo/with/254108)*

**Rein Zustand** · 2017-07-20 05:28 UTC

(#4756)

Making sure I have covered all the scenarios, but not yet for each type of
supported operating systems. Only in 14.04 so far.

dev:
  - fresh system to python3: this is handled by the first commit of #4756, which
    ensures that `tools/provision` will only set up a zulip-py3-venv, and to pave
    way for `tools/run-dev.py`
  - existing system on python2 to python3: I assume a dev env is always upgraded
    via a `git pull`, so this is handled by the first commit of #4756
  - existing system on python3 to python2: run `PYTHON=python2 ./tools/provision`.
    This shouldn't be added to documentation so that its content is more
    streamlined.

prod:
  - fresh system via tarball: this can be done without #4756.
    Build a python3 tarball from another machine with
    `./tools/build-release-tarball --py3` then install from this tarball
    https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/prod-install.html.
  - fresh system via git: this can be done without #4756. After a `git clone`,
    run `./tools/build-release-tarball --py3` then install from this tarball
    https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/prod-install.html
  - existing system on python2/python3 to python3 via tarball: this can be done
    without #4756.  All that needs to be done is to run
    `upgrade-zulip <python3 tarball>`
  - existing system on python2/python3 to python3 via git: My previous
    iteration was to patch `upgrade-zulip-from-git` with `PYTHON` param that can
    be toggled to be python2 or python3, but after testing (was stuck for a
    while, otherwise would have been sooner) this did not result in a python3 system since
    `upgrade-zulip-from-git` is called from `/home/zulip/deployments/current`,
    but only `upgrade-zulip-stage-2` is called from the cloned git repo. Between
    1) wiring a 2/3 binary switch to [manage.py, the libraries required by
    manage.py, the scripts called by
    `puppet/zulip/manifests/*`/`puppet/zulip_ops`], ensuring some of the steps
    in `upgrade-zulip-stage-2` to explicitly run on python3, documenting this to
    ensure so that any new script that is not called from within the venv has
    the switch 2) sed the shebang line to python3 in `upgrade-zulip-stage-2`,
    option 2) adds a smaller amount of upkeep complexity,
    limits the upgraded system to python3 only (this reduces testing overhead
    and aggregate headache), makes the second commit unnecessary, anticipates
    new scripts. Tested from 1.6.0 to this branch (works as long as `node`/`nvm`
    is fresh / doesn't have its permission botched).
    The steps are:
```bash
    # Purge ancient versions of node/nvm
    # to prevent node permission error
    rm -r /usr/local/bin/node /usr/local/bin/nvm

    # Steps as documented in prod-install
    do_install_zulip 1.6.0

    # Upgrade zulip
    echo -e "[machine]\npuppet_classes = zulip::voyager, zulip::static_asset_compiler\n[deployment]\ngit_repo_url = https://github.com/rht/zulip.git"
    rm -r /srv/zulip.git/
    /home/zulip/deployments/current/scripts/upgrade-zulip-from-git dev-py3-021
```
  - existing system on python3 to python2 via tarball: untested, but should be
    fine given that `upgrade-zulip-from-git` has been tested (which covers the
    `upgrade-zulip-stage-2` part).
  - existing system on python3 to python2 via git: tested from 1.6.0 to rht:dev-py3-021
    branch then to zulip:mater.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-21 22:50 UTC

@Tim Abbott I figured out why "count" is part of the `recent_topics` data structure.  It's not dead code, and it's not for unread counts.  It's for dealing with topic edits--we need to make sure that if somebody renames a topic, it disappears from their list of recent topics.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-21 22:50 UTC

ahh, right

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-21 22:50 UTC

Our mechanism for doing this now is kind of fragile--we use a count and incr/decr.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-21 22:52 UTC

For really old topics, we won't have counts, but it's also very unlikely the old messages would be renamed out of existence.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-21 22:53 UTC

Also, it's not absolutely the end of the world if we don't clear a topic--when the user goes to narrow from the sidebar, they'll simply get an empty list, which might be a head scratcher, but it might be no less of a head scratcher than their favorite topic disappearing from the sidebar.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-21 22:55 UTC

Topic edits are rare enough that the better mechanism here might be to some kind of did-we-kill-off-the-whole-topic check when the edit happens, rather than maintaining a count that we incr/decr on every new message.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-21 22:59 UTC

One slightly hacky thing we can do is have a topic-> oldest message id mapping, and just assume if somebody edits the topic for the old message in a topic, then that triggers the "remove" event.   But that has the problem that you could technically only edit the topic for the first message in a topic.  Which would be a strange thing to do, but it's possible.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-21 23:16 UTC

We have two sort-of-related problems that we need to solve:
* We can only remove "more topics" when we're completely confident that we've displayed all the topics for a stream (vs. having an incomplete history).
* We can only remove a defunct topic from the sidebar when we're completely confident all the messages we care about have been moved to a new topic (vs. having an incomplete history).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-21 17:11 UTC

There's a few larger projects that I think could be pretty valuable but aren't being worked on:
* Finishing the work done at PyCon to use thumbor to automatically thumbnail images for better network performance.
* Finishing the work done at PyCon to make the development environment test data much more complete.
* Making it possible to install Zulip from a (larger) tarball without Internet access.  Basically this would involve shipping our pip, node, etc. dependencies and then having a way to configure Zulip to try fetching those dependencies from disk rather than the Internet.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-21 17:12 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-21 17:24 UTC

So, there's some interesting things to think about in terms of how to order the changes.  We don't want to change e.g. the registration code path to stop checking whether a user exists in another realm until we've actually made it possible to have multiple users with the same email in different realms.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-21 17:26 UTC

I guess one step that I think we could do right now is improving our logging code in preparation for this.  In `zerver/middleware.py`, `zerver/lib/feedback.py`, `zerver/lib/error_notify.py`, and `zerver/logging_handlers.py`, we have various places where in either log lines or emailed error reports, we try to specify which user is involved in a given exception.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-21 17:26 UTC

Right now, all of those code paths basically tell you the user's email and expect you to be able to figure out which user that is.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-21 17:28 UTC

That will stop being the case.  So I think we probably want them to (with the exception of `middleware.py`, which has limited space) all include the `user_id`, `ream_string_id` (aka subdomain, or `realm_id` if it doesn't exist), etc., in the reports, to handle this ambiguity.  For the log lines in `middleware.py`, we should brainstorm a bit.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-21 17:29 UTC

(For `error_notify.py`, we can also get rid of the code related to `deployment`, since I think that's dead code; perhaps I should take that subtask)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-21 17:36 UTC

For brevity sake, I'm going to call this the chicken/egg problem:

* There are some pieces of code that you can't touch until we relax the DB constraint.
* We can't relax the DB constraint until we fix certain pieces of code.

It makes sense to fix as much code as we can until we truly get blocked by the above, but we're eventually going to get to a place where the only way to do things atomically is to squash a bunch of commits together.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-21 17:37 UTC

So it might be worth talking about a feature-branch/code-review strategy that can make that as easy to manage as possible.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-21 17:39 UTC

I think we're not really at the point where we need that yet.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-21 17:41 UTC

I think the next follow-up efforts we can do without the "big push" are:
* Finishing things like `recipient_for_emails`
* The logging work I described
* Look through the `UserProfile.objects.filter` and `UserProfile.objects.get` calls and migrate those.
* Preparatory refactoring of functions like `is_inactive` used in the registration flow to make sure we pass a `realm` object into the function, so that it would be possible to change their behavior.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-21 17:42 UTC

But I think there's a good chance that sometime next week we will get to the point where we start working on flipping the model.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-07-26 13:21 UTC

Also by the looks according to my current understanding this works something like:
* Client requests for an image from server using the `user_uploads` path.
* This request is returned with a response having a redirect in its header towards the thumbor server with the link to open file.
* Client again creates a request to server with the new link.
* This request is now satisfied by the thumbor server.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2017-07-26 13:21 UTC

What are the problems we need to fix:
* If we need to just get that PR working in production we can probably add a regex in nginx path configuration to not serve image files.
* Making two round trips to server to satisfy one image isn't a good idea I guess owing to the network usage. I guess we can make it work somehow with an internal redirect from nginx using the `x-accel-redirect` header.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-02-09 13:39 UTC

I guess I was not making any sense in the message on #**development help** so let me write a para on what's up:
Thumbor actually has a lot of dependencies but we only need to install what we are using. Since they have lots of dependencies, installation instructions get a bit confusing. For example: Here http://thumbor.readthedocs.io/en/latest/installing.html#alternative-installation they suggest to install a lot of lib's including `libjasper-dev`. This very list have dissimilarities with this file in there repo https://github.com/thumbor/thumbor/blob/master/requirements
So when I added the dependencies for this feature what happened was:
* Looked around for sometime what needs to happen.
* Found this [wiki page](https://github.com/thumbor/thumbor/wiki/Requirements) which said
>The other requirements for using thumbor depend on your choice of features, which is why we'll outline here the requirements per feature used, instead of overall requirements.
* So next what I did was looked through all the requirements in this [file](https://github.com/thumbor/thumbor/blob/master/requirements) for there purpose and added which we needed.
* These three lib's 
```
"libjpeg-dev",
"libjasper-dev",
"libpng-dev",
```
were related to different image format and there manipulation, so I figured we needed them.
* Open-cv is used as an Imaging Engine by thumbor and since we are using `pillow` for that I figured we didn't need it.
and so on I came up with the requirements commit.

**What I figured wrong**
The three lib's I mentioned weren't directly used by thumbor but are actually deps coming from the Imaging Engine.
Therefore `libjasper-dev` is a lib required by open-cv which we aren't using.

Now since I figured the deps from Imaging Engine might have issues I just went back to confirm we met all the deps required. Now since the Imaging Engine we are using is `Pillow` which was also being used in the app already I found out that the only two required deps for Pillow to work are `zlib` and `libjpeg` according to https://pillow.readthedocs.io/en/latest/installation.html#external-libraries

Now though I didn't explicitly specified `zlib` in `THUMBOR_VENV_DEPENDENCIES` it was meet because it is included in `VENV_DEPENDENCIES`and hence our server get's them anyway.

**What I think needs to happen to fix this**
* Remove  `libjasper-dev`.
(yeah, initial issue was this lib being removed in modern Ubuntu and we needed to deal with it. Its funny we can just remove it)
* Add `libz-dev` and `libjpeg-dev` (I think newer versions for these are `libjpeg8-dev` and `zlib1g-dev`) to `THUMBOR_VENV_DEPENDENCIES`.

One way you might find convenient to try things on Python 3.5 is to use a Docker image:
```
$ docker run -i -t python:3.5 bash
root@fcbeec829872:/# python -V
Python 3.5.9
```

https://launchpad.net/~deadsnakes/+archive/ubuntu/ppa
after which you should have a `/usr/bin/python3.5`.

Nix is an alternative that could work. It runs on any Linux distribution, and could replace our use of APT, nvm, pip, and Puppet. It would totally free us from system dependencies, allowing isolation and complete uninstallation.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-20 22:15 UTC

Hmm, that's an interesting idea!

I'm curious what that would look like. Does it have some kind of adapter logic to automatically take a package from e.g. PyPI and handle it as a Nix package? Or does it involve a Nix-side maintainer of some kind responding to new releases, like in Debian?

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-20 22:16 UTC

(In the Debian case there are tools to help automate, of course, but they're ultimately driven by a human maintainer for each package)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-20 22:33 UTC

There are tools to automatically generate Nix expressions from Python package sets. There’s also a large collection of human-maintained packages (Python and otherwise) in [nixpkgs](https://github.com/NixOS/nixpkgs). And crucially, there’s a powerful language for overriding packages from either of the above, in part or in full—for example, a simple version bump typically just involves passing in a new version and a new SHA-256 hash.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-20 22:53 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> And crucially, there’s a powerful language for overriding packages from either of the above, in part or in full—for example, a simple version bump typically just involves passing in a new version and a new SHA-256 hash.

Mmm. That does sound like a major, and quite appealing, advance over the state of the art for Debian packages.

IOW if I'm understanding right:
* you could take some human-maintained package from nixpkgs which corresponds to a PyPI package,
* and pass it a new version and a new hash,
* and typically that would just work? It'd apply the same adaptations the human-maintained package provides, just to the new version of the upstream package.

That's pretty great.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-20 22:58 UTC

Whereas in Debian-land, the same kind of version bump involves a lot more steps and layers. Even if the existing distro package is designed with Debathena levels of clean separation and non-redundancy -- and few are -- the workflow involves something like getting a source package which is basically a file tree, modifying a couple of files, and then performing an arcane build process and serving that up through a more-arcane repository system. (Or skipping the repository to manually schlep packages around, or doing the arcane build on every machine.)

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-20 23:00 UTC

(I know less about RPM-land, but I believe it's basically the same story except instead of modifying a couple of files in a file tree, you modify a spot or two in one big file with a multi-part format. Maybe the build process and/or repository system is less arcane, which would be something. But that's all moot for our practical purposes, as we don't live in RPM-land.)

I think we're going to need to a make a decision on our path forward on the Python front.  We have the following constraints
* We ideally would add Ubuntu 20.04 support soon after it releases (in 9 days), in the upcoming 2.2 release.
* Ubuntu 20.04 doesn't have Python 2 and thus requires upgrading Thumbor
* It would be sorta nice for our next release to still support Ubuntu 16.04 rather than requiring folks to upgrade.
* Ubuntu 16.04 has Python 3.5.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-14 19:04 UTC

So let’s decouple our Python version from the system Python. It’s not like we haven’t decoupled everything else.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-14 19:05 UTC

There's a few paths forward that make sense to me:
* We can drop Ubuntu 16.04 before the 2.2 release, and tell users to upgrade to 18.04.  We could even send out an email that we're planning to do that change ~today, so users have some preparation that we're going to start requiring 18.04+.
* We can ship Python.
* We can do the annoying work to make thumbor support Python 3.5 even though it is EOL in 6 months.

## unread_msgs re-subscribed

*2017-07-24 to 2017-07-24 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/unread_msgs.20re-subscribed/with/256356)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-24 17:49 UTC

@Tim Abbott @Boris Yankov For the issue of unsubscribed streams being part of our unread messages structure, the most expedient thing to do for 1.7 is probably to filter them out of page_params.  For the case of newly subscribed streams, I think the clients (web app and mobile) can just be responsible for setting the appropriate data structure of unread message ids just be an empty list (or make lookups default to an empty list, if you want to do it lazily).

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-24 17:50 UTC

The only tricky bit here is if you unsubscribe from a stream with unread messages, and then you re-subscribe to the stream.  I think for V1 this is enough of an edge case that we can punt on it, and just let the clients report zero unread counts.  This will be sort of a self-fixing problem if users end up scrolling back through their history, and I think generally it's a non-issue, since the most common re-subscribe case is probably a stream you mostly don't care about and occasionally get roped back into.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-24 18:09 UTC

Sounds good.  I think it'd be pretty reasonable to have unsubscribe mark the stream as read in the long term.

## bankruptcy

*2017-07-24 to 2017-07-24 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/bankruptcy/with/256395)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-24 18:23 UTC

I have some ideas/thoughts on bankruptcy:
* we want to figure out what happens on reactivation with unread counts
* I want some sort of automatic bankruptcy for completely absurd cases that endanger performance (cap unread messages at 10k) and where no user is realistically going to catch up
* I think we want features to make get-out-of-bankruptcy not completely all-or-nothing (i.e. don't flip last 24 hours to "read" status)
* We may want some kind of "soft" archiving of messages, where unread messages older than, say, two weeks are flipped to "read" status, but we have some kind or archive table of message ids that were never read, and we have some back door for users to get unread messages out of the archive

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-24 18:24 UTC

Oh yeah, one more bankruptcy thing is people have occasionally requested per-stream bankruptcy.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-24 18:29 UTC

Per-stream bankrupcty is something we should just open an issue for.  There's already a "mark all a read" option on the stream menu, it probably just doesn't do the right thing

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-24 18:31 UTC

Huh, I forgot about that...it's possible that it came up in discussion and I just didn't remember it was there.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-24 18:32 UTC

(I'm not sure whether that does the right thing or not.  `End` certainly does not do the right thing in the event that you're not caught up, but that's an unrelated issue, where if the browser isn't done fetching a stream's history, the display can be wrong)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-24 18:32 UTC

I wanted to mention all wish-list things together, since I think there may be some interactions.  For example, the exempt-the-last-n-hours wish is probably something that would apply to per-stream mark-all-as-read as well as overall declare-bankruptcy, although in this particular case we probably wouldn't need to solve both together.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-24 18:34 UTC

Yeah, makes sense; that one at least we should just check.  I think the `stream_obj` case of `do_update_message_flags` is supposed to cover that case.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-24 18:34 UTC

Yeah, and indeed, it looks like it does.  So I think the answer for "per-stream bankruptcy" is "use the item in the left sidebar caret menu"

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-24 18:37 UTC

To summarize my policy wishes:
* For really old unread messages, we should be ruthless and just flip them.  Performance trumps FOMO here.
* For old unread messages, we should flip them and provide some back door to find them.  (This is lowest priority for me, partly because the implementation cost is high).
* For normal unread messages, we should be able to declare bankruptcy.
* For very recent unread messages, I think we should exempt them from declare-bankruptcy.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-07-24 21:00 UTC

I think one of the challenges with the "cap at 10K" question is that probably we do want the user to keep unread counts for things like PMs.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-07-24 21:02 UTC

That might be an easy thing to exempt.  I think streams are where folks get really behind.  PMs tend to be self-regulating for obvious reasons.

I think we'll want to add a LIMIT clause to our queries for fetching unread message history to make this not slow, but it's actually much less slow than one might fear (~5s total time for `/` including collecting that data), which is an endorsement of our backend design.  Even capping it at something huge like 25K would resolve the issue. 

As a sidenote, I think we may want to have some algorithm for marking as read muted messages that are extremely old, since I don't think those unread counts are doing the user any good (perhaps in addition, we should have a UI feature to encourage users in this sort of state to unsubscribe from the things they're not reading).

## python 3

*2017-08-04 to 2017-08-18 · 67 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/python.203/with/262684)*

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-04 01:56 UTC

I spent today wrestling with the switch to Python 3.

Currently, for building a Python 3 release tarball, we have this clever scheme where we push everything to dispatch through shebangs (rather than invoke `python $script`), and make all our shebangs use `/usr/bin/env`, and then on `build-release-tarball` there's a `--py3` flag that causes it to rewrite the shebangs to all say `python3` rather than `python`.

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-04 01:57 UTC

This works great for ensuring that when the tarball is unpacked, everything you run out of there will be running on Python 3.

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-04 01:59 UTC

We'd like our strategy to be that for the next couple of weeks until the 1.7 release, we're still able to make a Python 2 version of the release tarball as well as Python 3. That means we want to continue to have Travis builds running tests under Python 2, and we want Python 2 to continue to be usable in the dev environment for debugging/fixing any bugs those tests turn up.

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-04 02:00 UTC

Unfortunately the weakness of the `#!/usr/bin/env python3` strategy is when you want to have some Python 2 around. A Python 2 virtualenv has no `python3`, which means that if you've activated a Python 2 virtualenv and then invoke such a script, it misses the virtualenv and goes right out to the system `python3`.

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-04 02:02 UTC

I'd been trying to get things working with all our shebang lines in the source repo switched to `python3`, in order to make `upgrade-zulip-from-git` run smoother. But that turns out to be a quagmire, for the reason above -- Travis is doing a lot of work from a source checkout, with a lot of scripts calling each other, and it trips over that issue in lots of places.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-04 02:04 UTC

What's our main reason for still trying to straddle back to python2?

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-04 02:04 UTC

## usermessage.id

*2017-08-15 to 2017-08-16 · 19 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/usermessage.2Eid/with/267413)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-15 13:58 UTC

So one thing I wanted to chat about with @Greg Price, @Steve Howell, and @Umair Khan (and others who had thoughts) is whether we should get rid of the `UserMessage.id` column.  Conceptually, that table's primary key is a `user_profile_id, message_id` pair; we only have `UserMessage.id` because Django created it automatically.   As best I know, we don't use those IDs for anything; it's probably worth trying to confirm that.  Since the table is our largest table, removing the extra large column would probably have significant disk savings, and it'd head off the need to do the work to change the ID to a 64-bit integer field to avoid overflow.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-15 14:03 UTC

The first question is whether Django's ORM has some implementation dependency on the column.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-15 14:05 UTC

I am actually using the ids in the fix script, and I can imagine things like `update()` use it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-15 14:05 UTC

Postgres doesn't have a dependency on them.  I think the Django ORM doesn't either, but we should confirm.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-15 14:06 UTC

Probably a good experiment to run quickly is to just add a migration that gets rid of the column and then see if sending messages and stuff works

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-15 14:06 UTC

My understanding is that you tell Django the primary key is (a, b) and it's smart enough to generate queries referencing rows with both values.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-15 14:12 UTC

Postgres definitely does not require them.  But they are convenient for doing multi-stage things like finding all rows that match a certain criteria, post-processing them, and then updating them.  I also imagine the indexes are a bit faster for ids than compound fields.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-15 14:13 UTC

Instead of saying `id in [2, 3, 4]` I'd have to do a much more verbose where clause.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-15 14:13 UTC

hmm, yeah, I see

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-15 14:52 UTC

If we got with the strategy that @Umair Khan proposes, we might want to think about how we handle unread messages.  I suspect we want to do unread-fixing completely independently from id-fixing, but if we are copying over data to a new table, it's possible we want to do the logic to remove unreads as part of that.   Like I said, the default plan here is probably the most sensible, but we should think it through a bit.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-15 15:09 UTC

I think we definitely don't want to couple those migrations.

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-15 22:56 UTC

@Steve Howell Do you know if we have things we do now that take advantage of the ids for that kind of multi-stage processing?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-15 23:11 UTC

I am only aware of the stuff I am working on.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-15 23:15 UTC

The other possible place would be the export tool, but that's unlikely to be fundamental.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-15 23:19 UTC

I think ids have hidden benefits.  Like if an import job crashes finding the last row is max(id).

**Umair Khan** · 2017-08-16 04:04 UTC

>The first question is whether Django's ORM has some implementation dependency on the column.

I think the only constraints will be related to foreign key (it seems we don't use this id in foreign key relationship) and the primary key index. Django doesn't allow a model without primary key.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-08-16 04:15 UTC

Combination of `(user_profile_id, message_id)` can work in my opinion. `max((user_profile_id, message_id))` should work as well. I'll read up on pros and cons though.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-16 04:21 UTC

My point about `max` was that `max(user_profile, message_id)` doesn't tell you the last row inserted into the table.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-08-16 04:22 UTC

True.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-08-24 17:27 UTC

@Tim Abbott #6264 should be pretty easy to merge, and it's the first step to migrating us to using stream_ids for topic mutes.  My thought is that we can have a lazy migration strategy to change the tuples from (stream_name, topic_name) -> (stream_id, stream_name, topic_name).  Or maybe we can do away with stream_name altogether--I think the client-side changes are fairly simple, but I'm not sure about mobile, and there's a bit of search-related code we'd need to clean up.

Cool.   I think phase one is something like this:
* store tuples as (stream_id, stream_name, topic_name)
* auto-upgrade tuples on any read or write (the noop penalty for this is minuscule, and the one-time hit is also small)
* add some code for stream-renames to fix up the stream_name (this is not super critical, since the app is already kind of broken for stream renames, but it should be easy enough)
* for almost all current consumers of topic mutes, we just returns `[(elem[1], elem[2]) for elem in db_value]`
* for internal stuff that needs performance, take advantage of stream_id
* migrate the app to use the new add/delete API that was added this year (pretty simple), and make the API able to accept stream_id

* Do a database migration to update all the existing ones to the new format; this should be really cheap to do.

And that finishes the database side of things (and lets us fix all the backend code to use stream IDs).  Then as a separate project later, we can migrate the apps.

## REALMS_HAVE_SUBDOMAINS

*2017-08-25 to 2017-08-26 · 17 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/REALMS_HAVE_SUBDOMAINS/with/273233)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-25 02:18 UTC

OK, I encountered a "fun" problem with the REALMS_HAVE_SUBDOMAINS model.  Right now, the root domain (i.e. zulip.example.com) is represented as having a subdomain of `""`.  This is great from a code perspective, but from a user perspective, this means that to interact with it in management commands, you need to do e.g. `get_realm("")`

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-25 02:19 UTC

And e.g. if you want to run a management command that interacts with it specifying a realm, you need to pass obscure-looking things like `--realm=''` on the command line

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-25 02:19 UTC

One idea for improving this is that we could use `root` as the human-readable name for the root domain.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-25 02:19 UTC

(Or some other string)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-25 02:20 UTC

From a code complexity perspective, it wouldn't be bad; we already ban `root` as a user-facing subdomain anyway, and everything accesses these via `get_realm()` anyway.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-08-25 02:52 UTC

The proposal is to keep "" in the database, but get_realm also accepts "root" for ""? Seems reasonable. We could also use something like "default"; root to me implies something special (like it's the administrator's realm, or something). I'm fine with root as well, though.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-25 02:54 UTC

Well, we could spell it as "root_domain" if we wanted.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-25 02:55 UTC

I would consider actually changing the database; as a practical matter, any code that interacts with the root needs to check for `""` and do something special anyway to avoid the leading `.`

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-08-25 03:16 UTC

yeah, good point.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-08-25 04:07 UTC

As a short term workaround, we can also create a constant `ROOT=''` and use it to get the root subdomain.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-08-25 04:10 UTC

It will create a layer of abstraction; once we shift to a different name in the DB we can update value of `ROOT`as well.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-25 04:41 UTC

I think we should just decide which way we're going to do this and implement that :)

**Umair Khan** · 2017-08-25 04:43 UTC

Both work for me :).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-25 23:16 UTC

For those of you who haven't been watching commits go by, I'm slowly fixing all the tests that would fail if we started hardcoding REALMS_HAVE_SUBDOMAINS.  Currently about 35 left :).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-08-25 23:16 UTC

Once that's done, I believe we get to delete all the !REALMS_HAVE_SUBDOMAINS code.

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-25 21:49 UTC

Evidently we're getting a "subject" value which is actually of type `bytes`, though at all the inner layers of that stack the type annotations say it should be `Text`.

The root issue appears to be here, in `send_to_missed_message_address`:
```
    result = redis_client.hmget(key, 'user_profile_id', 'recipient_id', 'subject')
    # [...]
    user_profile_id, recipient_id, subject = result
```
Adding a `reveal_type(result)` and `reveal_type(subject)` in there and rerunning mypy finds that both are `Any`. So the type-checker was powerless to spot that we were getting a `bytes` and passing it (a few lines lower) where a `Text` was expected.

**Greg Price** · 2017-08-25 21:52 UTC

Which in turn is because `typeshed` has no stubs for the `redis` library for Python 3! And the Python 2 version has a list of methods/attributes, and of parameter names for the methods, but no parameter or return types:
https://github.com/python/typeshed/blob/b6d08b81a/third_party/2/redis/client.pyi

Reading [the Django docs](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/1.11/topics/logging/#configuring-logging) on the `LOGGING` setting, it sounds like `disable_existing_loggers` shouldn't matter for your new logger -- it's documented like so:

> If the disable_existing_loggers key in the LOGGING dictConfig is set to True (which is the default) then all loggers from the default configuration will be disabled.

Django's default logging configuration is linked just above that -- it points [here](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/1.11/topics/logging/#default-logging-configuration), which describes the `django` and `django.server` loggers.

So it sounds like not "loggers configured before this point", but rather "loggers that Django would by default configure".

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-20 21:49 UTC

Oho, but that is a docs bug! The [actual implementation](https://github.com/django/django/blob/c4c128d67/django/utils/log.py#L64) just calls `logging.config.dictConfig`, from the stdlib, with first the default config, then the `LOGGING` config from settings. And `disable_existing_loggers` there does in fact just wipe out any loggers set up before then.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-20 22:14 UTC

Just read through a bunch of our logging setup, and it does indeed look like there's kind of a mess of different things going on! It'd be great to clean this up. Let me try to summarize some of what I see:
* We set a bunch of configuration in the LOGGING Django setting, which Django passes to `logging.config.dictConfig` at setup time.
* We also have a bunch of places that call `zerver.lib.logging_util.create_logger`, which sets up logging config at the given name. Those are all at module toplevel, so they run at import time and will be clobbered by the Django config.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-20 22:17 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-20 22:19 UTC

* The logging module has a nice hierarchy of loggers -- if you try to log to `foo.bar.baz`, and there's no configuration at that name or the configuration that is there hasn't set `propagate=False`, then it will continue on to `foo.bar` and see what logging config we have there, and so on up to the root, ``.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-20 22:22 UTC

So we should be taking advantage of that. The recommended practice in the upstream `logging` docs (https://docs.python.org/3/library/logging.html) is to say something like `logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)` and then do your logging on that `logger` object, so you're logging to your module name -- then the logging hierarchy you use effectively parallels the module hierarchy. That makes sense, and we already sometimes do it; those `create_logger` calls mostly pass `__name__`, and it returns the result of `logging.getLogger` on the given name.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-20 22:53 UTC

Anyway:
* We should set `disable_existing_loggers=False`. That will make some of this a lot easier to reason about: if you configure a logger, it stays configured, and doesn't get clobbered later depending on a subtle question of ordering. And it follows the recommendations of both the Django docs and the stdlib docs.
* We should stop calling `basicConfig` basically everywhere -- I think absolutely everywhere inside the Django app, where it appears in 5 places in `zerver/`. (It's fine at the top level of a standalone script that doesn't import a complex app codebase, like the examples in `scripts/`, `tools/`, and `puppet/`.) All of those should get deleted if they're just configuring the same thing we configure in `LOGGING`, or if they're trying to configure something different we should sort out what we want.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-20 23:01 UTC

* There's a lot of boilerplate in the `LOGGING` config dict, repeating the same information for a lot of different logger names. **Greg Price** · 2017-09-20 23:17 UTC

Here's another cleanup I think would be helpful, that's related to that:
* I'd like to shift more toward using standard `logging` methods directly, in a consistent way -- I think that will help in everyone seeing consistent good ways to do this. So our `create_logger` function looks like this:
```
def create_logger(name, log_file, log_level, log_format="%(asctime)s %(levelname)-8s %(message)s"):
    # type: (str, str, str, str) -> Logger
    logging.basicConfig(format=log_format)
    logger = logging.getLogger(name)
    logger.setLevel(getattr(logging, log_level))

    if log_file:
        formatter = logging.Formatter(log_format)
        file_handler = logging.FileHandler(log_file)
        file_handler.setFormatter(formatter)
        logger.addHandler(file_handler)

    return logger
```

The `basicConfig` should go away. And then I'd like to reduce it to a function that just does the stuff inside `if log_file`, and call sites will look like
```
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)
logger.setLevel(logging.WARNING)  # or skip this if just INFO
set_log_file(logger, settings.DIGEST_LOG_PATH)
```

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-20 23:17 UTC

Where the first two lines are totally standard examples of things everyone should become used to doing.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-21 23:48 UTC

> This is behavior must be because some how the logger is instantiated before the config is applied. I would think the config is only applied once at the start of the app and before the send_emails module is loaded, but I guess this is not the case.

The config is applied in the Django `setup` function. That'll be called as the app starts up -- there may be good docs on this, but I don't know offhand the specifics of when that happens. But imports are generally the first things to run at program startup because they're typically at the top level of the module, so it's likely that a given module of the application, if we use it, will get imported before all the initial imports are done and before code like `setup` is likely to run.

> How might I test this?

Good question to ask! I'd suggest adding some print statements and just running the code -- maybe a print at the top of each of the modules you're interested in, and also find a way to stick a print in to run when setup happens and the logging config is applied.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-21 23:50 UTC

One way to hack that in: see https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/1.11/ref/settings/#std:setting-LOGGING_CONFIG . That variable is a string which is the name of a function Django will call to set up logging. By default it's "logging.config.dictConfig", the name of a function in the standard library. You could make a little function that just prints a message and then calls that, and set LOGGING_CONFIG to the name of that function.

*2017-09-01 to 2017-09-01 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/fix_unreads/with/275723)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-01 12:53 UTC

@Tim Abbott I am in the process of turning fix_unreads into a migration.  I extracted into a library, which was easy.  The only problem is that fairly deep in the stack, the code calls build_topic_mute_checker, which uses a concrete instance of MutedTopic.  There are a bunch of workarounds to this:
* pass a muted_topic_manager all the way down the stack
* pass a build_topic_mute_checker all the way down the stack (and just clone it in the migration)
* turn fix_unreads into a class, so we can subclass it to override the build_topic_mute_checker (and thus avoid passing so many parameters around)
* have build_topic_mute_checker just use direct SQL (or Alchemy for sugar)  instead of the ORM (it's a pretty trivial query)
* don't attempt any code reuse and copy 200+ lines of code into the migration
* run fix_unreads outside the migration system (and figure out another mechanism to no-op it)
* add a not-exists-in-zerver_muted_topics clause to the direct SQL in `fix_pre_pointer` (depends on postgres being smart about it)

Thoughts?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-01 13:03 UTC

The calling sequence is migration -> fix -> fix_pre_pointer -> build_topic_mute_checker -> ORM MutedTopic.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-01 13:05 UTC

~~~ python

142

$ ./manage.py sqlmigrate zerver 0083_index_mentioned_user_messages
BEGIN;
--
-- Raw SQL operation
--

        DO $$
        BEGIN
            IF NOT EXISTS (
                SELECT 1
                FROM pg_class
                where relname = 'zerver_usermessage_mentioned_message_id'
                ) THEN
                    CREATE INDEX
                    zerver_usermessage_mentioned_message_id
                    ON zerver_usermessage (user_profile_id, message_id)
                    WHERE (flags & 8) != 0;
            END IF;
        END$$;
        ;
COMMIT;

## do_send_messages performance

*2017-09-10 to 2017-09-12 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/do_send_messages.20performance/with/278882)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-10 19:59 UTC

The Django ORM has 10x overhead for bulk operations on UserProfile and UserMessage.  If you mostly bypass the ORM, except for a little sugar in creating SQL queries, you make the bottleneck be markdown parsing for `do_send_messages`.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-10 20:02 UTC

Things that are fast:
* 99% of postgres queries (especially single-table queries)
* Python native types (set, dictionary, list, and friends)
* Python bit arithmetic

Things that are slow:
* metaprogrammed Django ORM objects
* Django bitfield object creation
* regexes
* fairly complex table joins that confuse postgres

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-10 20:04 UTC

Regexes are actually fast, and they should be maligned for much better reasons, haha.  The markdown parser just bangs really hard on regexes.  I need to get to the bottom of that.

see #6441

## postgres

*2017-09-15 to 2018-01-24 · 36 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/postgres/with/282727)*

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-15 22:49 UTC

@Steve Howell , I ran across https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/730da55bf and was a little sad that it seemed like we had to be working around the PostgreSQL query planner. Partly because I just gave a talk a week ago telling a bunch of PostgreSQL users how happy we were that we didn't have to do that since switching away from MySQL back in 2012. :-)

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-15 22:50 UTC

Looking at the description, I wondered if it's that postgres is choosing that plan because the realm_id you're searching for is actually most of the users in the database -- in which case it actually sounds like a pretty reasonable plan.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-15 22:54 UTC

So I took a look with `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` at some queries on the zulipchat.com database. Started with `select realm_id, count(*) as c from zerver_userprofile group by realm_id order by c desc limit 20;` to get a list of bigger realms of various sizes, then tried your example query with different realm IDs. I actually do get a variety of different query plans, each of which seems pretty reasonable for the respective values.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-15 22:55 UTC

And for the biggest realm, the execution time reported by EXPLAIN ANALYZE is 3.9ms.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-15 22:59 UTC

So I am not sure we're not actually better off in practice letting the query planner do its thing. All else equal, it saves us sending the data over to Python, deserializing it into a Python list of ints etc., then serializing it again and sending back.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-15 23:01 UTC

One thing I wonder about in your testing -- after you build up the large test realm, Postgres may not have updated statistics to guide its query planner.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-15 23:04 UTC

I think that can be controlled for by just running the `ANALYZE` statement after creating the data:
https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.3/static/sql-analyze.html

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-15 23:06 UTC

So one thing that complicates the UserPresence query is the timestamp check, which I didn't show in the commit message.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-15 23:14 UTC

Obviously, in an ideal world, where postgres always gets the query plan correct, it makes sense to just have one hop.  Of course, in an ideal world, the latency hop is also negligible, haha.

I'd be happy to do a controlled experiment here, where we re-combine some query and see what the impact is.  This particular query mostly impacts presence requests.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-15 23:27 UTC

One thought here is that we should just denormalize realm_id to UserPresence (and any other tables that have user_profile_id as a foreign key).  This would make it totally trivial for postgres to do query analysis (no table joins), and it would outperform the current model even with perfect analyze data (again, because no table joins).

And then another possibility is to just pull user_ids out of memcached for realms.  We can probably do that now, actually.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-15 23:54 UTC

I should echo one thing you said earlier--postgres has been super solid for this project.  There's some pretty heavy lifting in our queries to get messages, for example, and we've almost never had to worry about the DB part of it.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-15 23:57 UTC

But back to latency hops, I kind of wonder if we  should be assuming they're a big hit.  The nature of our system is that we can scale horizontally pretty easily, since realms are mostly disjoint.  (Realms share a few things, like welcome bots, but we want to fix that.)  So I think it's usually practical to just run postgres a short hop away from the Django instance.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-16 00:00 UTC

For the serialization costs, whether you do one big query or two small queries, most of the overhead isn't intrinsic to serialization, it's a byproduct of Django being a very dynamic ORM.  For most of our stuff, the ORM overhead is well worth it for the convenience.  But it's not super hard to optimize serialization of SQL results.  Most of the time, for minor optimizations, it's simple enough to use the ORM, but use `.values` instead of objects.  It doesn't make the code that much harder to read, because dictionaries are very readable in Python.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-16 00:01 UTC

Occasionally, for really big stuff, you want to bypass the ORM completely.  A good example of that is how we populate UserMessage objects, and that optimization was huge in impact.  It does create a bit more code, but it's not like the code is inscrutable or tricky.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-16 00:08 UTC

`UserMessageLite` is 7 lines of code, including class/def statements.

`bulk_insert_ums` is similar in size, and the fanciest thing in it is a list comprehension.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-16 00:20 UTC

@Steve Howell Back online, sorry for dropping off unannounced -- the wifi in the office stopped working, and after some fruitless fiddling with phone tethering, I just found something offline to do while officemates were fixing it :)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-16 00:22 UTC

No worries.  I actually have to leave myself now, but I'll be back later if you want to continue the conversation, and obviously I will understand if you start without me, haha.  These things are definitely worth discussing as we get closer to scaling up. :)

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-16 00:23 UTC

I think a controlled experiment, changing some query on zulipchat.com prod and seeing what the impact is, would be great. This looks like it could be a good query to do that on, or you might have other candidates. Not practical to do that for every query we try to optimize -- there were a lot of optimizations you made recently!, and I imagine it'd have been a big pain to study all of those in prod instead of dev -- but it'd be educational to see once or twice how the prod results compare to those in dev.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-16 00:28 UTC

Denormalizing `realm_id` into tables could be a good step, if we have a lot of queries that like this one are pulling a long list of things from across a realm. (It won't typically help, I think, with queries that are limited to something more specific like a user or a stream.)

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-16 00:30 UTC

Two tables I'd be hesitant to do that in: `message` and `usermessage`. Especially the latter; we almost surely don't want to do that.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-16 00:31 UTC

(Because there are so very many rows, and we've kept them quite small.)

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-16 00:48 UTC

In hops between the application and the database, my intuition would be that the serialization/deserialization is the slow part -- I agree that they should be kept close by in network terms. Definitely <2ms RTT, preferably more like 0.1ms; looks like for zulipchat.com we currently have around 0.2ms.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-16 00:59 UTC

FWIW, adding the timestamp condition to the query (as `timestamp > (now() - '2 weeks'::interval) and`) increases the time for the biggest realm on zulipchat.com to 6ms. The plan for that realm changes to an outright sequential scan on `zerver_userpresence`, in a hash join. Still seems like a pretty plausible plan, and potentially the same plan it'd choose if given an explicit list of `user_profile_id` values that's that long.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-16 02:17 UTC

Regarding the last point, I'd try decomposing the query manually and see what each one turns up.  The UserProfile query will be so fast it's almost a waste of time to measure, but you need it to collect the list of ids, and then do some somewhat tedious editing to make the follow up query.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-16 08:40 UTC

I think for doing this sort of testing, the `chat.zulip.org` data set is actually the one we want to work with.  Because presence is most inefficient there.

That's definitely an interesting dataset to work with. A key thing to bear in mind when looking at EXPLAIN ANALYZE results from there, though, will be that the planner is likely to skip any indexes that are all about `realm_id` -- because the main realm is the only one of any size.

This thread started with a commit where we'd changed from one query to a sequence of queries on account of seeing the query planner do a table scan and not trusting it to make the right choices. ## securing Zulip messaging using the Axolotl protocol

*2017-09-21 to 2017-09-21 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/securing.20Zulip.20messaging.20using.20the.20Axolotl.20protocol/with/285253)*

**Darin Gordon** · 2017-09-21 14:45 UTC

While reviewing the open source projects published by Wire, whose server is written in Haskell,  I discovered that they implemented the Axolotl protocol in Rust.  This is great news because Python can use Rust extensions.  If secure messaging is a priority for the Zulip project, you may not need to look further than this!  See the section on Proteus/Cryptobox:  https://github.com/wireapp/wire

worth considering, @tabbott?

**Matthias** · 2017-09-21 14:55 UTC

but there is a big difference between the two concepts: 
1) Zulip uses SSL by default to secure the transfer of msgs to the server,
2) Wire uses e2e encryption which is more secure but also has disadvantages like not being able to search endlessly into the past

if your Wire keys change (using different device, session reset) then your old msgs can't be decrypted and searching them would be impossible. Wire's security model just  doesn't match or fit Zulips.
What would be interesting though is how they make e2e work with their team server offer of recent weeks.

**Darin Gordon** · 2017-09-21 14:57 UTC

@Matthias that's a good point about message history.. I've personally experienced that loss when using Signal.  They absolutely must have considered that for team chat

**Matthias** · 2017-09-21 14:58 UTC

and I'm an avid Wire user and changed phone twice this year. I lost all my msg history due to Wire not syncing it like Whatsapp for example.
I love Wire but e2e has it's limits.

**Matthias** · 2017-09-21 15:12 UTC

btw Signal does have an export/import feature for msgs... Wire not (yet). But it might not backup images and other attachments.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-21 18:31 UTC

@Darin Gordon the problem with all of these e2e crypto systems is key distribution: when someone is subscribed to a stream, they need to somehow be given the secret keys to read messages on that stream.  I think probably one would need a browser/desktop app extension for doing the crypto stuff in the web browser to make E2E crypto work reasonably.  I don't think this is a small project.


## group alert words

*2017-09-22 to 2017-09-22 · 17 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/group.20alert.20words/with/285989)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-22 17:22 UTC

We have customers who use alert words like `@support`  as a convention for doing team/group things.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-22 17:24 UTC

Imagine you have an organization with 100 people, and there are 10 people on the support team.  You'll probably create a stream called "support," but you'll have non-support subscribe to that stream, because people not on the support team will go there to ask for support.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-22 17:24 UTC

So let's say you want to get just the attention of the support team, not all the subscribers.  If you do an at-all mention on the stream, it's too spammy.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-22 17:26 UTC

So the current workaround is to have an alert word convention, where you can say something like `@support` to get the attention of just the core support team.  (You don't actually need the `@` there, but it seems to be a common convention.)  The only problem there is that each person on the support team needs to set up the alert word.

It would be nice to have more "official" Zulip support for this alerting scheme.  There's gonna be some tension in here in figuring out what to build first:
* We want to do something pretty minimal to support this use case, since it's pretty clearly something customers want.
* We want to think a little bit about the end game of more pervasive teams support.  Think of things like being able to create teams and automatically subscribe team members to certain streams.

I don't think implementing the first bullet here really endangers any long term plans, but it's worth thinking it through a bit.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-22 17:29 UTC

But I'd start with doing a backend for this with tests, and then add a UI.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-22 17:29 UTC

Yeah.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-22 17:30 UTC

There can be another approach as well with two models: Groups and Users.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-22 17:31 UTC

Yeah, basically a many to many relation.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-23 01:07 UTC

Another one that looks potentially interesting is gdb-heap:
https://github.com/rogerhu/gdb-heap
In particular, that's the only one I've found yet that looks like it can take a core file dumped from a running process, then analyze it offline while the process continues on its merry way and/or you can kill the process and move on.

Looks like it might not be simple to install, though -- several system dependencies, and the fact that the README talks only about running on Ubuntu 12.04 (which is from 2012) suggests it hasn't seen much use. I'll set it aside for now but may come back.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-23 01:13 UTC

**tracemalloc** is a new tool in the stdlib since 3.4 that looks quite promising:

https://blog.fugue.co/2017-03-06-diagnosing-and-fixing-memory-leaks-in-python.html

It traces at allocation time, so I think it's not useful for an already-running process. But I may add this to what we run on this server so that after a little while we have some good data.

**Greg Price** · 2017-09-23 01:27 UTC

**pyrasite** is a tool for injecting Python code into a running process, which most other tools I'm finding depend on if you want to operate on a running process.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-09 00:21 UTC

@Steve Howell yes, memcached is capped at 1/8 of system RAM.  Because it's usually one of the largest processes at 1/8 of system RAM (especially if it is 6 UWSGI processes that are all leaking), it's likely to be the biggest and be hit by the OOM killer.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-09 00:21 UTC

Also, if the OOM killer were to kill an individual uwsgi process, nobody would notice since it'd just be replaced immediately.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-09 00:22 UTC

We do occasionally get weird tracebacks of the form "memcached is full" where I don't understand how that's possible since it's supposed to be an LRU cache.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-09 00:22 UTC

But we can be very confident memcached is not involved in our memory leak problem, since it's size doesn't change with time.

Probably we should make our `bulk_set` operations batch in smaller units and it'll be fine.

## stream owner

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-27 21:21 UTC

One of our biggest requests for improving Zulip is to have a "stream owner" concept.  As @Rein Zustand points out on #**issues**, this is something that Slack already has.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-27 21:22 UTC

This is a fairly large project, but it's worth getting some initial design ideas out there.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-27 21:23 UTC

One fairly low-risk project would be to just build the back end for **representing** stream owners, before giving them any actual power, and before building any additional UI.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-27 21:24 UTC

This would at least allow us to import data from Slack, for example, even if we don't use it in exactly the same way.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-27 21:27 UTC

Another way somebody can get the ball rolling here is to create a document that proposes a fairly complete security model.  Basically, outline the powers that stream owners should have, and emphasize things that they absolutely should not be able to do.  Also, maybe propose reductions for realm-admin power once we have stream owners.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-27 21:51 UTC

One thing that we're almost certainly going to support is multiple stream owners.  We might explicitly track the specific person who created the stream, but stream creators should be able to basically share all their power with stream owners.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-28 04:12 UTC

It feels like that the powers of the stream owner should be close to what an organization admin can do in that stream. So in a way an administrator can just delegate the responsibility to handle a specific stream to the stream owner.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 04:17 UTC

The stream owner of a private stream should actually have more power than an org admin.  Org admins should only be able to do blunt things like deactivate the stream.  Stream owners should be able to have finer control over membership privileges.  (The main context here is private streams, where privacy is paramount.  Stream owners aren't really needed for public streams, because we don't need to address any privacy concerns for realm admins doing stuff.  Having said that, we want stream owners on public streams too, it's just not as big a need.)

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-28 04:21 UTC

I see.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 04:26 UTC

I think the use case you describe is actually pretty common--you have realm admins in an organization where they basically have policy rights to administer all streams, and they simply want to delegate some of the admin work out.  But there are more complex scenarios where realm admins are entrusted with administrative tasks, but they shouldn't necessarily be privvy to the details of who subscribes to every private stream.  I know the latter scenario is at least plausible, but it's possible we punt on that for now.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-28 04:27 UTC

Yeah, the latter looks more cool.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-28 04:29 UTC

For example the stream owner can have access to different kind of statistics for that stream. Statistics like different counters, most popular words, most discussed topic etc.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-09-28 04:30 UTC

Words to ban.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 04:35 UTC

Indeed.  We will eventually have Zulip realms that service multiple organizations working on the same problem.  We want the realm admins to control the overall instance, but we want various factions to manage their own streams, so that people can have effective "offline" conversations that are still on Zulip, just on a private stream.

**Rein Zustand** · 2017-09-28 04:35 UTC

Btw, S###k has a more fine grained permission hierarchy -- owner, admin, member, multi-channel guest, single-channel guest. Yet there is no owner that is specific for administering a channel. Ref: https://get.slack.help/hc/en-us/articles/201314026-Roles-and-permissions-in-Slack

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 04:39 UTC

@Rein Zustand Along those lines, we've been asked for features like read-only subscriptions, guests users, etc.  So whoever does the initial work on "stream owner" should at least acquaint themselves with various long-term permissions models that we want to adopt.  It shouldn't necessarily prevent incremental progress--the stream owner concept is pretty solid in its own right--but it's good to have the big picture.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 04:40 UTC

s/we want to adopt/we want to consider adopting/

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-09-28 15:29 UTC

Interesting observation! I guess slack channels are less powerful than zulip streams in general, which could be one reason why they haven't felt a need for stream-admins. And we have some tasks like editing topics that are pretty natural for stream admins and which don't exist in slack.
That is good data, though, and does make me want to be more careful that there is a need for this feature before we do the large amount of work to implement it.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 15:57 UTC

One reason I like the idea of moving forward with "stream owner" is that the feature isn't inherently complex, and we can break up the tasks over time:
* the model is pretty simple--just create a many/many link between UserProfile and Stream
* we can have backend management scripts at first for appointing and removing stream owners
* we can have stream owners be "figureheads" at first and gradually give them more power
* a good feature to prototype is letting stream owners remove users from the stream--it's a full-stack thing, but some of the pieces are probably in place and just require changes to permission checks on the backend and some lightweight data classes on the frontend

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 16:00 UTC

I also think we can get marginal utility out of this feature almost from day one.  Just having our model set allows us to import data from Slack.  Having stream owners that are pure figureheads can still be helpful for users who want to know "who is in charge".  Allowing stream owners to do nothing but edit topics can immediately make streams work nicer for newbie-heavy realms.  Etc.


## Addressee.legacy_build

*2017-09-28 to 2017-09-30 · 27 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Addressee.2Elegacy_build/with/289116)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 18:44 UTC

@Tim Abbott @Neil Pilgrim Just some quick notes on killing off Addressee.legacy_build, since we were discussing that on #**development help**:

* There are very few direct calls to legacy_build, but there are tons of indirect calls.
* The lowest-hanging fruit cleanup is to fix about 50 webhooks with a bunch of similar one-line changes to directly send messages to a stream instead of janky lines like `check_send_message(user_profile, request.client, 'stream', [stream], subject, body)`.
* Similar to other projects like this, 80% of the cleanup will be easy and tedious, and then the last 20% may be a bit more subtle, although I don't think it's too bad.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-28 19:11 UTC

Hmm, yeah, we should start with migrating the webhook piece.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 19:20 UTC

If we get a volunteer, I can help with the initial effort to clean up the webhook calls.  If we don't get a volunteer, I'll eventually clean this up myself.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-09-28 19:21 UTC

I think we just need to pick what API we want to migrate to, and I bet @Eeshan Garg will be happy to do the rest.

**Eeshan Garg** · 2017-09-28 19:22 UTC

Absolutely, I am done with most of my current projects. So I'd love to help! :)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 19:23 UTC

Let me take a quick look...

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 19:25 UTC

I think the new API should be `check_send_stream_message(user_profile, client, stream_name, topic, body)`.  This eliminates the `message_type_name` parameter, and `message_to`is not an array; instead, we just pass in the stream name.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 19:25 UTC

And then the new function will be a simpler version of this:

~~~ python
1455 def check_send_message(sender, client, message_type_name, message_to,
1456                        subject_name, message_content, realm=None, forged=False,
1457                        forged_timestamp=None, forwarder_user_profile=None, local_id=None,
1458                        sender_queue_id=None):
1459     # type: (UserProfile, Client, Text, Sequence[Text], Optional[Text], Text, Optional[Realm], bool, Optional[fl     oat], Optional[UserProfile], Optional[Text], Optional[Text]) -> int
1460 
1461     addressee = Addressee.legacy_build(
1462         sender,
1463         message_type_name,
1464         message_to,
1465         subject_name)
1466 
1467     message = check_message(sender, client, addressee,
1468                             message_content, realm, forged, forged_timestamp,
1469                             forwarder_user_profile, local_id, sender_queue_id)
1470     return do_send_messages([message])[0]

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 19:26 UTC

We can eliminate a lot of the optional parameters, such as `forged_timestamp`.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 19:27 UTC

And instead of using `Addressee.legacy_build()`, we can call `Addressee.for_stream()`.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 19:27 UTC

Does that make sense, @Eeshan Garg?

**Eeshan Garg** · 2017-09-28 19:28 UTC

@Steve Howell: I'm going to say, yes! I'll definitely need to take a more in-depth look before getting started. :)

**Eeshan Garg** · 2017-09-28 19:29 UTC

So, we want to kill `Addressee.legacy_build()` in favor of `Addressee.for_stream()` and eliminate as many optional parameters in favor of a cleaner API, correct? And webhooks are the only place that this is being used?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-09-28 19:31 UTC

There might be other places, too, but cleaning up webhooks is the top priority.

**Eeshan Garg** · 2017-09-28 19:33 UTC

Cool, sounds good! I'll keep you updated! :simple_smile:

**Eeshan Garg** · 2017-09-28 19:34 UTC

Ideally, looking forward to getting this done *before* midterm week starts.

Another good "sweep" project here is to rename subject -> topic when it's easy and low-risk.

**Eeshan Garg** · 2017-09-28 19:52 UTC

I'll keep that in mind! :)

@Eeshan Garg I'd start with just doing 1-2, and then we can optimize the approach, and only then do more.

**Eeshan Garg** · 2017-09-28 20:34 UTC

Yeah that's what I was thinking! :)

## null bytes

*2017-10-02 to 2017-10-02 · 23 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/null.20bytes/with/291238)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-02 19:55 UTC

What should we do if there are null bytes in the message content?  Options include:
* Throw a JsonableError
* Just remove them

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-02 19:55 UTC

I can see the case either way.  Removing them is nice in that API users don't need to filter their content for obscure things like this

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-02 20:00 UTC

My vote is to throw an error.  I think for many API authors, they'll expect us to help them simply reject bad input.  For API authors that have to deal with kinda-legit incoming null data, I think it's generally better for Zulip to explicitly fail the messages than quietly massage them.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-02 20:01 UTC

The place where I worry about that is things where you're sending in log output from some other tool

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-02 20:01 UTC

You don't really want your log output to get discarded because it had some null bytes in it

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-02 20:02 UTC

We could potentially rewrite them to some zulip-markdown appropriate thing.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-02 20:13 UTC

Yeah, the logging case is probably common.  I think I'd still err on the side of rejecting null bytes entirely, but it's hard to speculate on what the worst case scenario is here, since there a couple plausible ones (losing important log data, making log data not 100% accurate, exposing us to null-byte strangeness, etc.).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-02 20:18 UTC

There's not much in the way of strangeness; postgrse throws an exception if it gets one, so we just 500 "cleanly" right now.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-02 20:18 UTC

I'd like to replace that with something that isn't a 500

**Greg Price** · 2017-10-02 20:19 UTC

I think the right solution to this probably looks like having a clear way to escape arbitrary text into a message. Then anything that's sending in arbitrary data like log messages, we can expect to use that, and we can help by giving a clear error (4xx, of course) when what they send is invalid.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-02 20:19 UTC

This seems to be a new issue for us; I suspect an upgrade in psycopg2 changed its behavior.

**Greg Price** · 2017-10-02 20:20 UTC

If you're sending log data, you want to prevent it from getting interpreted as Markdown anyway, so you're already doing some kind of escaping even if it's just prefixing with triple-backtick.

**Greg Price** · 2017-10-02 20:20 UTC

(Which isn't 100% enough by itself -- in addition to null bytes, the data could contain newline + triple-backtick.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-02 20:21 UTC

Right, aside from this issue, you'll do pretty OK if you just escape (+ maybe truncate).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-02 20:22 UTC

So there's some argument that we should just turn these into `\0` or something.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-02 20:23 UTC

To keep every client sending in logs from needing to write custom code for this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-02 20:23 UTC

As a data point, we seem to be getting this exception both from the Zulip mobile app and the email mirror.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-02 20:23 UTC

So there are multiple existing things that send stuff into Zulip that do this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-02 20:23 UTC

(Email mirror is typically people sending logs etc. into Zulip)

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-02 20:27 UTC

The less-than-perfect compromise is to make our endpoint reject null bytes but provide a simple does-nothing-but-escape-null-bytes encoder in our API client.

**Greg Price** · 2017-10-02 20:45 UTC

Yeah, whatever the recipe is for "escape properly", we should provide in our API client.

**Greg Price** · 2017-10-02 20:46 UTC

And "just escape" is exactly the point -- but I'm not sure exactly how to properly do that (what do you do if there's a newline-triple-backtick? are that and null bytes the only things to worry about?), which is why we should work out a sufficient recipe and write it down.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-02 21:45 UTC

Alright, I'm fine with making the backend reject null bytes and addressing this in the API client (and email mirror code, where we probably do need the server to do something since there's no "client").

*2017-10-02 to 2017-10-04 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/type.20annotation.20syntax/with/291274)*

**Greg Price** · 2017-10-02 20:34 UTC

Forking from the discussion [in topic "python3"](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/backend/subject/python3/near/290633) about switching from type comments to the Python 3 "def f(x: int) -> int:" type-annotation syntax from PEP 3107.

**Greg Price** · 2017-10-02 20:35 UTC

@Rein Zustand The other tools I'd consider as a substrate other than lib2to3 are [RedBaron](https://github.com/PyCQA/redbaron) and [rope](https://github.com/python-rope/rope). I've never used either, but I've heard good things about at least rope.

**Greg Price** · 2017-10-02 20:36 UTC

Awkwardly it looks like neither of them supports operating on Python 3... which only really matters when using Python 3-specific syntax, but of course we want this tool to start us doing that.

**Greg Price** · 2017-10-02 20:39 UTC

The powerful thing they do both provide, though, is that simultaneously
* whatever you change, you still get proper Python syntax in the result; and
* everything you don't change is spit back out unmodified, including formatting and comments.

The former is hard to do with anything less than a parser, and the latter is impossible with a parser like the one under `ast`, which is designed for executing the code and throws away the whitespace and comments.

**Greg Price** · 2017-10-02 20:43 UTC

https://github.com/PyCQA/baron/pull/115

So using redbaron, with that PR's version of baron, could be very helpful.

* you're trying to read the imports
* you're modifying the imports
* you're reviewing code
* you're trying to avoid merge conflicts

@Rishi Gupta and others,  in order to have vim remember your last position in a file, stick the below code in `~/.vimrc`.  (If you use a different editor, I imagine there's some way to configure it.)

~~~
function! ResCur()
  if line("'\"") <= line("$")
    normal! g`" 
    return 1
  endif
endfunction

augroup resCur
  autocmd!
  autocmd BufWinEnter * call ResCur()
augroup END

Depending on how the lines wrap, you can perturb up to 43 / 3 lines in the diff (assuming ~3 name per line).

## api limits

**Brock Whittaker** · 2017-10-17 22:20 UTC

I think the API limits are too low for a few things. When I run the "n" key to go through topics, some of which I don't care about so it goes through fast, it appears I can't do more than around 10 in a five to ten second space before I get this response:

```js
{"retry-after":4.6702561378,"msg":"API usage exceeded rate limit","result":"error"}
```

This feels perhaps like too low of a limit? It's from the `/messages` endpoint and the `/report_narrow_time` endpoint.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-17 22:33 UTC

I generally agree that we can probably make the rate-limiting values a bit less restrictive.  For the specific case of cycling through unread streams, I wonder if there's some kind of throttling that we should be doing on the client side, not so much to protect the server, but more to just make the app snappier.

**Greg Price** · 2017-10-17 22:34 UTC

This is extra easy to do because our rate-limiting supports different limits at different timescales -- so we could allow bigger bursts over a few seconds, without e.g. increasing how many are allowed over a minute.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-17 23:24 UTC

I suspect the problem here is more interesting.  We limit at like 100 API requests.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-17 23:24 UTC

I bet the problem is the limit for narrowing is fine, but one is hitting a rate-limit for something like "fetching an uploaded file"

def followup_email_delay(user):

It's a generally a good idea to structure your code so that it's easy to simulate what time and timezone is "present". *2017-10-22 to 2017-10-23 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/last_reminder/with/302626)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-22 00:26 UTC

@Tim Abbott I wonder how volatile `UserProfile.last_reminder` is in practice.  I haven't investigated fully, but I have suspicion that it might churn the cache a bit.  (The context here is that I'm trying to find out why page-load has so many queries, and if this field is not None, you spend two database hops to clear it.  The first hop is obvious (the update), but then you also have a query against subscriptions that's part of invalidating caches.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-23 17:57 UTC

@Steve Howell I suspect it's not volatile at all.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-23 17:58 UTC

Since it should only be set to not-none in the case that a bot the user owns threw an error.

The main source of cache churn in practice is going to be `pointer`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-23 18:12 UTC

BTW, we have an open issue for this, but the actual field that is really volatile on UserProfile is `pointer`.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-23 18:12 UTC

Ah, yeah, pointer is good to be aware of.  I think `last_reminder` is set to a non-None value in our page_params tests, which slightly inflates our query count beyond the normal case.  (We should leave it like, though, since we mostly care about the worst-case scenario in the query count tests.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-23 18:12 UTC

Which we try to manage a bit by not flushing caches when it changes.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-23 18:13 UTC

Yeah, unfortunately, we've had a caching bug for a while now where we over-churn the cache.  We had `updated_fields` instead of `update_field` in one of our codepaths.

Right.  Do you think it's worth putting that in for the release?  I think it requires some slight reordering of your commits in the relevant branch to make introducing `changes` not merge-conflict.
