## 2**n problem

*2017-10-27 to 2017-10-27 · 19 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/2.2A.2An.20problem/with/305849)*

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-27 20:08 UTC

So I'm start to think about adding a `client_gravatar` flag to our events registration code.  The tricky bit of this is that we instrinsically have 2**N possible payloads to send to clients when messages are sent, where N is the number of boolean configs.

Fortunately, N is only about to advance to 2 (apply_markdown, client_gravatar), so we'll only have four variations of the payload.

Right now N=1, and we handle this with two concrete variables.  We probably want to go to a more dynamic scheme with four possible payloads.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-27 20:11 UTC

I think with four variations, we can probably still get away with code like this:

~~~
dct[(True, True)] = finalize(raw_dict, True, True)
dct[(False, True)] = finalize(raw_dict, False, True)
dct[(True, False)] = finalize(raw_dict, True, False)
dct[(False, False)] = finalize(raw_dict, False, False)
~~~

And then
~~~
payload = dct[(client.apply_markdown, client.client_gravatar)]

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-27 20:12 UTC

But it also might make sense to have some kind of caching decorator/wrapper around `finalize`.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-27 20:12 UTC

where the wrapper is scoped to the current function call

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-27 20:18 UTC

@Steve Howell is the 2**n problem for testing, or more for sending events down to clients?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-27 20:18 UTC

It's a performance issue for the real code.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-27 20:18 UTC

Is this in `process_message_event`, I guess?

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-27 20:19 UTC

It's in `process_message_event`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-27 20:19 UTC

OK, great, so a performance-sensitive area.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-27 20:19 UTC

I guess `finalize` itself is pretty cheap.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-27 20:19 UTC

Yeah, especially at 2**2 scaling factor.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-27 20:20 UTC

So the main cost is actually just copying the message dict 4x

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-27 20:21 UTC

That might be OK; if I had to guess, that's a lot cheaper than some of the other things we're doing.  But I think an in-function cache that means we only copy-and-call-finalize for the cases that we actually use would not be a bad investment.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-27 20:21 UTC

Yeah, basically, and I'm working under the premise that the `actions.py` code does the superset of fetching/rendering you'd need, even if the only actual clients doesn't need rendering or server-side hashing of the gravatar URL.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-27 20:21 UTC

Yep, which I think is the right model.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-27 20:23 UTC

For N=1, we have two concrete variables.

For N=2, I'm proposing we compute four dict values with no caching.

And then when we get to N=3, I think we introduce a more lazy-copy strategy.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-27 20:24 UTC

N=3 will probably be the inflection point, since I think doing eight dictionary copies for a simple PM might actually start to be non-negligible.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-10-27 20:28 UTC

Yeah, that makes sense to me.  It took years to get from N=1 to N=2, so that's probably OK as a plan.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-10-27 20:32 UTC

The other option here, I suppose, is to just make sure our three clients can compute gravatar urls in the next N weeks.

We've put out the major fire for mobile, I believe, and they'll presumably be able to compute gravatar URLs soon if they don't already.  And then for the webapp and Python API, it's a simple enough fix.  And then our only backward compatibility concerns are people writing directly to the REST API (e.g. for non-Python clients) who care about displaying avatars.

## lint

*2017-11-08 to 2018-01-23 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/lint/with/315428)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-08 19:23 UTC

I've been thinking we should extract the linter as an independent project; for one thing, it'll let us reuse it between the Zulip backend and the Zulip Python API bindings, and it's also something that I'd like to blog about.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-08 19:24 UTC

We've basically stabilized the API for both the core linter framework and the `custom_check.py` system.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-08 19:24 UTC

I think step 1 is to extract things to a directory, where we have no Zulip linter configuration in that directory

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-08 19:25 UTC

E.g. `tools/zulint` would be a directory that only has reusable code.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-08 19:28 UTC

There's basically 2 material pieces of work required to make this happen.  Probably the big one to start with is making `custom_check_file` not have any hardcoded stuff, which means make the `max_length` and `firstline` block be things that are passed in via the DSL.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-08 19:29 UTC

The other one is just rearranging how the code is organized in `tools/lint` to have a thing you import and the main code.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-08 19:30 UTC

That second one requires more thought about the right way to do it, so I'd start with the first if you're thinking of working on this @Robert Hönig :)

**Robert Hönig** · 2017-11-08 19:32 UTC

Yup, would like to take this up.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-08 19:36 UTC

Oh, a third piece is modifying things like `pyflakes.py` to be able to put the "ignored rules" type things in a separate file from the definition.  I'd probably try to make it as small a change as possible: If the script expects code, pass in a function; if it expects a list of things, pass in a list, etc.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-08 19:36 UTC

I figure we can make the interfaces prettier once it's extracted, but best not to try doing 2 things at once :).

**Umair Khan** · 2017-11-09 05:11 UTC

This sounds great!

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-23 20:30 UTC

## email reuse

*2017-11-10 to 2017-11-22 · 15 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/email.20reuse/with/319027)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-10 18:20 UTC

So there's sorta a sequence that we need to merge things in for this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-10 18:21 UTC

First, we need to remove all use of `get_user_profile_by_email` (replacing with `get_user`) in code that isn't tests/management/commands

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-10 18:21 UTC

The big chunk of that is the auth backends, which have a prerequisite of making sure we pass in the realm unconditionally.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-10 18:21 UTC

That work is pretty tricky just in terms of code structure, because auth backends have a really weird model in Django.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-10 18:22 UTC

In parallel with that, we can try changing views like password reset to do something reasonable with emails not being unique, and also changing our logging middleware to include the realm ID in log lines somehow.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-10 18:23 UTC

Once that's all done, we can move the unique field email to a unique_together with realm, and test a lot.

**Steve Howell** · 2017-11-10 18:28 UTC

Is it hard to get realm ids in auth backends?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-10 18:38 UTC

Not hard, just requires some careful refactoring.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-10 18:38 UTC

The reason it requires care is that Django determines which auth backends to try based on the function signatures, which is super confusing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-10 18:39 UTC

Django 1.11 has a new feature that I want to try out where you can pass in the backend you want to use; we might want to try that out for the 80% of ones where we want a specific one.

**Rein Zustand** · 2017-11-13 03:05 UTC

This issue should have been tagged `priority: high`, shouldn't it?

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-22 19:29 UTC

@Vishnu Ks timabbott/email-rework now has 3 commits that I think should be all we need to do (totally untested, manually or automatically).  I think you can start with getting automated tests passing (will likely fix most of the bugs) and then do both manual and automated tests for making new accounts reusing emails.  For automation, I'd test (1) creating realm with an email used in another realm, (2) creating a later account with an email used in another realm, (3) login with various auth backends with an account that appears in multiple realms.  And include some for trying to use a system bot's email.

For manual testing, I'm thinking we can have `populate_db` create a new simple test realm called "kinglear" with Cordelia + King Lear in it.  (we may need to do something with DevAuthBackend to show the realm for users in the main screen to avoid confusion as to which is which)).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-15 00:22 UTC

What I meant is:
* It's rare that this sorting will even be relevant.  Testing, I found it'd move about 300 things to flip that setting on the whole codebase from one option to the other, and a lot of them are things where it's flipping `ujson` from top to bottom in a list of 4 things, where it looks about the same either way.  
* They look better grouped with all the `import foo` separated from the `from foo import bar` ones.
* I think it's not unlikely that I'd want to do a code sweep at some point to decrease the number of these mixed things, since a lot of them don't match our usual style without good reason.

So the isort config we have in master is great for everything where we don't have a lot of multi-line imports.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-15 00:22 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-15 00:22 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-16 00:04 UTC

We just merged re-sorting for collections of files that tend to not have multi-line imports and would have no merge conflicts (e.g. webhooks, migrations, etc.).  I estimate what is merged so far has covered about 30% of total changes `isort` would make .  @Rein Zustand I think I want to take a pause on doing further re-sorting at this point for a couple reasons:
* We aren't in agreement on what format strategy we want for multi-line imports.  Even if we decide we want to use our historical strategy in most places, I definitely don't want to change the strategy for `zerver/tests/test_events.py`, and so we at least need to figure out a way to exclude that.
* Most of the other stuff will have merge conflicts, and so we'll probably want to do in small chunks when we know a file is currently not being changed.
* We can't do scripts/ and tools/ until we figure out how to address the `sanity_check` issue.  This is the main issue for which we might need further tooling.

## utcnow

*2017-11-30 to 2017-11-30 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/utcnow/with/348852)*

**Greg Price** · 2017-11-30 01:20 UTC

(Moving a discussion from #7427.) I wanted to print the time (in some logging), so I had a bit of code that said `datetime.utcnow().strftime("%F-%T")`. I ran into the linter error that points at this docs section: http://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contributing/code-style.html#naive-datetime-objects

I then spent about 10 minutes searching through documentation to satisfy myself that the thing that recommends, which is `timezone_now` aka `django.utils.timezone.now`, would do what I wanted: to definitely always give something in UTC when I called its `strftime` method, rather than attempt to do something with a timezone, as the name suggests.

I'd like to make this clearer -- after all, the point of that lint rule is to try to make it easy to predict how our time functions will behave. I think calling the helper `utcnow` instead of `timezone_now` would basically do it. That seems a lot closer to what it actually does -- plus it matches `datetime.datetime.utcnow`, which experienced Python programmers may be accustomed to reaching for (certainly I am.)

@Rishi Gupta , does that rationale make sense to you?

**Greg Price** · 2017-11-30 01:21 UTC

> we don't ever want `from datetime import utcnow` in the codebase.

This actually isn't an issue -- `utcnow` is a class (or static?) method on the type `datetime`, which is in the module `datetime`. So you can only import as deep as `datetime.datetime`, and then you have to call it as `datetime.utcnow()`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-30 01:23 UTC

That makes sense to me.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-11-30 01:29 UTC

That logic does make sense. How about utc_now instead of utcnow? My main association with utcnow is that it is timezone-naive, and so I should be wary everytime I reach for it :).

**Tim Abbott** · 2017-11-30 01:42 UTC

I suppose we could also go with something verbose like `utcnow_tzaware`.

**Greg Price** · 2017-11-30 02:23 UTC

Hmm, my main association is that it is actually in UTC. :-)

**Greg Price** · 2017-11-30 02:24 UTC

I don't think I actually understand the underlying pitfall that motivates this lint rule. If a datetime object is "timezone-naive" but it is in fact in UTC, what goes wrong?

**Rishi Gupta** · 2017-11-30 03:10 UTC

The issue is if you pass it to something that by default interprets things in localtime (the timezone of the server).

E.g. I don't know what postgres does by default, but let's say you tell postgres that something happened at "9:00" on a certain day, without an associated timezone. A priori, it's hard to be sure that postgres will interpret that as 9:00 utc, rather than 9:00 localtime.

**Umair Khan** · 2017-11-30 04:40 UTC

@Greg Price, it seems that you can convert a timezone aware object easily to another timezone:

In [27]: naive = datetime.utcnow()

In [29]: karachi = pytz.timezone('Asia/Karachi')

In [30]: naive.astimezone(karachi)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
<ipython-input-30-8faa311a3720> in <module>()
----> 1 naive.astimezone(karachi)

ValueError: astimezone() cannot be applied to a naive datetime

In [31]: tz_aware.astimezone(karachi)

While working on adding strict-optional support to run-mypy, I was exploring the following change based on new python3 syntax that I remember @Greg Price mentioned recently; does this seem reasonable?
https://github.com/neiljp/zulip/commit/8f94f898f20230af283c09cfca7ce7461c814fb0

This only requires one change outside of the REQ code, and ensures parameter use is clear beyond the (optional) first (re-)name.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2017-12-24 06:05 UTC

Hi all. So I have been working on this feature which will enable scheduled messages / reminders in Zulip. I have created a [wip] PR #7967 which has my ongoing work in it. Please take a look and comment on what people think so far.

Rough roadmap on this beyond this point:

* Write some tests for the currently implemented backend aspect of feature.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-01-02 14:59 UTC

What I am most concerned about right now is extracting out date and time from the message. 
For the initial version I have been implementing this format for setting up reminders. 
`/remind <date and time> <message>`

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-01-02 15:07 UTC

What I have been thinking is striping out the `/remind` from the entire message and then splitting the message on *spaces* and then running dateparser lib's parse function repetitively on a message formed from joining components from the list of words after splitting. 
for example: Say we have this string `/remind 2nd jan at 2pm to start and lead backend meeting`
We strip out the '/remind' and get `2nd jan at 2pm to start and lead backend meeting`
Now we split it on spaces and get `['2nd', 'jan', 'at', '2pm', 'to', 'start', 'and', 'lead', 'backend', 'meeting']`
Now we repetitively take out elements from the above list and keep appending to a space separated string and feed it to the parse function. We continue this until we get two consecutive empty string response from the parse function (we can also have other forms of breakout).
The last date recognised is our date.
What do people think about this. I believe we might at max run parse 10 times per scheduling request.

The raw dictionaries are easier to manipulate, but then the unread messages result is nicer to go over the wire and matches what the mobile folks wanted the data to look at.  Think of `RawUnreadMessagesResult` as an intermediate result.

**Tarun Kumar** · 2018-01-16 14:40 UTC

@Steve Howell one more doubt, the stream_dict contains all the stream messages irrespective of whether the stream or topics in those streams are muted or not, right?
Also (Assuming above is true), for 'muting users implementation' the way I thought (see below in the fucntion) is to exclude the sender_id which matches one of those in the MutedUser table, so that way stream_dict, pm's, huddle_dict, mentions all would not have the messages send by a user who is muted (thereby implicitly assuming that those messages are read) , is this right, or we require to have separate dictionary for muted and unmuted for each of pm's, huddle_dict, mentions as is with stream messages?
In other words, does those stream_dict messages have any use except in testing? (because for unread messages we don't need them) .

```python
def get_raw_unread_data(user_profile: UserProfile) -> RawUnreadMessagesResult:

    excluded_recipient_ids = get_inactive_recipient_ids(user_profile)
	muted_user_ids = return [row for row in get_user_mutes(user_profile)]
	

    user_msgs = UserMessage.objects.filter(
        user_profile=user_profile
    ).exclude(
        message__recipient_id__in=excluded_recipient_ids,
		message__sender_id__in=muted_user_ids
    ).extra(
        where=[UserMessage.where_unread()]
    ).values(
        'message_id',
        'message__sender_id',
        'message__subject',
        'message__recipient_id',
        'message__recipient__type',
        'message__recipient__type_id',
        'flags',
    ).order_by("-message_id")

    # Limit unread messages for performance reasons.
    user_msgs = list(user_msgs[:MAX_UNREAD_MESSAGES])

    rows = list(reversed(user_msgs))

    muted_stream_ids = get_muted_stream_ids(user_profile)

    topic_mute_checker = build_topic_mute_checker(user_profile)

    def is_row_muted(stream_id: int, recipient_id: int, topic: Text) -> bool:
        if stream_id in muted_stream_ids:
            return True

        if topic_mute_checker(recipient_id, topic):
            return True

        return False

    huddle_cache = {}  # type: Dict[int, str]

    def get_huddle_users(recipient_id: int) -> str:
        if recipient_id in huddle_cache:
            return huddle_cache[recipient_id]

        user_ids_string = huddle_users(recipient_id)
        huddle_cache[recipient_id] = user_ids_string
        return user_ids_string

    pm_dict = {}
    stream_dict = {}
    unmuted_stream_msgs = set()
    huddle_dict = {}
    mentions = set()

    for row in rows:
        message_id = row['message_id']
        msg_type = row['message__recipient__type']
        recipient_id = row['message__recipient_id']
        sender_id = row['message__sender_id']

        if msg_type == Recipient.STREAM:
            stream_id = row['message__recipient__type_id']
            topic = row['message__subject']
            stream_dict[message_id] = dict(
                stream_id=stream_id,
                topic=topic,
                sender_id=sender_id,
            )
            if not is_row_muted(stream_id, recipient_id, topic):
                unmuted_stream_msgs.add(message_id)

        elif msg_type == Recipient.PERSONAL:
            pm_dict[message_id] = dict(
                sender_id=sender_id,
            )

        elif msg_type == Recipient.HUDDLE:
            user_ids_string = get_huddle_users(recipient_id)
            huddle_dict[message_id] = dict(
                user_ids_string=user_ids_string,
            )

        is_mentioned = (row['flags'] & UserMessage.flags.mentioned) != 0
        if is_mentioned:
            mentions.add(message_id)

    return dict(
        pm_dict=pm_dict,
        stream_dict=stream_dict,
        muted_stream_ids=muted_stream_ids,
        unmuted_stream_msgs=unmuted_stream_msgs,
        huddle_dict=huddle_dict,
        mentions=mentions,
)
```

One major headache here is that we don't actually use the server data here yet on our main client.  It's only used by the mobile client.  (For our main client, the client does all the logic to compute counts.)

The reason for this is that we had some edge cases for users who have ancient messages that are unread, due to having muted streams that go way back in time.

In some ways just immediately marking PMs as read is a lot easier to implement, and it might actually work better for users.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-16 15:32 UTC

We might want @Rishi Gupta to weigh in on this.  I can think of a couple decisions that can affect what we do for V1?

* Do we even care about streams?  (For V1 I am largely inclined to say no, since my experience as a user tells me that people who PM-spam me are generally well-meaning users who don't really annoy me by spamming streams, since there's usually other traffic there anyway that needs my attention.  And bad actors just get deactivated.)
* What should happen when I unmute a user?  (If I just temporarily blocked a user, then unmute them, do I really care about catching up on messages that were sent during the interim?  I would say no.  And it's not like I couldn't scroll back if I were really fearful that I missed out on something.  Or I'd just ask the other person, which is easier to do than on a stream.)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-16 15:35 UTC

If @Rishi Gupta were to agree with the above, then the simple V1 implementation would be to just immediately mark any incoming PM from a muted user as "read."  (I'd even exclude huddles from the V1, since it's plausible I'll have a 3-way conversation with a muted user and an admin or another person who's trying to coach them on etiquette or warn them about deactivation.)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-16 15:39 UTC

I guess the other thing for V1, or maybe V1.1, is that if you're in the `is:private` view, we want to keep that user's messages out of the view.   I don't consider that super pressing, since most of the time people narrow to a specific PM conversation.

## global-public streams

*2018-01-18 to 2018-02-05 · 156 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/global-public.20streams/with/453920)*

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-18 15:31 UTC

@Aditya Bansal and I have been discussing global-public streams, which are a proposed feature that's similar in nature to IRC archive/log sites.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-18 15:32 UTC

Basically, orgs can make a stream be global-public, and we would publish Zulip conversations for that stream to the web, and you, whether "you" are a human or web crawler, would not need a login to view the content.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-18 15:34 UTC

This has a couple benefits:
* we would get SEO hits for the content that direct people to Zulip (every page would have some kind of call-to-action to sign up for Zulip)
* orgs could publish their content to folks who don't desire to sign up for a full account

And then there are probably other benefits as well.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-18 15:37 UTC

We probably want to focus on some minimally viable prototype that we can launch fairly quickly.  To me the most important piece to get merged right away is some kind of DB model change/addition that says that a stream is global-public, and we probably want a min message id from which you can start considering messages to be global-public.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-18 15:38 UTC

(The reason I think a min message id is important is that we'll want to globally publish some czo content, but it would be too much of a legal pain to get retroactive consent.  And it shouldn't be that hard to implement a min message id.)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-18 15:39 UTC

One thing we **don't** need right away is any kind of settings-related UI.  Our very earliest experiment could be done by just manually setting the DB data.  And maybe we'd publish some content from the playground site first.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-18 15:43 UTC

I think we want to start solving problems in roughly this order:
* db model
* deal with emails being part of mentions (which maybe could be parallelized)
* create/modify API endpoints to allow getting public data for streams
* plunk data to HTML pages
* make pages link to Zulip sign-up
* figure out SEO issues
* figure out settings UI and automatic user-consents-to-publish legal stuff

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-18 15:43 UTC

@Aditya Bansal thoughts so far?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-18 15:45 UTC

BTW I definitely want the end goal of this conversation to be some kind of prioritized list, but we should feel free to discuss far-in-the-future nuances too, just to have the big picture in mind.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-18 15:47 UTC

It's not an implementation priority to get user consent-to-publish, but we'll need a mechanism for that before we do any kind of public release of this feature.  So when users join a global-public stream (or send their first message), we'll probably force them to accept that their content is global-public.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-18 15:49 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-18 15:51 UTC

For both the UI piece and the SEO piece, I think having some kind of starting implementation will move the discussion forward a lot, but I do have some thoughts before then.

* compose boxes
* buddy lists
* interleaved views
* Private messages

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-22 14:49 UTC

**date picker**

One of the challenges with a date picker interface is localization.  If I want all the messages for Jan 25th, that's going to produce a different page than if Aditya wants all the messages for Jan 25th.  So from an SEO standpoint that means the crawler has to follow every major timezone, which dilutes the values of each individual page.

Of course, I can see the argument that human usability trumps all of the time-zone complications; I'm just pointing out there are some serious tradeoffs.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-22 14:53 UTC

**near vs. at**

I am 99% sure the nomenclature of using "near" when you link to a message is exactly what @Aditya Bansal said.  It's just our way of indicating that you'll also see nearby messages.

My opinion is that for archives, we want "at" more than "near".  Being able to link to one specific message, without clutter, has benefits, I think, and then the "at" page would link to a page that "broadens" the narrow.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-22 14:55 UTC

**floating recipient bars**

I don't think floating recipient bars go completely away in an archived view.  I view them as mostly unnecessary in a topic-only view.  If we support interleaved views, they may become more like headings (no need to float).

* JS on client side will do AJAX and populated the left side bar.

Benefits of doing it this way rather than sending it as a page_params property as the actual web app does:
* If we have a bot visiting us and hitting us again and again we won't be doing db operations to collect all global public streams again and again. If the page actually is loaded and run using a browser or JS is rendered then only the streams would be fetched.
* We will eventually move to a world where clicking a topic won't reload the entire page and it would be therefore better just do a AJAX one time and sit tight.
Main advantage is we are basically saving db operation in case of bots hitting us to index. 

Just logging here what's on my mind :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-25 00:36 UTC

@cPhost OK, so here's the explanation:
(1) When we build releases, we use `tools/build-release-tarball`, which does a fresh clone of the repo and thus by construction cannot have older files.  That's not the case we're worried about here.  Those release get unpacked in production to `/home/zulip/prod-static/`, by just adding new files (the old ones hang around so they are available to older clients).
(2) Second, we run `update-prod-static` (and thus build webpack) in `scripts/upgrade-zulip-from-git`.  In that environment, it installs the new files directly under `/home/zulip/prod-static`; in that case, we don't want to delete the files from previous installations (again so they are available to older clients).

## finding event clients

*2018-01-24 to 2018-01-24 · 23 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/finding.20event.20clients/with/464488)*

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-24 19:32 UTC

@Tim Abbott, as we have mentioned elsewhere, in the future we will have occasions where we want to find out which bots are connected:
* need to tell users which bots are up
* prevent bots from running simultaneously
* shut down deactivated bots

Conceptually, we can find everything we need in the `clients` structure of `tornado/event_queue.py`.  But we're running into some confusion about accessing that data in Django, related to multiple processes.  Is it the case that Django code should never import `event_queue.py`?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:35 UTC

The current design is such that Django cannot have direct access to that sort of Tornado data since it is in-process data, and it would be very perf-expensive to provide it (part of the reason I've been pushing back against this).

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:35 UTC

I'm sure there's a way to work around that by getting data indirectly, let me think.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:35 UTC

One related feature we have is something that reports whether a zephyr_mirror service (for mirroring PMs) is running for a given user

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:36 UTC

That is handled via querying the UserActivity table (we show a visual alert if it's been >5min since the last time the user checked in)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:36 UTC

I think we handle that via the presence endpoints, though.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:37 UTC

(So to answer your direct question, Django importing data structures under `tornado/` is expected to be useless, since it's the wrong process)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:37 UTC

I think the UserActivity approach will be too slow of an update for your use case.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:38 UTC

The second thing we could do is when a bot does an `events_register` API request, that DOES connect to Tornado (to get the event queue created).  We could probably have some sort of unique key associated with an event queue (e.g. (realm_id, bot_name)), and have something special happen if you try to add a second bot with those parameters (either it shuts down the old one, or fails)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:39 UTC

We'd need to add a new dict to ensure O(1) access (everything in Tornado is ~required to be O(1)), but otherwise that implementation seems like it'd be pretty cheap

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:40 UTC

Shutting down deactivated bots should be handled automatically by the UserProfile object being deactivated (auth requests to Tornado will start failing)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-24 19:41 UTC

Are there ways to persist stuff out of Tornado?  Like is it allowed to hit redis?  (not suggesting we do this right away, asking out of curiosity now)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:41 UTC

For telling users which bots are up, I think we'd want to use a standard Events System approach (similar to typing notifications, where we send an event when a bot is activated/deactivated, and the initial state can be fetched in the `events_register` call when we're talking to Tornado anyway)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:42 UTC

Feels like something I'd want to be very careful about reviewing (Tornado doesn't have great unit tests), but that doesn't have anything super complex in it, so probably doable.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-24 19:42 UTC

Can you elaborate on the typing notifications?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:42 UTC

Ignore the timeouts part of typing: I just mean something where there is no state stored in the database.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-24 19:43 UTC

yeah, I just mean the simple part of how does Tornado know all the current typing notifictions during `events_register`?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:44 UTC

> Are there ways to persist stuff out of Tornado? Like is it allowed to hit redis? (not suggesting we do this right away, asking out of curiosity now)

Structurally, Tornado currently does queries to memcached(backed by DB) for auth, which is something that we'll want to remove long-term, and redis (for rate-limiting; which we also probably want to remove eventually).  But our setup doesn't have a way to do queries to network services from Tornado asynchronously (well, in particular, Django doesn't support that, and we do those network queries via Django today to avoid lots of duplicate sensitive code).  So major work could be done to add asynchronous database query support, but our overall goal is to have Tornado not need to talk to the database or other network services.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:45 UTC

Right, so for typing notifications, we just initialize to "nobody is typing" and let the every-n-seconds retransmit fill in the state.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-01-24 19:46 UTC

For this, we'd get the initial state from Tornado in `events_register`.  Maybe typing was a bad analogy; replace "typing notifications" with "like any other feature where we update clients dynamically using `send_event` and Tornado)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-24 19:48 UTC

Ah, so the complication there is that bots would need to keep sending keep-alive reports.  (So it would be a lot more similar to the human presence system, but kinda annoying for bots since bots don't walk away from their browser to get coffee, so it would be nice to just base everything off the existence of their queue).

We could probably have some sort of unique key associated with an event queue (e.g. (realm_id, bot_name)), and have something special happen if you try to …

@Robert Hönig and I are going to pursue this strategy and test it out on playground.  (We know that getting this merged may be difficult, but our exit strategy can be to at least document the overall approach.)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-01-24 20:41 UTC

* `bot_ids = lambda realm_id: {bot_id for bot_id, queue_id in active_bots[realm_id]}`

**Rein Zustand** · 2018-01-25 17:13 UTC

There are only 2 occurrences of `logging.critical` in the codebase:
```
$ ag logging.critical
tools/lib/provision.py
93:    logging.critical("Only x86 is supported;"
103:    logging.critical("Unsupported platform: {} {}".format(vendor, codename))
```
introduced in this commit, https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/75d0146d33372a50955aa9818147c7a28778149b, both has `sys.exit(1)` following them. The rest of `sys.exit(1)` error messages use `print`. **Rein Zustand** · 2018-01-25 17:21 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2018-01-26 01:42 UTC

@Rein Zustand In provision, we should just use `print` -- it's output going straight to the user (aka developer), and there's nothing to be gained from adding a bunch of fuss like timestamps and the word CRITICAL.

**Rein Zustand** · 2018-01-26 09:08 UTC

I see. I saw several `logging.error` being used in `tools` and `scripts` as well. Replacing them with `print`.

**Rein Zustand** · 2018-01-26 09:35 UTC

I actually found a case where `logging` is required. https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/tools/lint#L111-L114 for switching between verbosity level easily.

**Rein Zustand** · 2018-01-26 09:38 UTC

So I am proceeding with the policy that `logging` should be replaced with `print` except in places where there are verbosity flags.

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-08 21:30 UTC

@Aditya Bansal Moving here

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-08 21:31 UTC

Puppet is a great place to put conditionals on the OS release. How does that nginx config file change between the status quo and your change?

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-08 21:32 UTC

For detecting platform, grep for `xenial` for examples :)

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-02-08 21:32 UTC

so basically currently Nginx serves files directly

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-02-08 21:32 UTC

using the 
```
location /user_uploads {
        add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff;
        include /etc/nginx/zulip-include/uploads.types;
        alias /home/zulip/uploads/files;
    }
```
route.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-02-08 21:34 UTC

We want to have authentication on serving files but don't actually want django to serve files. So we want nginx to do the heavy lifting of serving files.
If we want authentication we need request to reach Django which essentially means removal of this route

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-02-08 21:35 UTC

but nginx below 1.5.9 doesn't expect quoted url's in internal redirects so doesn't unquote them so basically starts looking for wrong file paths and hence isn't supported in a unicode world

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-02-08 21:36 UTC

So hiding this route in Nginx behind OS flag will essentially make requests on Xenial installs reach Django and get authenticated

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-08 21:39 UTC

What does the Nginx config look like with your change?

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-02-08 21:40 UTC

```
location /serve_uploads {
        internal;
        add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff;
        include /etc/nginx/zulip-include/uploads.types;
        alias /home/zulip/uploads/files;
    }
```

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-02-08 21:40 UTC

basically we change the route and use Django sendfile to redirect requests internally to Nginx

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-02-08 21:42 UTC

in the updated PR we will have something like 

```puppet
if $zulip::base::release_name == "trusty" {
    location /user_uploads {
        add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff;
        include /etc/nginx/zulip-include/uploads.types;
        alias /home/zulip/uploads/files;
    }
  }

location /serve_uploads {
        internal;
        add_header X-Content-Type-Options nosniff;
        include /etc/nginx/zulip-include/uploads.types;
        alias /home/zulip/uploads/files;
    }
```

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-08 22:03 UTC

@Aditya Bansal Here's my suggested solution: use the `include` feature in the Nginx config file, to get the uploads bit of the config from elsewhere. Then have Puppet do a conditional to decide what file to put there to be included.

Specifically, I suggest in `.../nginx/sites-available/zulip-enterprise`:
```
    include /etc/nginx/zulip-include/uploads.*
```

Then have a file like `.../nginx/zulip-include-maybe/uploads.direct` that has the `/user_uploads` fragment, and `.../nginx/zulip-include-maybe/uploads.internal` that has the `/serve_uploads` fragment.

And in Puppet, have a conditional decide which of those two files to put into `/etc/nginx/zulip-include/`.

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-08 22:05 UTC

An alternative solution would be to just call the file a constant path `/etc/nginx/zulip-include/uploads`, and have Puppet decide which of two versions to copy to that same path. But that seems a little trickier to debug if something goes wrong in production for someone, so I'm inclined to the approach with two different filenames for the two cases.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-02-08 22:06 UTC

ohk, I will go with the first approach then. Thanks for the help.

**Sean Wallitsch** · 2018-02-08 22:07 UTC

Thank you both

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-21 02:26 UTC

Yeah. I think actually if you're interested in tackling this, the route I'd suggest is
* Try switching to rapidjson, on the most critical path (events, I think), and show that working and still being fast.
* Once that's done, just switch everything that's ujson to rapidjson en masse -- and if the tests pass, basically assume it's good. Maybe have a trivial wrapper like `zerver/lib/json.py` so we can just `from zerver.lib import json` everywhere, and never have to make a mass change like this again :)

## email queues on upgrade

*2018-02-28 to 2018-02-28 · 19 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/email.20queues.20on.20upgrade/with/519577)*

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-28 00:31 UTC

@Umair Khan @Tim Abbott Can you explain the thinking in commit c8f034e9a ?

The code that commit deletes was there for a reason -- as the comment on it explains, when a server is upgraded that code is what causes us to not just drop some messages on the floor. We can delete it after 1.8 is released, when we can tell people to upgrade to 1.8 first before upgrading further.

**Umair Khan** · 2018-02-28 03:46 UTC

@Greg Price  My mistake. I thought the upgrade code has already made into the previous release. Yeah, this commit should probably go in 1.8.1.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-02-28 16:14 UTC

It's a queue that's structurally ~always empty, and so the probability that anyone actually loses a single email notification with doing this migration in a single release  is low (especially since folks with busy sites tend to do upgrades at off times).  At the same time, many sites skip releases, so we'd still have about the same risk of losing an email notification unless we keep the migration compatibility code for like a year.  So it seemed worth just getting the migration done.  If we wanted to keep the code around forever, it would have been a mistake to open an issue for something that can't be worked on for a year (the comment in the code will do fine for a year-from-now cleanup).

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-02-28 16:38 UTC

I'm happy to be corrected if I'm missing something here though!

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-28 18:41 UTC

Low, perhaps, but not zero -- and by keeping this very small bit of code, we can make it structurally actually zero if the admins follow a pretty reasonable path that is very easy for us to recommend. You don't upgrade Debian across two releases at once if you don't want things to break, and you don't need to upgrade Zulip that way either.

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-28 18:47 UTC

I don't know what issue you're referring to (or is that a hypothetical?). I agree the comment in the code should do fine for a cleanup in the future -- preferably either at the time it says, which is sometime soon after 1.8, or else edit it to say a year from now or whatever if we decide to prefer that.

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-28 18:48 UTC

That is in fact precisely the purpose the comment in the code is there for :smiley:

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-28 19:11 UTC

OK, it looks like this got merged when it did basically due to a communication failure between me and Tim. (I just tracked this commit down to #8282.) I think the ri

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-28 19:12 UTC

err - sorry, new keyboard, more message coming :)

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-28 19:15 UTC

I think the right response is generally to undo the effect of the miscommunication promptly, so I'm going to go revert the commit now. (Then go deploy czo.) Happy to discuss more whether to remove this code after all, if you think that would be preferable.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-02-28 20:23 UTC

@Greg Price I was thinking about this problem on the way to jury duty.  I think a better approach for handling this sort of migration in the future would probably be to write a "database migration" that drains the old queue and just moves the items into the new queue.  That would happen atomically as part of the upgrade process, and would not require us to either leave around this code or require our administrators to follow a particular upgrade process in relation to this issue.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-02-28 20:25 UTC

I haven't looked into specifically how much code such a migration would be, but it seems like probably the right approach in the long term for handling changes in the format of events going into/out of our queue processors (which in general is not something that we have been careful about in past releases)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-02-28 20:25 UTC

The other approach to consider is running a job after we shut down the server to clear out all the queues from the order release before starting the new release; that would potentially be a more generic approach that doesn't require work on a given release..

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-28 20:27 UTC

Yeah, this will certainly be something we think about solutions to in the future. The problem is basically a form of database migration; the way it's handled in this case is basically the way we need to handle an incompatible migration when avoiding downtime.

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-28 20:31 UTC

That is, if you have a migration where the new schema is incompatible with the old code, and you want the new and old code (across each successive deploy) to be running simultaneously, you have to first deploy a version of the code that is compatible with both the new and old schema.

Normally, for upgrades for most admins, we've resolved this by just taking downtime so new and old code don't run at the same time.

But here, the meaning of "simultaneous" is different because it's a persistent queue -- even if you shut everything down, then start it all up with the new code, you may have effective simultaneity because the new code receives an event from the old.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-02-28 20:34 UTC

I'm not tracking to main part of this conversation, but just to give some additional context, we have needs for a more sophisticated migration process for things like building concurrent indexes, where limitations of Django provide interesting complications.  So there might be multiple benefits if we invest in some sort of of generic migration meta-layer.

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-28 20:34 UTC

In general we could handle these with either style, depending on what is easier. In a future where we make our releases non-disruptive, we'll need to handle incompatible migrations for the actual DB by making successive deploys anyway, and doing the same here can probably just piggyback on a system for handling that. Also in that future we won't be able to use the "migrate during downtime" solution anyway.

Prior to that future: this was a pretty easy solution, but a synchronous "database" migration might be easy too.

**Greg Price** · 2018-02-28 20:35 UTC

Aha, Steve and I were thinking similar thoughts. :)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-02-28 20:35 UTC

It would certainly be a non-trivial project, but conceptually it's just a graph. :smile:

**Greg Price** · 2021-04-30 00:28 UTC

Clever repro!

**Greg Price** · 2021-04-30 00:32 UTC

Yeah, I think this is just a case where the early authors of the mobile app should have done more copying the webapp code and less trying to reverse-engineer things. (At the time there weren't anything like the API docs we have now, so those were really the only two options.) Our logic for the unreads data structure looks like this, for the streams part of it:
```js
    case EVENT_NEW_MESSAGE: {
      const { message } = action;
      if (message.type !== 'stream') {
        return state;
      }

      if (message.sender_id === getOwnUserId(globalState)) {
        return state;
      }

      // prettier-ignore
      return state.updateIn([message.stream_id, message.subject],
        (perTopic = Immutable.List()) => perTopic.push(message.id));
    }
```

and it's essentially the same for PMs, just with a different underlying data structure in the last couple of lines.

IOW it's assuming that a new message is always unread unless you sent it yourself. Which I guess is very nearly true today, and becomes notably not true with muted users.

## incompatible migrations

*2018-03-10 to 2018-03-10 · 35 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/incompatible.20migrations/with/533093)*

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-10 02:23 UTC

Commit 777b6de68, merged today from #7978, contains a migration with the property that if you do the migration while the old code is still running anywhere, the code will break. (It removes a column.)

This means that if you want to deploy it without taking the server down for maintenance, you have to do a complex operational dance.

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-10 02:26 UTC

We have the expertise to do that dance when deploying zulipchat.com. But I would really like to get out of the habit of routinely having to do it -- it significantly increases the work required to deploy new code to the service; and because it requires careful human attention, it also makes it very difficult to add automation to the deploy process, so that it's less work, less risk, and can be done more frequently.

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-10 02:31 UTC

There's a spectrum of how high-tech a solution to this problem area can be. We don't have the resources to do something super high-tech in the near term. But I think there is a standard we can very reasonably hold ourselves to which would be a significant improvement.

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-10 02:35 UTC

The baseline, straightforward way to upgrade Zulip is to take some new commit, run all the migrations up to that point, then restart Zulip server processes into the new code.

Sometimes this won't be enough, because we'll want to do incompatible migrations like this one. But an upgrade process we can deliver is:
* Deploy some intermediate commit just like above, completely. Possibly repeat through a sequence of intermediate commits. Then deploy the final new commit the same way.
* The app does not fall over at any point.

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-10 02:38 UTC

In this example, we created a new column, and migrated some data there; then deleted an old column. The commit actually already has two separate migrations, one for creating and populating the new column and another for deleting the old. This is almost what we need!

What would suffice in this example would be
* First, a commit contains that first migration and also the code changes to stop using the old field.
* Then, a separate commit contains the second migration, deleting the old field.

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-10 02:39 UTC

Then when upgrading past those changes, it's enough to first deploy that first commit; then deploy the desired later new commit.

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-10 02:41 UTC

So when writing or merging that code, it'd be a very easy tweak to get it to meet this standard.

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-10 02:41 UTC

@Tim Abbott What do you think of that plan? Can I persuade you to try to hold migrations that you merge to this standard?

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-10 02:42 UTC

The main way this is less awesome than a super high-tech solution is that there is still a race: if someone actually *writes* to the data in question through the old code after the migration has happened, their writes will be lost, because they're writing to the old column.

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-10 02:43 UTC

To solve that problem without downtime would require some more machinery, to write any changes into two places during the transition.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-10 02:45 UTC

I guess I have mixed feeling on this.  I of agree with the technical observations about what's required on the upgrade process front to make this easy on the deployment side.  And I think I agree that it's about as much total work to do the 2-stage migration in the commits originally as it is to do the fixup later for zulipchat.com (for example).

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-10 02:46 UTC

That said, one of the challenges that I have to manage when merging things is the cost of constantly renumbering migrations and repeatedly re-reading the same code for a PR before merging it.  So, I think we might want to think through what's required to split such a commit just before merging, and think about whether there's tooling that can help here.

## catching up

*2018-03-12 to 2018-05-02 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/catching.20up/with/535755)*

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-12 13:01 UTC

@Tim Abbott I found another thing that's kind of ugly when you're far behind on messages.  If you try to send a local echo message, the message event gets queued, so ~5 seconds later the echo code detects a "broken" event loop and restarts the event loop.  I think the most obvious remedy here is to just wait till `server_events.home_view_loaded` gets called to turn on local echo.  (You can simulate slow catchup by settings `message_fetch.consts.catch_up_back_size` to a really small value like `10`.)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-12 13:07 UTC

A related issue with echo is that when you're in a specific narrow (e.g. topic narrow), you want to suppress echo if you know you're behind on that narrow.  That's conceptually easy enough, but we don't want to overfix this and have local echo basically not work every time you go to a new narrow.  So this would motivate the need for narrow's initial message fetch to accurately report that it's complete.  (You'll recall that I had a commit that I abandoned where I was checking whether the initial fetch was complete.  That was for an optimization where a "maybe" situation was ok, whereas the echo case needs a more precise answer.)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-12 13:13 UTC

So I'm thinking there are a couple todos here:
* suppress all local echo until `home_view_loaded` (to prevent the event loop restart)
* do the backend work to identify that backend fetches are "forward complete"
* make a reliable `fetch_status.has_newest()` function available on the client (which includes looking at the initial fetch)
* suppress echo if `!current_msg_list.fetch_status.has_newest()`

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-12 15:30 UTC

@Steve Howell that all sounds good to me, thanks for figuring that out :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-12 15:31 UTC

I think for local echo, we probably technically echo in all message lists, so that last line might be "for each msg list"

## num_extra_messages

*2018-03-13 to 2018-03-13 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/num_extra_messages/with/537617)*

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-13 11:44 UTC

@Tim Abbott The code below seems flawed to me.  If I specify num_before=3 and num_after=3 and anchor=100, I reasonably expect 7 results (97, 98, 99, **100**, 101, 102, 103), and the code below does the job for the non-narrow case.  What seems specious to me is the whole business about "if the narrow was specificied, the anchor message might not match the narrow anyway".  Yeah, but what if it does?  I still want 7 rows.  And let's say the narrow is `is:odd_number`, is it a terrible thing if the query produces 
(95, 97, 99, 101, 103, 107, **109**)? 

~~~
 633     # We add 1 to the number of messages requested if no narrow was
 634     # specified to ensure that the resulting list always contains the
 635     # anchor message.  If a narrow was specified, the anchor message
 636     # might not match the narrow anyway.
 637     if num_after > 0:
 638         num_after += num_extra_messages
 639     else:
 640         num_before += num_extra_messages
~~~

FWIW just so you realize I'm not being completely nitpicky here...I need the semantics here to be somewhat simple/precise to detect when I've gotten all results.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-13 17:44 UTC

@Steve Howell interesting.  I think what I think the ideal behavior is to match what the protocol advertises:
* The result should have exactly 3 messages before and 3 messages after the anchor, and potentially also the anchor itself if it matches the query (I don't think one should get 7 rows in your `is:odd_number` case, because that's not what the variable names we provide suggest).  
* If the anchor message matches the narrow, it's possible we should be doing the +1 thing and then doing some sort of post-processing step where we potentially drop an extra message at the end to ensure that the number before/after returned is exactly what was requested (no off-by-one errors).
* For the purposes of what you're building, I think the correct way to analyze is to just inspect the message IDs on the results we're sending to the user, and if the number of messages before the anchor is less than `num_before`, report `reached_beginning` (or whatever that variable is called).  That algorithm should be able to correctly report the answer, independent of the issue we're discussing here.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-13 17:50 UTC

Just to be clear, we're already breaking the `num_after` contract for the `is:even_number` case, and we're giving them **less** data than they asked for (which can mislead a client into thinking it has all the data).  I assume mobile isn't doing anything tricky with num_after/num_before yet?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-13 17:53 UTC

Yes, I agree with your assessment.  I think mobile will be excited to switch to using the new "reached_beginning" type flags once that's possible (and probably `zulip-terminal` as well), so hopefully we can get it in for the 1.8 release.

I'm just noting that if we provide this new reporting, the impact of giving the wrong number of messages drops dramatically, since the off-by-one error is less likely to cascade to other bugs.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-03-13 17:55 UTC

Ok, sounds good.  BTW I intend to do dumb O(N) sweeps to calculate reached-beginning and reached-end, even though you can technically do it in O(1) time.  (I tried the O(1) way and it is difficult to read.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-13 18:17 UTC

Yeah, that's fine -- we're writing these things out over the network, which is O(n) anyway.

## database migrations

*2018-03-21 to 2018-06-16 · 56 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/database.20migrations/with/545559)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-21 04:53 UTC

I just merged b94a24ffe3400de5e2d2d8cce96a395754fbaa6c, which fixes an unfortunate bug in one of our recently merged database migrations.  While probably chat.zulip.org is the only victim of this bug, we were close to not catching this before the release, and I think we should think about whether there's any tooling changes we can make for our database migrations (e.g. investigating a unit test system for them, if there's a good third-party Django thing for doing that?) to prevent this sort of thing in the future.

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-21 23:20 UTC

Yikes :-( -- glad you caught that!

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-21 23:21 UTC

Looks like the impact of this one wouldn't have been catastrophic if deployed more widely before the fix, but definitely not cool.

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-21 23:24 UTC

The issue here was in some custom code we wrote to run in this migration. I think the most valuable thing we could do to prevent similar issues is: when we write a migration function like this, pull the guts of it out into something that we can then thoroughly unit-test.

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-21 23:25 UTC

The low-tech version of that, which doesn't require any special support for testing a migration, would be to pull the central logic out into a function that doesn't refer to any migration infrastructure -- and then write a real unit test for that.

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-21 23:28 UTC

Here, I think that would look something like
```
def migrate(apps: StateApps, schema_editor: DatabaseSchemaEditor) -> None:
    Reaction = apps.get_model('zerver', 'Reaction')
    RealmEmoji = apps.get_model('zerver', 'RealmEmoji')
    migrate_models(Reaction, RealmEmoji)

def migrate_models(Reaction, RealmEmoji) -> None:
    ...  # the rest of the body of that function
```

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-21 23:29 UTC

IOW, just break the migration function after those `apps.get_model` lines and call the rest as a helper subroutine.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-21 23:29 UTC

Yeah, that's probably right.  I'm curious how easy Django makes it to actually write such a unit test.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-21 23:29 UTC

Might be worth writing a super trivial test for this migration using that model in a new `test_migrations.py` file, and just see if we can get it to work.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-21 23:30 UTC

@Aditya Bansal would you be interested in working on that?

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-21 23:30 UTC

(I read this migration function before it was deployed, too! I even fixed an unrelated, and less serious, bug in it...)

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-21 23:30 UTC

Yeah, that'd be good -- it'd give us practice, and also would help ensure there isn't another bug lurking in this one. :wink:

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-03-21 23:39 UTC

Hmm, I'm not sure that plan for doing a test would actually be writeable without basically mocking the model classes; the whole issue here is that the database models have a different format before and after the change.

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-03-21 23:40 UTC

how costly is taking DB snapshots. I mean something like restore points between migrations?

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-21 23:42 UTC

> the whole issue here is that the database models have a different format before and after the change.

We're treating them with different semantics, but the models themselves don't change -- that's why this is in custom code of ours, rather than a built-in migration primitive.

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-21 23:46 UTC

In this case there isn't an accompanying change to the underlying schema, so the test should be possible to run either before or after the migration is applied (probably after is what we'd actually do.)

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-21 23:47 UTC

In other cases, there may be schema changes too. For those cases, one thing we could do is split the migration into several commits. The naive approach gets a bit awkward, in that the tests will stop working in later commits if there's a schema change that breaks them (e.g. drops a column we were migrating off of.)

That won't be trivial to solve but I think should be solvable. Because it isn't relevant here -- and because this code would be really good to test :smiley: -- I think it would be valuable to go ahead and write a unit test for this migration without blocking on solving that problem.

**Greg Price** · 2018-03-21 23:48 UTC

## zero 500s goal

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-04-26 21:03 UTC

As Zulip has gotten more popular, we've been starting to see a range of rare 500s (usually sorta operational things like networking errors, but also few bugs in corner case code paths that used to just never be exercised).

So, I did an analysis of all the 500 errors that we get on chat.zulip.org and zulipchat.com, and am in the process of opening issues for all of these with high priority; the hope is that we can just clear these out, and then enjoy being in a state with no known 500 bugs for a long time :)

## performance of /

*2018-05-04 to 2018-05-05 · 26 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/performance.20of.20.2F/with/575334)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-04 20:18 UTC

So, I've noticed that the backend runtime time for `/` on this server are now often over 1s for most users, which is well above what I think is acceptable.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-04 20:18 UTC

So I'm doing a bunch of profiling in a `manage.py shell` on chat.zulip.org to debug why.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-04 20:18 UTC

So far, there's a few things that are basically sloppiness in recently added features (e.g. 300ms was a bug in the custom profile fields query)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-04 20:19 UTC

I'm currently debugging another 60ms (just for admins) related to bot configuration.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-04 20:30 UTC

In retrospect, probably all of these could have been found with something like `populate_db --number-users 5000`

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-05 00:20 UTC

OK, with those changes and the `attachment` fixes I did this afternoon, my personal page load time for `/` is now down to about 1.0s from 1.8s.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-05 00:20 UTC

There's basically only one more significant thing that's easy to fix, which is that we spend at least 500ms fetching and constructing lists of subscriber IDs.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-05 00:21 UTC

This is a place where we're paying a perf penalty per user account in the organization, and with chat.zulip.org now at 8000 registered users, that's getting to be expensive.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-05 00:23 UTC

(My user account is probably about 100ms slower than average, because I'm an org admin and thus more data gets sent down)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-05 00:23 UTC

So I think our next big scalability project we'll need to figure out is what to do with subscriber data as we approach 10K users.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-05 00:32 UTC

What level are we at now with the subscribers?  Are we doing the easy-ish things like avoiding heavy objects and bulking stuff?  Or are we starting to reach scale where we need more exotic remedies?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-05 00:32 UTC

We've already got all the optimizations one can do in Django of doing raw queries, etc.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-05 00:33 UTC

The problem at this point is that we're actually sending like 50K integers, because it's a list of user IDs per-stream.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-05 00:34 UTC

I suppose we could do a clever encoding for "popular" streams (e.g. default streams) to list the non-subscribers instead :)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-05 00:34 UTC

haha

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-05 00:34 UTC

I consider that starting to be in the realm of "exotic."  :smile:

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-05 00:35 UTC

Yeah, exactly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-05 00:35 UTC

I think the next thing to think about is turning that off for large organizations.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-05 00:35 UTC

(Or limiting it to non-`long_term_idle` users)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-05 00:36 UTC

Actually, that one might not be a bad idea; we can just send a `peer_add` event if those users come back

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-05-05 00:37 UTC

So for the uses cases where exact isn't important (e.g. for typeahead sorting), that could be fine

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-05 00:39 UTC

Do you know off hand what percentage of czo is long_term_idle?

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-05-05 00:50 UTC

why do we need to send all the subscribers per stream when we visit '/'. Like if its for the stream settings list only can't we put off the operation until someone actually opens those settings?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-05 01:20 UTC

Typeahead and compose fade use them but might not need every user right away

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-05 01:22 UTC

A good example is mentioning a non subscriber in a stream message

**Steve Howell** · 2018-05-05 02:10 UTC

But, as Tim was saying, for things that aren't super rigorous, we might be able to make compromises.  For example, if compose fade was the only thing we cared about, then we could intersect subscribers with only present users to have a much smaller download.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-05-03 15:31 UTC

I've been investigating the redis flakes on circleci bionic and I think this is the best place to post my findings, as they're related to the issue discussed above.

TLDR: Putting `` sudo sed -i '/^bind/s/bind.*/bind 0.0.0.0/' /etc/redis/redis.conf `` in "do Bionic hack" fixes running redis-server as a service, making it unnecessary to launch a separate instance as a hack (the way it was done so far) - also eliminating the occasional test flake caused by redis dying. Tested with 150+ Bionic runs on my circleci and the flake hasn't happened.

The redis-server instance started in "do Bionic hack" would mysteriously die before the start of the tests sometimes. I wasn't able to figure out why, all I found, when I got lucky and got this to occur on a job launched by "rerun job with SSH" is that there were two dead "redis-server" instances:
```
root@e69a3e9fa7bb:/home/circleci# ps -e | grep red
   69 ?        00:00:00 redis-server <defunct>
 4979 ?        00:00:00 redis-server <defunct>
```
On a "healthy" run, the first process wouldn't be <defunct> (this is the instance started in "do Bionic hack"). The second one is launched by "service redis-server restart" in the "install dependencies" step. It's always defunct, as expected, because that was the original issue. 

I tried to figure out what causes the server instance from Bionic hack to die, but I wasn't able to - I redirected stdout and stderr (when launching it) to a file, and then inserted another step (run before the tests, when this process is <defunct> already in the cases where the flake happens) to print out that file so that I could see it in the circleci report. But that didn't help, the file only had the usual startup messages
```
64:C 21 Mar 11:40:49.873 # oO0OoO0OoO0Oo Redis is starting oO0OoO0OoO0Oo
64:C 21 Mar 11:40:49.873 # Redis version=4.0.9, bits=64, commit=00000000, modified=0, pid=64, just started
64:C 21 Mar 11:40:49.873 # Configuration loaded
```
and no errors reported - yet the process mysteriously died. So I don't know what was going on with this.

Anyway, I decided to try to avoid launching this server instance in "do Bionic hack" and to just fix the standard "service redis-server start" method. This is a relevant issue for the problem: https://github.com/antirez/redis/issues/3241
(since `` Creating Server TCP listening socket ::1:6379: bind: Cannot assign requested address `` is the error when launching the service)
As explained in the comments to the issue, this can be worked around by replacing the line
`` bind 127.0.0.1 ::1 `` with `` bind 0.0.0.0 `` - redis-server won't try to bind on IPv6 thus avoiding the failure. My suggested, simple way of fixing this is by running `` sudo sed -i '/^bind/s/bind.*/bind 0.0.0.0/' /etc/redis/redis.conf `` in "do Bionic hack" to make this change to the default config file loaded when starting the service, right before the service gets restarted in the "install dependencies" step.

I tested this change by doing about 150+ Bionic test runs on my circleci and confirming that the flake doesn't happen. May have gotten very (un)lucky, but this amount gives me reasonable confidence that this fix indeed eliminates the flake.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-05-03 15:33 UTC

Link to PR: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/12256

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-03 18:35 UTC

Awesome investigation @Mateusz Mandera!  It's amazing how many random weird problems like this are caused by IPv6 weirdness on localhost.    (I can think of at least 3 extremely difficult to track down and very annoying Zulip bugs caused by the decision to use both IPv4 and IPv6 in localhost contexts, which in total have consumed at least a couple weeks of my life).

## provision perf

*2018-06-06 to 2018-12-07 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/provision.20perf/with/595841)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-06 20:50 UTC

Hey folks, just wanted to update you that we just merged #9625, which optimizes the common case where you're provisioning just to get a database migration that was just merged into master, which is pretty important, since we're currently going at a rate of about 90 new database migrations per year (crazy, I know!).

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-06 20:50 UTC

So, what you should experience is that if you're provisioning and the only thing that's changed is a new database migration, it'll be really fast.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-06 20:51 UTC

(One still needs to rebuild the database if you switch from a branch with a migration to one without one in development; that's a lot harder of a problem to solve generally, though as the person developing a new feature with a migration, you can do e.g. `manage.py migrate zerver 0172` before switching branches and save a bit of time the next time you provision)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-06 20:54 UTC

There are two remaining major things that we could do to make provision ultra fast, both involving networking:
* Work on eliminating the fact that we're installing a few Python dependencies from GitHub forks.  These are expensive, basically because `pip` isn't smart enough to know that they're the same each time.  One possible solution is to public on pypi packages with names like `zulip-ujson` and `zulip-talon` for our forks.
* Working on doing something like `virtualenv-clone` for our `node_modules` directories.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-18 14:41 UTC

We just merged some more optimizations to provision perf; we're now down to <5s on my laptop.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-18 14:41 UTC

There's some follow-up things we can do to get down to ~3s on that test, which I think are well worth doing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-22 22:06 UTC

Thanks to some more work by @Vishnu Ks, we're now down to 3.2s.  I think with the additional planned efforts, we'll end up landing somewhere between 2s and 3s for the no-op case.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-22 22:07 UTC

I'd love more feedback on the current provision performance experience now that we've done most of the easy optimizations.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-07 22:38 UTC

I opened a few issues (https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/10990 and https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/10991) for provision performance optimizations I identified today; with those changes and another I'm going to merge after CI finishes, we should be able to get no-op provision performance down to 2 seconds on my laptop (!).

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-07 22:45 UTC

Ooh, just noticed another fix which I'll just make; with that, we could get down to 1.5s.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-07 22:56 UTC

## private message data

*2018-06-07 to 2018-06-07 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/private.20message.20data/with/596235)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-07 17:26 UTC

So, one thing that has been on my mind is having data on the users who the user recently (or has ever) conversed with in PMs, which is a really important data set for typeahead and related features.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-07 17:28 UTC

For group private messages, we already have a data structure, `Huddle`, that keeps track of which sets of users have had a group private message conversation.  It would not be hard to add a `last_message_id` field to that table (or, perhaps less nicely, do a `Message.objects.filter(recipent_id__in=[huddle_recipient_ids]` query to compute it on the fly in the `page_params` algorithm) .

(CCing @Greg Price and @Steve Howell on this conversation).

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-07 17:29 UTC

I think probably the data we'd want for doing typeahead would be at most the number of total historical group PM messages with that set of users, and the date of the last one.  Possibly just the second is good enough.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-07 17:33 UTC

But it's a lot more awkward to do the obvious analog for single-user private messages, because.  So one thing I've been thinking about is whether we should eliminate `Recpient.PERSONAL` and replace that with 2-user huddles in our database table structure.  That's already how things are (mostly) structured in the API and frontend, and so I think it'd be a relatively easy migration compared to other things touching core database tables.

**Greg Price** · 2018-06-07 20:01 UTC

I think the total number of messages would be nice, but the date of the last one is good enough.

(And is actually closer to what we really want, if we were to use only one of them. The ideal thing is something like a recency-weighted count of messages... or not even that but like a recency-weighted count of days on which there were messages. The ideal thing is more complex to compute than makes sense for us to do, but "date of last message" is an OK zeroth-order approximation.)

**Greg Price** · 2018-06-07 20:03 UTC

> whether we should eliminate `Recpient.PERSONAL` and replace that with 2-user huddles in our database table structure.

I think that'd be pretty reasonable. It makes some things a bit more indirect... but also more uniform. And the indirection is basically something we already have for most messages, so it can't be too terrible performance-wise.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-06-07 20:23 UTC

Right, exactly.  OK, I'll plan to spec out what this migration would look like, at a technical level.  The main downside is probably going to be something subtle like the `Subscription` table becoming a lot bigger; so we might find we need to add some new partial database indexes on e.g. just the Stream type subscriptions.

**Akash** · 2018-06-22 16:09 UTC

I think easiest method is using ngrok -
* Install ngrok
* Start a Zulip server
* `./ngrok http 9991`
* Copy the ngrok URL
* Replace following settings in `dev_settings.py` -

```shell
if EXTERNAL_HOST is None:
    user_id = os.getuid()
    user_name = pwd.getpwuid(user_id).pw_name
    if user_name == "zulipdev":
        # For our droplets, we use the external hostname by default.
        EXTERNAL_HOST = os.uname()[1].lower() + ":9991"
    else:
        # For local development environments, we use localhost by
        # default, via the "zulipdev.com" hostname.
        EXTERNAL_HOST = 'ngrok_url:9991'
        # Serve the main dev realm at the literal name "localhost",
        # so it works out of the box even when not on the Internet.
        REALM_HOSTS = {
            'zulip': 'ngrok_url'
        }
else:
    REALM_HOSTS = {
        'zulip': EXTERNAL_HOST,
    }

ALLOWED_HOSTS = ['ngrok_url']
```

I think the key points that aren't in this discussion already are:
* You need to connect your phone and laptop to the same wifi network

**Aditya Bansal** · 2018-06-19 17:03 UTC

Hi @mohsen fotrosi 
If I am right you are trying to install Zulip on an Ubuntu Xenial system where the said version of Ubuntu is most probably a Desktop version? or basically has a GUI interface. 
So upstart is needed for GUI interface to work, but Zulip requires upstart not to be installed (I won't go into details I don't know about why it is like that)
So what I find useful in this case which I use when I have to test something out temporarily in a production environment in a local Ubuntu VM is this process:
* Boot into Ubuntu.
* If right now GUI starts up fine, good; otherwise install it from the ttly by installing unity. I think this was the command `apt-get install unity`. After that you can just run `startx` command to start GUI interface.
* Once inside GUI interface, if we remove upstart GUI won't shutdown until a reboot or a logout maybe. So basically what I used to do was remove upstart, install zulip, run it, do stuff,....
* When I needed to reboot now, just reboot; CLI interface will show up (or you can reach a CLI by choosing the right options from the low graphics menu that pops up. Install upstart, start GUI and remove upstart!

PS: 
* Most probably this kinda question is more suited for #**production help** stream.
* I don't think the solution I gave you to get by the error is something dev's might be using in actual production env's. Probably as the error says upstart has been replaced by systemd, most probably you get to install some other thing instead of upstart and get to run GUI without doing installs/uninstalls on every boot.

Hope this helps :)
