**Robert Hönig** · 2018-06-28 18:10 UTC

So nginx brotli support ships as a third party module: https://github.com/google/ngx_brotli

Installing 3rd party modules in nginx is a pain for our setup:

* With nginx < 1.9.11, external modules could only be installed as static modules. This means that you have to clone the module's source and nginx's source and build both from source. To disable/enable modules, you need to rebuild nginx.

* With nginx >= 1.9.11, external modules can be installed as dynamic modules. This means that you still have to do the building from source, but now, these builds generate .so binaries for the modules that can be included and excluded in nginx.conf.

* With nginx >= 1.11.5, external modules can be installed in "compatibility mode". This means that you can build the .so module binaries with an nginx source version, and use them with an already installed nginx. 

We currently have
> nginx version: nginx/1.10.3 (Ubuntu)

This is a problem, because it means that we cannot build and install external modules in compat mode (to install a module built in compat mode one needs an nginx version built in compat mode). We cannot just build nginx from source, because Ubuntu ships with a special nginx:
> The Debian package provided by ppa:nginx/stable sets up configuration to monitor and start Nginx on system boot (Upstart/SysInit), logrotate and other system needs. 

It's possible to compile external modules into Ubuntu's nginx, but it's an even bigger pain [see instructions](https://serversforhackers.com/c/compiling-third-party-modules-into-nginx).

It'd be much more convenient if we could upgrade to an nginx >= 1.11.5.

**Robert Hönig** · 2018-06-28 18:10 UTC

Thoughts on how to proceed?

**Robert Hönig** · 2018-06-29 11:16 UTC

Also, I just tried upgrading to nginx >=  1.11.5 and it didn't help: Apparently, `--compat-mode` is not a guarantee that the generated brotli binary can be used with an existing nginx, but more a "we'll try our best but it doesn't work with every module". It doesn't work with ngx_brotli. Therefore, I went over the alternative route: Cloning the nginx debian repo source and building and installing it with the brotli module. This process is wonderfully explained here: https://serversforhackers.com/c/compiling-third-party-modules-into-nginx

And it worked! Brotli is now enabled on playground.zulipdev.org (along with gzip).

**Robert Hönig** · 2018-06-29 11:17 UTC

Go visit the page, open chrome dev tools and see for yourself :)

You can check if a file is transferred with brotli encoding by looking for `Content-Encoding: br` in the HTTP response headers.

**Robert Hönig** · 2018-06-29 11:20 UTC

Here are some stats from my observations:

* no compression: 1.7 MB | 9 MB

* gzip: 539KB | 6.9 MB

* brotli: 444KB | 4.7 MB

I obtained these numbers from the Chrome dev tools network inspector by recording the network log for a single hard reload. The first number is the amount of data in JS files transferred. The second number is the amount of data in total transferred.

**Robert Hönig** · 2018-06-29 11:21 UTC

Here are the nginx settings used for gzip and brotli:

```
    brotli on;
    brotli_comp_level 4;
    brotli_types text/plain text/css application/javascript application/json image/svg+xml application/xml+rss;

    gzip on;
    gzip_disable "msie6";
    gzip_proxied any;
    gzip_types
      audio/ogg
      application/javascript
      application/json
      application/xml
      application/x-javascript
      image/png
      image/svg+xml
      text/css
      test/javascript
      text/plain;
    gzip_vary on;
```

**Robert Hönig** · 2018-06-29 11:25 UTC

Note the `brotli_comp_level 4;`. This is the brotli compression level. We could achieve even greater compression rates with brotli by setting this to a higher number (11). With such a compression rate, however, brotli slows down significantly. Therefore, it is recommended to use this compression rate for all static files (I think for us these are in webpack?) I didn't do this yet, but apparently it's easy: Just run a brotli comrpession tool in the directory that serves the static files.

## empty message history

*2018-06-27 to 2018-06-27 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/empty.20message.20history/with/604316)*

**Yago González** · 2018-06-27 10:47 UTC

Hi! I just noticed that the backend isn't able to handle when we try to fetch the edit history of a message that hasn't been modified before (it just throws an HTTP 500).

So I'm working on fixing this, but I'm not sure about what should we return. This is what a normal response looks like:

~~~json
{
    "message_history": [
        {
            "content": "hello",
            "user_id": 5,
            "timestamp": 1530095369,
            "rendered_content": "<p>hello</p>",
            "topic": "bar"
        },
        {
            "topic": "bar",
            "content_html_diff": "<div><p><span class=\"highlight_text_inserted\">howdy</span></p> <p><span class=\"highlight_text_deleted\">hello</span></p></div>",
            "prev_content": "hello",
            "timestamp": 1530095461,
            "content": "howdy",
            "rendered_content": "<p>howdy</p>",
            "prev_rendered_content": "<p>hello</p>",
            "user_id": 5
        },
        {
            "topic": "bar",
            "content_html_diff": "<div><p><span class=\"highlight_text_inserted\">(deleted)</span></p> <p><span class=\"highlight_text_deleted\">howdy</span></p></div>",
            "prev_content": "howdy",
            "timestamp": 1530096052,
            "content": "(deleted)",
            "rendered_content": "<p>(deleted)</p>",
            "prev_rendered_content": "<p>howdy</p>",
            "user_id": 5
        }
    ],
    "msg": "",
    "result": "success"
}
~~~

**Yago González** · 2018-06-27 10:48 UTC

I feel like the optimal response would be something like this (if the message hadn't been modified):

~~~json
{
    "message_history": [
        {
            "content": "hello",
            "user_id": 5,
            "timestamp": 1530095369,
            "rendered_content": "<p>hello</p>",
            "topic": "bar"
        }
    ],
    "msg": "",
    "result": "success"
}
~~~

**Yago González** · 2018-06-27 10:50 UTC

Although another option would be sending an empty `message_history` (which is what we actually store in the database).

**Vishnu KS** · 2018-06-27 10:51 UTC

I think the first version makes more sense. (Sending the message over sending an empty message_history)

**Yago González** · 2018-06-27 10:53 UTC

Great, I'm going to try that. Thanks Vishnu!

```python
actual_email = models.EmailField(blank=True, db_index=True)  # type: str
```

**Joshua Pan** · 2018-07-03 04:21 UTC

**Shubham Dhama** · 2018-07-03 05:00 UTC

@Joshua Pan Just a try, 
```python3
def set_initial_value_for_actual_email(apps: StateApps, schema_editor: DatabaseSchemaEditor) -> None:
    UserProfile = apps.get_model("zerver", "UserProfile")
    for user in UserProfile.objects.all():
        user.actual_email = user.email
        user.save(update_fields=["actual_email"])
```
And confirm the changes in dbshell/shell if this works or not.

**Joshua Pan** · 2018-07-03 05:02 UTC

How do access the dbshell? That'll be really helpful.

**Joshua Pan** · 2018-07-03 05:02 UTC

That's definitely plausible: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/41500811/copy-a-database-column-into-another-in-django

**Shubham Dhama** · 2018-07-03 05:04 UTC

`./manage.py shell`would be better (dbshell requires PostgreSQL knowledge.

**Joshua Pan** · 2018-07-03 05:04 UTC

Ah, got it. `./manage.py dbshell`.

> That's definitely plausible: https://stackoverflow.com/questions/41500811/copy-a-database-column-into-another-in-django

## pika error

*2018-07-03 to 2018-07-03 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/pika.20error/with/607396)*

**Oktay X** · 2018-07-03 15:40 UTC

zulip@z:~/deployments/current$ ./manage.py change_user_email xxxx xxxx
2018-07-03 15:39:00.367 WARN [pika.adapters.base_connection] Connection to ::1:5672 failed: [Errno 111] Connection refused


I am getting this error. The command seems to go through. How would the problem exhibit itself if pika isn't running?

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-07-03 15:43 UTC

@Oktay X so, pika is the Python library for rabbitmq that we use

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-07-03 15:43 UTC

And port 5672 is the rabbitmq port

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-07-03 15:45 UTC

Oh, I bet that error is actually harmless (and fixed in master); what's happening is that it's trying the ipv6 address for localhost in addition to the ipv4 one, and the ipv6 address is failing (since rabbitmq doesn't listen there)

**Oktay X** · 2018-07-03 15:47 UTC

OK. That's a nonissue then.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-07-03 15:54 UTC

(Though my comment had been based on the assumption that it went through; if it actually failed, you'll want to edit `/etc/hosts` to not include `localhost` on the list of IPs for `::1`)

**Oktay X** · 2018-07-03 16:06 UTC

::1     localhost ip6-localhost ip6-loopback
This is there already

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-07-03 16:07 UTC

Right, what I'm saying is you should remove the `localhost` from that line if you want the warning to not happen :).

**Oktay X** · 2018-07-03 16:07 UTC

Oh sorry. I misread.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-07-04 15:29 UTC

Ohhh,apparently this is the error that gets thrown if you try to ALTER a table you have changed data in, in one transaction - https://stackoverflow.com/a/12838113/11708575

Postgres doesn't allow ALTERing in one transaction with other stuff generally  - perhaps we should have kept the DELETEs and altering the field in separate migrations - or the `` atomic = False `` way should do the job here too. I think we prefer to just split the migration into two though? Since we will want all the DELETEs in a single transaction.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-07-04 15:33 UTC

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-07-04 21:39 UTC

It's clearing out the archive tables, so that `` archive_transaction ``column  can be changed to not null. There's no sensible way of assigning a default for existing rows (from before the migration), so we delete them.

**Ricardo Duarte** · 2019-07-04 21:41 UTC

Ok. But what messages will be gone?

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-07-04 21:44 UTC

The archive is for use in a yet-incomplete feature, so this should have no meaningful impact. Any messages moved to the archive, have already been deleted for you. You won't have any messages disappear from your zulip as a result of this. It's just cleaning out a table that's essentially invisible for you for now.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-07-04 22:05 UTC

I believe the only way of messages going into the archive is through "delete message(s)" features (unless you manually set retention policies for reals and ran the archive_messages management command - which is the incomplete feature) - so you've opted for getting rid of them. The way this will work once things are finished, is that you will be able to restore messages from the archive - but that hasn't been a possibility yet.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-07-04 22:05 UTC

I updated the PR https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/12717 to include this deletion ordering fix.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-04 23:42 UTC

Thanks for debugging @Mateusz Mandera, merged.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-04 23:43 UTC

(Just to note, restoring deleted messages is not intended to be a user-facing feature; it's intended as a protection against potential bugs in the retention policy deletion implementation)

## new api key after pass change

*2018-07-09 to 2018-07-10 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/new.20api.20key.20after.20pass.20change/with/609933)*

**Yago González** · 2018-07-09 09:26 UTC

While discussing some issue in the mobile app (#M2770 for context), we noticed that we don't generate a new API key whenever the user changes their password.

I don't know if this is intented, but maybe we should consider automatically creating a new API key whenever the password is modified/reset.

**Yago González** · 2018-07-09 09:26 UTC

cc @Boris Yankov

**Greg Price** · 2018-07-09 18:39 UTC

I think it'd be good to offer that explicitly when the user has just changed their password. I'm not sure I'd want to just do it automatically, since it's a potentially disruptive operation.

**Greg Price** · 2018-07-09 18:41 UTC

It's kind of awkward here that you have just one key, rather than each bot or client that you've authorized having its own key that can each be separately revoked. There isn't really a good UX here that's possible without making that more fundamental change.

**Greg Price** · 2018-07-09 18:44 UTC

The UX that many services have and that works great is that the service can show you a list of all the integrations / apps / clients / etc. that you've given any kind of authorization to, with a "remove" button on each one.

**Greg Price** · 2018-07-09 18:51 UTC

Ha, in fact @Yago González I just read #M2770 and I see you made that very suggestion:
>  I wonder whether it may be worth having an endpoint in the REST API that works like the current /fetch_api_key, but only generates a per-application token (sort of how the OAuth flow works in some other platforms). This way, changes in the user's credentials or main API key wouldn't affect other services, unless the user revokes the authorization for that specific app.

I agree! I guess I would go a little farther in that I think we ultimately wouldn't have a concept of your "main API key".

In particular, one thing we could do that would eliminate that concept while being fully compatible with existing bots/etc. that expect to be given a key would be to let the user manage a list of API keys, each with a short text field for them to label what it was for, and make new ones or revoke specific old ones at will.

**Greg Price** · 2018-07-09 18:53 UTC

See https://github.com/settings/keys for something a lot like that list.

Or hey, actually https://github.com/settings/tokens is basically exactly that list.

**Yago González** · 2018-07-09 18:53 UTC

That's a very good idea! That would probably be much easier to implement, and it keeps the advantage of letting the user have full control over the API keys around.

**Greg Price** · 2018-07-09 18:56 UTC

Looks like GitHub also does the serious-about-security thing where they won't show you an old token. You see it once, when you generate it. If you need a token again, they'd rather you generate a fresh one, which isn't any harder anyway.

**Greg Price** · 2018-07-09 18:57 UTC

Somewhere in the Google developer console I've gone through a UX a lot like that one, too -- you make a token, they show it to you just that once; you can always make more later, and revoke individual tokens at will.

**Yago González** · 2018-07-09 19:00 UTC

Yeah, I've seen that a lot as well.

**Yago González** · 2018-07-09 19:01 UTC

We could probably make `/fetch_api_key` only generate new tokens.

**Yago González** · 2018-07-09 19:02 UTC

Although, now that I think of it, we should probably require a `label` parameter or something when querying that endpoint, which could pose retrocompatibility problems.

**Greg Price** · 2018-07-09 20:31 UTC

I think we probably want something like
* There's `/fetch_api_key` which is compatible with existing clients/bots. It doesn't require a label, but maybe we can make it secretly generate a new key instead of providing a single shared one.
* There's a new endpoint that behaves exactly as we'd like. It requires a `label`, and/or maybe a bit more structured info. It has a different name, because "fetch API key" doesn't quite sound right anyway for the operation of generating a new key and returning it.

Then `/fetch_api_key` can be deprecated -- which doesn't mean it needs to stop working anytime soon, but we tell people not to use it and we update everything we ourselves maintain. And then if we want we can look around after a while at what's still using it on e.g. chat.zulip.org and zulipchat.com, and try to get people to update.

**Yago González** · 2018-07-10 04:24 UTC

Sounds good! Maybe we can use the client's `User-Agent` as the user-visible label when a new API key is generated via `/fetch_api_key`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-07-10 07:20 UTC

The design just discussed is exactly what I'd had in mind for how we'd migrate this to a multiple API keys model.  I think it's not a super huge project if someone's excited about working on it.

We do make the optimization of not going to the server for id:N.  For near:N we keep things simple and don't even look for the id.  To do near:N locally we'd need to write some special anchor-like code before applying the filter (and possibly change the filter not to be always-true).

## multiple api keys per user

*2018-07-14 to 2018-07-15 · 32 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/multiple.20api.20keys.20per.20user/with/612311)*

**Yago González** · 2018-07-14 12:27 UTC

So I've been asked about some more context on this, and maybe this can be useful for other people interested in the backend.

I'm working on a feature that allows users have more than one API keys on their account. The idea is to have something similar to what other platforms do to manage personal authentication tokens: a list of keys where the user can create new ones or revoke previously existing keys.

The idea behind this is that every client should have its own API key, and if the user decides to revoke authorization to any of those clients, they can just delete the specific key without affecting other services that rely on API key auth.

We decided to do this after I noticed that regenerating a user's API key automatically logs them out of our mobile app, which is inconvenient (and a big pain if you have more than one application connected to your Zulip account).

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-14 12:29 UTC

Thanks for the explanation!  I was wondering about this after skimming some conversations, and now it makes perfect sense. :smile:

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-14 12:29 UTC

Will bots still be limited to one key?

**Yago González** · 2018-07-14 12:33 UTC

Well, from a database perpective bots are just a type of user, so it may be technically possible for a bot to have multiple API keys.

**Yago González** · 2018-07-14 12:35 UTC

But there are no plans to implement it for bots in the UI or anything, so that probably is a no.

**Yago González** · 2018-07-14 12:36 UTC

How do you feel about that? Do you think that bots could benefit from it?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-14 12:37 UTC

I think 99% of the time you just run one program per bot user, so having multiple API keys would confuse matters for people running bots.  But I do think it's at least plausible to want to have one bot "personality" that actually runs several programs that get deployed in various places.  Of course, that wouldn't work very well now with the mentioning scheme.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-14 12:38 UTC

So I'd probably err on the side of keeping the one-API-key restriction for bot users.

**Yago González** · 2018-07-14 13:49 UTC

After talking to Greg, he has also made an interesting point on why it could be valuable letting bots have multiple API keys: say that you want to change your bot's API key, but want to minimize the downtime. You could just create the new key, make the required changes in the bot's code/settings (or even try it out while the main instance is running) and then doing the actual change.
After that, you could remove the old API key.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-14 13:53 UTC

Yeah, that makes a lot of sense, and I've done that dance before with production systems.  Hopefully we can make this happen in a way that still seems simple to most bot authors.  A lot of bots are important but not in a 24/7 kinda way.  And some are just flat out toys. :smile:

**Yago González** · 2018-07-14 14:00 UTC

I wonder if maybe, as a followup feature, we could implement saying "okay, so I'm going to regenerate this API key, but want the old one to remain usable for X time before deleting it"

**Yago González** · 2018-07-14 14:01 UTC

So maybe as an optional argument when DELETing/regenerating an API key, say `expiration_time`, that can be used for that.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-14 14:18 UTC

That starts getting complex.  Some other alternatives to keeping programs running despite API key changes:
* only require the API key to establish a session (I believe this is kind of how Zulip works now)
* allow API keys to give you tokens back with limited expiry

**Yago González** · 2018-07-14 14:46 UTC

But limiting the expiry doesn't fix what we're talking about, does it=

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-14 14:52 UTC

Maybe I'm misunderstanding the use case but the idea is that if the old program is already authenticated, you change the API key without stopping the old program.  And then downtime is just stopping the old program than launching the new program with a slightly different config.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-14 14:53 UTC

I don't know if we actively shut down event queues or something like that.

**Yago González** · 2018-07-14 14:56 UTC

If I understood correctly, by "limiting the expiry" you mean being able to set a date when the API will stop being valid, right?

**Yago González** · 2018-07-14 14:56 UTC

(setting the date at creation time)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-14 14:57 UTC

I said "limit the expiry" with **tokens**, not API keys.  The idea is that your API key gets revoked whenever you change it, but programs who asked for tokens can keep running with the tokens.

**Yago González** · 2018-07-14 14:58 UTC

Oh, I see! So you could grab one of these tokens with the API key, and then use them to authenticate as if they were API keys?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-14 14:58 UTC

yeah

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-14 14:59 UTC

Huge caveat that I'm not recommending any of these solutions, just trying to say there are multiple ways to solve the problem.

**Yago González** · 2018-07-14 15:00 UTC

But if you revoke an API key, shouldn't all their associated tokens be revoked as well?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-14 15:01 UTC

The general scheme makes sense in lots of things, but maybe not this case specifically.  A good example is if you have a credit card, the way responsible vendors protect your credit card info is that they only use the card number at the edges, and then everything in the subsequent transaction is based off of some limited-use token.

**Yago González** · 2018-07-14 15:05 UTC

Didn't know that! But I agree, I don't think that it can apply to this specific case.

**Greg Price** · 2018-07-15 13:20 UTC

A token sounds to me a lot like another kind of API key, so I think it'd probably keep things simpler to just have the one kind.

**Greg Price** · 2018-07-15 13:21 UTC

> saying "okay, so I'm going to regenerate this API key, but want the old one to remain usable for X time before deleting it"

@Yago González Now that you mention it, I've actually seen a system where this was the only option! You had a choice of what X would be, but IIRC all of them were quite finite, like maybe the longest was 24 hours.

**Greg Price** · 2018-07-15 13:22 UTC

And that seemed like a pretty reasonable solution. (This is for the case of a bot user, of course.)

**Yago González** · 2018-07-15 13:40 UTC

Well I guess that we could probably set our own maximum lifespan, depending on our own needs.

**Yago González** · 2018-07-15 13:41 UTC

From a logic perspective it felt like it made sense, but I don't know how difficult would it be to implement from a backend perspective.

**Yago González** · 2018-07-15 13:44 UTC

I know for certain that some parts in the backend allow doing actions in the future (like a deferred email, for instance).

**Steve Howell** · 2018-07-15 14:37 UTC

@Yago González It's worth getting a quick data point on this.  Try starting a simple bot like `helloworld` and then change the bot user's API key while it's running.  My hypothesis is that it will keep running.  This will purely be a data point, since I don't think we'll  necessarily rely on the behavior, but we should know how it works currently.

Each call to `access_message` does at least one database query, and potentially a few, so we could end up doing ~20 database queries here if we're not careful.

I think even just checking whether the stream's history is public to the user, and if so, skipping the `access_message` calls (but otherwise doing an `access_message` loop) would be a significant optimization, since most traffic is in streams where history is public to the user.

(I would try to structure this as a function `bulk_access_messages_in_thread` in `zerver/lib/message.py`, and implement it as returning the subset of those messages that the user can access, since this seems like a concept that may eventually be reusable logic.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-07-26 16:38 UTC

And then v1 of that function can just be an `access_message` loop that we can write tests for, and then we can add commits on top to optimize from there.

## is_private flag

*2018-08-07 to 2018-08-08 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/is_private.20flag/with/627094)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-08-07 23:04 UTC

@Shubham Padia @*mobile* @Aman Agrawal I'd like to chat a bit about https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/9753/files.

We're adding this flag on `UserMessage` basically as a denormalization performance optimization (it'll make the `is:private` narrow a lot faster for corner cases where the user mostly receives stream messages, and is what we need on the backend to support anything else around recent private message conversations with fast queries).  Currently, the fact that we're implementing it as a flag would leak into the API.  I'm currently thinking we should address this by having the ~3 touchpoints where UserMessage objects get sent down to users be modified filter out the `is_private` flag, basically making this flag hidden from API clients, because the opposite would just be confusing (why should a client receive both the message type and this flag?)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-08-07 23:04 UTC

But I wanted to bring it up for a gut check before we commit to that plan.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-08-07 23:06 UTC

(The list of places would be basically making `flags_list` and `flags_list_for_flags` in `zerver/models.py`, which are the functions that interact with it, pretend the flag doesn't exist).

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2018-08-08 03:51 UTC

Yup, it doesn't make sense to send both message type and flag to the client. This sounds like a great improvement BTW.

**Shubham Padia** · 2018-08-08 08:29 UTC

Using the flag only internally sounds good to me.

**Greg Price** · 2018-08-08 11:43 UTC

Yeah, I agree -- better to keep this out of the API.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-08-08 16:55 UTC

@Shubham Padia OK, cool, can you make an attempt at patching those two functions in your PR, then?

**Shubham Padia** · 2018-08-08 16:58 UTC

I've done it already in the PR :). Patching only `flags_list_for_flags` was necessary since `flags_list` used that function. The relevant commit is ef58f969686384f990ffc378a545cde9cab440d2

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-08-08 17:20 UTC

@Shubham Padia makes sense.  There's a few tweaks I think we want to make on top of it for robustness, still thinking through them (but I think we want a nice variable name like `NON_API_FLAGS`)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-08-08 17:22 UTC

As the comments indicate in that function, that function used to be a surprising performance bottleneck.  (The recent changes seems fine, so maybe no need for extra warning here.)

> This probably should just be moved to a new issue since it's a backendy thing and not directly related, but I'm not sure the right thing happens for users who set e.g. their editor to "Emacs" before that choice value is deleted; I think everyone should be reverted to the "Not selected" value, but I' …
The issue here is that, when user select any choice from listed choices, we store order of that choice in backend modal. So when choices are changed, removed, reordered by admin, at end user it will show choice of stored order(if doesn't exist then `null`). 
Either we can change how values are stored in modal for choice type field or we can delete `CustomProfileFieldValue` when admin changes/removes/reorder choices and reset to `null`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-08-13 18:47 UTC

I think the latter makes the most sense (deleting the values when the admin removes the choice).

**Greg Price** · 2018-08-14 23:56 UTC

There's two different things being described in your respective comments here. When the admin just reorders the choices, we shouldn't delete everyone's answers -- we should make them stay effectively the same (so if they said "Emacs" before, they still say "Emacs" even though that's at a different point in the order.)

That could be done by going through and swapping everyone's values in that case, or it could be done by adjusting how we store the answers.

**Yashashvi Dave** · 2018-08-15 14:33 UTC

Right, we should not remove all values. 
If we go with same model structure(storing order of choice), this is we can do, when admin modifies choices of custom field:
* Retrieve all values `CustomProfileFieldValue` corresponding to modified choice-field `CustomProfileField`
* Traverse to all each `CustomProfileFieldValue` and get its choice-text-value from old choices list
* Check if choice-text-value exists in new choices list:
         - if exists, replace choice-order stored in `CustomProfileFieldValue` by new order from new choices list
          - if not reset it to null, delete from backend

**Yashashvi Dave** · 2018-08-18 05:48 UTC

Submitted #10349
it doesn't removes everyone's values, only choices which are deleted by admin

```
        # The key detail is that e.g.
        #   UserMessage.objects.filter(user_profile=user_profile, flags=UserMessage.flags.starred)
        # will generate a query involving `flags & 2 = 2`, which doesn't match our index.
        return 'flags & 2 <> 0'

**Greg Price** · 2018-08-21 23:53 UTC

**Joshua Pan** · 2018-08-22 00:41 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2018-08-22 00:55 UTC

It's described in the comment I quoted above.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-08-22 19:25 UTC

@Greg Price well, it's more complicated than that; we're using the `django-bitfield` library (which is unmaintained upstream and doesn't support creating indexes).  So our indexes are manually generated.  Most of our important queries to this index are from `zerver/views/messages.py`, the one section of Zulip that uses sqlalchemy.  And our indexes are designed to match the queries that our sqlalchemy code generate.

(I did, in the next commit, add a helper for the one other flag that we do queries on outside `messages.py`)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-08-22 19:27 UTC

I think if we were to put significant investment into this, we could redo the sqlalchemy queries to match the ones `django-bitfield` would generate, and redo our index structure to match that, and get rid of these bits of code, and we might do that someday.  But I think it's fair to say this construct is our own fault :)

**Greg Price** · 2018-08-21 20:25 UTC

The great bulk of realms are closed -- a spammer can't just show up and spam from the realm, unless it's theirs. And the great bulk of those are older than a few days. The purpose of this rule is to apply a tight limit to the spam realms a spammer might create in a burst, without catching up that great bulk of other realms in the same net.

**Greg Price** · 2018-08-21 20:26 UTC

The limit we apply here during an ongoing spam attack is far tighter than we would want to apply to the total invites sent from all normal realms on the server.

diff --git a/zerver/lib/openapi.py b/zerver/lib/openapi.py

@@ -43,11 +47,16 @@ class OpenAPISpec():

+            self.reload()

 class SchemaError(Exception):

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-06 23:07 UTC

And then I ran `test-help-documentation` off of #10481 so I could see the output easier.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-06 23:13 UTC

Most of the time I run it, due to the crawler spider many connections, you'll get a race where one of the processes is waiting for another process to populate `self.data`, even though that process has already populated `self.last_update` on the module-level `openapi_spec` variable.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-06 23:18 UTC

For me the race window is about 3.5s, which seems like a long amount of time to parse 1722 lines of YAML.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-06 23:21 UTC

It actually only takes 300ms to parse the YAML, so I think YAMOLE is 10x more costly for some reason.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-06 23:23 UTC

The race is this:
* client 1 calls spec(), which calls reload(), which sets `last_update`
* client 1 starts reading the file
* client 2 calls spec(), which sees `last_update` set
* client 2 does not call reload(), since it thinks the data is current
* client 1 is still in the 3-second window of actually populating `data`
* client 2 tries to access `data`, which isn't set

**Steve Howell** · 2018-09-06 23:24 UTC

And then you see this (without my above patch):

  File "/home/zulipdev/zulip/zerver/lib/openapi.py", line 46, in spec

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-02 19:05 UTC

There are two known issues with imports being slow:
* UserMessages take a while to load (kind of hard to avoid if there are zillions of them, although we do bulk-insert fairly efficiently as of a couple weeks ago)
* rendering is expensive

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-02 19:06 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-02 19:08 UTC

For rendering the main bottleneck is **hitting the database** for no reason.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-02 19:08 UTC

You can avoid reading the message (since it's already in memory) and writing the message (by doing rendering before you insert the message into the DB).

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-02 19:09 UTC

You can also do a one-time query to get the Realm (which requires passing it down the stack, of course).

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-02 19:11 UTC

You can also avoid a couple realm queries related to **previews**, which were just kind of a result of sloppy code.  The fix here is to treat `current_realm` like we handle `db_data` and `current_message`.  It's kind of sketchy to set these globals--I'm not convinced all of our hackery in this regard is truly necessary, but it's a huge refactoring for another day.

We also had an unnecessary query for user groups.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-02 19:13 UTC

Actually, the user group query didn't send any SQL over the wire, but Django's ORM is just super slow even for tasks that it can eventually short-circuit.

I am experimenting with eliminating the need to have 2N bugdown engines in memory, where N = number of realms, and 2 is for whether or not we're using the email gateway.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-03 14:33 UTC

The reason we have up to 2N bugdown engines in memory (plus a few more for situations where we don't know the realm or are supporting Zephyr) is that it's costly from a speed standpoint to build a new instance of `Markdown` with all the extensions.  And the reason we have 2N extensions is that we have different behavior for different realms, mostly driven by realm filters, plus different behavior for `email_gateway` being `True` or `False`.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-03 14:35 UTC

Another factor is that we can't necessarily just inject new  configuration into a new engine, since by the time you render, the engine may already have baked in the old configuration into its data structures.  (I'm not sure this is really a problem, so I may come back to this.)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-14 20:13 UTC

But the server will never send "topic" in fetch results or outbound events unless the client **specifically registers** for it.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-14 20:14 UTC

Of course, your point is still well taken--the earlier we can get the latest mobile app to be topic-smart, the better.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-11-14 20:14 UTC

## provision script run as root

*2018-11-22 to 2018-11-26 · 13 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/provision.20script.20run.20as.20root/with/663708)*

**Antonio Salazar Cardozo** · 2018-11-22 04:35 UTC

I'm poking at Dockerifying the dev/potentially runtime environment in a minimal way using Alpine Linux… One interesting thing I'm running into is that the provisioning script is designed to bail if it's run as root. This isn't entirely unusual during Dockerfile execution, since you're setting up the base environment in a declarative way and can later  switch up the functional user for when the docker container actually executes.

**Antonio Salazar Cardozo** · 2018-11-22 04:36 UTC

Unfortunately the [introducing commit](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/789ae8648ada471cf0f51e18c8f1b7b941e397c5) doesn't really explain the reasoning behind the root abort, so it's not clear if it was just a “don't clobber yourself” decision, or if it's necessary in a more docker-like environment as well.

**Antonio Salazar Cardozo** · 2018-11-22 04:37 UTC

Any ideas here? Would it be crazy to introduce some sort of detection or flag for docker to use that removes the need for what `Dockerfile-dev` does right now? (For reference, `Dockerfile-dev` creates a `zulip` user and give it `NOPASSWD` `sudoers` rights, AKA make it root for any important purposes.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-26 20:05 UTC

@Antonio Salazar Cardozo hello and welcome!

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-26 20:06 UTC

I believe the context for 789ae8648ada471cf0f51e18c8f1b7b941e397c5 is that `provision` expects to run as a non-root user with sudo access, and the commit was just checking for that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-26 20:08 UTC

The broader context is that (1) you generally want to be running the dev server (etc.) as a non-root user that you're going to login is, (2) provision needs access to that user account to do some setup steps (e.g. `tools/setup/emoji/build_emoji`).

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-26 20:08 UTC

So, if we wanted to support `provision` being run directly as root, we'd need to (1) pass into that provision mode the user to run those commands as, and (2) do some refactoring.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-26 20:09 UTC

The first refactoring step we'd like to do for other purposes, is change `run(["sudo", ...]` to `run_as_root([...])`, so that we can make those commands be a no-op in the case that the user is already root.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-26 20:09 UTC

(That refactor to add a `run_as_root` wrapper function has other benefits for production use anyway, where we currently require `sudo` to be installed just so `root` can `sudo` to itself, which I'd really like to fix)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-26 20:10 UTC

I can't remember whether @Rohitt Vashishtha was planning on working on that `run_as_root` refactor, but it's high on my list of projects for our provisioning/installer codebases.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2018-11-26 20:28 UTC

We have `is_root` from a recent refactor that we can use to write `run_as_root` in `zulip_tools`, in case someone else takes this. 

I found 26 instances of this needing refactoring. I'm currently not able to get any work done, but in a couple of days will get to this (if still left).

**Antonio Salazar Cardozo** · 2018-11-26 21:18 UTC

Hello! Thanks for the extra detail, it all makes a lot of sense! I stopped going down this path for now in favor of the existing docker setup, but I'll ask more questions if and when I feel compelled to pick docker back up :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-11-26 21:53 UTC

OK, probably belongs on your list then, Rohitt.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-11 18:52 UTC

OK, makes sense, we'll need to change some code then.  This function in `zerver/views/auth.py` is the direct place that this gets called:

```
@require_post                                                                                                                        
def logout_then_login(request: HttpRequest, **kwargs: Any) -> HttpResponse:                                                          
    return django_logout_then_login(request, kwargs)                                                                                 
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-11 18:52 UTC

The actual code of `django_logout_then_login` is this:

```
@deprecate_current_app
def logout_then_login(request, login_url=None, extra_context=_sentinel):
    """
    Logs out the user if they are logged in. Then redirects to the log-in page.
    """
    if extra_context is not _sentinel:
        warnings.warn(
            "The unused `extra_context` parameter to `logout_then_login` "
            "is deprecated.", RemovedInDjango21Warning
        )

    if not login_url:
        login_url = settings.LOGIN_URL
    login_url = resolve_url(login_url)
    return LogoutView.as_view(next_page=login_url)(request)
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-11 18:53 UTC

So I think we can just try changing our `auth.py` code to do this:
```
return django_logout_then_login(request, login_url=settings.LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL, kwargs)
```

and then use `LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-11 18:55 UTC

(Or we could make up our own setting name, but I think that's probably not the right approach)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-11 18:56 UTC

It's also possible that the correct fix is instead to just change our code to be 

`return LogoutView.as_view()(request)`, which I think is the default recommendation for modern Django, and it would respect `LOGOUT_REDIRECT_URL` automatically.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-11 18:58 UTC

@ZulipLover for user auto-creation with REMOTE_USER, that's absolutely supported.  IIRC, you just need to have LDAP configured to set the user's full name (otherwise they'll get a simple registration form to pick it).

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-11 21:18 UTC

I just wanted to highlight some great work by @Rein Zustand in c9d54f785455aea216665cf9fee2ae8134216338, which removed our copies of several-year-old versions of various standard Puppet modules.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-11 21:18 UTC

Our experience has been that those modules are trouble in a bunch of ways (and we can't upgrade them without breaking Zulip installation on Xenial/Trusty, because the newer versions require the latest Puppet language)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-11 21:19 UTC

So it's great to just get rid of them; we were only using 3 functions in any case, so it was pretty easy to eliminate them from the codebase once we restructured the way we're managing our apt repositories.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-11 21:20 UTC

As a bonus, we don't get complaints from the GitHub web UI about how we should update versions of various things in the Gemfile.lock files for those dependencies (which weren't used, so there wasn't an actual issue, but spurious alerts are always annoying)

https://zulipchat.com/api/update-subscription-properties is for editing your properties (e.g. notification settings); `/streams/` is for the stream's global settings (e.g. whether it's private).

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-17 20:18 UTC

In any case, our endpoints as a general rule support changing several properties in a single request, and both of those endpoints have that property.

@Tim Abbott how does the backend feel about the values not being actually new?
For example:
1. We have `{ name: "Boris", age: 36 }`
2. We want to update `age`.
3. The backend receives `{ name: "Boris", age: 37 }`

**Boris Yankov** · 2018-12-18 23:16 UTC

Do you want the client to do the diffing for every value and only pass the changed props or is it Ok to simplify and give you the whole object?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-18 23:20 UTC

It’s ideal if you diff cause your data may be stale.

**Boris Yankov** · 2018-12-18 23:29 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-18 23:41 UTC

For stream names, the backend will throw an error if you try to change the stream name in a no-op way.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-18 23:41 UTC

So you actually need to check what fields the user edited locally.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-18 23:41 UTC

(Which is best practice anyway because of staleness)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-18 23:58 UTC

@Boris Yankov Generally, you can send multiple fields, as long as each field actually changes values.

payload = {}

  payload.salary = form.salary
send_data_server('/zulip/endpoint', payload)

## which shell shebang to use

*2018-12-18 to 2018-12-18 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/which.20shell.20shebang.20to.20use/with/673479)*

**Rein Zustand** · 2018-12-18 02:24 UTC

(Redirected from https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/11004#issuecomment-447678745)
To make an informed decision on whether to use (1) `#!/usr/bin/env bash`, (2) `#!/bin/bash`, (3) `#!/bin/sh`.

Other systems:
1. Shellcheck itself uses (1) for its script (see https://github.com/koalaman/shellcheck/pull/1125) because it has to anticipate being run on darwin with bash 4.
2. Elasticsearch prefers (2) since it doesn't support BSD systems, and is worried about the security concern of (1) (see https://github.com/elastic/elasticsearch/issues/23443).
3. Git strictly uses (3). This makes sense since most of its subcommands are written in shell anyway and has to run smoothly across *NIXes. Additionally, its test suite is entirely in shell as well.
4. Kubernetes has 331 lines of (1), 67 lines of (2), 181 lines of (3)
5. Chromium has 16 lines of (1), 272 lines of (2), 501 lines of (3)

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-18 02:27 UTC

@Anders Kaseorg since he's also been involved in this discussion.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-18 02:28 UTC

Is there a reason `#!/usr/bin/env bash` would be any worse than `#!/usr/bin/env python3`  security-wise?  I suspect not, and that there's no reason for us to prefer (2) "for security".

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2018-12-18 03:08 UTC

If you’re writing shell scripts that run from setuid binaries, then (don’t, but in particular,) you’d need to be concerned about someone inserting a malicious `python3` binary into your `PATH`. Not a concern for us.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2018-12-18 03:09 UTC

Not a concern for elasticsearch either, but it’s easier for them not to change anything and make up whatever justification makes the bug reporter go away.

## replace minor of PROVISION_VERSION with content version

*2018-12-18 to 2018-12-18 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/replace.20minor.20of.20PROVISION_VERSION.20with.20content.20version/with/673585)*

**Rein Zustand** · 2018-12-18 13:08 UTC

By replacing the minor part of PROVISION_VERSION with a hash of `requirements/*.in` or `requirements/*.txt`, no manual minor version bump is necessary. Would this be a good idea?

**Rein Zustand** · 2018-12-18 13:48 UTC

One drawback is that this adds more ms to the time spent on no-ops runs.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-18 14:41 UTC

@Rein Zustand probably knows most of the history here, but for others' benefits, the `PROVISION_VERSION` scheme he refers to is Zulip's effort to make it so that users are forced to run provision before running various testing tools, but **only** when necessary.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-18 14:43 UTC

If provision could truly run in zero seconds when none of our dependencies changed, we would obviously abandon the scheme, but it's hard to get it down to zero seconds, since provision still needs to do things like load up Django, check on versions of external dependencies, make sure local assets are properly built, etc.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-18 14:45 UTC

Back when we introduced the scheme, Tim basically made the same suggestion as Rein, but there are two problems with hashing `requirements/*`:
* some things that affect provision, such as building local assets like emojis, wouldn't show up there
* you might get false positives for trivial edits to requirements file that don't actually change anything structurally

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-18 14:48 UTC

I think you could have **both** a minor version number and a hash in the file.  And we could have a tool that makes sure the hash is correct.  If the hash is wrong, we'd urge the developer to both bump the minor version **and** hash, but a savvy developer could just update the hash if they determined that the hash changed for something negligible like adding a comment to a requirements file.

And then we would still rely on devs to bump the version for things where the hash didn't change (with the added check/balance of Tim looking out for these types of changes).

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-18 14:52 UTC

Another possibility is that we just abandon the `PROVISION_VERSION` scheme and just force users to run the provision for every checkout.  This would add a bit of overhead the first time you checked out a commit that otherwise wouldn't have required a provision, and we could prevent multiple runs per version by writing the commit version to a local file.  Unfortunately, this isn't quite as simple as it sounds--you need to account for devs working on long series of commits, where they may be rebasing frequently,  etc., or switching between branches.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-18 19:31 UTC

Here's my thoughts on this:
* I don't think abandoning PROVISION_VERSION is reasonable; it saves me a ton of time when switching branches, and I suspect that's true for others as well.
* In addition to `PROVISION_VERSION`, which we'd still need for various manual changes, we could add a separate mechanism for checking a hash of the requirements files, so that those specific categories (which change often) don't require manual editing of PROVISION_VERSION..

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-18 19:32 UTC

So I think if we change "replace the minor part ..." in @Rein Zustand's proposal with just "Add a separate bit of code for automatically handling requirements/ and package.json updates", that'd be great.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-18 19:34 UTC

Going back to one of my earlier concerns, I think we'd get very little noise on the hash scheme within the specific context Tim mentions.  I just did `git log requirements`, and almost every change is substantive and would truly motivate a new provision.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-18 19:35 UTC

(So I like Tim's proposal.)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-18 19:36 UTC

Basically, 95% of changes are straightforward upgrade of single packages, and most of the rest are even bigger changes.  I didn't find anything that seemed cosmetic.

## pinning users

*2018-12-27 to 2019-01-15 · 49 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/pinning.20users/with/676157)*

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-27 15:41 UTC

There's some chance I'll work on pinning users in the near future.  The most fundamental decision is how to model it, and I'm thinking `PinnedUser` with two fields, `viewing_user` and `pinned_user`, that are of course foreign keys to `UserProfile`.

I'm highly inclined to just use the simple, concrete solution here for the problem at hand.  I'd love to hear a counterargument, though, perhaps in favor a more generalized friend/relationship model.  I can imagine other "friend" features, like selecting a small group of friends for PM notifications.

The closest thing we have now is `UserGroup`, and you could actually do something really hacky where each person's collection of pinned users is a specially named or specially flagged group of users, but that seems like it extends the user-group concept a bit too far and would complicate lots of code.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-12-27 16:03 UTC

I'm still partial to the direction we were going in a few months ago, e.g. always including anyone you have a recent PM with

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-12-27 16:04 UTC

Followed by a toggle to limit the buddy list to your current stream (which is needed for guest users anyway)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-27 16:06 UTC

You might want to add some commentary here:

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/10513

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-12-27 16:06 UTC

I think the "always include recent PMs in buddy list" will solve a lot of usability issues users are having with PMs

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-27 16:08 UTC

I like the idea of just pinning users based on observed behavior (recent PMs), but I also feel like some users will want more control.  I assume we would only count PMs where both parties participate, which would help, but I think there are definitely occasions where a) I'd need to PM somebody who I don't want to pin and b) I want to pin somebody despite not having reason to PM them.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-27 16:13 UTC

I think the best-of-both-worlds scenario would be this:
* users can pin/unpin as simply as they do for streams (which makes the app more consistent, too)
* after you send a 2nd or 3rd response to a user who's not pinned, we prompt you with a modal that makes it super easy to pin them

This gives the user 100% control, with minimal manual effort and interruption.

(It would probably make sense to occasionally prompt users to pin streams as well, but that seems less urgent.  The left-sidebar pinning approach hasn't gotten major pushback, by the way. )

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-27 16:16 UTC

Ideally when we detect that an unpinned user is a candidate for pinning, we could make it 100% automatic, and then have the modal be something like this:

~~~
Alice will be pinned!  [Don't pin]

Since you are conversing with Alice, we are pinning her.
~~~

And it would be like the mute-undo dialog (which is easier to replicate with one of my latest PRs), where it would go away after 4 seconds if you do nothing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2018-12-28 02:00 UTC

I think backend-wise, we'll want a ManyToManyField or something similar.  I'm partial to the approach of having it be automatically managed (e.g. auto-add users you send/receive a PM with) with manual overrides (e.g. you can remove or add a user you haven't exchanged PMs with)

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-28 02:02 UTC

Can you elaborate on ManyToMany?

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-12-28 02:05 UTC

I think my feeling is that the basic buddy list updates (include PMs, and limit to stream members) are so high value that we should likely implement those first and then see where we are. "Include PMs" I think will make us more competitive with Rocket.chat and Mattermost for PM-heavy workloads, and limit-to-stream-members will enable us to provide a real "guests" feature.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-28 02:11 UTC

I still think users prefer control above all other concerns, but I think a basic implementation of a pinning relationship on the backend is the first step for any approach—whether we let users pin, or we decide for them, or we decide and allow overrides.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-28 02:14 UTC

I haven’t thought much about limit-to-stream.  On the one hand I would argue that compose-fade already solves that.  But on the other hand I know compose fade is kinda confusing for users and just feels generally hacky in nature.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-12-28 02:14 UTC

the "include PMs" would be a purely frontend thing, similar to how mobile does it

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-28 02:16 UTC

I am not really happy with the mobile experience to be honest, although I am not 100% sure what it’s trying to achieve.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-12-28 02:16 UTC

the mobile experience is just using whatever PMs it has in the last N messages, for a small N. The webapp will have the luxury of using a much larger N.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-28 02:16 UTC

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-12-28 02:17 UTC

(I'm just referring to the choice of who to list; I don't recall how the mobile app does presence)

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-12-28 02:18 UTC

anyway, I think using 10x the number of messages will make it a lot nicer, and I think we're already planning on adding an endpoint for mobile that will let clients know the list of recent PMs?

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-28 02:21 UTC

I think we’re basically on the same page if we all agree to a somewhat hybrid approach of manual and automatic pinning, and we probably need to iterate on how much is automatic.

**Steve Howell** · 2018-12-28 02:23 UTC

But in terms of building it I am still pretty firmly in the camp of manual control first that gets us backend infrastructure and may satisfy 80% of users that care either way.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2018-12-28 03:03 UTC

I agree that eventually we'll want something that supports pinning and removing individual users, but I do think that the infrastructure needs are somewhat different between the two features. My guess is there are two types of PM workloads:
* Majority of a user's PMs are with a handful (< 5) of users 
* A large fraction of a user's PMs are conversations with people they talk to < once/month

For the first group, I agree that something that looks like pinning could make sense. For the second group, I think showing all the recent PM-recipients is the primary concern.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-01-14 03:42 UTC

> only render in a minimal number of functions 

We should only render in these places:
(1) The functions that edit a stream's description
(2) The function that creates a stream (might need to render the default description)
(3) A data migration that runs when we first deploy the feature.

(And in each case, store the rendering to the database).

If we do those, then we won't need to render stream descriptions anywhere else, since other code paths will just be pulling the data from the database.

  5 exports.get_message_events = function (message) {

 26         };
 27     });
 28
 29     return events;
 30 };

            for (option in opt.options) {

    });

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2019-02-13 19:02 UTC

Slightly tangentially, do you know if this is equivalent to using `parametrize` in pytest?
(https://docs.pytest.org/en/latest/parametrize.html)

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-13 19:03 UTC

> Slightly tangentially, do you know if this is equivalent to using `parametrize` in pytest?

I do!  I liked the example that you linked to a couple days ago.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-13 19:04 UTC

https://github.com/zulip/zulip-terminal/blob/master/tests/cli/test_run.py

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-13 19:05 UTC

~~~ python
@pytest.mark.parametrize('color, code', [
    ('red', '\x1b[91m'),
    ('green', '\x1b[92m'),
    ('yellow', '\x1b[93m'),
    ('blue', '\x1b[94m'),
    ('purple', '\x1b[95m'),
    ('cyan', '\x1b[96m'),
])
def test_in_color(color, code, text="some text"):
    assert in_color(color, text) == code + text + "\x1b[0m"
~~~

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2019-02-13 19:07 UTC

Doesn't it make the test so concise :D

**Steve Howell** · 2019-02-13 19:08 UTC

Yeah, and I also like that it signals the type of function you're dealing with.  You know it's a fairly simple function that can act on lots of inputs, as opposed to, say, a more complex function where the testing focus is maybe more on sequence of operations or interactions with other functions.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2019-02-13 19:29 UTC

>>  1 @pytest.mark.parametrize('i', range(0, 6))

    4     Test that numbers between 0 and 5 are all even.
    5     """
    6     assert i % 2 == 0
```
compared to the example in the unittest docs here:
https://docs.python.org/3/library/unittest.html#distinguishing-test-iterations-using-subtests

## test-backend performance

*2019-02-19 to 2023-07-09 · 38 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/test-backend.20performance/with/704151)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-19 22:53 UTC

I just merged 4dc7f5354ddfbde3b732b31d46ec2981b47c427c aka the first part of https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/11055, which makse the default behavior for `test-backend` when run on the command line not run the tests for `zerver/webhooks`.  @Eeshan Garg FYI.

The main benefit is a 25% reduction in the runtime of `test-backend` for folks who aren't working on webhooks; for folks who are, we already recommend e.g. `test-backend zerver/webhooks/github` because it's way faster to just run the tests for a single webhook, so there isn't much downside.  CI behavior is the same as before (using `test-backend --include-webhooks`).

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-19 22:55 UTC

#11055 has a much of other ideas that we intend to look into for further optimizing `test-backend` performance, which I'd really like to get back down significantly below 1 minute on my quad-core laptop (it's currently a bit over 70s, down from 94s with this change)

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-19 22:57 UTC

Many of the fixes ideas discussed in #11055 involve improvements to tests to be more efficient, but others may be fixable by just optimizing some of our user-facing code that is run a lot in the tests even if it's not as heavily used in production.  E.g. optimizing /help/ page rendering.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-06-27 15:48 UTC

FWIW it would have saved me a little bit of time if the `--profile` option either automatically ran single-threaded or forced me to specify how many threads I wanted to run. **Steve Howell** · 2023-06-27 15:53 UTC

Given that DB-related activity seems to be the clear bottleneck here, I think the next step would be to try to track down the following:
* Are any single queries particularly slow?
* Do any single tests run a whole bunch of queries?

For the latter, I could see us having some kind of test-runner tweak where we disallow any single test from running more than N queries, unless at some point they call `assert_database_query_count`.  This would ensure us that most O(N)-queries bugs either get caught or get explicitly called out by the tests.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-23 00:59 UTC

I just merged https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/11654, which re-enables our linters enforcing "no unused imports".  This is an experiment.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-23 01:02 UTC

For background, we previously had it turned off for 2 reasons:
* The relevant upstream Python linter didn't support type comments, so it would produce lots of bogus stuff given that we were using mypy.  This was fixed upstream a few weeks ago.
* In early Zulip development, we had a lot of merge conflicts and PRs failing CI due to linter errors from unused imports that wasted a lot of time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-23 01:02 UTC

I think it makes sense to try turning this on because with Zulip's backend fairly mature, we don't move things between files super often (as we already have a file structure we're happy with).

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-02-23 01:03 UTC

But I'd love to hear about instances of folks finding this linter annoying, as we may find that it's of negative value to run in CI (and we should go back to our previous model of running it and doing a bulk clear every few months)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-02-25 20:27 UTC

Here’s my perspective: I configure my editor to highlight flake8 (= pyflakes + pycodestyle) warnings, so (1) I don’t need to round-trip through `lint` to find those warnings, but (2) if we write some pattern to exclude those particular warnings from `lint`, they’d still show up in my editor, which makes real warnings (FSVO “real”) a bit harder to spot.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-02-25 20:31 UTC

Since your profile says you’re also using Emacs, maybe you’d be interested in giving [Flycheck](https://www.flycheck.org/) a try. It’ll show you flake8 warnings by default if you have flake8 installed. I use this global ~/.flake8rc to exclude the pickiest categories:
```
[flake8]
# E302: expected 2 blank lines, found 1
# E305: expected 2 blank lines after class or function definition
# E501: line too long
# W503: line break before binary operator
ignore = E302, E305, E501, W503
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-02-25 20:37 UTC

If we decide we want to exclude unused `typing` imports anyway, we’d probably need to upgrade `suppress_patterns` from substrings to regexes. It’d be pretty easy—I’d just be a little annoyed at the inevitable result.

**Steini** · 2019-04-23 20:40 UTC

so my manual solution was to disable port80-section in the nginx.conf, then restart nginx, then run certbot-auto renew, restart nginx and re-enabled the port80-section in the nginx.conf
As far as i understand, in default certbot uses the webroot-method and certbot-auto uses anything he can get a hand on and used in my case standalone, so it had to bind to port80 what was possible, after i modified the nginx.conf.
So a not so well crafted solution would be to disable port 80 all together in the nginx.conf and set up some kind of certbot-auto renew cronjob. That's more of a shitty-crafted solution but i worked for me. So hopefully this is helpful to some other people out there.
@Tim Abbott Maybe somebody with more nginx and certbot-skills could take a look at the config to make sure that a fully integrated solution with certbot on the webroot-method does a smooth certificate renewal.

## PM glitch

*2019-03-02 to 2019-03-02 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/PM.20glitch/with/711850)*

**Steve Howell** · 2019-03-02 21:06 UTC

Boris just ran into a problem that I ran into a month ago.  If you do a search that pulls up a really old conversation, the client adds that old PM conversation to "Private messages", and it makes it look like you have a "gap" between new conversations and old.  Which, in fact, you do, at that point.  We could possibly fix with a Conversation table, or more backend support, or just ignore search-related messages when computing stuff client-side.  Not a huge priority, but good to be aware of, at least.

I think the right plan is to follow through on our plans to use the "private messages" narrow data to populate that feature directly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-03-02 22:17 UTC

Though I do think not adding messages from search to that widget would be an improvement in any case.

*2019-03-27 to 2022-11-02 · 39 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/REQ.20vs.20Pydantic/with/725197)*

Pydantic appears to be a new approach to a similar problem, and is now being used in things like FastAPI (using starlette for an async web backend). Pydantic doesn't extract the parameters I believe, but the validation has been very similar to what I wondered might be possible by interpreting the types literally for us, using REQ.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-04-04 00:51 UTC

@Neil Pilgrim interesting.  I think it probably doesn't solve the problem REQ does, in that REQ takes care of parsing the request data from Django, not just at a function level.

I'm also not really a fan of the model of defining a separate class for each view function's argument validation; django-rest-framework takes that approach and my experience is that it makes the code a lot less readable by splitting the validation explaining what the argument types are from the view code that actually parses those types.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-10-28 01:20 UTC

Some observations posted on the PR:
- `cattrs` provides quite detailed error messages when parsing fails. But they are not really concise especially when we have deeply nested structures with multiple errors:

```
  + Exception Group Traceback (most recent call last):
  |   File "/home/pig208/zulip/zerver/tests/test_events.py", line 2339, in test_add_attachment
  |     add_event = cattrs.structure(events[0], AttachmentAddEvent)
  |   File "/srv/zulip-py3-venv/lib/python3.8/site-packages/cattrs/converters.py", line 309, in structure
  |     return self._structure_func.dispatch(cl)(obj, cl)
  |   File "<cattrs generated structure zerver.lib.event_schema.AttachmentAddEvent>", line 24, in structure_AttachmentAddEvent
  |     if errors: raise __c_cve('While structuring ' + 'AttachmentAddEvent', errors, __cl)
  | cattrs.errors.ClassValidationError: While structuring AttachmentAddEvent (1 sub-exception)
  +-+---------------- 1 ----------------
    | Exception Group Traceback (most recent call last):
    |   File "<cattrs generated structure zerver.lib.event_schema.AttachmentAddEvent>", line 15, in structure_AttachmentAddEvent
    |     res['attachment'] = __c_structure_attachment(o['attachment'], __c_type_attachment)
    |   File "<cattrs generated structure zerver.lib.event_schema.AttachmentType>", line 34, in structure_AttachmentType
    |     if errors: raise __c_cve('While structuring ' + 'AttachmentType', errors, __cl)
    | cattrs.errors.ClassValidationError: While structuring AttachmentType (1 sub-exception)
    | Structuring class AttachmentAddEvent @ attribute attachment
    +-+---------------- 1 ----------------
      | Traceback (most recent call last):
      |   File "<cattrs generated structure zerver.lib.event_schema.AttachmentType>", line 20, in structure_AttachmentType
      |     res['path_id'] = __c_structure_path_id(o['path_id'])
      | ValueError: invalid literal for int() with base 10: '2/87/WoqhJzoaO8LUV7doiIn7s92e/zulip.txt'
      | Structuring class AttachmentType @ attribute path_id
      +------------------------------------
```
- It coerces data into the destined primitive type when possible. For example, if a data structure has a field `count: int`, then structuring the dict `{"count": "12"}` works fine, while `{"count": "abc"}` fails as expected. This is different from what `check_data`. We can probably fix this with a hook similar the one here https://github.com/python-attrs/cattrs/issues/44.
- It allows extra keys by default. This behavior is also different from `check_data`, which rejects unknown keys. This can be fixed by using a custom converter `c = cattrs.Converter(forbid_extra_keys=True)`.

To replicate other behaviors of our current event schema construct (checking the presence of `type` field, auto-adding `id`), we can probably make use of the extensibility of the `cattrs`/`attrs` APIs. An advantage of this might be that we can reuse the schema data structures in other places like `queue_json_publish` without the cost of validating them. This is valuable because we gain the advantage of static type checking.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-10-28 01:22 UTC

I'm trying similar things with `marshmallow-dataclass`.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-10-28 02:03 UTC

`marshmallow-dataclass` does not provide [static type checking](https://github.com/lovasoa/marshmallow_dataclass/blob/master/marshmallow_dataclass/__init__.py#L224-L228) for the parsed data structure with the desired type.

The usage of `marshmallow-dataclass` in our test case might look like this:
```python
        add_schema = marshmallow_dataclass.class_schema(AttachmentAddEvent)()
        add_event = add_schema.load(events[0])
        reveal_type(add_schema)  # zerver/tests/test_events.py:2341: note: Revealed type is "marshmallow.schema.Schema"
        reveal_type(add_event)   # zerver/tests/test_events.py:2342: note: Revealed type is "Any"
        self.assertEqual(add_event.upload_space_used, 6)
```

We will have to use `marshmallow_dataclass.class_schema` to generate a `marshmallow.schema.Schema` first, then use the `.load` method defined on the generated schema.
AFAIK, `Schema` does not preserve the typing information of the generated schema, which probably requires a complicated mypy plugin as type annotations are insufficient.
Since this does not guarantee type safety at the library level, `marshmallow_dataclass` does not meet the requirements.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-31 22:09 UTC

Yeah, status type checking is pretty clearly one of our goals for doing something other than basic dataclasses.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-11-02 04:37 UTC

Just an extra thought here. It seems that `attrs` might be unnecessary since `cattrs` also supports `dataclass` alone for type-checking purposes.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-11-02 04:51 UTC

Actually, we might be bumping into [some limitations of `dataclasses`](https://github.com/python-attrs/cattrs/pull/215), so `attrs` is not off the table.

## Deactivated users social auth backend

*2019-04-10 to 2019-04-11 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Deactivated.20users.20social.20auth.20backend/with/730844)*

**Shubham Padia** · 2019-04-10 07:54 UTC

Re #11937 (Fix social auth backend handling of attempts to login by deactivated users)

** Why Google Oauth shows the error: **
- **TLDR:** [finish_google_oauth2](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/zerver/views/auth.py#L393) does not have a check for inactive user
- And further steps continue after which [log_into_subdomain](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/zerver/views/auth.py#L493) calls [login_or_register_remote_user](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/zerver/views/auth.py#L150) with the `user_profile` as `None`.
- The reason for the user_profile being none:  As the user is deactivated and cannot be authenticated, `authenticate_remote_user` returns None
- Due to the `user_profile` being `None`, `login_or_register_remote_user` calls `maybe_send_to_registration`.
- `maybe_send_to_registration` uses `HomepageForm`. 
- `HomepageForm.clean_email` calls [validate_email_for_realm](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/zerver/lib/actions.py#L4765) which raises the validation error with the message 'The account for %s has been deactivated'.

**Github/social auth:**
- The [social_auth_finish](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/zproject/backends.py#L754) has a check for inactive user and it returns the user to the login page without any errors.

**Q:** What should be the approach to solve this issue? While removing the check for `inactive_user` may solve the issue immediately, I'm not sure if it is the right thing to do.

## postfix

*2019-04-23 to 2019-04-24 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/postfix/with/736208)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-04-23 23:37 UTC

For https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/12167, it'd be really helpful if someone did the investigation of what version of postfix introduced these options that are now required.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-04-23 23:37 UTC

(Probably a project of mostly reading their changelogs)

**Shubham Padia** · 2019-04-24 04:46 UTC

(if this was what you asked)

From http://www.postfix.org/COMPATIBILITY_README.html:

Using backwards-compatible default setting smtpd_relay_restrictions = (empty)
The smtpd_relay_restrictions feature was introduced with Postfix version 2.10, as a safety mechanism for configuration errors in smtpd_recipient_restrictions that could make Postfix an open relay.

The smtpd_relay_restrictions implicit default setting forbids mail to remote destinations from clients that don't match permit_mynetworks or permit_sasl_authenticated. This could result in unexpected 'Relay access denied' errors after Postfix is updated from an older Postfix version. The backwards-compatibility safety net is designed to prevent such surprises.

When the compatibility_level less than 1, and the smtpd_relay_restrictions parameter is left at its implicit default setting, Postfix may log the following message:

postfix/smtpd[38463]: using backwards-compatible default setting
    "smtpd_relay_restrictions = (empty)" to avoid "Relay access
    denied" error for recipient "user@example.com" from client
    "host.example.net[10.0.0.2]"
If this request should not be blocked, then the system administrator should make the backwards-compatible setting "smtpd_relay_restrictions=" (i.e. empty) permanent in main.cf:

# postconf smtpd_relay_restrictions=
# postfix reload

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-04-24 21:36 UTC

OK, cool, looks like even Ubuntu Trusty had 2.11.0, so we should be safe to use it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-04-24 21:37 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-28 21:38 UTC

It doesn't account for all the time (that first `0.86s` is probably importing Django, etc.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-28 21:45 UTC

Needs more investigation, but those two elements are:
* `manage.py showmigrations`, to figure out whether there are new migrations since we last rebuilt the database.  I bet we can optimize that significantly by caching e.g. `sha1sum */migrations/*.py` and only doing that check if the content has changed.  This could save ~0.5s (out of the 4s on my machine).  Definitely worth doing.
* `./tools/setup/generate-fixtures`, the somewhat misleadingly named thing that dumps and recreates the test database from the template, takes 1.6s.  It will probably require some deeper investigation into options, but one possibility that seems very doable would be to optimistically do this reset work at the end of the test (and check its state), rather than the start, so it doesn't delay access to whether the test worked.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-28 21:50 UTC

Actually, probably the most promising thing here is that I'm not sure why we need to run `generate-fixtures` at all in the case that we determined the template database is up to date.
