**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-28 21:54 UTC

This code in `zerver/lib/test_runner.py` looks like it does that correctly:
```
    def run_tests(self, test_labels: List[str],                                                                 
                  extra_tests: Optional[List[TestCase]]=None,                                                   
                  full_suite: bool=False,                                                                       
                  include_webhooks: bool=False,                                                                 
                  **kwargs: Any) -> Tuple[bool, List[str]]:                                                     
        self.setup_test_environment()                                                                           
        try:                                                                                                    
            suite = self.build_suite(test_labels, extra_tests)                                                  
        except AttributeError:                                                                                  
            # We are likely to get here only when running tests in serial                                       
            # mode on Python 3.4 or lower.                                                                      
            # test_labels are always normalized to include the correct prefix.                                  
            # If we run the command with ./tools/test-backend test_alert_words,                                 
            # test_labels will be equal to ['zerver.tests.test_alert_words'].                                   
            for test_label in test_labels:                                                                      
                check_import_error(test_label)                                                                  
                                                                                                                
            # I think we won't reach this line under normal circumstances, but                                  
            # for some unforeseen scenario in which the AttributeError was not                                  
            # caused by an import error, let's re-raise the exception for                                       
            # debugging purposes.                                                                               
            raise                                                                                               
                                                                                                                
        self.test_imports(test_labels, suite)                                                                   
        if self.parallel == 1:                                                                                  
            # We are running in serial mode so create the databases here.                                       
            # For parallel mode, the databases are created in init_worker.                                      
            # We don't want to create and destroy DB in setup_test_environment                                  
            # because it will be called for both serial and parallel modes.                                     
            # However, at this point we know in which mode we would be running                                  
            # since that decision has already been made in build_suite().                                       
            destroy_test_databases(self.database_id)                                                            
            create_test_databases(self.database_id)                                                             
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-05-29 22:09 UTC

@hi-ko so the way using LDAP + Email authentication works is that we only allow email authentication for users whose accounts are definitely not managed by LDAP.

This is to prevent security issues where users set a Zulip password when their account is supposed to be managed by LDAP.

## unicode emojis

*2019-06-24 to 2021-04-23 · 45 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/unicode.20emojis/with/758828)*

**Vishwesh Jainkuniya** · 2019-06-24 18:25 UTC

I was debugging **Keypad emoji fail to render (sometimes) #M3517** and found that on some phones, font is not able to recognize continuous unicodes generated by codePoints which have `-` in them like `0030-20e3` (which is the codePoint of 0 ( :zero: )). Basically `0030` denotes `0` and latter one denotes box, which will enclose previous char. 
On debugging this on server we (me & Greg) found that we are using `non_qualified ` instead of `unified ` (https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/zerver/models.py#L1703) from https://raw.githubusercontent.com/iamcal/emoji-data/master/emoji_pretty.json. Why :thinking: . If we are always using `unified` one, then that issue on mobile will get fixed easily. @Tim Abbott @Harshit Bansal  cc @Greg Price

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-06-25 05:31 UTC

I do not recall the backstory for this; @Harshit Bansal do you?  I think 99e1a810552ac2665270a6312e229986012d7293 is relevant but I don't remember the details.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-06-25 05:32 UTC

@Vishwesh Jainkuniya FYI

**Greg Price** · 2019-06-25 10:27 UTC

A bit more context: from attempting to read the relevant Unicode spec, I think the two-codepoint sequence `0030-20e3` is simply invalid according to the spec, and it should be `0030-fe0f-20e3`.

See in particular http://www.unicode.org/reports/tr51/#def_emoji_keycap_sequence , and search that document generally for `20e3`; and see http://www.unicode.org/Public/emoji/12.0/emoji-sequences.txt with the same search.

**Greg Price** · 2019-06-25 10:31 UTC

Clearly a lot of browsers do accept the `\x{0030} \x{20e3}` form, and maybe it was allowed, or ambiguously allowed, in a previous version of the spec. But we should do the version that actually appears in the `emoji-sequences` reference and is described by the TR51 emoji spec.

**Greg Price** · 2019-06-25 10:40 UTC

BTW here's the names of those three codepoints:
```
$ unicode --brief 0030 fe0f 20e3
0 U+0030 DIGIT ZERO
 U+FE0F VARIATION SELECTOR-16
 U+20E3 COMBINING ENCLOSING KEYCAP
```

In particular U+FE0F is a "variation selector", specifically the "emoji presentation selector". It contrasts with U+FE0E the "text presentation selector", and can be used after certain codepoints listed in http://www.unicode.org/Public/emoji/12.0/emoji-variation-sequences.txt to say to display the character as an emoji-style glyph or a more text-style glyph.

**Greg Price** · 2019-06-25 10:42 UTC

E.g. here's U+1F6F0 SATELLITE in emoji style and text style, as interpreted by my terminal:
[pasted image](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/73/nHtCBobOaEPWotZRS9hbu3pT/pasted_image.png)

**Harshit Bansal** · 2019-06-25 18:32 UTC

As far as I remember the back story is that iamcal introduced this `qualified` and `non-qualified` thing to comply with the unicode standard which dictates that emoji unicode codepoints should have both text and emoji style glyphs available. So the `qualified` codepoint represents the emoji style glyphs while the non-qualified one represents the text style glyphs. The standard also states that environments like chat applications don't need to use `qualified` codepoints to display emoji style glyphs. So we don't need to use the `qualified` version.
Also the problem with multi-codepoint emojis is that we need to write regex in our markdown parser so that if someone pastes a multi-codepoint emoji we can convert it. If we write that regex (and test it properly), then the rest of the infrastructure work can be done (I had even made some progress in this direction).

**Vishwesh Jainkuniya** · 2019-07-02 22:05 UTC

So should we go with fixing (do changes) in backend (not sure whether it will break web frontend or not) or should we handle it in mobile itself?

**Vishwesh Jainkuniya** · 2019-07-03 19:39 UTC

Currently we are getting `'0': '0030-20e3',` as codePoint  from server. We are first splitting it by `-`, then getting unicode string from both (`0030` & `20e3`) and then joining both strings.
```javascript
const parseUnicodeEmojiCode = (code: string): string /* force line */ =>	const parseUnicodeEmojiCode = (code: string): string /* force line */ =>
  code	  code
    .split('-')	    .split('-')
    .map(hex => String.fromCodePoint(parseInt(hex, 16)))	    .map(hex => String.fromCodePoint(parseInt(hex, 16)))
    .join('');
```
Some Android phones font consider it has invalid. As :zero: is a result if two codePoint, one is digit (`0030`) and other one is box (`20e3`) which is enclosing it.
One hack which I tried on mobile is 
```javascript
const parseUnicodeEmojiCode = (code: string): string /* force line */ =>
  code	  code
    .split('-')	    .split('-')
    .map(hex => String.fromCodePoint(parseInt(hex, 16)))	    .map(hex => String.fromCodePoint(parseInt(hex, 16)))
    .join('');	    .join('\uFE0F');
```

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-10 01:19 UTC

Based on having read the emoji spec, aka TR51 linked above, my understanding is
* U+1F329 is a perfectly good "emoji character", on its own
  * And every emoji character is also a valid length-one "emoji sequence", which is the object we're usually dealing with when we speak of "an emoji" in Zulip
* The sequence U+1F329 U+FE0F is also a valid emoji sequence, one that explicitly says to render in an emoji style. It's valid because it appears in http://www.unicode.org/Public/emoji/12.0/emoji-sequences.txt .

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-10 01:22 UTC

But
* U+0030 aka good old `0` is certainly not an emoji character
* So U+0030 U+20E3 would only work as an emoji if it were an emoji sequence...
* ... which it isn't. It's not in the list.
* Rather, U+0030 U+FE0F U+20E3 is a valid emoji, specifically a valid emoji sequence.

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-10 01:26 UTC

> I would have assumed we had the relevant sprite sheet embedded in the mobile app, and used the CSS and other files generated by the `tools/setup/emoji/build_emoji` pipeline for other reasons, in which case I would not have thought there would be any divergence from the webapp behavior?

Aha -- we don't use a sprite sheet. Instead we use the actual Unicode, and let the browser take care of rendering it.

That may also explain why the webapp isn't affected by the invalid emoji sequence. If you're never actually taking these down to the sequences of Unicode codepoints that they represent, then these strings like `0030-20e3` are just abstract names with a helpful-and/or-confusing resemblance to lists of codepoints, and it doesn't matter whether the lists of codepoints they resemble have anything to do with valid or invalid Unicode emoji sequences.

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-10 01:30 UTC

> * What is the correct way to get the list of emoji that are affected by this issue?

The complete list of emoji that we handle invalidly in the way I'm aware of are the "emoji keycap sequences" as TR51 calls them. These are the entries in http://www.unicode.org/Public/emoji/12.0/emoji-sequences.txt that say `Emoji_Keycap_Sequence`. There are 12 of them.

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-10 01:30 UTC

They overlap a lot with `REMAPPED_EMOJIS`. But the latter has 11 of the 12 -- it doesn't have :asterisk: -- and has 10 others that look unrelated.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-10 05:28 UTC

Ok given there are 12 and we already have a hack for 11 of them, migrating seems simplest.  Is there a field in iamcal we should switch to using for these?  Or do we need to remap differently?

**Greg Price** · 2021-04-23 00:28 UTC

With or without that workaround, there's still a symptom caused by the server not having the correct codepoint sequences here.

If you go and send a message and you include one of these emoji as the actual Unicode -- so like 1️⃣, not as `:one:` -- then the Markdown renderer doesn't recognize it as emoji, and so it gets passed through verbatim rather than getting our emoji formatting.

That means it looks like 1️⃣ vs. :one: -- it's smaller than we normally make emoji appear.

**Greg Price** · 2021-04-23 00:31 UTC

This is probably most likely for someone to run into if they're using an iPhone, either in the mobile app or in the webapp. That's because these emoji are in the iOS emoji keyboard; I don't see them when I look in the Google keyboard on Android, and of course they're not on physical keyboards like people use on desktop. (But maybe they're also in the Samsung keyboard or other Android keyboards; I don't know.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-11 18:23 UTC

On Python 2 support:
* 16% is huge and would definitely be worth doing work to support if we thought it was a random subset of the userbase.  
* While upstream support for Python 2 ends up in 2020, RHEL 8 will contain Python 2 and it'll be around as a thing one can use on RHEL at least for like another decade, supported by Red Hat.  So it's not like it's leaving the world as a thing people use anytime soon.
* Since zulint doesn't integrate tightly with third-party code, it's mostly not a problem for a Python 2 shop to run a Python 3 linter toolchain.  

I think it's reasonable to just declare we're doing Python 3 for this.  Though we shouldn't confuse ourselves: We will get likely complaints if zulint gets any adoption, because tons of people use Python 2, and not supporting Python 2 will make it hard for folks to do things like run linter tests as part of their Python 2 test suite.

## OpenAPI validation

*2019-07-11 to 2019-07-11 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/OpenAPI.20validation/with/766651)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-11 18:16 UTC

Hey folks, I just wanted to highlight the work on our API documentation at zulipchat.com/api that's  we've been doing in https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/12751 (more details in #12521) , since it'll likely come up as folks modify our API.

With this new test change, our automated tests for our API documentation will include:
* Running the `python` example code in `tools/test-api` to confirm that it actually works and returns the expected output documented in the documentation.
* Comparing the `REQ()` parameters defined in the actual views code defining the API against the declarations in the OpenAPI docs, which lets us confirm that we 

There's still a bunch of anomalies to investigate and fix (`git grep documentation_pending` has a bunch of examples), and of course we haven't documented every endpoint that we'd like to, but this new testing system should ensure that we always update the documentation when we extend the arguments for an existing API endpoint in the common cases, which is really important.  

This will not eliminate human error; for now the `curl` and `zulip-js` docs are still hand-maintained (though one could imagine further work to fix that by generating them from the OpenAPI data, which would likely be an improvement), and it's impossible to do that with the prose.

I wanted to flag this for everyone here both because you'll be potentially seeing some new error messages related to this (which I'd love any feedback on), and also just because it's an example of the kind of high-value work that we continue to invest in to reduce the effort required to write and review changes so that the project can move quickly without breaking everything.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2019-07-11 23:03 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-11 23:36 UTC

## test-backend

*2019-07-13 to 2020-05-06 · 2 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/test-backend/with/767561)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-13 00:55 UTC

I just merged 86f762bc753aba6b6adea6fc0c0cfb6f8e4bca31 / #12540, which completes our effort to clean up how `test-backend` interacts with the filesystem to avoid disk leaks.  The new documentation is at https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/testing/testing-with-django.html#testing-code-that-accesses-the-filesystem, but the relevance to everyone is this fixes two problems with the old setup:
* Leaking disk if you run `test-backend` a bunch of times, which is obviously bad.
* Potential problems where parallel test threads conflict with each other, resulting in nondeterministic failures.

Developers may want to do one-time cleanup of their `var/` directory, especially: `"var/$(cat ~/.zulip-dev-uuid)"/test-backend`; following this change, nothing new should leak there.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-06 05:25 UTC

## hidden emails

*2019-07-15 to 2019-08-13 · 49 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/hidden.20emails/with/768316)*

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-15 22:07 UTC

I'm working on #M3196, with a draft branch that switches to using the `.email` from `/register` everywhere we use "this user's own email", instead of the email they logged in with. I have a test realm with the hidden-emails setting enabled -- i.e. "who can see people's emails" -> "admins only".

The draft branch breaks various things, which is natural, so I'm debugging them.

One of the breakages appears to stem from us getting unobfuscated email addresses from the server! Specifically, it looks like in a `/messages` response, the `display_recipient` properties have the real email addresses, not the obfuscated ones.

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-15 22:09 UTC

Here's a fragment from my console:
```
display_recipient: Array(3)
0: {email: "greg+t1@zulipchat.com", full_name: "Greg 試し", short_name: "greg+t1", id: 101712, is_mirror_dummy: false}
1: {email: "greg+t2@zulipchat.com", full_name: "Greg 2", short_name: "greg+t2", id: 101713, is_mirror_dummy: false}
2: {email: "reminder-bot@zulip.com", full_name: "Reminder Bot", short_name: "reminder-bot", id: 108224, is_mirror_dummy: false}
length: 3
```

User `greg+t2@zulipchat.com` is the one I'm testing as. This is a group PM message, as you can work out from the shape of the `display_recipient`.

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-15 22:11 UTC

That fragment comes from a layer or two inward from the raw `/messages` response, but I'm pretty sure we haven't done any processing of this part of the data at this point. And in any case this client should have no knowledge at all of the email address `greg+t1@zulipchat.com`, belonging to the other user -- the user I'm testing as isn't an admin.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-15 22:12 UTC

@Greg Price hmm, interesting.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-15 22:13 UTC

It's possible this is a cache-flushing issue.

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-15 22:13 UTC

Oh huh could be -- I did just switch this test org over to the new setting.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-15 22:13 UTC

If you look at `get_display_recipient_remote_cache`, which is what constructs that attribute, it clearly only accesses the `email` attribute, not the `delivery_email` one.

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-15 22:14 UTC

And that's certainly a cache that should be flushed on this settings change, and it'd be an easy bug to forget to do so.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-15 22:15 UTC

```

```

which seems like it should handle this cache...

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-15 22:15 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-15 22:16 UTC

If you're testing somewhere you have console access, you can do a `manage.py shell` and print-debug to figure out if it's indeed a caching issue?

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-15 22:34 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-16 23:10 UTC

Aha, perhaps this is the problem:

The *message* dicts are also cached. The cached data for them includes a version of `display_recipient`.

And I don't see an obvious place where we're invalidating *that* cache on this change.

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-16 23:13 UTC

Specifically, `get_messages_backend` gets its data from `messages_for_ids`, which gets the bulk of it from `generic_bulk_cached_fetch(to_dict_cache_key_id, ...)`.

That cache key appears to be populated by `message_to_dict_json` (perhaps there's another path too, because I don't see how that connects to `generic_bulk_cached_fetch`? but if there are multiple, they ought to agree). Which is just `MessageDict.to_dict_uncached`. Which via `MessageDict.to_dict_uncached_helper` defers to `MessageDict.build_message_dict`.

Which has
```
        obj['raw_display_recipient'] = get_display_recipient_by_id(
            recipient_id,
            recipient_type,
            recipient_type_id
        )
```

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-16 23:16 UTC

The most direct fix would be to have `delete_display_recipient_cache` go track down all those messages, and invalidate those cache keys too.

Probably it'd be good to first fix a perf-bug where `delete_display_recipient_cache` currently goes and invalidates the cache for streams the user is subscribed to, in addition to personals and huddles.

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-16 23:20 UTC

At that point the work we're doing when this setting is flipped becomes pretty steep indeed if the realm is significantly lived-in. (I see there are already TODO comments pointing out that the current version is already a lot.) So probably more work is needed. But that would at least fix the correctness issue, and would put all the burden on the rare event of flipping this setting, with no effect on normal operation.

**Greg Price** · 2019-07-16 23:22 UTC

Perhaps a helpful deeper change would be to un-denormalize a bit, taking `raw_display_recipient` out from the message dicts? Would need to make sure the bulk-fetch code then bulk-fetches the display_recipient values... but once done, that should be more efficient than the status quo anyway because there will typically be far fewer distinct recipients than there are messages.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-17 21:36 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-18 19:28 UTC

@Greg Price I think I just realized why this wasn't discovered on the webapp.  We generally ignore everything but the `ID` attribute of users from the `display_recipient` objects in the webapp; including the denormalized values is primarily useful for (1) Making life easier for API clients that aren't implemented to look up users (which I suppose includes in the mobile app, in this case) and (2) perhaps making there be no user-visible impact for certain classes of data synchronization bugs.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-18 19:29 UTC

So I think there's probably a few things we should think about here:
(1) Denormalizing `display_recipient` here, as you describe, which has unclear impact on performance.
(2) Offering an option to not bother including values beyond just `stream_id` or list of `user_ids` for the `recipient`, for clients that don't need those extra details, which is an opportunity to basically skip the query described in (1) in many cases.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-08-06 21:22 UTC

`` get_display_recipient_by_id `` also has a local cache:
```
# Doing 1000 remote cache requests to get_display_recipient is quite slow,
# so add a local cache as well as the remote cache cache.
per_request_display_recipient_cache = {}  # type: Dict[int, Union[str, List[Dict[str, Any]]]]
def get_display_recipient_by_id(recipient_id: int, recipient_type: int,
                                recipient_type_id: Optional[int]) -> Union[str, List[Dict[str, Any]]]:
    """
    returns: an object describing the recipient (using a cache).
    If the type is a stream, the type_id must be an int; a string is returned.
    Otherwise, type_id may be None; an array of recipient dicts is returned.
    """
    if recipient_id not in per_request_display_recipient_cache:
        result = get_display_recipient_remote_cache(recipient_id, recipient_type, recipient_type_id)
        per_request_display_recipient_cache[recipient_id] = result
    return per_request_display_recipient_cache[recipient_id]
```

I think we should clear this as well in `` delete_display_recipient_cache ``? Something like
```
def delete_display_recipient_cache(user_profile: 'UserProfile') -> None:
    from zerver.models import Subscription  # We need to import here to avoid cyclic dependency.
    recipient_ids = Subscription.objects.filter(user_profile=user_profile)
    recipient_ids = recipient_ids.values_list('recipient_id', flat=True)
    keys = [display_recipient_cache_key(rid) for rid in recipient_ids]
    cache_delete_many(keys)

    from zerver.models import per_request_display_recipient_cache
    for recipient_id in recipient_ids:
        if recipient_id in per_request_display_recipient_cache:
            del per_request_display_recipient_cache[recipient_id]
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-07-24 23:22 UTC

I'm forking a separate topic for this specifically, because I feel like anecdotally a lot more folks have been having trouble with the Vagrant development environment than in the past, likely indirectly related to our upgrade to Ubuntu Bionic.  It's hard to tell from individual reports how isolated they are; a lot of issues like out-of-disk an out-of-memory are things that Zulip could do better logging for (or we could adjust the default settings for how large of a disk to create, for example).

## mypy follow_imports

*2019-08-07 to 2019-08-07 · 32 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/mypy.20follow_imports/with/776740)*

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-08-07 00:29 UTC

From mypy.ini:

```python
# Error on importing modules that are present but not part of the
# build.  If the module can't reasonably be made to not error, errors
# can be suppressed with ignore_errors.
# (The mypy daemon only supports error and skip for follow_imports)
follow_imports = error
```

This is a problem, because it also prevents mypy from reading type annotations in third-party modules—it just uses `Any` for everything imported.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-08-07 00:30 UTC

Now that `run-mypy --no-daemon` runs in about 3 seconds on a warm cache, maybe it’s reasonable to disable the daemon entirely?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-08-07 00:55 UTC

I did, it does not.

Because that comment was written when we were the first non-Dropbox project to integrate the daemon

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-08-07 00:55 UTC

OK, annoying.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-08-07 00:56 UTC

I guess this was known—it’s why we have `[mypy-zulip] follow_imports = skip`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-08-07 00:56 UTC

`zulint` is going to have the same problem when we give it a `py.typed` file.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-08-07 00:58 UTC

I thought we had an approach that involved explicitly listing modules that had type data to check in `mypy.ini` for things we know have typing data, though I don't see an example.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-08-07 00:59 UTC

In practice, we do not use `zulip` type-correctly.

## cache: Replace cache key functions with cache key classes?

*2019-08-16 to 2019-08-16 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/cache.3A.20Replace.20cache.20key.20functions.20with.20cache.20key.20classes.3F/with/780374)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-08-16 22:05 UTC

Inspired by some cache-clearing bugs I've worked with lately - I've had an idea with the aim of increasing safety in our workflow for adding new cache keys.

How it is right now:
When we want to add a new cache - let's say for caching ``UserProfile``s - we define a new cache key function:
```
def user_profile_by_api_key_cache_key(api_key: str) -> str:
    return "user_profile_by_api_key:%s" % (api_key,)
```
apply it for caching the object (``UserProfile``)  where we want (probably by decorating some function of ours with ``@cache_with_key`` with the cache key function we just defined) and then figure out where we need code for deleting objects from this cache when needed (for example in ``delete_user_profile_caches`` in a simple case). 
My impression is that this makes it easy to forget/miss something and not delete objects from the cache, causing tricky to find and debug issues.

What could be done:
To promote safety in doing this kind of thing, hopefully decreasing the frequency of these mistakes happening, instead of just defining raw cache key functions, we could define class objects which would specify, upon creation, what are the conditions under which objects should be deleted from the cache.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-08-16 22:07 UTC

This would require quite some work, and good design,  but we'd end up with a nice framework for defining new caches, which would be safer, and perhaps also provide a way for additional customization of it if appropriate (perhaps custom ``set_cache`` functions or things like that).

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-08-16 22:14 UTC

For example, instead of manually putting all these various caches to delete from in ``delete_user_profile_caches``, this function would delete all appropriate objects from caches that have specified "delete if UserProfile changed" in their definitions.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-08-16 22:21 UTC

Interesting idea.  It would be cool if it could be done cleanly.  I'd worry a bit about the transition introducing new cache clearing bugs, and maybe also about complexity.  Not sure we need a class vs. just a decorator argument to register

## Rename 'pub_date' column to 'timestamp' in the Message table

*2019-08-27 to 2019-08-27 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Rename.20.27pub_date.27.20column.20to.20.27timestamp.27.20in.20the.20Message.20table/with/783101)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-08-27 18:50 UTC

So we have this issue - https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/1727 where we want to rename ``message.pub_date to message.timestamp``. 

But there is one nuisance with this - our ``timestamp`` column will actually be datetime and not a "timestamp" in the sense of the various time conversion functions (Unix timestamp), which leads to awkwardness like:
``timestamp = datetime.datetime.fromtimestamp(epoch_seconds)``
or
``timestamp         = datetime_to_timestamp(timestamp)`` (where the argument to the function is a "timestamp" in the sense of being the timestamp field of a Message - but the ``timestamp`` we're assigning value to is in the sense  of Unix timestamp)

What would be the best way to approach this? Do we just ignore it accept this quirk? The type could just be changed from ``datetime`` to Unix timestamp for consistency, but I'm guessing there must be some reasons for us wanting the column specifically as datetime?

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-08-27 18:53 UTC

Yeah, that's not great.  @Greg Price @Rishi Gupta I'd love your thoughts on this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-08-27 18:54 UTC

I think it probably is good terminology-wise to be consistent, and maybe `timestamp` is a good consistent name for a UNIX timestamp (hard to come up with a better name for that).

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-08-27 18:54 UTC

The thing I really don't like about `pub_date` is that "publish" isn't a term we use anywhere.  Something like `date_sent` or `sent_at` would be significantly better if we wanted to avoid using `timestamp`.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2019-08-27 18:58 UTC

out of those `date_sent` seems most in line with `date_created` and `date_joined`

**Rishi Gupta** · 2019-08-27 18:59 UTC

I think I would be ok with just having all of these timestampy fields named `date_created`, though maybe the confusion is not worth the consistency

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-08-27 19:08 UTC

I think `date_sent` makes sense for a sent message.

## commit line length

*2019-09-05 to 2020-03-13 · 50 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/commit.20line.20length/with/784952)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-09-05 00:04 UTC

So, we appear to have some lack of clarity/inconsistency in what we're using as the maximum line length for commit messages.   
https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/13119 is a PR that suggests one possible fix.  We're currently using 76 for everything.  A few thoughts on the topic:
* The most important requirement is that `git show` doesn't wrap in a normal 80-column terminal, which requires a 76 limit on body width.  I think this is reasonable.
* Some folks argue for a lower limit for the title line, e.g. 72, 68 or even 50.  I think 50 is a terrible idea because you can't express anything and nobody in the Zulip world emails patches with the terminal-based email clients where a subject line of short length is valuable.

Thoughts?

**Rishi Gupta** · 2019-09-05 00:06 UTC

I think the expressiveness of 76 is nice.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-09-05 00:08 UTC

Data from the last 10K commits is helpful:
```

    280 64
    239 65
    251 66
    230 67
    202 68
    198 69
    152 70
    131 71
    138 72
     63 73
     69 74
     61 75
     38 76
      7 77
      7 78
      3 79
      4 80
      5 81
      3 82
      2 83
      2 84
      1 87
      1 88
      1 90
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-09-05 00:09 UTC

Aside from the few dozen mistakes, essentially everything is within the 76 limit.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-09-05 00:09 UTC

Looks like:
* About 200 (~2%) commits between 72 and 76
* About 600 (~6%) commits between 68 and 72.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-09-05 00:11 UTC

So I think it'd be to describe our current de facto policy as "aim for <=70, maximum of 76" based on that.

**Rishi Gupta** · 2019-09-05 00:12 UTC

what's the benefit / general argument for going below 76? 
I guess one is that the github UI wraps title lines at some length < 76?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-09-05 00:16 UTC

GitHub ellipsizes subject lines longer than 72.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-09-05 00:22 UTC

I tend to wrap at the Emacs default fill-column (70) because it’s easy, but that’s not a proposal to impose a specific number. I don’t think there should be a “hard limit” because sometimes you want to copy and paste naturally long URLs or code or literal output into a commit message.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-09-05 00:28 UTC

linux/Documentation/process/submitting-patches.rst says subject at 70–75, body at 75.

**Greg Price** · 2019-09-05 00:49 UTC

I've generally been asking for prose to be wrapped to "around 68 columns, 70 max" in the mobile repo.

This isn't a hard limit in the sense that it's enforced by a machine that won't realize something is a URL or some literal output. The main way a machine gets involved is to set the wrapping width in your text editor to 70 columns.

**Greg Price** · 2019-09-05 00:53 UTC

The reason for that is that when lines actually get to 76, I usually feel like they're annoyingly wide to read. And at 72 I often feel that way, and when they're 70 usually not.

**Greg Price** · 2019-09-05 00:57 UTC

For the summary line, I mostly keep it to the same 70-column maximum but I'll sometimes go a bit over when it feels hard to fit all the key information otherwise.

In particular this means I'm often OK with a *longer* summary line than any line of normal prose. That's basically because in prose there's never a pressing need to squeeze more in: just wrap onto the next line.

(If there's a giant URL or something that's a large fraction of the line's length and shouldn't be broken across lines, I'll usually want to set it off indented on its own line anyway. Most recent example in `git log` on mobile:
```
commit 532d4358125025dd38ebad2da465b4005f5fe9bf
Author: Greg Price <greg@zulipchat.com>
Date:   Thu Aug 22 14:43:41 2019 -0700

    logging: Let `console.log` and friends do their work in release mode, too.
    
    The effect of these is, on Android, to log the messages to the device
    log with tag `ReactNativeJS`.  So this command finds them:
      adb logcat -s ReactNativeJS:V
    I'm not sure if it does anything helpful on iOS, though I'd hope so.
```
)

**Greg Price** · 2019-09-05 01:01 UTC

One specific thing about a width of 76 is that in an 80-column terminal, it means the message can go all the way to the last column. I find that to my eye that makes it look strongly *like* it may be extending off to the right and just not being wrapped -- so I really want a couple of columns of right margin, which means a max of 74 columns of text. This isn't really an issue for an occasional isolated line like a longish summary line; it's mainly about the routine width of prose.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-09-05 21:33 UTC

I think "around 68" as what to aim for is reasonable.  I think given that we end commit messages with a period, I'm not sure hitting 76 is really an issue?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-09-05 23:20 UTC

A commit message has a subject line and a body, and the context from the PR you linked is that we’re talking about both.

**Greg Price** · 2019-09-06 01:59 UTC

> I think given that we end commit messages with a period, I'm not sure hitting 76 is really an issue?

Yeah, plus for summary lines (which is what I think you mean here) I think the exact maximum is less sensitive than for prose. Partly because in prose, whatever you set as the maximum you'll often hit because in every paragraph $$ n-1 $$ of the lines are bumping up as close to the limit as they can get.

**Greg Price** · 2019-09-06 02:01 UTC

So I'd be quite happy with "around 68 columns" as the headline rule -- together with the key practical advice of please set up auto-wrapping in your editor and set the wrap width to a value 70 or less. That's the thing that makes it automatic so there's no need to nag nor to fix it up ourselves.

**Greg Price** · 2019-09-06 02:02 UTC

And then if an information-dense summary line is up to 76 or so columns, being OK with that.

**Wyatt Hoodes** · 2020-03-13 07:50 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-13 21:57 UTC

(replying to Yash RE)
> kinda unrelated to this... but what's a good line length to wrap in-code comments?

For paragraphs of prose, the width that's good for reading is basically the same as for the prose in the body of a commit message, for the same reasons. So a width of 68 of 70 columns is a good one to wrap at.

See for example discussion around [here](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/3-backend/topic/commit.20line.20length/near/786552), a few months ago in this topic.

That's 68 columns of *text*, though -- and one thing about code comments is that the text usually starts out fairly indented. E.g. 4 or 8 or more columns of code indentation, then 2-3 columns for `# ` or `// `. So when the text is 68 columns wide, the total length of the line might be 74 or 83 or more.

For getting your editor to wrap the comment for you, you typically have to set a total line length, rather than a width for just the text. I set that to 80, which makes a pretty good approximation of "68 columns of text".

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-12-31 15:17 UTC

Probably some issue with the attribute statements. Yes, the IdP needs to pass email. From the instructions for the setting ``SOCIAL_AUTH_SAML_ENABLED_IDPS`` :

> The values needed in the attr_ fields are often configurable in your IdP’s interface when setting up SAML authentication (referred to as “Attribute Statements” with Okta, or “Attribute Mapping” with GSuite). You’ll want to connect these so that Zulip gets the email address (used as a unique user ID) and name for the user.

**Anusha Harish** · 2019-12-31 15:18 UTC

@Mateusz Mandera Thank you. I will check

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-12-31 15:23 UTC

Ah, I see. The attribute statements your idp is sending:
```
    <saml:AttributeStatement>
      <saml:Attribute Name="urn:oid:0.9.2342.19200300.100.1.1" NameFormat="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:uri">
        <saml:AttributeValue xsi:type="xs:string">student@gmail.com</saml:AttributeValue>
      </saml:Attribute>
      <saml:Attribute Name="urn:oid:1.3.6.1.4.1.5923.1.1.1.1" NameFormat="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:uri">
        <saml:AttributeValue xsi:type="xs:string">member</saml:AttributeValue>
        <saml:AttributeValue xsi:type="xs:string">student</saml:AttributeValue>
      </saml:Attribute>
    </saml:AttributeStatement>
```
Which is fine, but it uses the codes ``urn:oid:XXXX`` for names. So you either need to make your idp send attribute names like ``email``, ``first_name``, ``last_name``, or putting the codes in the ``SOCIAL_AUTH_SAML_ENABLED_IDPS`` dictionary in the ``attr_*`` configuration. @Anusha Harish

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-12-31 15:25 UTC

You should also send the ``first_name`` and ``full_name``.  Here is a template of attribute statements that okta sends, that the server does understand easily:
```
    <saml2:AttributeStatement>
        <saml2:Attribute Name="first_name" NameFormat="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:unspecified">
            <saml2:AttributeValue
                xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"
                xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:type="xs:string">user.firstName
            </saml2:AttributeValue>
        </saml2:Attribute>
        <saml2:Attribute Name="last_name" NameFormat="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:unspecified">
            <saml2:AttributeValue
                xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"
                xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:type="xs:string">user.lastName
            </saml2:AttributeValue>
        </saml2:Attribute>
        <saml2:Attribute Name="email" NameFormat="urn:oasis:names:tc:SAML:2.0:attrname-format:unspecified">
            <saml2:AttributeValue
                xmlns:xs="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema"
                xmlns:xsi="http://www.w3.org/2001/XMLSchema-instance" xsi:type="xs:string">user.email
            </saml2:AttributeValue>
        </saml2:Attribute>
    </saml2:AttributeStatement>
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-09-13 20:11 UTC

Well, the default configuration is
```
OnCalendar=*-*-* 6,18:00
RandomizedDelaySec=12h
Persistent=true
```
and you didn’t override any of this except `RandomizedDelaySec`, so I think all you’re doing is adding more invocations.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-09-13 20:12 UTC

But any kind of time-based solution is going to be fragile.

**Vishnu KS** · 2019-09-14 19:01 UTC

hmm. Makes sense. I thought the file will override the default.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-09-14 21:20 UTC

`override.conf` is just an arbitrary filename (and, by the way, it would be clearer to call it something like `zulip-droplet.conf`). All the `*.conf` files in the `.d` directory are parsed after the unit file itself. (Documentation: [systemd.unit(5)](https://www.freedesktop.org/software/systemd/man/systemd.unit.html).) So you can override lines on a line-by-line basis, but it won’t automatically assume you want to override *everything*.

I'm migrating RealmAuditLog.event_type from charfield to int. From preliminary investigation it seems like postgres (and django) do support the following:
* For each row, replace the str value of event_type (e.g. 'user_created') with the string version of the new value (e.g. '123')
* AlterField event_type from charfield to int

Another option though would be something like
* Rename event_type (str) to event_type_old (str)
* Create a new field event_type (int)
* Copy the data from event_type_old to event_type, doing the str->int conversion
* Delete event_type_old

Please correct me if I'm wrong here, but I don't think that we support sending users' custom profile field data in our API yet right? I can't find any entries for this in the docs nor can I find any support for this in the source code. We have `^realm/profile_fields$` to be able to create or modify the custom profile fields themselves but nothing for getting the user-by-user data. **Hemanth V. Alluri** · 2019-10-16 14:51 UTC

If we're okay with adding this functionality, I'd be more than happy to write the code for it. I was thinking that we could just modify the `/users` endpoint to take an optional parameter and the return custom profile fields id that optional parameter is set to true (akin to what we're doing with `client_gravatar` right now). Since we don't currently have a feature like "private custom profile fields" vs "public custom profile fields" (everything is just public) we don't need to do any extra privacy checks (people only add data if they want to let it be public). ## Memcached Bad Key Error

*2019-10-20 to 2019-10-21 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Memcached.20Bad.20Key.20Error/with/792624)*

**Hemanth V. Alluri** · 2019-10-20 18:18 UTC

I was testing some changes, and when I ran `get_realm_user_dicts(Realm.objects.get(id=2))`, I made when I noticed:
```
pylibmc.BadKeyProvided: error 33 from memcached_get(:1:f5cf256661499e215683f9d5847cb): (0x3326770) A BAD KEY WAS PROVIDED/CHARACTERS OUT OF RANGE, Key provided had invalid character. -> libmemcached/key.cc:103
```

I initially thought that I might have accidentally messed something up but then I checked out master and after running `./tools/do-destroy-rebuild-database` and running `get_realm_user_dicts(Realm.objects.get(id=2))` again, I noticed the same issue. Does this mean that our caching system is broken somewhere, or is this something that we could ignore?

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-10-21 04:49 UTC

@Hemanth V. Alluri that's just a bug in your code.  `get_realm_user_dicts` expects a `realm_id`, not a `Realm`, and memcached doesn't know how to serialize a Realm object correctly.  (And the Django/memcached error message isn't great for this case).

**Hemanth V. Alluri** · 2019-10-21 05:21 UTC

Oh, right, that was quite a stupid mistake. Thanks for helping!

```
# This is a 2-stage Docker build.  In the first stage, we build a
# Zulip development environment image and use
# tools/build-release-tarball to generate a production release tarball
# from the provided Git ref.
FROM ubuntu:18.04 as base

# Set up working locales and upgrade the base image
ENV LANG="C.UTF-8"

ARG UBUNTU_MIRROR

RUN { [ ! "$UBUNTU_MIRROR" ] || sed -i "s|http://\(\w*\.\)*archive\.ubuntu\.com/ubuntu/\? |$UBUNTU_MIRROR |" /etc/apt/sources.list; } && \
    apt-get -q update && \
    apt-get -q dist-upgrade -y && \
    DEBIAN_FRONTEND=noninteractive \
        apt-get -q install --no-install-recommends -y ca-certificates git locales lsb-release python3 sudo tzdata


FROM base as build

# Add a zulip user
RUN useradd -d /home/zulip -m zulip && \
    echo 'zulip ALL=(ALL:ALL) NOPASSWD:ALL' >> /etc/sudoers

USER zulip
WORKDIR /home/zulip

# You can specify these in docker-compose.yml or with
#   docker build --build-args "ZULIP_GIT_REF=git_branch_name" .
ARG ZULIP_GIT_URL=https://github.com/zulip/zulip.git
ARG ZULIP_GIT_REF=master

RUN git clone "$ZULIP_GIT_URL" && \
    cd zulip && \
    git checkout -b current "$ZULIP_GIT_REF"

WORKDIR /home/zulip/zulip

ARG CUSTOM_CA_CERTIFICATES

# Finally, we provision the development environment and build a release tarball
RUN ./tools/provision --production-travis
RUN . /srv/zulip-py3-venv/bin/activate && \
    ./tools/build-release-tarball docker && \
    mv /tmp/tmp.*/zulip-server-docker.tar.gz /tmp/zulip-server-docker.tar.gz


# In the second stage, we build the production image from the release tarball
FROM base

ENV DATA_DIR="/data"

# Then, with a second image, we install the production release tarball.
COPY --from=build /tmp/zulip-server-docker.tar.gz /root/
COPY custom_zulip_files/ /root/custom_zulip

ARG CUSTOM_CA_CERTIFICATES

RUN \
    # Make sure Nginx is started by Supervisor.
    dpkg-divert --add --rename /etc/init.d/nginx && \
    ln -s /bin/true /etc/init.d/nginx && \
    mkdir -p "$DATA_DIR" && \
    cd /root && \
    tar -xf zulip-server-docker.tar.gz && \
    rm -f zulip-server-docker.tar.gz && \
    mv zulip-server-docker zulip && \
    cp -rf /root/custom_zulip/* /root/zulip && \
    rm -rf /root/custom_zulip && \
    export PUPPET_CLASSES="zulip::dockervoyager, zulip::postfix_localmail" \
           DEPLOYMENT_TYPE="dockervoyager" \
           ADDITIONAL_PACKAGES="expect" && \
    /root/zulip/scripts/setup/install --hostname="$(hostname)" --email="docker-zulip" --no-init-db && \
    rm -f /etc/zulip/zulip-secrets.conf /etc/zulip/settings.py && \
    apt-get -qq autoremove --purge -y && \
    apt-get -qq clean && \
    rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/* /tmp/* /var/tmp/*

COPY entrypoint.sh /sbin/entrypoint.sh
COPY certbot-deploy-hook /sbin/certbot-deploy-hook

VOLUME ["$DATA_DIR"]
EXPOSE 80 443 25

ENTRYPOINT ["/sbin/entrypoint.sh"]
CMD ["app:run"]
```

        ):
            first_step_data = {"username": email,
                               "password": password,
                               "two_factor_login_view-current_step": "auth"}
            result = self.client_post("/accounts/login/", first_step_data)
            self.assertEqual(result.status_code, 200)

            second_step_data = {"token-otp_token": str(token),
                                "two_factor_login_view-current_step": "token"}
            result = self.client_post("/accounts/login/", second_step_data)
            self.assertEqual(result.status_code, 302)
            self.assertEqual(result['Location'], 'http://zulip.testserver')

            # Going to login page should redirect to `realm.uri` if user is
            # already logged in.
            result = self.client_get('/accounts/login/')
            self.assertEqual(result.status_code, 302)
            self.assertEqual(result['Location'], 'http://zulip.testserver')
```

Specifically, why do we set the ldap password as the "normal" password in the database?
```
        password = self.ldap_password()

        user_profile.save()
```

```
user_profile = get_user_profile_by_email("username@example.com")

## recipient_id denormalization

*2019-12-04 to 2019-12-05 · 23 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/recipient_id.20denormalization/with/800350)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-04 01:42 UTC

In #13453, we're planning to denormalize the Recipient ID for a user_profile object into the UserProfile table, basically because it makes it easier for us to do important database queries efficiently.  There's limited potential risk to the change since Recipient mappings never change.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-04 01:43 UTC

We're likely to end up wanting to add similar denormalization for the Stream and Huddle tables, in part for symmetry and in part because there are a number of other places where queries are complicated by the need to e.g. first fetch a Stream object and then do a second query to get its Recipient ID for joining (i.e. the same situation that made us want to do this for UserProfile).

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-04 01:45 UTC

Which suggests we should think about naming for such denormalization columns in concert.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-04 01:46 UTC

The current proposal is `user_profile.personal_recipient_id`, which makes sense in isolation, but when thinking about the use case of Stream, for example, I think a `stream.recipient_id` or `huddle.recipient_id` makes more sense.  In which case we should probably make it `user_profile.recipient` as well.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-04 01:46 UTC

Thoughts?

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-04 01:49 UTC

(The PR is otherwise ready to merge and something we want for the release since it avoids what would otherwise be a significant performance regression)

**Greg Price** · 2019-12-04 01:54 UTC

`recipient_id` sounds good to me.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-04 17:51 UTC

@Mateusz Mandera @Steve Howell any thoughts?

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-12-04 17:52 UTC

If we want to add to Stream and Huddle, then I also think uniformly having  ``recipient_id`` makes the most sense.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-04 17:54 UTC

Sounds good.  Thoughts on whether it's worth writing the migration for `Stream` at this time?  I think we'd be able to use that in a few places for small performance gains fairly immediately.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-04 17:55 UTC

Seems like it might be advantageous to do it while we have this in mind.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-04 17:55 UTC

(We essentially never interact with the `Huddle` table itself, so I'm not sure I'd bother with that at this time)

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-12-04 18:03 UTC

If the UserProfile change ends up without issues, i think it  would make sense to do it for ``Stream``, since the migration should be very analogical. I can take care of it if we want that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-04 18:18 UTC

Yeah, let's do it.  I've already test-deployed on chat.zulip.org without issue, so I think we've confirmed the migration works.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-04 18:18 UTC

(I'll need to remember to undo the migration when we deploy the next version)

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-12-04 18:22 UTC

Do we want it in a single commit (And migration file) with the ``UserProfile`` one?

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-04 18:24 UTC

Yeah, I think that's reasonable.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-04 18:24 UTC

BTW we don't need to clear caches -- when one deploys a new Zulip version, we change all cache keys (by changing the cache prefix)

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-04 18:24 UTC

So you can simplify the second migration a bit.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-12-04 18:26 UTC

ah, cool!

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-12-05 20:39 UTC

Basically every place where we call ``get_personal_recipient``, ``get_stream_recipient``, ``bulk_get_recipients`` (or similar) seems like an obvious candidate to see if things can't be improved there. That's quite a few places. Do we want to go over all the low-hanging fruit before the release?

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-12-05 22:10 UTC

Okay, PR updated.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-05 23:44 UTC

I don't think there's urgency to convert all of those places, but I think it'd be worth opening a follow up issue to track that.

I want to hard code the redirect_uri to IP like 10.0.0.1  ,  which code should I modify it ?
I know that Zulip is use social-auth to do the SSO. So I think we should pass the redirect_uri to  GithubOAuth2. but I don't know how to write the code.
GitHubAuthBackend(SocialAuthMixin, GithubOAuth2):

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2019-12-07 17:39 UTC

You can try overriding this original function (or the self.redirect_uri attribute itself) in the backend (it's inherited from ``OAuthAuth`` class - you may need to dive into ``python-social-auth`` internals):
```
    def get_redirect_uri(self, state=None):
        """Build redirect with redirect_state parameter."""
        uri = self.redirect_uri
        if self.REDIRECT_STATE and state:
            uri = url_add_parameters(uri, {'redirect_state': state})
        return uri
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-09 00:29 UTC

@willy you can also just register a DNS name mapping to that IP address.

**willy** · 2019-12-09 01:42 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-12-18 03:07 UTC

This might work:
```udiff
--- a/puppet/zulip/manifests/base.pp
+++ b/puppet/zulip/manifests/base.pp
@@ -91,9 +91,17 @@ class zulip::base {
   ]
 
   # $::memorysize_mb is a string in Facter < 3.0 and a double in Facter ≥ 3.0.
-  # Either way, convert it to an integer.
-  $total_memory_mb_array = scanf("${::memorysize_mb} ", '%i')
-  $total_memory_mb = $total_memory_mb_array[0]
+  # Either way, convert it to an integer in one of two ways, both of which are
+  # stupid, depending on the Puppet version.  (╯°□°）╯︵ ┻━┻
+  case $::puppetversion {
+    /^3\./: {
+      $total_memory_mb = 0 + inline_template('<%= @memorysize_mb.to_i %>')
+    }
+    default: {
+      $total_memory_mb_array = scanf("${::memorysize_mb} ", '%i')
+      $total_memory_mb = $total_memory_mb_array[0]
+    }
+  }
 
   group { 'zulip':
     ensure     => present,
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-16 16:08 UTC

Just to clarify, we do not have CentOS support today and there are 0 installations using it, so the [specific issue](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/18179) that I think was bugging @Alex Vandiver (writing upgrade code to instalupgrading a CentOS machine) isn't a problem - we don't need code to support that.

What we have today is 80% of the plumbing for doing CentOS support, which is useful for making it within striking distance when we want to do that, and it's nice to preserve that plumbing, but because it is not functional, I don't think we should apply undue effort to avoid breaking it (it's reasonable to defer challenging/annoying new work for supporting that to a focused effort to support the enterprise Linux).

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-04-16 16:54 UTC

What sparked this was not just the upgrade, but also two other things in quick succession:
 - writing code to stop apache is different, so it affects #14959, which I'm also working on.  I'll ignore it, but I know it's another incompatibility.
 - the yaml package name in 3314fefaec8d754e039c73fba5710bedc0c63313 for CentOS is wrong, so installs have been broken since at least then, if not before.

My point is that its mere existence causes more effort; every time code touches something which is inside a CentOS conditional, we have to decide (without testing) what the appropriate change is inside that if clause for the CentOS side.  Leaving it unchanged increases the effort by making the Debian/Ubuntu code less clear, by obscuring the parallelism of what the clause was trying to do - e.g. making it look like Ubuntu needs an extra package, when really it was never added to the CentOS side.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-16 17:15 UTC

Yeah, makes sense.  Effectively we're paying the tax of maintaining our almost-CentOS support while not getting the benefit of having it.  It may be that we're not doing too much more work than what we'd need to do anyway if we were to start on CentOS support from scratch now, but we have been carrying the incomplete feature for a few years now without actually focusing on finishing it, which is annoying.

I guess as another option for dealing with this sort of situation, I think it's OK to post a comment on the CentOS PR when changing something likely to break CentOS.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-04-16 17:17 UTC

2. Open the mobile web browser on the same phone, and try to log in to the same server.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-24 20:09 UTC

I think probably what we should do is as follows:
(1) Report an issue to `python-social-auth` upstream for the thing @Anders Kaseorg noted; I think at the very least, they should offer an option to clear the session on authentication flow startup, but likely it's actually just a bug that they don't unconditionally clear `FIELDS_STORED_IN_SESSION`.
(2) If we don't get a reply on that, we can likely patch this without forking by providing our own definition of `social_django.views.auth`; the base definition is, and it's included via `social_django.urls`:

## subscribers perf

*2019-12-28 to 2021-01-19 · 90 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/subscribers.20perf/with/804765)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-28 20:21 UTC

So, thanks to @Steve Howell's recent work, our frontend performance in handling the quadratic size of subscriber lists in large, public organizations like this one is improving significantly.

There's another significant performance problem caused by this data structure, which @Anders Kaseorg and I did some digging into maybe 2-3 months ago.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-28 20:22 UTC

That other problem is that the work of fetching, marshalling, and compressing the section of `page_params` data related to subscribers gets to be quite expensive in those organizations, for the same quadratic reasons.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-28 20:23 UTC

The current data structure lists, for each stream, a list of user IDs that are subscribed to it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-28 20:24 UTC

The problem with that data structure is that while all the default streams (i.e. the ones every user is on when they join) on chat.zulip.org have 12K-13K users subscribed, each one has a slightly different list of subscribers, so it doesn't compress super well.

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-28 20:24 UTC

However, probably 12K of those users have never changed their subscriptions from the set of streams when they joined, and among those users, there's only probably a dozen different sets of streams.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-12-28 20:51 UTC

Ideally we can find a generic compression algorithm for this. I am pretty sure we sort user_ids within streams, so typical data would look roughly like this (where users 5, 1, and 6 unsubscribed):

~~~
101: 1, 2,3,4,6,7,8,9,10
102: 2,3,4,5,6,7,8,9,10
103: 1,2,3,4,5,7,8,9,10
~~~

In the above we'd want a compression algorithm that could find long strings like "2,3,4" and "7,8,9,10" compress them to a few bits.

**Steve Howell** · 2019-12-28 20:58 UTC

I would be worthwhile to see how well gzip compresses real-life czo data.  Basically you want to compute (a - b) / (c - d) where
* a = len of gzipped page_params
* b = len of gzipped page_param sans subscribers
* c = len of page_params
* d = len of page_params sans subscribers

You want to do this instead of slightly simpler calculations, because it's important that the rest of the payload doesn't undermine gzip's ability to compress just the subscribers part.  (It's a bit complex--if subscribers truly dominates the payload, it should dominate the compression algorithm's choices of what to compress, but I don't want to make too many assumptions.)

**Steve Howell** · 2019-12-28 21:00 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2019-12-29 02:40 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2019-12-29 03:53 UTC

Right, I tried a couple of different explicit compression schemes in September.

1. current (each stream has a sorted list of user IDs): 6118539 uncompressed, 1506981 compressed
2. each user has a sorted list of stream IDs: 5591334 uncompressed, 748484 compressed
3. each user has a “stream set ID” pointing to a deduplicated sorted list of stream IDs: 4180933 uncompressed, 741109 compressed
4. users are sorted lexicographically by their sorted list of stream IDs, which are then delta-compressed against the previous user’s list: 4109543 uncompressed, 738485 compressed
5. subscriptions are stored in some crazy trie structure: 4151884 uncompressed, 743230 compressed
6. subscription data is deleted entirely (for a lower bound): 3957432 uncompressed, 688850 compressed

The compressed benefit of anything more complicated than 2 is minimal.

~~~ py
 10 def transpose(data):
 11     d = {}
 12

 14         stream_id, user_ids = row
 15         for user_id in user_ids:
 16             if user_id not in d:
 17                 d[user_id] = []
 18             d[user_id].append(stream_id)
 19
 20     d = list(d.items())

 22
 23     res = {}
 24     for k, g in itertools.groupby(d, key=lambda d: d[1]):

 26         res[str(k)] = users
 27     return res
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2019-12-31 10:20 UTC

For the three things that need subscribers:
* Stream Edit UI - could be fetched on demand for unsubscribed streams (most people edit streams infrequently)
* compose fade - subscriber info is only needed for streams you subscribe to
* mentioning unsubscribed person - subscriber info is only needed for streams you subscribe to

There's also a fourth edge case, where you can technically attempt to create a stream link to a public stream that you're not subscribed to, while composing to a private stream you do subscribe to.  And we check there to ensure that the subscribers to the linked stream are a subset of the subscribers of the stream the message is going to (so as not to link the private stream's name).  But I think this check already returns false if you're not subscribed to the other stream.  I think we could work around that.

So, again, I don't think we really need subscriber data for your unsubscribed streams until you go to the edit UI.  Which seems like a reasonable tradeoff.

But it could be significant for anyone who's dropped a few subscriptions, or in organizations with a less pathological data case.
* I believe mobile is using `include_subscribers=false`, and so won't be directly affected by changes here.  If it is, the right model would be to add an option to the functions called by the `page_params` code path.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-01-09 10:08 UTC

@Dinesh ch Okay, so for this test (and ``test_github_oauth2_email_not_associated``) to keep testing what they're intended to test (user choosing an email we don't want to accept, so a ``noreply.github.com``email in this test) you need to change the ``email_data`` dict (that's the dictionary of email associated with the github account we're simulating). It is:
```
        email_data = [
            dict(email="notprimary@zulip.com",
                 verified=True),
            dict(email="hamlet@zulip.com",
                 verified=True,
                 primary=True),
            dict(email=account_data_dict["email"],
                 verified=True),
        ]
```

so with the new behavior, the ``hamlet@zulip.com`` will get picked. I think it makes sense to change that to a different email that doesn't have an account in the realm. And then test should make sense again.

The reason the ``chosen_email`` is ``None`` in your debugging session is because `` chosen_email = backend.strategy.request_data().get('email')``. This code actually gets called twice on paths with the "choose email screen" - once without ``email`` GET param - then the user ends up with the "choose email" screen displayed, and chooses the email which then will get passed in the ``email`` GET parameter, and the code gets called again and this time ``chosen_email`` won't be ``None``.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-01-09 10:12 UTC

But after adjusting this test, we'll indeed also need new ones to test other cases - such as the ``email_data`` dict having a verified email belonging to an existing account in the realm, but the user passing an invalid (in any sense) email in the ``email`` get param - then the existing account should get picked I think, except the ``is_signup`` case where the path to an error will be correct. We need to make sure behavior around these cases (and similar) makes sense and have tests for that.

In general, the social backends testing system is fairly complicated compared to most other tests, so it is a steeper learning curve to figure it out.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-01-09 10:13 UTC

As a final note, in your current code:
```
        if not chosen_email:
            avatars = {}  # Dict[str, str]
            existing_account_emails = []
            for email in verified_emails:
                existing_account = common_get_active_user(email, realm, {})
                if existing_account is not None:
                    existing_account_emails.append(email)
                    avatars[email] = avatar_url(existing_account)
            if (len(existing_account_emails) > 1 or backend.strategy.session_get('is_signup') == '1'):
                return render(backend.strategy.request, 'zerver/social_auth_select_email.html', context = {
                    'primary_email': verified_emails[0],
                    'verified_non_primary_emails': verified_emails[1:],
                    'backend': 'github',
                    'avatar_urls': avatars,
                })
            else:
                chosen_email = existing_account_emails[0]
```

you have a bug occurring when there are no ``existing_account_emails`` - because the code goes to the ``else`` case and tries ``chosen_email = existing_account_emails[0]`` which will fail. I believe ``len(existing_account_emails) != 1`` will be correct (and you have ``>``).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-01-02 22:27 UTC

In `puppet/zulip/templates/memcached.conf.template.erb`:

```
<% if scope["zulip::base::release_name"] == "xenial" -%>
# Use "modern" features.
-o slab_reassign,slab_automove,lru_crawler,lru_maintainer,maxconns_fast,hash_algorithm=murmur3
<% end -%>
```

That should have been `!= "trusty"` and enabled on bionic, right?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-01-02 22:31 UTC

Oh, maybe all the modern features are default now.

**Greg Price** · 2020-01-03 02:43 UTC

Rereading the commits and the links from them, I think the answer is that since v1.5.0 these options are enabled by default.

Haven't 100% fact-checked that -- the remaining question is whether `-o modern` in v1.4.39 included all the things we have in that line. The answer to that should be in the release notes somewhere. But it sounds like it's very likely yes.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-03 20:05 UTC

Might still be wrong for Debian, though; I think Anders is right that we want to delete that conditional.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-03 20:06 UTC

My guess is what happened here is the `grep`s that I did to look for Xeniak-checks to audit for ones that should have been `!Trusty` only looked in `puppet/zulip/manifests`, not the templates.

**Greg Price** · 2020-01-03 23:38 UTC

> Might still be wrong for Debian, though; I think Anders is right that we want to delete that conditional.

I'm not sure which direction this is intended to mean.

I think most likely we want to have that `-o` line just for a set of moderately-old releases: the releases new enough to have those options, but old enough that they're not just all on by default. If we carry them on into the future, that (a) is messy and (b) potentially disables further improvements in later versions.

**Greg Price** · 2020-01-03 23:39 UTC

Specifically, Trusty was too old to support them (or some of them, at least). But memcached v1.5.0 enables many of them, and I think probably all of them, by default. The open fact-checking question I mentioned above is to confirm that it includes all of them.

**Greg Price** · 2020-01-03 23:41 UTC

Debian buster introduced 1.5.x: https://packages.debian.org/memcached

Ditto Ubuntu bionic: http://packages.ubuntu.com/memcached

**Greg Price** · 2020-01-03 23:43 UTC

Oh, I see we support Debian stretch (aka oldstable). That has memcached 1.4.33, newer than xenial's 1.4.25 but older than 1.5.0. So stretch should probably get the same treatment as xenial.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-04 00:44 UTC

It might make sense for us to just resync our memcached config file defaults based on what Debian Buster ships.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-04 00:44 UTC

(with options for backwards-compatibility)

**Greg Price** · 2020-01-04 01:06 UTC

Sure. I'd want to think of it more as merging -- there'll have been some changes in Debian, and there are also changes we made that we presumably want to keep, like to the user and the memory allocation. (And fixing the trailing whitespace.)

## email_mirror renaming

*2020-01-14 to 2020-01-14 · 13 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/email_mirror.20renaming/with/808892)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-01-14 18:57 UTC

So as was discussed in a PR [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/13643#issuecomment-573506793) our "email mirror" system's naming is rather messy - files with code are named ``email_mirror.py``. In the main user documentation we call it "incoming email integration" - https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/production/email-gateway.html - and in some places we call it "email gateway".
We definitely should rename the ``email_mirror`` files - the main question is what naming we should settle on. Do we want ``email_gateway.py`` (and ``email-gateway`` for some other files instead of ``email-mirror``) or ``incoming_email`` or something else altogether?

**Rein Zustand** · 2020-01-14 19:16 UTC

I'd vote for `email_gateway`, `email-gateway`. `incoming_email` restricts the functionality too much. In the future, the bridge could be bidirectional, i.e. someone posting a reply in the stream could have their message also sent to the email sender.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-01-14 19:33 UTC

I actually vote for a name that most specifically describes what it does now, unless we are planning extensions in the pretty near future.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-14 20:47 UTC

Yeah, fundamentally, the outgoing email system is `zerver/lib/email_notifications.py`, and I am happy with our structural separation of those as different components (even if they are designed to work together).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-14 20:48 UTC

I think giving that we're calling it the "Incoming email integration" as the title in the user-facing documentation, which I think makes sense, probably `zerver/lib/incoming_email.py` or `zerver/lib/email_integration.py` would be appropriate.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-14 20:49 UTC

I think `incoming_email.py` is probably most explicit about its purpose: It's the library for processing emails sent into Zulip.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-01-14 21:16 UTC

I suppose one argument in favor of ``email_gateway`` could be that the main setting for the system is called ``EMAIL_GATEWAY_PATTERN``, which would be nicely consistent. Or we could rename that setting in some way, though setting renaming is somewhat annoying.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-14 21:41 UTC

Well, I guess one way to name components would be that:
* The postfix or IMAP component is the "email gateway" part of the system (which is what those settings ultimately configure)
* The part of the Zulip server that processes incoming emails that it receives from there is the "incoming email" processing system, so `zerver/lib/incoming_email.py`, an `incoming_email` queue, etc.

Does that make sense?

**Greg Price** · 2020-01-14 22:24 UTC

It seems simpler to me to have one name, like "incoming email" / "incoming-email integration".

For me, the name "email gateway" has never conveyed much meaning, other than as an arbitrary bit of Zulip-specific jargon. It doesn't make particularly more sense to me as describing the Postfix or IMAP configuration than as describing the corresponding application code within our server.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-01-14 22:31 UTC

My vote:
- rename the module to `incoming_email.py`
- leave the docs as "incoming email integration"
- don't worry about the setting, they are indeed a pain to change (but maybe add a comment there)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-14 23:12 UTC

I'm happy with Steve's proposal, extending it to include renaming the cron job and RabbitMQ queue to `incoming_email` as well.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-14 23:12 UTC

(From "email_mirror", which is what it is today)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-14 23:15 UTC

So I think we should start with a series of commits like this:
* Rename `email_mirror.py` -> `incoming_email.py`
* Rename `email_mirror_helpers.py` -> `incoming_email_encoding.py`
* (Maybe any other simple changes with no side effects)
* Rename the `email_mirror` cron job (requires some care in puppet to delete the old file)

And then figure out a technical plan for renaming remaining references to `email_mirror`.  (In particular, renaming the queue may be somewhat annoying since we need to figure out how to kill the old one).


## websockets removal

*2020-01-15 to 2020-12-30 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/websockets.20removal/with/809227)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-15 06:33 UTC

Just an update that we're about to merge #12862, which removes Zulip's direct use of `sockjs`/Websockets.  Historically, it was only ever used in an attempt to reduce connection startup latency when sending messages, which with our current HTTP/2 configuration, at least, is no longer material.  When we first wrote the Tornado/sockjs code back in 2014, we had planned to consider moving our server-to-client push system to use it, but we've been happy with the longpolling experience thus far, so I'm not sure what would cause us to feel a strong need to switch.  And the `sockjs-tornado` library we've been relying on is more or less unmaintained upstream.  

So removing this system from the codebase lets us decrease complexity significantly and remove what was a critical unmaintained dependency with no real downsides, which is a big win.  We're still indirectly using sockjs in the development environment at least via Webpack.

(It's currently test-deployed here as of ~30 minutes ago, but we've been testing a setting that disabled it without deleting the code for months on zulipchat.com without anyone noticing, so I don't expect any issues)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-15 06:34 UTC

If we later decide to re-introduce using a third-party library for websockets or similar, we'll likely want to use the new Django channels rather than base something off the old system anyway.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-15 06:35 UTC

ea6934c26d226055f0d1fac6737e4b235f0d7783 has more details for anyone curious.  It's always really nice whenever we get to remove big pieces of code from Zulip; especially so in this case, where the code was some of the least well-tested code in Zulip.

**Rein Zustand** · 2020-01-15 11:18 UTC

I'm kind of surprised that even zulipchat.com is used for testing.

**Greg Price** · 2020-01-15 18:31 UTC

> I'm kind of surprised that even zulipchat.com is used for testing.
I think the key thing to be tested here was whether there were networks out there (that users were on), or browsers (that users were using), that behaved poorly with the new configuration. For that, basically the only way to test is to deploy to a large set of users and watch closely. Google regularly does the same thing on google.com, for things like HTTP/2 and new TLS/SSL features.

The code itself was, I'm sure, well tested already.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-15 19:32 UTC

Yep, that is correct.  We'd tested it extensively in other environments before.  The setting to disable websockets has been in production use for years.

**Rein Zustand** · 2020-01-15 19:35 UTC

> Yep, that is correct. We'd tested it extensively in other environments before. The setting to disable websockets has been in production use for years.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-15 20:32 UTC

"Other environments" here means self-hosted users who have proxy/network constraints that didn't support websockets.

**Greg Price** · 2020-01-23 19:42 UTC

## presence API

*2020-01-24 to 2020-01-24 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/presence.20API/with/811593)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-24 21:17 UTC

So, inspired by the issue report about "two weeks ago", I spent some time thinking about how we want this to actually work.  See https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/13734 for my issue writeup.  There's several things we need to discuss here before that's something we can work; the one I'd like to focus on is what we want the new presence data encoding to be, for which we'll want the @*mobile* folks involved.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-24 21:17 UTC

I think it's clear we don't want a JSON dictionary keyed by email addresses in any case; this is one of the last bastions of not using user IDs to refer to users.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-24 21:25 UTC

One simplified protocol format would be roughly this:
```
{
user_id: {
    timestamp: <timestamp>,  # timestamp for the most recent activity record
    status?: "idle", # Optional; if the timestamp is old or status is offline, this is implied and added by the client.
}
```

There's a few other fields one could optionally include, and we might want to support, but perhaps should be optional:

* `pushable?: True` (Whether the user will receive notification if you PM them)
* `clients: ["ZulipMobile", "ZulipElectron"]` (Something indicating what clients types the user is offline?)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-24 21:26 UTC

It's a little too bad that there's not an easy way to get it down to just a `user_id -> timestamp` dictionary; I suppose we could have the format optionally allow that structure for users who are offline.
