## 'anchor' API design

*2020-01-28 to 2020-02-07 · 17 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/.27anchor.27.20API.20design/with/812682)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-28 02:33 UTC

The wart that has long been present inin Zulip's `get_messages` API is how to request "the latest messages" in the API.  In https://github.com/zulip/zulip-mobile/issues/3654 we discuss a bug caused by this, which came up with a proposal I like.

Currently, the recommendation is basically to pass `anchor=10000000000` (for an appropriately huge number).  An accident of the server's implementation meant that specific number was actually important to avoid a buggy value for `found_newest`.  Anyway, @Greg Price's proposal is to allow passing `anchor='latest'`, basically a special string-type value that the server can interpret as meaning the user really just wants the most recent messages.  We might also want an analogous `anchor='first'` or similar to avoid folks needing to write a somewhat ugly `anchor=0` for fetching the very first messages.  While it's not always ideal to make a value have a variable type like this, it feels to me like a really clean way to express the idea of what the user is asking for in the API.

One question I'm a bit uncertain about is whether we want `latest` or `last` (and e.g. `first` vs. `earliest`).  I think maybe `last`/`first` feels more natural to me because that's what Django and jQuery (and probably a lot of other software) use for use cases like `queryset.last()` (to fetch the very last value), and also because `earliest` (what's closest to `latest`) feels way less intuitive than `first`.  Thoughts?

@Steve Howell I'd like your thoughts on this especially since I think you've spent nearly as much time as I had being sad about this API detail in the past.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-01-28 02:57 UTC

First/last seems fine to me.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-28 06:07 UTC

Opened https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/13747 with an implementation of that concept using last/first.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-28 22:51 UTC

Greg proposed "newest" and "oldest", which matches existing fields; I think we can proceed with that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-29 02:12 UTC

Updated here: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/13747

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-29 02:13 UTC

@Greg Price thoughts on the name for that field?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-29 02:13 UTC

The `first_unread` is probably a sensible name; the one thing that makes me hesitant is the semantics are "the first unread message, or the latest message if there are no unreads"

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-29 02:14 UTC

Which I guess is conceptually the same thing if we treat the first unread as "the next message that will be sent".

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-29 02:14 UTC

So maybe that name is fine.

## server initialization

*2020-01-30 to 2020-02-12 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/server.20initialization/with/813470)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-30 20:44 UTC

@Mateusz Mandera @Anders Kaseorg @Steve Howell FYI.

Following #13774, it's now the case that we share a our Zulip server initialization code between the development environment and the production environment, which is great.  It's run inside `populate_db` and `manage.py initialize_production_database`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-30 20:44 UTC

Looking at the code there, however, I'm now wondering whether it'd make sense to rework things so that we can delete this block of code.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-30 20:45 UTC

The main thing that it does is create the "system bot" realm and users, and we have in the past put together a design where we eliminate them as a concept (basically, moving them to be bot users that are automatically generated in each realm during realm creation).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-30 20:46 UTC

(There may be other designs, e.g. just creating them when the first realm is created)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-30 20:47 UTC

The main advantage of eliminating this initialization step is that it'd simplify the installation process to not require us to touch the database in production from the `zulip` container (i.e. after settings are created) and it'd remove some confusion involving users seeing this "system bot realm".

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-30 20:48 UTC

That initialization process detail has been a source of trouble with Docker, where folks accidentally replace the database but not a hidden file in the `zulip` container; there are other ways to fix that which involve just inspecting the database rather than a stamp file, but that bug is why we were spending time on this installer detail.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-30 20:50 UTC

So, I wanted to get thoughts on how we want this to actually work.  I'm somewhat tempted by the design approach of just eliminating `initialize_production_database` (formerly `initialize_voyager_db`) now by calling its code inside an `if not Realm.objects.exists("zulipinternal")` check in the realm creation code path, to reap the benefits of a simpler installer experience, and then we can decide later on the merits of removing the cross-realm-bot arrangement.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-01-30 20:53 UTC

If we did want to change cross-realm system bots to in-realm system bots, the main downsides are (A) a somewhat complex database migration that we'd need to write and (B) needing to think through a bunch of UX design decisions about to what extend the system bots are something organization administrators can directly administer.  (E.g. can you rename or delete "Welcome bot?")

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-02-11 14:13 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)

Meaning we'd be creating the system bot realm upon creation of the first "actual" realm on the server? That sounds like a good idea.

I'm also very in favor of moving system bots into normal realms - reasoning about cross-realm messages is rather difficult in their current form so it'd be nice to get rid of them. They also cause some headache if we want to denormalize ``realm_id`` into ``Message`` (which was discussed in https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/13857) as well as in ``zerver/lib/retention.py``.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-11 14:24 UTC

(replying to Mateusz Mandera)

Likewise!

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-02-12 01:28 UTC

> Meaning we'd be creating the system bot realm upon creation of the first "actual" realm on the server? That sounds like a good idea.
Yeah, let's start with doing this part; it'll let us get a lot of benefits.  It's probably 5% of the work of a removing cross-realm bots as a concept entirely (which involves database migration complexity and also decisions about the administration model complexity) and lets us improve the installer API significantly.

## SOCIAL_AUTH_SUBDOMAIN

*2020-02-06 to 2020-02-16 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/SOCIAL_AUTH_SUBDOMAIN/with/815127)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-02-06 18:49 UTC

So ``SOCIAL_AUTH_SUBDOMAIN`` is the subdomain that we use for the callback URLs in our "social" auth backends - github, google etc. send their response (after authenticating the user) to that subdomain to the appropriate endpoint. We store some data in the session of the user on that domain at the beginning of the flow, so that after coming back from Github/Google/others. we know which realm to log the user into etc.

So its only use is just as intermediate step to pass through in the authentication flow - it doesn't host a realm and shouldn't really ever be accessed by a user manually. Some auth errors end up happening and being shown to a user while on that subdomain though, which is one way in which the user can end up with a page from that subdomain showing in the browser. Which can be confusing because that's how it looks:
[pasted image](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/3c/D-QOsxFDUvfFd0lVsNo3igtE/pasted_image.png)

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-02-06 18:52 UTC

So it has the login buttons in the center, and also login/signup in the upper right corner. Of course trying to use them won't lead the user to anything good, because there is no realm on this subdomain. So I think what gets displayed when the subdomain is opened should be changed to something that makes it clear it's not meant for normal use. Question is, how would we want to make this work and look.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-02-06 22:37 UTC

Yeah, we need to figure out how to have the error handling redirect them back to their original subdomain.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-02-16 19:54 UTC

Posted a PR to fix this at https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/13924

The urls to the python-social-auth backends (``/login/github`` etc.) are included in this line:

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-02-07 11:20 UTC

I don't think ``/login/openid`` should be a thing, "openid" is just an abstraction, it's the protocol. Just like ``/login/oauth`` isn't a thing. **Greg Price** · 2020-02-10 21:49 UTC

On a very large table, you'd always want a new column to be created as nullable (and convert to NOT NULL only after backfilling the values) because otherwise the DBMS has to write in the values atomically when you do the ALTER TABLE.

In particular for PostgreSQL, I read up about this in the docs a couple of years ago, and determined IIRC that if you add a non-nullable column it will lock the whole table for as long as it takes to basically rewrite the entire thing on disk, as it goes through and adds the new column's default value to each row.

I'm not sure any of our tables other than `Message` and `UserMessage` are quite big enough, even on zulipchat.com, that that'd be a real problem in practice at our current scale. But probably best avoided even on moderately big tables like `UserProfile` and `Stream`.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-02-16 10:55 UTC

What about a scheme like this (inspired by the cloudflare post) for the ``UserProfile``-based limiting (could be done for IPs too, or in general based on any ``identifier``):
1. In-memory store that maps ``identifier -> is_over_limit (True or False, if True also the nearest timestamp when another request will be accepted) `` 
2. Thread (queue worker?) handling the slow communication with redis, updating the in-memory store based on redis data.
3. The code that's applied to requests only checks the in-memory store and decides based on it - this will be super fast. If the request gets allowed, it tells the redis-handling thread  about the request  for ``identifier``.

Sometimes some extra requests will be "incorrectly" allowed due to the redis-handling thread updating the in-memory store slowly, but that shouldn't be problematic, because the sender will get blocked as soon as the updates happen.
Main upside is this will stop the rate limiting logic from slowing down processing requests to almost 0. And this scheme is agnostic to the actual rate-limiting algorithm, so it can be freely changed if ever needed.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-03-02 12:40 UTC

@Tim Abbott said:
> I'm a bit surprised that accessing request.GET takes 100us; if I had to guess, that may be a lazy-evaluation thing where whatever code accessing request.GET first pays a big penalty? It's a bit odd that request.POST doesn't experience the same thing; it may be worth reading the code for Django's Que …

``WSGIRequest`` defines the ``GET`` method in what seems to be a "lazy" approach indeed (unlike ``POST``):
```
    @cached_property
    def GET(self):
        # The WSGI spec says 'QUERY_STRING' may be absent.
        raw_query_string = get_bytes_from_wsgi(self.environ, 'QUERY_STRING', '')
        return QueryDict(raw_query_string, encoding=self._encoding)
```
``@cached_property`` means that subsequent access to ``.GET`` will be fast, but the first one does a bunch of encoding stuff in `get_bytes_from_wsgi` and `QueryDict.__init__` - so that seems to confirm the lazy-evaluation explanation.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-03-02 13:20 UTC

> Which to me argues for "we should have an if settings.RUNNING_INSIDE_TORNADO alternative rate-limiter implementation that is entirely in-memory using the same API as the redis-based system.

It shouldn't be a big issue, but I think we'll have to use a different algorithm. The redis-based one is very reliant on redis - it stores timestamp of every request (then uses this log of timestamps to calculate whether the user is over limit for each new request), and relies on redis ``EXPIRE`` to expire the old timestamps that are no longer relevant for future calculations. Re-implementing this expiry thing for the in-memory approach seems needlessly complicated.
The ``Sliding window`` approximate approach from https://blog.cloudflare.com/counting-things-a-lot-of-different-things/ sounds much simpler though. They have to do it with memcached and in async way, but as has already been discussed, we can do this in a synchronous, purely in-memory way.

```
    'api_by_user': [
        (60, 200),  # 200 requests max every minute
    ],
```
So each timestamp can be forgotten after a minute. If there is a longer-term rule is configured, then we need to remember timestamps that much longer.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-02 13:31 UTC

i.e. it's like 65us to pop the top off of a list that's in the 10k range:

~~~ py
import time

n = 20000
t = time.time()
lst = list(range(n))

while lst:
    lst = lst[1:]
print((time.time() - t )/ n)
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-02 13:35 UTC

I imagine we rarely process more than 600 requests per minute, so one possibility here is to just every time:
* slice old entries off the front
* count number of keys
* if bad, stop
* if good, push new key to end of list

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-02 13:36 UTC

plus, we only care about small fractions of requests anyway per minute?

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-03-02 13:43 UTC

Hmm, yeah I think that could work :thinking: The ``sliding window`` approach should be simpler though - at the cost of us using two different algorithms, which probably isn't great...

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-02 13:48 UTC

I honestly think we could replace the whole redis thing with a simple node server where you only have one round trip per rate limit request.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-02 20:33 UTC

Yeah I think the list algorithm Steve suggests should work well.  You'll do O(1) work amortized work per request

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-02 20:33 UTC

Well we'd not want to count keys instead keeping it as a separate variable to avoid O(n) work counting a list

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-02 20:41 UTC

Dict of lists?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-02 23:30 UTC

If you’re doing a lot of `lst = lst[1:]` operations, you wanted a `collections.deque`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-02 23:35 UTC

This runs 150 times faster:
```python
from collections import deque
import time

n = 20000
t = time.time()
deq = deque(range(n))

while deq:
    deq.popleft()
print((time.time() - t )/ n)
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-02 23:38 UTC

(And whether you believe we’ll ever hit the pathological quadratic cases in practice or not, our rate-limiting system is supposed to be our last line of defense against pathological quadratic cases, so it would be good if it didn’t have any of them itself.)

I think we could sensibly work out a way to disable that within Tornado (or perhaps more broadly within API routes; it's really not intended for that use ca …

## Continue coverage

*2020-02-15 to 2020-02-17 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Continue.20coverage/with/817260)*

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-15 18:02 UTC

@Anders Kaseorg You hit the annoying coverage glitch with continue in one of your PRs.  This is a known bug related to some optimization that Python does.  I ran into it a couple years ago.  I vaguely remember that I was able to work around it by extracting a function or something similar.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-15 18:05 UTC

I remember somebody filed an issue against Python with some pretty spicy 🌶 commentary.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-15 18:32 UTC

It’s the peephole optimizer.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-15 22:01 UTC

* https://bitbucket.org/ned/coveragepy/issues/198/continue-marked-as-not-covered
* https://bugs.python.org/issue2506

Fun stuff!

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-15 22:04 UTC

According to Raymond Hettinger, this has never almost never been a problem in the real world, which makes me wonder what :earth_africa: I'm living in:

~~~
This has basically almost never been a problem in the real world.  No 
need to complicate the world further by adding yet another option and 
the accompanying implementation-specific knowledge of why you would 
ever want to use it.

Also, when the peepholer is moved (after the AST is created, but before 
the opcodes), then little oddities like this will go away.

Recommend closing as "won't fix".

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-15 22:05 UTC

https://bugs.python.org/msg64726 (comment from 2008)

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-17 21:42 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell)
> According to Raymond Hettinger, this has never almost never been a problem in the real world, which makes me wonder what :earth_africa: I'm living in:

Not to mention Ned Batchelder, who reported the bug! I think it's pretty clear from his original report that this is something he saw in the real world (a point he then made in reply to Raymond.)

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-17 21:44 UTC

And then several others over the years since then. I think in short this is an issue that is inevitably going to be real for any project maintaining 100% code coverage on much of its codebase.

**Greg Price** · 2020-02-17 21:45 UTC

There's always this workaround of Alex Gaynor's:
https://github.com/pyca/cryptography/pull/3968/commits/3b585f803891e750d0ca5861b5a29e16b779bc16
```diff
+            # Random garbage to defeat CPython's peephole optimizer so that
+            # coverage records correctly: https://bugs.python.org/issue2506
+            1 + 1
             continue
```

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-17 21:48 UTC

Ha, that’s clever.  Using continue is often a code smell, but it has its place.

## typing indicators

**Steve Howell** · 2020-02-23 17:25 UTC

One of the things that I clean up in #13998 is that if I start typing a message to 2 or more users that I've never talked to before, the server is creating the following rows before I send a message:
* Huddle
* Recipient
* Subscription

I don't think we want to do that.  Hopefully it's never been a real issue, but I know I've started messages before that I aborted, so it will be nice to save a little database churn. In `unread_msgs`, the answer turns out to be
* in `huddles`, the sender is included (and so is the current user) 
* in `pms`, only the sender is included (so the current user is excluded -- except for self-PMs)

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-03 10:54 UTC

This is what I recommend:

~~~ py
def make_rate_limiter(time_window, max_count):
    buckets = dict()

    def _garbage_collect(t):
        '''
        Remove all timestamps that are too
        old.
        '''
        t_old = t - time_window
        for key, q in list(buckets.items()):
            while True:
                if len(q) == 0:
                    del buckets[key]
                    break

                if q[0] >= t_old:
                    break

                q.pop()

    def need_to_limit(key):
        t = time.time()
        _garbage_collect(t)

        if key not in buckets:
            buckets[key] = deque()

        q = buckets[key]

        if len(q) > max_count:
            # don't append key, since we won't
            # actually service request
            return True

        q.append(t)
        return False

    return need_to_limit

~~~

Here N is probably small enough that it's not a huge concern, but you can pretty easily mitigate this as follows:
* on every request, just manage the one bucket for your key
* on every 100th request, garbage collect all the keys (and fully delete expired keys)

We should also configure `time_window` to be somewhat small.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-03 22:34 UTC

If we’re willing to slightly loosen the semantics from

* each key may make at most $$C \cdot \left\lceil\frac{t}{W}\right\rceil$$ requests within any $$t$$ second interval

to

* each key may make at most $$C \cdot \left(\frac{t}{W} + 1\right)$$ requests within any $$t$$ second interval

(which is different by at most a factor of 2), then there’s a much simpler implementation that’s less memory-intensive. You only need to store a single reset time for each key, rather than a deque of all requests that were made within the window:

```python
reset_times = dict()

def need_to_limit(key):
    t = time.time()
    r = max(t, reset_times.get(key, t)) + time_window / max_count
    if t < r - time_window:
        return True
    reset_times[key] = r
    return False
```

and you can garbage collect any reset times in the past.

This also has the advantage that you can only ever lock yourself out completely for $$\frac WC$$ seconds instead of $$W$$ seconds.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-03 23:38 UTC

Something like this:

```python3
import heapq

# Each key has a bucket of used requests that empties at a
# constant rate such that a full bucket will empty in time_window
# seconds.  Each new request fills 1 / max_count of the bucket,
# and is allowed as long as it would not overfill the bucket.

# reset_times[key] is the time at which the bucket will
# finish emptying.
reset_times = dict()

# reset_heap is a min heap of (reset_bound, key) tuples where
# reset_bound is a lower bound on reset_times[key].
reset_heap = []

def need_to_limit(key):
    now = time.time()

    while reset_heap and reset_heap[0][0] <= now:
        # We may have empty buckets to garbage-collect.  Since
        # reset_heap only stores a bound, first check whether the
        # bucket is really empty.
        key = reset_heap[0][1]
        reset = reset_times[key]
        if reset <= now:
            heapq.heappop(reset_heap)
        else:
            # This bucket was further filled since being added to
            # the heap.  Re-insert it with a better bound.
            heapq.heapreplace(reset_heap, (reset, key))

    if key in reset_times:
        # Check whether the new request would overfill its bucket.
        new_reset = reset_times[key] + time_window / max_count
        if new_reset > now + time_window:
            return True
        reset_times[key] = new_reset
        # This key is already in the heap; don't re-insert it.
    else:
        # The bucket was empty, so one request cannot overfill it.
        reset_times[key] = now + time_window / max_count
        heapq.heappush(reset_heap, (reset_times[key], key))
    return False
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-03 23:40 UTC

~~~
def need_to_limit(key):
    now = time.time()

    while reset_heap and reset_heap[0][0] <= now:
        # We may have empty buckets to garbage-collect.  Since
        # reset_heap only stores a bound, first check whether the
        # bucket is really empty.
        key = reset_heap[0][1]
        reset = reset_times[key]
        if reset <= now:
            heapq.heappop(reset_heap)
        else:
            # This bucket was further filled since being added to
            # the heap.  Re-insert it with a better bound.
            heapq.heapreplace(reset_heap, (reset, key))

    if key in reset_times:
        # Check whether the new request would overfill its bucket.
        new_reset = reset_times[key] + time_window / max_count
        if new_reset > now + time_window:
            return True
        reset_times[key] = new_reset
        # This key is already in the heap; don't re-insert it.
    else:
        # The bucket was empty, so one request cannot overfill it.
        reset_times[key] = now + time_window / max_count
        heapq.heappush(reset_heap, (reset_times[key], key))
    return False

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-07 13:13 UTC

Ooh. Now that I’m thinking about this again, I realized it’s possible to replace the heap with a deque and get amortized O(1) for all operations (as long as we use a different deque for each rule when there are multiple rules).

```python
from collections import deque
import time

# Each key has a bucket of used requests that empties at a
# constant rate such that a full bucket will empty in time_window
# seconds.  Each new request fills 1 / max_count of the bucket,
# and is allowed as long as it would not overfill the bucket.

# reset_times[key] is the time at which the bucket will
# finish emptying.
reset_times = dict()

# gc_queue is a deque of (check_time, key) tuples.
gc_queue = deque()

def need_to_limit(key):
    now = time.time()

    while gc_queue and gc_queue[0][0] <= now:
        # We may have empty buckets to garbage-collect.
        gc_key = gc_queue.pop_left()[1]
        if reset_times[key] <= now:
            del reset_times[key]
        else:
            # This bucket is not empty yet.  Re-insert it for later
            # checking.
            gc_queue.append((now + time_window / max_count, gc_key))

    if key in reset_times:
        # Check whether the new request would overfill its bucket.
        new_reset = max(reset_times[key], now) + time_window / max_count
        if new_reset > now + time_window:
            return True
        reset_times[key] = new_reset
        # This key is already in gc_queue; don't re-insert it.
    else:
        # The bucket was empty, so one request cannot overfill it.
        reset_times[key] = now + time_window / max_count
        gc_queue.append((reset_times[key], key))
    return False

def clear_history(key):
    now = time.time()
    reset_times[key] = now - time_window
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-07 13:16 UTC

This time the amortization argument is that each request for a key increases its`reset_time - check_time` by at most `time_window / max_count`, while each key the GC loop re-inserts into the deque decreases its `reset_time - check_time` by at least `time_window / max_count`, so there are at most as many re-inserts as requests.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-07 13:20 UTC

Some keys may be garbage collected up to `time_window / max_count` later than they could be, but they never stay around more than twice as long as necessary.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-07 21:57 UTC

The same O(1) amortization argument can be made for @Steve Howell’s collector, *if* you change the sweep frequency from a hard-coded number of requests to a calculated amount of time.

```python
reset_times = dict()
last_gc_time = time.time()

def need_to_limit(key):
    nonlocal reset_times, last_gc_time
    now = time.time()

    if last_gc_time <= now - time_window / max_count:
        last_gc_time = now
        reset_times = {k: t for (k, t) in reset_times.items() if t > now}

    new_reset = max(reset_times[key], now) + time_window / max_count
    if new_reset > now + time_window:
        return True
    reset_times[key] = new_reset

def clear_history(key):
    now = time.time()
    reset_times[key] = now - time_window
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-07 23:12 UTC

A key with only one request should stay around for only `time_window / max_count`. This collection frequency is the sweet spot where both memory and computation are within a constant factor of optimal. Waiting any longer costs proportionally more memory without saving much computation (because the less frequent collections take longer), and waiting any shorter costs proportionally more computation without saving much memory (because the more frequent collections don’t remove as much).

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-03-30 14:01 UTC

One more detail that could be worth discussing is about the headers that we set on the response, namely `X-RateLimit-Remaining, and `X-RateLimit-Reset`. The way this has worked is that this gets set to:
1. If not blocked, `X-RateLimit-Remaining` becomes the number of requests until the "longest" rule is violated. `Reset` is time until complete freedom from the longest rule (call counter for it becomes 0)
2. If blocked, `Remaining` is 0, `Reset` is time when the next request can be made without violating the "shortest" rule that was violated right now. But it doesn't mean that the request won't violate a different rule at that time.

Is that how we want this to work? Would it be better to at least - in case `2`, call it `Retry-At` instead of `Reset`, since it's not any reset, it's just  a moment where the client can try again and *maybe* the request will be accepted. Or we could calculate the *actual* time at which the user can make the next request - that would be the `max` of the set of these timestamps across all rules that are being violated by the current request.

* If we do a parallel Python implementation, that implementation will be limited to just the critical `GET /events` codepath.  It's very much worth doing if we can save a significant portion of total `GET /events` request time, but if the optimizations discussed above are big enough (and network latency to the rate-limiter server is low enough), it might not end up being worth doing. | concurrency | main    | redis-ratelimit | regexes + user-cache | regexes + user-cache + redis-ratelimit |
| ----------- | ------- | --------------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
| c=1         | 10.4789 | 11.5322         | 8.065                | 8.6359                                 |
| c=3         | 30.6801 | 32.8495         | 22.6686              | 26.3271                                |
| c=5         | 49.1325 | 53.1502         | 37.8877              | 41.4119                                |

| concurrency | main    | redis-ratelimit | regexes + user-cache | regexes + user-cache + redis-ratelimit |
| ----------- | ------- | --------------- | -------------------- | -------------------------------------- |
|             |         | (vs main)       | (vs main)            | (vs main)                              |
| c=1         |         | 110.05%         | 76.96%               | 82.41%                                 |
| c=3         |         | 107.07%         | 73.89%               | 85.81%                                 |
| c=5         |         | 108.18%         | 77.11%               | 84.29%                                 |

So going to (same-host) redis is a 8-10% performance hit.  #38322 shaves 25% off the time, and so going to Redis claws some of those wins back.

```c
/* Data for deque objects is stored in a doubly-linked list of fixed
 * length blocks.  This assures that appends or pops never move any
 * other data elements besides the one being appended or popped.
 *
 * Another advantage is that it completely avoids use of realloc(),
 * resulting in more predictable performance.
```

IOW the author likes that push and pop (on either side) are O(1) even non-amortized.

Which is nice... but seems to me pretty hard to justify in a counterpart to Python's lists, which have only amortized O(1) append/pop in exchange for O(1) random access. Hard even to justify calling the performance "predictable", when it's surprisingly divergent from the ubiquitous lists.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-04 11:48 UTC

I think Raymond (most of this code was written by Raymond Hettinger) was probably comparing his choice to another possible implementation, where you just have a long circular buffer with random access.  The problem with a  long circular buffer is that you eventually need to expand it.  When you expand the buffer, the worst case scenario is that you have to move all N of your items to a new place in memory (because realloc returned a new pointer instead of just extending the allocation).  And even when realloc simply extends your region of memory, you may still have to move some subset of your N elements so far, which is usually somewhat proportional to the number of popLefts that you already have completed.  Let me find the Rust code...

~~~ 
    /// Frobs the head and tail sections around to handle the fact that we
    /// just reallocated. Unsafe because it trusts old_capacity.
    #[inline]
    unsafe fn handle_capacity_increase(&mut self, old_capacity: usize) {
        let new_capacity = self.cap();

        // Move the shortest contiguous section of the ring buffer
        //    T             H

        //    T             H

**Vishnu KS** · 2020-03-07 08:55 UTC

Yeah. I initiated a ZulipTestCase object  to make use of some helper functions so that I could avoid some code duplication.  These are the functions.

---
* send_stream_message
* subscribe
* get_stream_id

---

* example_user
* example_email
* nonreg_email
---

The first category of functions don't access the self variable. So there should not be any side effects or issues from them. I think we can move them to a test_helpers file or turn them to `staticmethod`.

The second category of methods do access the self variable. But the attributes they are accessing through self are static and hence should not be having any side effects or issues as well. They can be rewritten to  be accessed through Class instead. So the second category of functions can be turned into `staticmethod` or `classmethod`.

The advantage of changing methods to` staticmethod` or `classmethod` (for second set of functions) over moving to test_helpers file is that we don't have to make any modifications in the way they are currently accessed in tests (except for `curl_param_value_generators`) .

Once the changes are made we can remove the creation of the ZulipTestCase instance in `curl_param_value_generators` and also maybe add a lint check that prevents further initiations like this in the future.

`self.client_post` does not fit into either of the two category of methods since its accessing the `client` attribute in self. So an alternative mechanisam, something like Steve suggested should be used for that.

## Checking password strength on login

*2020-03-11 to 2020-06-22 · 44 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Checking.20password.20strength.20on.20login/with/830027)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-03-11 17:15 UTC

Currently we use ``zxcvbn`` on both the frontend and backend to check password strength when the user is registering (or changing password) and enforce a minimal "strength". We actually override  `UserProfile.set_password` to ensure no bug can cause a weak password to be set:
```
    def set_password(self, password: Optional[str]) -> None:
        if password is None:
            self.set_unusable_password()
            return

        from zproject.backends import check_password_strength
        if not check_password_strength(password):
            raise PasswordTooWeakError

        super().set_password(password)
```

This leaves the question of old users logging in with their weak passwords, set before we introduced these checks. I think we should in some way detect those cases and get the user to change their password.  I see two potential approaches that could be good:

1. Refuse to log in the user if the password is weak and show a page saying to reset the password.

Pros:
- Most secure

Cons:
- Perhaps too strong, and annoying to the user?
- Uncomfortable implementation - there are multiple places, in each it'd be required to account for this special case.

2. Log in the user, but tag the ``UserProfile`` (perhaps ``user_profile.weak_password = True`` attribute). For users tagged in this way, add `weak_password` to `page_params` and have the webapp display the red warning banner on top nagging the user to change password.

Pros:
- More gentle for the user
- Cleaner to implement (only one place to do `user_profile.weak_password = True`, and then `page_params` and warning banner).

Cons:
- Less secure

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-11 17:48 UTC

There's a third option, which is to serve a redirect on /home to a password change UI (effectively, treat it as a password reset).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-11 17:49 UTC

I think in most installations this is a rare state, since the frontend was blocking setting weak passwords before we added backend support for doing the same enforcement.  So I think the main situation this will happen is when a server adjusts the password strength settings (E.g. perhaps through a new, fancier version of zxcvbn).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-11 17:50 UTC

I'm a little bit tempted by the option that tells them their password is weak and they need to reset it; it's more secure and if we think this isn't going to happen often, having a more secure and simpler flow to reason about is probably going to be a better overall experience.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-03-12 13:18 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I'm a little bit tempted by the option that tells them their password is weak and they need to reset it; it's more secure and if we think this isn't going to happen often, having a more secure and simpler flow to reason about is probably going to be a better overall experience.
This would require handling this possibility in all places where we do an `authenticate()` call with a password. From what I see so far, that's `json_change_settings`, `json_fetch_api_key`, `api_fetch_api_key`, and of course `OurAuthenticationForm`. That seems rather awkward, but perhaps I'm missing a better approach?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-12 19:01 UTC

Well, I think for all of those, we already (should) have code to display a `json_error` sent from the code path.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-12 22:14 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> There's a third option, which is to serve a redirect on /home to a password change UI (effectively, treat it as a password reset).

I think this is the best option, if it's not too painful to implement. It meets the goal of getting the user to an adequately strong password, without causing as much trouble for the user.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-12 22:16 UTC

I think the tradeoff would be different if we had reason to think the old password had leaked, or there was a security vulnerability involved. The password strength requirement feels to me more like a hardening measure than a question of a vulnerability.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-12 22:18 UTC

One consideration here is that from time to time a server admin might increase the password strength requirement, or we might ship a new zxcvbn that rejects some passwords the old one accepted.

It'd be a pretty bad user experience, and as a server admin I would not feel good about making/deploying the change, if that meant that lots of users had to go to reset their passwords by email. What I'd want instead is to force them to choose a new password upon their next login.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-13 00:11 UTC

The main downside of the redirect experience is it won't work on mobile and similar clients without extra work.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-13 00:26 UTC

True. One option would be to provide the redirect where we can, and an error where we can't.

The error then could recommend logging in on the web/desktop in order to change the password. (Doing a reset by email would involve going there anyway, I think.)

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-13 00:30 UTC

Because logging in again on mobile is very infrequent, that might mean that even most mostly-mobile users see the redirect experience.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-11 21:04 UTC

So, I want to start a discussion on naming for a bundle of fields discussed in #14166, and specifically this bundle of them:
```
development_environment = settings.DEVELOPMENT,
max_file_upload_size = settings.MAX_FILE_UPLOAD_SIZE,
max_avatar_file_size = settings.MAX_AVATAR_FILE_SIZE,
server_generation = settings.SERVER_GENERATION,
server_inline_image_preview = settings.INLINE_IMAGE_PREVIEW,
server_inline_url_embed_preview = settings.INLINE_URL_EMBED_PREVIEW,
password_min_length = settings.PASSWORD_MIN_LENGTH,
password_min_guesses = settings.PASSWORD_MIN_GUESSES,
jitsi_server_url = settings.JITSI_SERVER_URL,
server_avatar_changes_disabled = settings.AVATAR_CHANGES_DISABLED,
server_name_changes_disabled = settings.NAME_CHANGES_DISABLED,
initial_servertime = time.time(), # Used for calculating relative presence age
```

We're moving these to be available via the `/register` API (the mobile equivalent of `page_params`) rather than only being available to the webapp (which is basically a bug).  The question is how to name them.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-11 21:06 UTC

I think the ones named with `server_` as the prefix are already fine.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-11 21:07 UTC

Probably it'd be correct to rename to `realm_jisti_server_url` for clarity.  And probably `max_file_upload_size` might be best namespaced under `realm`, in that one can imagine that being per-realm configuration and it seems appropriate to namespace it in a way that suggests that as we do other parameters with that property.  

`max_avatar_file_size` seems unlikely to have the same argument apply; so maybe `server_max_avatar_file_size` is appropriate.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-11 21:09 UTC

I know flatter is generally better than nested, but I think there is an argument to nest some of the server settings into their own struct.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-11 21:09 UTC

And @Steve Howell I feel like perhaps `initial_servertime` should be restructured to be part of the presence structure we send?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-11 21:09 UTC

OK, I took `initial_servertime` off the list of things in the issue that we're thinking of moving in the first pass of "easy things".

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-11 21:11 UTC

I'm imagining if we decide to restructure things to be less flat, we'd do a bulk move of all the `realm_` or `server_` properties at once; probably that's an independent decision from this because any migration code would probably just loop over the fields with names starting like that to move them.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-11 21:11 UTC

So we can consider that out of scope for the naming question here :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-11 21:13 UTC

@Greg Price @Chris Bobbe to make sure some mobile folks see this.  My thinking here is that we should first move the ~12 above that are easy, and then potentially move the remaining TODO list into comments in the codebase detailing the plan for them (and potentially extract an `add_webapp_only_data` function name to make it really feel bad to add things there that don't belong.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-11 21:16 UTC

Structs aren’t completely orthogonal to naming decisions, because you can avoid some prefixes.  But I don’t care that much.  I am actually more of the opinion that clients should decouple themselves from server names at the edges.  And mobile should mostly drive this.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-12 22:31 UTC

That general plan sounds good to me.

I agree with Steve that clients should decouple themselves from server API names at the edges. I think it's helpful for the name inside the client to be the same as in the API (or at least the same modulo predictable conventions like for underscores and capitals), because that means fewer names to juggle when trying to understand the code. But that should be a choice the client explicitly makes at the edge.

Even when a client codebase picks a completely unrelated name, though, the name in the API is still part of the API people rely on to understand the system. So it's worth thinking about that API choice.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-12 22:38 UTC

The `max_file_upload_size` and `max_avatar_file_size` examples suggest to me that perhaps we shouldn't try to have the API encode whether a setting is per-server or per-realm.

Partly because it might change for a given setting, and it seems like that should remain an implementation detail within the server. (I was about to say "except the org settings UI"... but even there! There can be settings that are per-realm/org but org admins can't set, only server admins. Those might appear read-only in the org settings UI... but the same could be true of some per-server settings.)

Then partly because that distinction doesn't seem like a high-order bit for understanding a setting. Those two settings seem awfully parallel from a client perspective, even in a future where one can vary per-realm while the other can't.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-12 22:45 UTC

Oh interesting, I see there's both a `realm_inline_image_preview` and a `server_inline_image_preview`. I'm guessing that the latter controls whether the former will be offered in the settings UI?

So effectively the former is the one that matters to any part of the client other than the org settings UI. (Which doesn't exist on mobile and isn't in a near-term roadmap.) The latter controls the bit of the org settings UI that controls the former.

Oh, but also it looks like the webapp doesn't actually care about the former either, except in the org settings UI (as the current state of that same checkbox.) That likely means we won't on mobile until we someday also build an org settings UI. (Just checked, and we don't look at that value now.)

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-12 22:46 UTC

Same story for `server_inline_url_embed_preview`, unsurprisingly.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-12 22:58 UTC

Looking at `server_avatar_changes_disabled`, there's the same kind of pairing ~~with the same effect in the org settings UI~~ (actually, where the org settings UI appears to have a bug that it shows the checkbox with no indication of whether it has any effect). But that one does get looked at in the web frontend outside that.

It's a bit awkward what the code has to do -- it has to manually combine the two settings:
```
static/js/settings_account.js
42:    if (page_params.realm_avatar_changes_disabled || page_params.server_avatar_changes_disabled) {
```

I think the ideal API for this kind of realm + server setting would be instead like:
* The unadorned name `foo` has the setting that's actually in effect.
* For the org settings UI, a prefixed name like `server_foo` conveys any server-level setting that constrains what the org admin can do.

No rush to migrate things like `*avatar_changes_disabled`, but where we're freely choosing new names it'd be good to make them that way.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-04-09 20:49 UTC

My guess is that this is again because of the issue with us not having access to the original user session because of the `Lax` cookie setting and the response is POSTed to the server. The subdomain to which the user is authing is saved in their session in the initial step of the flow - in this we won't have access to that. So the social pipeline doesn't know to what subdomain to try to authenticate the user and returns the redirect to /accounts/find/.

We'll want to store this (and all the other `SOCIAL_AUTH_FIELDS_STORED_IN_SESSION`) under the `state`-derived key in redis. That's how we'll be able to retrieve all this data when the user comes back from Apple with the POST response. The backend should retrieve all that and `session_set` it in the new user session - this will make it available to the social pipeline the way it expects.

~~~ py
function get_last_active_date_html(user) {

    }
    const today = new XDate();

}
~~~

## presence scalability

*2020-03-23 to 2020-03-23 · 15 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/presence.20scalability/with/836507)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-23 00:47 UTC

I've been thinking more and more that we should change the model for presence live-updates when a user comes online to replace the `events` notices, at least for large organizations, with code in the typing notifications / message sending code paths to mark a user as present when you see a message from them and, to improve scalability of presence in larger organizations with hundreds of users who might be constantly going on/offline while still preserving the nice touch that you don't see a user as offline right after they send a message.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-23 13:49 UTC

My biggest question about `do_update_user_status` is why we broadcast the event to all `active_user_ids()` (*).  I would think we only need to broadcast presence events to other users who are actually present themselves.   Unlike other events, presence events have a short shelf life, so it seems silly to put them on the event queue for any idle users who may still have an event loop running just cause they haven't shut down the browser.

(*) Tim knows this, but for others, `active_user_ids` returns users who are simply "active" in the sense that their account has been deactivated.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-23 13:52 UTC

So when @Tim Abbott is talking about using typing/message-sending activity as perhaps a more efficient (and perhaps more stingy?) way of determining **actual** presence more pragmatically, I am wondering if we can use that data on both sides of the equation:
* be more stingy about who announces their presence
* be more stingy about to whom we announce presence

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-23 13:53 UTC

FWIW I am finally dusting off an in-progress PR from over a month ago related to presence.  I will be at least making the payloads a bit smaller, although I doubt my change will be more than just a small percentage performance improvement.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-23 13:56 UTC

I guess the nicer part of my upcoming PR is that we will just be simplifying the protocol for modern clients, which should make it easier to adapt it to any changing requirements here.  (We still need to support the ugly legacy protocol for old mobile apps.)

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-23 18:09 UTC

I think the suggestion at the top of the thread is that we would actually stop directly announcing presence in events at all.

It'd then be conveyed two ways:
* explicitly in the presence heartbeat, once a minute, just like today
* implicitly by new-message and typing-status events, and possibly a few others (like message edit?)

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-23 18:11 UTC

I think a protocol like that makes sense to me.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-23 18:18 UTC

I think it's somewhat common for somebody to be online for a while where they're just reading messages.  So I do think there's some value in clients telling the server, at some point, that Greg is actually online, he just hasn't been typing messages or doing anything else visible.

But I could see all kinds of optimizations here based around inferences about user activity that come from non-presence events, so I like where this is going.

Certainly if we only needed to guarantee presence was accurate within a minute, we could do just heartbeats and make everything simple.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-23 18:20 UTC

The one limitation of typing indicators and message events is that they aren't true broadcast events.  Typing indicators barely go to anyone--it's just the other potential PM recipients.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-23 18:21 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell)
> So I do think there's some value in clients telling the server, at some point, that Greg is actually online, he just hasn't been typing messages or doing anything else visible.

Yeah definitely. But if "at some point" extends over a minute, then the regular presence heartbeat takes care of that.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-23 18:21 UTC

And then the use of those other events is basically to avoid visibly broken-looking situations where you see activity from a user, so clearly they're online, but they're showing as offline in the sidebar.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-23 18:21 UTC

Yep, hence my comment that if we only needed to guarantee presence accuracy at one-minute granularity, then everything becomes simple.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-23 18:23 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> And then the use of those other events is basically to avoid visibly broken-looking situations where you see activity from a user, so clearly they're online, but they're showing as offline in the sidebar.

Oh, I see.  Yeah, I have always thought one-minute granularity is fine, so I'd be fine with it as long as we don't make things look funny.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-23 18:25 UTC

It's ironic that I procrastinated on my presence PR for about five weeks until the exact day Tim proposed this.  (It's possible some piece of my PR will still be useful, but not actually sure.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-23 19:25 UTC

Great, I think we're on the same page for the goals here.

I did some research on azure.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-27 17:12 UTC

@Kartik Srivastava This is an artifact of how the id gets passed in from the REST api:

~~~
228     url(r'^attachments/(?P<attachment_id>[0-9]+)$', rest_dispatch,
229         {'DELETE': 'zerver.views.attachments.remove'}),
~~~

Even though it's effectively an integer in the URL, the actual conversion takes place in the view.  I kinda hate REST for this kind of stuff, because now if the attachment id is mis-formatted, we just get a 404 instead of possibly a more useful error message.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-27 21:24 UTC

Yeah, agreed; the fact that REST results in parameters potentially being in the URL or elsewhere is annoying.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-27 21:25 UTC

That said, I think one can/should name those using `REQ(..., path_only=True)`, and we could add support for running validators/converters on such parameters (there's a TODO for this in `zerver/lib/requests.py` if you search for `path_only`)

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-27 18:41 UTC

One thing I'd like to fix is that `internal_send_private_message` and its cousins should probably go into `zerver/lib/message.py`.  This would also force us to move `do_send_messages`.

At one point we were trying to enforce that anything that actually updated the database was to remain in `actions.py`, but I think we've already strayed from that, and I'm not sure that's the best rule to follow, as it cuts down on our ability to keep things organized.  (It's also a bit irritating to always be jumping between `actions.py` and `messages.py` when you're working on the message codepath.)  I think the better convention is just to maintain the `do_` prefixes for places where we're actually having side effects (where `do_send_messages` is a great example).

## developer productivity

*2020-03-27 to 2021-02-12 · 148 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/developer.20productivity/with/842122)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-27 23:00 UTC

So I wanted to start a thread about pain points in the development experience; it's been a while since we've done one, and there's a bunch of new folks with fresh perspective, so now's a great time to do it.  We'll likely fork off several threads for deeper investigation into individual issues as we talk.  

The main philosophical point here is that the better the developer experience, the more time we can spend on actually improving Zulip vs. fighting with tooling.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-27 23:09 UTC

webpack takes 30s in Casper tests (although it's somewhat mitigated by the `--interactive` mode that @Rohitt Vashishtha added)

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-27 23:09 UTC

`run-dev.py` still feels sluggish

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-27 23:10 UTC

I'll start with mentioning a few things on my mind:
* We've been having a lot of issues with CI stability over the last few days.  While some issues are human error, there's a lot of things we can do to help with human error.  There's an ongoing discussion on this in #**automated testing**.
* There's this annoying bug where Tornado, unlike Django, sometimes doesn't auto-restart properly when switching branches, resulting in one needing to manually restart `run-dev.py`.  This especially affects me, since I switch branches 25+ times every day to look at PRs, but I bet it's annoying for others too.  It seems like it should be fixable, because the Django auto-reload logic doesn't have this bug.
* run-dev.py takes too long to startup.  
* Right after you (re)start `run-dev.py`, if you try loading a page in the webapp, for like 5 seconds, you'll get "connection refused" because the Django process isn't ready to accept connections yet.  I'm pretty sure it should be possible to have `run-dev` retry requests (or hold them) to avoid this gap.

But really I'm hoping to hear from you folks on what bothers you!

Having many points of partial reformatting would mean the rebase would need to happen in many stages. ## Empty string model

*2020-03-28 to 2020-03-28 · 15 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Empty.20string.20model/with/842913)*

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-03-28 21:10 UTC

I need to use a CharField with the ability to store string both empty and non-empty. I read that null=True is not advisable but I could not find an alternative. Can anyone help me with this please?

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-03-28 21:11 UTC

The issue is that the values can both be None and '' for a string. I could hack it by querying and checking for both but would like someone's advice on this.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-28 21:21 UTC

What’s the field gonna be used for?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-28 21:22 UTC

The empty string `''` is distinct from `NULL`. You can still store the empty string whether or not you can store `NULL`. Just keep the default `null=False` unless you specifically need to be able to store `NULL`.

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-03-28 21:32 UTC

Got it. Thanks @Anders Kaseorg

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-03-28 21:33 UTC

@Steve Howell it's for the stream specific linkifier issue I'm working on

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-28 21:35 UTC

I am curious why we would even allow the empty string, much less null, for that?

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-03-28 21:37 UTC

The empty string will mean that it is a linkifier for the entire realm

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-03-28 21:37 UTC

The null part is just me not understanding everything clearly

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-28 21:38 UTC

What is the field here?  The regex or the stream?

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-28 21:39 UTC

It seems like stream linkifiers should be their own table??

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-03-28 21:43 UTC

There's a new field called stream_name. If it is empty, you render it. If it has a value, you check if is same as current stream and then only render it.

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-03-28 21:44 UTC

You'll check for all linkifier objects. We can have multiple ones as long as the stream_name is different

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-28 21:45 UTC

At the very least this should be stream_id.

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-03-28 21:48 UTC

That's a good approach too. I guess I'll go with stream_id. It'll then be immune to stream name changes


## Never mind (flush_per_request_caches())

*2020-03-29 to 2020-03-30 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Never.20mind.20.28flush_per_request_caches.28.29.29/with/843202)*

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-03-29 18:10 UTC

Didn't know how to delete :sweat:. Fixed the issue

**Cyphase** · 2020-03-30 00:52 UTC

Personally, I would recommend that instead of deleting a question that you resolved on your own, you post what you learned for everyone's future reference, and potentially as something that could end up in documentation. :smile:

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-03-30 19:43 UTC

Yeah, I agree; I find it helpful to see what issues folks are getting stuck on, even if they resolve them, because it's valuable data about what kinds of things folks get stuck on; a lot of our improvements to the development experience are driven by patterns in that kind of report.

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-03-30 19:48 UTC

The issue was that `flush_per_request_caches()` deleted the created objects (realm filters here) but I failed to notice that we create instances of `RealmFilterPatterns` in `bugdown/__init__.py` which have the necessary data. So, instead of using `RealmFilter.objects.filter()` in HandleMatch, I slightly modified the area which creates the instances mentioned above (`register_realm_filters`) to store the necessary data in a way that I wanted it to.  The work is in https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/14397 where you can take a look if you want to.


## malformed API call

*2020-03-30 to 2020-03-30 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/malformed.20API.20call/with/843821)*

**Divyanshu Agrawal** · 2020-03-30 18:52 UTC

Is a malformed API call that causes a 500 internal server error considered a bug?

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-30 18:55 UTC

Yeah, a 500 is always a bug. If the API call is malformed, the proper response code is 400 (or another 4xx).

**Steve Howell** · 2020-03-30 18:59 UTC

@Divyanshu Agrawal Can you give us more detail on why you're asking the question?  If you're seeing a 500 in dev, then the server log should tell us something interesting.  Is this on master or in a branch that you're working on?

The main way we defend against malformed data is with our `REQ` system, although sometimes there may be more semantic checks that we need to do within the function itself.

**Greg Price** · 2020-03-30 19:00 UTC

One practical reason for drawing the line in that way is that, by declaring that and then making a practice of doing it, we keep the 500s relatively few -- which means in turn we can make a practice of investigating them when they appear in production, and fixing them. That's a very useful signal for spotting bugs, and fixing bugs that people are hitting.

## incorrect youtube link preview

*2020-03-31 to 2020-04-27 · 39 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/incorrect.20youtube.20link.20preview/with/844352)*

**Hashir Sarwar** · 2020-03-31 01:03 UTC

There is an issue with the inline preview of YouTube links. The problem is that `youtube_re` (inside the function `youtube_id(url)`) is matching with the URLs like `https://www.youtube.com/<any_string>`. So, inline preview will be displayed for a link like [https://www.youtube.com/123](https://www.youtube.com/123)
and it causes unexpected behaviour for the youtube links of "channels" (more detail here [#14376](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/14376)) and "playlists" etc.

**Hashir Sarwar** · 2020-03-31 14:52 UTC

I've refactored the regex logic for `youtube_id(url)` from 
```python3
schema_re = r'(?:https?://)'
host_re = r'(?:youtu\.be/|(?:\w+\.)?youtube(?:-nocookie)?\.com/)'
param_re = r'(?:(?:(?:v|embed)/)|' + \
    r'(?:(?:(?:watch|playlist)(?:_popup|_videos)?(?:\.php)?)?(?:\?|#!?)(?:.+&)?v(?:ideo_ids)?=))'
id_re = r'([0-9A-Za-z_-]+)'
youtube_re = r'^({schema_re}?{host_re}{param_re}?)?{id_re}(?(1).+)?$'
```
to
```python3
schema_re = r'(?:https?://)'
host_re = r'(?:(?:www\.)?youtube(?:-nocookie)?\.com/)'
param_re = r'(?:(?:(?:v|embed)/)|' + \
    r'(?:(?:(?:watch|playlist)(?:_popup|_videos)?(?:\.php)?)?(?:\?|#!?)(?:.+&)?v(?:ideo_ids)?=))'
id_re = r'([0-9A-Za-z_-]+)'
youtube_re = r'(?:^(?:{schema_re}?{host_re}{param_re}){id_re}(?(1).+)?$|^{schema_re}?(?:youtu\.be/){id_re}$)'
```

The aim is to
* distinguish the URLs based on domains (`youtube.com` and `youtu.be`)
* Avoid unwanted URLs from matching. Examples of incorrect URLs are: 
  * `youtube.com/channel/<id>`
  * `youtube.com/playlist?list=<list-id>`
  * `youtube.com/<any_string>`
  * `youtube.com/`
  * `youtu.be/<id1>,<id2>`


I've tested my regex logic for links like:
* https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=123
* www.youtube.com/watch?v=123
* youtube.com/watch?v=123
* https://www.youtube.com/watch_videos?video_ids=123,456
* https://youtube.com/channel/1234
* youtu.be/123
* youtu.be/123,444
* youtube.com/playlist?list=1112

@Tim Abbott @Anders Kaseorg does it look okay?

**Hashir Sarwar** · 2020-03-31 14:55 UTC

This logic will return `id` as `match.groups(1)`for `youtube.com` and `match.groups(2)` for `youtu.be` links.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-03-31 17:33 UTC

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2020-04-21 17:48 UTC

I looked at it briefly, and I learnt that we have code to fetch open graph data in two places - `zerver.lib.url_preview` and a `fetch_open_graph_image` function in the `zerver.lib.bugdown`. 

The `fetch_open_graph_image` tries to fetch the open graph data while the message is being rendered, instead of using the `embed_links` queue worker. Currently, we use it only for Dropbox images, and the external request is set to timeout in 1sec. We could decide to use the same mechanism for YouTube or decide, as @Hashir Sarwar did in his PR, or move to use the queue worker. 

@Tim Abbott do you have thoughts on what should be the way forward here?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-21 21:25 UTC

@Puneeth Chaganti I think probably it makes sense to eventually migrate everything to use the `embed_links` system.  Basically, the stuff in bugdown is the original one-off things we did for a few specific tools early on, and it seems silly long-term to maintain two independent, redundant systems.

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2020-04-22 04:27 UTC

So, as I see it, we would use the `embed_links` system, but still show previews for YouTube links even if the `inline_url_embed_preview`flag is turned off, right? This would keep the preview behavior for YouTube similar to the current state of things. Eventually, when inline previews are out of beta, and more organisations choose to turn on this flag, we could toggle YouTube and Twitter previews too with this flag.

Yeah, I think that's right; it's a bit awkward because the inline previews are spammy for other sites, but we don't have a fast path forward there.

## how to upgrade python from 3.6 to 3.7 in Zulip

*2020-04-02 to 2020-04-02 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/how.20to.20upgrade.20python.20from.203.2E6.20to.203.2E7.20in.20Zulip/with/846148)*

**lixiran** · 2020-04-02 10:44 UTC

the python version was 3.6 when I install zulip. now I need to upgrade the python version from 3.6 to 3.7.
I have upgraded the python to 3.7 at the OS level. but seems the zulip has its own zulip compiler (which is still using 3.6 in /srv/zulip-venv-cache ) 
is there a way to upgrade it ?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-02 19:55 UTC

@lixiran can you explain more what you're actually trying to do?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-02 19:56 UTC

Zulip is designed to use the version of Python that comes with the base OS.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-02 19:56 UTC

So if you want to use a newer Python, our recommended approach would generally be to upgrade to a new version of the base OS supported by Zulip that has the target Python version.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-02 19:56 UTC

Or if you're writing your own custom application using Python 3.7, you can install that on the system and use that if you like.

Okay this is what I figured out 
When we run commands like ```manage.py runserver or shell ``` Django system check framework runs and one of the checks is the URL check.

instead of

```
ZULIP_PATH = os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.dirname(os.path.abspath(__file__))))

```
so it is appending the wrong path.

## Unlikely race between user logging in and being deactivated

*2020-04-12 to 2020-04-12 · 2 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Unlikely.20race.20between.20user.20logging.20in.20and.20being.20deactivated/with/851997)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-04-12 12:16 UTC

This should be virtually impossible, but I'm wondering if we should address it nonetheless - or perhaps it's not worth it?
In `do_deactivate_user`, after setting `is_active=False` on the user, we do `delete_user_sessions(user_profile)`. Hypothetically, we could have an admin deactivating  the user and at the same the user logging in, which may end in the `do_login` function:
```
def do_login(request: HttpRequest, user_profile: UserProfile) -> None:
    """Creates a session, logging in the user, using the Django method,
    and also adds helpful data needed by our server logs.
    """
    django_login(request, user_profile)  # creates the session
    # ... some other irrelevant stuff
```

So, if the ordering of events turns out like this:
1. the auth flow checks if user is active and other checks
2. do_deactivate_user  does `is_active=False` and deletes user sessions
3. the auth flow, having finished all the verification, calls do_login

We may have a deactivated user with an active session. Is this worth addressing, or is there already something I'm missing that prevents this?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-12 19:26 UTC

@Mateusz Mandera hmm, good question.  The race is unlikely, but it does seem not ideal for that to be possible in any circumstance.  There's a few ways we could approach the issue:
* Defense in depth -- make our API validators check `is_active` defensively before letting the user do anything with their session.  Probably a good idea in any case.  I just verified we already do this in all of the `zerver/decorators.py` code paths.
* Using the right sort of database transaction around both blocks, to ensure they're serialized with respect to each other at the database level.  I'm not sure if memcached would make this piece more complicated than we want.
* A different form of defense-in-depth: Adding after that `django_login` line a check if the account is deactivated, and if so, immediately calling the delete-all-sessions function for the user to correct the issue.

**Greg Price** · 2020-05-08 20:18 UTC

In this case I think that actually didn't play a role -- the first update in Debian since last June was this March:
https://tracker.debian.org/pkg/puppet
which is after Focal had its Debian Import Freeze:
https://wiki.ubuntu.com/FocalFossa/ReleaseSchedule
so Focal actually had the latest Debian package as of then.

Instead the issue was just that the Debian maintainers of that package were apparently focused on stable, not testing. (Which seems pretty sensible for this particular package.) And so when Buster froze, they stopped uploading new upstream releases; and when Buster released, they stopped uploading anything at all for a while.

Which was not at all convenient for Ubuntu's LTS cycle, seeing as it's a year out of phase with Debian's. But nobody was particularly trying to make the package up to date for Ubuntu.

I reproduced the memcached failure, and with a `git bisect` on memcached, tracked it down to 1.5.7~3 “Use HAVE_SASL_CB_GETCONFPATH” ([memcached/memcached#366](https://github.com/memcached/memcached/pull/366)).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-05-14 22:55 UTC

That commit has a bug that wasn’t fixed until [1.6.0~15](https://github.com/memcached/memcached/commit/6207330c2705fdb5f02de13b99a0d994f7c4f14a) “fix bug where sasl will load config the wrong path”.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-05-14 23:00 UTC

Workaround: create `/etc/systemd/system/memcached.service.d/zulip-sasl-fix.conf` with these contents:
```
[Service]
Environment=SASL_CONF_PATH=/etc/sasl2
```
(and run `systemctl daemon-reload; systemctl restart memcached`).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-05-14 23:09 UTC

That also works on 18.04, so it’s probably fine to apply that unconditionally.

**Matt** · 2022-07-28 14:05 UTC

Speaking generically, choosing a config management or orchestration framework (Puppet, Ansible, Salt, etc.) is a bit of a dogmatic choice, and one that is increasingly difficult to change over time. I recommend giving them all a little go, and figuring out what's "best" for your needs for your application. Often these decisions are made based on the experience of the people who need to make the decision and their tech stack. 

I can't speak to Zulip's Puppet decision, but will say that historically Puppet has had more brainshare available than the other technologies. Said differently, it's easier to find someone who has used Puppet than someone who has used <something else>.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-28 18:34 UTC

We picked `puppet` for this role in late 2012, and I can't say I've been thrilled with Puppet for this job. That said, I'd have been much sadder with the other options that were popular at the time, like cfengine.

It has been successful in allowing us to provide a reliable installation and upgrade process for a variety of configurations, which I'm glad for, but we've certainly spend a substantial amount of time on working around issues with its tooling where a different choice available today would have avoided that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-28 18:37 UTC

Directionally, we will likely be reducing how much we manage with `puppet` over time, and we may port our implementation to a different tool at some point. But I'd say our overall architecture goal is to try to make it easy for users to configure a wide range of different styles of Zulip installations with only manually entering configuration in a few files in `/etc/zulip` that don't require knowing an obscure programming language to edit, and that's been fairly successful.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-28 21:05 UTC

Even if one wasn't going to use `Nix`, it's probably the case that a more modern configuration engine like Ansible or Salt would be better as a direct replacement, but I've not evaluated them for the purpose in any detail.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-28 21:26 UTC

My plan is to fully replace Puppet with Nix.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-28 21:35 UTC

Yeah, that's my goal as well. I just haven't done a thoughtful audit through all the things we do with Puppet to try to determine if any of them might be awkward to do that with, so don't want to claim that we'll definitely end up with that outcome vs. having "Nix plus X" be a reasonable description of where we end up.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-28 21:36 UTC

I definitely don't want there to be any Puppet remaining at the end :)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-28 21:39 UTC

Although Puppet is a bad language, the real problem with Puppet, Ansible, and Salt is that they solve the wrong problem. They give you languages for saying “these are some *changes* I want to make to the system”. Nix is the only tool that lets you express “this *is the system* I want”, and you can be confident that the result doesn’t depend on the path you took to get there (except for the explicitly stateful parts like data in your database).

**Matt** · 2022-07-28 22:29 UTC

When used appropriately, Ansible is used to abstract system definitions, and describe the system you want. You can then either deploy changes to existing systems or a whole new system that reflects the new state. I have plenty to complain about all of these, but Ansible does make system description a first class thing. (When used appropriately)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-28 22:29 UTC

Yeah, I mean I think a Puppet fan would say its concept is that you declaratively state "I want directory X to exist and have these permissions", or whatever -- that's certainly how it's language is expressed. But it's got the wrong set of abstractions for that goal, and thus is leaky and you end up spending a bunch of time dealing with the fact that it doesn't quite obey the high-level contract.

There's older configuration management systems that didn't have Puppet's model, and they'd have been very much unsuitable for what we're trying to do. Puppet's core flaw, in my view, is that it was built with a practical devops mindset, rather than a "we should have a sound design" mindset. I should give it credit for improving over time as a tool -- some problems that drove me crazy in 2013-2017 with Puppet have been fixed ... but it's not designed for the class of problem we have, and it shows.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-28 23:06 UTC

No. With Ansible or Puppet, if you say “I want directory X to exist”, directory X will exist. If you then *stop* saying “I want directory X to exist”, directory X will *continue to exist*.

This is because what you have expressed is a change, from a system where directory X may or may not exist, to a system where directory X exists. Your system is then the product of all the changes you expressed in the past.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-28 23:11 UTC

This has two consequences. Firstly, the existence of directory X might have undesired side effects, and so you need to write an explicit migration to remove directory X.

Secondly and more importantly, if you are still implicitly relying on directory X, but directory X had previously been created as a side effect of something else, you might not realize that your change description no longer causes it to be created. Your system will appear to work, but then you bring up a new deployment from scratch and it breaks.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-29 00:14 UTC

I certainly agree with those criticisms of Puppet! But I thought it important to highlight that Puppet/Ansible/etc. have syntax and advertising that suggest a "describe the state of the system you want and it'll make it so" model -- they just aren't able to do that correctly in situations that are actually quite simple/common, like in your example above, if the developer decides to rename a directory.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-29 00:36 UTC

Why’s it important to highlight their syntax and advertising? I’m interested in what the model actually is. For Ansible and friends, the model is changes. Obviously they provide a pretty syntax for changes, tools for managing and abstracting and deploying large collections of changes, etc. but they do not provide *anything at all* in the direction of modeling systems rather than changes. There are many axes on which they are better than a shell script that runs `mkdir -p /directory/x`, but the underlying model is *exactly the same*.

**Jussi Talaskivi** · 2022-07-29 05:38 UTC

Changes for the system are always tricky if the start state anything but blank. In our experience Nix is a great tool for abstracting dependencies for different parts of the system (same system independent of packaging format or configuration for example).  It is excellent for ensuring that each developer have the exact dependencies installed for the development. 

For running things in production I'm biased for container images. Our current model is using Nix to create these images and running them with Hashicorp Nomad or with Podman in a single server. Containers have an excellent portability. You can run them pretty much on any operating system nowadays (as long as it has some Linux capability). Orchestrating the containers is a bit of muddy story. Single containers are fine with Podman or Docker but things get difficult when running multiples of them. Docker-compose doesn't go far enough and Kubernetes is often an overkill. Hashicorp's Nomad is a fine choice if one needs to run the infrastructure also. 

We (as in Digital Services in University of Jyväskylä) have went through the route of Puppet to Ansible to Nix. Puppet we have eliminated but Ansible still has a role for setting up the servers and I don't see any need for replacing it. Nix is being used for development and creating container images.

A user account is deactivated either by the person who owns it, or by an org admin. It means that user is gone, but the record of them in the database is still there so that e.g. old messages sent to and from them can still exist and history still makes sense for other users.
