I was reading the docs and I think this is a very nice way to handle users. It's actually pretty cool. Didn't know Django used this too.

**Abhishek B Chakravarthi** · 2020-04-15 18:09 UTC

Thanks for pointing this out.


## topics I follow naming

*2020-04-15 to 2023-05-16 · 24 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/topics.20I.20follow.20naming/with/854541)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-15 23:08 UTC

Hey folks, I have a naming question, related to the backend for the "notifications for topics I follow" feature detailed here:
https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/14555/files#diff-c29a639b9c074638e5b08d59f0be3997

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-15 23:09 UTC

The feature as described would initially let you configure notifications for threads you sent messages to recently, and then I imagine in the future we'll add manual controls as well (to let you follow/unfollow a thread without sending a message).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-15 23:09 UTC

I'm imagining the default configuration for new users would be to get notifications for topics one follows; especially in an OSS organization like this one, it'd be very helpful in ensuring folks who ask for support get notifications.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-15 23:10 UTC

But the current implementation just has the setting and notifications implementation.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-15 23:10 UTC

The question for now is what to call the field in the database.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-15 23:11 UTC

The branch here has e.g. `enable_topic_email_notifications`, in analogy with e.g. `enable_stream_email_notifications` for your default notification settings for stream messages, but I think it's a bit too broad of a name, since this is a configuration for a subset of all topics.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-15 23:12 UTC

My current thinking is `enable_followed_topic_email_notifications` or perhaps `enable_topic_follow_email_notifications`, but I really don't like how that latter sounds like it's telling you whether the topic was followed.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-15 23:15 UTC

I prefer `enable_topic_follow_(email,desktop,...)_notifications`.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-15 23:17 UTC

Is it too late to introduce a `UserNotificationSettings` table with these fields?
* user_profile
* event (FOLLOW_TOPIC=1, ...)
* kind (EMAIL=1, DESKTOP=2, ...)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-15 23:19 UTC

I mean, it's never too late in some sense, but I think the expedient thing is to proceed with this direction.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-15 23:19 UTC

The current model feels like the worst of both worlds.   I'd either want a more standard DB structure here (like above), or just put all these settings in a big blob, so we don't need to constantly be doing db migrations.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-15 23:19 UTC

I'm not sure what the right structure would be for that kind of table.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-15 23:20 UTC

And we do get a lot of structural simplicity from the `property_types` framework that we might lose with that type of system.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-15 23:21 UTC

My guess is the migration we'll end up doing is more in the direction of a `UserPreferences` table that tries to move out of UserProfile data that isn't relevant to code running on behalf of other users (E.g. your personal settings), but I'm not really sure.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-15 23:22 UTC

The thing I like about `enable_topic_follow_*_notifications` in the database is that it more nicely works with other local variable names in the logic for deciding on notifications, like  `stream_email_user_ids` -> `topic_follow_email_user_ids`, etc.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-15 23:22 UTC

So I'm OK with that option as well.  Would love to hear some more opinions.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2023-05-15 13:41 UTC

Bumping this up as we have resumed work on it.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2023-05-15 13:53 UTC

I'd prefer `enable_followed_topic_email_notifications` for the reason @Tim Abbott mentioned above.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-15 15:55 UTC

I like that proposal! Reads better than the "topic_follow" variants I'd been thinking about above.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2023-05-15 18:00 UTC

Also, I think [`stream_email_user_ids`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/actions/message_send.py#L258) and `stream_push_user_ids` should be renamed.

**Reason:**
Whether notification is sent or not is now [determined by](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/lib/notification_data.py#L177) both `topic_specific_settings`(global)  and `stream_specific_settings` (global or per stream); not only `stream_specific_settings` (global or per stream).

`topic_specific_setting` will take precedence as [discussed here](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/3-backend/topic/Follow.20Topics/near/1564073).

**Proposal:**
* `stream_or_followed_topic_email_user_ids`
* `stream_or_followed_topic_push_user_ids`

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-15 22:28 UTC

@Prakhar Pratyush I think we might actually just want a new `followed_topic_email_user_ids` parallel field in those objects, because I'm guessing we do need to plumb which of those possibilities was the case all the way through the system, so that the little text at the bottom of notification emails can say "You're receiving this email because you follow this topic."

Specifically this block in `templates/zerver/emails/missed_message.html`
```
{% block manage_preferences %}
<div class="email-preferences">
    &mdash;<br />
    {% if personal_mentioned %}
    {% trans %}You are receiving this because you were personally mentioned.{% endtrans %}<br />
    {% elif mentioned_user_group_name %}
    {% trans %}You are receiving this because @{{ mentioned_user_group_name }} was mentioned.{% endtrans %}<br />
    {% elif wildcard_mentioned %}
    {% trans %}You are receiving this because everyone was mentioned in #{{ stream_name }}.{% endtrans %}<br />
    {% elif stream_email_notify %}
    {% trans %}You are receiving this because you have email notifications enabled for #{{ stream_name }}.{% endtrans %}<br />
    {% endif %}
```

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2023-05-16 03:27 UTC

This makes sense.

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2023-05-16 03:32 UTC

However, with regards to the UNMUTE feature we have already implemented, it feels like the last text here (`You are receiving this because you have email notifications enabled for #{{ stream_name }}.`) would be incorrect if someone received a notification from an UNMUTED topic in a muted stream?
That person has specifically _disabled_ notifications for that stream, but we're saying they have _enabled_ notifications for that stream just because one topic in that stream is UNMUTED.
Should we also add fields like `unmuted_topic_email_user_ids` to correct this?

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-16 18:50 UTC

Yeah that seems right to me, though I think in most cases they'll only be getting an email because of a mention, it does seem possible to get a notification not due to that if you have email notifications enabled by default in streams.

If you run provision after removing/updating `dev-secrets.conf`, we will call the following program, which generates/updates the secrets file, and `local_database_password` in particular.  That's all good:

~~~
run(["scripts/setup/generate_secrets.py", "--development"])

* `zulip_test`

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-19 15:19 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-19 15:20 UTC

```
**Greg Price** · 2020-04-23 21:04 UTC

Cool, glad I mentioned it :slight_smile: 

That bit "sudoers(5)" can be read as "the 'sudoers' page in section 5 of the manual".

The idea of "section of the manual" is kind of obsolete in a literal sense -- it comes from talking about physical paper manuals -- but what it means operationally is you use the command `man 5 sudoers` and you get that page.

**Greg Price** · 2020-04-23 21:05 UTC

See also `man man`:
```
DESCRIPTION
       man is the system's manual pager.  Each page argument given  to  man
       is  normally the name of a program, utility or function.  The manual
       page associated with each of these arguments is then found and  dis‐
       played.   A  section,  if  provided, will direct man to look only in
       that section of the manual.  The default action is to search in  all
       of  the available sections following a pre-defined order ("1 n l 8 3
       2 3posix 3pm 3perl 3am 5 4 9 6 7" by default, unless  overridden  by
       the  SECTION directive in /etc/manpath.config), and to show only the
       first page found, even if page exists in several sections.

       The table below shows the section numbers of the manual followed  by
       the types of pages they contain.

       1   Executable programs or shell commands
       2   System calls (functions provided by the kernel)
       3   Library calls (functions within program libraries)
       4   Special files (usually found in /dev)
       5   File formats and conventions eg /etc/passwd
       6   Games
       7   Miscellaneous  (including  macro packages and conventions), e.g.
           man(7), groff(7)
       8   System administration commands (usually only for root)
       9   Kernel routines [Non standard]
```

**Greg Price** · 2020-04-23 21:08 UTC

So in general if in some Unix- or Linux-flavored documentation you see something that looks like an identifier and then a number in parens after it -- like "florble(3)" -- then you translate that to a `man` command like `man 3 florble`, to look up that man page in that "section of the manual".

**Greg Price** · 2020-04-23 21:11 UTC

A related handy resource while I'm talking about man pages: you can browse a comprehensive set of manages on the Web here:
https://manpages.debian.org/
(for all man pages in Debian, which will also cover virtually any you'd find in Ubuntu, and in any other Linux distro most things will be very similar.) E.g. enter "sudoers" and you get:
https://manpages.debian.org/buster/sudo/sudoers.5.en.html

I almost always look man pages up with the `man` command, but manpages.debian.org is very handy for posting a link to one in, say, a Zulip message.
```

```
**Arpit Sharma** · 2020-04-22 20:45 UTC

After removing python-pip dependency I could install dev server on Focal. Looks like ```Python-pip-whl ``` issue ( ipaddress module missing) with python2  got fixed in upstream. 

One slight issue is that - 
Some dependency like ``` importlib-metadata ``` and ```importlib-resources ``` are built-in for python 3.8 and 3.7 respectively. So if we install a dependency that depends on them, our requirements.txt will differ for python versions. 

Earlier in ``` pip-tools 4.4.1 ``` there were no annotations to primary requirements in the compilation output and so they did not include reverse dependencies. So adding these dependencies in our primary requirements solved this issue.
But since we upgraded pip-tools Focal tests are failing.

@Anders Kaseorg  So Should we restrict pip-tools (till we merge the PR that allows us to ship python) or there is any other way possible?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-04-22 20:52 UTC

The [upstream recommendation](https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools#should-i-commit-requirementsin-and-requirementstxt-to-source-control) is to compile `*.txt` for each Python version separately, which is not great. There’s some further relevant discussion in https://github.com/jazzband/pip-tools/issues/826.
```

**Greg Price** · 2020-06-11 21:12 UTC

Introduced here, last year:
```
commit a046a0957b30cd90ffe29e9a0379aa6e7e24c9d0
Author: Kouhei Sutou <kou@clear-code.com>
Date:   Sat May 4 07:32:49 2019 +0900

    docs: Fix upgrade process for Ubuntu 16.04 -> 18.04.
    
    We need to disable "CREATE EXTENSION pgroonga" in zulip-puppet-apply
    by creating /usr/share/postgresql/10/pgroonga_setup.sql.applied.
    Because PostgreSQL 10 isn't running in this case. If PostgreSQL 10
    isn't running, we can't run "CREATE EXTENSION pgroonga".
    
    We can't use pg_upgrade with PGroonga. PGroonga's install SQL
    https://github.com/pgroonga/pgroonga/blob/master/data/pgroonga.sql has
    conditions to support multiple PostgreSQL versions. So it's not safe
    to use pg_upgrade. pg_upgrade copies metadata for PostgreSQL 9.5 to
    PostgreSQL 10. We need to use pg_dump and pg_restore to upgrade
    PGroonga correctly for PostgreSQL 10.
```

## Django squashmigrations

*2020-04-25 to 2025-08-13 · 130 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Django.20squashmigrations/with/862735)*

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-04-25 17:13 UTC

After reading some blog posts, I can say there are 2 general ways of making our migrations faster.

1. Use Django's `squashmigrations`. This has a few problems:
* We need to manually move a lot of RunPython migrations we have. This is highly risky too.
* We need to keep our old migrations until all the systems have migrated to the release in which squashmigration was applied.

2. We recreate migrations.
Copied from - https://www.karimoff.me/articles/squash-migrations-in-django.html

This method is similar to above, but you pretend you have written all models at once and have never ever had any migrations applied.

**Steps**
* Delete existing migration files, keep migrations folder empty with only migrations/__init__.py.
* Remove all records from django migrations table in database. Run django-admin dbshell and execute TRUNCATE django_migrations; query.
* Create new migration files. Run django-admin makemigrations.
* Apply new migrations with fake flag. Run django-admin migrate --fake

**In Production**
* We can use our `upgrade-zulip-stage-2` script to do required steps for us based on the version.

**Drawbacks**
* This method requires you to write SQL query and execute directly which is risky and you might accidentally drop a table/database instead 🤯.


Rebuilding our current test db takes 22s,
```
./tools/rebuild-dev-database  22.76s user 1.02s system 50% cpu 46.817 total
```

Which I think is pretty decent compared to the trouble we will have to go through to make sure all the different instances of zulip while doing provision and `upgrade-zulip-stage-2` don't run into trouble and same migration files are generated on all systems.

**Greg Price** · 2024-08-13 18:11 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> I wonder how complicated the implementation is. It's possible that the most efficient way to handle at least some of these limitations is to actually improve the generic `squashmigrations` code.

The driver of squashmigrations is [this MigrationOptimizer class](https://github.com/django/django/blob/b99c608ea10cabc97a6b251cdb6e81ef2a83bdcf/django/db/migrations/optimizer.py), with a loop I don't fully understand the logic of but it's not much code.

The bulk of the implementation is in `reduce` methods on the various Operation subclasses.

**Greg Price** · 2024-08-13 18:11 UTC

For example for this situation:

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> But I think it's also just not that smart; e.g. it won't squash the AlterField to change a default in a model into its `CreateModel` entry.

the relevant logic is [here](https://github.com/django/django/blob/b99c608ea10cabc97a6b251cdb6e81ef2a83bdcf/django/db/migrations/operations/models.py#L233-L245):
```py
class CreateModel(ModelOperation):
    # …
    def reduce(self, operation, app_label):
        # …
        elif (
            isinstance(operation, FieldOperation)
            and self.name_lower == operation.model_name_lower
        ):
            # …
            elif isinstance(operation, AlterField):
                return [
                    CreateModel(
                        self.name,
                        fields=[
                            (n, operation.field if n == operation.name else v)
                            for n, v in self.fields
                        ],
                        options=self.options,
```

## Unique id for topic

*2020-04-26 to 2020-04-26 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Unique.20id.20for.20topic/with/862900)*

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-04-26 07:54 UTC

Does it make sense to have unique ids for topics too?
In frontend, we need to update a lot of stuff after a topic edit, and we even miss out updating in some places like `recent_senders.js`, also there are issues like #13726. 

I suggest we set `id of a topic` to be the `id of the last msg` in the topic as every topic has at least one last msg and most of the times that is all what we are looking for when querying info related to a topic.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-26 16:56 UTC

@Aman Agrawal it's a good question.  This is a somewhat tricky issue.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-26 16:56 UTC

Our current backend data structure for topics is just a string field on the `Message` table, so there's no well-defined ID attached to topics there.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-26 16:57 UTC

And the message-editing semantics of being able to move a message to another topic mean that a hack like what you describe would be no better than just using the topic as a string (because your IDs wouldn't be stable across message deleting/editing).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-26 16:59 UTC

A topic table would only help with #13726 on public streams or private streams with shared history; for other situations, we still need to go to the UserMessage/Message tables to see which topics the current user has access to.  

(This is why my proposal for #13726 is that we have to add that index regardless of what else we do)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-26 17:00 UTC

I think in the absence of a stable, backend-provided ID, we're better off using (stream_id, topic_name) pairs, i.e. the actual unique key for the topic, than trying to work with a non-stable ID that we make up on the frontend.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-26 17:01 UTC

And even if we had that sort of stable ID, we'd still need to write special code for the message-edit and message deletion code paths to update things like `recent_senders` to deal with messages that just changed topics.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-26 17:03 UTC

So while I agree that message-editing and message-deletion require a lot of care to get right with topics, I don't think that work becomes particularly more or less if we were to migrate to a data model where there's a `topic_id` integer field somewhere.  The main way that such a field could help us is if we wanted to have other state attached to topics where a ForeignKey structure would be helpful.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-04-26 17:45 UTC

Interesting thanks for explaining this to me. I understand this issue better now.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-04-26 18:18 UTC

It's possible we should put a version of that text in our documentation somewhere.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-04-30 00:09 UTC

What happens now is that the dev database fails the `database_exists` check, so it runs the init for the dev database, but then when we go to check the test database, we're using the `zulip` account to find that the **test** database exists, which it does, so then we don't update anything for the test database, and then the `zulip_test` account is still locked out.  Or something like that--I don't remember the exact details.

I do think for this particular scenario we can add `dev-secrets.conf` to the digest, and then both databases will just do a complete rebuild.  I think, but I haven't tested this yet.

The bigger point here is that these scenarios are really hard to debug when you don't have a fail-fast mentality.  I'm not saying you should *never* recover--in fact, for 98% of cases, there's a logical happy path where we cleanly detect what we need to do next, and we do it--it's just when we're in that other 2% of cases that I think we should just fail hard.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2020-05-02 08:37 UTC

Thinking out loud here, maybe a good syntax would let me express this sequence of declarations:
* An expression matching the pattern `logging` has tag `LOGGER`.
* An expression matching the pattern `logger` has tag `LOGGER`.
* If `$L` has tag `LOGGER`, then an expression matching the pattern `$L.debug` has tag `LOGGER_CALL`.
* If `$L` has tag `LOGGER`, then an expression matching the pattern `$L.info` has tag `LOGGER_CALL`.
* If `$L` has tag `LOGGER`, then an expression matching the pattern `$L.warning` has tag `LOGGER_CALL`.
* If `$L` has tag `LOGGER`, then an expression matching the pattern `$L.error` has tag `LOGGER_CALL`.
* If `$L` has tag `LOGGER`, then an expression matching the pattern `$L.critical` has tag `LOGGER_CALL`.
* If `$C` has tag `LOGGER_CALL`, then an expression matching the pattern `$C(... % ...)` is an error.
* If `$C` has tag `LOGGER_CALL`, then an expression matching the pattern `$C(... .format(...))` is an error.

## markdown size limit

*2020-05-03 to 2021-03-17 · 33 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/markdown.20size.20limit/with/867068)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-03 18:09 UTC

In production, in some of our mathematics-focused communities, we've been throwing this markdown processor exception: `Rendered content exceeds 100000 characters`

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-03 18:16 UTC

Our limit on raw content for a message is 10K characters.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-03 18:17 UTC

And that code is there to prevent pathological cases where the markdown output explodes being a big problem.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-03 18:17 UTC

However, KaTeX, as a system, has a blowup factor that's significantly larger than 10, so folks talking about math have this come up with what are likely reasonably-sided messages.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-03 18:24 UTC

I'm curious for thoughts on how we should proceed; ideally, one should be able to post 5K character messages full of math.  But with KaTeX, a simple expression like `\int_0^1 f(x)` that's ~14 characters turns into like 1600 characters of HTML.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-03 18:24 UTC

So we'd need to increase that limit ~10x, e.g. to 100K, to achieve that goal.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-03 18:25 UTC

I suppose if we're not worried about DoS, just about bugs (which may be the case at this size), we could have the limit be 10x higher if the message contains KaTeX.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-03 18:44 UTC

We could just render Tex client-side.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-04 04:47 UTC

My guess is it'd be a bad experience to do that if you have a screen full of messages full of math, which is exactly the use case in these communities.  But I suppose we could do that only if there's a lot of KaTeX content  -- basically have the backend markdown processor decide to just store the raw TeX input on an element and request that the client render-and-replace it to handle this sort of corner case.  Not sure how messy that would be as a system; it could be pretty reasonable.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-04 12:09 UTC

One data point here is that we actually use the JS parser in both places for KaTeX here, right?

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-05-04 16:19 UTC

Yes, we use subprocess to call `katex/cli.js`

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-04 16:29 UTC

Correct, which makes it technically reasonable to do what I describe.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-04 16:30 UTC

I think it's important to do backend-side validation that it doesn't throw a parse error, so we'd still run KaTeX in the backend processor in any case.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-05-04 16:31 UTC

We could also take a note of all the Katex strings length and subtract them from the 100k rendered text limit? Seems easy enough to get this data in fenced_code.py.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-04 16:37 UTC

Is the backend validation necessary for the sender or the sendees?  I guess it’s plausible you could maliciously construct a message that expands to really nasty html?

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-05-04 16:38 UTC

That's mostly to find any kind of weird recursive bugs, I think. I think its reasonable to assume that if we have that large of an explosion from raw to rendered, there's something wrong in the message.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-05-04 16:40 UTC

I'm wondering if we can craft something like:

~~~
"```py\nx\n```" * 500
~~~

and have this explode to 100k+. That's one of the few potential ways to break this check with an actual message.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-04 23:40 UTC

It's important for the sender as a user experience thing -- it's a lot nicer to get a compose error message for broken syntax than for your broken message to be sent.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-04 23:41 UTC

(replying to Rohitt Vashishtha)
> That's mostly to find any kind of weird recursive bugs, I think. I think its reasonable to assume that if we have that large of an explosion from raw to rendered, there's something wrong in the message.

That isn't the case with KaTeX -- HTML is a much less efficient way to represent math than the raw LaTeX.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-04 23:41 UTC

Which is where the 100x blowup comes from.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-05 12:49 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> It's important for the sender as a user experience thing -- it's a lot nicer to get a compose error message for broken syntax than for your broken message to be sent.

If we're concerned about the sender, then what I'm proposing is that we just validate in the front end, since it's the exact parser that we use in the backend anyway.  But I assume there's also some concern about the sendees here.

**Wesley Aptekar-Cassels** · 2021-03-16 04:20 UTC

fwiw, i've run into the 10k limit just writing "normal" messages/PMs on zulip, and i've seen other people run into it as well. i think bumping up that limit would be good in general, and would be a good short-term way to help folks in math communities running into this problem (it sounds like there's linear benefit here, which is actually pretty good — if we double it, that ~doubles the size of message that people can send, which seems like a significant improvement)

**Wesley Aptekar-Cassels** · 2021-03-16 04:22 UTC

from a DoS perspective, is sending a 100k message significantly worse for the server than sending 10*10k messages?

**Wesley Aptekar-Cassels** · 2021-03-16 04:24 UTC

oh, i see that the 10k is just the raw limit, so maybe that's a separate concern. but still, i think if users are bumping into limits like this, just increasing the limits is a reasonable option unless we have a reason to suspect that'll create problems

**Wesley Aptekar-Cassels** · 2021-03-16 04:41 UTC

10xing the rendered limit in messages with latex seems reasonable to me, i don't think that having a handful of 1MB rendered messages should hurt the server much, especially given that we upload uncompressed images/etc all the time (although maybe that's equivocating, if those go to S3 or whatever).

we could also set the limit to 100x the size of the raw message, to offer even more protection against bugs (or more reasonably, `max(1000, raw_msg_size*100)`, or maybe even something slightly fancier). that way long katex messages have enough space, but short messages would quickly hit limits if there's some sort of blowup bug.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-16 19:16 UTC

(replying to Wesley Aptekar-Cassels)
> from a DoS perspective, is sending a 100k message significantly worse for the server than sending 10*10k messages?
Well, we have rate limits on how fast a user can send messages (or hit any API endpoint).  I could imagine our trying to modify that rate-limiting logic to have a "total size of messages per unit time" resource to manage the issue.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-16 19:18 UTC

But I think we should first test the question of how long KaTeX actually takes to transform LaTeX into text -- if it's fast enough, moving that rendering to the frontend might be a better structure.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-16 19:22 UTC

I don't think I've previously heard of folks feeling unhappy about the limit of 10K characters for their raw input of a message.  I think we could probably make that number 20K without material server-side issues.  That said, I don't think it's super pleasant to actually read a 20K input character Zulip message in most cases, because it's likely to take up multiple screenfuls of height and thus isn't readily keyboard-accessible (as our main keyboard scrolling interface of up/down doesn't support sub-message granularity).  Maybe that's OK and we should let folks do it -- they'll see what their message looks like and each community can decide how they want to handle the social issues around it.

But I think there's also a perspective that having people composing messages hit the 10K character limit and need to split their message might result in a better reading UX than allowing folks to write extraordinarily long individual messages.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-16 19:22 UTC

I guess the other thing that needs testing is what KaTeX's actual typical explosion factor is -- I have no specific reason to believe that 100x is the right number to model.

**Wesley Aptekar-Cassels** · 2021-03-17 06:54 UTC

> But I think we should first test the question of how long KaTeX actually takes to transform LaTeX into text -- if it's fast enough, moving that rendering to the frontend might be a better structure.

my experience with mathjax is that client side rendering almost always leads to various flavors of jank (since the height isn't known until rendering is complete). maybe katex is good enough not to have this problem, but i'd be surprised? i guess the solution is to block rendering any messages that were sent after (and including) any katex message until katex rendering is complete, so then the question is if katex rendering is fast enough that the bandwidth-saving is worth it. i also wonder if there are malicious katex messages one could craft that would result in exponential rendering time? that can be fixed with a timeout, of course, but a timeout means a message may render on one persons computer, but fail for another, which seems bad. there are ways to fix all of this, of course, but it does seem like it would add a significant amount of complexity, relative to just increasing the rendered message size limit :)

> I don't think I've previously heard of folks feeling unhappy about the limit of 10K characters for their raw input of a message. I think we could probably make that number 20K without material server-side issues. That said, I don't think it's super pleasant to actually read a 20K input character Zulip message in most cases, because it's likely to take up multiple screenfuls of height and thus isn't readily keyboard-accessible (as our main keyboard scrolling interface of up/down doesn't support sub-message granularity). Maybe that's OK and we should let folks do it -- they'll see what their message looks like and each community can decide how they want to handle the social issues around it.

i think it's unusual — i've only run into it a couple times, and i only know of three other people who have run into it. somehow i seem to remember the behavior being that the message was truncated on send, but checking now it doesn't seem like that's the case (i found someone complaining that it did in 2015, so maybe this changed since then? and one person complaining that reply-by-email truncated their message, which seems like a real bug). instead, the inputbox just stops accepting input (there should probably be more feedback here, but that's a separate issue, i'll file that in a bit). anyway, all of this isn't really relevant to the rendered size limit, so i'll just file these as issues or start other threads :)

**Alex Dehnert** · 2021-03-17 18:12 UTC

> instead, the inputbox just stops accepting input (there should > probably be more feedback here, but that's a separate issue, i'll file > that in a bit).

IIRC Twitter lets you keep typing and just tells you the character count and refuses to let you send, which means you can figure out what you want and then edit it. This is probably a lot less important for 10K characters, but it is pretty nice.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-17 18:31 UTC

That’s probably the best solution here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-17 20:32 UTC

@Wesley Aptekar-Cassels I think this is the truncation logic used by the email gateway:

```
    if len(content) > MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH:                                                            
        content = content[0:3900] + "\n\n[message was too long and has been truncated]"              
```

Note that 3900 is much less than MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH; my vague recollection was that this was intentional at the time we added it (many years ago) because many emails in the wild have infinite junk at the bottom of them, but that was done before we introduced `talon` for stripping replies and the like.

Re editing etc, that's evolving and there's a WIP PR for updating settings from inside the app.

**Greg Price** · 2020-05-05 18:34 UTC

Great :)

**Greg Price** · 2020-05-05 18:37 UTC

One nice thing about the dotfile model is that (assuming the config is in some reasonable config-file format, of which there are many) it's completely under my control, as the user. I can read it; edit it; back it up; copy it from one machine to another, and then edit specific pieces; version it in Git, so I know exactly what changed when I discover something broke, and can go back exactly to a previous version.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2020-05-05 18:43 UTC

Right, I'm all in favour of controlling that stuff :) That said, having a 'backup' in the server is pretty useful. I was thinking earlier about the priority order, as typically there's command-line > local-config > defaults. With server data that could become command-line > local-config > server-config > defaults. If you lost the config file, you could retain the config.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2020-05-05 18:46 UTC

With all those options, my concern is that you end up handling syncronization between them all, ie. do you "magically" update server config from default+local each time, or some other combination, or only do things explicitly.

**Greg Price** · 2020-05-05 18:56 UTC

From a "backup" perspective, while my Zulip message history is important data, I think my Zulip user settings are pretty low in the list of things I'd be sad to have lost if my disk failed/vanished and I didn't have working backups.

**Greg Price** · 2020-05-05 18:59 UTC

I think most of us who spend a lot of time in a terminal will have other config files in our homedir that we'd be pretty sad to lose. (For me my Emacs and Bash configs, for a start.) So any local config for ZT that's in a standard config-file place will get covered by whatever backups we have for all that.

**Greg Price** · 2020-05-05 19:03 UTC

If you were to have something like command-line > local-config > server-config > defaults, I think one way to frame the question of how they interact is: what happens when you adjust some setting from inside the app? Where does that get written to?

If it's just command-line > local-config > defaults, then the answer is clear: it gets written to the local config. (The `~/.config/zulip-terminal/config` file or whatever.) But if there's also server config, then when do you write to which one?

Git has a pretty good answer to this in the form of `git config --global` -- by default you write changes to the local repo's settings, but you can explicitly do it to your global homedir settings instead. If you think there's a strong case for both local and server-side settings, you could potentially do something similar in the ZT settings UI.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-05 19:55 UTC

My two cents is that we should decouple the authentication stuff in `zuliprc` from other configuration.  Keeping secret and non-secret info in the same file creates a few problems that I would want to avoid:
* If you want to change your API key and download a new `zuliprc`, there's a chance you would blow away other settings.
* If you want to share your settings (kinda like people share tricked out vimrc and gitconfig files), it's inconvenient if the file has secrets in it.
* If you simply want to back it up or source control it, it's inconvenient to have secrets in the file.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2020-05-05 20:26 UTC

@Steve Howell That's the likely outcome from this discussion in any case, including the related discussion on #**zulip-terminal**.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2020-05-05 20:26 UTC

(probably best to follow up there, too)

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I think we still haven't looked into this, and it could be useful: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/3470

I'd be interested to hear what @Anders Kaseorg thinks about immutable caching.  Here's the article for convenience: https://hacks.mozilla.org/2017/01/using-immutable-caching-to-speed-up-the-web/

I agree with the premise that 304s may be nearly as expensive as fetching some smaller items.  For the particular case of emojis, I don't think this would help much, since we already prevent lots of round trips with the sprite.  It seems promising for the avatars, though.

To Tim's point, since most of our static assets are built with hash-names, maybe there's no real downside here.

We can enable immutable caching on everything in `/static/webpack-bundles` except `/static/webpack-bundles/5xx.html` (probably a browser wouldn’t immutably cache an error page, but it’s good to be sure). We’re not as consistent with the rest of `/static`.

I am reluctant to go down that rabbit hole in that I think there's a lot of hidden complexity involved in trying to do that involving violating assumptions of the model.

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2020-05-12 17:16 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> Thoughts on how we might want to relax the others?
If the source and destination are both public, does it make sense to allow anyone to move the topics? If a particular user is allowed to edit topics, they should be able to move between streams which are public.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-12 17:17 UTC

Well, I'm not sure about that -- there's more mischief possible with moving topics to another stream than renaming a topic within a stream, and so we need to be thoughtful about the permissions model.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2020-05-12 17:18 UTC

Admins could also move things from public to private. Suppose someone accidentally reported a COC violation here in a public stream that we would rather discuss somewhere else?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-12 17:18 UTC

The other consideration here is that we're add a "stream admin" permission, and that may play into what options make sense to allow.

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2020-05-12 17:19 UTC

(replying to Rohitt Vashishtha)
> Admins could also move things from public to private. Suppose someone accidentally reported a COC violation here in a public stream that we would rather discuss somewhere else?
Or vice-versa, if we want to make a discussion public that seems to be relevant for a bigger audience.

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2020-05-12 17:23 UTC

At least in the realms I'm a part of, I'd be comfortable with admins being able to move messages out of a private stream. I'd expect the admin to check with the OP or the participants in the topic before doing the move, when moving from private streams. (I'd do that in the realms where I'm an admin)

**Wyatt Hoodes** · 2020-05-12 17:41 UTC

Would a 'request' make sense? In the sense that any member can make a request to move a topic, and an admin would approve or deny.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-12 17:43 UTC

Yeah, I think potentially stream administrators should be able to move content out of a private stream; one can (1) always repost the content and (2) always make the stream no longer private, anyway.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-12 17:44 UTC

The same argument likely applies to moving content into a private stream; you move it to a stream you administrer and then make that stream private.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-12 17:44 UTC

So I think we just need to adjust the automated notifications to be appropriate (with "a private stream") instead of a direct link?

**Puneeth Chaganti** · 2020-05-12 17:51 UTC

> (1) always repost the content and (2) always make the stream no longer private

I'm thinking of a scenario where a few of us have started discussing a topic, and then we realize the discussion is relevant to a wider audience. Reposting the content would work, but it'd be a summary of the discussion or a copy/paste of the messages already sent. Being able to move all the messages might be nicer, than either of these options.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-12 18:16 UTC

Yeah, just to be clear, I'm talking about the security model considerations.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-12 18:17 UTC

I.e. the fact that the stream administrator can make the stream no longer private means that we're not providing any additional security protection by preventing a move of the content to another stream.

**Greg Price** · 2020-05-12 21:30 UTC

I think (2) is a good reason to generally let a stream's admins move a topic out of that stream.

It's not a perfect one! When reasoning about security and security models, a wall with a small crack in it pretty much might as well be an open gate a truck could drive through. But privacy is not only about security of that kind, but also about social expectations.

From an expectations point of view, an admin of a private stream making the whole stream public is a nuclear option. In a lot of situations you might be pretty confident the admins wouldn't do that... but maybe not as confident of how they'd use the option to make just one conversation public, selectively.

**Greg Price** · 2020-05-12 21:37 UTC

Similarly, from a security perspective (1) means anyone who can read a conversation might as well have the ability to move it (or at least copy it) to any stream they can post to.

But from an expectations perspective, I think it can actually feel very different -- I think a lot of private streams would feel a lot less private if there were a handy product feature that anyone in the stream could use to turn a given conversation public. In that world, a private stream would only feel reasonably private if I were confident that *everyone* in the stream had a shared social understanding of how to appropriately decide whether/when to do that.

That's what makes it important to limit the feature to stream admins -- it makes it a lot more likely that there'll be that confidence so that the private stream still feels private.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-12 22:59 UTC

Yeah, I agree, the "stream admin" restriction seems important.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-12 22:59 UTC

Which effectively gates doing this properly behind having "stream admins" beyond just "realm admins".

**Steve Howell** · 2020-05-12 23:01 UTC

I think we should err on the side of caution when it comes to moving from private to public.  I have always resisted this feature, as even moving from a small public stream to a big public stream feels like a violation of trust to me, even though it’s technically not a security violation.

**Greg Price** · 2020-05-12 23:02 UTC

It could be just realm/org admins for now, right? Seems like the feature is pretty orthogonal.

Would probably benefit from a comment like
```
// TODO(stream-admin): This should be extended to stream admins when we have those.
```
to make sure the stream-admin work comes back to it.

**Greg Price** · 2020-05-12 23:04 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell)
> I think we should err on the side of caution when it comes to moving from private to public. I have always resisted this feature, as even moving from a small public stream to a big public stream feels like a violation of trust to me, even though it’s technically not a security violation.

Yeah, I agree with this feeling. I think it's dependent on the admin who'd do it having a good sense of people's expectations, and typically doing it only after asking the people who talked in the topic.

**Greg Price** · 2020-05-12 23:05 UTC

Puneeth was saying upthread that in Zulip communities he's in, he feels confident stream admins would indeed handle that appropriately.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-13 19:05 UTC

See #**desktop>IDEA: Go to TOP of TOPIC** for a discussion of a bug we need to track down.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-13 19:06 UTC

**Pragati Agrawal** · 2020-07-10 08:55 UTC

Can we split `access_stream_for_delete_or_update` function like this. Now we can simply use `check_stream_access_for_delete_or_update` in `list_to_streams` (not sure code is right, just pointing out the idea of splitting the function)
```python3
def check_stream_access_for_delete_or_update(user_profile, stream, sub):
    # We should only ever use this for realm admins, who are allowed
    # to delete or update all streams on their realm, even private streams
    # to which they are not subscribed.
    if stream.realm_id != user_profile.realm_id:
        raise JsonableError(_("Invalid stream id"))

    if user_profile.is_realm_admin:
        return

    if sub is not None and sub.is_stream_admin:
        return

    raise JsonableError(_("This action requires administrative rights."))

def access_stream_for_delete_or_update(user_profile: UserProfile, stream_id: int) -> Stream:
    try:
        stream = Stream.objects.get(id=stream_id)
    except Stream.DoesNotExist:
        raise JsonableError(_("Invalid stream id"))

    try:
        sub = Subscription.objects.get(user_profile=user_profile, 
                                       recipient=stream.recipient,
                                       active=True)
    except Subscription.DoesNotExist:
        sub = None

    check_stream_access_for_delete_or_update(user_profile, stream, sub)
    return stream
```

def create_tornado_application(port: int) -> tornado.web.Application:

        r"/api/v1/events",
        r"/api/v1/events/internal",

## edit_history

*2020-05-15 to 2020-05-16 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/edit_history/with/878944)*

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2020-05-15 18:55 UTC

We've just been discussing how to show the edit history in ZT in #**zulip-terminal**. A previous PR that @Preet Mishra is building on (by @Shreya Malviya) used `edit_history` in the Message dicts from get_messages and various events, which includes a lot of content. Tim noted the presence of a specific history endpoint. Often the webapp doesn't necessarily use extra endpoints, and an initial review made me think it was tracking message history using the same approach we planned - but it seems that the webapp specifically uses this endpoint to show the history.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2020-05-15 19:00 UTC

So:
* Is there a reason the history is in every message that's sent out, rather than relying on the user calling the extra endpoint like the webapp does? Historical?
* Does the frontend rely on this for some other reason? (I've not dug deeply)
* Is this eventually going to go away? It seems like duplication, if the webapp relies on the extra endpoint alone.
* Is this a prod needed to help it go away? ;)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-15 23:32 UTC

I think in theory if we could do client-side highlighting well, we wouldn't need that webapp endpoint.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-15 23:32 UTC

The main thing the frontend uses edit history for is to check if the message was edited at all.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-15 23:33 UTC

I agree we should resolve in one of two directions:
* Either we only send `edited: bool` in message objects from the server (probably best)
* Or we expect clients to use the `edit_history` endpoint to fetch details.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2020-05-16 00:35 UTC

I'm sure that the extra data load isn't much, but it seems duplicated work to handle both, and also unclear from an API perspective, so it seems like a good decision to make. The extra feature of the diff from the extra API call is also useful, but we could use a parameter to determine whether rendered or regular content is included and/or with the diff, a little like with get_messages?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-05-16 22:32 UTC

Yeah, I think my temptation would be to do the `edited: bool` approach.  @Greg Price thoughts on the right backwards-compatibility approach for this?


## user group mentions

*2020-05-17 to 2021-06-06 · 37 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/user.20group.20mentions/with/880148)*

**Hashir Sarwar** · 2020-05-17 07:07 UTC

Suppose a user is added in two groups and both the groups are mentioned in a single message. Right now the user gets only one new mention and the notification email states "You are receiving this because you were mentioned in Zulip Dev".

But now we want to replace "you were mentioned" with "@userGroupA was mentioned", for example (reference: [#13080](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/13080)). How can we handle multiple user group mentions in a single message? IMO, we should still indicate 1 mention count with an email stating something like "You are receiving this because @userGroupA, @userGroupB, @userGroupC were mentioned in Zulip Dev". Does this sound good?

**Hemanth V. Alluri** · 2020-05-17 07:31 UTC

@Hashir Sarwar that approach seems to be a bit to verbose/overkill. Mentioning any one of the groups should fine.

To quote @Tim Abbott  from when he opened the issue:
> If a user's mentioned multiple ways, we use the highest priority (personal over user group) and a random user group (doesn't matter which).

The main purpose of this change is to let the person know if they were mentioned personally or via. a group mention (since that indicates how directly the mention applies to them and in a way the urgency of the notification). The exact group is usually not that important so that's why we're using any single user group in the push/email notification.

**Hemanth V. Alluri** · 2020-05-17 07:35 UTC

If we really want to make it so that we specify every mentioned group the user belongs to, we could always add that later. But for now we want to keep the notification simple and crisp.

**Hemanth V. Alluri** · 2020-05-17 07:36 UTC

This way the push notification would also be smaller and displayed better on the mobile side I guess.

**Hashir Sarwar** · 2020-05-17 07:37 UTC

Sounds good. Thanks @Hemanth V. Alluri!

The problem with having a separate flag in UserMessage plumbed through to clients is that existing clients wouldn't support the flag, so we might feel the need to set the `mentioned` flag for them as well.  So we'll probably need to do a `client_capabilities` transition.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-04 14:43 UTC

We may eventually want to adjust UserMessage to have such a separate flag, but we don't have any current features that would treat that any differently from `flags.mentioned`, and it's a decent amount of work involving a new database index, API transitions, etc.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-04 14:44 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-04 14:48 UTC

I think the main motivation for not doing that is just that it's nontrivial work; e.g. we probably need a migration like `zerver/migrations/0099_index_wildcard_mentioned_user_messages.py` to make sure we have a fast database index for "is the user mentioned" with the updated data model.

2. Have the database store user group mentions information in `UserMessage` too, but keep the `mentioned` flag for the API to be `personal_mentioned | user_group_mentioned`.
3. Actually send user group mention data to clients, if and when we have any client-side features which can make use of this data.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-06 15:26 UTC

(replying to Abhijeet Bodas)
> If we were to store user group mention data in `UserMessage`, would an `ArrayField` better suit the requirement than a boolean flag? (Since a message could mention multiple user groups)
We need to be extremely careful with adding additional columns to the UserMessage table, because it is our largest database table, something like 2-3x as large as the rest of a Zulip database combined.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-06 15:27 UTC

And that's with it containing just 3 numbers in each row.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-06 15:29 UTC

I don't think we have a vision for user-facing UI where we'd need to show the list of user groups mentioned in a message efficiently, which is the only reason we'd need such an ArrayField in the database.  (One can do it inefficiently today by parsing the rendered message for user group mention elements and taking the union of their `data-user-group-id` attributes).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-06 15:30 UTC

So I think that vision makes sense, where we potentially would imagine step 3 to be the simple extension of having a `user_group_mentioned` flag available to clients.

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-06 16:13 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-06 16:24 UTC

Well, the benefit of having it as a dedicated column in the database is that we could in the future add an independent search operator for it.  And the API motive would be to allow desktop notifications to in the future be adjusted to indicate whether a user group was mentioned or not.

But I think none of these things are product features we have as a near term goal, and those migrations are nontrivial work, so I'd be tempted to, after considering the steps we could do, just do step 1 for now and declare victory.  Does that make sense to you @Abhijeet Bodas?

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-06 16:29 UTC

## auth backend loggers

*2020-05-20 to 2020-06-02 · 15 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/auth.20backend.20loggers/with/882092)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-05-20 13:30 UTC

Currently in `zprojects/backends.py` the way we do logging (necessary in the social auth backends that have more complex logic) is through `logging.xxxx()` calls. This isn't great, because it may be not obvious which backend generated the log unless you remember to clarify that every time you're writing a line of code to log something :slight_smile:  Like:
```
logging.info("/login/saml/ : Bad idp param: KeyError: %s.", str(e))
```
or
```
            error_msg = "Missing idp or subdomain value in relayed_params in SAML auth_complete: %s"
            logging.info(error_msg, dict(subdomain=subdomain, idp=idp_name))
```

So my idea, that I wanted to see what people think about it, is that we should set up a different logger for each backend:
1. Add a top-level logger in settings.LOGGING `zulip.auth` with the default handlers `DEFAULT_ZULIP_HANDLERS` (and perhaps an extra handler to also write to `/var/log/zulip/auth.log`?).
2. Each auth backend should use its own logger `self.logger = logging.getLogger(f"zulip.auth.{self.name}")` to log its stuff.

I think that should make these auth logs much easier to analyze and eliminate the need to think "will it be clear which backend generated this log message?" when writing new backend code?

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2020-05-27 07:25 UTC

This is how our fronted handles it:
```
exports.server_update = function (opts) {
    channel.post({
        url: '/json/users/me/status',
        data: {
            away: opts.away,
            status_text: opts.status_text,
        },
        idempotent: true,
        success: function () {
            if (opts.success) {
                opts.success();
            }
        },
    });
};
```
This is how our frontend does it, you can see https://zulipchat.com/api/rest for more implementation details, (this specific case is not mentioned there, but there are examples that will help you get the desired output).

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-09-05 09:37 UTC

I'm pretty sure this is part of the events system.

There's a `user_status`event type for the /api/register-queue and /api/get-events. The register response will send an object with all the status of all users in the organization who have set one. And then a `user_status` event will be sent to the client when a user updates their status.

There isn't currently an API endpoint for getting the status of all users in the organization though. The /api/update-status endpoint is for updating the current user's status and generates the event above.

## Consider removing our own custom key validation

*2020-06-04 to 2020-06-04 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Consider.20removing.20our.20own.20custom.20key.20validation/with/894196)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-06-04 11:10 UTC

Issue for the context: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/13504

We fixed that in 2470fba95ccc3239aa5386fd3853666d196b804f

In 2.2.13 Django seems to add their own validation in https://github.com/django/django/commit/07e59caa02831c4569bbebb9eb773bdd9cb4b206
It actually basically duplicates our own logic.
Their code:
```
def memcache_key_warnings(key):
    if len(key) > MEMCACHE_MAX_KEY_LENGTH:
        yield (
            'Cache key will cause errors if used with memcached: %r '
            '(longer than %s)' % (key, MEMCACHE_MAX_KEY_LENGTH)
        )
    for char in key:
        if ord(char) < 33 or ord(char) == 127:
            yield (
                'Cache key contains characters that will cause errors if '
                'used with memcached: %r' % key, CacheKeyWarning
            )
            break
```

Our code:
```
def validate_cache_key(key: str) -> None:
    if not key.startswith(KEY_PREFIX):
        key = KEY_PREFIX + key

    # Theoretically memcached can handle non-ascii characters
    # and only "control" characters are strictly disallowed, see:
    # https://github.com/memcached/memcached/blob/master/doc/protocol.txt
    # However, limiting the characters we allow in keys simiplifies things,
    # and anyway we use make_safe_digest when forming some keys to ensure
    # the resulting keys fit the regex below.
    # The regex checks "all characters between ! and ~ in the ascii table",
    # which happens to be the set of all "nice" ascii characters.
    if not bool(re.fullmatch(r"([!-~])+", key)):
        raise InvalidCacheKeyException("Invalid characters in the cache key: " + key)
    if len(key) > MEMCACHED_MAX_KEY_LENGTH:
        raise InvalidCacheKeyException("Cache key too long: {} Length: {}".format(key, len(key)))
```

This is basically the same I think.
Do we want to to keep our own validation or try to remove as much of it as possible and rely on Django?

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-04 13:32 UTC

@Mateusz Mandera  The logic that is unique to us is below, correct?  It seems like this code should enforce a consistent policy for whether the caller prepends the key here, although I can sort of understand how this is pragmatically fine.    See 4f2897fafc09213832318d0f198b8870739b628d (from you) for more context.

~~~ py
    if not key.startswith(KEY_PREFIX):
        key = KEY_PREFIX + key
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-04 13:34 UTC

To your broader question, I am mostly ambivalent, but I think I'd want to mostly leave this alone for now, given the small amount of code to maintain here, and the fact that we seem to error whereas Django warns.  OTOH I think we've been pretty aggressive about removing Zulip-specific code once Django add features that we were duplicating, and I don't believe we've ever regretted it.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2020-06-04 15:06 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell)
> @Mateusz Mandera The logic that is unique to us is below, correct? It seems like this code should enforce a consistent policy for whether the caller prepends the key here, although I can sort of understand how this is pragmatically fine. See 4f2897fafc09213832318d0f198b8870739b628d (from you) fo …
 
Hmm, the problem there is that the low level functions like `cache_get_many`, `cache_get`, etc. assume you give them the key without the prefix - and that seems wise, because the callers shouldn't worry about such low level details as the key prefix. But then slightly higher level functions such as `safe_cache_get_many` (helpers used by `generic_bulk_cached_fetch`) need to both do validation of the keys *and* call the base functions `cache_get_many`, `cache_set_many`, which don't expect the key. So it's hard to be consistent in having/not havingthe prefix on keys when validating them.

(replying to Steve Howell)

OTOH I think we've been pretty aggressive about removing Zulip-specific code once Djang …

validate_cache_key(final_key, has_prefix=True)

~~~ py
if not key.startswith(KEY_PREFIX):
~~~

I have been trying to find a case when the query `UserMessage.object.filter(flags=UserMessage.flags.active_mobile_push_notification` will not give correct results ([here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/15179#discussion_r434863689) is the background discussion) but I couldn't find one. In order to fetch `active_push_notification` both the following `flags` conditions seem correct to me:
* flags & 4096 <> 0 (as implemented in `where_active_push_notification()`)
* flags & 4096 = 4096 (which is `UserMessage.object.filter(flags=UserMessage.flags.active_mobile_push_notification)` equivalent)

Here is the explanation:
If we perform bitwise addition of any value of flag with 1000000000000 (which is the binary of 4096), all the digits of flag except for the 1st one doesn't matter because of the AND operation. We will always be getting 4096 if the first digit of `flag` is 1, in other words, the query `UserMessage.object.filter(flags=UserMessage.flags.active_mobile_push_notification)` will always give result if `active_mobile_push_notification` flag is set.

This is an exceptional case because `active_mobile_push_notification` is the last entry in `ALL_FLAGS`.
Did I get it right or there is still a case where this can fail? (So that we can update our existing tests to cover that case)

```
    def by_is(self, query: Query, operand: str, maybe_negate: ConditionTransform) -> Query:          
        if operand == 'private':                                                                     
            cond = column("flags").op("&")(UserMessage.flags.is_private.mask) != 0                   
            return query.where(maybe_negate(cond))                                                   
        elif operand == 'starred':                                                                   
            cond = column("flags").op("&")(UserMessage.flags.starred.mask) != 0                      
            return query.where(maybe_negate(cond))                                                   
        elif operand == 'unread':                                                                    
            cond = column("flags").op("&")(UserMessage.flags.read.mask) == 0                         
            return query.where(maybe_negate(cond))                                                   
        elif operand == 'mentioned':                                                                 
            cond1 = column("flags").op("&")(UserMessage.flags.mentioned.mask) != 0                   
            cond2 = column("flags").op("&")(UserMessage.flags.wildcard_mentioned.mask) != 0          
            cond = or_(cond1, cond2)                                                                 
            return query.where(maybe_negate(cond))                                                   
        elif operand == 'alerted':                                                                   
            cond = column("flags").op("&")(UserMessage.flags.has_alert_word.mask) != 0               
            return query.where(maybe_negate(cond))                                                   
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-05 16:49 UTC

In an ideal world, the indexes would be managed by `django-bitfield`, and perhaps it would use the `!= 0` format queries which negate more naturally than the `= x` ones.  (Or really, Django mainline would have merged a bitfield feature)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-05 16:51 UTC

And perhaps we should have rewritten our sqlalchemy queries as the way to handle the discrepancy; I think we just didn't consider doing that (or maybe we thought the `!= 0` approach was better, which I think is true)

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-05 16:51 UTC

One possible motivation for preferring the `!= 0` version is I think that's likely to compose better natively inside postgres for the similar `mentioned` query, where we want to check if any of two flags is nonzero.

**Greg Price** · 2020-06-05 22:50 UTC

I am surprised to learn that `.filter(flags=UserMessage.flags.active_mobile_push_notification)` actually has the desired semantics! I expected it to mean the `flags` field was *equal* to the given value, not that it contained it.

**Greg Price** · 2020-06-05 22:50 UTC

Honestly I would say that is a pretty terrible API choice made by django-bitfield. It's never a good idea to overload equality to mean something that is not at all like equality.

The right choice would have been to use the ["lookup type"](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/3.0/topics/db/queries/#field-lookups) concept that's used in the Django ORM generally: so something like `.filter(flags__contains=UserMessage.flags.active_mobile_push_notification)`.

**Greg Price** · 2020-06-05 22:54 UTC

In any case, the need to make the expression one that Postgres can recognize as matching the index condition remains an important reason to use the provided method.

That does make it hard to usefully unit-test. I think it's fine not to unit-test this distinction.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-05 22:59 UTC

Yeah, I agree that `django-bitfield` didn't make the right choice here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-24 21:26 UTC

@Zixuan James Li yeah, we should keep pushing on E2E encryption for push notifications, it is pretty important.

**Vaclav Bartik** · 2023-07-25 06:37 UTC

Hi, I've been using Zulip since 2015, running two small self-hosted instances. The development state of encrypted mobile notifications feature is something I'm checking on regularly for years now, as for someone not willing to go unencrypted/redacted(very little value there), this is something that severely impacts the value of what Zulip can bring to discussions where both parties aren't necessarily online.

One thing has been running through my mind lately though. When implementing a reliable encryption mechanism is not a trivial thing to do to an extent of not having this feature for many years now, is this *really* necessary to deliver the feature?

I mean, delivering a non-encrypted signal 'hey, there is something new on the server for you' that doesn't carry any content at all and then using this as a trigger to have the client pull the actual content from the server (using the same security level that is configured for interactive use in the first place) seems to be way easier thing to implement.

Is there something I'm missing why the issue shouldn't really be approached this way? From my point of view, separating the content flow from push notification service to the path server<->client seems like a good idea.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-25 17:25 UTC

I suppose that approach would have a few architectural differences:
* The Zulip server would need to store the set of push notifications for collection by the client; this would involve some complexity since it'd likely require a new per-device-per-message database table. Using the vendor push notifications APIs sorta saves us from having to do interesting/stateful per-mobile-device storage in the server.
* It would reduce deliverability of notifications in limited network situations where the mobile app can receive push notifications via the Google systems but can't reliably make outgoing network connections directly to the Zulip server. I'm not sure how real a problem that might be -- but it would be an extra moving part for the system.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-25 17:27 UTC

I don't think the current plan we have for actually encrypting the notifications is a huge amount of implementation work, though it probably is a more complicated design.

**Vaclav Bartik** · 2023-07-25 20:03 UTC

Regarding tracking - would it be necessary though? If the message ids (only message ids) in question would be part of the trigger, every client would know what to ask for as it would have worked as notifications work now, right?

Also, when you mention the limited network situations - I don't know if the value of getting the contents through notification is really so great. In that case, it would be similar as getting redacted notifications - you would need server connection anyway.

On the other hand, I would tend to see a value in *not* implementing cryptographic mechanism at all.

Either way, I'm fine with whatever path chosen, just wanted to bring up the idea...

## Python codebase migrations

*2020-06-11 to 2020-06-15 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Python.20codebase.20migrations/with/902161)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-11 23:53 UTC

In the last couple week or so, we merged several more major Python codebase migrations, notably including the addition of `isort` as a linter (which sorts imports) as well as converting most strings to f-strings.  Expect all of your pull requests with Python changes to have resulting merge conflicts, and please resolve them as soon as you can so that they're reviewable again.

We like to time this sort of big one-time change with low risk late in release cycles to minimize how much backporting of changes across these we'll need to do in the future.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-11 23:54 UTC

Huge thanks to @Anders Kaseorg for driving these migrations, many of which required changes to third-party upstream tools to make them suitable for Zulip (often filing good bug reports and working with maintainers to get them fixed).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-15 07:15 UTC

An update: We just added a linter rule enforcing the use of f-strings over `%` formatting in the Python codebase.  We still allow `.format()`, though in most cases it's more readable to use f-strings with an added local variable.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-14 19:58 UTC

So I think there's an interesting question on whether we want to move Zulip to using postgres from the Postgres upstream Debian repositories (where you can choose whatever version you want), and default Zulip to use the latest postgres release (E.g. 12) for new installations.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-14 19:58 UTC

We already have done the work to support telling Zulip you want to be running a specific postgres version via a single line in `/etc/zulip/zulip.conf`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-14 19:59 UTC

And we already use those repositories on zulip.com so that we can run Postgres 11 on Ubuntu Bionic, which seems to work well.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-14 20:00 UTC

The long-term benefit is that if we end up wanting to use features of newer postgres, we'll be in a much better position to do so (And we can document a clear process for upgrading postgres on your Zulip server for folks who want to move to postgres 12; it's bad at all if you're OK taking downtime to do the upgrade).

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-14 20:00 UTC

## UserProfile model

*2020-06-16 to 2020-06-17 · 33 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/UserProfile.20model/with/905733)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-16 08:05 UTC

This is probably a rabbit hole we won't want to go down just before a release, but at some point we'll want to rename `UserProfile` to `User` in the backend codebase.  I did 15 minutes of investigation into this idea:
* Changing the class name from UserProfile to User (and then doing a find-replace on `zerver/models.py` and adding `UserProfile = User` to make existing imports work) results in a large number of generated migrations by Django, including in third-party apps that seemed pretty broken and corrupted my virtualenv.
* Adding `User = UserProfile` and then doing a s/UserProfile/User/` in a random file runs happily.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-16 08:14 UTC

So I think we do have the option of using that second bullet to allow a bulk codebase migration to s/UserProfile/User/` everywhere outside migrations and models, and then deal with the messy problem of changing the name in the actual database schema later.  

We can use https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/2.2/ref/models/fields/#django.db.models.Field.db_column to rename the variables for accessing models to e.g. `.user` while leaving the ForeignKey fields in the actual database as e.g. `user_profile_id`.  E.g. I think something like this would allow us to rename all the `subscription.user_profile` references to `subscription.user` except in raw SQL queries:
``` python3
diff --git a/zerver/models.py b/zerver/models.py
index 8dd74d059e..e6ad714f5c 100644
--- a/zerver/models.py
+++ b/zerver/models.py
@@ -2142,7 +2142,7 @@ def get_old_unclaimed_attachments(weeks_ago: int) -> Sequence[Attachment]:
     return old_attachments
 
 class Subscription(models.Model):
-    user_profile: UserProfile = models.ForeignKey(UserProfile, on_delete=CASCADE)
+    user: UserProfile = models.ForeignKey(UserProfile, db_column="user_profile_id", on_delete=CASCADE)
     recipient: Recipient = models.ForeignKey(Recipient, on_delete=CASCADE)
 
     # Whether the user has since unsubscribed.  We mark Subscription
@@ -2169,7 +2169,7 @@ class Subscription(models.Model):
     wildcard_mentions_notify: Optional[bool] = models.BooleanField(null=True, default=None)
 
     class Meta:
-        unique_together = ("user_profile", "recipient")
+        unique_together = ("user", "recipient")
 
     def __str__(self) -> str:
         return f"<Subscription: {self.user_profile} -> {self.recipient}>"
```

https://stackoverflow.com/questions/25091130/django-migration-strategy-for-renaming-a-model-and-relationship-fields is probably somewhat useful.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2020-06-16 16:17 UTC

What's the reasoning for this?

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-16 17:03 UTC

It's a code cleanup to use the `user` name rather than `user_profile`.  The UserProfile name is a legacy consequence of Django's history -- in ~2013, Django didn't support customizing the User model, so all your custom fields (not email, name, etc.) needed to be in a separate UserProfile model.  When we updated to newer Django the next year, we decided to merge the models in a way that left the UserProfile name, not the User name, because that was easier to implement the migration correctly.  We've been in a state where it would be more readable to just call it User ever since.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-16 17:08 UTC

I personally don’t feel any urgency to do this renaming.  I actually feel it may be a step backwards for certain things.  Just my opinion though.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-16 17:10 UTC

Do you have examples of places it'd be a step backwards?  I'm not presently aware of any places we intentionally use `user` and `user_profile` as variables for different objects, for example.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-16 17:12 UTC

Just grep noise.  We eventually want to rename people.js, for example.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-16 17:12 UTC

I should probably retract the step backwards comment

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-16 17:12 UTC

I just don’t feel it’s worth the effort.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2020-06-16 17:39 UTC

Greppability does seem an interesting argument against.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-16 17:44 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell)
> I just don’t feel it’s worth the effort.
Yeah, I think that's really the question here -- how much effort is it?  If we can do it as a find/replace, it'd be cheap to transition.  The thing that might make that not really viable is the Django migrations system side of the problem.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-16 17:45 UTC

The greppability consideration is interesting; though could `git grep User[^a-zA-Z]` successfully find just User references?

**Greg Price** · 2020-06-16 20:13 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> The greppability consideration is interesting; though could `git grep User[^a-zA-Z]` successfully find just User references?

Even easier: `git grep -w User`. That's the feature I use all the time for finding references to identifiers.

**Greg Price** · 2020-06-16 20:17 UTC

When I started working on Zulip, it took me quite a while to fully absorb that "user profile" was truly just a funny name for the user record, and there wasn't some *other* thing elsewhere that was the bare "user". I imagine I'm not the only one who's been confused by it.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-17 01:22 UTC

It took a lot of effort to rename subject to topic, speaking very much from first hand experience.  Part of the complication there was that “subject” also is used for email code.  And columns might be trickier than table names.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-17 01:23 UTC

I mentioned above a nice solution for columns; Django has an option that lets us rename the variables in the Python objects without any changes to the database itself.

**Tim Abbott** · 2020-06-17 01:24 UTC

(Which means we can migrate the codebase to all user `.user_id`, and then later do a party of migrations to rename all the foreign key columns which would at that point only appear in the raw SQL queries)

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-17 01:24 UTC

Obviously if there were no opportunity cost here, I would fully support the rename.  But I have never felt great pain here.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-17 01:26 UTC

Mypy has some surprisingly powerful tricks up its sleeve:

```python
LengthT = TypeVar("LengthT", bound=int)

class CappedString(Generic[LengthT], str):
    pass

def check_capped_string(length: LengthT, value: str) -> CappedString[LengthT]:
    assert len(value) <= length
    return CappedString(value)

a: CappedString[Literal[30]] = check_capped_string(30, "hello")  # ok
b: CappedString[Literal[20]] = check_capped_string(30, "hello")  # type error
```

However, I would be really cautious about actually trying to use this feature because it’s probably full of bugs.

**Steve Howell** · 2020-06-20 00:16 UTC

Most of my branch just cleans up stuff to build to this very simple code:


~~~ py
def validate_the_validator(func: FuncT, mypy_type: Any) -> None:
    if USING_TYPE_STRUCTURE:
        def check(type_structure: TypeStructure, mypy_type: Any) -> None:
            if type_structure == 'skip':
                return

            if isinstance(type_structure, tuple):
                if type_structure[0] == Union:
                    print(mypy_type, type_structure)
                    assert mypy_type.__origin__ in [Union]
                    return

                if type_structure[0] == List:
                    assert mypy_type.__origin__ in [Iterable, List, Sequence]

                    sub_type_structure = type_structure[1]
                    sub_mypy_type = mypy_type.__args__[0]
                    check(sub_type_structure, sub_mypy_type)
                    return

                # TODO: validate other complex types
                return

            if type_structure.startswith('any'):
                return

            if type_structure == 'bool':
                assert mypy_type == bool
                return

            if type_structure == 'int':
                assert mypy_type == int
                return

            if type_structure == 'str':
                assert mypy_type == str
                return

            print(func.type_structure)
            print(mypy_type)
            raise Exception('invalid validator', type_structure)

        check(func.type_structure, mypy_type)
~~~
