## Add denormalized Stream.subscriber_count field.

*2021-01-27 to 2021-05-20 · 74 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Add.20denormalized.20Stream.2Esubscriber_count.20field.2E/with/1108552)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2021-01-27 20:41 UTC

I think it makes sense to discuss #17101 here a bit further, as @Steve Howell [suggested](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/2-general/topic/bulky.20subscriber.20data/near/1108024). Opinions seem fairly split at this point between the 3 approaches:
1. Caching approach - cache `subscriber_count` per stream rather than using the database.
2. "Triggers" approach - put `subscriber_count` in the database and use either database triggers or `post_save`
3.  Manual approach - have `update_subscriber_counts_for_stream_ids` function and call it in all the relevant code that does something that should alter the count.

As Tim [pointed out](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/17101#issuecomment-768483989) using `generic_bulk_cached_fetched` should let us avoid the concern of doing large amounts of cache hits to send subscriber counts of streams upon page load. On the other hand, for cache invalidation we will have to make explicit function calls in the code that adds/removes subscriptions so in that sense it seems analogous to (3) where we'd call `update_subscriber_counts_for_stream_ids` in all those places. I suppose that this analogy might be reducing the dilemma (between 1 and 3) to the question of whether `stream subscriber count` data philosophically (or practically) belongs more in the database or the cache?

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-27 20:58 UTC

I don't think the query itself is gonna be super expensive either on the write side (`update_subscriber_counts_for_stream_ids`) and certainly not the read side (since we're getting Stream objects).

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-27 20:58 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-01-27 21:44 UTC

Latency is immaterial to performance here -- we're talking about a data structure that currently takes seconds to compute, and an RTT to the database or cache is like 1ms.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-01-27 21:47 UTC

I guess the reason that I've been thinking a cache would be appropriate is that structurally, what we are doing is caching a value that would be expensive to compute (in large organizations).  That doesn't imply we need to use an in-memory memcached structure to do so, but I think we should understand what we're doing.  One advantage of using memcached is that people are used to working with caches from other items in the codebase, and many of the performance/accuracy tradeoffs present there are relevant here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-01-27 21:48 UTC

(I'm not sure which is simpler -- both are a small amount of code, and the database option involves a database migration, and thus more deployment complexity, so I think it's very likely the cache will be less work).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-01-27 21:49 UTC

One downside of memcached is that items in memcache expire with load (etc.), and that doesn't happen if we store it in the database.  One reason that we might strongly prefer the database option (perhaps in a dedicated small database table, if we don't want to churn `stream` every time someone subscribers/unsubscribers, which seems worth avoiding) is that we flush memcached as part of the server restart process, and subscriber data is something that is mainly accessed when loading the webapp.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-01-27 21:51 UTC

I think another structural question here is whether we want to maintain this value for all streams, or just for "large streams".  I could imagine a version where we fetch all subscribers for streams with <200 members and use the count-based approach only for big streams, with the reasoning being that it's not a big deal if the number is off by a bit for caching reasons (or bugs in a more complex algorithm) when it's going to tell you whether the number is 11574 or 11572 than whether it's 4 or 2 members.

## denormalization and sharding

*2021-01-28 to 2021-02-10 · 131 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/denormalization.20and.20sharding/with/1109330)*

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-28 12:55 UTC

(replying to Mateusz Mandera)
> Also worth noting that if `realm` was denormalized into the Message model (a possibility that has been discussed quite a bit in the past iirc), this query (as well as the one for archiving normal personal/huddle messages) could get rid of another JOIN

I am in favor of denormalizing `realm` to all of our big tables (and updating appropriate indexes).

**Greg Price** · 2021-01-28 21:25 UTC

Denormalizing realm_id into almost all of our tables is fundamentally the right long-term architecture, so I think in general whenever we feel motivated to do so for a given table we should go ahead and do it.

The only table I'd hold back from is zerver_usermessage, because it's such an enormous number of very small rows. (That and the few miscellaneous tables where each row doesn't have a particular realm it belongs to.)

**Greg Price** · 2021-01-28 21:30 UTC

The reason it's the right long-term architecture is that eventually as we scale we'll want to shard by realm -- different realms' data will live on different database servers. So then, except for the few queries which are truly cross-realm, every query will need to explicitly know which realm it's looking for data in (so it can talk to the right database server) and every join will need to be explicitly within a single realm (because it can only operate within the one database server, and that can only be guaranteed if it's within the realm.)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-28 21:32 UTC

Yeah, well said, and I agree that UserMessage is probably the last one we would tackle or consider.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-01-28 21:33 UTC

Why does sharding require that denormalization?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-01-28 21:36 UTC

The query can know which realm it’s looking for without *every table* knowing.

**Greg Price** · 2021-01-28 22:04 UTC

It's true, the query knowing which realm it's looking for doesn't require that the realm_id be denormalized. What it does mean is that the query won't be disadvantaged by having the realm_id denormalized, and in particular by having the indexes the query wants to use all start with the realm_id. The query just makes sure to include something like `AND realm_id = {realm_id}` along with whatever other information it has, and the database gets to use the index the same way.

And then the other fact about our queries related to sharding is that generally these queries that are doing larger scans are really only interested in a single realm. Once there's a realm_id in the table, we can express that fact and that can make them a lot more efficient.

**Greg Price** · 2021-01-28 22:09 UTC

There was a mention above about removing a JOIN. I'm not sure that's an important goal in itself. Ran some measurements on the bulk_get_subscriber_user_ids query in dev environment.

Set up with `./manage.py populate_db --extra-users=2000 --extra-streams=400` followed by deactivating 300 users to have some variance in the `is_active` state. 

Running the SQL query WITHOUT the denormalization: `1.58 -> 1.51 -> 1.49` executions times (seconds).
For additional control and comparison, let's add a db index on the `Subscription.active` column: `1.39, 1.42, 1.39` execution times, a small improvement

Now we add the denormalization of `Subscriber.is_user_active` (and run a backfill migration + simplify the query to remove the JOIN of course)
Without any indexes: `1.41, 1.31, 1.30, 1.33` times.
Add index on Subscription.is_user_active: `1.25, 1.24` times
Also adding the index on Subscription.active as in the "no denormalization" case: `1.22, 1.23, 1.19, 1.18`
---------------------------------------

I think this clearly suggests that adding the denormalized column AND index gives a  modest but meaningful improvement. There might be a case to be made for also adding the index on `Subscription.active`  as it seems to give a little bit of an improvement, though it might not be meaningful.

*2021-01-28 to 2025-02-27 · 15 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/PoWA/with/1110221)*

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-01-28 22:02 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2021-01-29 02:16 UTC

> HypoPG allows you to create hypothetical indexe. A hypothetical index is an index that doesn’t exists on disk. It’s therefore almost instant to create and doesn’t add any IO cost, whether at creation time or at maintenance time. The goal is obviously to check if an index is useful before spending too much time, I/O and disk space to create it.

> With this extension, you can create hypothetical indexes, and then with EXPLAIN check if PostgreSQL would use them or not.

Huh, that sounds quite interesting!

That’s not even the most interesting part.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-10 23:21 UTC

The slow query log in postgres is fundamentally the wrong system, because it tells you what queries are slow in an absolute sense, not those that are slow compared to what they should be.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-10 23:22 UTC

So if you have something that takes 450ms and happens all the time, it won't find it (or whatever threshold you pick).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-10 23:23 UTC

E.g. at one point we had an issue where PreregistrationUser or something similar I think had no index on a frequently queried key, and we only found out once the total time consumed by that got to be large on zulip.com.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-10 23:23 UTC

Whereas it should have been obvious from any tooling that could see that we were doing queries that did table scans on a large table (can't remember but I think it was ~100K entries at the time) and that started getting slow.

@Alex Vandiver FYI in case you have bandwidth to try setting this up.

(replying to Steve Howell)
> I am not against this solution, but all I really want for Xmas is a slow query log that we aggressively monitor and react to.

4.08 years later I am still in favor of aggressively monitoring the slow query log with automated scripts.  Maybe there's better technology today, including PoWA.  But a simple Python script that checks the query log and ignores the most basic exceptions can be so easily evolved.  There are so many dials that can be easily tuned.  Make it noisier when you're paranoid, and quiet it down when you are busy.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-02-27 16:16 UTC

You're welcome to contribute such a script if you find it useful for your production maintenance.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-27 17:34 UTC

I think the thing that would be useful for me in that space is something in `zerver/lib/db.py` that recorded slow queries in a usable format -- say, it logged slow queries with `traceback.format_stack` or ideally some shorter, more semantic thing as the key (so it's easy to back it out to what line of code generated the query) and the query runtime as a the value.

Then you could do statistics/graphing/monitoring trends for those, like observing that a type of query is newly very expensive.

Maybe there's a feature in Sentry's performance tracing functionality that could do something of that form without us needing to reinvent the wheel. I certainly don't have time to go down that rabbit hole for how much value I'd expect it to add over "just skim the slow query log manually from time to time".

Historically we have rarely experienced Tornado problems for instances that are just running a single realm.  Even a large realm like this one.  (Granted this realm, while having many more users than yours, isn't quite as busy in terms of actual messages, I'm guessing.)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-29 17:33 UTC

We have actually run multiple realms on a non-sharded Tornado setup in the past.  I wanna guess hundreds?  It obviously helps to have a powerful CPU.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-29 17:35 UTC

When we've hit our bottleneck it's just because we have **so many** realms.  And then that leads to the solution of sharding by realm.  Which has certain benefits:
* simplicity (all traffic for a single realm hits the same shard)
* flexibility (you can put known-busy realms on their own shard)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-29 17:36 UTC

Our main strategy for the single-realm case is to just make Tornado performant enough to run in single-process mode.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-29 17:37 UTC

This isn't really my area of expertise, so maybe somebody more knowledgeable will jump in.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-29 17:39 UTC

It's worth noting that Tornado just kinda pulls work from a queue, so if it falls behind for a little bit, it might not be any worse than the amount of time it takes messages to deliver over the wire.  And presumably your other three cores can keep up with the other work of the system.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-01-29 17:40 UTC

@Robert so, Tornado scalability is an issue that has gotten a lot of active development of late.  One specific issue that we have fixed since the 3.x release has to do with when a lot of users are signing up around the same time -- could that describe your situation?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-01-29 17:41 UTC

If so, I'd highly recommend upgrading to master -- there's a set of optimizations that we did in the Fall that for our own installations completely fixed issues we saw with Tornado being overloaded during large events that resulted in many signups around the same time in a large organization, which sounds like it describes exactly what you're seeing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-01-29 17:42 UTC

@Steve Howell (showell), you actually did the optimizations -- this was the issue where creating new users resulted in a large number of events being sent to Tornado, so if you had a lot of users joining around the same time, it'd overflow Tornado -- but of course the actual work was in `actions.py`, not Tornado itself.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-01 17:36 UTC

@Robert you can try applying this patch:
```
Author: Tim Abbott <tabbott@zulip.com>
Date:   Sun Sep 13 15:45:02 2020 -0700

    presence: Disable live presence updates in larger realms.

diff --git a/zerver/lib/actions.py b/zerver/lib/actions.py
index fe17a2e263..9fcf9f9757 100644
--- a/zerver/lib/actions.py
+++ b/zerver/lib/actions.py
@@ -4075,13 +4075,17 @@ def do_update_user_activity(user_profile_id: int,
         activity.save(update_fields=["last_visit", "count"])
 
 def send_presence_changed(user_profile: UserProfile, presence: UserPresence) -> None:
+    # Performance mitigation for excessive presence changes.
+    user_ids = active_user_ids(user_profile.realm_id)
+    if len(user_ids) > 100:
+        return
     presence_dict = presence.to_dict()
     event = dict(type="presence",
                  email=user_profile.email,
                  user_id=user_profile.id,
                  server_timestamp=time.time(),
                  presence={presence_dict['client']: presence_dict})
-    send_event(user_profile.realm, event, active_user_ids(user_profile.realm_id))
+    send_event(user_profile.realm, event, user_ids)
 
 def consolidate_client(client: Client) -> Client:
     # The web app reports a client as 'website'

```

Just to provide some context, what it'll mean is that when a user goes from completely offline to online in the morning, it'll take a minute for them to appear as active, rather than the <1s that it is without this patch.  The benefit is that it'll remove 100% of the load related to presence that you're seeing, which sounds like 90% for your server.  My guess is this will completely resolve your problem with pretty minimal downside.

## updating events

*2021-01-30 to 2021-02-10 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/updating.20events/with/1111240)*

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-30 16:17 UTC

I have recently had conversations in three different contexts where there might be some utility in having a two-step process for registering for events:
* register for most events when the client starts
* register for additional events later

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-30 16:18 UTC

Basically, all three use cases are lazy-load sort of situations.  You want the app to get up and running quickly, and then later (either fairly immediately after page load or when somebody finally invokes a feature) you want to get more data.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-30 16:19 UTC

All three use cases were basically about subscribers.  The webapp example is that we might want to load subscribers for non-long-term-idle users first, and then only load long-term-idle users when we go into Manage Streams.  (The exact details of the examples here aren't super important, by the way.)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-30 16:20 UTC

It's pretty easy to implement lazy-load strategies where, when the time comes to get additional data, you just ask the server via normal GET requests, i.e. via the normal API, to just get more data.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-30 16:20 UTC

But there can be subtle races when you do that.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-30 16:21 UTC

So I've been thinking about a mechanism where you basically have an option to re-register events.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-01-30 16:21 UTC

Before I go too deep into my thought process, I am wondering if @Tim Abbott has thought about this all.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-09 01:48 UTC

Registering for additional events later is definitely something we could in theory support; it requires a bit of thinking about race conditions.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-09 01:49 UTC

I'm not sure that there'd be a benefit to not just registering for the whole set of `events` and specifying a narrower set of `fetch_events` for that sort of situation.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-09 14:13 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I'm not sure that there'd be a benefit to not just registering for the whole set of `events` and specifying a narrower set of `fetch_events` for that sort of situation.

The premise here is that the app does multiple fetches over time.  It gets a somewhat minimal fetch initially, then later tries to fetch additional subscribers or things like that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-10 01:42 UTC

Yeah, understood.  I think in 99% of cases, it'd be fine to just get the full set of `fetch_events` that the app supports from the beginning, though; there's not that much savings to skipping a few event types.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-10 01:43 UTC

(It might be like <1% of total `GET /events` load)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-10 12:22 UTC

I think I must be misunderstanding Tim's terminology here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-10 22:41 UTC

The `fetch_event_types` and `event_types` parameters to https://zulip.com/api/register-queue#parameters are what I'm talking about.

## status-expire

*2021-02-07 to 2021-03-23 · 78 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/status-expire/with/1114757)*

**Gaurav Pandey (ligmitz)** · 2021-02-07 08:06 UTC

I am looking to incorporate a feature to remove the status after certain interval of time. Is this feature feasible and desirable ? Also what is the optimum way to implement this.

**Gaurav Pandey (ligmitz)** · 2021-02-07 08:08 UTC

I am thinking of storing the time period as a field in the UserStatus model and then running a timer after the userstatus is set to remove it after the specified time period.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-07 12:11 UTC

@Gaurav Pandey There are a few possible approaches here:

* Have a cron job that runs every minute on the backend to reset statuses (and we'll want an index on UserStatus to make it fast).
* Have timers run on the front end to automatically expire statuses (including other people).
* Have the timer only run for the user who set the status, and then remind them to change their status.  (And if they are loading the page and have an expired status, remind them then.)

I am in favor of the last approach, as it has the fewest moving parts, and it gives users a little more control.  For example, if I set my status to "out to lunch" I might say "Remind me in 60 minutes".  And then if I have a long lunch and get back in 90 minutes, I just change it when I actually get back.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-07 12:15 UTC

People have asked for this feature, so I think there is some desire for it.  I'm not personally convinced we need it.  The root problem here, which I know folks have rightly complained about, is that we don't show your own status prominently on the main screen.  Of course, that problem is hard to solve when we're concerned about not using up screen real estate.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-07 12:17 UTC

If it were up to me, we'd first figure out how to improve the UI for the current data model before adding any new features.

## message.realm

*2021-02-09 to 2021-02-10 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/message.2Erealm/with/1115561)*

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-09 14:06 UTC

@Mateusz Mandera Let me try to persuade you that we should wait until we do cross-realm fixes before denormalizing realm onto Message.  (I hope I lose this argument, but I want to do due diligence.)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-09 14:06 UTC

As you mentioned in our PM convo, even though sender_id's for cross-realm messages may be outside my realm, the recipient will be **inside** my realm.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-09 14:08 UTC

So if we define `Message.realm` to be the realm of the recipient, then things like retention code can just use `Message.realm`.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-09 14:08 UTC

I guess we don't yet have `realm_id` on `Recipient`, since presumably recipients can now include participants from multiple realms.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-09 14:10 UTC

For recipients of type `PERSONAL` or `STREAM` the `realm_id` is implicit enough.  But what about huddles?

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-09 14:10 UTC

(As an aside, does it possibly make more sense to just add `Recipient.realm_id`?  Or possibly even both tables, but start with `Recipient`?)

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2021-02-09 14:17 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell (showell))
> For recipients of type `PERSONAL` or `STREAM` the `realm_id` is implicit enough. But what about huddles?
The comments detailing this more are lost somewhere in an old PR, but I remember doing an investigation into this and the conclusion was basically that:
1. We don't actually send huddle message via cross-realm bots anywhere in the code.
2. It might be theoretically possible to manually generate such messages via `manage.py shell` using the `internal_send_` helper functions, but they'll refuse to cooperate if the recipient users aren't all in the same realm. So for such hypothetical huddles, `realm` would still be well-defined.

I'll try to find the PR comments as well to double-check my memory on this.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2021-02-09 14:35 UTC

I can't find the comment, but confirmed now with some fiddling that `internal_send_huddle_message(realm, bot, emails, "test")` can work with `bot` being a cross-realm bot , but only if `emails` are all users in `realm`.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-09 14:37 UTC

Would it make sense to put `realm_id` on to `Recipient` first?

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-09 14:41 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell (showell))
> Would it make sense to put `realm_id` on to `Recipient` first?

I think the answer is no, but it would make the `Message.realm_id` backfill easier.  I can't think of any time we do queries at realm granularity to get all recipients from a realm that don't also involve messages.  Hrm, maybe streams?

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-09 14:41 UTC

I guess `get_active_streams` already takes advantage of `Stream.realm_id`.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2021-02-09 14:54 UTC

Yeah I can't think of any place where we query for Recipients by realm and would benefit from avoiding the JOIN that much. So likely it's best to just do `message.realm` only?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-10 01:41 UTC

I'm pretty sure we have logic, effectively in the soft-deactivation code path, that effectively computes a `realm(message)`.  The algorithm ends up being:
* If recipient is a stream, `stream.realm`
* If a 1:1 PM, the users will be in the same realm unless there's a cross-realm bot involved, and then we do the non-internal realm.
* If it's a huddle, all the users will be in the same realm, so pick one.

So obviously we can save some work in that migration if we kill the "cross-realm bot" complexity first, but I think killing "cross-realm bot" complexity might be multiplicatively more total work than just creating a `message.realm` and backfilling as described above.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-10 01:41 UTC

I'm OK with doing the cross-realm bot migration first, though, if we're going to end up doing both anyway.

```
def make_safe_digest(string: str,
                     hash_func: Callable[[bytes], Any]=hashlib.sha1) -> str:
    """
    return a hex digest of `string`.
    """
    # hashlib.sha1, md5, etc. expect bytes, so non-ASCII strings must
    # be encoded.
    return hash_func(string.encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()
```

so we're doing SHA1 of it.

## subscribers [] / None

*2021-02-17 to 2021-02-18 · 25 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/subscribers.20.5B.5D.20.2F.20None/with/1119877)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-17 21:07 UTC

Hmm.  One challenge with that is that we end up enforcing in the API the invariant that every stream has at least one administrator.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-17 21:09 UTC

Hmm, maybe not -- a client still knows whether it sent `include_subscribers`, and so it can infer that the empty list of subscribers means it had no access, and thus an empty list of admins is because the client doesn't get that data, rather than because there are none (which would appear as some subscribers with no admins).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-17 21:09 UTC

So, yeah, I think that's the right plan.

**Greg Price** · 2021-02-18 00:06 UTC

(replying to Sahil Batra)
> I am rebasing my PR after a long time now, so there have been many changes till now, one of them being to include "subscribers" field for the users even when user is not allowed to see subscribers and pass empty list in those cases.

That change sounds puzzling to me. Was it made intentionally? It seems like an API bug.

**Greg Price** · 2021-02-18 00:08 UTC

That is, if the client isn't allowed to see the subscribers, I'd much rather have the response simply not include `subscribers`, rather than provide a value the client is supposed to figure out is a lie.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-18 00:11 UTC

It’s an empty list.

**Greg Price** · 2021-02-18 00:17 UTC

Right, so it's saying there are no subscribers. Which is untrue.

**Greg Price** · 2021-02-18 00:17 UTC

(except sometimes when it happens to be true)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-18 00:18 UTC

It’s not a lie.  There are zero subscribers that you are authorized to know about.

**Greg Price** · 2021-02-18 04:28 UTC

Do we have now a concept in general of "subscribers you're not allowed to know about"? Like, there are 12 subscribers I can know about, but there might be 10 more that I can't?

If so, that is much more worrying than this broken bit of API. That's a serious privacy failure waiting to happen. As you've said before, people rely on knowing who their audience is when they send to a private stream. I doubt we can craft the UI so that people see the list of 12 subscribers they can know about, but then also effectively communicate "BTW, there might be any number of secret lurkers, could be anyone, JFYI, keep that in mind."

Or more precisely: we *cannot* accurately communicate that without just creeping people out all the time. Because it is creepy.

**Greg Price** · 2021-02-18 04:30 UTC

If we don't have that as a concept, and instead it's either "here's the list of subscribers, all of them" or "sorry, you can't see who the subscribers are", then consider what a UI should say in the latter case. Is it going to just show an empty list, exactly like it would if there were no subscribers?

It should not do that. That would be a lie, told to the user. The truthful message is "you can't see the list of subscribers", not "there are no subscribers".

**Greg Price** · 2021-02-18 04:33 UTC

So the client needs to know the difference, and it needs to handle the two situations "empty subscriber list" and "unknown subscriber list" very explicitly differently.

That means the right semantics for this field isn't "here's the list of subscribers that you can know about", where "there are no subscribers" and "you can't know the list of subscribers" both get represented as `[]`.

The right semantics is "here's *the actual list of subscribers*, or else an explicit lack of data." Some reasonable ways to represent an explicit lack of data include leaving the field out, or sending it with the value `null`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-18 06:56 UTC

There's no current circumstance where one would only see some of the subscribers.  And it's an invariant that every stream has at least one subscriber.  But think the background here is that we previously had buggy behavior where the server would effectively randomly send `[]` or `null` for the case of "you're not allowed to see subscribers".  @Greg Price this thread is relevant background: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/17046#pullrequestreview-570084875, but basically for historical reasons clients need to handle both possibilities :/.

I agree with the premise that `null` is better for "access denied", even if it isn't super important because a correct client is unlikely to send an `include_subscribers` request.  But I'm not sure that's actually the right model.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-18 06:57 UTC

With the behavior in master, "[]" on subscribers means you have no access, because of invariants of the system.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-18 06:59 UTC

But one could argue that we should just throw an error if you pass `include_subscribers=true` and you don't have access to subscribers.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-18 07:00 UTC

I guess there's one funny corner case, which is that in the Zephyr mirroring realm, users have access to streams where they don't have access to subscribers; other than that weird corner case, I'm not aware of a distinction between having access to a stream and having access to its subscribers.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-18 07:01 UTC

And I might argue that it doesn't make sense to have a situation where one will have access to a stream but not access to the set of administrators, even if there's a world where you don't get access to the set of all subscribers?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-02-18 07:02 UTC

But maybe there's some future use case where that'd be relevant, and I think we'd be better off with the `null` interface in such a world?  Not sure, and heading AFK, but those are the things to think about.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-18 12:54 UTC

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/d9740045a5aa61b3031e713eec7ba75a2d7856c0

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-18 12:58 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> So the client needs to know the difference, and it needs to handle the two situations "empty subscriber list" and "unknown subscriber list" very explicitly differently. The right semantics is "here's *the actual list of subscribers*, or else an explicit lack of data." Some reasonable ways to represe …

Even if we accurately distinguished `[]` vs. `None` vs. `nil` vs. `null` vs. `undefined` vs. `false` vs.  omitting the key for the list of subscribers, the client wouldn't be able to do much with that  information.  For example, as soon a user gets promoted from a guest to a normal user, their ability to access (and add subscribers) to a public stream would change.  Or if we made a public stream private.  Or if we revoked your admin privileges.

It's much more sensible for a client to implement logic like this:

~~~
    sub.can_access_subscribers =
        page_params.is_admin || sub.subscribed ||
        (!page_params.is_guest && !sub.invite_only);

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-18 13:10 UTC

And then there are possible additional business rules on top of that.  For example, we might allow an admin to access subscribers for a private stream that she is not subscribed to, but we might give her an extra warning before she can add herself.

None of these things are easy to communicate with by omitting keys or sending `None`.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-18 13:13 UTC

We document the current behavior (non-optional arrays) in zulip.yaml.  Edits are welcome:

~~~
subscribers:
  type: array
  items:
    type: integer
  description: |
    A list of user IDs of users who are subscribed
    to the stream. Included only if `include_subscribers` is `true`.

    If a user is not allowed to know the subscribers for
    a stream, we will send an empty array.  API authors
    should use other data to determine whether users like
    guest users are forbidden to know the subscribers.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-18 14:08 UTC

(The fact that we have an `include_subscribers` flag would also make any strategy of using `[]`/`None` distinctions for business logic even more fragile.)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-18 15:41 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I guess there's one funny corner case, which is that in the Zephyr mirroring realm, users have access to streams where they don't have access to subscribers; other than that weird corner case, I'm not aware of a distinction between having access to a stream and having access to its subscribers.

Guests are not allowed to see the subscribers for public streams that they have unsubscribed from, but they are still allowed to see messages from that stream.  You can demonstrate this to yourself by doing these steps with Polonious:
* send a message to Denmark
* unsubscribe from Denmark
* reload and narrow to Denmark

You will notice that the "All" tab is disabled in "Manage Streams" for guests.

We actually do a good job of documenting this business rule in https://zulip.com/help/stream-permissions#public-streams

**Steve Howell** · 2021-02-18 15:58 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> [...] And it's an invariant that every stream has at least one subscriber

I don't believe we have ever relied on that invariant to determine whether a user has access to their subscribers, and it certainly stopped being necessary in February 2018 due to 20311185451ce5e3f670bbfb2f86b6a7cdb4d6a2

The fact that the invariant holds isn't entirely irrelevant to the discussion, though.  Unless a dev had tested with Zephyr users or guests, it would have been difficult to identify bugs related to wrong interpretation of false-y values.

**Sourabh Saini (100RABHpy)** · 2021-03-03 12:16 UTC

**Greg Price** · 2021-03-04 04:38 UTC

(replying to Sean Yuan)
> I have concerns about a global compression on all uploaded images. There are times when my team uploads images containing text that they would like to share. Overly aggressive compressions risk blurring such text. I would prefer if this was an option perhaps?

I think this is one of the reasons that by far the biggest impact to be had here is by generating thumbnails and using those when the image appears in the message list.

When we're making a thumbnail, fundamentally it's to be shown at a small size, so there aren't that many pixels and it will be quite a lot smaller than the original image. And the uploaded image is always there in the lightbox for when a user actually wants to see the detail. That means a thumbnail can perform a very steep reduction in size that we couldn't do at upload time.

**Greg Price** · 2021-03-04 04:39 UTC

And because a message is sent once and read many times, the great majority of the benefit to be had is by reducing the size of what ultimately gets downloaded, not what gets uploaded.

**Greg Price** · 2021-03-04 04:40 UTC

Generating thumbnails is a server-side job, and it's tracked as #16210. It's been stalled for a long time, though.

We also have a mobile issue for shrinking images at upload time: #M2749.

*2021-03-04 to 2021-03-04 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/get_user_messages.20in.20test.20for.20bots/with/1126826)*

**Wesley Aptekar-Cassels** · 2021-03-04 08:20 UTC

i'm testing #17332, and seeing something odd: in the test, `self.get_messages()` includes:

```
{'id': 31, 'sender_id': 4, 'content': '<p><span class="user-mention silent" data-user-id="10">King Hamlet</span> created a new stream <a class="stream" data-stream-id="6" href="/#narrow/stream/6-Verona2">#Verona2</a>.</p>\n<p><span class="user-mention silent" data-user-id="10">King Hamlet</span> created a new stream <a class="stream" data-stream-id="7" href="/#narrow/stream/7-Denmark5">#Denmark5</a>.</p>', 'recipient_id': 120, 'timestamp': 1614845775, 'client': 'Internal', 'subject': 'new streams', 'topic_links': [], 'is_me_message': False, 'reactions': [], 'submessages': [], 'flags': ['read'], 'sender_full_name': 'Notification Bot', 'sender_email': 'notification-bot@zulip.com', 'sender_realm_str': 'zulipinternal', 'display_recipient': 'Denmark', 'type': 'stream', 'stream_id': 1, 'avatar_url': 'https://secure.gravatar.com/avatar/0fc5476bdf03fe8640cc8fbc27a47549?d=identicon&version=1', 'content_type': 'text/html'}
```

but `zerver.lib.test_helpers.get_user_messages(self.notification_bot())` returns `[]`.

what's up with that? does `get_user_messages` not work for bots?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-04 19:09 UTC

@Wesley Aptekar-Cassels indeed, `get_user_messages` doesn't work for certain classes of bots.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-04 19:10 UTC

I'm not convinced this is the right design, but basically for E.g. incoming webhook bots, which only have permissions to post messages, it's a substantial waste of resources to record UserMessage rows for messages sent to streams that they might be subscribed to for the purpose of having permissions to post there.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-04 19:10 UTC

Notification Bot is a system-level bot which is a bit different, but it also only sends messages by design.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-04 19:12 UTC

So I would instead, if you want to check `get_user_messages`, use a normal user subscribed to the relevant stream.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-04 19:13 UTC

(That said, I'm not sure there's a reason to call that rather than just `self.get_messages` in a test for that feature)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-04 19:16 UTC

I guess the critical point for Notification Bot here is that it isn't subscribed to the stream or a recipient of the message, and we only create UserMessage rows for recipients.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-22 19:42 UTC

For #17742, we basically just need to pick what we think is an appropriate timeout for how long a server has to reply to a Zulip outgoing webhook message.  I think we don't need to be exceedingly generous here, in that clients that need extremely long processing times can get essentially equivalent functionality with a loop and our `call_on_each_message` API, so there's a workaround for anyone whose handler is very slow/expensive.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-22 19:42 UTC

Has anyone seen documentation from another service on how much processing time they offer for this?  I feel like I've seen both 5s and 10s for different services, but can't quickly find an example by googling so figured I'd ask.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-22 19:43 UTC

If we can't find a clear reason to do something specific here, I suppose we can just implement 10s and iterate from there.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-23 22:39 UTC

Any thoughts on this?  Or should we just go with 10 seconds and iterate from there if we get feedback arguing for another value?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-03-24 00:12 UTC

We could stick some logging in there and see what the p99 is of current requests.  Some quick googling finds 3s or 10s to both be defaults people use.

1.270672
1.820220
2.756498
2.835955
3.250471
4.096407
30
```
The 30s is a queue worker-level timeout.  So 5s or 10s is likely a fine timeout here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-04 01:02 UTC

I feel like 5s is pretty reasonable for us to require, but probably folks whose handler is really slow will fail occasionally; it might be best to just do 10s.  (I think we just need to set the value and then document it somewhere on https://zulip.com/api/outgoing-webhooks).

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-05-12 19:27 UTC

From more data, 10s is p99.4 or so -- we've seen one response come back after 10.2s, and a few more hit the 30s timeout.  Which is Fine, I think.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-12 19:27 UTC

Yeah, agreed.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-12 19:28 UTC

Thanks for the follow-up!

## blueslip in production

*2021-03-24 to 2021-03-24 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/blueslip.20in.20production/with/1141505)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-03-24 01:12 UTC

The `blueslip` system is great in development, since it surfaces exceptions to developers right in the browser, in order to make them more obvious.  In production, it shovels exceptions into email and/or the `#errors` channel.  Those interfaces aren't well-suited for doing aggregation on exceptions to look for trends and patterns in client-side exceptions.

We already have integrations with Sentry (https://sentry.io/) for server-side exception monitoring and aggregation.  It would be nice to be able to use the same interface for tracking client-side errors as well.

If we add that integration, is it worth keeping the production integrations with blueslip that put client-side exceptions in `#errors` and/or email?  Unlike server-side errors, where they're accessible in the error logs, no matter what, dropping the blueslip-to-server pipeline means that tracking exceptions will no longer be possible without a Sentry account.  They do have a free pricing level, but having the requirement to use them to see the exceptions seems only somewhat-OK.

But I also don't know if anyone but Zulip Cloud cares about tracking these (@*selfhosters* ?).

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-24 02:25 UTC

I personally think it’s fine to optimize this for our own use case and let self-hosters manage it on their own.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-24 03:41 UTC

Yeah, I'd be tempted to keep the logic for emails -- I don't think `#errors` support is something I'd want to encourage a self-hosted installation to use, in part because it has nonzero risk of an exception loop.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-24 03:43 UTC

I also do appreciate the `blueslip.log` system in production -- I'm not sure how the Sentry exception system works, but I think I prefer a model where exceptions are send through the Zulip server rather than submitted directly to Sentry from the browser for security reasons anyway?  I guess the downside of that aspect of the current setup is that if we ever have a total outage, we can't get access to the JS errors during during that window, which may or may not be useful.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-24 03:47 UTC

I also to some extent like the current property we have that the logic for detecting production errors 

But I don't really have a sense for how Sentry's protocol works, and whether it's really possible to arrange data the way we might want to.  

I suppose one could also imagine reimplementing the "non-Sentry" error reporting to use Sentry's JS library pointed at a URL hosted by the Zulip server -- I haven't looked at their protocol but given that mostly all we need is the stacktrace, that's probably possible.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-24 03:49 UTC

And I certainly see the appeal of just plugging in Sentry's library and not having to figure something complicated out.

## server version upgrade nag

*2021-03-26 to 2021-04-27 · 25 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/server.20version.20upgrade.20nag/with/1144560)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-26 21:38 UTC

I opened https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/17826 to track a proposed release goal, namely having a mechanism through which folks who are running very old Zulip servers will get nagged about upgrading.

This sort of feature is particularly important to get into a release, because it'll only really start to help us like a year after we implement it, as users of course don't get its code until it's implemented.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-26 23:18 UTC

I've implemented much of this design in https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/17982.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-26 23:18 UTC

One thing I realize we kinda need here is a page this can link to that talks about Zulip's security release process and why it's important to upgrade regularly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-26 23:18 UTC

Here's a sample screenshot:

[image.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/6/SePd8HyunfqAUmuR5zUjpS2O/image.png)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-26 23:20 UTC

My thinking is we can merge this to master (to make it easier to iterate on) with the "Learn more" link pointing to the general upgrade instructions, and then we can fork smaller issues for the remaining things we want to do (E.g. we need to figure out a way to see if the current install is from a release tarball created sometime deeper in the past, finalize whether we think 1 year is the right time window, etc.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-27 19:20 UTC

OK, #17982 is merged, so we have the basic infrastructure in place.  To complete #17826, we need a few things:
* A discussion on how we feel about "1 year" as the default time period before servers get nagged about upgrading.
* A better page about Zulip's release schedule and security to link to; my current thought is to rewrite docs/roadmap.md to be that page (it's been stale for years).
* A way to check on what date the release tarball that was installed on a Zulip server was created.  (Basically as a way of avoiding the notice being cleared for a year if you upgrade from one ancient release to a slightly less ancient release, at least if done via the default release tarball method).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-27 19:21 UTC

I don't remember if we install our releases using a `cp -a` type mechanism where the `mtime` on files generated during the release process would work, or if we need to generate a new file with a timestamp in it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-27 19:21 UTC

`unpack-zulip` does this: `subprocess.check_call(["tar", "-xf", tarball_path, "-C", extract_path])`

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-27 19:23 UTC

It would appear so; so I think we can check if a `os.path.join(settings.DEPLOY_ROOT, "version")` file exists, and if so, what its mtime is, to answer this question.

**Cyphase** · 2021-04-27 19:31 UTC

Do you not want to have servers phoning home to check the latest release version? Or maybe this time-based nag could be a fallback for a future opt-in release-based nag?

**Cyphase** · 2021-04-27 19:31 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> ...; my current thought is to rewrite docs/roadmap.md to be that page (it's been stale for years).
I was just noticing that page's staleness yesterday. :+1:

**Greg Price** · 2021-04-27 19:33 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> * A discussion on how we feel about "1 year" as the default time period before servers get nagged about upgrading.

I think the terms it makes most sense to think about this time period in is as time since the *next* release that you should have upgraded to, rather than the release you're on.

I understand that for the implementation it's helpful to avoid any need for outside information, so implementing as time since the release you're on is helpful. But for choosing the duration, I think it's best thought of as a way of approximating "time since subsequent release that you should have upgraded to".

**Greg Price** · 2021-04-27 19:35 UTC

Recent minor releases have come 3-4 months apart. So "1 year since release you're on" would roughly correspond to "6 months since you should have upgraded", plus some buffer for variability in how often we make a release.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-27 19:35 UTC

(replying to Cyphase)
> Do you not want to have servers phoning home to check the latest release version? Or maybe this time-based nag could be a fallback for a future opt-in release-based nag?
Yeah, I think we may want to add that, but it's more complicated and we'd want a fallback anyway.

**Greg Price** · 2021-04-27 19:36 UTC

That feels a bit fast to me for server software.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-27 19:36 UTC

(replying to Greg Price)
> Recent minor releases have come 3-4 months apart. So "1 year since release you're on" would roughly correspond to "6 months since you should have upgraded", plus some buffer for variability in how often we make a release.
I think actually frequency of minor releases is not important; what's important is when the last security release with an important security bug relevant for their installation happened.  Which historically is "every 3-4 months" for a security release at all, but much harder to guess for "a security bug that affects your configuration".

**Greg Price** · 2021-04-27 19:38 UTC

Well, the point is that it's pretty annoying if you start getting a nag because you're "out of date", but it actually hasn't been very long at all since the new release you should have upgraded to.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-27 19:39 UTC

Yeah, so maybe we want 18 months -- basically a year for "there's probably a security bug, whether in Zulip or one of its dependencies" and then 6 months as a buffer beyond that?

**Greg Price** · 2021-04-27 19:39 UTC

SGTM.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-27 19:39 UTC

(And we'll have clear instructions for how to just change a setting and adjust the nag deadline if you don't want to upgrade)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-27 19:40 UTC

I think 18-24 months or so is also likely to end up being the point at which we would consider making the mobile/desktop apps stop supporting old versions, which is sorta the other analysis point we want to have here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-27 19:40 UTC

And ideal version of this feature would have a way to phone home and ask whether in fact there's an important security issue, etc., but I don't want to design that right now and it'd likely be simple enough that we could backport it if desired.

**Greg Price** · 2021-04-27 19:41 UTC

Yeah

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-27 20:01 UTC

OK opened https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/18288 for the two changes that are not just documentation that we want for this release.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-27 20:01 UTC

And then I'll do some later project on the documentation front, probably next week.


## Double Escaping

*2021-03-28 to 2021-03-29 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Double.20Escaping/with/1145946)*

**Akshat** · 2021-03-28 21:18 UTC

I was adding test cases in #17511 when I got a doubt that:
Should `&lt;` be **rendered** as `<`(its HTML version is still `&lt;`) or `&lt;` (its HTML version is `&amp;lt;`)?

**Akshat** · 2021-03-28 21:18 UTC

I tried to this at several places like: [commonmark](https://spec.commonmark.org/dingus/?text=%5C!%5C%22%5C%23%5C%24%5C%25%5C%26%5C%27%5C(%5C)%5C*%5C%2B%5C%2C%5C-%5C.%5C%2F%5C%3A%5C%3B%5C%3C%5C%3D%5C%3E%5C%3F%5C%40%5C%5B%5C%5C%5C%5D%5C%5E%5C_%5C%60%5C%7B%5C%7C%5C%7D%5C~%0A), github.com, etc. They all **render** `&lt;` as `<`.
But when I checked this on Whatsapp Web, they do **double escaping** (i.e. `&amp;lt;`)

**Akshat** · 2021-03-28 21:18 UTC

I wonder, is this because Whatsapp doesn't use that heavy Markdown formats?
I mean, the upstream version that we use renders `&lt;` as `<` because of the intended behaviour?

**Akshat** · 2021-03-28 21:18 UTC

I can't see by not doing double escaping how is it useful.
According to me, `&lt;` must be rendered as `&lt;` (i.e. double escaping should be done).

**Akshat** · 2021-03-28 21:21 UTC

To be more clear: What I mean by **double escaping** is that `&lt;` is already an escape version of `<` but `&amp;lt;` is the double escaped version of `<`.

**Akshat** · 2021-03-28 21:23 UTC

I am trying to put here that we are missing the escaping in cases like `&lt;`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-03-28 21:52 UTC

Converting the text `&lt;` to the HTML `&amp;lt;`, which renders as the text `&lt;`, is not double escaping; that’s just normal escaping.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-03-28 21:55 UTC

[Example 300](https://spec.commonmark.org/0.29/#example-300) in the CommonMark spec clarifies the expected behavior of `\<` and `\&`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-03-28 22:01 UTC

And [section 6.2](https://spec.commonmark.org/0.29/#entity-and-numeric-character-references) specifies how HTML entity references work when `\` is not involved.

**Akshat** · 2021-03-29 05:44 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> Converting the text `&lt;` to the HTML `&amp;lt;`, which renders as the text `&lt;`, is not double escaping; that’s just normal escaping.
Yeah, I agree! That's why I clarified [here](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/3-backend/topic/Double.20Escaping/near/1145952). :sweat_smile:

## chat.zulip.org send times

*2021-03-31 to 2021-03-31 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/chat.2Ezulip.2Eorg.20send.20times/with/1148114)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-31 01:23 UTC

So, I noticed that there's getting to be nontrivial lag when posting to public streams in chat.zulip.org, and just checked servers logs and confirmed that it often takes 2-3s on the backend to send a message to a stream with 17k subscribers like this one:
```
POST    200  3.0s (mem: 7ms/6) (md: 14ms/1) (db: 996ms/19q) /json/messages (7@root via website)
```

That's a multiplicative factor higher than seems reasonable.  It's been a while since we last looked into optimizing this.  I opened https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/17898 after noticing this as a clever idea that will save 300ms or so in terms of visual UX, but that's only 10% of the total.  So we should do some profiling/investigation here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-31 01:25 UTC

Specifically of interest to me is that we spend almost 1s in the database, which I definitely don't remember being a significant chunk of time in the past; I kinda suspect we have some sort of regression here.

That all said, one other bit of context is that everything seems to take much longer on chat.zulip.org than it used to since sometime in December when we hadn't changed anything, so part of this could be a hardware issue.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-31 01:26 UTC

E.g. one other observation is that `GET /events` on zulipchat.com takes ~3ms whereas it's ~8ms on chat.zulip.org, and I don't have think there's a good reason that should be the case.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-03-31 01:29 UTC

We're taking a restart on czo tonight.  That may move us to a different underlying host, which may adjust performance.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-31 13:04 UTC

Has there been any recent bump in the number of queries?  It seems high to have 19 queries for sending a stream message.  I thought at one point message sending was single digits.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-31 20:27 UTC

Yeah, it did used to be single digits; we of course add them from time to time, but that is definitely unexpectedly high.  Which suggests hardware isn't the only thing that has regressed here.


## Investigating slow / times

*2021-03-31 to 2021-03-31 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Investigating.20slow.20.2F.20times/with/1148906)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-31 18:59 UTC

I think it could be useful to figure out an instrumentation system for `fetch_initial_state_data` or `GET /` that lets us figure out where the time is going when `/` is slow in production (might want it for other endpoints too).  There's a few ways I can see getting at that.

We actually track all the database queries in a request using this in `zerver/lib/db.py`:
```
        self.connection.queries.append(                                                              
            {                                                                                        
                "time": f"{duration:.3f}",                                                           
            }                                                                                        
        )                                                                                            
```

These numbers are added up in `zerver/middleware.py`, and used for logging the total query time and number of queries for every request.  However, there's more we can do here -- e.g. we could log a special log line or data structure with details on all the specific queries that took more than 10ms, say, for key endpoints where we care a lot about latency.  Might require a bit of care -- I don't want to log user IDs or the like -- but that'll usually be good enough to figure out where the time is going.

I could imagine imagine having a context manager that we put around specific likely expensive queries that we want to log details for in every request for the purpose of graphing the distribution of those values.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-03-31 19:33 UTC

I did a refactoring of the fetch code a while back that had this as one of its goals. My initial approach was a bit clumsy, so I ended up abandoning it.  But this is definitely feasible and worthwhile.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-31 20:24 UTC

Yeah -- my proposal was one that wouldn't require any refactoring at all, but for `/`, I'd ideally want something more detailed, sorta like this test in `test_event_system`:
```
        flush_per_request_caches()                                                                   
        with queries_captured() as queries:                                                          
            with mock.patch("zerver.lib.events.always_want") as want_mock:                           
                fetch_initial_state_data(user)                                                       
                                                                                                     
        self.assert_length(queries, 29)                                                              
                                                                                                     
        expected_counts = dict(                                                                      
            alert_words=1,                                                                           
            custom_profile_fields=1,                                                                 
            default_streams=1,                                                                       
            default_stream_groups=1,                                                                 
            hotspots=0,                                                                              
            ...
           )                                                                                            
```

except with total elapsed time (so we can see Python time).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-03-31 20:25 UTC

the other thing I should mention is that `manage.py profile_request`, in the `zilencer` module, might be a reasonable path for this with a bit more work -- for a `GET` request, one could just simulate it.

## The Difference "return json_error" and "raise JsonableError"

*2021-04-01 to 2021-07-07 · 22 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/The.20Difference.20.22return.20json_error.22.20and.20.22raise.20JsonableError.22/with/1149549)*

**Zixuan James Li** · 2021-04-01 13:20 UTC

It seems that `return json_error` and `raise JsonableError` are sometimes interchangeable. For example, in `zever/views/message_edit.py`, there are three ways to do the same thing:
```python
    if propagate_mode != "change_one" and topic_name is None and stream_id is None:
        return json_error(_("Invalid propagate_mode without topic edit"))
```
```python
    else:
        return JsonableError(_("You don't have permission to edit this message"))
```
```python
    if content is not None and user_profile.realm.message_content_edit_limit_seconds > 0:
        deadline_seconds = user_profile.realm.message_content_edit_limit_seconds + edit_limit_buffer
        if (timezone_now() - message.date_sent) > datetime.timedelta(seconds=deadline_seconds):
            raise JsonableError(_("The time limit for editing this message has passed"))
```
Perhaps this might be a result of having part of it extracted from `action.py`, part of it written after that as a part of the view.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-04-01 13:57 UTC

I think your code excerpt is a bit inaccurate--we never say `return JsonableError`.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-04-01 13:58 UTC

Your hypothesis is probably correct, though.  I think any inconsistencies are just due to how the code emerged.  I think we generally prefer the `raise JsonableError(...)` idiom in 2021.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-01 16:32 UTC

They do the same thing.  I think most accurate is that `json_error` is a bit cleaner to read and thus often what one uses directly in a view function.  

We need `JsonableError` when we want to raise the error from code that returns data without modifying types (e.g. it's super great for a validation method you call).

There's an argument that we should just migrate away from using `json_error` at all to have one less thing to learn, and also to not need to change error handling when refactoring error checking code between different functions.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-01 16:34 UTC

This is perhaps somewhat informative:
```
(zulip-py3-venv) tabbott@coset:~/zulip$ git grep json_error  | grep -v assert_json_error | grep -v import | wc
    199    1289   18010
(zulip-py3-venv) tabbott@coset:~/zulip$ git grep JsonableError | grep -v import | wc
    378    2136   32427
```
so about a 2:1 usage ratio.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-04-01 16:35 UTC

Yeah, I've always been on the fence on this.  I think the 2:1 ratio is compelling.  I wouldn't miss `json_error`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-01 16:40 UTC

I think the main benefit for me would be refactoring; e.g. this morning when working on 08116a17b0dfec59b5eba7e97facb13fcad56309, I ended up spending some time changing this as part of moving code (mostly because I split it out of a larger commit that did the `json_error` import, and didn't want to churn the imports).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-01 16:40 UTC

So I think I'm in favor of that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-06 15:58 UTC

Do we want to open an issue for doing this migration?  I think it's the kind of thing that can be nice to do soon before a release, because it'll churn a lot of code, and thus make backporting changes across it a little more annoying.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2021-04-06 16:36 UTC

I just skimmed through many of the functions that return `json_error(...)` and I found that it should be safe to replace most of them with `raise JsonableError(...)` without refactoring. But I'm uncertain of whether there are any cases in which we want `return json_error(...)` instead of `raise JsonableError(...)`

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-06 16:37 UTC

The discussion above I think suggests the answer is no.  `raise JsonableError` is converted into `return json_error` in `middleware.py`, so they're functionally equivalent in terms of the resulting `HttpResponse`.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2021-04-06 16:40 UTC

OK, then I think it would definitely be great to migrate for consistency. I have seen these two approaches being used in the same function so many times.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-28 23:35 UTC

@Zixuan James Li would you be interested in doing this migration?  In #**api design>Rate limits**, we just came across another motivation for doing this. And I think you're now pretty good at doing big codebase cutovers, and with the mypy stuff are the main person doing big backend migrations one would want to serialize the work with.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2021-06-29 02:26 UTC

Yeah, sure.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2021-07-01 02:49 UTC

So now we have merged #19066 that brings `git grep json_error  | grep -v assert_json_error | grep -v import | wc -l` from 199 to 53.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2021-07-01 02:52 UTC

The remaining ones are not migrated mainly because they use parameters like `data` and `status` that `JsonableError` is not able to handle without overriding it in subclasses.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2021-07-01 02:56 UTC

The question here is that whether it is better to allow the `__init__` function of `JsonableError` to take these additional properties, or to create subclasses to cover these use cases?

**Zixuan James Li** · 2021-07-01 04:01 UTC

I just came to read #5598. For the following use cases, I would say that subclassing `JsonableError`should be the right direction here for both readability and reusability.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-01 18:28 UTC

@Zixuan James Li yeah, I think that's probably the better model. Certainly in places where we'd be copying an error string/code combination in several places, it'd be cleaner to raise an exception.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-01 18:31 UTC

While we don't necessarily want to do the investment to make every since JsonableError have a `code` (Certainly the `BAD_REQUEST` response seems correct for cases of malformed user input, which is a large portion of errors), it's probably cleaner for 401s at least `raise JsonUnauthorizedError` as a subclass rather than passing a `code` property to `JsonableError`, if we don't feel the need to have a more specific code for that reason for an unauthorized error.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-01 18:33 UTC

I think we want to avoid defining large numbers of unique `code` values that are unlikely to be useful for clients, since it is a lot of API naming decisions and thus would be time-consuming, but we should define them for any specific error that we'd expect an API or mobile client to want to do something special for (not just display the `msg` to the user).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-07 00:56 UTC

We've now completed the migration to eliminate `json_error` in favor of `JsonableError`.  

Since we deleted the old functions, folks rebasing old branches that use `json_error` will see test failures.

## login problem / internal server error

*2021-04-06 to 2021-04-06 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/login.20problem.20.2F.20internal.20server.20error/with/1154584)*

**Oktay X** · 2021-04-06 12:27 UTC

I have an install running the latest zulip with LDAP authentication. It just stopped letting logins. People already logged in are fine.  When I try to log in, it hangs for a long time until eventually it displays an internal server error. I can't find anything obvious in the logs. It seems to be chugging along fine with the logged in users. A reboot did not fix it. Where should I look?

**Oktay X** · 2021-04-06 12:31 UTC

Oh. I think this is a cloudflare caching issue. Checking.

**Oktay X** · 2021-04-06 12:44 UTC

That was it.  In case anyone has a similar issue. The LDAP url pointed to a domain that was proxied by cloudflare. Changed it to an unproxied domain name pointing directly to the ldap server and it's fixed.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-06 15:57 UTC

@Oktay X thanks for the report!  That's a subtle possibility I hadn't thought about, so it's useful to know about in case someone else runs into the same situation.

**Rein Zustand** · 2021-05-01 17:24 UTC

How does downgrading work in case when there is a problem with the currently running CZO instance? From reading #**learning>Downgrading** , it looks like it is nontrivial to downgrade?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-05-01 20:57 UTC

An individual commit that doesn’t do a state migration can generally be downgraded safely. We always keep track of which commits involve migrations, because they have special deployment considerations on Zulip Cloud.

**Rein Zustand** · 2021-05-02 01:57 UTC

I see. Also documented at https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/production/upgrade-or-modify.html#rolling-back-to-a-prior-version.
1. Do you think it is worth it for `/home/zulip/deployments/DATE/scripts/restart-server` to contain a sanity check to assert that the difference between the chosen-to-be-current version only differs by the current version in their minor numbers, when downgrading?
2. Found this issue #280 for downgrading that involves migrations. But why not also just document the current best practice used in CZO and zulipchat.com when deploying a new server version that involves migration? I assume you have to create an EC2 snapshot or something equivalent, before doing the non-backward compatible upgrade?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-05-02 05:08 UTC

"the difference between the chosen-to-be-current version only differs by the current version in their minor numbers" is insufficiently safe, because 4.0-dev and 4.0-dev are not safe to downgrade between. :)

But yes, we should document that downgrading is generally safe when there are not database migrations involved.  Ideally Django would provide a way to help enforce this, but `./manage.py migrate --check` seems happy to declare "no migrations to apply" on a checkout of a commit with an earlier schema.

**Rein Zustand** · 2021-05-02 05:27 UTC

But at least `restart-server` should be able to catch incompatible downgrades that are 100% sure to cause problems, like 4.0-dev to 3.3.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-05-02 05:33 UTC

Sure.  Though we should probably catch it before restart-server, in upgrade-stage-2.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-05-02 05:34 UTC

Though, there's a bit of a pickle that because that's the old version of the code, we won't actually be able to catch this except for folks downgrading to 4.x (or whenever we add such code).  But that's certainly not a reason to not put it in, it's just an upper bound on how often it will *currently* help.

**Rein Zustand** · 2021-05-02 12:56 UTC

Additionally, it should be possible to prevent the user upgrading from a very old version (e.g. #**general>Upgrade from Zulip 2.1** straight to the latest version. Since the upgrade need to be done in stages for each upgrade that requires a migration.

(replying to Rein Zustand)
> Additionally, it should be possible to prevent the user upgrading from a very old version (e.g. #**general>Upgrade from Zulip 2.1** straight to the latest version. Since the upgrade need to be done in stages for each upgrade that requires a migration.

I was actually wondering recently whether we shouldn't make it a rule to require upgrades to only go up by one major version? So upgrading from e.g. 3.0 to 5.4 would require doing the sequence of upgrades `3.0 -> 4.0`, `4.0 -> 5.4`. It adds some hassle for old, unupgraded deployments, but the added simplicity from not having to worry about the upgrade system working across large leaps in versions might be worth it.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-05-02 15:40 UTC

There's currently no need for that restriction. Upgrades by multiple versions should work fine as long as the OS is still supported (which we already check).

def do_login(request: HttpRequest, user_profile: UserProfile) -> None:                                               
    """Creates a session, logging in the user, using the Django method,                                              
    and also adds helpful data needed by our server logs.                                                            
    """                                                                                                              
    django_login(request, user_profile)                                                                              
    request._requestor_for_logs = user_profile.format_requestor_for_logs()                                           
    process_client(request, user_profile, is_browser_view=True)                                                      
    if settings.TWO_FACTOR_AUTHENTICATION_ENABLED:                                                                   
        # Log in with two factor authentication as well.                                                             
        do_two_factor_login(request, user_profile)                                                                   
```

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2021-05-03 20:46 UTC

Ah, perhaps this is at least part of the story https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/3.2/topics/auth/default/#session-invalidation-on-password-change 

>  If your AUTH_USER_MODEL inherits from AbstractBaseUser or implements its own get_session_auth_hash() method, authenticated sessions will include the hash returned by this function. In the AbstractBaseUser case, this is an HMAC of the password field. Django verifies that the hash in the session for each request matches the one that’s computed during the request. This allows a user to log out all of their sessions by changing their password.

So when the password gets rehashed, the session will have a mismatching HMAC of the `.password` field. Which would explain this behavior reported by the user:
> ok! I got logged in that time. it simultaneously logged my out of this browser.

With OAuth, the zulip-terminal flow from the user perspective would be:

1. You tell zulip-terminal you want to log into chat.zulip.org.
2. zulip-terminal opens a browser (or prints a URL); you log in to chat.zulip.org in your browser.
3. chat.zulip.org displays a single-use token with a copy button; you paste the token into zulip-terminal and you are now logged in there.
4. zulip-terminal may persist the OAuth session to disk so that it remains valid for future launches if it isn’t revoked or expired.

**Sahil Batra** · 2021-04-09 05:32 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-09 05:39 UTC

As a bit of a digression on how we make decisions: in a large asynchronous community like this one, there's a tradeoff between waiting for everyone's input vs. making decisions quickly.  

For decisions that are easy to change/undo later (E.g. one can just revert a commit), our strategy is to err on the side of being decisive after a few people have given their thoughts (including at least a couple people who are highly familiar with the topic) if they largely agree.  This is a useful optimization -- because in that situation, it's likely that the result would be the same if we waited for everyone, and it's a lot more pleasant experience for folks working on something to be able to proceed with work that depends on the question at hand.  And as long as it is indeed easy to change our mind later with additional input, at worst we end up redoing some work, which isn't a big deal if this is relatively rare.

However, an important part of this working is that folks who disagree with the consensus reached in a conversation that they missed speak up.  So if you think the people who were online at the time made the wrong choice here (or in any other thread) in a quick 5-minute conversation -- please be encouraged to reply with additional thoughts.  Nothing is set in stone.

(For bigger decisions that have a high cost to undo, we try pretty hard to wait several days for a broader part of the community to have an opportunity to provide input, because this reasoning doesn't apply in those situations).

## mypy __init__

*2021-04-16 to 2021-04-16 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/mypy.20__init__/with/1164248)*

**Rein Zustand** · 2021-04-16 05:04 UTC

It appears that annotation of `__init__(self, ...)` no longer requires a `-> None` (see https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/604). Do you think it is worth refactoring the codebase to remove those `-> None`s?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-04-16 05:09 UTC

[PEP 484](https://www.python.org/dev/peps/pep-0484/#the-meaning-of-annotations) still requires it.

> (Note that the return type of `__init__` ought to be annotated with `-> None`. The reason for this is subtle. If `__init__` assumed a return annotation of `-> None`, would that mean that an argument-less, un-annotated `__init__` method should still be type-checked? Rather than leaving this ambiguous or introducing an exception to the exception, we simply say that `__init__` ought to have a return annotation; the default behavior is thus the same as for other methods.)

**Rein Zustand** · 2021-04-16 05:15 UTC

But https://github.com/python/mypy/pull/5677 is newer than PEP 484.

https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/604#issuecomment-390737052

**Rein Zustand** · 2021-04-16 05:15 UTC

https://github.com/python/mypy/pull/5677 is the PR that closed https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/604.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-04-16 05:21 UTC

PEPs are [regularly updated](https://github.com/python/peps/commits/master/pep-0484.txt). But my point is that the implicit `-> None` on `__init__` is a mypy extension. The line between the specification and the mypy implementation is blurry sometimes, but it nominally exists, and there are other Python type checkers.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-04-16 05:23 UTC

I don’t mind relying on mypy extensions when they’re useful, but this one doesn’t seem to add anything.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-16 16:10 UTC

Yeah, and it's an extension designed to make mypy more useful for incompletely typed codebases. Zulip is a fully typed codebase, and I don't think there'd be any benefit in our changing the rule from "every function is annotated" to "every function but the `__init__` category is annotated" -- that's effectively just going to create an extra rule we have to explain to folks working on the codebase.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-16 16:11 UTC

One of the principles that's really important for scaling an open source project as we have with Zulip is minimizing the amount of rules/complexity/etc. one needs to explain to someone in order for them to be an effective contributor to the project.

## TODO/compatibility convention

So, the discussion in #18164 caused me to want to start a new convention of `TODO/compatibility` comments, which we can audit periodically when doing major releases, for the purpose.  The way I'm imagining this should work is:
* When we add a change to the server that's to support upgrading from older versions of the Zulip server, we add a comment including that string that also explains the condition at which the code will be no longer useful (ideally with a test that isn't the number for a future release that we can't predict the time for).
* Here's a couple examples: 260861426c95ae73b6c255a347a2936f41336f6b and 48d99886fd409adf5ae448a01c4d25ca653cc3b2.
* I imagine we can also use this for all the little things in `upgrade-zulip-stage-2` like `class_renames` or the pyyaml3 migration.  I'm a little less worried about that file in particular because it's something one looks at.  @Alex Vandiver FYI since you've been thinking about our server upgrade infrastructure.

Proposals for changing the name appreciated!  I just wanted to create something so I could merge #18164, and figure the cost of a rename commit is low compared to needing to keep re-reviewing that PR.
