## `hl_lines` regex #2036

*2021-04-16 to 2026-08-09 · 37 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/.60hl_lines.60.20regex.20.232036/with/1164886)*

**Akshat** · 2021-04-16 18:38 UTC

The original conversation starts from [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/16984#discussion_r583001775) (Related PR: #16984) where `FENCE_RE` modified by me was ambiguously matching the empty string with [either alternative](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/f566df5bf048dbe7e4931a83e8c6ddc321c7d4bb#diff-292c566e278db475f65a0606c41333c79553d2b2dbfdb87f94f637c3b3fb780dR112). As a result of this, I was unknowingly modifying [this line of code](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/f566df5bf048dbe7e4931a83e8c6ddc321c7d4bb#diff-292c566e278db475f65a0606c41333c79553d2b2dbfdb87f94f637c3b3fb780dL207-R210) (That time I thought that I had to modify because of my new changes).

To understand how the new `FENCE_RE` was ambiguously matching the empty string, I used https://regex101.com.

# Following is how original `FENCE_RE` matches the empty string:

```python3
FENCE_RE = re.compile(
    """
    # ~~~ or ```
    (?P<fence>
        ^(?:~{3,}|`{3,})
    )
    [ ]* # spaces
    (
        \\{?\\.?
        (?P<lang>
            [a-zA-Z0-9_+-./#]*
        ) # "py" or "javascript"
        \\}?
    ) # language, like ".py" or "{javascript}"
    [ ]* # spaces
    (
        (hl_lines=(?P<quot>"|')(?P<hl_lines>[0-9 ]*)(?P=quot))?
        | # hl_lines to emphasize certain lines of code
        \\{?\\.?
        (?P<header>
            [^~`]*
        )
        \\}?
    ) # header for features that use fenced block header syntax (like spoilers)

# Following is how:

```python
FENCE_RE = re.compile(
    """
    # ~~~ or ```
    (?P<fence>
        ^(?:~{3,}|`{3,})
    )

    [ ]* # spaces

    (
        \\{?\\.?
        (?P<lang>
            [a-zA-Z0-9_+-./#]*
        ) # "py" or "javascript"
        \\}?
    ) # language, like ".py" or "{javascript}"
    [ ]* # spaces
    (
        hl_lines=(?P<quot>"|')(?P<hl_lines>[0-9 ]*)(?P=quot)
    )? # hl_lines to emphasize certain lines of code
    (
        \\{?\\.?
        (?P<header>
            [^~`]*
        )
        \\}?
    ) # header for features that use fenced block header syntax (like spoilers)
    $
    """,
    re.VERBOSE,
)
```

`{py}`

Probably an ideal behavior would instead only accept a list of forms like
`py`
`.py`
`{py}`
`{.py}`

**Emmanuel Yusufu Kimaswa** · 2026-06-04 18:43 UTC

Hi all, I picked up #2036 and opened a PR (#39455) that adds hl_lines to code fences. On the implementation, I avoided the FENCE_RE issue from #16984: rather than parsing hl_lines inside FENCE_RE, I read it from the header group that FENCE_RE already captures, so FENCE_RE stays unchanged. I went with the space-separated hl_lines="1 3" form and left ranges out, to avoid the DoS concern raised earlier.
Before taking it further I wanted to check the syntax direction, since the thread never really settled it. @Tim Abbott , you said you'd prefer the  {1,3-5,7} form with ranges. @Anders Kaseorg , you pointed out the space-separated form isn't Python-Markdown's current syntax (the attrs {.python hl_lines="..."} is), and you weren't sure this was worth adding right now.
So two questions: is this still something you'd want, and if so, which syntax should I target, the hl_lines="..." form I've built, the attrs form, or {1,3-5,7} with ranges (capped to a safe length)? Happy to adapt either way.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-06-23 16:58 UTC

In general we've been aiming to conform to `CommonMark` patterns on this sort of detail, since we expect to replace the existing implementations with more modern CommonMark-with-extensions processors.

**Emmanuel Yusufu Kimaswa** · 2026-06-30 19:29 UTC

That makes sense, and I think it points at a syntax that covers all three concerns here. The CommonMark-with-extensions convention is the curly-brace attribute block on the fence line, the Pandoc and Python-Markdown form, so the language stays as-is and highlights go in `{hl_lines="1 3-5 7"}` after it.

That fits the CommonMark direction you're describing, it's the syntax Python-Markdown already uses (matching Anders's point), and the hyphen ranges inside the attribute give the 3-5 style ranges you preferred earlier, just in attrs form rather than a bare {1,3-5,7}.

So if the feature still makes sense in principle, I'll rework the PR to read hl_lines from the `{...}` attribute block instead of the bare `hl_lines="..."` it uses now. Does that direction work for both of you?

## supervisorctl restart order

*2021-04-27 to 2021-04-29 · 31 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/supervisorctl.20restart.20order/with/1169623)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-04-27 02:56 UTC

Moving over from github comments in https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/18215#issuecomment-824244931:

I wrote:
> I think there's a separate question of if we actually need to onion-restart things, so that both django and the workers are down at the same time. I don't think the goal of `restart-server` is to have a point in time when everything is stopped -- after all, we kick tornado first, and it's not like we take the DB schema upgrades inside that restart. So I think we could restart the supervisor'd jobs one at a time, instead of stopping django and workers, and then bringing both of them back, which results in a longer worker backlog.

@Tim Abbott responded:
> Yeah, I think that's right. The consideration we haven't discussed much here is that it is a goal to limit how many processes we restart all at once, especially at the moment we're restarting Django, so that we don't overload the CPU with "Python process startup", resulting in a longer period where no requests are handled at all. And that's maybe the right motivation for delaying worker startup -- though it is less significant now that we've deleted several processes from the overall queue worker bundle (most importantly, the `message_sender` bundle).

I'm not entirely sure if we're agreeing or not, because I don't know for sure what you mean by "delaying worker startup."

I think that "stop all; start all" (what we do now) is probably *worse* for having all of the services starting at the same time.  With "stop django; start django; for each worker: stop worker && start worker" we space the time out and each supervisor process is, when it starts, not competing with anything else starting up at that *exact* second, since it's spaced out from the previous one by the time to stop it.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-04-27 03:30 UTC

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/14959#issuecomment-827287011 is also tangentially relevant here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-27 18:42 UTC

Great.  Thanks for doing all this investigation.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-27 18:48 UTC

Given all this research, I think our policy should be:
* For the `zulip-tornado` processes, to restart them one-at-a-time to make downtime as minimal as possible and avoid restarting several at once.  This is in part motivated by the fact that we have a bug of unknown nature where sometimes one of the Tornado processes does not stop on its own and needs to be forcibly killed, which can result in the `stop` step taking 10+ seconds, and we'd like to avoid that ever happening with all processes.  
* For the `zulip-django` process bundle (managed by `uwsgi`), we want to minimize downtime, since everything 500s if this is down for long enough to overflow the number of requests that `nginx` will buffer for us.  
* For the `zulip-workers` bundle, the main goal is just to keep them out of the way of the restarts for Django and Tornado, since by design, they are all things where 15 seconds of queueing delay has minimal user-facing impact.

I'm not entirely sure how that translates into a conclusion for what we want to do.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-04-27 20:53 UTC

Do we have any ordering on django <-> tornado enforced by potential backwards-compatibility considerations?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-27 21:41 UTC

I think Tornado first is better, mainly because it's particularly unpleasant for Tornado to be not up again yet (since we don't have `uwsgi` buffering requests for us).

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-04-28 22:49 UTC

Hm, sure.  It's a bit unfortunate that kicking the tornado processes is what leads to a bunch of requests to Django to `/`, prevcisely at the same time that we're about to kick it.  Which means that doing a hot-restart of some sort with Django is probably worth it.

So I think rolling restarts are likely the right path here:
 - rolling restart tornado
 - then rolling restart each of the uwsgi Django processes
 - then rolling restart each of the workers

This spreads out the time that we have code skew.  Which is inherently a risk we have already, but not really an avoidable one -- so leaning into it to get a bit better availability seems entirely reasonable.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-28 22:53 UTC

Hmm, Tornado kicks shouldn't result in a large number of requests to Django for some number of minutes.

The logic is in `reload.js` -- the Tornado restarts send an event, but what that event does is causes each client to schedule a reload at a random time according to certain parameters (it waits longer if the user is using the app at the time).

The observed behaviour is a fairly immediate spike in requests, though.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-28 22:56 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-28 22:57 UTC

But I think you're right that the ideal world would be that we first restart Django, wait until some sense of "all Django processes are healthy again" and then do Tornado one process at a time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-28 22:57 UTC

Because the Django restart should be extremely cheap, in that it shouldn't result in any change in client requests from stready-state (with some catchup from buffering/retries).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-28 22:58 UTC

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-04-28 22:59 UTC

It's not *not* totally disruptive, though.  I did a quick local test of using [chain reloading](https://uwsgi-docs.readthedocs.io/en/latest/articles/TheArtOfGracefulReloading.html#chain-reloading-lazy-apps) and it seems to work entirely reasonably.  The memory costs are slightly higher, because it's doing all of the loading post-fork, but it ensures that there are always n-1 uwsgi workers ready.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-28 23:00 UTC

From a "how broken is the website" perspective, `GET /` will fail if Tornado isn't running properly, but that's also unlikely to happen unless we have a database format change, and in any case, `GET /` requests are relatively rare as long as we didn't just restart Tornado.

**Cyril Pletinckx** · 2021-04-28 11:25 UTC

I investigated this error and here is what I found.

In the development environement the email backend that is created is an `EmailLogBackend`, a subclass of `django.core.mail.backends.smtp`. This object is initialized with the parameters contained in `zulip.zproject.computed_setting.py`. To understand why the error mentioned above is happening inside the devlopment environment it is important to notice that the following parameters are instantiated as follows :
- host = ""
- port = 25
- username = ""
- password = None
- use_tls = False
- use_ssl = False

When the development environment is starting it initializes an `EmailSendingWorker` and thus calls `initialize_connection(None)`. This call returns an `EmailLogBackend` instance on which the `open()` method was called. 

Refering to https://github.com/django/django/blob/6e742dabc95b00ba896434293556adeb4dbaee8a/django/core/mail/backends/smtp.py#L41, the connection of the backend object will be initialized to an `smtlib.SMTP` object. The latter is instantiated as detailed in https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/master/Lib/smtplib.py#L229. 

As host is empty it will not call the `connect()` method which is supposed to initialize the socket : https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/master/Lib/smtplib.py#L315. This means that the returned connection was opened but doesn't contain a socket. 

Thus when trying to send an email through the worker's `send_email()` function, the `initialize_connection()` function is called again with the former created `EmailLogBackend` object. As it is an instance of `django.core.mail.backends.smtp.EmailBackend` the `noop()` function will be called with an unintialized socket leading to the error above-mentioned.

I tried to implement a fix by calling the `connect()` method manually if the `noop()` call raises a `"please run connect() first" SMTPServerDisconnected` exception but it triggered the following error : `ConnectionRefusedError: [Errno 111] Connection refused`. I guess this is because I'm calling `connect()` without any argument and thus it is trying to connect to localhost on port 25 which is probably blocked by my firewall or something ?

I'm not sure how I have to fix this as it depends on the development environment's settings and I don't know which values they should take.

@Alex Vandiver @Tim Abbott I could quickly implement a fix if you gently enlighten me  about the dev environment's requirements and how I should initialiaze the socket in it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-28 15:02 UTC

One other possibility would be to overwrite the `connect()` method of https://github.com/python/cpython/blob/master/Lib/smtplib.py#L315 to avoid using a socket or to pass arguments in order for the connection to be a sort of self-loop ?

I don't think we may just overwrite `open()` and `close()` as they must remain as it is for the special cases where it is needed to send outgoing emails. I also wonder how the dev environment was not reporting any issue before these changes if it was also based on `EmailLogBackend` ?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-28 16:29 UTC

Yeah, one theory would be that we make two classes extending the same base class: `EmailLogBackendBase`, with one subclassing that and the locmem one, and the other subclassing `EmailLogBackend` conditional on `settings.FORWARD_ADDRESS_CONFIG_FILE` (which seems to be how we do sending actual outgoing email in development?)

```
        if get_forward_address():
            self.prepare_email_messages_for_forwarding(email_messages)
            num_sent = super().send_messages(email_messages)
```

**Cyril Pletinckx** · 2021-04-28 17:03 UTC

I think I found what is the source of the problem. Before implementing the EmailSendingWorker to use a single smtp connection we never had to worry about it (= we opened new connections over and over again) thus we never had to access the `connection` field of a django SMTP EmailBackend directly. All the traffic was going through `mail.send()` in `send_email()` :

```python
    template = template_prefix.split("/")[-1]
    logger.info("Sending %s email to %s", template, mail.to)

    if mail.send() == 0:
        logger.error("Error sending %s email to %s", template, mail.to)
        raise EmailNotDeliveredException
```
According to https://github.com/django/django/blob/6e742dabc95b00ba896434293556adeb4dbaee8a/django/core/mail/message.py#L278 this call will initialize a new `smtplib.SMTP` connection with `self.get_connection()` (or actually a connection depending on `settings.EMAIL_BACKEND` which is an `EmailLogBackEnd` in our case) and then call `send_messages()` on it. As `EmailLogBackEnd` overwrites this method it never uses the `connection` attribute of the `smtplib.SMTP` instance (except when `get_forward_address()` returns True which is for the special cases mentioned before I suppose).

In the new implementation of `send_email()` we also use `send_messages()` so everything is fine but before calling `send_email()` we refresh the connection with `initialize_connection()` and this function tries to send a `noop` command to the SMTP server while the socket was never initialized in the dev environment (except for the special cases). This triggers the exception that you mentioned in the first message of this thread. 

To avoid that we could add a special case in `initialize_connection()` that checks if we have an instance of `EmailLogBackEnd` and to return immediately if it is the case or to proceed with the `noop()` call if it is an SMTP backend of django. I just wonder if it would not break the special cases where we want to send outgoing emails in the dev environment as this additional check would not re-open the connection if it was closed by the server. We could eventually also use `get_forward_address()` to detect the special cases in `initialize_connection()` as well ? Or maybe this is not necessary ?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-28 17:09 UTC

I think something like that is reasonable.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-28 17:09 UTC

(It also sounds like this is a development-environment only issue, which is good to know)

**Cyril Pletinckx** · 2021-04-28 17:20 UTC

I will try to implement that and see if it is working but I'm not sure how to test the special cases ? And yes I think it is. If the default settings of Zulip are to use a classic SMTP backend of django in a "real" environment (with a real connection and senders/recipients) when someone wants to create its own server then everything should be fine. And I guess one issue would have been opened by someone if the impacts of this mistake go beyond the dev environment ?

## moving topic between streams

*2021-04-30 to 2021-06-02 · 55 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/moving.20topic.20between.20streams/with/1172302)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-04-30 23:49 UTC

With #18051, we're hoping to add support for configuring who has permission to move topics between streams.  I want to bring this up since there's some security sensitivity for this operation, and I'd like to make sure we're reasoning about it correctly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-01 00:00 UTC

OK, I think we need to add additional security checks before we can merge this.  The basic problem is users who are subscribed to a stream but don't have full access to history.  This isn't a security concern for organization administrators, because they have the ability to just change history access to any stream they are subscribed to anyway.  But for a normal user, I believe you would be able to use this API endpoint to fish for messages that you shouldn't have access to by trying to move "anything with topic `secret project`" to another stream, with `propagate_mode=change_all`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-01 00:01 UTC

So the structural thing that we need to do before merging this is to do a `bulk_access_messages` call inside `update_messages_for_topic_edit`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-01 00:05 UTC

Except that's really slow.  We could do `get_topic_history_for_stream` or we could support optionally passing in parameters to `has_message_access`, I guess.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-05-01 00:05 UTC

That doesn’t stop a user from learning whether the topic `secret project` ever existed.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-01 00:06 UTC

How so?  You need a specific message ID that you have access to in order to attempt a message edit, so I think you need to send a message to the target topic first in order to do anything.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-01 00:06 UTC

So you can determine ... that topic has at least one message, the one you can see.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-01 00:07 UTC

```
    message, ignored_user_message = access_message(user_profile, message_id)                         
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-01 00:07 UTC

(There's no parameter for old topic or old stream -- just a message -- so I think we're good there).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-05-01 00:07 UTC

Depends on whether it throws errors for the previous messages that may or may not have existed; I thought the implication was that it would.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-01 00:07 UTC

Ahh, no, `bulk_access_messages` just filters those that don't match

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-05-01 00:07 UTC

Okay.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-01 00:08 UTC

``` python
def bulk_access_messages(user_profile: UserProfile, messages: Sequence[Message]) -> List[Message]:   
    filtered_messages = []                                                                           
                                                                                                     
    for message in messages:                                                                         
        user_message = get_usermessage_by_message_id(user_profile, message.id)                       
        if has_message_access(user_profile, message, user_message):                                  
            filtered_messages.append(message)                                                        
    return filtered_messages                                                                         
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-01 00:13 UTC

So I think we can do that by plumbing through something like this:
```
@@ -677,14 +677,19 @@ def access_message(
 def has_message_access(
-    user_profile: UserProfile, message: Message, user_message: Optional[UserMessage]
+        user_profile: UserProfile, message: Message, user_message: Optional[UserMessage], *,
+        stream: Optional[stream]=None,
 ) -> bool:
     if user_message is None:
         if message.recipient.type != Recipient.STREAM:
             # You can't access private messages you didn't receive
             return False
 
-        stream = Stream.objects.get(id=message.recipient.type_id)
+        if stream is None:
+            stream = Stream.objects.get(id=message.recipient.type_id)
+        else:
+            assert stream.recipient_id == message.recipient_id
+
         if stream.realm != user_profile.realm:
             # You can't access public stream messages in other realms
             return False
```

In order to make `bulk_access_messages` only need to fetch the Stream/Subscription objects once, without creating risk of correctness bugs if someone passes the wrong stream into something.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-01 00:14 UTC

@Aman Agrawal (amanagr) @Sahil Batra perhaps you can coordinate on doing this refactoring over the next week.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-01 00:26 UTC

In summary, we're currently enforcing:
* The user doing the move has access to both the old and new streams.
* The organization has chosen a configuration where this user is allowed to move messages between streams.  Guests cannot be given that permission.  (Replacing master's state that only organization administrators can move messages).
* The user has access to the target message in the original topic.

We will need to add enforcement of:
* The user doing the move has current read access to all of the individual messages being moved (as discussed above).  Thus any content in the messages, the user could already have shared with others via taking a screenshot and posting to the new stream if they really wanted to.  (There's some difference in whether the screenshot can be authenticated -- you can doctor content in via the browser inspector before taking it if you really want to fabricate a screenshot -- but this detail likely has little practical significance).
* The `stream_post_policy` allows the user moving messages to post to the new stream.  This was previously not required, because administrators can post to any stream, but probably we don't want someone to be able to circumvent `stream_post_policy` by moving messages even if the organization decided anyone can move messages between streams.
* We should make sure we're enforcing the "permission to edit topics at all" checks we use for moving messages within a stream.  I believe the first block in `update_message_backend` does this, but we should have test coverage for `!user_profile.realm.allow_community_topic_editing`.

I imagine in practice, large organizations will limit this permission to moderators, but your 10-person company might want to give all members access to use this feature, so I think it makes sense to allow the full set of policies for who can move content.

## send_message slowness

*2021-05-07 to 2021-05-12 · 123 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/send_message.20slowness/with/1176710)*

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 19:42 UTC

I am trying to figure out why it takes a long time to send messages to streams with lots of recipients.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 19:43 UTC

I set up my test db with 8k users of whom only 400 were non-long-term-idle.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 19:43 UTC

Here are my timings:

~~~
start query
0.02997303009033203 SELECT "zerver_subscription"."user_profile_id", "zerver_subscription"."push_notifications", "zerver_subscription"."email_notifications", "zerver_subscription"."wildcard_mentions_notify", "zerver_subscription"."is_muted", "zerver_userprofile"."enable_stream_email_notifications" AS "user_profile_email_notifications", "zerver_userprofile"."enable_stream_push_notifications" AS "user_profile_push_notifications", "zerver_userprofile"."wildcard_mentions_notify" AS "user_profile_wildcard_mentions_notify" FROM "zerver_subscription" INNER JOIN "zerver_recipient" ON ("zerver_subscription"."recipient_id" = "zerver_recipient"."id") INNER JOIN "zerver_userprofile" ON ("zerver_subscription"."user_profile_id" = "zerver_userprofile"."id") WHERE ("zerver_subscription"."active" AND "zerver_recipient"."type" = %s AND "zerver_recipient"."type_id" = %s) ORDER BY "zerver_subscription"."user_profile_id" ASC
end query 0.057945966720581055
start UserProfile query
0.041599273681640625 SELECT "zerver_userprofile"."id", "zerver_userprofile"."enable_online_push_notifications", "zerver_userprofile"."is_bot", "zerver_userprofile"."bot_type", "zerver_userprofile"."long_term_idle" FROM "zerver_userprofile" WHERE ("zerver_userprofile"."is_active" AND (id IN %s))
end UserProfile query 0.06280851364135742
get_recipient_info 0.15200328826904297
0.03327822685241699 INSERT INTO "zerver_message" ("sender_id", "recipient_id", "subject", "content", "rendered_content", "rendered_content_version", "date_sent", "sending_client_id", "last_edit_time", "edit_history", "has_attachment", "has_image", "has_link") VALUES (%s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s, %s) RETURNING "zerver_message"."id"
2021-05-07 19:28:11.114 INFO [zr] 166.170.34.226  POST    200 416ms (db: 125ms/12q) /json/messages (29@zulip via website)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 19:45 UTC

The call to `get_recipient_info`, which has two queries that return 8k users, accounts for 152/416ms, or 36% of the time.  So it's not necessarily the only bottleneck, but it might be the bottleneck for even larger streams.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 19:47 UTC

The two queries take 58ms and 63ms for Django to process (including the time in the DB), and then the other 31ms (20%) is Python slinging around sets and lists and calling one-line helper functions.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 19:49 UTC

The total Django time in the function is 121ms, of which 62ms is the DB, so the ORM overhead is 95%, or 59ms.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 19:50 UTC

The DB itself accounts for 47% of the time within the function.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 19:55 UTC

The reason we have two queries is somewhat an artifact of `get_recipient_info` handling not just streams, but also PMs and huddles, so that is why we somewhat redundantly query the `long_term_idle` column, but the two queries are otherwise disjoint.  (We could certainly combine them into one query to avoid a latency hop, but that would add some extra complexity.)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 20:06 UTC

To summarize:
* 47% in DB
* 32% in ORM
* 20% in regular Python
* 1% rounding error

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 20:06 UTC

The slower query here (against UserProfile) has a sane enough query plan.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 20:09 UTC

I'll wait for @Tim Abbott to advise on next steps.  I think we could micro-optimize in many directions here, but the only way to get more like a 10x speedup is to do more aggressive optimizations to defer any kind of work for users who are long-term idle.  This might be complicated by things that still need to happen in "real time" for long-term idle users.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-07 20:56 UTC

Well, it probably is worth refactoring to get the `long_term_idle` bit in that first query, since it sounds like that would save some resources.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-07 20:58 UTC

None of these things account for possible taking a full second to for the API request to send a message on chat.zulip.org.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-07 20:58 UTC

So we should probably do broader profiling for where the time is going.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 20:59 UTC

About half the time is in `do_send_messages`, which also increases for larger streams.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 21:00 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> Well, it probably is worth refactoring to get the `long_term_idle` bit in that first query, since it sounds like that would save some resources.

To be clear, the bit is already there in the first query.  The second query is shared by the non-stream codepath.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 21:11 UTC

`create_user_messages` accounts for 10% of the time, and it has some straightforward optimizations.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-07 21:19 UTC

I think it's worth doing a an actual profile for this with Python's cProfile to get a full understanding of where the time goes.  We have the infrastructure for that in `test-backend --profile`.  Maybe with a bit of cleanup you can make `zerver/lib/profile.py` work to do a flame graph profile.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-07 21:19 UTC

(This is also a code path where using line_profiler wouldn't be a bad idea, but that's more of a pain because you have to decorate every function)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 21:22 UTC

I've been print-debugging to re-familiarize myself with the code, and the results are pretty conclusive already.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 21:24 UTC

The vast majority of the time is spent in `get_recipient_info` and `do_send_messages`, and both functions are super sensitive to the number of users.  `get_recipient_info` is just slow because it's doing lots of work (and 47% of that is in the DB itself, so it's hard to get anything more than a 2x speedup without an architecture conversation).  And then `do_send_messages` spends a lot of time in `create_user_messages`, which inefficiently creates 8k lite objects, when it can be tuned pretty quickly by moving a conditional up in the loop.

I'll do a full profile soon, but I can pretty much guarantee that the solution here is to actually defer work for long-term-idle users more aggressively...

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 21:27 UTC

If long-term-idle users didn't have to get UM records for alert words and mentions in real time, and if we didn't have to account for them being in either `stream_push_user_ids` or `stream_email_user_ids` in real time, then we'd get an easy ~20x speedup in the bottlenecked code, which I believe is most of the code.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 21:27 UTC

(assuming 95% long term idle)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 21:28 UTC

So we might want to think about a little queue processor that checks every message to see if any of the long-term-idle users need action, and we can create their UserMessage record for alerts/messages and push out any email notifications.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-07 21:43 UTC

I'd like to avoid the queue processor complexity if we can, but that is certainly an option.  It's not clear to me that we that we can't use some sort of clever OR gate to only fetch data all for `long_term_idle` users who have a notifiable excuse.  I'd expect the union of:
* Users with at least one alert word (166 / 18K in CZO).
* Users who are configured to get email or push notifications for all stream messages or for this stream
* Users who are possibly mentioned by the message

... to have a very small overlap with `long_term_idle` users.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-07 21:44 UTC

(And for what we're optimizing here, basically the entire realm is subscribed to the stream).

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 21:50 UTC

The tricky part is getting the DB to detect alert words and mentions, which are now handled by the markdown processor.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-07 21:51 UTC

That's why my proposal is:
* For alert words, just return every user who's subscribed and has at least one alert word, regardless of whether it's in the message -- and then we can do the actual filtering in Python.
* For mentions, we already have `possibly_mentioned_user_ids` as a superset of who could be mentioned (and we'll need to assume everyone could have been mentioned if `possible_wildcard_mention`, but that's a 0.1% case so it's fine if it's slow).

**Steve Howell** · 2021-05-07 22:12 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-05-08 02:42 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-08 02:50 UTC

It looks like django-auth-ldap has new maintainers and thus is actively maintained again.  We should probably participate in https://github.com/django-auth-ldap/django-auth-ldap/pull/150#issuecomment-779222449 with the goal of no longer running a fork.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-08 02:51 UTC

Looks like no new features in https://github.com/django-auth-ldap/django-auth-ldap/blob/master/CHANGES.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-05-08 02:52 UTC

Why *does* that feature need to live in django-auth-ldap? (Cc @Mateusz Mandera.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-08 03:11 UTC

The `_LDAPConnectionMixIn` refactor might be the main reason: Having a way to use the LDAP connection without the rest of LDAPUser.  It seems reasonable for django-auth-ldap to offer a way to get at the LDAP connection you configured already with the library so that settings are in one place.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-05-08 03:15 UTC

Alright, but just making a separate LDAP connection seems preferable to living on a perpetual fork.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-08 03:18 UTC

Well, that's why a PR was submitted upstream.  I don't remember the context though.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-08 03:18 UTC

(Going AFK)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-08 05:52 UTC

Relatedly, I'm doing a chat.zulip.org deployment with #18400 so we can start burning that in.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2021-05-08 10:30 UTC

Yeah, there isn't a super great reason for that feature needing to be in django-auth-ldap. For us the motivation is that django-auth-ldap already takes care of the configuration and making of connections, and all our current ldap code is based on what the library provides, so it's clearly better if we can use its framework for "reverse email search" instead of having to mix in ldap code of another module.

I'm not sure how to convince upstream to merge though - because ultimately they're right in that this feature is kind of tangential to the "auth" purpose of the library. So either they consider this to be sufficiently useful to the users to warrant merging such a side-feature or they don't - and if they want to keep the scope of the project super focused on "django authentication", that's a perfectly good stance for them to take.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-08 15:55 UTC

I posted a comment on the django-auth-ldap thread.  It's up to the maintainers whether they want to provide said hook, but I think there's good reasons it might make sense to do so.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-08-23 23:05 UTC

@Mateusz Mandera If the django-auth-ldap proposal is not moving ahead upstream, then we should do whatever workaround we need to do in Zulip to get back on the upstream version, so we don’t remain on a perpetual fork.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2021-08-24 12:58 UTC

Thanks for the reminder! I think I'll give it one more try to revise the PR to be in line with what upstream would be willing to merge, before resorting to dropping the fork and using a workaround in our code

This will be converted to https://$MYDOMAIN/external_content/$hash/$digest, and it expects a running camo instance behind /external_content/, because CAMO_URI is set in /etc/zulip/settings.py.
But camo is not installed in the docker image: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/puppet/zulip/manifests/profile/docker.pp
In the standalone profile, it is installed: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/puppet/zulip/manifests/profile/standalone.pp
If I manually add that include statement to the docker profile, and rerun puppet, than camo will be installed in the zulip container.
But requests to /external_content/ still fail, because camo listens on [::1]:9292 by default and not 127.0.0.1:9292, so I changed the nginx upstream from 127.0.0.1 to localhost in /etc/nginx/zulip-include/upstreams, see also https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/master/puppet/zulip/files/nginx/zulip-include-frontend/upstreams
Then requests to camo from outside happens, but camo just answers with "Not Found" (literal string). Enabled debugging on camo, and it reports a checksum mismatch.... Now I need your help.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-19 01:22 UTC

@Rene Pasing thanks for the report!  I think the bug here is probably the camo is not installed in `docker-zulip`; ideally, we'd have that running in all production installations.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-19 01:22 UTC

But probably a short-term workaround is to disable it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-19 01:23 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-19 01:24 UTC

**Alex Vandiver** · 2021-05-21 21:01 UTC

This doesn't work out-of-the-box because camo is expecting to run as its own service, and Docker only runs supervisor services.

So we'd need to write a supervisor file for camo, and install `/etc/nginx/zulip-include/app.d/camo.conf` like `puppet/zulip/manifests/localhost_camo.pp` does.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-23 21:05 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-23 22:22 UTC

Currently, in message send events, we send the following data for users-
```python
        users = [
            dict(
                id=user_id,
                flags=user_flags.get(user_id, []),
                always_push_notify=(user_id in send_request.push_notify_user_ids),
                stream_push_notify=(user_id in send_request.stream_push_user_ids),

I feel the `always_push_notify`, `stream_push_notify` and `stream_email_notify` variables have slightly misleading names. At face value, they seem to answer the question "Should this message notify the user?" while, actually they are more about "*If* the message were to contain mentions/were a PM/etc, should it trigger a notification?" Avatars with EXIF orientation metadata are being rotated improperly on upload. See that it looks normal in some browsers, but rotated 90° *clockwise* in others—despite the fact that the image's "Orientation" in the metadata is `6`, which marks a 90° counterclockwise rotation. Then, on a recent dev server, comment out all of `exif_rotate`'s callsites and then upload the image as a user's avatar. In the browsers where it looked normal, it'll be 90° counterclockwise; in the browsers where it was rotated 90° clockwise, it'll look normal. Presumably the ones where it looks normal are the ones that handle the metadata appropriately, and other browsers will catch up in the (hopefully near) future.

We would like input as which is the best option.

We think there are three options:
- In `create_user` have `ext_auth_id` as a paramter e.g. `create_user(ext_auth_id={"ldap":  "..."})`
- In `create_user` have `ext_ldap_id` and `ext_saml_id` es separate string paramters
- Calling a seperate method to set the id.

- #16208

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-26 19:37 UTC

Good question!

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-26 19:38 UTC

I tend to prefer setting properties of the `UserProfile` object atomically with the creation of the object where possible, since that involves less thinking about possible race conditions where you get a failure partway through the process.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-26 19:39 UTC

I think the actual concern @Mateusz Mandera has here is that we want to manage the complexity of what we pass into the user creation functions, which is very reasonable.  It'd be OK to have a single parameter for the "External authentication ID" purpose, but not to have one per authentication backend, for example.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-26 19:41 UTC

There's sorta a related concern with what we want to do with the data model -- so maybe we should talk about that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-26 19:42 UTC

One model is a `user_profile.external_auth_permanent_id` + `user_profile.external_auth_backend` -- basically a single field with an ID + backend identifier.  This is simple and avoids one field per backend, but has the downside of limiting us to only one such unique ID per user, which may come to bite us down the line if we want to extend this feature down the line to associate e.g. your GitHub user ID with your Zulip account.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-26 19:45 UTC

Another model is a separate database table with `(zulip_user_id, external_permanent_id, external_backend)` tuples, which would probably work as well as the above and doesn't limit a user to a single associated backend.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-26 19:46 UTC

And then the other problem we need to solve is how to encode the `external_backend` part -- with most things it's not a big deal, but with SAML, the user can change the name for the backend from `saml:name1` to `saml:name2` in the configuration and then restart the server, so we'd need to think about how that should work (possibly just something to document that if you're using this feature, you need to do some manual work if you rename the backend, because probably that ~never happens in production anyway).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-26 19:48 UTC

If we're going with a separate database table, though, then Mateusz' proposal is right that we'll want to do the association operation outside `do_create_user`.  I think that might make sense anyway, since we may want to attach the association on every successful login as well.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-05-26 19:49 UTC

We should also look at whether python-social-auth has a table for this purpose that we can just reuse for everything but LDAP.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2021-06-09 12:37 UTC

1. `associate_user` is a function for including in the pipeline - which means that it doesn't seem usable for us directly, since what we have in `SOCIAL_AUTH_PIPELINE` is very custom-built and won't directly integrate well with it - but I imagine we might end up writing our own (similar) version of the function and adding it to the pipelin.
2. `social_auth_usersocialauth` (https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-app-django/blob/master/social_django/models.py#L65 is the model) also seems like something that we'll need to customize rather than be able to re-use directly exactly because we need to support multiple organizations. And this table and the related code make the assumption that a `(uid, provider)` pair uniquely identifies a `UserProfile`, which won't be true. E.g.
https://github.com/python-social-auth/social-app-django/blob/master/social_django/storage.py#L108
```
    @classmethod
    def get_social_auth(cls, provider, uid):
        if not isinstance(uid, str):
            uid = str(uid)
        try:
            return cls.objects.get(provider=provider, uid=uid)
        except cls.DoesNotExist:
            return None
```

We could do something weird like appending the subdomain to the backend name when creating the  `provider` string, but I think we may be better off just making our own, slightly tweaked to support subdomains, model and `associate_user` etc. code

**Robert (ro-i)** · 2021-07-01 20:08 UTC

Hi :)
I think that @Felix (strifel) and I need some more clarification in order to be able to finally proceed with this issue.

To start with, I think we need to clarify the flow of authentication using the new `ext_auth_id`. Some points:
- `ext_auth_id` is the configurable parameter of an appropriate authentication system used for this realm. There may also be other authentication systems for this realm which may or may not use an own `ext_auth_id` parameter.
- This parameter will be asked for (as "username") upon login in our login mask. If the authentication method uses an external login page (e.g. SAML), we need to obtain the `ext_auth_id` parameter from them, so we need to have appropriate fields in the config. Which is already the case for SAML, see `attr_user_permanent_id`.
  - ~~Problem 1: What if someone made a mistake and the parameter is not unique? We need a fallback for this case, probably the good old email address.~~ Edit: That does not make sense, sorry :)
  - Problem 2: What if the realm uses multiple authentication systems? I think that should not be a problem. We can use the `ext_auth_id` parameter where possible and the email address otherwise, as usual.
- There is a new column `ext_auth_id` in the `userprofile` table of Zulip's database. There, the `ext_auth_id` parameter is associated with the realm and the authentication provider.
- Ok, now a **new** user **registers** to our realm.
  1. We check whether they use one of the authentication systems for which we provide the `ext_auth_id` facility.
    a) If not, they can register as usual, i.e. we use the email address as identifier. Problem: What if this user later decides to login using another authentication method where we **would** consider `ext_auth_id`? The value of `ext_auth_id` in the database would be `null` for this user, so that is not possible without further ado. But we could add an option to the user settings where the users can specify their usernames (= `ext_auth_id` values) for all authentication systems that would require them. Just as it is possible to change the email address (= the "`ext_auth_id`" we used so far) in the settings.
    b) If yes, let's move on...
  2. We determine the `ext_auth_id` value for this user either using the username field of our login mask or by getting the parameter from the authentication provider if an external login page is used for this authentication method.
       If this `ext_auth_id` is already in use, we show an error message to the user and ask them to contact the admin.
  3. Otherwise, we continue by adding the `ext_auth_id` value to the database, associated with both the realm and the authentication provider.
- Now, an **existing** user **logs in**.
  1. They enter the `ext_auth_id` parameter as username into our login mask or we get the parameter from the authentication provider. Now, we check whether this `ext_auth_id` is in our database, associated with this realm and this authentication provider. If that is the case, we found the user. If not, we deny access.

Is this correct as a rough overview?

Why would you want to add the `external_auth_id` value upon **login**? We need to match a user to their `external_auth_id` (per provider) in a reliable way, so either
1. upon registration. Let's assume a user registers using SAML. Assume we use the Shibboleth attribute `eduPersonTargetedID` (see [german docs](https://doku.tid.dfn.de/de:common_attributes#a11)) as unique identifier `external_auth_id`. So the user gets forwarded to the external login page of the authentication provider. The user enters their credentials. Now, the user is identified unambiguously. We do not care how the authentication provider identified the user unambiguously, but now we can get the `eduPersonTargetedID` from the Identity Provider. From now on, the user can be identified by this parameter in our DB. In case the user likes to use another authentication method, the user need to give us their `external_auth_id` parameter for this authentication system **in advance**. See case 2.
2. using the user settings. Assume the user registered using SAML. Now, the user likes to use email for login, too. For email, the unique identifier is the email-address. So the user has to specify their email address in the user settings in order to associate the email account which the user wants to use for the login with the existing Zulip account.

So as far as I understand now, the flow would be as follows:
- The user is internally identified using their email address.
- This email address is used for all authentication methods.
- If an authentication method is used where the email is not the actual unique identifier (LDAP, SAML):

  2. We fetch the `external_auth_id` attribute from the account with the given email address. From now on, we will also be able to identify this user with this attribute (for this authentication method).
  3. If the user logs in using an authentication method for which we use an `external_auth_id` attribute, we only use this attribute to identify the user **but** we additionally update their email in our db.

## get_active_presence_idle_user_ids

*2021-06-08 to 2021-06-17 · 45 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/get_active_presence_idle_user_ids/with/1203823)*

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-08 15:39 UTC

I think I found a bug with per-stream email/push notifications. If you've turned **on** push notifications for **a stream**, and someone sends a message to that stream, you won't get a notification if you're idle.
This is because of how `get_active_presence_idle_user_ids` works.
```py
def get_active_presence_idle_user_ids(...):
    """
    Given a list of active_user_ids, we build up a subset
    of those users who fit these criteria:

        * They are likely to need notifications (either due
          to mentions, alert words, or being PM'ed).
        * They are no longer "present" according to the
          UserPresence table.
    """
    user_ids = set()
    for user_id in active_user_ids:
        flags = user_flags.get(user_id, [])
        mentioned = "mentioned" in flags or "wildcard_mentioned" in flags
        private_message = is_pm and user_id != sender_id
        alerted = "has_alert_word" in flags
        if mentioned or private_message or alerted:
            user_ids.add(user_id)

    return filter_presence_idle_user_ids(user_ids)
```

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-08 15:40 UTC

If the message doesn't mention you and isn't a private message, you won't be in the `presence_idle_user_ids` set, even if you are idle:
```py
    presence_idle_user_ids = get_active_presence_idle_user_ids(
        realm=sender.realm,
        sender_id=sender.id,
        message_type=message_type,
        active_user_ids=send_request.active_user_ids,
        user_flags=user_flags,
    )
```

and replacing it with a single function call, one which we can also rely on when enqueueing the task.

In order to have a shot at working correctly, one thing that function will probably need is to be passed some indication of what kind of notification this is, so that it can look at the right preference :wink: . I.e., whether it's a PM or @-mention notification on one hand, or a stream notification on the other.

**Greg Price** · 2021-06-15 07:41 UTC

That could be a boolean (with PMs and @-mentions lumped together), or maybe ideally it would be an enum with values like "PM", "@-mention", "plain stream message (i.e. with no @-mention)". There's already a notion like that in some places in `zerver/lib/push_notifications.py` -- it shows up in the API of what's sent to the device.

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-15 08:11 UTC

> Alternatively I wouldn't really be unhappy with checking the preferences twice. But -- if we're going to do that, we should arrange things so that there's only one piece of *code* that checks the preferences, and we're just calling that same code in two places. I.e., we should factor it out into an appropriate function.

Not sure how we could do that, since the enqueueing code gets its data from the message send function, which intentionally uses bulk database queries to get the data for efficiency. (And we'd want the settings data for only the single user in the queue consumer)

**Greg Price** · 2021-06-15 08:35 UTC

Hmm. Well, at a minimum if there are two implementations, I'd want it to be easy to compare them. E.g. having them right next to each other, plus having their structure be as similar as possible in the circumstances.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-16 00:56 UTC

Yeah, I think I'd like to keep the 2-check model, and agree that's a good model.  If necessary, two functions that sit next to each other and have a shared test suite (which it calls both functions with the same data setup and compares the results) is a great way to make sure they agree.

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-17 14:28 UTC

I've added a commit to #18853 which fixes the bug in the OP about `get_active_presence_idle_user_ids`.
What remains is having `maybe_enqueue_notifications` (and the like) to take in this new dataclass instead of the individual fields.

*2021-06-09 to 2021-06-11 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Message.20send.20event.20user.20data/with/1205130)*

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-09 15:46 UTC

@Ryan Rehman @Steve Howell (showell) @Tim Abbott After #**backend>get_active_presence_idle_user_ids**, I do think we could benefit from introducing a `TypedDict` or `dataclass` to hold together the user data sent in message events:
```py
        users = [
            dict(
                id=user_id,
                flags=user_flags.get(user_id, []),
                online_push_enabled=(user_id in send_request.online_push_user_ids),
                stream_push_notify=(user_id in send_request.stream_push_user_ids),
                stream_email_notify=(user_id in send_request.stream_email_user_ids),
                wildcard_mention_notify=(user_id in send_request.wildcard_mention_user_ids),

            )
            for user_id in user_list
        ]

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-09 15:47 UTC

I thought about how we could do that, and the only blocker seems to be that we don't properly calculate the `mentioned` and `wildcard_mention_notify` fields until `event_queue`
Here's a snippet from `event_queue.py/process_message_event`
```py
mentioned = "mentioned" in flags and "read" not in flags
wildcard_mention_notify = (
    user_data.get("wildcard_mention_notify", False)
    and "wildcard_mentioned" in flags
    and "read" not in flags
)
```

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-09 15:48 UTC

Although we could calculate these in `do_send_messages`, and then create a `TypedDict` like:
```py
class MessageSendEventUserData(TypedDict):
    id: int
    flags: List[str]
    mentioned: bool
    online_push_enabled: bool
    stream_push_notify: bool
    stream_email_notify: bool
    wildcard_mention_notify: bool
    sender_is_muted: bool
```

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-09 15:49 UTC

...and we could use this new type in:
- The `send_event` call in `do_send_messages`
- A subset of arguments to `maybe_enqueue_notifications`
- The new function proposed in #**backend>get_active_presence_idle_user_ids**

Thoughts?

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-09 16:00 UTC

(replying to Abhijeet Bodas)
> Here's a snippet from `event_queue.py/process_message_event` ```py mentioned = "mentioned" in flags and "read" not in flags wildcard_mention_notify = ( user_data.get("wildcard_mention_notify", False) and "wildcard_mentioned" in flags and "read" not in flags ) ```
(One thing I did not understand about this is that, why do we need to look at the `read` flags here? We do that downstream in `lib/email_notifications.py` and `/lib/push_notifications.py` too.)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-09 16:15 UTC

I think it’s just that if the user has read the message, they don’t need to be notified?

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-09 16:18 UTC

Yeah, I was thinking whether we could centralise that logic?

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-09 16:45 UTC

I don’t know why we couldn’t.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-09 20:19 UTC

I think that structure may be historical, from before we had a delay in email/push notifications that could provide time for a user to read the message (and thus added a check in those places).  Since generally the only user who will have a message marked as read at this stage is the sender, in practice the function of that logic is to save a bit of work for messages you yourself sent -- without that check, a wildcard mention you send will waste a tiny bit of CPU time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-09 20:21 UTC

So yeah, I think we can safely just remove that check.  I think there's another copy in `missedmessage_hook` that is similarly useless (it runs later, but there is no refetch of the data, so it's just looking at a stale `read` flag value).

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-06-11 14:36 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> So yeah, I think we can safely just remove that check. I think there's another copy in `missedmessage_hook` that is similarly useless (it runs later, but there is no refetch of the data, so it's just looking at a stale `read` flag value).
I opened #18803 in that direction.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-17 16:53 UTC

@Riken Shah (Riken-Shah) I think it's a good question about the semantics of the feature whether we need these 3 parameters.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-17 16:54 UTC

The 3-field model (or really, the 2 fields `emoji_code` and `reaction_type`) are required to unique encode an emoji in a permanent fashion, supporting both custom emoji and unicode emoji.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-17 16:56 UTC

If we do an `emoji_name` as the encoding, we create two potential issues:
* If we adjust the emoji data set, and that emoji name no longer exists in the emoji names dataset, now we have a somewhat corrupted data structure.
* We need to do a lookup in our emoji data set in order to communicate to clients what to do with the emoji name.  

It would also mean that if someone uploaded a new custom emoji with that name, that'd change the glyph, but that's probably OK.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-17 16:57 UTC

That first issue seems like a good reason to copy the design we have for reactions -- we don't want to have to deal with error handling logic of this form whenever we make an adjustment to the emoji data set.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-17 16:59 UTC

I think that refactoring looks essentially correct; we should double-check that it doesn't result in two `UserProfile` fields being on `UserStatus`, but I think the subclassing will do the right thing.

The other thing we may need is decision of what to set as the "current: emoji for existing UserStatus elements.

**Riken Shah** · 2021-06-22 18:44 UTC

> The other thing we may need is the decision of what to set as the "current: emoji for existing UserStatus elements.

I think so setting the empty string ( for `emoji_name` and `emoji_code`) for existing `UserStatus` elements seems like the right choice as it would be like in the "unset state". Also, we are using the same approach for the `status_text` i.e. When we remove the `status_text` we set it to an empty string instead of deleting the element.  



I have opened [WIP PR](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/18955)  implementing the above approach, It'd be great if it can get a review.

Also, we have already set the default for [`reaction_type` (i.e. `unicode_emoji`)](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/85e19b2bde72524cbb3b20272037205d1d3162bb/zerver/models.py#L2436) so I decided to go with it instead of overriding its default value with the empty string.

## dataclasses for queue workers

*2021-06-22 to 2021-06-23 · 40 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/dataclasses.20for.20queue.20workers/with/1216099)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-22 18:05 UTC

I noted in https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/18950/files#r656462275 that we don't have a particularly satisfying registry of types for our queue workers in `zerver/worker/queue_processors.py`.  I'd like to start a discussion about adding one.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-22 18:06 UTC

On theory is we make a `zerver/worker/queue_types.py` library, that would declare a `dataclass` for each queue worker, that would be imported and used in `actions.py` and `queue_processors.py`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-22 18:06 UTC

(And I guess the `deferred_work` queue processor would be a Union type of these, and its processor might have various `assert isinstance()` logic?).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-22 18:07 UTC

We may want to do something similar for the events themselves, but I want to mostly consider that out of scope, mostly because the interfaces for our normal queue workers are largely simple, and thus it's much more of a quick migration if we can decide what we want to do.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-22 18:09 UTC

And then I can imagine that when we change an event format, we might preserve a `ZulipLegacyEventFoo` data type that's the pre-migration type, and the queue worker can accept a `Union` of the legacy and current types, so that type-checking helps us verify that we're handling legacy events that might be in a queue when we upgrade.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-22 18:09 UTC

Thoughts?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-22 18:11 UTC

For naming, perhaps `UserActivityWorkerEvent` would be the event type for queue events going into `UserActivityWorker`, and `UserActivityWorkerLegacyZulip4Event` could be a naming scheme for legacy formats?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-06-22 18:54 UTC

I don’t see the migration concern. Dataclasses are a Python-specific in-memory concept. They need to be serialized for communication, and there’s no reason not to serialize them to the same JSON format we already have. I think the [dataclasses-json library](https://pypi.org/project/dataclasses-json/) is an easy way to set up that serialization.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-22 19:24 UTC

I don't think there's any migration concern for switching those types to data classes; we already have `queue_json_publish` functions that take a dictionary and pass it through as the API, so the simplest change from what we have currently would be to just have the `dataclass` call `to_dict` type methods; and then I imagine things would be cleaner further moving to `dataclasses-json`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-22 19:26 UTC

The migration consideration is not for switching to dataclasses, but instead the long-term codebase consideration of how to handle events already in the queue when we upgrade to a new Zulip version in general that has, e.g., added or adjusted the fields in one of these interfaces (and we want to not drop the those events already in the queue).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-22 19:27 UTC

(Where it'd be nice to have a less manual verification process than what we do now, which involves manual testing and maybe some automated tests, but does not benefit from any type-checking)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-06-22 19:37 UTC

I have wondered whether we actually get a scaling benefit from RabbitMQ, or whether we could move most or all of our queues to the database where we could apply our normal migration system to them.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-06-22 19:52 UTC

(The answer to that question may have changed since the addition of PostgreSQL 9.5’s [`SELECT FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/9.5/sql-select.html#SQL-FOR-UPDATE-SHARE), which greatly [simplifies](https://www.2ndquadrant.com/en/blog/what-is-select-skip-locked-for-in-postgresql-9-5/) building correct work queues.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-23 18:55 UTC

That's a good question, that I don't know the answer to.  Certainly a few of our queue workers exist because database writes were 5-10x more expensive than RabbitMQ writes at the time (E.g. IIRC, `user_activity`, `user_activity_interval`  and `user_presence` exist mostly for that purpose).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-23 18:57 UTC

I don't think I'd expect RabbitMQ to have a material scaling benefit over Postgres necessarily (though latency is certainly a consideration).

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-23 18:58 UTC

I would love to get rid of RabbitMQ.  I suspect it would simplify efforts to do more asynchronous/parallel processing of queue requests.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-23 18:58 UTC

(That's basically also the reason we use redis for rate-limiting rather than Postgres; better latency for cheap queries in the hot path for endpoints that we want to return in just a few milliseconds).

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-23 19:01 UTC

For queue processes aren’t we more concerned about throughput than latency? (Not suggesting we get better throughput with DB solution)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-06-23 19:10 UTC

Another advantage of putting the queues in the database would be that we could create jobs transactionally with other database changes.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-06-23 19:11 UTC

And the development environment wouldn’t constantly consume 5% CPU while not even running anything.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-23 20:40 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell (showell))
> For queue processes aren’t we more concerned about throughput than latency? (Not suggesting we get better throughput with DB solution)
For these queue processors, we're concerned about latency for the HTTP request that generates the enqueued event, not latency for the queue processor doing the work, if that makes sense.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-23 20:43 UTC

https://github.com/SweetProcess/django-pg-queue looks like a library we could use if we wanted to go in this direction.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-23 20:44 UTC

In general I would be very happy to be able to remove `rabbitmq` as a dependency, in that it's operationally just an unpleasant service to run/debug (it mostly just works, but when it doesn't, it is very hard to figure out why).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-23 20:47 UTC

(There's also e.g. [celery](https://docs.celeryproject.org/en/stable/getting-started/introduction.html) as a third-party thing for queue workers with various properties, though I don't think it supports postgres as its data store, it can do `redis`).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-23 20:47 UTC

That said, our choice of RabbitMQ was primarily motivated by the Tornado use case; our other queue workers are a very much secondary application for that service.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-23 20:48 UTC

So we'd need a replacement for `RabbitMQ` for that purpose in order to stop running RabbitMQ in production.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-06-23 20:48 UTC

django-pg-queue looks like it’s doing the right thing from a cursory scan.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-23 20:55 UTC

Ah, for the latency of putting  the request into the DB, I assume that’s mostly negligible.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-23 21:00 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell (showell))
> Ah, for the latency of putting the request into the DB, I assume that’s mostly negligible.
My last profiling of this was a couple years ago, but my vague recollection is that the difference was a few milliseconds vs. a few hundred microseconds, which is important at least for `GET /events` scalability.  It is unclear to me whether that difference is important for other endpoints.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-23 21:02 UTC

But that's certainly something we can measure.  Do you think if we were able to migrate all but 2 queue processors to something like `django-pg-queue`, but found it difficult to migrate 1-2 queue processors and/or Tornado, so we'd still be stuck with RabbitMQ, that such a state would be an improvement?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-23 21:02 UTC

(I think that determines to what extent we should focus our attention on the hardest migration or the easiest for investigating that direction)

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-23 21:02 UTC

When does /events lead to any deferred work?

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-23 21:04 UTC

Oh nvm

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-06-23 21:04 UTC

I don’t think there’s a theoretical barrier to migrating Tornado, though there may be some implementation limitation.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-23 21:05 UTC

I think it’s worthwhile to proceed here.

**Steve Howell** · 2021-06-23 21:07 UTC

If we can migrate most things to the DB except Tornado interactions, I think that could set the stage to use Celery for super simple problems.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-23 21:49 UTC

I don't think we should be excited about the idea of using a mix of Celery and a database-powered deferred work queue library; ideally we want to have just one to do X that satisfies the needs for all of things that need queues, not N different systems.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-23 21:51 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-06-23 21:51 UTC

I think it probably doesn't really change the fact that it'd be nice to have type-checking of our objects, since that's a property we'd want to preserve with how we use any of these alternative approaches (basically a common type for what we put into the queue and what we pull out of it). ## furl

*2021-07-01 to 2021-07-02 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/furl/with/1223624)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2021-07-01 14:55 UTC

Do we want to consider migrating to `furl` https://github.com/gruns/furl for doing URL manipulations? As the project descriptions says:
> Python's standard urllib and urlparse modules provide a number of URL related functions, but using these functions to perform common URL operations proves tedious. Furl makes parsing and manipulating URLs easy.

This has popped up in https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/19063#discussion_r661725931 but we have a bunch more places where we manipulate URLs using `urllib.parse` which does tend to be very fiddly and sometimes just doesn't support some operations one would want to do etc. So we could potentially benefit from `furl` by getting more readable code and just making it generally more straightforward to manipulate URLs.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-01 18:27 UTC

Hmm, it does look to be more pleasant than urllib after a quick skim of the documentation.  I'd appreciate other folks looking at it a bit more closely.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-07-02 00:42 UTC

I would rather use the standard library unless it’s actually broken. I don’t think the convenience advantage of allowing you be sloppy with slashes is actually an advantage.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2021-07-02 13:19 UTC

I don't think it's about being sloppy with slashes (in this particular example discussed) - it's about having a function for expressing "add this to the path in the URL" - and `urljoin` isn't quite that (exactly because of the subtleties around `/` positioning) thuogh can be used for doing this task. Aside of this situation, it just seems like a friendlier and easier to use library - e.g. less verbose without all the `urlparse` and `urlunparse`ing back and forth.

It also allows doing more things - manipulating parts of the `netloc` is what comes to my mind. 
```
In [7]: p = urllib.parse.urlparse("https://google.com:20/path/x/?x=5")
In [14]: p.port
Out[14]: 20

In [15]: p._replace(port=21)
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
ValueError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
<ipython-input-15-4a9934a714be> in <module>
----> 1 p._replace(port=21)

<string> in _replace(_self, **kwds)

ValueError: Got unexpected field names: ['port']
```

Compared to:
```
>>> furl.furl("https://google.com:20/path/x/?x=5")
furl('https://google.com:20/path/x/?x=5')
>>> f = furl.furl("https://google.com:20/path/x/?x=5")
>>> f
furl('https://google.com:20/path/x/?x=5')
>>> f.port = 11
>>> f.url
'https://google.com:11/path/x/?x=5'
```

or even more control:
```
>>> f = furl.furl("https://user:pass@google.com:20/path/x/?x=5")
>>> f.username = "user2"
>>> f.url
'https://user2:pass@google.com:20/path/x/?x=5'
>>> f.username = None
>>> f.password = None
>>> f.url
'https://google.com:20/path/x/?x=5'
```

It's possible we don't need to do such things anywhere right now though.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2021-07-02 13:21 UTC

The main benefit could be just lowering the amount of time and effort needing to be spent figuring out `urllib.parse` for less experienced contributors - because arguably the library is quite painful at first contact - at least it was for me

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-02 18:41 UTC

I think we don't have enough total URL manipulation in the codebase that it'd be worth a migration for that reason.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-07-02 20:39 UTC

I also don’t like how `furl` is mutable. The global confusion caused by accidental mutation is much more confusing than the local confusion of learning a standard API.

Hmm, quoting [from this Django ticket](https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/22431#comment:1):

The ticket was [later fixed](https://github.com/django/django/commit/fcd08c175787e909b3eb98f756317a07741c48dd), by adding checks for deferred database constraints at the *end of the test*.

I thought it was unncessary because only the `.save()` will alter the database state, and a single insert query will by itself be ato …

There's still a benefit to using a transaction even if we only have a single write, since it ensures the database gives us a consistent view for the multiple independent fetches one might do.

That said, since we're not using `select_for_update`, it doesn't do any locking (and we already have a lock for the process itself anyway), so I think I agree that transaction is not useful.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-22 19:38 UTC

I think it's potentially OK to not have test coverage for an exception case of this form if we can't efficiently figure out how to write a test for it; I'd just include a comment for why next to the `nocoverage` comment.

## transaction.atomic

*2021-07-15 to 2026-07-31 · 99 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/transaction.2Eatomic/with/1231749)*

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-07-15 13:08 UTC

Regarding #18559, I'm don't understand when to use `savepoint=False` or `durable=True`.
How does `savepoint=False` help us deal with nested transactions? And why are nested transactions undesirable at all?

If we wanted to absolutely avoid nested transactions, we could put `durable=True` everywhere, but:
> django.test.TestCase disables the durability check to allow testing durable atomic blocks in a transaction for performance reasons.
so it would be difficult to verify it in tests, and it could raise `RunTimeErrors` in production if used incorrectly.

**Abhijeet Bodas** · 2021-07-15 13:08 UTC

Pasting the relevant docs here for reference, from https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/3.2/topics/db/transactions/

> It is sometimes useful to ensure an atomic block is always the outermost atomic block, ensuring that any database changes are committed when the block is exited without errors. This is known as durability and can be achieved by setting durable=True. If the atomic block is nested within another it ra …

> Under the hood, Django’s transaction management code: * opens a transaction when entering the outermost atomic block; * creates a savepoint when entering an inner atomic block; * releases or rolls back to the savepoint when exiting an inner block; * commits or rolls back the transaction when exiting …

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-15 15:45 UTC

Hmm, I think we probably just want `savepoint=False` everywhere, since we avoid having long transactions and it's easier to reason without them (And I think savepoints confuse our vision of using `SELECT FOR UPDATE` and `on_commit` hooks predictably).

Structurally, when we're using `atomic`, we want to ensure that the block of code is executed transactionally, whether the code path is called from an outer transaction or not, because we want to be able to reason about the code under the assumption that certain classes of issues with a failure causing an invariant violation are impossible because of the transaction.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-15 15:46 UTC

That said, I think the Django design intent is that we use `durable=True` whenever we have an atomic block that we want to ensure is never called from within another atomic block.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-15 15:46 UTC

So if we have a specific atomic block where we think it'd be a bug to have the transaction be longer-lived than that block, we'd want to use it there.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-07-15 18:44 UTC

This reminded me that the new `durable=True` flag would have caught the `do_send_messages` bug we fixed in #16507 ([previous discussion](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/3-backend/topic/do_send_messages/near/1031559)), so I tried adding it there and found another bug in topic resolution: #19265.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-15 19:59 UTC

Would `savepoint=False` on that atomic block prevent that from being a bug?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-07-15 19:59 UTC

No.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-15 20:01 UTC

Can you explain why that would be a bug if we always used `savepoint=False`?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-07-15 20:03 UTC

The only effect of `savepoint=False` is that it breaks exception handling in the case of

```python
with transaction.atomic():
    db_update_1()
    try:
        with transaction.atomic(savepoint=False):
            db_update_2()
            raise Exception:
    except Exception:
        # here db_update_2() is still incorrectly visible
        raise
# here both updates have been rolled back anyway
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-07-15 20:05 UTC

It does not cause your partially completed atomic transaction to remain permanently visible after an exception. That would defeat the entire point of transactions.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-15 20:06 UTC

Well, it also avoids creating postgres subtransactions, which are not postgres' best feature.  See e.g. https://buttondown.email/nelhage/archive/22ab771c-25b4-4cd9-b316-31a86f737acc.

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-15 20:09 UTC

Looking at the specific case flagged by `durable=True`: We have an atomic block for sending a message, and one for message editing. In the "resolve topic" case where topic editing triggers a new message being sent, to what extent would be unhappy with a world where a single atomic block surrounds both moving the topic and sending the message?

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-15 20:10 UTC

(We'd want to do `transaction.on_commit` for the `send_event` side effects for both code paths, so I guess not doing that is a bug, though one present for most of our `send_event` calls).

**Tim Abbott** · 2021-07-15 20:12 UTC

I guess I used `durable=True` for both of these because they're things that I expect us to definitely not call within another transaction; I'm kinda thinking we want the rule to be that we use `savepoint=False` only for things like sending a message that we expect to potentially be nested.  But probably we don't want any `transaction.atomic` calls in `actions.py` that don't specify one or the other.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2021-07-20 01:18 UTC

After experimenting with this more, I think wrapping our `post_save` flush callbacks in `on_commit` is not quite the right strategy. Many of our tests trigger a `save`, causing caches to be flushed, and then try to read the same values from the cache shortly thereafter. Delaying the flush leads to stale values being read. I have no reason to think this couldn’t happen in our real code too.

Perhaps our cache library itself should, during database transactions, buffer all `cache_set` and `cache_delete` operations to thread-local memory, where they can be used to satisfy `cache_get` operations from within the transaction, until the transaction commits and the operations are propagated to memcached.

> After experimenting with this more, I think wrapping our `post_save` flush callbacks in `on_commit` is not quite the right strategy.
