**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-08 01:38 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> All topics could be a lot of data in realms that have existed for years. Of course, not all topics will be in the topics table yet, but if we ever want that to change, we should make sure our APIs are sufficiently lazy.

One thing that we need to be really careful about with a vision of having a topics table appear in the API is that it creates a lot of additional permissions issues. While I think we can reasonably set the rule that if you have access to a stream, you get to see the names of pinned topics regardless of whether it has shared history (Or maybe better would be to just not allow pinned topics in streams without shared history, since it's sorta an incoherent concept in that new users won't be able to see anything in the topic). As a result, for pinned topics in particular, we can potentially avoid needing to deal with some of the extra complexity involved in security around topics in streams without shared history.

More generally the types of permissions/security issues we're talking about here become dramatically more complex if we're trying to have a shared `topic` data structure, since at present access to see which topics exist in a stream without shared history is mediated entirely by whether you can access any messages with said topic.

This is one of several subtle technical reasons why I am still not convinced it would make our life any easier to have a topics table that aims to contain all topics (in addition to being a huge pain to migrate). Other big concerns are the risk of creating a performance leak where it becomes impossible to load large organizations with years of history efficiently, the fact that we have carefully considered product design around topics being case-preserving but insensitive that would become more awkward to manage and the concern that we'd be spending many hours to just rearrange complexity around topic edit, but not end up with any less complexity at the end.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-08 01:39 UTC

If we discard the design goal of having our `topics` data be something we could readily extend to sending you every topic that's every happened in the organization on page load, and instead think of it as a "special topic settings" object, then I think that does help manage complexity for this conversation.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-08 01:41 UTC

I think the designs of having `topics` be a separate top-level object vs. a key inside `subscriptions[stream_id]` are essentially isomorphic; we could even have `post_process_state` convert from one format to the other if we wanted our `events.py` system to structurally avoid needing security code when removing a user from the stream to remove their `topics` data from the state object.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-08 01:42 UTC

The reason I preferred a separate `topics` object between these two structurally equivalent shapes is mainly that it felt to me that it'd be a real tangle to design the event if we were to put them inside the subscription objects.

**Steve Howell** · 2022-03-08 14:08 UTC

## splitting actions.py

*2022-03-01 to 2022-04-15 · 58 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/splitting.20actions.2Epy/with/1337373)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-01 22:50 UTC

We should consider splitting `actions.py` into multiple files. Since we moved to Black for code formatting, it's been pretty annoying to work in that file because it takes several seconds to run the code formatter on it (3-4s even on fast machines); and in any case an 8.7K line file can be unwieldy.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-01 22:50 UTC

(Thanks to @Evy Kassirer for bringing this up to me).

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-01 22:52 UTC

There's a few considerations that we should be mindful of when doing this sort of project:
* Doing this just before a major release is a good idea because a lot of bugs that we would want to backport would touch this file.
* Doing this will likely make a large number of open stale PRs have major merge conflicts. This is kinda unavoidable but I guess argues for trying to not need to move everything multiple times.
* We should give some thought to __how__ we want to split it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-01 22:52 UTC

One question is whether we like the name `actions`; the most natural split in some sense would be a directory, e.g. we'd create `zerver/actions/message_edit.py` and similar files.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-03-01 22:53 UTC

What's our delineation of what's `zerver/actions/` vs `zerver/lib/` ?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-01 22:54 UTC

I feel like even though `actions` is a name that was chosen in like 2012, it's probably still a decent description of the category of things we have there -- structurally, it's the functions that user-level code (views, etc.) is supposed to call to change the database in a way that correctly live-updates clients.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-01 22:55 UTC

I suppose there is still a question of whether we think it's worth having a separate file for that purpose, or we should instead be e.g. just moving the user groups related actions functions into e.g. `zerver/lib/user_groups.py`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-01 22:57 UTC

The original motivation for having a single file for this purpose was basically to help make it easier to use the codebase correctly; e.g. if you're writing a new view or a test or whatever, and you need to change a user group thing, you should just look at the actions function for user groups.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-03-01 22:57 UTC

It feels like we're trying to make a views -> actions -> lib hierarchy.  I think it's clear what's a view, but in the hypothetical world where we enforced that libs couldn't import actions, that would pretty much drive everyone to write libs.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-03-01 22:58 UTC

But I do like the concept that we make clear which are the higher-level abstractions that we point people toward.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-01 23:00 UTC

For example, for user groups, we have this function in `zerver/lib`:
```
def create_user_group(                                                                                   
    name: str,                                                                                           
    members: List[UserProfile],                                                                          
    realm: Realm,                                                                                        
    *,                                                                                                   
    description: str = "",                                                                               
    is_system_group: bool = False,                                                                       
) -> UserGroup:                                                                                          
    with transaction.atomic():                                                                           
        user_group = UserGroup.objects.create(                                                           
            name=name, realm=realm, description=description, is_system_group=is_system_group             
        )                                                                                                
        UserGroupMembership.objects.bulk_create(                                                         
            UserGroupMembership(user_profile=member, user_group=user_group) for member in members        
        )                                                                                                
        return user_group                                                                                
```

and then this function in `actions.py`:
```
def do_send_create_user_group_event(user_group: UserGroup, members: List[UserProfile]) -> None:          
    event = dict(                                                                                        
        type="user_group",                                                                               
        op="add",                                                                                        
        group=dict(                                                                                      
            name=user_group.name,                                                                        
            members=[member.id for member in members],                                                   
            description=user_group.description,                                                          
            id=user_group.id,                                                                            
            is_system_group=user_group.is_system_group,                                                  
        ),                                                                                               
    )                                                                                                    
    send_event(user_group.realm, event, active_user_ids(user_group.realm_id))                            
                                                                                                         
                                                                                                         
def check_add_user_group(                                                                                
    realm: Realm, name: str, initial_members: List[UserProfile], description: str                        
) -> None:                                                                                               
    try:                                                                                                 
        user_group = create_user_group(name, initial_members, realm, description=description)            
        do_send_create_user_group_event(user_group, initial_members)                                     
    except django.db.utils.IntegrityError:                                                               
        raise JsonableError(_("User group '{}' already exists.").format(name))                           
```

So a problem statement is avoiding folks new to the codebase choosing which of those to call at random. We address that right now through two conventions: The `do_` and `check_` naming conventions for Actions, and having them live in that file.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-03-30 23:59 UTC

For the Black and Prettier reformattings, there was a proposal to handle them incrementally, formatting a few files at a time. We rejected that approach because:

* It would not have added information to the history: you can always view part of a large diff by file after the fact if that’s what you want.
* It would not have made manual conflict resolution any easier: you get exactly the same conflicts either way.
* It would have significantly complicated the automatic tool to rebase branches across the reformatting.
* Until we were able to enforce the formatting as a linter, intervening commits might have regressed the formatting in already-formatted files.

None of those rationales apply to this migration.

* The history will make it clear exactly where each piece of `actions.py` was moved to and where each `actions/foo.py` was moved from. (This would be partially computable by `git diff --color-moved`, but that’s easily fooled by common lines when there’s a lot going on, and there only so many useful colors.)
* Manual conflict resolution will be easier when you have the option of dealing with one move at a time. Of course, you still have the option of doing the rebase all at once if you want.
* We’re almost certainly going to need to do some manual adjustments, so a fully automated rebase tool will be too complicated or impossible anyway.
* Functions don’t get moved by accident, so intervening regressions are unlikely.

I considered both approaches and chose the multiple-commit approach intentionally.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-03-31 00:07 UTC

Additionally, the multiple-commit approach of #17259 turned out to be extremely helpful for bisecting bugs. As much as we hope there won’t be any bugs, side effects from rearranging imports are significantly more likely than side effects from reformatting.

*2022-03-02 to 2022-03-08 · 17 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Email.20gateway/with/1337586)*

We currently use Mailman.  Since I expect some of our users will participate largely via email, the email gateway functionality is very important to us, and was a focus in my testing.  I opened [PR 21229](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/21229) to address two usability issues when replying to a topic via email.

Thoughts?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-02 22:43 UTC

@Jason Hildebrand thanks for bringing this up! The other potential issue I'm worried about is risk that forwarding an email you received from the email gateway will give someone else the ability to forge emails as you.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-02 22:43 UTC

I think the main thing that needs to happen is some investigation into how/if other platforms like GitHub that support replying via email address this problem.

**Jason Hildebrand** · 2022-03-03 04:43 UTC

Github is closed source.  They may have have security mechanisms in place, to protect against abuse, but we can't get insight into what they do  unless it is documented (which I doubt it is).

Instead, I looked at several open source projects: Gitlab, Discourse, rocket.chat.  I dug into the source code for each of them.  As far as I can tell, none of them apply expiration dates or limit the number of replies to a thread (from inbound email).  rocket.chat is different from gitlab & discourse in that the Message IDs (to which users reply) are not linked to a single user, like they are in Zulip.  Rocket.chat appears to accept any inbound message and post it using the from address in the email (creating a guest account on the fly if the sender does not already have an account).  

In summary, these 3 projects do not take measures to protect against abuse from inbound email. 

For the scenario with someone forwards a message to a 3rd party, the original Reply-To would not be used if that 3rd party then uses reply or reply-all.  They'd have to look through the source headers of the forwarded email (which are usually not even included, unless the MUA is configured to forward using attachments).  So this seems a low risk in my estimation.

If abuse occurs in Zulip, the offending messages could be removed by a moderator, right?  If that is not sufficient, one thing we could do is make these constants configurable.  So if a zulip installation started seeing abuse, they could tighten them up to reduce exposure.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-03 07:02 UTC

Yeah, I think I agree with that analysis; my guess is this logic was just not well thought through in the first place. The types of things we might want to add to do further hardening here would be checking signatures and the like that the email sender is as expected, but it's possibly the case the best answer is to just delete both of those checks. In particular, email clients generally won't include a `Reply-to` header when forwarding an email, so it's only going to be cases where someone forwards the full email.

(And maybe do something to discourage forwarding emails with the full headers)

The worst thing one can do if one were forwarded the email with original headers is forge emails as having been sent by another user, and you can only send those replies to the precise conversation where you got the email notification.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-03 07:03 UTC

@Greg Price @Alex Vandiver I'd appreciate your checking my thinking on this, but I think probably we'd be better off deleting the checks rather than limiting them to a specific time period (the draft PR linked above changes that from 7 days to a year and from 1 message to 25, but I don't really see either as being particularly useful).

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-03 07:08 UTC

For context, this restriction was implemented probably in 2014 in the very first commit that allowed email notifications to trigger a message with the user as the sender (not Email Gateway Bot), 2a5ec202956dc3465fd50292f0b066e4cddcc717, which I'm pretty sure was during Dropbox Hack Week. So I don't think we should assume these restrictions actually make sense.

**Jason Hildebrand** · 2022-03-04 01:45 UTC

What about someone doing a brute force attack - emailing to a bunch of hashes to try to spam whichever ones  happen to be valid.  Is the address space of the generated hashes large enough that they wouldn't find very many valid hashes?  This is one reason why an expiry limit might make sense.  I'll do some math and will follow up.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-03-04 01:50 UTC

The search space is 16^16, or 2^64.  That's a big space to find needles in.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-03-04 01:59 UTC

I don't think we need to be concerned with brute-force, here.  Even if Zulip Cloud grows by a couple orders of magnitude, *and* we have someone who can send us emails 1/sec for a year, it'd need to be an attacker that doesn't care where the one message they get lucky with successfully ends up.

And we can easily extend the space.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-03-04 02:00 UTC

Ah, sorry, did my math wrong, since `token_hex(16)` is 16 bytes.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-03-04 02:02 UTC

So we're *very* OK here, with 2^128 bits of space.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-03-04 02:08 UTC

We already have a unique index on `email_token`, so we're not in danger of accidentally generating duplicates, in the exceedingly rare case that happens.

So I think I'm fine with removing the time and use limits.  We can leave the `times_used` and `timestamp` fields in-place for a bit to see if they get abused in any way, but not act on them.  And even if we remove them, we can even reverse this decision without too much work; just give every message 0 uses and a timestamp of `now()`, and a week later we'll be back to status quo.

**Jason Hildebrand** · 2022-03-04 02:21 UTC

Thanks for that analysis.  And yes, it would be straightforward to put the limits back in place. @Greg Price do you have anything to add?

**Jason Hildebrand** · 2022-03-08 14:37 UTC

I'm going to assume we have consensus on this.  When I have time I will work on these changes and update the [PR](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/21229).

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-03-08 16:06 UTC

Sounds good to me.  Thanks for bringing it up, and helping us re-think it!

## Website inline preview

*2022-03-14 to 2022-03-14 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Website.20inline.20preview/with/1343955)*

**Pat Roam** · 2022-03-14 13:46 UTC

I was just reading another topic about disabling website preview of linked websites and the question occurred to me. Do those previews pose a security risk to the backend if Zulip tries to render a preview to a malicious website? I’m sure this has been considered internally but still curious to the answer.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-14 17:55 UTC

@Pat Roam it's certainly a potential security concern with any feature that displays third-party content, in that the code for generating previews could have security bugs. We have put substantial care into the security design for our preview features. For the website previews feature in particular, processing on the backend is largely limited to downloading the page and parsing its HTML attributes (such as Open Graph meta tags). And then we rely on the frontend configuring browser sandboxing configuration to protect clients from embedded content.

Particularly security-conscious customers who do work on malicious websites disable this feature just in case.

**Pat Roam** · 2022-03-14 21:16 UTC

Okay good to know and thanks for the answer! I think pretty much every website these days needs to be considered potentially malicious. Sometimes the operators don’t realize they have been compromised and are unknowingly serving up malware.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-23 17:47 UTC

I think while working on #20136, I've identified a subtle bug in how our `zerver/lib/retention.py` logic handles restoring a deleted message in the situation where multiple messages have claimed a given Attachment object. Specifically, I think if you:
* Upload an attachment.
* Send message 1 referencing the attachment.
* Send message 2 referencing the attachment.
* Delete message 1.
* Restore message 1.

Then I think this sequence will have cut the `attachment.messages` from the attachment to message 1.

@Mateusz Mandera can you check my reasoning here?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-23 17:50 UTC

We should at least get it into the issue tracker if so; I'm not sure it's actually important given how rare restoration is, and the fact that multiple messages referencing an upload isn't super common either. I think that a correct solution probably involves adding an `ArchivedMessage` => `Attachment` `ManyToManyField` so that we can preserve these records?

Every query that anyone writes, whether in production code or migrations, on half a dozen tables, would need to check this flag or produce invalid output. 

If we wanted to change this, I agree we'd want to basically lint-ban direct queries against those tables not using the special `QuerySet` function, but even that in insufficient, because one can do buggy joins via the Django ORM or raw SQL.

For instance, adding an index on a column which is true a minuscule fraction of the time (0.0007% in CZO, for instance) will *never be chosen unless you're looking for that minuscule fraction*.  In the majority of cases, adding the index would at best be ignored because it is so non-selective, and at worst would bloat the database and serve to put pressure on postgres' index pool and push out useful indexes.

I think there are reasonable arguments against merging the tables -- primarily being bulletproof against leaking data across them.  But indexing is *not* such a reason, much less a simple one, and claiming so very much undermines your position.

def restore_attachment_messages_from_archive(archive_transaction_id: int) -> None:
    query = SQL(
        """
    INSERT INTO zerver_attachment_messages (id, attachment_id, message_id)
        SELECT zerver_archivedattachment_messages.id,
            zerver_archivedattachment_messages.archivedattachment_id,
            zerver_archivedattachment_messages.archivedmessage_id
        FROM zerver_archivedattachment_messages
        INNER JOIN zerver_archivedmessage
            ON  zerver_archivedattachment_messages.archivedmessage_id = zerver_archivedmessage.id
        WHERE zerver_archivedmessage.archive_transaction_id = %(archive_transaction_id)s
    ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING
    """
    )
    with connection.cursor() as cursor:
        cursor.execute(query, dict(archive_transaction_id=archive_transaction_id))
```

It does `INSERT`s of the `Attachment.messages` rows that got archived back into the table, so it should successfully re-append the restored message id :thinking: What in the retention system made you suspect this bug? @Tim Abbott

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-25 23:57 UTC

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2022-03-26 10:45 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> Hmm, how does that work? Do we create an ArchivedAttachment row even when deleting message 1 in this corner case?
Yup. When archiving a chunk of Messages (or a single message etc.) we pass the ids to this: 
```
def move_related_objects_to_archive(msg_ids: List[int]) -> None:
    move_models_with_message_key_to_archive(msg_ids)
    move_attachments_to_archive(msg_ids)
    move_attachment_messages_to_archive(msg_ids)
```
Which will create  `ArchivedAttachment` rows (with `.messages` to go with it, containing the relevant ArchivedMessages):
```
def move_attachments_to_archive(msg_ids: List[int]) -> None:
    assert len(msg_ids) > 0

    query = SQL(
        """
    INSERT INTO zerver_archivedattachment ({dst_fields})
        SELECT {src_fields}
        FROM zerver_attachment
        INNER JOIN zerver_attachment_messages
            ON zerver_attachment_messages.attachment_id = zerver_attachment.id
        WHERE zerver_attachment_messages.message_id IN {message_ids}
        GROUP BY zerver_attachment.id
    ON CONFLICT (id) DO NOTHING
    """
    )
    move_rows(Attachment, query, message_ids=Literal(tuple(msg_ids)))
```

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2022-03-26 10:46 UTC

The original `Attachment` only gets deleted if it has no remaining `Message`s left. (`delete_expired_attachments`)

## Adding --rotate-api-keys option to logout_all_users

*2022-03-25 to 2022-05-23 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Adding.20--rotate-api-keys.20option.20to.20logout_all_users/with/1352919)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2022-03-25 18:18 UTC

In #19397 we want to add an option to `manage.py logout_all_users` to also rotate affected users' API keys (to log them out on mobile). There's a small decision to make of how to structure the implementation. The command is super simple:
```
    def handle(self, *args: Any, **options: Any) -> None:
        realm = self.get_realm(options)
        if realm:
            delete_realm_user_sessions(realm)
        elif options["deactivated_only"]:
            delete_all_deactivated_user_sessions()
        else:
            delete_all_user_sessions()
```
so an approach would be to add a `rotate_api_keys: bool = False` optional arg to these three `delete_...` functions.

@Tim Abbott Proposed

> I think I might prefer to just have an independent `bulk_rotate_api_key` type of parallel method, since one can imagine settings where one wants to rotate one but not the other in either direction.

Which sounds right to me too, and we can just pass  the list of user ids to the  `rotate_api_keys` function, but it'd still leave the minor question of whether we want to call it inside the `delete_...` functions `if rotate_api_keys is True`, or just have the management's command `handle()` code figure out the user ids and call `rotate_api_keys`. 

An argument against the latter would be that it duplicates the work of `delete_...` functions in figuring out the `UserProfile` set. But API-wise, having rotation of API keys doesn't feel quite right in "delete *session*" functions.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-25 18:44 UTC

Yeah, I think it's the queryset determination isn't that hard.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-25 18:45 UTC

We could also consider refactoring to support just passing a set of user IDs rather than having the logic like this:

```
def delete_realm_user_sessions(realm: Realm) -> None:                                                    
    realm_user_ids = [user_profile.id for user_profile in UserProfile.objects.filter(realm=realm)]       
    for session in Session.objects.filter(expire_date__gte=timezone_now()):                              
        if get_session_user(session) in realm_user_ids:                                                  
            delete_session(session)                                                                      
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-25 18:46 UTC

And then we could try to reuse the common `management` library code for specifying a set of users.
```
    def get_users(                                                                                       
        self,                                                                                            
        options: Dict[str, Any],                                                                         
        realm: Optional[Realm],                                                                          
        is_bot: Optional[bool] = None,                                                                   
        include_deactivated: bool = False,                                                               
    ) -> List[UserProfile]:                                                                              
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-25 18:46 UTC

I guess we'd need to add an `only-deactivated` variant, but that seems manageable.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2022-03-27 20:52 UTC

Hmm, opened https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/21577 for now, just duplicating UserProfile queries. More refactoring can be added, but after thinking more about this more, the `delete_realm_user_sessions` etc. functions are nice utils for calling them in `manage.py shell` etc., and I'm not sure we want to delete them in favor of some kind of generic `bulk_delete_sessions`? Also because they even have some tests for themselves in `test_sessions.py` - seems like a waste :thinking: 

The problem with using `get_users` is that it doesn't support  getting large bulks of users from more than one realm at once - and even if we changed that, that's a *lot* of UserProfiles, so the function's convention of returning entire UserProfiles instead of a list of ids makes it not very suitable I think?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-03-28 19:58 UTC

I think it could be OK performance-wise if it's returning a QuerySet rather than actual objects (since it'll be lazily evaluated in an iterator context or potentially just included as a where clause in a single database query depending on what one does with it), but I think the approach you've taken is fine.

**Harshit Bansal** · 2022-05-22 11:55 UTC

Just thinking out loud and may not be completely related to this discussion but as an user for this command won't one expect that when someone calls this command like this:

```
./manage.py logout_all_users --realm 1 --deactivated-only
```
it would just logout only the deactivated users with realm id 1. Current implementation (even without this PR) doesn't seem to follow it. Any reasons for it?

>I'm not sure we want to delete them in favor of some kind of generic bulk_delete_sessions?

Agree on those being handy but may be these can be refactored to use a common `bulk_delete_sessions`? Also the command might just construct the query set based on the options passed and pass the queryset to `bulk_delete_sessions` and `bulk_regenerate_api_keys` for further actioning?

P.S.: Was just going through some random PRs and came across this one. Please feel free to ignore if not relevant :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-23 22:55 UTC

@Harshit Bansal I think that sort of refactoring would be productive, yeah.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-23 23:04 UTC

The actual thing we likely want to do is extend the `Session` table to have `UserProfile` and `Realm` columns, so that one can filter that table directly -- it'd simplify this code substantially in addition to just being a cleaner database model.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-23 23:04 UTC

I think we haven't figured out a good plan for how to subclass Django's session system to support that -- could be a nice project for someone.

Maybe, yeah.  I'm looking [here](https://github.com/Supervisor/supervisor/blob/d76f548019745d1ef74a6f50c1d52c99575a32c8/supervisor/supervisord.py#L156-L172):
```python3
    def ordered_stop_groups_phase_1(self):
        if self.stop_groups:
            # stop the last group (the one with the "highest" priority)
            self.stop_groups[-1].stop_all()

    def ordered_stop_groups_phase_2(self):
        # after phase 1 we've transitioned and reaped, let's see if we
        # can remove the group we stopped from the stop_groups queue.
        if self.stop_groups:
            # pop the last group (the one with the "highest" priority)
            group = self.stop_groups.pop()
            if group.get_unstopped_processes():
                # if any processes in the group aren't yet in a
                # stopped state, we're not yet done shutting this
                # group down, so push it back on to the end of the
                # stop group queue
                self.stop_groups.append(group)
```

## Tornado sharding

*2022-04-08 to 2022-05-17 · 100 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Tornado.20sharding/with/1362374)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-04-08 00:27 UTC

@Tim Abbott and I had a conversation the other day about how to best shard Tornado instances.  Feedback on this idea appreciated!

I think our current proposal is:
 - Add a shard-id (either just a port, or something opaque) to every realm.
 - When a request for `/` comes in, set a `tornado_instance=9804` cookie in the response (based on the value in the user's realm), and register the queue on that server.
 - Have the nginx proxy do dispatch based on the cookie set in the request.  If the cookie isn't present, or isn't a valid port, pick a backend at random, or just a fixed default.
 - When a request comes in to Tornado, we check if the cookie matches the value in the user's realm.  If it does, act as normal, re-sending the cookie just to be explicit.
 - If the cookie doesn't match the realm's, we are moving this user to a different shard.
    - Serialize the user's queue, if we have one, and POST it to a dedicated `transfer_queue` endpoint on the shard defined for the realm, using the private key to authenticate to the other shard.  If we don't have a relevant queue, do nothing.
    - The other Tornado instance needs to be able to *start* getting events from rabbitmq before it's seen the queue registration, since the database change (and thus event queueing from django) will not happen at a clean request boundary.  I don't think the current Tornado processes with this at all currently.
    - Immediately send an empty response to the user, without any longpoll.
    - In the response, set the cookie pointing to the new shard.

Note that this is still aligning *whole realms* to specific shards -- we currently assume in `send_event` that all of the users that might need the event are on the same shard, and thus just we're just choosing _which_ shard to enqueue a message to.  This means less processing in general, and also correlated outages, which is probably a feature here.  but being able to *temporarily* split users across shards would be useful, as it lets us slew the user-base of large realms.  Without this, it means that we have to move the queue of every active user in a realm whenever they show up within the 1min longpoll window, which may cause a lot of load on the tornado shards in question.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-08 00:30 UTC

> - Serialize the user's queue, if we have one, and POST it to a dedicated endpoint the shard defined for the realm, using the private key to authenticate to the other shard. If we don't have a relevant queue, do nothing.

I think this is missing a word or two?  We're posting to a dedicated `transfer_queue` endpoint on the Tornado shard for the realm.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-04-08 00:32 UTC

Yup, sorry, lost something in editing; inserted some words.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-08 00:33 UTC

> Have the nginx proxy do dispatch based on the cookie set in the request. If the cookie isn't present, or isn't a valid port, pick a backend at random, or just a fixed default.

I guess this is a detail I hadn't thought about. In theory, this shouldn't happen unless the client forget its cookies in the protocol, so yeah I think any of those options is likely reasonable.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-04-08 00:33 UTC

Yeah, and we'll bounce it to the right queue from wherever we send it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-08 00:34 UTC

Right, or more likely, return an authentication error because the client also forgot their session cookie :).

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-04-08 00:34 UTC

Probably. :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-08 00:34 UTC

The other option would be for `nginx` to return an error in that case; it might be a better experience for buggy API clients if we thinks that's the only situation where this will happen.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-04-08 00:35 UTC

There's also a little hidden question in here of how much pre-planning we do for being able to put the shards on different hosts, not just different ports.  I think the port number is fine, but there's a clear extension point with what you stick in the cookie

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-04-08 00:37 UTC

I waffled in this write-up as to if we should bother sending the client the current events that we have in the queue, rather than serializing them and sending them to the other Tornado instance, and sending back an empty response.  I *think* it may be better in the idealized sense to not have to pass the events around, but I think serializing them and merging them into the other Tornado instance's may be more robust to race conditions.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-08 00:39 UTC

A few things to highlight about this proposal:
* This design in theory allows us to further refine the implementation to shard different users within a realm to different shards in the future, without much complexity in the changes. (The main thing that would require is having the `send_event` logic send the event to all shards that users in the realm are configured to use, which would be pretty straightforward). A few alternative designs we considered (E.g. ones that start sharding by hashing the `Host` header) would not have this property.
* Existing clients with a compliant HTTP client implementation should not need to be modified to "upgrade" to this protocol, since all they need to do is support sending a cookie. We should probably do some early logging for to what extent there are existing API clients connecting to Zulip Cloud that would have a problem here that we should bug to update.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-04-08 00:40 UTC

And, to the second point, we already know that the clients support sending cookies in some form, since they're sending the session cookie.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-08 00:41 UTC

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> There's also a little hidden question in here of how much pre-planning we do for being able to put the shards on different hosts, not just different ports. I think the port number is fine, but there's a clear extension point with what you stick in the cookie
I think if the value we store is `events_shard_id=N`, then we can have our internal code that maps a shard ID to a (host, port) pair be free to work however we like.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-08 00:41 UTC

(replying to Alex Vandiver)

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-04-08 16:04 UTC

To take a step back, we fundamentally need some shared storage between the load-balancer and the backend which distributes messages into queues, so we can change that shared store to repoint load.  Right now, that shared state is a static JSON file / config which we write out, and restart everything to pick up.

There are a bunch of ways of making that dynamic, which pretty much equate to where we're comfortable sticking that state:
 1. Store that state on the client.  That includes amending the session cookie, or adding a new cookie, or stuffing it into the hostname or query-string in the URL and using redirects.  Almost all of these are going to require some subset of clients to get smarter to handle this change -- there are arguments to be made about which of these are likely to require changes to more clients.
 2. Build a separate dispatching service between nginx and the tornado servers.  This is *effectively* what @Anders Kaseorg's last suggestion is, of forwarding to a backend which uses `X-Accel-Redirect` to bounce nginx to the right place.  Either we're distributing those request across all of the shards (doubling the number of requests on them) or we concentrate those onto one server whose sole job is to do the repointing (which becomes a SPOF).  Regardless, nginx remains stateless and doesn't have any direct connections to databases or memcached, though does depend on the redirection service.
 3. Move a database connection into nginx itself; this is the `ngx_http_upstream_consistent_hash` 3rd-party module option.  No round-trips into a redirect service are necessary, though nginx now has a startup dependency on memcached.
 4. Make nginx itself into the database.  That is, make nginx itself stateful in some way -- by observing outgoing responses with lua, and using that data to redirect incoming event requests, or by switching nginx for something like Envoy which has its own reconfigurable API plane.  Any of these make loadbalancer restarts much more fraught.

* A "Connection server" tier has as its sole job holding open connections and managing long-polling, but holds no state other than what HTTP connections are open right now.  These are stateless and can be load balanced between freely by clients, and basically just look up what queue server is associated with that client via some algorithm.
* A "Queue server" is an individual database shard of the actual queue data, and communications with connection servers via some protocol (perhaps just HTTP).

I think the main benefit this would have over having the routing be inside `nginx` is that a 500-line connection server might be a lot easier to reason about, preserve our extensible existing logging format for, etc., than an `nginx` plugin.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-05-13 21:18 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> I think you should go actually skim the ngx_http_upstream_consistent_hash documentation. It stores sharding information in memcached.
Looking at the [`ngx_http_upstream_consistent_hash`](https://www.nginx.com/resources/wiki/modules/consistent_hash/) docs more closely, I don't think this is the case.

The only directive that it adds is `consistent_hash $something`, which is a technique to select from one of the $$n$$ `server`s in the server group, in such a way that the choice is consistent for a given `$something`, and that minimizes the number of `$something`s moved if a new server is added.  The only interaction with memcached is that this particular choice strategy is already used in some sharding-into-memcached strategies.  `consistent_hash` doesn't itself read anything from memcached, and certainly doesn't read any sharding information from there -- it only takes as input the var it was given, and selects a server from that.

`memcached_pass` is part of [`ngx_http_memcached_module`](http://nginx.org/en/docs/http/ngx_http_memcached_module.html), whose job is to serve whole responses out of a memcached server.  The idea is that you pre-fill HTTP responses into memcached, and nginx can serve it quickly.  The content in memcached is served as the response body, with headers fixed as `Content-Type: application/octet-stream` and not adjustable from the memcached data.

We can probably write the behaviour as a C extension or LUA, but I'd prefer to avoid both of those.

The `consume` method expects `Mapping[str, Any]` or `Dict[str, Any]`, so does `queue_json_publish`. The actual shape of the mapping is event-specific, and we enforce that manually. Do we have plans for typing the event queue system? Or is it a design choice we made?

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-04-12 21:33 UTC

It appears to me that there is no "convenient" way to implement this. The expected data structure of the json objects might need to be typed as `dataclass` or `TypedDict`. This approach requires overloading with string literals, and potentially requires us to make QueueProcessingWorker generic.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-04-12 21:37 UTC

However, I'm not entirely sure if the type signature will become a lie between enqueuing the object and invoking the consume method.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-04-12 21:45 UTC

*All* annotations involving `Any` are [unchecked legacy relics](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/testing/mypy.html#avoid-the-any-type) that need to be replaced. We have no reservations about using generics when that’s how an  interface is accurately annotated.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-04-12 21:48 UTC

I think [dataclasses-json](https://github.com/lidatong/dataclasses-json) is the mechanism we need to check the types at runtime to guarantee that the annotations aren’t a lie.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-12 22:55 UTC

Yeah, I think `dataclasses-json` is probably the easiest way to connect the types used in `queue_json_publish` with that read out in the queue processor.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-25 16:35 UTC

With #21611 about to merged, the core backend part of allowing groups to contain subgroups as part of #19525 will be complete. There's still a lot of work to do before we can start adding new permissions settings that are controlled by groups rather than roles. But I figured I'd flag that one of the things we're going to want is to be able to sync the direct membership of a user group from LDAP (aka #9957), and I figured I'd start a thread on it since likely @Mateusz Mandera will be driving that.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2022-04-25 17:04 UTC

Yeah, hopefully this should be relatively straightforward - `django-auth-ldap` seems to give simple ways of accessing an ldap user's groups  - https://github.com/django-auth-ldap/django-auth-ldap/blob/master/django_auth_ldap/backend.py#L449. So if all works as expected, it should just be a matter of grabbing the list of  groups e.g. upon login (or `manage.py sync_ldap_user_data`) and modifying the user's Zulip group membership based on that and some simple configuration dict in `settings.py`

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-25 17:11 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-25 17:13 UTC

It's decently likely that we'll find we want to have a setting on the group for whether it's managed via an automatic synchronization thing like this (preventing you from editing its membership in the Zulip UI). ## Race condition in realm creation #21160

*2022-04-26 to 2026-08-03 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Race.20condition.20in.20realm.20creation.20.2321160/with/1373743)*

**Matt** · 2022-04-26 17:57 UTC

Hi :wave: I'm working on [#21160](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/21160) (Proper handling of an exception within ``accounts_register``), and am pretty sure I have a fix, but after wading through the registration code, tests, and whatnot, am struggling a bit to reproduce the problem, as hammering away at ``accounts_register`` isn't producing the race, nor are there existing tests that cover the function in question (that I could find). Any thoughts/pointers? Thanks!

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-26 18:15 UTC

@Matt Keller My guess is you won't be able to easily trigger a race -- the best idea I have for manual testing is to add a `time.sleep` inside the `do_create_realm` transaction, or similar, and then just use your browse to double-trigger a post.

**Matt** · 2022-04-26 18:17 UTC

I did contrive an event similarly, but as it's "untestable" didn't want to lean on that too much. Thanks!

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-26 18:17 UTC

For an automated test, one is likely to want to simulate an effective sequence by using `mock.patch` on `set_realm_permissions_based_on_org_type` (or some other function called from inside that block), and have the mock's replacement function trigger a second registration attempt, while you have the first one's execution paused.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-26 18:18 UTC

And then have the test verify the return status of both requests.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-26 18:20 UTC

I think the a key question for how important it is to write a difficult automated test is whether the fix is one that is unlikely to be accidentally undone in future refactoring; but I think such a mock might be fairly doable (and we might end up wanting to reuse the technique to, for example, test for a potential similar race with registration).

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-26 18:21 UTC

In terms of how a user actually triggered this (I'm pretty sure we opened that issue because it actually happened), my guess would be that they managed to double-click the Submit button on the realm creation form in quick succession.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-26 18:21 UTC

(So both requests likely came from the same browser).

**Matt** · 2022-04-26 18:21 UTC

I will think of a better way to abstract this for testing, and follow the ``mock.patch`` route. Again, thank you for the pointers! :smile:

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-26 18:22 UTC

Thinking a bit more, I suppose it's possible that if that's the real-world scenario, the ideal user experience would be to have whichever request loses the race return the same thing as the one that succeeded (i.e. serve a redirect to the app), rather than a 400 error, so that it's transparent to the user. But you can play with it :)

**Ahmad Jafari** · 2026-07-28 07:23 UTC

I’m working on #21160 in PR #39830.

The current fix catches the unique-constraint IntegrityError and returns
a user-facing 400 response. After reproducing the race manually, we are
considering how the accounts registration page should present the error.

Which user experience would be preferable?

1. Render the registration form again with an error banner.
2. Show a separate error page.
3. Redirect to the organization created by the first request.

The redirect option was discussed in the previous PR, but it may introduce
another race during user creation.

**Ahmad Jafari** · 2026-08-03 11:09 UTC

Update: I implemented and manually tested the form-based approach.

When realm creation loses the subdomain unique-constraint race, the
registration form is now rendered again with a field-level error on the
organization URL. The response is HTTP 400, submitted values are preserved,
and the user can choose another subdomain.

I reproduced the race manually: the first request created the organization,
while the second request displayed:

“Subdomain is already in use. Please choose a different one.”

This avoids redirecting to an organization that may belong to another
registration flow.

There are a number of criteria for an organization being eligible for the directory, which changes whether the setting is enabled or disabled:

## Self-hosted homepage

*2022-04-28 to 2022-04-28 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Self-hosted.20homepage/with/1375349)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-28 18:00 UTC

So there's a somewhat complex question that needs to be settled before we can integrate #21940.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-28 18:01 UTC

First, I have only tested in a development environment, so confirmation would be appreciated, but my belief from reading the code is that if you visit the root domain of a freshly installed self-hosted Zulip server, you'll redirected to an apparent login page that throws a 500 if you try to login. (Someone testing this would be very much appreciated!).

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-28 18:02 UTC

This outcome doesn't make sense. Its saving grace is that this isn't a thing one actually does in a new server; the installation process ends with printing out a link to create your first realm, most people create that realm on the root domain of their self-hosted server, and then the login page actually works.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-28 18:03 UTC

Changes to make the public access view load directly if a realm is present on the current domain caused me to look at this, which is why it related to #21940.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-28 18:04 UTC

The approach we currently have in that pull request is to serve the save 404 that we serve in other situations where you visit a Zulip server subdomain that doesn't have a realm (you can see it on https://invalid.zulipchat.com/)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-28 18:06 UTC

We likely will want to do a follow-up to both improve that 404 page and also perhaps provide a nicer specialized one for the root domain of a self-hosted Zulip server that hosts no realms (E.g. it could link to instructions).

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-28 18:07 UTC

The consequence of that 404 page detail that we need to make a decision about before we can merge #21940 is that changing the response from a direct to that 200 login page to a 404 page results in this change to the HTTP headers in one of the health checks that we do in CI for a newly setup production system:

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/21940/commits/b092c0a0342a3eb1b57db439e065519faf48fd19#diff-617507e83aa2531092a9b6eee9f839f873186b031db4ab2a1bea2ac1a8cd273b

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-28 18:08 UTC

Basically, `tools/ci/production-verify` does this little bit of logic and then compares the HTTP headers for the Zulip server to what was expected:

```
curl -ILk https://localhost -o /tmp/http-headers                                                         
grep -vi -e '^content-length:' -e '^date:' -e '^expires:' -e '^set-cookie:' /tmp/http-headers >/tmp/http\
-headers-processed                                                                                       
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-28 18:09 UTC

## GitHub workflow for partial merges

*2022-04-30 to 2022-08-10 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/GitHub.20workflow.20for.20partial.20merges/with/1376438)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-30 16:52 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> You do it manually from the Git command line. It’s not a concept GitHub knows about, so it has some disadvantages. GitHub doesn’t remember the association between the merged commits and the PR they came from, and the PR usually ends up showing as having conflicts in the GitHub UI.

GitHub could, in theory, add support for knowing about that. But GitHub was quite late in adding support for rebase merges at all, and still considers it to be a secondary/advanced option, so I wouldn't count on that happening anytime soon. 

But for me, the tradeoff of being able to merge part of a pull request to reduce the amount of code one needs to keep track of reduce risk of future merge or migration numbering conflicts generally feels worth it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-30 16:53 UTC

I suppose we could try a more GitHub-aware version of this workflow, where we make a tool that, given a commit and pull request ID, turns the commits between the merge-base with upstream`/main` into a new PR that is configured to merge automatically once CI passes.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-30 16:53 UTC

If the tooling was done right, it could create cross-links between the two pull requests in an automated fashion that made it less of a chore.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-04-30 16:54 UTC

(And this would potentially eliminate a class of CI failures in `main` due to linter issues fixed in the wrong commit when partially merging a PR, etc.)

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2022-08-04 02:15 UTC

I know the test overhead in the server is higher, but would the linter issues you mention here be resolved through per-commit linting? The basic tool added to ZT this year has been very useful for automated 'yes these commits are independent' (and passing linting), whether finally or during reviews.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-04 19:02 UTC

One can definitely run the linter or tests locally before doing a partial merge. That said, a pretty common problem is new code without test coverage added in the first few commits (and then tested later in the branch), and that currently requires running the full test suite to verify easily.

**Greg Price** · 2022-08-10 20:26 UTC

I definitely agree we should plan on the assumption that GitHub is not going to add support for this workflow.

The idea of a tool to make a new PR is an interesting one. It wouldn't take much code to implement, I think.

**Greg Price** · 2022-08-10 20:27 UTC

FWIW the solution I generally apply in zulip-mobile is that I'll rewind the PR branch to include just the commits I want to merge, then merge that, and ask the author to send the rest as a fresh PR. This works 100% for getting the association between commit and PRs in GitHub's metadata.

**Greg Price** · 2022-08-10 20:33 UTC

That solution is ideal in the case when the commits I'm ready to merge include the main part of the PR, and the code that most of the discussion in the PR thread has been about.

When there's some existing review discussion on the commits not getting merged, it's a bit annoying in that the discussion on the new PR may have to refer back to those subthreads on the old PR.

But I think some sort of compromise on that dimension is unavoidable for this problem statement. For example, the proposed tool would have a similar split, affecting the initial ready-to-merge commits instead of the later still-in-progress commits.


## saving DB queries to get realm user groups.

*2022-05-02 to 2022-05-03 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/saving.20DB.20queries.20to.20get.20realm.20user.20groups.2E/with/1376835)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-05-02 13:50 UTC

As discussed [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/21927#issuecomment-1111282660), we are trying to save database queries in `user_groups_in_realm_serialized`. Currently we need to do two separate queries on `UserGroupMembership` and `GroupGroupMembership` tables to get direct members and direct subgroups of the user group.

We initially thought of using `prefetch_related` but that does not reduce the number of DB queries as mentioned in the above linked github comment.

Posting it here in case anyone has suggestions or ideas here to improve this.

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-05-02 13:50 UTC

The function code for easy accessibility -
```python
def user_groups_in_realm_serialized(realm: Realm) -> List[Dict[str, Any]]:
    """This function is used in do_events_register code path so this code
    should be performant.  We need to do 2 database queries because
    Django's ORM doesn't properly support the left join between
    UserGroup and UserGroupMembership that we need.
    """
    realm_groups = UserGroup.objects.filter(realm=realm)
    group_dicts: Dict[str, Any] = {}
    for user_group in realm_groups:
        group_dicts[user_group.id] = dict(
            id=user_group.id,
            name=user_group.name,
            description=user_group.description,
            members=[],
            subgroups=[],
            is_system_group=user_group.is_system_group,
        )

    membership = UserGroupMembership.objects.filter(user_group__realm=realm).values_list(
        "user_group_id", "user_profile_id"
    )
    for (user_group_id, user_profile_id) in membership:
        group_dicts[user_group_id]["members"].append(user_profile_id)

    group_membership = GroupGroupMembership.objects.filter(subgroup__realm=realm).values_list(
        "subgroup_id", "supergroup_id"
    )
    for (subgroup_id, supergroup_id) in group_membership:
        group_dicts[supergroup_id]["subgroups"].append(subgroup_id)

    for group_dict in group_dicts.values():
        group_dict["members"] = sorted(group_dict["members"])
        group_dict["subgroups"] = sorted(group_dict["subgroups"])

    return sorted(group_dicts.values(), key=lambda group_dict: group_dict["id"])
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-03 19:22 UTC

I'm sure it's possible to do what we want with raw SQL. I would have expected Django's `prefetch_related` to be the way to do this in Django.

## message sorting design

*2022-05-23 to 2022-05-25 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/message.20sorting.20design/with/1383753)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-05-23 22:42 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> Preserving the timestamps won’t be possible in any case, since Zulip assumes that timestamps are monotonically increasing with message ID.
I assume that we only have that restriction across messages in a single realm, or imports would never work.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-05-23 22:44 UTC

Right.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-05-23 22:48 UTC

Ideally we’d relax this; we’d need to change lots of `id` sorts to `date_sent` sorts, probably add some corresponding database indexes, and extinguish the cursed floating-point local `id` dumpster fire in the frontend.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-23 23:31 UTC

I think the main thing that'd be unpleasant about changing this is rethinking the `GET /messages` API model -- it's a helpful simplification for reasoning about what we've fetched from the server that the thing we use as a unique identifier (the message ID) is also the sort key. 

The current API of sending an anchor message ID and how many messages before/after you want works fine if the message ID you request exists, but the logic around what happens when that ID doesn't exist (of getting the nearest message ID to it matching your narrow) would become incoherent in a world where message IDs are no longer sorted.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-23 23:32 UTC

Another direction we could take here is moving to at least 64-bit message IDs (which we need to do for scaling reasons anyway), and then leaving large gaps between consecutive message IDs in a realm in some strategic way that would support bulk inserting message IDs where we please.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-23 23:34 UTC

There's also a possible approach where we split what is currently the message ID into two things -- one that's an unordered unique ID, and the other that's an ordering ID, and have the ordering ID be mutable (with a client restart, say) even if the unique ID is not.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-05-23 23:34 UTC

> and then leaving large gaps between consecutive message IDs

How many more dumpster fires do we need to light before we realize that playing stupid games with numbers is not a substitute for correctly modeling data…?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-05-23 23:35 UTC

> and the other that's an ordering ID,

We could call it `date_sent`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-23 23:35 UTC

Does `date_sent` have enough resolution that we don't risk having two messages with the same value of it due to races?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-05-23 23:36 UTC

[1 microsecond resolution](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/datatype-datetime.html).

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-23 23:37 UTC

Yeah, I'm pretty sure that one was on the reasons we rejected the idea of ordering by `date_sent`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-05-23 23:37 UTC

We can order by `(date_sent, id)` tuples.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-05-23 23:38 UTC

We should probably move this conversation to #**backend**.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-23 23:38 UTC

Yeah, such a move seems reasonable.

**Notification Bot** · 2022-05-23 23:40 UTC

14 messages were moved here from #**zulip cloud>Importing eMail into a Zulip stream** by @Alex Vandiver.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2022-05-25 02:49 UTC

## email auto-reply headers

*2022-05-24 to 2022-05-27 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/email.20auto-reply.20headers/with/1384330)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-24 23:03 UTC

https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/13193#issuecomment-1136487378 has a detailed comment giving what headers Front uses to detect whether an email is auto-generated and thus should not trigger a vacation auto-response.

It's be useful if we can figure out whether any of these headers are somewhat standard and thus we could start including in our outgoing email notifications.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-05-24 23:05 UTC

https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc3834#section-5.2 applies, I thnk

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-24 23:11 UTC

Looking at GitHub's email notifications for inspiration, I see they have this header: 

`X-Auto-Response-Suppress: All`

Googling suggests Exchange supports avoiding auto-responses to emails with that header, which seems promising.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-24 23:12 UTC

I do not see `Auto-Submitted` on GitHub's headers, perhaps because there is a human who triggered the notification in their case (and ours)?

"The Auto-Submitted header field SHOULD NOT be supplied for messages that were manually submitted by a human."

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-24 23:13 UTC

So I think the correct action for us to take is to make all emails generated by Zulip have `X-Auto-Response-Suppress: All`?

**David Albert** · 2022-05-26 16:04 UTC

I'm the person who posted the list of headers Front uses to classify auto-generated emails. From an initial glance at RFC 3834, it frustratingly doesn't seem like `Auto-Submitted` will help that much. Front only ignores `Auto-Submitted: auto-replied` and `Auto-Submitted: auto-notified`, neither of which seem quite right. Zulip's notifications aren't themselves auto-replies, and auto-notified is from [RFC 5436](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc5436.html), part of a system called Sieve, that I'm not familiar with, but doesn't seem like it would apply here.

From looking at all the other options, and reading a bit about `X-Auto-Response-Suppress`, I agree that `X-Auto-Response-Suppress: All` is most likely to be the correct header for Zulip to use.

Given the lack of an obvious standardized way to get the behavior we want, I think this is a situation where the best tack is to add the first header, mark the bug as resolved, and see if anyone reopens it with another email provider who's vacation responder doesn't respect X-Auto-Response-Suppress, and go from there.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-26 22:25 UTC

That seems right to me. @Alex Vandiver do you think there's any added testing we'll want to do before adding such a header?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-26 22:26 UTC

I guess the other question is whether we want that applied to all emails Zulip sends -- my theory is yes, since I can't think of any specific case where we'd want a vacation autoresponder reply to any outgoing transactional email.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-26 22:26 UTC

(Even the ones that don't have a `noreply` reply address, generally are only interested in replies from people)

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-05-27 00:21 UTC

Yeah, I think that's a reasonable thing to add to all outgoing emails.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-05-27 00:21 UTC

As another point in support of it, it appears that's the only such header that Github sends.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-05-27 00:34 UTC

Pushed #22134.

## transaction.on_commit when sending multiple events

*2022-05-26 to 2022-06-09 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/transaction.2Eon_commit.20when.20sending.20multiple.20events/with/1384735)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-05-26 10:59 UTC

I noticed a bug  when sending multiple events in a transaction and using `transaction.on_commit` callbacks to send the events. Sharing this here as @Tim Abbott [suggested](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/22109#discussion_r879917502).

The problem is when we send multiple events like in below code and same variable is used for the event object, the event object defined last is sent to both the events since the event variable stores that object at the time of sending events. 
```python
def notify_linkifiers(realm: Realm, realm_linkifiers: List[LinkifierDict]) -> None:
    event: Dict[str, object] = dict(type="realm_linkifiers", realm_linkifiers=realm_linkifiers)
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_event(realm, event, active_user_ids(realm.id)))

    # Below is code for backwards compatibility. The now deprecated
    # "realm_filters" event-type is used by older clients, and uses
    # tuples.
    realm_filters = realm_filters_for_realm(realm.id)
    event = dict(type="realm_filters", realm_filters=realm_filters)
    transaction.on_commit(lambda: send_event(realm, legacy_event, active_user_ids(realm.id)))
```

It works fine if I update one variable for event object to `legacy_event` as I did [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/21686/commits/90f6ac0a66cc2ed6bfce0722c54be0e0953d90ae).


I am facing the same problem in #22109 where events are sent in a loop in `bulk_remove_subscriptions` and the first commit in the PR is to avoid using `transaction.on_commit` in events sent by `bulk_remove_susbcriptions`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-26 22:27 UTC

@Sahil Batra thanks for flagging this!

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-26 22:27 UTC

This is a pretty nasty Python scoping issue, and I think structurally the problem is that we shouldn't be using this `lambda` construction.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-26 22:28 UTC

What I don't have a clear idea of is what the best alternative is.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-26 22:30 UTC

There's probably some tactical things we could try, like making it so that the function passed to `transaction.on_commit` does all the fetching of data to send to clients itself.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-26 22:31 UTC

But it also makes me think again about whether we should prioritize trying to migrate to a world where we are writing events to Postgres as part of the transaction, perhaps with a (hopefully temporarily) compatibility layer that just pushes events from the queue's Postgres table into RabbitMQ.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-05-26 22:33 UTC

Agreed on moving to get rid of RabbitMQ long-term.

A typical workaround for the immediate problem is `lambda event=event: …`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-26 22:34 UTC

Hmm, can you be explicit about how that workaround works?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-05-26 22:35 UTC

It (ab)uses the Python quirk that default arguments are evaluated at function definition time rather than call time.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-05-26 22:36 UTC

It’s mentioned [in the Python FAQ](https://docs.python.org/3/faq/programming.html#why-do-lambdas-defined-in-a-loop-with-different-values-all-return-the-same-result).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-05-26 22:39 UTC

In this case, avoiding mutation seems best, either by renaming one of the `event` variables or inlining them so there isn’t an `event` variable at all.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-26 22:42 UTC

Yeah, I suppose inlining is probably a pretty good option for the loop case.

(I preferred renaming for readability in the case where the function just does two calls, so I'm decently happy with that solution)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-05-26 22:44 UTC

Inlining wouldn’t solve this in the case of a loop, since Python implements loops by mutating the loop variable.

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-06-08 14:57 UTC

Since we cannot use `lambda event=event: …` for loop cases, should we continue with the changes in #22109 to use `with` block instead of `@transaction.atomic` decorator for now?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-06-08 20:40 UTC

What do you mean? We can use `lambda event=event: …` for loop cases, and I don’t see what a `with` block has to do with this.

**Sahil Batra** · 2022-06-09 14:19 UTC

Ohh, sorry. I tried doing it and was failing before, but then caught my mistake and it works. Extremely sorry for the confusion.


## topic IDs

*2022-05-27 to 2022-05-27 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/topic.20IDs/with/1385319)*

**Evy** · 2022-05-27 00:50 UTC

Related to my [paper doc](https://paper.dropbox.com/doc/Topic-IDs--BiSFQ52tSxw63Ouv3jh_z_ZEAg-9iSYEXlik9BMMK9uqmTh2) on why topic IDs would be nice, one of which being renaming a topic wouldn't have to involve moving all the messages. When the messages are being moved, you end up with UI like this:

[image.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/42/TTjHo3bsSzHv4bkQyxJrBiJX/image.png)

**Evy** · 2022-05-27 00:51 UTC

(this is both the old and new name for the topic)

**Evy** · 2022-05-27 00:52 UTC

Oh whoa only half my messages were moved. I have no idea how that happened -- I was using the pencil icon in the recipient bar. :shrug:

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-27 22:28 UTC

@Evy Kassirer I think this is a known permissions issue -- I think this is a case where you don't have permission to move the older messages, or something messy like that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-27 22:29 UTC

I think there's an extended #**design** conversation about how to fix the UI around this -- but it's primarily our having a suboptimal solution to a messy policy issue, specifically about the tradeoff between making it easy for users to edit topics but not easy for a malicious user to merge all the messages in a stream into a single topic.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-27 22:34 UTC

Topic IDs are relevant to this class of problem in terms of how we implement things, but one can implement moving content correctly regardless of the data model -- what topic IDs would change is primarily where the tangly technical complexity of message editing lives within the system. Some details would get simpler and others more complex.

In this specific example, in a world with topic IDs, if one wanted to move only half the messages in one topic to another, we'd needs to change the topic ID of the moved messages, whereas if we were moving all of them, the real-time update event would instead need to change the name/location of the topic with that ID. As a result, those two classes of move actions would look more dissimilar in terms of the real-time sync API than they do now.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-05-27 22:35 UTC

I think all 3 plausible models are viable here (no topic IDs, topic IDs that only exist in the server and are invisible to clients, and topic IDs synced to clients) can all be made correct with our message editing product experience.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-06-03 16:46 UTC

We added soft-reactivation in #22124 #21812 triggered by password reset requests and mentions. As Tim [mentioned](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/22124#issuecomment-1140055287), we should improve the user experience by having an indicator in the UI to let the user know that soft-reactivation is in progress.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-06-03 16:53 UTC

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-06-03 16:54 UTC

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-06-03 16:55 UTC

But I'm not sure if it will be the best practice to approach this, what is our general approach to show something is "in progress"?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-06-03 17:01 UTC

We can make `long_term_idle` not a bool, but some sort of enum.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-06-03 17:01 UTC

Another reason to want this is that we can use it to prevent re-queueing the reactivation for a user (e.g. if they get multiple messages).  The reason this is important is not safety (reactivation is safe to do even if the user is not long_term_idle) but rather queue management -- reactivations can take a bit, and our "is the queue backed up" logic for alerting admins multiplies the size of the queue by the average time taken recently.  So a user reactivation could take 10s -- but if it has 100 copies of the same user queued up behind it, we should *not* estimate that the queue will take 100*10s to clear them all.  The later ones are nearly instant.

The cleanest way to fix this is to not re-enqueue the work for the user more than once.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-06-03 17:05 UTC

That makes a lot of sense! Relying on the field to prevent re-queuing seems to be subjected to a race condition here. Though rare, we should handle that as well.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-06-03 17:09 UTC

For sure.  Erring on the side of queueing more than once is clearly preferred. :)

## Typing keyword variadic arguments for test client helpers

*2022-06-06 to 2022-06-28 · 22 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Typing.20keyword.20variadic.20arguments.20for.20test.20client.20helpers/with/1389250)*

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-06-06 20:10 UTC

We wrap the client functions in ZulipTestCase, which takes a `**kwargs`. Now I'm thinking of the proper way to give them more specific types. Several keyword arguments that might present as an entry in `**kwargs` need to have certain types, like `follow` and `secure` needs to be `bool`.

There are some ways to type this.
One will be to write out the keyword arguments in the signatures:

So
```
def client_put(self, url: str, info: Dict[str, Any] = {}, **kwargs: ClientArg) -> HttpResponse:
```
will become
```
def client_put(self, url: str, info: Dict[str, Any] = {}, follow: bool = False, secure: bool = False, **kwargs: ClientArg) -> HttpResponse:
```
This requires us to copy over the default values for `follow` and etc defined in Django, which does not comply with the practice of having a single source of truth.

One will be getting rid of `**kwargs` in its entirety, and create a `TypedDict` holding the type definition
```
class ClientArgs(TypedDict, total=False):
   follow: bool
   secure: bool

def client_put(self, url: str, info: Dict[str, Any] = {}, kwargs: ClientArgs) -> HttpResponse:
```

The caller needs to create and validate the dictionary to call the test client method with (which is not a bad property for the sake of type checking). This approach does not have the flexibility of using keyword variadic arguments.
This might be improved with support of [typing `**kwargs` with `TypedDict`](https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/4441), but it will require a PEP (which can take a long time to be drafted and implemented).

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-06-07 03:42 UTC

To add questions with this: What will be preferable to type this? What are some other options available?

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2022-06-07 15:15 UTC

(replying to Zixuan James Li)
> This might be improved with support of [typing `**kwargs` with `TypedDict`](https://github.com/python/mypy/issues/4441), but it will require a PEP (which can take a long time to be drafted and implemented).

Ah, that's a shame that ``**kwargs: TypedDict`` doesn't work like we'd wish for. I see there's already a PEP PR at https://github.com/python/peps/pull/2620 - it'd be cool if it gets accepted, though I'm not familiar with how the process goes :smile:

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2022-06-07 15:17 UTC

I like the second approach of
```
class ClientArgs(TypedDict, total=False):
   follow: bool
   secure: bool

def client_put(self, url: str, info: Dict[str, Any] = {}, kwargs: ClientArgs) -> HttpResponse:
```
since it avoids having excessively big function signatures - though might be somewhat of a hassle to call them, having to explicitly construct the `TypedDict` first. But the type-checking seems worth it :smile:

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-06-07 15:43 UTC

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-06-08 00:39 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-06-08 00:59 UTC

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-06-14 01:10 UTC

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-06-14 03:03 UTC
