**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-06-14 03:06 UTC

The issue with the original wrappers is that we were calling django's test client methods with the unpacking `**kwargs: ClientArg`, which had types that might collide with the defined keyword arguments (`follow` and `secure` for example). This version fixes the problem by ensuring that a duplicated key error must be raised when the caller is sneaking keyword arguments with incompatible types.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-06-14 21:03 UTC

(replying to Zixuan James Li)
> If we copy over the defaults without making `**kwargs: ClientArg` -> `kwargs: Dict[str, ClientArg]` and appropriate refactorings to use `kwargs` as a regular keyword arugment, all the callers need to copy the defaults as well if they want to unpack a dictionary.
This turns out to be untrue as the callers can construct a `TypedDict` to be unpacked to avoid having incompatible types for the keyword arguments.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-06-14 21:05 UTC

With that insight taken, #22247 is updated with `ClientArg` removed. An example of a refactored client method looks like this:
```
    @instrument_url
    def client_post(
        self,
        url: str,
        info: Union[str, bytes, Dict[str, Any]] = {},
        skip_user_agent: bool = False,
        follow: bool = False,
        secure: bool = False,
        intentionally_undocumented: bool = False,
        **headers: str,
    ) -> "TestHttpResponse":
        django_client = self.client  # see WRAPPER_COMMENT
        self.set_http_headers(headers, skip_user_agent)
        result = django_client.post(url, info, follow=follow, secure=secure, **headers)
        self.validate_api_response_openapi(
            url,
            "post",
            result,
            info,
            headers,
            intentionally_undocumented=intentionally_undocumented,
        )
        return result
```

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-06-14 21:06 UTC

I think I should have covered all the flags that got mixed into `kwargs` previously. Any feedback will be appreciated.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-06-28 23:40 UTC

Having seen the implementation resulting from this, obviously it's a bit annoying that we repeat ourselves a bit with the prototypes for `follow` and friends, but I think it does read clearer and certainly self-documents itself better following these changes.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-06-28 23:41 UTC

BTW one thing that we might want to do following this as add brief docstrings for these methods; they seem important enough when writing tests that it'd be helpful?  Or at least an extended docstrings for one of them, with the others referencing that one for more information.

```
            # Note that request.user is a Union[RemoteZulipServer, UserProfile, AnonymousUser],

It doesn't seem to be important for authentication itself, because the way that works is that in the `authenticated_rest_api_view` decorator we do
```
# profile is a Union[UserProfile, RemoteZulipServer]

...

```

so actually the `profile` object returned by `validate_api_key` is the important one, getting passed on to the view function as the authenticated entity. The fact that `request.user` gets set in `validate_api_key`to the `RemoteZulipServer` doesn't seem terribly important.

## smokescreen

*2022-06-28 to 2022-07-11 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/smokescreen/with/1397782)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-06-28 01:39 UTC

We had a plan to authenticated various parts of Zulip to the outgoing Smokescreen instance -- which would let us limit which parts of the system could make requests to where.  Doing this requires auth'ing to Smokescreen in some way; the simplest is to set a request header, which Smokescreen can trust.

Smokescreen used to support this out of the box, but they've removed that functionality, and [don't want to add it back in](https://github.com/stripe/smokescreen/pull/161).  Smokescreen is easy to compose arbitrary auth callbacks into, but that means that we have to build and install `zulip/smokescreen`, and version bump that in parallel with changes to `stripe/smokescreen`.

It's a little frustrating to manage with version changes, but I think still easier than managing up the TLS client certs that are the only built-in option for smokescreen from upstream.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-06-28 01:44 UTC

The attack that using TLS certs protects against, over header-based auth, is if the attacker has compromised the process entirely, has the ability to make arbitrary requests with arbitrary headers, is limited at the network level to make them only to the proxy, and only has access to a single client TLS certificate as the user they're executing code as.

That doesn't feel like a situation which maps onto how Zulip code currently runs, so I think it's reasonable to use the header solution.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-06-28 01:50 UTC

One alternative would be to ship some deliberately insecure certificates with the code, all with the same hard-coded private key.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-06-28 01:58 UTC

:nod:  That doesn't provide any of the security benefits of the client-side certs, but means we can use the built-in auth support.

It forces TLS over the wire between the Zulip process and smokescreen, which is silly if it's on localhost, but it's not always.  It makes adding new smokescreen roles a little fiddlier, since you need to jump through the CSR hoops to make them.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-06-28 02:00 UTC

We could ship the CA and generate certificates in memory on demand.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-06-28 19:18 UTC

I guess that makes it very clear that these certificates provide no real authentication.

We do need to distribute the signing cert to the smokescreen host so it can validate those certs -- which is straightforward if it's the same host, but a little irksome to do otherwise.

* Django 1.10 supports PostgreSQL ≥ 9.2.
* Django 1.11 supports PostgreSQL ≥ 9.3.
* Django 2.1 supports PostgreSQL ≥ 9.4.
* Django 3.0 supports PostgreSQL ≥ 9.5.
* Django 3.2 supports PostgreSQL ≥ 9.6.
* Django 4.0 supports PostgreSQL ≥ 10.
* Django 4.1 will support PostgreSQL ≥ 11.
* Django 4.2 will support PostgreSQL ≥ 12.

## request.user being nonexistent

*2022-07-08 to 2022-07-15 · 36 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/request.2Euser.20being.20nonexistent/with/1402003)*

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-07-08 21:24 UTC

I'm perplexed by the if condition here: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/context_processors.py#L54-L55

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-07-08 21:25 UTC

How is it possible for `request` to not have the `user` attribute?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-08 21:27 UTC

It’s not. That was clearly written by someone who didn’t want to think about which attribute their `AttributeError` was coming from.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-07-08 21:32 UTC

6d452e87a540e99fd82447497fee9e80a3993b9d ?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-08 21:37 UTC

Mm, this runs before `AuthenticationMiddleware`? I guess that could happen (but might indicate that this is isn’t a good use case for the context processor API).

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-07-08 21:38 UTC

That's an implicit assumption about `request.user`. I wonder which middleware is accessing that before `.user` gets assigned.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-07-08 22:19 UTC

Yeah, I don't know if it's currently possible to call `render` before the auth middleware.  If that's *not* the case anymore, then it can of course be cleaned up.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-07-08 22:20 UTC

That commit is from 2017, so some invariants may have shifted since then.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-08 22:22 UTC

Maybe that happens when rendering the error page for an exception thrown inside one of our auth backends?

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2022-07-10 17:20 UTC

I don't think auth backends ever run before middleware?

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2022-07-10 17:20 UTC

But perhaps this https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/6d452e87a540e99fd82447497fee9e80a3993b9d/zerver/middleware.py#L373 `render(` in `SessionHostDomainMiddleware` was triggering before `AuthenticationMiddleware` sometimes? (`AuthenticationMiddleware` is the last in the middleware chain)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-11 21:10 UTC

(replying to Mateusz Mandera)
> I don't think auth backends ever run before middleware?
Correct, authentication backends should always run after middleware.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-11 21:11 UTC

Yeah, I think @Mateusz Mandera flagged the right code; `AuthenticationMiddleware` sets `request.user`, and it runs after other middleware, so this block of code in our `HostDomainMiddleware`, which runs before `AuthenticationMiddleware`:
```
        request_notes = RequestNotes.get_notes(request)                                                  
        try:                                                                                             
            request_notes.realm = get_realm(subdomain)                                                   
            request_notes.has_fetched_realm = True                                                       
        except Realm.DoesNotExist:                                                                       
            if subdomain == Realm.SUBDOMAIN_FOR_ROOT_DOMAIN:                                             
                # The root domain is used for creating new                                               
                # organizations even if it does not host a realm.                                        
                return None                                                                              
                                                                                                         
            return render(request, "zerver/invalid_realm.html", status=404)                              
```

would crash.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-11 21:11 UTC

I think that points to a possible solution of setting `request.user` explicitly to `AnonymousUser` in that exception handler, since we only have that one, rather than having the context processor believe it's possible for `request.user` to be `None`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-11 21:13 UTC

I guess this block in `zulip_default_context` is probably motivated by the same issue:
```
    user_is_authenticated = False                                                                        
    if hasattr(request, "user") and hasattr(request.user, "is_authenticated"):                           
        user_is_authenticated = request.user.is_authenticated                                            
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-11 21:14 UTC

@Zixuan James Li I think a good path forward would be to try to find or write a test that uses that `invalid_realm` code path, above, and then use that code path to verify that we can do a refactor like what I described.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-11 21:28 UTC

That seems reasonable. But also, do we need to be running our `HostDomainMiddleware` before Django’s `AuthenticationMiddleware`?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-11 21:30 UTC

All `AuthenticationMiddleware` does is create a *lazy* `request.user` property, so it should be totally fine to move that earlier in the chain.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-11 22:03 UTC

I've confirmed 3 tests fail if we delete that code, so we do have some coverage here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-11 22:10 UTC

That's a good idea; we should check how the CSRF middleware works, but it seems very possible we could just move AuthenticationMiddleware 2 slots up and then get to delete this code.
```
    "zerver.middleware.HostDomainMiddleware",                                                            
    "django.middleware.csrf.CsrfViewMiddleware",                                                         
    "django.contrib.auth.middleware.AuthenticationMiddleware",                                           
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-11 22:11 UTC

(I have no reason to believe CSRF wouldn't commute with HostDomainMiddleware, but obviously we should make a reasoned decision about how we order that)

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-07-13 02:36 UTC

> but it seems very possible we could just move AuthenticationMiddleware 2 slots up and then get to delete this code.

This seems like a promising way to resolve this. Looking at the source code, I don't see how `CsrfViewMiddleware` would require `request.user`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-13 22:50 UTC

@Zixuan James Li ok, go ahead and put in a PR with a first commit that reorders these and then clenas up these checks for `request.user` not being set.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-07-14 13:42 UTC

#22478

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-07-14 13:43 UTC

Note that there is still another check in `LogRequests` that cannot be solved by reordering the middleware.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-07-14 13:44 UTC

In this case, any error that is raised before the auth middleware and after `LogRequests` makes the middleware chain end up without `request.user`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-14 17:44 UTC

What stops us from reordering `AuthenticationMiddleware` before `LogRequests`?

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-07-14 18:00 UTC

Actually, I was wrong. If we reorder `SessionMiddleware` as well and put it before `AuthenticationMiddleware` and `LogRequests`, the test cases pass without the `hasattr` check.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-14 21:58 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> What stops us from reordering `AuthenticationMiddleware` before `LogRequests`?

I think the only potential downside of that move is hinted in the comment at the top of our middleware block -- namely that anything happening before `LogRequests` isn't counted in our logged runtime for the request.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-14 21:59 UTC

`AuthenticationMiddleware` is instant, so that's not a problem; but `SessionMiddleware`, which needs to run before it, might parse the session and/or try to look the user up in the database?

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-14 22:00 UTC

So depending whether it in fact does that immediately, or just sets things up lazily so that access to `request.user` will do so, we could end up accidentally moving most of the runtime for an endpoint that does nothing beyond checking authentication out of what we're tracking in `LogRequests`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-07-14 22:25 UTC

`SessionMiddleware` doesn’t do any database lookups on `__init__` or `process_request`. It [constructs](https://github.com/django/django/blob/3.2.14/django/contrib/sessions/middleware.py#L22) some Python objects that can be used to do lookups [later](https://github.com/django/django/blob/3.2.14/django/contrib/sessions/backends/base.py#L238).

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-15 00:24 UTC

Great, I'll note that in the commit message and then merge this.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-07-15 01:44 UTC

As a side-note, since we always force evaluate the lazy `.user` attribute in `LogRequests`, are we kind of sacrificing the performance for logging? Though I imagine that the performance penalty exists only for views that do not end up needing `.user`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-15 03:21 UTC

I think we always evaluate it as part of the decorators system for (say) authentication anyway, so no.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-07-15 03:22 UTC

So I think we're getting exactly what we want -- it gets setup lazily early, potentially outside the window that we log, but the actual work of evaluating it will be inside the window that we log.

## dmypy using experience

*2022-07-19 to 2022-07-19 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/dmypy.20using.20experience/with/1406600)*

Recently, we added an option to run mypy daemon in #22346. Because I frequently rerun mypy on the entire codebase, when checking out different revisions to generate diffs of errors, mypy daemon is particularly useful for working on django-stubs refactorings. So far, there aren't any drawback when compared to the mypy cli.
The only thing is that when the configuration is changed, the daemon needs to start over, but that is not so much of a problem for the similar performance when restarted.

# This stub is a lie. These are all actually classes that inherit from a common
# base Field class. But their usage is to be attached to Model classes like this:

#   class MyModel(Model):
#       name = CharField(...)

# Due to Django metaclass magic, the effect of this assignment is that the

# string, not an instance of the `CharField` class. But this of course confuses

# objects in our codebase (and going forward, our use of the Django ORM should

## improved read-tracking with HyperLogLog ?

*2022-08-01 to 2022-08-01 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/improved.20read-tracking.20with.20HyperLogLog.20.3F/with/1413795)*

**Adam Sah** · 2022-08-01 17:32 UTC

I was re-reading about [soft deactivation](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/subsystems/sending-messages.html#soft-deactivation)...

Instead of tracking precisely which messages each user has read, I was wondering if it's worth testing a modern sketching algorithm (e.g. HyperLogLog) which approximates this data with very high accuracy using a small number of bits per user. HLL is widely used by a who's who of apps and virtually every infrastructure company.

HLL sketches can be downloaded and updated into the browser as part of local echo. On the server, we can either use a python implementation or the [pg HyperLogLog extension](https://www.google.com/search?q=postgresql+hll+extension) which is supported for self-hosted PostgreSQL, and PostgreSQL on AWS, GCP and Azure.

Obviously, what we have now works so it's not urgent, but could be valuable for scaling to large numbers numbers of messages, compressing memory or pg footprints, etc.

LMK if helpful, happy to look into a prototype. No worries if distracting...

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-08-01 17:50 UTC

Read message counting isn’t a good use case for HyperLogLog. Firstly, if there are 1413795 messages on the server, and HyperLogLog tells me that I’ve read 1430000 ± 2% of them, that doesn’t help me distinguish between zero unreads and a few thousand unreads, which is a very important difference. Secondly, it doesn’t tell me which messages are unread, it only gives me a count.

**Adam Sah** · 2022-08-01 20:58 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> Read message counting isn’t a good use case for HyperLogLog. Firstly, if there are 1413795 messages on the server, and HyperLogLog tells me that I’ve read 1430000 ± 2% of them, that doesn’t help me distinguish between zero unreads and a few thousand unreads, which is a very important difference. Sec …
Sorry for not being precise: one can use the same sketch to perform set membership testing, i.e. whether a user has read a message or not. Also, the 2% error number that's often thrown around in fact can be (dramatically) improved for cases like ours with lower cardinality and more storage bits available per user. If you look at the Google HLL++ version they use, error rates drop to <0.5%, i.e. very unlikely to tell you someone has read something that they haven't.


## Breaking down rest_dispatch

*2022-08-01 to 2022-08-02 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Breaking.20down.20rest_dispatch/with/1413798)*

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-01 17:36 UTC

We have a all-in-one `rest_dispatch` function that dynamically handles all kinds of requests and dispatches them to the appropriate view function. I found this pattern particularly not so good for type checking in terms of the function signature.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-01 17:40 UTC

When there is the flag `allow_anonymous_user_web`, the second parameter of the view function is required to be `Union[UserProfile, AnonymousUser]`;
When the view is only intended for remote servers, the second parameter is required to be `Union[UserProfile, RemoteZulipServer]` for authenticated views;
When the view is not authenticated, there is no requirement for the second parameter (we simply use `path` instead of `rest_path` in this case);
When the view is authenticated, the second parameter should be `UserProfile`;
In all cases, the first parameter should be `HttpRequest`.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-01 17:43 UTC

The current `rest_path` does not handle the variety of authentication methods and the authenticated entity (if there is one), which is understandable prior to `ParamSpec`. But I think now that we have the tool available for us, we might want to figure out a way to properly type check the parameters of view functions.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-01 17:50 UTC

I think a way to do this will be breaking `rest_path` into something like `remote_server_rest_path`, `public_rest_path`, and `user_rest_path`.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-01 17:51 UTC

To avoid duplication, we wrap common logic for handling REST requests in a separate function.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-08-01 17:53 UTC

I definitely want `rest_dispatch` split up; it does way too much. I’d also like to split its authentication jobs from its method-dispatch jobs; the latter would be better handled by Django’s built-in [class-based views](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.0/topics/class-based-views/).

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-01 17:53 UTC

Then each `*_path` function will have an accurate type annotation for what kind of view function will be expected. A limitation of this new API though is that we cannot pass multiple view functions in one call to the `*_path`function, because `ParamSpec`will bound to a single view function and it will not become compatible with the signature of other view functions unless we define one `ParamSpec` for each HTTP method.

## The proper way to deal with `Promise` objects

*2022-08-05 to 2022-08-08 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/The.20proper.20way.20to.20deal.20with.20.60Promise.60.20objects/with/1415638)*

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-05 16:07 UTC

Django's `gettext_lazy` returns a proxy object as a subclass of `Promise`, whose value is evaluated every time when a method on it is called, converted to a `str`, or used with operators like `%`, `+`, and `<`.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-05 16:10 UTC

The fact that it is a proxied object makes it behave essentially the same as a regular `str` in most situations; we can call `.format` on it with no problem.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-05 16:14 UTC

However, we can't narrow it to a `str` with an `isinstance` check, and it cannot be serialized by `orjson`. This gets brought up is in [012113c5](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/012113c5426444e9dd0f9b9cc642f3af2074e604). So it is necessary to always acknowledge the type checker that we are dealing with a `Promise` object.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-05 16:21 UTC

But then the question is how we are supposed to properly type `Promise` in the stubs. The very minimal type annotation would look like this:
```
class Promise:
    def __init__(self, args: Any, kw: Any) -> None: ...
    def __reduce__(self) -> Tuple[Any, Tuple[Any]]: ...
    def __lt__(self, other: Any) -> bool: ...
    def __mod__(self, rhs: Any) -> Any: ...
    def __add__(self, other: Any) -> Any: ...
    def __radd__(self, other: Any) -> Any: ...
    def __deepcopy__(self, memo: Any): ...
```
Since `Promise` is not a subtype of `str`, it causes problems when we call a library function where a `str` is expected. 
This also forbids the use of methods like `format` proxied from `str`.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-05 16:23 UTC

One approach will be supporting comprehensive type checking on `Promise`, which will take a lot of work to implement and test the plugin.
Since `Promise` actually represents other kinds of proxied objects where the underlying classes might not be `str`, there is some added complexity to the implementation.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-05 16:26 UTC

Another approach will be requiring us to deal with `Promise` objects carefully whenever it is used: call `str()` before passing a `Promise` object; always use `getattr` to call methods instead of `.` accessing members.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-05 16:31 UTC

I'm more inclined to solve it the second way after [learning the mypy apis and running into solving the edge cases for a plugin](https://github.com/PIG208/django-stubs/blob/5199a662443a356ec8b19afc4b8341073bceb5b0/mypy_django_plugin/transformers/functional.py). It was fun implementing a plugin hook, but it will take too much work for this infrequent use case. I'd love to hear what other people feel about this solution.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-05 17:00 UTC

Opened #22665.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-05 19:55 UTC

I posted a couple comments, but I don't understand the places where you switch from the `_lazy` variant to the non-lazy form. The reason we often want to do the lazy version is when defining a string variable at top-level, we want the string to be translated using the request language, not the process startup language (of always English), and doing so requires the lazy construction.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-05 20:05 UTC

We weren't using the `_lazy` form in the first place, so I removed the alias to avoid changing the behavior. This issue is now fixed.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-08-05 21:56 UTC

I think you overcomplicated things for yourself trying to write a mypy plugin that deals with `Promise[…]` in full generality. My proposal would be to write a django-stubs-specific `class _StrPromise(Promise)` (similar to `class _MonkeyPatchedWSGIResponse(_WSGIResponse)`) that has the string-specific methods. For anything more complicated than that, we should explicitly force the promise with `str()` or [`force_str()`](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.0/ref/utils/#django.utils.encoding.force_str) at the appropriate point.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-08-05 22:01 UTC

It’s a *feature* that mypy will prevent you from passing an arbitrary `_StrPromise` to a function that expects `str`, because that won’t always work at runtime (for example, anything that checks `isinstance(…, str)` would fail), and even things that work at runtime might work unexpectedly (because they evaluate differently in different `with django.utils.translation.override(…)` blocks).

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-06 01:07 UTC

Yes, that sounds like a fair plan.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-08 14:55 UTC

To implement this, we can either copy the typeshed definitions for all methods on `str` or create a plugin to proxy the `str` specific methods.
My proposal is that we will keep copying definitions for magic methods for operators because mypy doesn't have a hook for refining operator types, and implement a plugin hook for the rest.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-08 14:56 UTC

This plugin should be simpler than the full-blown one since we only deal with `builtins.str` in this case.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-08 17:59 UTC

#22665 and https://github.com/typeddjango/django-stubs/pull/689 are updated.

**Christopher Chong** · 2022-08-14 10:27 UTC

I would like to get your thoughts on the implementation if it achieves "do a sub-select with an ORDER BY ... FOR UPDATE" described [here](https://stackoverflow.com/a/27015834) — which I would like to get your confirmation first before I create a common helper method and apply them to all methods that do message flags bulk updates.

1. 2. I have tried to create a deadlock scenario by trying to send 2 requests simultaneously (using xargs and curl in terminal) to `/mark_all_as_read`, however from the server logs it seemed those 2 requests still got executed sequentially — so I failed to reproduce the deadlock scenario — though I have tested that `/mark_all_as_read` still worked fine after the changes I made to `do_mark_all_as_read` in the PR.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-14 16:55 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-14 16:56 UTC

@Tim Abbott I was able to reproduce the deadlock situation! And also verified that the changes I introduced [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/22710) stops deadlock from happening anymore.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-27 23:40 UTC

**Christopher Chong** · 2022-08-28 10:16 UTC

**Christopher Chong** · 2022-09-04 04:01 UTC

Yeah, it's hard to know. I've talked a decent number of people using Flask, which is one of the lightweight Python frameworks that also supports python-social-auth, and many of them would not recommend Flask over Django for the sort of thing we're building. 

There's probably newer frameworks that would be better if we were starting today, especially if we were willing to consider a different programming language, for example. Certainly Python and Django are not great for asynchronous services, and probably even if we project forward the progress being made on those areas, it's still only be kinda OK, not amazing. But I think no matter what we'd picked, we'd either run into the constraints coming from the third party's design decisions that we disagree with, or discovering that we need to write our own thing because the third party doesn't provide it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-16 02:45 UTC

I think to some extent, our perspectives are different in part because I spend a lot of my time supporting folks doing feature work, where one sees a lot more cases where the framework made our lives easier by avoiding us needing to write an X because the framework came with a perfectly suitable or easily adapted X. Whereas you spend more time on classes of things that tend to focus attention on things that are problematic.

For me, this feels like a neat solution to not have our own version method dispatching, and we don't really have to follow django's way of writing views.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-16 03:05 UTC

I suspect our difference in perspective is less about the area of code we focus on, and more about what it means to “understand” something. This may be an unfair characterization, but perhaps: you want an interface that corresponds with what the developer was thinking at the time they wrote the code, while I want an interface that corresponds with what actually happens so one can easily verify that it corresponds to what one’s thinking now.

**tatsuya6502** · 2022-08-16 06:24 UTC

> Does PGroonga do stemming for different languages?

I got answers for my questions by @kou , a PGroonga/Groonga maintainer.

1. There is a stemmer called `TokenFilterStem` in PGroonga, but you need to install it separately and enable it when creating a PGroonga index:
  - Install `groonga-token-filter-stem` package from `ppa:groonga/ppa` PPA. ([doc](https://groonga.org/docs/install/ubuntu.html))
  - Create a PGroonga index with token filter(s). ([doc](https://pgroonga.github.io/reference/create-index-using-pgroonga.html#custom-token-filters))
2. The stemmer is built upon Snowball and [supports various European languages](https://snowballstem.org/algorithms/):
  - When creating an index, you can specify the language of the stemmer as `TokenFilterStem("algorithm", "french")`. ([doc](https://groonga.org/docs/reference/token_filters/token_filter_stem.html))
  - English is the default.

Note that to support searching in multiple languages, you need to create multiple indices with different languages; one index for each language.

**Matt** · 2022-08-16 13:14 UTC

I don't think we want to get into stemming- at least not initially. That adds a lot of complexity. I looked into it last week and it's messy. From a usability standpoint, each organization would need to declare a language, if it's not one we index for we'd need to add one, then use that column, etc. PGroonga does substring matching fine: So a search for "obvious" returns "obvious" and "obviously", etc. If you're giving the search too much, and searching for "searching" you will not get "search" or "searches"... That's a pretty natural pitfall. Some of us might remember when having to do the same to webcrawler... I mean yahoo ... I mean dogpile... I mean google. :)

So for a more accurate comparison, wouldn't we want english stemming enabled on PGroonga?
(but still skipping any configuration along those lines)

**Matt** · 2022-08-16 16:22 UTC

I will dig more, but at first blush, if you let PGroonga "be", it does a "good" job of understanding all of the languages, but if you tell it to look at a specific index, it will then do a "great" job  of that language, and a "poor" job of the other languages.

Of course, we could allow each organization to pick its "natural" language, with "all" being an option. For multi-org setups this could result in a large number of indices on the message table, as each supported language would need its own stemmed index, and every message would need to then get indexed accordingly- probably not an observable latency for 3-4 languages, but absolutely 3-4x index bloat versus a single.

**Matt** · 2022-08-16 16:50 UTC

It's also worth noting that PG does support [Snowball](https://snowballstem.org/) dictionaries now (since PG10), https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/textsearch-dictionaries.html#TEXTSEARCH-SNOWBALL-DICTIONARY so that's a potential upgrade as well.

**kou** · 2022-09-01 02:15 UTC

For stop word:
We can implement it with the search-time approach not the index-time approach.
The search-time approach means that we replace a stop word in query with a word that is never matched such as "XXXXXXXXX".
We can implement the search-time approach by synonym expansion: https://pgroonga.github.io/how-to/synonym-expansion.html
We need to register a record per stop word like the followings:

```sql
 INSERT INTO synonyms (term, synonyms) VALUES ('i', ARRAY['XXXXXXXXXX']);
 INSERT INTO synonyms (term, synonyms) VALUES ('my', ARRAY['XXXXXXXXXX']);
-- ...
```

Pros for the search-time approach:
* We don't need to reindex when we update our stop words. (We need to reindex with the index-time approach.)
Cons for the search-time approach:
* Index size isn't reduced. (Index size is reduced with the index-time approach.)

Search performances of them will be same. (No big difference.)

**Matt** · 2022-09-06 18:24 UTC

escape_html is pretty simple, and easy to customize.
```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION zulip.escape_html(text)
 RETURNS text
 LANGUAGE sql
 IMMUTABLE
AS $function$
  SELECT replace(replace(replace(replace(replace($1, '&', '&amp;'), '<', '&lt;'),
                                 '>', '&gt;'), '"', '&quot;'), '''', '&#39;');
$function$
```

## Using has_request_variables with positional-only parameters

*2022-08-24 to 2022-08-24 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Using.20has_request_variables.20with.20positional-only.20parameters/with/1423969)*

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-24 01:42 UTC

We have wrapper functions returned decorators that use `has_request_variables`. To type such functions with `ParamSpec`, the concatenated parameters need to be positional-only. `has_request_variables` does not support the use case of positional-only variables, so there needs to be some change.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-24 01:43 UTC

Specifically, we are talking about `webhook_view` and `authenticated_uploads_api_view`.

This is how `authenticated_uploads_api_view` is supposed to be typed with `Concatenate` and `ParamSpec`:

```python
def authenticated_uploads_api_view(
    skip_rate_limiting: bool = False,
) -> Callable[
    [Callable[Concatenate[HttpRequest, UserProfile, ParamT], HttpResponse]],
    Callable[Concatenate[HttpRequest, str, ParamT], HttpResponse],
]:
    def _wrapped_view_func(
        view_func: Callable[Concatenate[HttpRequest, UserProfile, ParamT], HttpResponse]
    ) -> Callable[Concatenate[HttpRequest, str, ParamT], HttpResponse]:
        @csrf_exempt
        @has_request_variables
        @wraps(view_func)
        def _wrapped_func_arguments(
            request: HttpRequest,
            api_key: str = REQ(),
            /,
            *args: ParamT.args,
            **kwargs: ParamT.kwargs,
        ) -> HttpResponse:
```

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-24 01:44 UTC

This use case is pretty rare and in fact, it only occurs in the above-mentioned decorators.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-08-24 01:46 UTC

There’s no reason for `authenticated_uploads_api_view` to be a decorator. It’s only ever used to decorate a function that’s then immediately called.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-24 01:46 UTC

One way to solve this is to support positonal-only parameters with `has_request_variable`. This can be done with a reasonable amount of work, but it adds complexity to the already complex implementation. Another approach will be inlining `api_key` by accessing `request.POST` and `request.GET`.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-24 01:47 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> There’s no reason for `authenticated_uploads_api_view` to be a decorator. It’s only ever used to decorate a function that’s then immediately called.
Then probably coming up with a solution is more necessary for `webhook_view`. We can refactor away `authenticated_uploads_api_view`.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-08-24 01:49 UTC

Getting `api_key` from `request.POST` and `request.GET` seems fine. I question whether a decorator is the best idiom for `webhook_view` too, but we can delay that question to another day.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-24 01:56 UTC

We can potentially get rid of decorators used in `rest_dispatch` as well. There should be a cleaner way to handle authentication and other side effects.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-08-24 01:59 UTC

It does seem like we have too many decorators. I suspect what happened was that someone copied one of the Django decorators in order to make a little change, and started an avalanche of decorators.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-24 02:13 UTC

Opened #22781. Refactoring away `authenticated_uploads_api_view` falls outside the scope of this fix. That change is better done by restructuring `rest_dispatch` along with the removal of other similar decorators.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-08-24 02:17 UTC

`get_api_key_from_request` could be written to use `has_request_variables` itself, if you want this to be a more minimal change.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-24 02:20 UTC

## Usage of asyncio in django

*2022-08-28 to 2022-09-29 · 13 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Usage.20of.20asyncio.20in.20django/with/1426680)*

**Christopher Chong** · 2022-08-28 10:42 UTC

I have heard a lot about the benefits of using asynchronous framework in backend server code (reducing API latency for API that involves blocking I/O)  — I noticed that we're using `asyncio` in our tornado codes, but not in the main django codes. What's the reason behind not using `asyncio` in the django codes (or are we already using it)?

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-08-28 17:55 UTC

Django's asynchronous support came out in [3.1](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.1/releases/3.1/), while it does come with performance improvements, it also requires quite a bit of refactoring/investigation to get it working, and we can't really drop-in `asyncio` and expect that it will just work.

Since this feature is relatively new, there are still some parts missing, such as [transaction support](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.1/topics/async/#queries-the-orm), and [async cache API](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.1/releases/4.0/#cache) was just added in 4.0. To fully take advantage of async views, it's better that we migrate entirely from WSGI to ASGI. These are something that we likely will do but there isn't a clear plan for that yet.

**Aman shenoy** · 2022-08-28 18:17 UTC

Hello

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-08-28 23:06 UTC

One of the upstream problems I ran into when experimenting with the async cache API is https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/33625.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-08-28 23:12 UTC

More fundamentally, Django’s ORM architecture where property accesses might be implicitly converted into database queries is problematic, since there’s no way to make those accesses implicitly asynchronous. The whole point of `async` is to be explicit about where execution might yield to other tasks.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-29 19:37 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> More fundamentally, Django’s ORM architecture where property accesses might be implicitly converted into database queries is problematic, since there’s no way to make those accesses implicitly asynchronous. The whole point of `async` is to be explicit about where execution might yield to other tasks …

Yeah, that's a problem. I wonder if we should try contributing a patch to upstream Django that adds a Django setting to disable lazy evaluation of queries, with that async context as the background for why it's important for their async roadmap.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-29 19:38 UTC

Because I'd love to just enable such a setting overall. And I think it might be one of the blockers for us being able to use asyncio for a couple API endpoints where we'd benefit from it substantially.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-29 19:41 UTC

One of the most significant visible benefits we might get if we were able to use `asyncio` in Django requests would be converting the `/` endpoint, which currently does about 70 database queries in series, to instead do them in parallel; I'd expect that to potentially shave 50% or more from the app's initial loading latency, if we were just able to do the handful of most expensive things asynchronously with each other.

But probably converting some of our queue workers to async would be easier to do first (since it wouldn't require ASGI or anything) and also have significant benefits.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-08-29 19:42 UTC

And I suspect we could use an audit-based or "mocking in tests" based approach to guard some  queue workers against doing database queries; a lot of them are only a few dozen lines of code total.

**v3ss0n** · 2022-09-29 08:37 UTC

how is with django 4.1 now , since it is async ready on ORM and Handlers , Would it possible to replace tornado in this place?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-09-29 09:44 UTC

That’s an exaggerated reading of the release notes—the word “ready” doesn’t appear anywhere in them. In truth, there are still huge holes in the async APIs. Just in the ORM, there’s still no async support for accessing related fields, saving/refreshing objects, or transactions. What async support it has is still just an async wrapper around synchronous code, which will be slow. Async handlers aren’t new; what’s new is async handlers for class-based views, which we don’t currently use much. There’s been no progress on my [cache pooling issue](https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/33625). Meanwhile, there’s a more pressing [`AutoField` regression](https://code.djangoproject.com/ticket/34058) that blocks us from updating to Django 4.1 at all for the moment.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-03-15 01:00 UTC

I think the thing that I actually want to do here is work towards bot email addresses not being a thing that exists in the API. I've been vaguely thinking in the direction of moving our API authentication structure away from the current (username, api_key) pair that you send as an HTTP Basic authentication combined `{email_address}:{api_key}` to just a single API key token that we generate that might have the form `{human-pneumonic}-{api_key}`, where the human-readable part is really just there to help you figure out, given one of these entries in a configuration file, which account it goes with. I've not through about the precise encoding details, but I'm imagining something like:

* If you named a bot "GitHub Bot" when creating it, we'd generate a token that looks like "github-bot-abcd1234" for you. If you rotate its API key, it'll do the same algorithm but using the new/current name.
* If you're a human user, we'd generate an API token that looks like "tim-abbott-abcd1234".

The nice thing about needing only one thing rather than two things is that  (1) the email addresses we're currently using are mutable and thus bad and (2) their main purpose is to help you, when reading your `zuliprc` file, figure out which bot something is.

## django-stubs

*2022-10-06 to 2022-10-06 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/django-stubs/with/1445351)*

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-10-06 02:23 UTC

With thousands of typing errors fixed, [django-stubs](https://github.com/typeddjango/django-stubs) has now been integrated (#18777) into the codebase.

This change allows us to type-check important features of Django such as `QuerySet`s and frequently used classes like `HttpRequest`, `HttpResponse`, `django.conf.settings`, etc., along with a pretty comprehensive set of stubs. Without us having to provide type annotations on our own.

---

For people who aren't familiar with it, django-stubs is superpowered by a mypy plugin that comes with it, which helps type-checking some really dynamic features that can't really be described with static type annotations.

For example, some methods available on a `Manager` such as `all`, return a `QuerySet` of the managed instance of a model. The mypy plugin is able to narrow down its type to be `QuerySet[UserProfile]`, and further knows the attributes (as well as their types) on the `QuerySet` object when type checking.

It is also capable of checking the types of arguments passed to the `create` method.
```
Book.objects.create(publisher_id=None)
```
or the arguments for `.filter` calls.

In the future, we no longer need to provide type annotations for the model fields.

For example, a `TextField()` no longer needs to be defined with a type annotation of `str`:
```diff
class Realm:
   ...
-   default_code_block_language: Optional[str] = models.TextField(null=True, default=None)
+   default_code_block_language = models.TextField(null=True, default=None) 
```

---

Integrating django-stubs also brings a lot of positive side effects. We have reworked the helper methods like `client_get` to be type safe in terms of `kwargs`, stopped monkey-patching `HttpRequest` and instead introduced `RequestNotes` as a type-safe workaround, tightened type annotations, none-checks,  and `TypedDict`s throughout the codebase. 

Huge thanks to @Anders Kaseorg, @Tim Abbott, as well as many others for reviewing and helping with all of the django-stubs-related work.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-10-06 02:24 UTC

We will probably work on some follow-ups like providing better type annotations for the events.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-10-06 02:37 UTC

This is huge -- in multiple meanings of the word.  Thank you for your perseverance getting all of the issues fixed!

As discussed in the above thread, as we do not want to allow the user to move messages that are too old and since we cannot always check such condition at the client itself (because we may not have all messages of the topic), we would show the modal and then when user tries to move the messages we show a confirmation prompt. ## check_message realm argument

*2022-10-30 to 2022-10-31 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/check_message.20realm.20argument/with/1457039)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2022-10-30 19:41 UTC

Our core function for creating the Message object when a message is being sent (through a variety of codepaths), is `check_message`:
```
def check_message(
    sender: UserProfile,
    client: Client,
    addressee: Addressee,
    message_content_raw: str,
    realm: Optional[Realm] = None,
    ....
) -> SendMessageRequest:
```

The `realm` argument was `Optional` so far, which wasn't a big deal until the recently merged `Message.realm` denormalization. Now the function needs to know the `realm` value to set it correctly on the Message.  Which poses the question of whether we should make it a required argument? 

In the commit adding `Message.realm` column I made this function simply infer the right value based on the sender:
```
    if realm is None:
        realm = sender.realm
```
but this just creates a perpetual question of `are we sure every cross-realm bot message-sending codepath delivers a realm value in the argument so that the sender.realm inference doesn't get used`? (because that'd be a bug, creating a Message in the system bot realm instead of recipient realm).  I didn't find any bugs in my investigation right now, but there isn't much preventing a regression being introduced in a refactoring etc.

Making this a required argument will be a bit messy though, forcing a whole bunch of functions to plumb the value through, when it's mostly unnecessary, because `sender.realm` is almost-always right. An alternative answer could be that we should just finally push on  getting rid of cross-realm bots which would make this whole problem non-existant. Any thoughts on this?

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-10-30 22:47 UTC

I think it is quite valuable to continue the work in #17520, so that we are guarded by the invariant that `message.realm` is always `sender.realm`. It would than be easy for us to remove the `realm` parameter.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-10-31 13:40 UTC

I think removing cross-realm bots is a useful step to take in general, to reduce unused complexity.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-31 22:03 UTC

I think #17520 is something we definitely want to do.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-10-31 22:06 UTC

The long term design of this detail probably depends a little bit on how we want to design any future native "Cross-realm stream" feature, which I kinda don't want to think through designing right now. 

I **think** probably any reasonable version of that design, which includes variants where we have cross-realm streams that live in a special "Cross-realm messages" realm or all sort of other weird designs, would have the `Realm` be a function of the `(sender, addressee)` pair; and any additional complexity would go into how `addressee` objects are put together? I'm not sure.

    // Now, we can just compare the first cached message to the first                                    
    // message ID in the stream; if it's older, we're good, otherwise,

    // cache.                                                                                            
    const first_cached_message = all_messages_data.first();                                              
    return first_cached_message.id <= sub.first_message_id;                                              
```

I would expect those `api_post` calls to fail with the `/json/` style URLs; so ideally we'd figure out if that is indeed a bug, and if so, fix it as well as sweep the tests that might be relying on it.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-11-04 19:03 UTC

I think the problem lies in `zerver.lib.rest`.

```python
    elif not request.path.startswith("/api") and request.user.is_authenticated:
        # Authenticated via sessions framework, only CSRF check needed
        auth_kwargs = {}
        if "override_api_url_scheme" in view_flags:
            auth_kwargs["skip_rate_limiting"] = True
        target_function = csrf_protect(authenticated_json_view(target_function, **auth_kwargs))

    # most clients (mobile, bots, etc) use HTTP basic auth and REST calls, where instead of
    # username:password, we use email:apiKey
    elif "Authorization" in request.headers:
        # Wrap function with decorator to authenticate the user before
        # proceeding
        target_function = authenticated_rest_api_view(
            allow_webhook_access="allow_incoming_webhooks" in view_flags,
        )(target_function)
```

Usually prior to accessing a `/json/` endpoint in the test suite, we use `self.login_user` to get an authenticated session.
This is not the case in `test_realm_playgrounds`. So `not request.path.startswith("/api") and request.user.is_authenticated` evaluates to `False`,
and since `api_post` sets the `Authorization` header, we proceed to
```python
        target_function = authenticated_rest_api_view(
            allow_webhook_access="allow_incoming_webhooks" in view_flags,
        )(target_function)
```
without verifying if the endpoint actually is for api.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-11-04 19:06 UTC

Logically, it is a bug *because* it allows the user to access views where HTTP basic auth is not allowed.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-11-04 19:10 UTC

I'm not sure if there is anything out there that relies on the behavior (i.e. a bot that uses its `email:api_key` to access json endpoints), but if there is any they should have just switched to the correct `/api/` URL instead.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-11-04 19:13 UTC

This bug also allows the client to access views that are `/json/`-only, namely `json/fetch_api_key` and `json/subscriptions/exists`, with an API key.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2022-11-04 19:39 UTC

Opened #23444

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-11-04 20:24 UTC

(replying to Zixuan James Li)

Yeah, I feel confident enough that such clients should be rare to just change it; the fix for users is trivial and we've never at any point documented/suggested using the /json/ endpoints with API key authentication.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-11-04 20:25 UTC

I'd like to pitch moving `propagate_mode` on message updates to being a full-on proper Enum (either in the vanilla Python stdlib sense, or in the sense of any Parse Don't Validate schema-ing libraries that may come to be - I know there's currently chatter about this already in this stream).

On that basis I'd split the commit into the former and latter, to separate the simple add/switch situation from where thought goes into specific renaming. I don't know the code well enough to suggest if some of the short exception names could be more descriptive, but `Invalid`, `Custom` and `Diff` seem rather terse just reading the summary :)

- Get `docker-zulip` out of the cert management game entirely and replumb the entrypoint to stop doing certbot-related things (there's several places this will touch)

I think I need to do some refresher reading on docs I'm fairly sure I've seen about where TLS termination has to happen in the Zulip stack, and try to work backwards from what is typical in containerized deployment environments to see what the path from A to B is.

I noticed someone in the docker-zulip repo PRs/issues had called out that we have a bit of a "supercontainer" doing many things in one image; after a quick read I think they're not wrong, and that this complicates matters a bit: if I'm imagining a typical containerized deploy of something like Zulip, it'd have a separate ingress container entirely when running locally/homelab/etc. (and when deployed to some hosting provider, that ingress "container" is unlikely to even be a container I control, but is instead a load balancer provided by the platform), a container dedicated to the database, a container running just the bare Python app as exposed by Django, etc. This makes our use of certbot within the container probably surprising behavior.

**Josh Klar** · 2022-12-28 20:53 UTC

Though, it does seem like there's a bit of existing art from respectable sources on this: `docker-swag` for nginx+certbot+php deployments also manages certbot within the container, on a cron job: https://github.com/linuxserver/docker-swag. That said, that image seems to be a "for local use" image, judging by the existence of the smaller https://github.com/linuxserver/docker-nginx which still does nginx+php, but skips the TLS bits.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-12-28 22:45 UTC

Prior art for full applications like Discourse, Gitea, Mastodon, and Nextcloud might be more relevant than for individual application components like nginx.

**Josh Klar** · 2022-12-28 23:00 UTC

Good thought:

- Gitea is a complicated example to a degree: the application itself supports plaintext HTTP end-to-end (no HTTPS redirects in the app), implements self-signed certificate creation and ACME themselves, *or* is happy to be spoken plaintext HTTP behind a TLS-terminating load balancer. This seems different enough from our case to be difficult to use as an example (I personally used to run Gitea behind nginx+letsencrypt, I believe actually the linuxserver.io image I linked above). https://docs.gitea.io/en-us/https-setup/
- Mastodon seems to rather strongly hint at following the "speak plaintext to me, terminate your TLS at a reverse proxy" pattern: https://github.com/mastodon/mastodon/blob/main/Dockerfile (plus other grepping around the source tree)
- Discourse is happy either way: [they document how to make a bundled nginx server speak HTTPS](https://meta.discourse.org/t/set-up-https-support-with-lets-encrypt/40709) as well as [providing your own SSL cert](https://meta.discourse.org/t/allow-ssl-https-for-your-discourse-docker-setup/13847). This seems so far to be the closest analogue to what we do (they use s6 init in their container(s) to do a "supercontainer", too)

**Josh Klar** · 2022-12-28 23:02 UTC

That said, it appears neither Gitea or Discourse do any fiddling with `/etc/certbot` in their certificate pipeline, so there's still a good bit of digging I'll need to do here.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-12-28 23:05 UTC

I think we do that to help you avoid tripping Let’s Encrypt [rate limits](https://letsencrypt.org/docs/rate-limits/) if you rebuild your container too frequently.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-12-05 19:47 UTC

Hm.  I don't feel like I go looking through the audit logs frequently enough to have a strong opinion here.  In the abstract, the "JSON dict with keys named `1` and `2` to store old/new values" pattern is ... very odd, and not really one I would have naturally chosen.  It looks like this came about from 01bf99ec65af650f019a7997e7dd7ddaf1ca4797, when we started tracking user counts.  Which I *guess* is useful, in that we can do [this](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/c3475e83ecb0632a28af570a3c96cb2650c5f164/zerver/actions/users.py#L201-L214) during role change:

The creator of CommonMark just introduced [djot](https://github.com/jgm/djot), a lightweight successor to Markdown with sane parsing rules and extensibility.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-05 21:29 UTC

Cool! Reading their list of variations from CommonMark on the Rationale page, most of them seem great. The one that I think would be problematic for our context is this:

> Block-level elements can't interrupt paragraphs (or headings), because of goal 7. So in djot the following is a single paragraph, not (as commonmark sees it) a paragraph followed by an ordered list followed by a block quote followed by a section heading: ```` My favorite number is probably the numbe …

Requiring people to put a blank line between text and a list works out very poorly -- Zulip's markup originally worked that way, because Markdown did, and it was a source of constant complaints.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-05 21:34 UTC

I guess some existing Zulip Markdown extensions we'd need to think about were we building on top of this include:
* Spoiler blocks and math blocks; seems like we could use the same extension strategy on top of code blocks we use today. (Perhaps we could suggest them to `djot` as options to include in their official syntax, since they're of general interest)
* Linkifiers -- that's something that would need to integrate into the parser somehow, but perhaps could be a postprocessor just fine.
* Implementation considerations like security/runnability in a browser frontend.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-05 21:35 UTC

I suppose we could consider opening issues in `djot` for some of those items we'd want with a view towards being able to switch to it without ending up with our own nonstandard model, without first deciding we definitely will be able to.

In CommonMark, a numbered list starting from 1 interrupts a paragraph, but not starting from [any other number](https://spec.commonmark.org/0.30/#example-304). This also [confuses](https://github.com/commonmark/commonmark-spec/issues/599) [people](https://talk.commonmark.org/t/ordered-sublists-must-start-with-1-or-they-dont-embed/2704).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-12-06 01:03 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-06 02:45 UTC

Structurally I think the issue is basically a problem of priorities: needing to automatically hard wrap text where you have a `1.` in the middle of the paragraph are rare. Wanting to write a bulleted or numbered list and not have it render wrong if you don't follow particular whitespace rules is a common need. (Hard wrapping of paragraphs isn't even a thing one usually does in the Zulip compose box at all).

A good solution here should make the common need Just Work, at the cost of making hard wrapping a bit messier to implement correctly, and this decision in `djot` feels like a misprioritization.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-12-06 03:00 UTC

I dunno, I don’t think the priorities are *wrong*.

Maybe the least-bad solution would be for djot to standardize two modes:

* a default mode where paragraphs can be wrapped without changing the output, and the extra blank lines before lists are required, intended for longer documents to be maintained over time where source readability is more important,
* a significant-newlines mode where newlines indicate a line break, and the extra blank lines before lists are optional, intended for short comments and chat messages that are probably going to be written once and rendered.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2022-12-06 03:03 UTC

This split already exists to some degree in the Markdown world, with e.g. GitHub rendering `*.md` files more like the former and comments more like the latter.

## /etc/zulip/zulip.toml?

*2022-12-06 to 2022-12-07 · 22 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/.2Fetc.2Fzulip.2Fzulip.2Etoml.3F/with/1475060)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-06 18:58 UTC

One of the quirks of Zulip's [server-level settings](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/subsystems/settings.html) is that they split between two places: `/etc/zulip/settings.py` and `/etc/zulip/zulip.conf`. 

(We also have `/etc/zulip/zulip-secrets.conf` for secrets, but I think we're happy with that aspect of the design). 

While both files can be accessed by Python code, only the `zulip.conf` settings are available to puppet within using the (very slow) `scripts/get-django-setting` helper; this can result in some duplication and unnecessary complexity. Additionally, while we can edit `zulip.conf` programmatically via `crudini`, that isn't easy to do safely with `settings.py`, which makes life harder if we want to do things like rename settings or set an explicit default value for something without requiring the system administrator to manually handle that during an upgrade.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-12-06 19:00 UTC

(Tangential to this discussion, but it seems like a notable omission that https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/subsystems/settings.html doesn't even mention `/etc/zulip/zulip.conf`)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-06 19:00 UTC

@Anders Kaseorg proposed that we consider merging these into a single TOML file, say `/etc/zulip/zulip.toml`. This would solve basically all of the problems noted above:
* Unlike `settings.py`, TOML files are machine-editable.
* Unlike the `zulip.conf` format,  TOML files support lists/dictionaries, so it can express more complex things like the SAML configuration that currently live in `settings.py`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-06 19:02 UTC

The messiest issue we'd need to deal with is this:
* Zulip's LDAP configuration configuration currently involves importing some things; we'd need to tweak the configuration language for those nontrivially, or have an escape hatch of a `/etc/zulip/extra_settings.py` where you could put extra Python code to do things like set additional Django settings that might involve importing modules or whatnot.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-12-06 19:02 UTC

Does it provide enough rope to have settings preference previously-set values, à la:
```python3
SOCIAL_AUTH_SAML_SP_ENTITY_ID = "https://" + EXTERNAL_HOST

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-06 19:04 UTC

But aside from that, I think it would be doable to write a tool that generates a `zulip.toml` from your existing configuration (and maybe even automates the "upgrade documentation comments" step of our upgrade process) that would work smoothly for most installations.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-06 19:04 UTC

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> Does it provide enough rope to have settings preference previously-set values, à la: ```python3 SOCIAL_AUTH_SAML_SP_ENTITY_ID = "https://" + EXTERNAL_HOST ```

I think we'd need to just move that code to Python, as the default, and you'd only set that property if you actually need to override the default value.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2022-12-06 19:06 UTC

I don't see any way around repetition for things like:
```python3
SOCIAL_AUTH_SAML_ORG_INFO = {
    "en-US": {
        "displayname": "Example, Inc. Zulip",
        "name": "zulip",
        "url": "{}{}".format("https://", EXTERNAL_HOST),
    },
}
```

But I think that's a small price to pay.

**Josh Klar** · 2022-12-06 19:06 UTC

@Alex Vandiver no, but you can have something like [Dhall](https://dhall-lang.org/) (or do as Pulumi and Terraform CDK did and have TypeScript output config files) generate your configs to get to that world. I've done this for "type safe YAML", eg CI configs

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-06 19:06 UTC

One question I have is whether TOML is the right language; in particular, would this workflow provide us a path to reworking the insanity of how `docker-zulip` manages its settings to no longer involve a YAML file containing values that get passed via the environment as individual strings and then parsed and dumped into a Python file.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-06 19:07 UTC

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> I don't see any way around repetition for things like: ```python3 SOCIAL_AUTH_SAML_ORG_INFO = { "en-US": { "displayname": "Example, Inc. Zulip", "name": "zulip", "url": "{}{}".format("https://", EXTERNAL_HOST), }, } ``` But I think that's a small price to pay.

I think that would be fine -- we'd just make the Python code that computes the Django setting for `SOCIAL_AUTH_SAML_ORG_INFO` loop through each entry in the TOML representation, and if there is no `url` field specified, insert the default before exposing it to Django.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-06 19:08 UTC

One benefit we're getting here is because we more explicitly have our own code sitting between reading the configuration file and Django, doing mutations on a value written by the end user to fill in defaults now is a natural thing to do rather than changing what was supposed to be an immutable value.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-06 19:10 UTC

I wouldn't want to do it a ton, since each instance would want to be documented, but I think there's <5 places where we do that sort of thing in the existing configuration file anyway.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-06 19:10 UTC

(We obviously would need to talk about this transition in the upgrade notes, since in theory an end user could be doing something fancy in `settings.py`, which is a possibility we probably would prefer to not exist).

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-06 19:11 UTC

But it'd be a one-time transition at least.

**Josh Klar** · 2022-12-06 19:11 UTC

(I'd also pitch https://cuelang.org/ for config files that straddle the "type safe, strong schema, some repetition, maybe should look vaguely YAML familiar" lines)

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-06 19:13 UTC

How would you think about it in comparison to TOML? 

Part of the motivation for this would be to eliminate the "editing a Python file" part of setting up a Zulip server; it can be a barrier for system administrators who are not programmers that they don't understand significant whitespace and other Python quirks.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-06 19:15 UTC

I haven't worked with TOML a huge amount, but my sense is that it's likely to be more intuitive for someone who's not a programmer than the Python files, and probably comparable to the INI format used by `zulip.conf` (which unfortunately doesn't support lists and things).

**Josh Klar** · 2022-12-06 20:19 UTC

Ah, yeah, if I'm taking the Programmer hat off and putting the Ops/SysAdmin hat on, Dhall directly would be a horrible move (though I've always found it excels most to me personally as a YAML generator, not a standalone config format).

CUE I find more interesting with this hat on: its syntax is rather familiar to those coming from YAML (with some niceties added around folding structs into a single line), and most of its functionality is opt-in: take https://cuelang.org/docs/tutorials/tour/intro/fold/ and the other `intro` examples as an example, it caters well to the "just be like YAML" usecase until you choose to, say, make use of its merge behaviors or extra type narrowing or etc.

TOML I have rather tenured experience with on both the user and developer ends. tl;dr of my thoughts: it's great until you get into nested structures, and then quickly starts frankly being less readable than even the worst ["get your carpentry squares out to horizontally align your screen"](https://twitter.com/abock/status/1117056887072145409) YAML files I've seen. If what we're after is "INI, but supports lists and structs", however, it's great for that, and it's easily writeable by higher-level tools for users who want to get fancy with repetition or code-sharing (see endorsement of Dhall for this, above).

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-06 20:32 UTC

I think the most complicated structure we're likely to have is the SAML configuration blocks:
```
SOCIAL_AUTH_SAML_ENABLED_IDPS: Dict[str, Any] = {                                                        
    ## The fields are explained in detail here:                                                          
    ##     https://python-social-auth.readthedocs.io/en/latest/backends/saml.html                        
    "idp_name": {                                                                                        
        ## Configure entity_id and url according to information provided to you by your IdP:             
        "entity_id": "https://idp.testshib.org/idp/shibboleth",                                          
        "url": "https://idp.testshib.org/idp/profile/SAML2/Redirect/SSO",                                
```

So we can probably experiment with what those will look like in a TOML format as a way to validate that concern.

**Jussi Talaskivi** · 2022-12-07 06:11 UTC

INI-files can be extended to support hierarchies... kinda. We have done this by defining multipart section names like [section:subsection:subsubsection]. I'm not saying it is the optimal way but works in some situations.

**Tim Abbott** · 2022-12-07 21:36 UTC

Yeah; I think ideally we want something a standard parser will like and that can happily support both lists and dictionaries, and given those needs, TOML/YAML/etc. are a better fit. And TOML feels more ergonomic and friendly to folks who are not programmers; a lot less quotation mark fiddling is involved.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2022-12-16 06:09 UTC

The frontend is actually sending requests to the backend in a loop. See `mark_all_as_read` in `unread_ops.js`.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2022-12-16 06:11 UTC

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2022-12-16 06:11 UTC

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2022-12-16 06:14 UTC

(replying to Rohitt Vashishtha)
> I'd always assumed the backend just batched the database writes in bataches of 1k, didn't know it was actually the frontend controlling it all.
We recently changed this behaviour. Also, we handle the API limit exceeded case:
```js
        error(xhr) {
            // If we hit the rate limit, just continue without showing any error.
            if (xhr.responseJSON.code === "RATE_LIMIT_HIT") {
                const milliseconds_to_wait = 1000 * xhr.responseJSON["retry-after"];
                setTimeout(() => mark_all_as_read(args), milliseconds_to_wait);
            } else {
                // TODO: Ideally this would be a ui_report.error();
                // the user needs to know that our operation failed.
                blueslip.error("Failed to mark messages as read: " + xhr.responseText);
            }
        },
```

but looks like it not useful if the whole app is affected by it.

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2022-12-16 06:16 UTC

I wish I'd opened the console before running this, but maybe this can be replicated on a devserver?

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2022-12-16 06:16 UTC

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2022-12-16 06:16 UTC

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2022-12-16 06:17 UTC

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2022-12-16 06:20 UTC

**Rohitt Vashishtha** · 2022-12-16 06:24 UTC

(replying to Aman (amanagr))
> (replying to Rohitt Vashishtha) ```quote Surely there must be a better way to handle bankruptcy, especially in extreme cases like this, than to wait for minutes and minutes? ``` We switched to this mechanism instead of just marking everything in the database as read and reloading to avoid the reload …
If the webapp purely pretends that everything is read, basically, here:

```js
export function message_unread(message) {
    if (message === undefined) {
        return false;
    }
    if (currently_marking_as_unread && message.id < latest_message_id_at_time_of_op_start) return false;
    return message.unread;
}
```

And later, a server event sets `currently_marking_as_unread` to false, that should work.

## splitting provision.py

*2022-12-28 to 2023-01-08 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/splitting.20provision.2Epy/with/1483067)*

**Josh Klar** · 2022-12-28 22:24 UTC

Looking to see what dragons I might unearth if I go down a road of attempting to split `provision.py` into chunks, with a rationale of improving Docker image layering. I'm currently working on a local-only-for-now solution to https://github.com/zulip/docker-zulip/issues/357 but, typical for cross-compilation, running into quirks along the way (yarn especially seems unhappy with networking in this QEMU world right now). When, say, `yarn` fails, the *entire* provisioning layer is invalidated, meaning all the native and python dep steps must be re-run, wasting bandwidth, CPU time, wall clock time, etc.

Typically in a Docker world I'd split these provision steps out into multiple `RUN` lines, perhaps `RUN provision --only=dpkg`, `RUN provision --only=pip`, etc. I'm inclined to hack on `lib/provision.py` to get towards that world, but want to make sure I'm not heading down a path someone has already tried and tripped over. FWIW cache *invalidation*, at least, shouldn't be a major issue here: since the image itself clones the Zulip repo rather than, say, mounting a host volume in (or copying files in), the provisioning scripts shouldn't change between layers (in other words, Docker's built-in layer cache invalidation should suffice).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-09 20:12 UTC

@Lachie Chapman we do offer a similar feature for LDAP, so it could be done for Zulip. One big challenge with that class of feature is that we only get to inspect the expected state during login -- so if a user just remains logged in, their set of groups will not be updated (either added or removed). LDAP doesn't have that failure mode, because an automated job can query LDAP directly on a regular basis in order to do updates.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-09 20:13 UTC

So such a feature would always be unreliable for syncing a set of groups. It could still be potentially useful for "setting the initial groups for a user" , and we might build it for that purpose, but we'd need to be very careful to explain exactly what that class of integration can and cannot do.
