Just to lay out the plan for this -- once we merge this PR, it'll be possible for start having the presence API be much more compressed -- the client can start asking the server "Please send me all the presence updates since time T", where T is roughly the time of the last time the server looked up the answer for this client the last time. Because of queuing delay and other possible races, we'd probably want T to be something like "5 minutes plus the time since the last request", but we'd be able to entirely stop sending presence update data for anyone who's been offline for the last half hour (I think the current API has a value for that which is something like 2 weeks).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-09 18:38 UTC

Just an update on this PR -- I think the thing we're stuck on is https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/16381#discussion_r1100891702; apparently while the Zulip web app has consistently used `OFFLINE_THRESHHOLD_SECS=140`, the server has used both that value and `5 * 60 = 300`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-09 18:48 UTC

OK, I think I understand the previous state of the world. @Mateusz Mandera FYI:
* We use the 300s version in exactly two places.
* One of them is unimportant (the "Go invisible" code path's made up time stamp to have the user appear as offline immediately), though of course it should agree with the others.
* The other is that the `presence` API endpoint reports users as "offline" using the 300s value. I think this is mostly non-operative, because clients are supposed to use their own understanding of time to decide what's offline, to manage lag issues. I'll post the JS code shortly.
* Mobile has `OFFLINE_THRESHHOLD_SECS=140` hardcoded as well.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-09 18:49 UTC

Here's the web frontend's core logic here:
```
const OFFLINE_THRESHOLD_SECS = 140;
....

/*                                                     
    If the server sends us `active_timestamp`, this    
    means at least one client was active at this time  
    (and hasn't changed since).                        
                                                       
    As long as the timestamp is current enough, we will
    show the user as active (even if there's a newer   
    timestamp for idle).                               
*/                                                     
if (age(active_timestamp) < OFFLINE_THRESHOLD_SECS) {  
    return {                                           
        status: "active",                              
        last_active,                                   
    };                                                 
}                                                      
                                                       
if (age(idle_timestamp) < OFFLINE_THRESHOLD_SECS) {    
    return {                                           
        status: "idle",                                
        last_active,                                   
    };                                                 
}                                                      
                                                       
return {                                               
    status: "offline",                                 
    last_active,                                       
};                                                     
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-09 18:50 UTC

I think in the new API, that will just look like:
```
if (age(last_connected_time) > OFFLINE_THRESHOLD_SECS) {
    // treat as offline
}

if (age(last_active_time) > OFFLINE_THRESHOLD_SECS) {
    // treat as idle
}

// treat as active
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-09 18:53 UTC

Overall what I think this means is that:
* We should standardize on a single value, which is currently 140s, and perhaps have that live in the `settings.py`
* We should add that value to the `server_settings` section of the API, so that clients can just get this value from the server, making it possible to change it meaningfully from 140s. 
* The initial value of that should be 140s, which I'm pretty sure was selected as "plenty of network/other latency more than 2 x ACTIVE_PING_INTERVAL_MS". This is a pretty aggressive value; even a single request being missed or 500ing can result in a user appearing offline. (Since there's a lag of up to one full ping interval between when the other client checks in and when you check in, and so we'll be at almost 2 ping intervals when you issue your next request that might get an updated connection time from that user ). We want to change this to at least `3 x ACTIVE_PING_INTERVAL_MS + 20s`, while still having it small enough that a user who leaves appears gone reasonably quickly -- so probably 180s given that the ping interval is currently 50s.
* We should also add the other similar constant to the API: `const ACTIVE_PING_INTERVAL_MS = 50 * 1000;`, since those two likely need to be related for a coherent experience.

I note that the dostring here at least suggests it may not be correct to use the same rule?
```
def format_legacy_presence_dict(presence: UserPresence) -> Dict[str, Any]:
    """
    This function assumes it's being called right after the presence object was updated,
    and is not meant to be used on old presence data.
    """
    if (
        presence.last_active_time
        + datetime.timedelta(seconds=settings.PRESENCE_LEGACY_EVENT_OFFSET_FOR_ACTIVITY_SECONDS)
        >= presence.last_connected_time
    ):
        status = UserPresence.LEGACY_STATUS_ACTIVE
        timestamp = datetime_to_timestamp(presence.last_active_time)
    else:
        status = UserPresence.LEGACY_STATUS_IDLE
        timestamp = datetime_to_timestamp(presence.last_connected_time)

    return dict(client="website", status=status, timestamp=timestamp, pushable=False)
```

OK, I'm prepping to deploy this here on CZO.  While deploying it "straight" would work, I'd like to test the deployment plan in the first commit:
> The way to deploy is to start the backfill migration with the server
down and then start the server *without* the user_presence queue worker,
to let the migration finish without having new data interfering with it.
Once the migration is done, the queue worker can be started, leading to
the presence data catching up to the current state as the queue worker
goes over the queued up events and updating the UserPresence table.

I believe this we can do this by:
1. `upgrade-server-from-git [...] --skip-restart` which will abort due to the migrations.
2. `cd ~zulip/deployments/next` and adjust `scripts/start-server` to skip the `user_presence` worker
3. Then:
```
./manage.py fill_memcached_caches --skip-checks
./scripts/stop-server --skip-checks
./manage.py migrate zerver 0443 --skip-checks
./scripts/start-server --skip-checks
./manage.py migrate zerver 0444 --skip-checks
supervisorctl start zulip-workers:zulip_events_user_presence
```

This should leave the old table in place (since it doesn't run 0445, which is the drop), the user_presence worker only started after the backfill is done (0444), and django started ASAP after the schema is in place (0443).

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-08-09 01:17 UTC

e566e985e4d2e824ecbafef74f171883e3a77b2a looks like it made an important change that affects perf here -- it moved from `messages.update()` to `Messages.objects.bulk_update(messages_list, update_fields)` which is O(n) as opposed to O(1) `UPDATE` queries.  It also should have updated the [comment above it](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/lib/topic.py#L180-L183), which no longer makes sense without an `.update` call.

There look to be a few parts to why we have `messages_list`:
 1. We need to return `messages_list` to `do_update_message`, which uses it:
   1. To check that it has more than one element (it always does, since `changed_messages = [target_message]` at the top and is only ever added to)
   2. To run various `DELETE` and `UPDATE` queries via `id__in`, which become much less performant when they have giant `CASE` statements
   3. To call `.exclude(id__in=...)` to find out if we're moving the whole topic, which is going to be very slow in cases when we _are_ moving the whole topic, and it is big
2. To adjust the `edit_history` of each of the messages, individually, by JSON-parsing, prepending, and re-serializing.

All of the uses in `do_update_message` seem like they would benefit greatly from having a queryset to act on.  The `edit_history` is a `text` field in the database, so (lacking #18146) we could possibly write a query that adjusts every row using a single `UPDATE` by casting it to `jsonb` and back.  But #18146 looks like it was essentially done, and just needed to be adjusted to do some batching on the migration.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 01:02 UTC

@Prakhar Pratyush I think moving to a world where there is just a `set_topic_visibility_policy` is the right abstraction. However, I think our intent is to have 4 possible states for a topic:
* MUTED  (This topic is muted regardless of whether the stream is muted)
* INHERIT (represented as no UserTopic row existing) -- this topic is not explicitly muted, and will be treated as muted or not depending on whether the stream is muted or not.
* UNMUTED (This topic is not muted even if the stream is muted).
* FOLLOWED (Not in scope for this project, but would be both unmuted and have additional notifications enabled)

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 01:03 UTC

If the stream is currently muted and you remove the "UNMUTED" state, we probably want to set the topic's state to INHERIT (i.e. remove the UserTopic row) -- but that would be implemented via the browser sending a request to the server with INHERIT as the requested policy, not MUTED.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 01:04 UTC

Anyway, I like the idea of having a single function `set_topic_visibility_policy`, which just accepts the desired policy and implements that in whatever way is appropriate given the current state.

@Alya Abbott there's a product question here that's sufficiently in the implementation weeds that I think we can just talk about it here. When you move messages from one topic to another, we currently migrate the UserTopic rows (i.e. everyone's "muted topics" configuration for that stream, but of course the "followed topics" and "unmuted topics" features should work similarly) in some circumstances; I don't remember the precise algorithm, but for the purpose of this question, assume it's the obvious case where someone has moved the entire old topic to another topic.

The question is how to handle the situation when the destination topic already has messages, and not only messages, but actually had UserTopic configuration. (For example, they'd explicitly unmuted a topic that is merged into an explicitly muted topic).

While thinking about this comment of @Abhijeet Bodas 
> Not specific to this PR, but is there a specific reason to use the delete-and-update pattern in the message edit code (where in, old topic UserTopic rows are first deleted, and new topic UserTopic rows are then created)? I am thinking of another way of doing this:

Here's some pseudocode to explain
```python
        user_topics = get_user_topics(stream_being_edited.id, orig_topic_name)

        user_topics_to_remove: QuerySet[UserTopic] = user_topics.filter(user_profile_id__in = delete_event_notify_user_ids)
        user_topics_to_update: QuerySet[UserTopic] = user_topics.exclude(user_topics_to_remove)

        # If the messages are being moved to a stream the user
        # cannot access, then we treat this as the
        # messages/topic being deleted for this user. This is
        # important for security reasons; we don't want to
        # give users a UserTopic row in a stream they cannot
        # access. Remove the user topic rows for such users.
        bulk_do_set_user_topic_visibility_policy(
            user_topics_to_remove,
            stream_being_edited,
            orig_topic_name,
            operation="remove",
        )

        # If the messages are being moved to a stream the user
        # can access. We move the user topic records for such
        # users.
        bulk_do_set_user_topic_visibility_policy(
            user_topics_to_update,
            new_stream if new_stream is not None else stream_being_edited,
            topic_name if topic_name is not None else orig_topic_name,
            operation="update",
        )
```
Now in the bulk_ function, we can do
```python
if operation == "remove":
    user_topics.delete()
    return 

user_topics.update(stream_id=stream_id, topic_name=topic_name, recipient_id=recipient_id, last_updated=last_updated)
```
and the send_event using a loop.

thoughts?

Hm, I would imagine something like this:

1. If original and target match, use that policy:

| original topic | target topic | final behaviour
| --- | --- | ---|
| nvp | nvp | nvp
| muted | muted | muted
| unmuted | unmuted | unmuted

2. Otherwise, use the higher-visibility policy, regardless of whether it's the target or the original. This only applies if there is some content in the target, so if the target is a brand new topic, you'd use the visibility for the original topic.

| original topic | target topic | final behaviour
| --- | --- | ---|
| muted | nvp | nvp
| nvp | muted | nvp
| nvp | unmuted | unmuted
| unmuted | nvp | unmuted
| muted | unmuted | unmuted

## scheduled email worker

*2023-01-27 to 2023-01-27 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/scheduled.20email.20worker/with/1498040)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-01-27 18:31 UTC

@Lauryn Menard bumped me to think about scheduled email forever-retries (#**issues>email-delivery-spam**) again.

We have three situations in terms of how we send email and handle failure:
1. Things which send email synchronously (e.g. password resets, invitations, realm downgrades due to failure to pay) which fail just ... fail, and we never retry.
2. Things in the `email_senders` (which is only missed message emails and new logins) queue use the `retry_send_email_failures` decorator which means they get 3 retries with ~no backoff besides being re-queued at the tail of that queue.
3. Scheduled emails retry forever every 10s.

We can't have the third case use the same codepath as the second, since it's not actually an event queue, just a table we're using as an event queue.

I feel like the More Right solution in this space is to unify our three email-sending regimes.  I know @Tim Abbott has pushed back against combining the scheduled emails and the email_senders queues, since the former can get a giant bolus of emails dumped into it from digests, and it'd be bad to block missed-message emails behind thousands of those.  Which is a reasonable argument -- but we can have separate queues and shared email-sending code with two workers pulling from two different queues.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-01-27 18:34 UTC

The short-term solution would be to catch `EmailNotDeliveredError`s and to adjust the `scheduled_timestamp` to later.  But we don't have a place to store number of failures to not retry forever, or to implement exponential backoff.  We can add a column for that, but that feels like building parallel functionality to our actual queue workers.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-01-27 18:35 UTC

There is also the even larger project of rebuilding our queueing system entirely, not on RabbitMQ, but I don't think anything in this problem necessitates that -- moving scheduled emails to the existing framework makes that easier to do later, not harder.

**Notification Bot** · 2023-01-27 18:39 UTC

3 messages were moved here from #**issues>email-delivery-spam** by @Alex Vandiver.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-27 23:30 UTC

Hmm, I think the problem is that while `ScheduledEmail` could be used to manage emails to be sent immediately, the opposite isn't true -- the queue worker system cannot be used to send an email 2 days from now.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-27 23:31 UTC

I agree we can manage the digest issue in a number of ways, potentially including just having a "priority" column.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-27 23:34 UTC

I think unifying scheduled emails and `email_senders` makes a lot of sense. For synchronously sending emails, it's arguable -- it may be a better user experience to just give a user-facing failure for a password reset attempt than to have the password reset email show up hours or days later after outgoing email gets fixed -- and I think that's why we have code paths that do that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-27 23:34 UTC

(More complex operations like invitations and downgrades feel different on that point).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-01-27 23:36 UTC

I think maybe the right direction, given all that, would be to replace the `email_senders` queue with an extension of `ScheduledEmail`, with a view in the design towards that scheduling system being extended in the future for moving other queue workers off RabbitMQ?

## get_realm_user_dicts size

*2023-02-01 to 2025-02-05 · 32 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/get_realm_user_dicts.20size/with/1500619)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-01 15:38 UTC

Last night we had an outage of chat.zulip.org because `get_realm_user_dicts` started being large enough that it no longer fit into the 1MB memcached size.  I temporarily mitigated it by increasing the max object size in memcached.

This isn't the first time this has happened.  We ran into this issue in Zulip Cloud previously with a large realm, and it's [been reported here](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/31-production-help/topic/Internal.20server.20error.20-.20zulip.20ui/near/1436271) for a self-hoster as well.

#23215 was one technique for slimming down the size of that cache, but clearly wasn't a big enough hammer.  What can we do to not have such a giant datastore that we ship to clients?  The sheer size of that is not only a problem for memcached, but also is the majority of the 1.5MB that we push down to users when they load `https://chat.zulip.org/`

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-01 15:53 UTC

Reverting 5db53029a590284f63414b2172c6bfd1c661d1d5 is one potential step, but that's a very small amount of gain -- we should be considering techniques to make this significantly smaller.

I know we've previously discussed limiting the contents to users that are not `long_term_idle` -- what failure modes would that have?

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 01:06 UTC

The contents of that cache for each user are as follows:
```
realm_user_dict_fields: List[str] = [
    "id",                            
    "full_name",                     
    "email",                         
    "avatar_source",                 
    "avatar_version",                
    "is_active",                     
    "role",                          
    "is_billing_admin",              
    "is_bot",                        
    "timezone",                      
    "date_joined",                   
    "bot_owner_id",                  
    "delivery_email",                
    "bot_type",                      
    "long_term_idle",                
]                                    
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 01:07 UTC

We store items in these caches in compressed form. So for the memcached problem, what will be most useful is adjustments that will compress better.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 01:10 UTC

From a programming simplicity standpoint, ideally, we'd avoid needing to write client code to do asynchronous fetches of data that the web app displays on a user in order to use a user object for typeahead, messages, and user cards... it significantly impacts the snappiness of the experience and ends up being reasonably complex. Obviously at a certain scale, like 1M users in a realm, that becomes impossible.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 01:12 UTC

I feel like it may be worth playing with the data structure in chat.zulip.org and trying to see what easy adjustments would improve its compressed size.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 01:12 UTC

For example, we could readily drop the `is_bot` field and just compute it from `bot_type`, which will be `None` whenever `is_bot=False`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 01:13 UTC

But I have no idea if that actually does anything of value -- maybe the compression algorithm has figured that out and that tweak would only be a 0.2% adjustment in size.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 01:16 UTC

Anyway the things I would look at trying of that form are:
* Compute `is_bot` from the `bot_type` field, and only include the `bot_type` field if its value is not `None`.
* Include `bot_owner` only if its value is not `None`.
* Make `is_billing_admin` only present if the value is `True`, which should be the case for only a very small portion of users.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 01:17 UTC

The next class of thing one could try is to have fields that are only displayed when interacting with a user's profile or user card be fetched only when viewing those elements; this could include the following:
* timezone
* date_joined (would also be needed for the "Users" table in settings, which is annoying)
* custom profile fields, which are fetched via a separate database query anyway.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 01:19 UTC

And one more class of thing we can do is look at further adjustments to how we manage avatars; I haven't thought that through but the block in `format_user_row` around `user_avatar_url_field_optional` is useful context.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-02 02:36 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> We store items in these caches in compressed form. So for the memcached problem, what will be most useful is adjustments that will compress better.
To be explicit, bmemcached uses zlib to compress the pickled data.  We're storing 1MiB of zlib-compressed data which we unzip to 3.75MiB of pickled data, which we unpickle and the json-serialize:
```
In [1]: from django.core.cache import cache
   ...: from orjson import dumps
   ...: from timeit import timeit
   ...:
   ...: client = cache._cache
   ...: timeit(lambda: dumps(client.get(":1:e26e352c9cc13496d29a996d1c0dc4b3:realm_user_dicts:2")), number=100)/100
   ...:
Out[1]: 0.1492796527966857
```

So it takes us ~150ms to pull this out of memcached on our local host -- and that's skipping all of the transforms that we do on the raw value we pull out of memcached.  This is a significant performance cost, even pulled from memcached -- and not just a case of "too big."

(As a point of reference, it also "only" takes 330ms to pull the same data from the database and json-serialize it)

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-02 02:39 UTC

Dropping `is_bot` moves us from 1048920 bytes to 1046703, which isn't very significant.  I suspect many of the other trimmings of the "width" of the cache are places where they're low-entropy, which is why we expect to get away with removing them.

I think we probably need to address the *length* of the cache, not the width.  We're never going to get rid of the id, name, and email, which is where most of the entropy and thus size comes from.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-02 02:41 UTC

Limiting to just `'id','full_name','email', 'delivery_email'` is still 660k.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-02 02:43 UTC

Limiting to non-long-term-idle users, but keeping the original full width is *88k*.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-02 02:44 UTC

I don't think those extra 935k are doing us much good, and it seems like we should lazy-load them as needed, rather than upfront.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-02 02:47 UTC

I can imagine cases where this is would bite us (a zulip instance fallow for 28 days would soft-deactivate everyone, and might thus thrash at load-time pulling in the user-data for every user it needed to render information for) so we may need to be a little cleverer than that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 20:58 UTC

I don't think we can easily just not send at least the id/name pair for all users; a lot of components, like mention and private message recipient typeahead, need to be able to access all users that exist, not just those who have been active recently, and there's basically 3 simple options for how to handle that:
* Include the full `users` data set in the initial response.
* Fetch the full data `users` data set slightly lazily, e.g. the first time that the user tries to access it.
* Have the typeahead query the server after every keypress before it can show results. This is what GitHub's typeahead does, which makes sense given that they're a global namespace for users, but it's a visibly slow experience.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 20:58 UTC

I think probably the short-term answer here is to just allow this cache to be 2MB, given that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-02 20:59 UTC

There are other fancy things that are theoretically possible, involving caching data on clients between sessions, but I'd rather avoid them if at all possible.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-02-06 14:54 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I think probably the short-term answer here is to just allow this cache to be 2MB, given that.
This feels pretty unsatisfying.

That we have a fundamental scaling problem which is O(n) in both time and space for the number of users that have ever signed up, during first page-load, seems pretty unfortunate.  Even what we do for web-public sessions, where we at least ship `/` so it can render s a spinning loading progressbar (and get users in a second request), seems probably preferable to what we do for logged-in sessions, where we wait for you to pull down and parse the huge JSON blog before we render *any* Zulip UI.

I guess the point that I'm making isn't that 2MB is onerous on the server-side for the memcached limit, but rather that it's a smell for a protocol decision which I think has bad effects for clients trying to load Zulip.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-06 20:22 UTC

Well, this was the short-term answer, not the long-term answer -- and my claim is there isn't a localized/cheap change that we can make here that would solve those problems.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-06 20:25 UTC

I agree we can and should shift the way the that the app loads to work like the public access view, where we do the `/register` API request after showing a loading page; probably worth forking a separate thread for that. (Or at least do that for organizations above a certain size; the current model saves an RTT and maybe that could be significant in smaller organizations with high latency to the Zulip server). But that just changes when we do the fetch -- we'll still not be able to let you do anything until we fetch the full data set.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-06 20:37 UTC

There are longer-term options for changing how we manage the `users` data set. Just to spell out probably the most credible idea:
* `long_term_idle` is not suitable for not including a user in typeahead -- one does need to be able to mention someone who was active in the community a year ago and have that work. 
* I think probably we just need the entire user data set to be accessible there. But we could potentially do something like lazy-load the full data the first time you do one of the ~5 tasks that actually require it -- filtering in the right sidebar, various typeaheads, the "Users" panel in settings, etc. We have precedent for this -- we do the same thing for "what topics exist in a stream's history" today. 
* And then we could have whatever clever optimization algorithm we want for a smaller set that is sent on page load; might be `!long_term_idle`, or maybe a significantly larger but still small subset like "has sent a message or been present in the last 3 months". But the key thing would be that to arrange things such that nothing breaks if we don't have data on a user cached. 
* We would need to change all the message fetching/display logic to fetch data for users that they need to display if that's not already available. Possibly it' d be simplest to just have those code paths all use the same "Get me the full `users` data set" function rather than fetching the individual users they need, and that's just an at-most-1-time thing you do per session.

But that doesn't feel like a quick refactor, and that's not even the biggest chunk of the `/` response on extremely large organizations like this one. (I'm pretty sure it's the "which users are in which streams" structure, which is slightly quadratic but just a bunch of IDs, and we had some ideas for how to compress much better but haven't had a chance to pursue).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-02-06 20:43 UTC

So I think probably for the next 3 months, just increasing those cache sizes will buy us the time to do that without any cliff-shaped user-facing impact.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-04 20:09 UTC

Debugging of #**issues>read receipts fail randomly.@2077717** suggests that this cache is active enough to have race issues preventing it from functioning properly. I'd like to talk about some options for how to improve it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-04 20:13 UTC

One idea that's been in the back of my mind for a while is to add a column like `last_update_id` to `UserProfile`, like what we designed for presence in [#api design > presence rewrite &gt; add last_update_to /register?](#narrow/channel/378-api-design/topic/presence.20rewrite.20.3E.20add.20last_update_to.20.2Fregister.3F).

This could be used by the server and/or possibly a synchronization protocol to determine which user objects have been modified since the last data the client has available. So for example, the algorithm to fetch the set of users to a client could look like:
- Fetch data from the cache, which includes both the set of users and a `last_update_id`.
- Go to the database to fetch just those user rows whose `last_update_id` is newer than the cutoff, and merge their data on top of what was in the cache.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-02-05 16:52 UTC

So this makes the cache bigger, and just doesn't update it as often in exchange?

**Greg Price** · 2025-02-05 17:48 UTC

I read the idea as not including `last_update_id` in the user rows in the cache — just a single `last_update_id` value that represents effectively the time the cached value was computed. So it's only a trivial amount bigger.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-02-05 17:58 UTC

Ahhh, for some reason I was parsing it as per-row, yeah, which doesn't make any sense.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-05 23:15 UTC

Yeah this doesn't solve the size issue at all; we need API changes to meaningfully do that, but it would allow us to eliminate races resulting in erroneous `realm_user` output. And the `last_update_id` concept, if exposed in the API, would be very helpful for a client to fetch "just the users that have changed since what I have in my local cache" on startup, which could be huge for the mobile apps, which could just store `realm_user` in their local database. 

The main cost is we'd need to write the code to maintain the field.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-02-05 23:42 UTC

ITYM "API changes" not "AI changes". :)

## #DZ388

*2023-02-21 to 2023-02-21 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/.23DZ388/with/1510800)*

**Josh Klar** · 2023-02-21 19:31 UTC

Soooooooo I guess the curse of working not only west coast hours, but generally more of a 9:30 or 10am start, is that I miss stuff like https://github.com/zulip/docker-zulip/pull/388 when it's opened, and so I'm getting this feedback in *after* the merge. But anyway, I think requiring use of DC 2.1.1+ features is a bit too bleeding edge to be a good UX, given that [very many distros haven't packaged DC 2.x to begin with](https://repology.org/project/docker-compose/versions), despite [its (then-immediate) deprecation upstream](https://www.docker.com/blog/announcing-compose-v2-general-availability/). That list (to save you a click, and assuming Repology is correct) includes all versions of Fedora, Alpine, Debian, Guix, all but the latest version of NixOS, all versions of Raspbian (Debian fork for RPis), and all stable versions of Ubuntu (other than those using PPAs for Docker).

In short, this is a bad user experience for a huge number of users. I think we should discuss either a roll back, or a roll forward to something more backwards compatible. If we do neither of those, we need to document this somewhere as an expected bit of breakage for all of those distros (many of which are very common Docker host systems).

What we used to do for this purpose was have containers run via a `wait-for` wrapper script (or just `sh -c "wait-for-whatever; my-service"`). Some examples of that flow are discussed in https://github.com/docker/compose/issues/8351

## process_client

*2023-02-22 to 2023-03-04 · 18 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/process_client/with/1511623)*

**Josh Klar** · 2023-02-22 22:33 UTC

So we do a check against `client_name` in `zerver/decorator.py#process_client`:

```python
def process_client(
    request: HttpRequest,
    user: Union[UserProfile, AnonymousUser, None] = None,
    *,
    is_browser_view: bool = False,
    client_name: Optional[str] = None,
    query: Optional[str] = None,
) -> None:
    """The optional user parameter requests that a UserActivity row be
    created/updated to record this request.

    In particular, unauthenticate requests and those authenticated to
    a non-user object like RemoteZulipServer should not pass the
    `user` parameter.
    """
    request_notes = RequestNotes.get_notes(request)
    if client_name is None:
        client_name = request_notes.client_name

    assert client_name is not None

    # We could check for a browser's name being "Mozilla", but
    # e.g. Opera and MobileSafari don't set that, and it seems
    # more robust to just key off whether it was a browser view
    if is_browser_view and not client_name.startswith("Zulip"):
        # Avoid changing the client string for browsers, but let
        # the Zulip desktop apps be themselves.
        client_name = "website"

    request_notes.client = get_client(client_name)
    if user is not None and user.is_authenticated:
        update_user_activity(request, user, query)

```

After trying to figure out why one of the commits in the series that becomes #24231 was so important that the `AssertionError` came back without it, I end up with `request_notes` of `RequestNotes(client=<Client: <Client: website>>, client_name='internal', client_version=None, ...)`

The change in https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/24231/commits/e8122ae3e0e26a0b4e5db5bb8d05670b7cd4f6f8 was worded differently, which I think might have led to the concern over its inclusion: I'd originally tracked down errors related to `request_notes.client.name` being *none*, and thus prioritized `request_notes.client_name` over it, falling back to the nested lookup. However, in this case, it's not a null-coalesce, it's outright differing values.

Three thoughts come to mind, two are probably more actionable:

- One, I could change `process_client` to ignore overriding the local stack `client_name` if `client_name.startswith("internal")`
- Two, I could reword the commit that already exists in this series to reflect this other way of ending up hitting the new codepath (and thus the wording becomes more simple: `rate_limiter: Always prefer request_notes.client_name over request_notes.client.name to determine exemptions.` (subject to character limit...)
- Three, we could start tearing things apart to figure out why we have two confusingly similar (one character difference in lookup code...) strings stored in this struct to begin with (from some commit message reading I did of stuff that landed last summer/fall, it seems to be a transitional step of organic growth) and see if one can go away, though this seems both somewhat unbounded, and also somewhat out of scope for this PR.

I guess this is me asking for input from anyone with opinions, but particularly @Tim Abbott since he has the blocking comment in the PR.

These are all of our use of Jinja in Markdown files (after #24520):

```jinja
{% for event_type in all_event_types -%} {{- comma() -}} `{{ event_type }}` {%- endfor %}
{% if 'IRC' in integration_display_name %}
{% if all_event_types is defined %}
{{ api_url }}
{{ api_url_scheme_relative }}
{{ external_uri_scheme }}
{{ hubot_docs_url }}
{{ integration_display_name }}
{{ integration_name }}
{{ integration_url }}
{{ recommended_stream_name }}
{{ support_email }}
{{ zulip_url }}
```

The conditionals are unnecessary since each integration knows whether it’s IRC and whether it has `all_event_types`. So we could replace all use of Jinja with a tiny Markdown plugin that replaces specific known variables. **Alex Vandiver** · 2023-03-02 02:33 UTC

Thanks for that long history dive, @Josh Klar!

Let me try to lay out what I think I understand of our constraints:
1. `certbot` writes its config file based on how it was last run, and renewals use that.  We don't have a programmatic way of modifying the config files written by `certbot`, so we need to do a `--webroot` run at some point during the setup process.
2. If we're running cerbot with webroot, `nginx` needs to be started by then to serve http.
3. If nginx is started, it needs a certificate to serve TLS.
4. We can only run `certbot --webroot` and *also* be running `nginx` if one of them is in the background somehow.

So this is mostly about *what* certificate we're seeding nginx with.  We *could* fudge a couple of those constraints a little:
- We could hackily regex-edit the certbot config file post-certbot to say webroot.  I don't like this because it lays a time bomb for 3 months down the road if anything goes wrong, and it's very likely to.  This option is pretty much off the table, but I mention it for completeness.
- We could start nginx with an http-only config, run certbot to get a cert with that, and then install and reload into an http+https nginx config.  This has the mild upside that we never serve a bad cert on https, but adds some of complexity to swap between http_only and not.  But this *only* saves us presenting the bad cert temporarily, because...

...there's no getting around point (4) on the first list.  That `&` "hack" is *forced* because we have to run webroot because of (1), so nginx has to be running at the same time.  Juggling making a cert using `--standalone` first, as @Josh Klar suggests above, doesn't save us from this -- the post-hook would need to start nginx and also run the webhook renewal, so one of those would need to be backgrounded.  The juggling of the post-hook trigger in standalone mode doesn't actually solve it.

We can pull tricks to hide the `&` better, but we're forced into its existence by point (1) and (4) on the first list.  Personally, I don't find it all that much of a hack -- we can pretty it up by moving it into a one-shot supervisor service if we want, but a `nginx reload` to pick up a new cert isn't all that disruptive.   And I agree with Anders' logic that it's helpful to essentially do a full end-to-end test-run of the normal (re)new-and-reload process during first boot, to suss out problems.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-03-08 15:33 UTC

So the goal is to return a different response (text, or image) depending on what the browser sends as an `Accept` header.  The [list Anders linked to](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Web/HTTP/Content_negotiation/List_of_default_Accept_values) shows that in different contexts, browsers ask for different things.  For instance, Chrome for an `<img>` tag sends:
```
Accept: image/avif,image/webp,image/apng,image/*,*/*;q=0.8
```

This means that it would like any of:
- `image/avif`
- `image/webp`
- `image/apng`
- `image/*`
- `*/*` but only with [quality 0.8](https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/Glossary/Quality_values) -- so everything else not listed above is not preferred, but will work.

The [built-in Django `.accepts()`](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.1/ref/request-response/#django.http.HttpRequest.accepts) only tells you a binary "yes" or "no," but because of that last "anything goes, but not as preferred" sort of value, we need more than a binary yes/no -- we need to be able to answer "does the browser prefer `text/html` or `image/svg`, based on its quality ranking?"

You should write a commit to provide a function which takes a list of potential content-types we can return, and return the highest-ranked one which the browser will accept, or None if it won't accept any of them.

You will want to use [the `.accepted_types` method](https://github.com/django/django/blob/32d4b61c313be5169137047e9fb3668da20a5d89/django/http/request.py#L107) and the resulting [MediaType objects](https://github.com/django/django/blob/32d4b61c313be5169137047e9fb3668da20a5d89/django/http/request.py#L663).

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-03-08 15:37 UTC

Once you have that, we can use it to either return a normal `text/html` `HttpResponseNotFound` *or* a 404 status with an internal redirect to the static image content via nginx.  We can discuss how to do that second part once you've tackled the first part.

@Alex Vandiver  I wrote a general-purpose function to sort the accept header. Here's the function

```python
def sort_func(request:HttpRequest) -> List[str]:
    acc = str(request.accepted_types)
    med = acc.split(',')
    sorted_media = sorted(med, key=lambda mt:float(mt.split(';q=')[1] if ';q=' in mt else '1.0'), reverse=True)
    return sorted_media
```

## cdn

*2023-03-08 to 2023-03-14 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/cdn/with/1520933)*

**Stpn** · 2023-03-08 18:40 UTC

Hello could someone please advise if Zulip (self-hosted) supports CDN for file uploads? Trying to setup Cloudfront for S3 and adding `S3_ENDPOINT_URL` doesn't seem enough - images won't upload or load

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-03-08 19:35 UTC

Zulip serves the file uploads directly from the server, because it wants to apply access control to the requests.  If you're storing files in S3, Zulip 5.x and earlier send a redirect to a temporary URL in S3, which serves the file; in `main` (what will be 6.x and later) the Zulip server fetches the content from S3 and serves it directly, so the browsers can cache it.

So theoretically in 5.x we could serve a slightly different redirect to clients which was fronted by a CDN -- but that request is not a good one to cache, since it's a time-limited signed request.  And in 6.x the only place oner could apply a CDN is between the user and the Zulip server -- and the user uploads are still not cacable by an intermediate proxy because they're private, so you'd only be benefiting from the accelerated distribution networks that CDNs often offer.

`S3_ENDPOINT_URL` is only if you have a S3-compatable-but-not-S3 service you're using (e.g. [DigitalOcean Spaces](https://www.digitalocean.com/products/spaces))

**Stpn** · 2023-03-09 07:59 UTC

thank you. any suggestion how to speed up image upload? Or is there nothing on Zulip side that we could do and any optimizations are on the user side (reducing size etc)

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-03-09 14:54 UTC

Are you using the [S3 storage backend](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/stable/production/upload-backends.html#s3-backend-configuration), or the default on-disk storage?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-03-09 14:56 UTC

But the biggest impact adjustments are always going to be to have fewer bytes to upload, by having smaller files, yes.  Other things to optimize include reducing latency from users to the server (e.g. putting it in a location close to them) or reducing latency to the S3 storage if you're using that (e.g. choosing the right AWS region).

**Stpn** · 2023-03-14 16:33 UTC

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> Are you using the [S3 storage backend](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/stable/production/upload-backends.html#s3-backend-configuration), or the default on-disk storage?
The S3 storage. Do you have any extra suggestion for  it by any chance? The most issues we have are with uploading videos from mobile however.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-03-14 18:12 UTC

My notes above about S3 storage apply, then --- make sure you're storing them in the same region, and are using [AWS S3 VPC endpoints](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/vpc/latest/privatelink/vpc-endpoints-s3.html) to keep the traffic inside the region.

But that's only going to solve the "server saves it to S3" part of the latency -- if you're uploading large videos from mobile, te bottleneck is likely in the client's network, which is not really something you have any real control over.

## Scheduled message races

*2023-04-02 to 2023-04-03 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Scheduled.20message.20races/with/1539789)*

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2023-04-02 21:23 UTC

When modifying a scheduled message, how should we handle the race to sending the scheduled message vs modifying it? Should just using `transaction.atomic` would be enough since it locks the row for us and changing `delivered=true` would fail if we are trying to send the message in parallel? 

There is a possibility of a scheduled message being sent between us locking the row and the user sending the patch request, which I am not sure how to handle. The best option is probably to just send an error message to the user, right? or, should we delete the scheduled message when the user clicks on edit button in the UI to avoid this behaviour altogether?

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2023-04-02 21:25 UTC

Should I also be worried about any more races? I am not sure any other races are possible since we're using `lte` when deciding which messages to send.

```py
messages_to_deliver = ScheduledMessage.objects.filter(
                        scheduled_timestamp__lte=timezone_now(), delivered=False
                    ).select_for_update()
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-03 05:04 UTC

@Aman (amanagr) a transaction sounds correct, and I think if the scheduled message is sent during a request to modify its state, it should just return an error indicating it was already sent.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-04-03 13:13 UTC

(replying to Aman (amanagr))
> Should just using `transaction.atomic` would be enough since it locks the row for us and changing `delivered=true` would fail if we are trying to send the message in parallel?

Locking the rows won't cause "changing `delivered=true` [to] fail" -- the lock just means that the changes are serialized.

> There is a possibility of a scheduled message being sent between us locking the row and the user sending the patch request

I'm a little confused by this.  We shouldn't be (and can't, really) hold a lock across HTTP requests -- so the edit button can't take a row-level lock.  When we get the PATCH request, we should take a lock, check that `delivered=False`, and if that fails tell the user that the message was already sent.  Since sending it should also take a lock, we know that if `delivered=False` that the mesasge truly hasn't been sent yet and we can modify it as we wish.

We should, probably as a follow-up, do something to the edit UI if the frontend gets an event via longpoll which says that the message was sent.  But I think that it makes sense that the scheduled send time takes precedence even if the edit box is open -- I don't think we want something to appear to fail to send if someone accidentally left the edit box open.  I think it's more understandable that it "timed out" and sent as the user originally asked.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-03 17:34 UTC

Yeah, that sounds right to me, thanks for writing it out.

Merged! Thanks @Prakhar Pratyush for doing this cleanup.

I was reflecting a bit on the fact that we named this test helper function about 10 years ago, in b02770440ac8d9082730c7a0557269a9d8fab837, and despite it being useful enough that we're using it in over 100 places, somehow it's taken this long for me to notice that its name and interface should be improved. Not that it was terrible, and certainly at the time we named it, we were always just talking about "tornado" to refer to the real-time sync system, since we were just getting it working well. But the fact that names are so sticky is part of what motivates me to make so many review suggestions about what to call things -- if you're not watchful about these things, the codebase just slowly gets harder and harder to read.

@Steve Howell FYI as I thought you might enjoy this :)

**Steve Howell** · 2023-04-07 17:40 UTC

@Prakhar Pratyush and @Tim Abbott  I definitely enjoyed this change!  When I looked at the particular case of fixing `test_example.py` I wondered whether we should also change the name of the test.  I think there are arguments in both directions.  The test is still named `test_tornado_redirects` if I am reading the diff correctly.  It can be helpful at times to still concretely talk about Tornado as the underlying mechanism, but I think I would lean in this particular case to a more abstract name.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-04-07 18:34 UTC

Yeah, I think now that `send_event` is one of our important, documented interfaces that we call in 50+ places, that's the right word to use when referring to it, but certainly back in 2013 we might not have known how things were going to settle.


## remote dev with https proxy

*2023-04-04 to 2023-04-04 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/remote.20dev.20with.20https.20proxy/with/1540962)*

**Tam Le** · 2023-04-04 16:45 UTC

While trying to set up a remote development environment with the application server running behind an SSL-certified domain according to the instructions at https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/development/remote.html#using-an-nginx-reverse-proxy, I encountered an issue in which any backend/JSON requests were returning a 403/CSRF error.

Since Django 4.0 it seems that if running the server behind a reverse-proxy such as Nginx, then we require the CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS setting containing the exact value for scheme + hostname.

I've created a PR to address this issue here: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/24730

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-04-04 16:53 UTC

In production deployments, we handle this by configuring the proxy to forward the `Host` header unchanged from its incoming request (e.g. [for `nginx`](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/production/deployment.html#nginx-configuration)).  That seems like it might be a simpler fix here?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-04-04 16:57 UTC

Does using a config more like prod remove the need for the `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` change?

i.e.
```diff
diff --git tools/droplets/zulipdev tools/droplets/zulipdev
index 0c37e0e80f..59b49a0091 100644
--- tools/droplets/zulipdev
+++ tools/droplets/zulipdev
@@ -12,16 +12,12 @@ server {
     ssl_certificate_key /etc/ssl/private/zulip.key;

     location / {
-        proxy_set_header Connection "";
-        proxy_set_header Host $host;
-        proxy_set_header X-Real-IP $remote_addr;
-        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
-        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
-
-        proxy_pass          http://127.0.0.1:9991;
-        proxy_read_timeout  1200;
-
-        proxy_redirect off;
-        proxy_next_upstream off;
+        proxy_set_header   X-Forwarded-For $proxy_add_x_forwarded_for;
+        proxy_set_header   X-Forwarded-Proto $scheme;
+        proxy_set_header   Host $http_host;
+        proxy_http_version 1.1;
+        proxy_buffering    off;
+        proxy_read_timeout 20m;
+        proxy_pass         http://127.0.0.1:9991;
     }
 }
```

**Tam Le** · 2023-04-04 18:18 UTC

tried updating the Nginx config as you suggested but would still get the same error (reloaded the nginx config and everything).

Note that an alternative option to get past the error, instead of setting `CSRF_TRUSTED_ORIGINS` in `dev_settings.py`, would be to set:
```python
SECURE_PROXY_SSL_HEADER = ("HTTP_X_FORWARDED_PROTO", "https")
```

Reduced test case:

```python
import ctypes
import threading
import time

thread = threading.Thread(target=lambda: time.sleep(1))
thread.daemon = True
thread.start()
time.sleep(0.1)
ctypes.pythonapi.PyThreadState_SetAsyncExc(
    ctypes.c_ulong(thread.ident), ctypes.py_object(TimeoutError)
)
time.sleep(0.1)
thread.is_alive()
time.sleep(0.1)
assert thread.is_alive()
```

Under Python 3.10, 3.10 with coverage, or 3.11, `thread.is_alive()` immediately returns `True`. Under 3.11 with coverage, the first `thread.is_alive()` blocks for the thread’s `sleep` to finish and the second one returns `False`.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2023-05-08 22:32 UTC

This is the overall technical design I planned for implementing the **notification aspect** of the "Follow Topics" feature:

1. We plan to make notifications configurable for each topic.

So, notifications are sent for messages sent in a topic or not is determined by:
[`user_allows_notifications_in_StreamTopic`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/lib/notification_data.py#L177)
```diff
def user_allows_notifications_in_StreamTopic(
    stream_is_muted: bool,
    visibility_policy: int,
    stream_specific_setting: Optional[bool],
+   topic_specific_setting: Optional[bool],
    global_setting: bool,
) -> bool:
    """
    Captures the hierarchy of notification settings, where visibility policy is considered first,
    followed by stream-specific settings, and the global setting in the UserProfile is the fallback.
    """
+   if visibility_policy == UserTopic.VisibilityPolicy.FOLLOWED:
+      return topic_specific_setting

    if stream_is_muted and visibility_policy != UserTopic.VisibilityPolicy.UNMUTED:
        return False

    if visibility_policy == UserTopic.VisibilityPolicy.MUTED:
        return False

    if stream_specific_setting is not None:
        return stream_specific_setting

    return global_setting
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-29 18:27 UTC

For self-hosted systems, we do migrations with the server down, since it's generally pretty easy for an individual organization to take a minute of downtime, and usually all migrations finish in less than that on a single-organization system.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-29 18:29 UTC

I don't have time to write up how Zulip Cloud manages things in detail, but if someone who knows what they're doing is managing it, it's possible to make the window between the migration being applied and the relevant part of the server being restarted be a few seconds, and the downtime impact of a few seconds of downtime of any form is pretty minimal, but especially when it's a thing that each user does once per account.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-29 18:30 UTC

For migrations on tables like `Message`, where a brief downtime would affect every user, not just the users joining that moment, we usually do a series of migrations that each can be done without downtime, where you first add a nullable column, and then fill it, and then make it not nullable anymore.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-29 18:30 UTC

## Data model internals for DMs #25713

*2023-05-24 to 2023-05-29 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Data.20model.20internals.20for.20DMs.20.2325713/with/1575463)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-24 00:29 UTC

So in #25713, there's interest in having Zulip support per-user settings for direct message conversations of various sorts.

The challenge for doing this in Zulip is that while we could very easily hang data off the `Subscription` table for group direct message conversations just like we do for users' subscriptions to Streams, this is not possible for 1:1 private message conversations, because the internal database representation for those involves a single `Recipient` object for the user who the direct message was sent to, and the conversation is determined by the pair of that user's ID and the user ID of the sender.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-24 00:30 UTC

I think the most straightforward way to solve that problem would be to just change how we store 1:1 direct messages to have a group direct message conversation object (`Huddle` in the database right now, though we're definitely going to rename that eventually) for every direct message conversation, rather than having this weird special case of 1:1 direct messages in how the database stores things.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-24 00:31 UTC

I am not sure there would be any major downsides to such a refactor of our direct message conversation storage internals, other than the transition costs. I think the main one would be that we'd increase the size of the `Huddle` table by some substantial multiplicative factor like 5-10; it's not exactly a large table and is rarely accessed.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-24 00:34 UTC

And I think it might come with significant benefits in terms of removing the need to have special case logic like this:

``` python
# If the private message is just between the sender and                            
# another person, force it to be a personal internally                             
if len(recipient_profiles_map) == 2 and sender.id in recipient_profiles_map:       
    del recipient_profiles_map[sender.id]                                          
                                                                                   
assert recipient_profiles_map                                                      
if len(recipient_profiles_map) == 1:                                               
    [user_profile] = recipient_profiles_map.values()                               
    return Recipient(                                                              
        id=user_profile.recipient_id,                                              
        type=Recipient.PERSONAL,                                                   
        type_id=user_profile.id,                                                   
    )                                                                              
                                                                                   
# Otherwise, we need a huddle.  Make sure the sender is included in huddle messages
recipient_profiles_map[sender.id] = sender                                         
                                                                                   
user_ids = set(recipient_profiles_map)                                             
return get_huddle_recipient(user_ids)                                              
```

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-24 00:37 UTC

I agree that there would be some transition costs here, but this feels like a really good idea to me.  Insofar as you always have to think about `Huddle` logic in the backend, you might as well make it support the 1:1 case and eliminate a lot of code.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-24 00:39 UTC

I have some nostalgic fondness for the "Huddle" name, but I also agree that it's probably overdue for a rename, haha. :laughter_tears:

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-24 00:45 UTC

There has always been a ton of fiddly code on the JS side as well related to this general problem.  (Which possibly means you should be a little careful about transition costs, but I think the long-term changes would be good.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-24 19:48 UTC

Thoughts on what we should rename it to? `DirectMessageGroup` is the most natural option in my mind.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-05-26 20:53 UTC

The only drawback is that it seems like it'd be very easy to accidentally have more than one 1:1 DM for a pair of users.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-29 18:31 UTC

I think that's what `huddle_hash` is for -- we have a `UNIQUE` index on a hash of the pair of user IDs. (With modern databases, probably there's a fancier thing we could do that skips the hash).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-29 18:32 UTC

(And we already would have that problem for groups of 3 users anyway, if we didn't have a way to prevent it).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-05-29 18:49 UTC

PostgreSQL has had array fields [forever](https://www.ucolick.org/~de/PG/OldManual/advanced.html#arrays), and Django has supported them [since 1.8](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/1.8/releases/1.8/#new-postgresql-specific-functionality).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-29 18:58 UTC

Yeah, we've not touched the Huddle model since 2013; I think I remember being annoyed that Django didn't support it.

The main work would be just making sure we get the indexes right, which despite https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.2/ref/contrib/postgres/fields/#indexing-these-fields is probably easy for our use case, since the only query we have a reaason to do on that table is "Given this exact list of user IDs, find me the object that corresponds to that".

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-05-29 19:01 UTC

Yeah the default B-tree index should do what we need there. (A hash index would be better except those [can’t be declared unique](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/indexes-unique.html) for some reason.)


## Django logs to stdout vs stderr

*2023-05-24 to 2023-05-25 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Django.20logs.20to.20stdout.20vs.20stderr/with/1576186)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-24 22:52 UTC

I'd appreciate feedback on my proposal to move Django `logging` output to use `stdout` rather than the default of `stderr`, see #25750 / #23937. I think we're using `redirect_stderr=true` in all our supervisor jobs already, so this mostly affects manually running things on the command line and maybe cron jobs.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-05-24 23:01 UTC

Looking at the original motivation:

> otherwise it's hard to determine if anything is wrong with backup/export

That’s what exit codes are for, no?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-05-24 23:04 UTC

My main concern is that this could have weird side effects on commands like `manage.py showmigrations` where `upgrade-zulip-stage-2` is parsing its stdout.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-24 23:18 UTC

Yeah, probably that's the right thing to audit for.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-24 23:20 UTC

I am more motivated by the console logging output that we've ourselves written for management commands being primarily written/intended to be informative output, not error output, and thus conceptually something belonging in `stdout`. 

I was unable to find any useful references on why Django picked that default, but the `showmigrations` case, or deprecation warnings that Django issues itself might be the sort of thing that motivates it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-24 23:20 UTC

I suppose the more conservative option for us would be to define a `console_stdout` separate output location, and configure the specific loggers that we control there.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-05-24 23:21 UTC

The logging system is not really intended for stuff that belongs in stdout in the first place. That’s what `print()` is for.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-25 23:52 UTC

We use the Django/Python logging system in a number of places to ensure that changes get logged to the log file for that subsystem, in addition for being printed, and that's definitely an expected use case for it. What I'm not sure about is whether it's worth the effort to make our configuration match our intention here; I mostly decided to work on this because it looked simple.


## api narrow failure

*2023-05-27 to 2023-07-04 · 65 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/api.20narrow.20failure/with/1578935)*

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 16:47 UTC

When you call `client.get_messages` the narrow filter is modern:

~~~
narrow = [dict(operator="streams", operand="public")]

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 16:49 UTC

When you call `client.call_on_each_event(handle_event, event_types=["message"], ...)` you have to use old style tuple narrows:

~~~
narrow = [["streams", "public"]]

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 16:51 UTC

That is obviously somewhat inconvenient, because it is fairly natural when developing an API program to start by testing with `get_messages` and then, once you have that working, switch over to `call_on_each_event`.  In fact, you may possibly want to support both at the same time.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 16:55 UTC

The evil thing, however, is that if you mistakenly call `call_on_each_event` with a new-style narrow, the API sends it off to the server with no warning that you are on the wrong schema.  And then the register event seems to happily accept the narrow, but when it actually processes the event, it interprets the narrow as always-return-false.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 16:57 UTC

I am still investigating, but there are two possible fixes here:
* Just solve it in the API client by either doing a basic type check to fail hard or just auto-downgrade the modern format
* Solve it on the server side.

The latter seems smarter to me for a couple reasons.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 17:00 UTC

Apart from some mypy yuckiness, it seems like we could trivially upgrade this code to the modern format while staying backward compatible:

~~~ py
 135 def build_narrow_filter(narrow: Collection[Sequence[str]]) -> Callable[[Mapping[str, Any]], bool]:
 136     """Changes to this function should come with corresponding changes to
 137     NarrowLibraryTest."""
 138     check_supported_events_narrow_filter(narrow)
 139
 140     def narrow_filter(event: Mapping[str, Any]) -> bool:
 141         message = event["message"]
 142         flags = event["flags"]
 143         for element in narrow:
 144             operator = element[0]
 145             operand = element[1]

~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 17:04 UTC

Apart from tests, though, it only has one caller, which is `ClientDescriptor`, although that method is supposed to be a pretty dumb bucket of parameters, so that might not be the right place either.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 17:08 UTC

Hrm, `events_register_backend` claims to be validating that the narrow is a tuple:

~~~
 76     narrow: NarrowT = REQ(
 77         json_validator=check_list(check_list(check_string, length=2)), default=[]
 78     ),

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 17:14 UTC

Well, the server is at least legitimately complaining to the client (insofar as the server is too inflexible to support the modern format):

~~~
{'result': 'error', 'msg': 'narrow[0] is not a list', 'code': 'BAD_REQUEST'}

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 17:22 UTC

So `do_api_query` has a retry loop, and it's called by `do_register`, which has its own retry loop.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 17:25 UTC

Ok, this is the same problem as #**feedback>api client silent failure**, except that here it's ignoring validation of parameters, while there it is ignoring validation of API keys.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 17:25 UTC

Let's mostly talk over there about the API side of things.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 17:28 UTC

On the server side, fixing `build_narrow_filter` won't help anything, because the view layer at the edge of the server won't even let the modern format in.  So you basically have to fix `events_register_backend` to accept both flavors.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 17:29 UTC

Then the quick fix is that `e_r_b` just downgrades the modern version to tuples for its callees.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 17:30 UTC

The only slightly longer fix would be that it upgrades the ancient versions to dictionaries for its callees, and then we tweak all the callees.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-05-27 17:30 UTC

I saw about five tests that would have to be touched.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-05-29 17:48 UTC

I am also available to do remote pairing with somebody on this (assuming, of course, that they have a working dev environment).  I am pretty experienced with this type of change, and it's not rocket science, but it seems like this will be at least a couple hours of work.

In other words, I am not yet broadening the set of acceptable types that the server accepts at the edge; instead, I am just making the internal code, particularly `build_narrow_filter`, more consistent with other server-side code.  I want `build_narrow_filter` to work with dictionaries instead of tuples.     @classmethod

            d["client_type_name"] = d["client_type"]                                                    
        if "client_gravatar" not in d:                                                                  
            # Temporary migration for the addition of the client_gravatar field

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-06-05 20:05 UTC

(replying to Brijmohan Siyag)
> I went through some libraries, and none of them were maintained and fully fit for our project, So I'm going with our own implementation.

I'm not wild about maintaining our own implementation of the protocol, which has a bunch of fiddly bits to it (e.g. [concatenation](https://tus.io/protocols/resumable-upload#concatenation), which is required for parallel uploads).

> will re-factor the code after that and will post the approach here. Currently I'm updating the LocalUploadBackend.

When using the S3 backend, the simplest implementation is to store the chunks locally and upload the complete file all at once, when we have all of the parts locally.  That has the nice property that the Backend implementation stays essentially unchanged -- give it all of the bytes in the file, and it will durably store them.  However, it means that there is now file upload state stored on the server, which would have to be copied over if someone were to transition the server over to another instance.  It also defers all of the data transfer into S3 until the very env, making the final upload take potentially a very long time.  We may need to extend the LocalUploadBackend and S3UploadBackend to be aware of chunked uploads, and use the [S3 multipart upload](https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/mpuoverview.html) APIs.

Keep in mind that we will need some way to garbage-collect partial file uploads.  The [TUS FAQ suggests a week](https://tus.io/faq#how-are-pauseresume-handled-when-should-i-delete-partial-uploads).

*2023-06-01 to 2023-08-08 · 32 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Migrate.20extra_data.20on.20audit.20log.20models.20to.20JSONField/with/1583509)*

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-01 21:59 UTC

I'm reviving #23116 so that we can complete the migration from hacking random stringified Python objects into `TextField` to storing just `dict`s with `JSONField`.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-01 22:03 UTC

Just incorporated the recent change in #25625. Most of the migration aren't that stale, so no major updates are needed.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-01 22:03 UTC

I just need to go through the commits again to make sure that everything else is still up-to-date.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-03 04:27 UTC

I have went through the commits and made some changes organizing them. The plan is to organize them into four PRs of incremental changes.
1. #25877: Prepare zilencer for a API change that adds compatibility support for `extra_data` being either `str | None` or `dict`.
1. #25878 : Add `extra_data_json`, a transitional field that will replace the original `extra_data`. This implements a double-write mechanism such that the newer entries of audit log models will always have it populated. As long as the older entries get backfilled, `extra_data_json` will be consistent with `extra_data` for all audit logs.
1. #25879: A backfilling migration that processes all existing audit log entries in chunks and updates their `extra_data_json` by looking at `extra_data`. We expect that the server does not contain extra data converted to string using `str` to have `Decimal` values.
1. #23116: The final migration that renames `extra_data_json` to `extra_data`, safely dropping the old values. This also contains all the changes necessary so that the server interacts with `extra_data` being a `JSONField` instead of `TextField`.

## reducing minimal memory usage

*2023-06-06 to 2024-02-14 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/reducing.20minimal.20memory.20usage/with/1586585)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-06-06 18:10 UTC

After reviewing https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/25906, I'm thinking it might be worth doing some more little configuration tweaks to reduce Zulip's memory requirements for low-memory systems. Each `zulip` process seems to be about 140MB on that system. I see two opportunities for optimization:
* One idea is to reduce `uwsgi_processes` from the default of 4 (for systems under 4GiB of total memory) from 4 to some lower number; maybe 2 or 3. I'm not sure this is a great idea; cutting the parallelism too much will result in latency issues.
* A possibly easier idea would be trying to combine/reduce the two `delivery_scheduled_*` workers, which currently are each independent processes from the multi-threaded `process_queue` bundle. 
* Doing some memory profiling to see if there's any large third-party dependencies that we're hardly using that we should switch to a conditional/deferred import. E.g. maybe `talon` is huge and we should only be importing it in the email gateway process.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-06-06 18:10 UTC

I think the last option is likely to be the most fruitful if there are good tools for doing it; I've not investigated that topic.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-01-29 14:55 UTC

We've gotten more reports of this in 8.1 -- e.g. #**production help>Sending message takes too long**

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-01-29 14:56 UTC

I've got a lot on my plate right now; it would be good if someone else could take a look at this, because it seems like a notable regression which is negatively affecting users' experience.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-30 20:11 UTC

There's a memory leak in `uwsgi` processes that we should probably debug using a production system. But that's unlikely to be the cause of a new problem on upgrade to 8.x -- it appears to be a fairly slow leak. One thing we've noticed is that the minimal memory usage of Zulip `uwsgi` processes in production seems to be higher than I remember in past versions.

I wonder if there's a good way to investigate whether there's unexpectedly huge dependencies being pulled in to our Python processes? I remember we found a bunch of bugs a couple years ago involving unused Python code imported by badly written modules consuming a ton of CPU (and presumably also memory) resources.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-30 20:12 UTC

Any ideas on how to investigate that?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-30 20:13 UTC

For an 8.2 release, the stopgap answer is to reduce `uwsgi_processes` in some memory range; let me see about doing a quick PR for that.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-01-30 20:14 UTC

I have [heard](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bw5AHdZA7e4) that [Memray](https://bloomberg.github.io/memray/) is useful in such cases.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-01-30 20:37 UTC

Opened #28755 with a proposal for how to adjust how many processes we use:
* Moves the minimum memory for multiprocess mode to 3800MiB from 3500MiB; this is still higher 4000MB that you sometimes get from hosting providers selling "4GB" systems.
* Changes how we calculate the default for `uwsgi_processes` to increase in a more stepped fashion, and in particular not increase from 4 to 6 until 6000MB.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-02-14 19:15 UTC

I just played with memray, and it was indeed pretty useful -- worth pointing at our workers and django processes, for sure.

We need `PARENT_GROUP_CHANGED` because otherwise we don't have any indexed way to look *up* and find out when we were moved to another subgroup -- we have to limit by `realm` and `SUBGROUP_MEMBERSHIP_*` and check every `extra_data` to find out if it applies to the subgroup we care about.
