## UserGroup race conditions

*2023-06-15 to 2023-08-24 · 37 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/UserGroup.20race.20conditions/with/1593918)*

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-15 19:56 UTC

When adding a subgroup B to a user group A, we do a [check](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/ea1357be668112b3e96d82776c6bbc71f60d76f2) to see if the B already recursively contains subgroup A. Let's say this is transaction T1.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-15 19:58 UTC

I think this is fine in a world where the transactions are all serializable. But it appears that we potentially have a race condition when the recursive query that gets all the subgroups finishes before another insertion is complete.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-15 20:04 UTC

Suppose that in transaction T2, A is being added to user group C, and that C is a subgroup of B;
it occurs that A gets added to C after the recursive check in T1. We proceed to add B to A.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-15 20:09 UTC

In the default [read committed isolation level](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-READ-COMMITTED), even if we put the queries inside a single `atomic.transaction` block, it is still subject to *phantom reads*. @Alex Vandiver [suggested](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/23634#discussion_r1230325201) a similar issue in the backfilling migration for audit log entries of user group membership changes.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-06-15 20:25 UTC

We could create `SERIALIZABLE` transactions with [django-pgtransaction](https://django-pgtransaction.readthedocs.io).

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-15 21:13 UTC

A [comparison](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/transaction-iso.html#XACT-SERIALIZABLE) between *Serializable* transactions and *Read Committed*/*Repeatable Read* transactions:

> The monitoring of read/write dependencies has a cost, as does the restart of transactions which are terminated with a serialization failure, but balanced against the cost and blocking involved in use of explicit locks and SELECT FOR UPDATE or SELECT FOR SHARE, Serializable transactions are the best performance choice for some environments.

Because `SERIALIZABLE` transactions can fail:

> It is important that an environment which uses this technique have a generalized way of handling serialization failures (which always return with an SQLSTATE value of '40001'), because it will be very hard to predict exactly which transactions might contribute to the read/write dependencies and need to be rolled back to prevent serialization anomalies.

we need to have a standard way to deal with serialization failures. Depending on how often this happens, would multiple retries and fallback to a JsonableError suffice?

We also need to use the isolation level consistently. This should result in some refactorings with all the writes related to user groups.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-06-16 00:28 UTC

There are ways to write this with the default *read committed* isolation level (e.g. taking "SELECT FOR UPDATE" locks whenever you are recursively checking a group's contents, to prevent edits to the set of things in them) but these also admit the possibility of deadlock -- if group A is added into group B in T1, and group B is added into group A in T2, postgres will detect a deadlock and abort one of them.  I suspect that any solution to this sort of problem may have some possibility of deadlock or serialization error.

We do have deadlock possibilities elsewhere in the codebase, and when PostgreSQL fails, we just 500.  This is probably fine at the scale we're at -- as long as we expose some sort of error message to the user, they're free to retry.  That sort of behaviour is probably totally ifne here as well.  I am very wary of hiding retry loops in the middle of code like this -- you have to be careful to include every database ACL and consistency check inside the transaction, or the retry will happily put you into invalid state based on some properties which were passed into the transaction by way of Python variables whose values are now out of date.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-06-16 00:48 UTC

I think `SELECT FOR UPDATE` takes a lock on the rows it returns, but does not take a lock on the nonexistence of the rows it doesn’t return—those predicate locks are only used under `SERIALIZABLE` isolation.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-06-16 00:54 UTC

Agree, and that's what can result in phantom reads.  But if A has-many-B, selecting for update the B's provides no guarantee -- but selecting A `FOR UPDATE`, if you're consistent about doing that before updating B's membership in A, can provide that guarantee.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-06-16 01:02 UTC

I don’t follow. Consider two empty groups being added to each other simultaneously. Both processes do `SELECT FOR UPDATE`, they both return zero rows and take zero locks, they both decide to go ahead, both transactions commit, and now you have a cycle.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-06-16 01:05 UTC

Oh okay I see. You want to lock the group rows themselves, not the membership rows.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-06-16 01:09 UTC

So before adding group foo to group bar, either (a) we lock foo, bar, and all recursive supergroups of bar, or (b) we lock foo, bar, and all recursive subgroups of foo?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-06-16 01:27 UTC

Yeah, locking the group rows -- sorry for being unclear.  And if we're adding *to* group bar, I think (a) makes more sense.  But I think either would work.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-06-16 01:53 UTC

We’d need to be careful to lock the recursive {super,sub} groups with the same CTE query that finds them, rather than as a separate step.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-06-16 01:56 UTC

Yup.  And ordering in there is fraught -- I think we want to lock bottom-to-top, but that may be hard to arrange.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-16 02:05 UTC

I feel that (b) is more natural, and it is more consistent with the predominant use of subgroups in the codebase at the time. This can change though.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-17 03:02 UTC

/me created a pull request for the initial implementation: #26048

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-17 03:04 UTC

Haven't tested this yet. I'm not sure if we have a way to set up race conditions and test for that concurrently with the existing testing infrastructure.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-06-20 19:57 UTC

Testing race conditions is unfortunately notoriously hard. :/

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-28 00:27 UTC

I think it will probably be easier if we utilize the testing infrastructure for `test-api`.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-28 00:29 UTC

So that we hit the server via actual HTTP requests, instead of spawning threads to use Django test clients concurrently. The latter doesn't sound like its intended use case.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-28 03:58 UTC

Did some testing by utilizing the `test-api` infrastructure. I came to the realization that probably there is nothing stopping me from sharing the test client across threads, so that's worth trying.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-28 04:15 UTC

Some discoveries so far:
1. It is probably best to do `SELECT FOR UPDATE NOWAIT` with the recursive query. When the lock cannot be initially acquired, it is possible that after the lock becomes available, more rows that ought to be locked get committed. So there is no point waiting on the lock.
2. Django's `TestCase` wraps the test case into a transaction. It silences the error raised when `select_for_update` is not in a transaction as it expects it to be.
3. Knowing the exact points where deadlocks and database error due to `nowait`, a possible way to implement error handling is to raise a `JsonableError` on `DeadlockDetected` or `LockNotAvailable`. This aborts the transaction managed by the helper context manager where we restrict the scope of the row locks to.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-06-28 18:10 UTC

> When the lock cannot be initially acquired, it is possible that after the lock becomes available, more rows that ought to be locked get committed. So there is no point waiting on the lock.

Doesn't that defeat the point of doing the locking entirely?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-06-28 18:11 UTC

Tests being run in a transaction is a big headache when working with transactions.  It makes sense from a test performance point of view, but it makes it real hard to test rollbacks and post-commit hooks.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-06-28 19:28 UTC

I think `nowait` should only apply to the recursive query. We can wait on the second lock as usual.

**Topic Bridge Bot** · 2023-07-04 05:58 UTC

@Zixuan James Li mentioned this topic in **[#backend > TransactionTestCase](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/3-backend/topic/TransactionTestCase/near/1603434)**.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-04 06:53 UTC

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-04 06:55 UTC

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-06 01:45 UTC

I'm running into some trouble when using `select_for_update` within the `WITH` part of the recursive CTE.
The error: `FOR UPDATE is not allowed with UNION/INTERSECT/EXCEPT`.
This is a [documented behavior](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-select.html#:~:text=Currently%2C%20FOR%20NO%20KEY%20UPDATE%2C%20FOR%20UPDATE%2C%20FOR%20SHARE%20and%20FOR%20KEY%20SHARE%20cannot%20be%20specified%20either%20for%20a%20UNION%20result%20or%20for%20any%20input%20of%20a%20UNION.)
I also found a relevant response [here](https://www.postgresql.org/message-id/27164.1551987517%40sss.pgh.pa.us), where it's explained that they are incompatible because of the ambiguity introduced.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-06 01:45 UTC

Is there a way to rewrite the CTE such that `UNION` is avoided?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-07-06 02:24 UTC

That may not be possible, because a group could be a subgroup via more than one path.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-06 04:49 UTC

I see. We can still acquire the lock on the full set of recursive descendants. This is less ideal than progressively acquiring the lock as we descent with the CTE.

However, assuming we don't have too deep of a hiearchy, the window for race conditions during the recursive query is pretty narrow. The adversary has to complete a full request to add an subgroup in midst of the query in order to abuse this.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-07 16:37 UTC

I imagine most of these hierarchies will be relatively simple.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-07 16:38 UTC

But we do need to be careful here to avoid intentional DoS nonsense.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-08-24 23:55 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-08-24 23:55 UTC

## TransactionTestCase

*2023-07-04 to 2023-07-06 · 21 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/TransactionTestCase/with/1603433)*

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-04 05:57 UTC

Opened #26178 for implementing a Zulip variant of `TransactionTestCase`.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-04 05:58 UTC

This is related to #**backend>UserGroup race conditions** where we wanted to test some transaction-specific behaviors with Django.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-04 06:00 UTC

The idea is that we can refactor `ZulipTestCase` into `ZulipTestCaseMixin`, which is a subclass of Django's `SimpleTestCase`. And then make use of mro so that we can combine `ZulipTestCaseMixin` with either `TransactionTestCase` or `TestCase`.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-04 06:02 UTC

By default, `TransactionTestCase` truncate the database by using the `flush` command. It effectively clears the test database of the current worker during the `tearDown` stage. Because our test runner is set up to only initialize the database once, this behavior is not viable.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-04 06:05 UTC

So I decided to turn it into no-op, at the cost of losing isolation between tests. This can be problematic because `TransactionTestCase` does not wrap tests into atomic transactions, so running tests *does* cause changes to be committed, leaving side effects that can interfere with other test cases.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-04 06:17 UTC

There are some possible ways to go around this:
- Isolate transaction test cases from regular test cases with a separate worker, and write test cases being aware of possible side effects
- Use the [`serialized_rollback`](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.2/topics/testing/tools/#transactiontestcase:~:text=you%20can%20set%20serialized_rollback%20%3D%20True%20inside%20the%20TestCase%20body.) feature. It serializes the database before each test and loads it back afterward. I couldn't get it working for some reason. It is also known to be very slow.
- (Current implementation) Make transaction tests separate so they only get run when the `--include-transaction-tests` argument. Manually restrict side effects when writing transaction test cases and leave transaction tests to the last for the test runner minimizing the impact.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-04 06:22 UTC

Scenarios where transaction test cases are needed are rare. And committing transactions is not always necessary for these test cases. So it is probably unlikely to have side effects that make backend tests flakey.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-07-05 14:29 UTC

The loss of isolation is mildly problematic, since it means that running the whole testsuite a second time may fail, when it passed the first time.  That's a recipe for frustration.

I wonder if we could have the tearDown assert what changes are allowed to have happened to the database, so if someone writes a bad TransactionTestCase, that the test will fail rather than pollute the database state.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-07-05 14:30 UTC

Well, I guess it'd fail *and* pollute the database test state.  But at least it'd only affect the person writing the test, who is going to be more amenable to re-provisioning to a clean test db.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-05 17:38 UTC

Looks like Django already runs `TestCase` before `TransactionTestCase`: https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.2/topics/testing/overview/#order-of-tests

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-05 17:40 UTC

This is good because `TransactionTestCase` won't pollute regular tests in this way. For detecting database changes, I'm not sure if there is a good way. Maybe we can use an `on_commit` hook on all transactions?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-07-05 17:47 UTC

(replying to Zixuan James Li)
> This is good because `TransactionTestCase` won't pollute regular tests in this way.

It can still pollute the database for the *next* run of the `TestCase` runs.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-07-05 17:49 UTC

I think we want to assert that there are no new rows in the database -- so maybe fingerprint the set of ids in every table, and compare post-test?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-07-05 17:49 UTC

(obviously, edits to rows could also cause problems, but inserts or deletions are much easier to test)

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-05 17:54 UTC

> for the *next* run of the TestCase runs.

Oh, I see the point. We [clone the test database per worker](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/086d6be8e255c868db8cb5d58a4506d7970da5d7/zerver/lib/test_runner.py#L208) every time we run the tests, so at least we have isolation between runs.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-07-05 18:04 UTC

Ah, great, so we can't drift there.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-07-05 18:05 UTC

ISTR (back when I was last working on test performance for a different project) that in PostgreSQL 9 cloning from a template DB was *really* slow.  I guess we only do it once per worker, so I guess they haven't improved perf of that too much.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-05 18:14 UTC

Yeah, we clone once per worker. I think assertions would be doable without compromising much performance. The alternatives such as cloning the database per transaction test/testcase will be a lot slower.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-06 04:55 UTC

I have updated `ZulipTransactionTestCase` to have checks for all tables for insertion/deletion, so one writing test cases would be responsible for restraining leakage.

**Notification Bot** · 2023-07-06 11:40 UTC

This topic was moved here from #**backend>TransactionTestCase** by @Vihaan M.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-06 18:02 UTC

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> ISTR (back when I was last working on test performance for a different project) that in PostgreSQL 9 cloning from a template DB was *really* slow. I guess we only do it once per worker, so I guess they haven't improved perf of that too much.

Yeah, it takes like a few hundred milliseconds, which is fine as a one per worker thing, but not a thing we want to do in general.

*2023-07-10 to 2023-07-11 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/realm.20default_code_block_language.20setting/with/1607075)*

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-07-10 17:49 UTC

So it was noted in #**feedback>Using code blocks with "Enter to send" set, #26085**, that here in CZO the composebox typeahead header is being rendered even though a default syntax/language isn't set.

[Screenshot-from-2023-07-10-18-54-01.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/5d/7lxrdBLkZ28ys2hDRRRHUwu-/Screenshot-from-2023-07-10-18-54-01.png)

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-07-10 17:49 UTC

It looks like in commit 5c0a52585c1bd6d60227d5a52fcb327e0299cd38, we changed the frontend code to check for `null` instead of an empty string. But I don't think that addressed the underlying issue, which is how this realm setting is updated when an organization sets and then unsets this setting.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-07-10 17:49 UTC

The field in the `Realm` class is: 

```python
default_code_block_language = models.TextField(null=True, default=None)
```

So, it's `null` or `None` when an organization is created, but then if at any point the organization sets and unsets this realm setting, then it is saved as an empty string in the database, not `None`. I'm guessing this is what happened at some point in CZO since I can reproduce in the dev environment.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-07-10 17:49 UTC

There is [this block](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/views/realm.py#L324-L329) in `update_realm` in `zerver/views/realm.py`:
```python
    if default_code_block_language is not None:
        # Migrate '', used in the API to encode the default/None behavior of this feature.
        if default_code_block_language == "":
            data["default_code_block_language"] = None
        else:
            data["default_code_block_language"] = default_code_block_language
```

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-07-10 17:49 UTC

But that only updates the data in the success response for the realm setting change. The events sent to other users and what's returned as the realm setting moving forward is the empty string, because this is done via the normal `do_set_realm_property` loop earlier in that same function.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-07-10 17:49 UTC

Here's a screenshot of the documentation for this realm setting api/register-queue:
[Screenshot-from-2023-07-10-18-50-21.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/50/fp72wi_Vmp7ovhV08RcZwE8p/Screenshot-from-2023-07-10-18-50-21.png)

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-07-10 17:50 UTC

The realm description is the only other realm setting that's a text field and is in `Realm.property_types`. The realm description has a default value as an empty string, instead of `None`. So, I don't think there are other realm settings with this particular issue.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-07-10 18:24 UTC

Good sleuthing -- do we want to make the default just the empty string, and make the field non-nullable?  That seems potentially cleanest here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-10 22:56 UTC

Yeah that solution seems fine.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2023-07-11 13:50 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-10 23:15 UTC

Hmm. I can't say I love the bulk database query runtimes; the bulk cache query times are even worse. I feel like there must be something wrong with how we're doing the cache queries -- `memcached` should be doing something very cheap here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-10 23:17 UTC

One theory is that we're pickling complex objects to put them into the cache, and THAT is what is expensive. I suspect a few categories of things:
* Metadata objects hanging of `class Stream` or `class Realm` like `COMMON_POLICY_TYPES` that aren't actually part of the data object.
* The `select_related` chaining.

I think the best fix here is probably to figure out how to limit the scope of the `select_related` calls here to just get the direct relations we care about -- mostly the direct properties on the `.realm` field, and not any of the `.foo_group` things, in that what we're doing is wrong for the DB there too, and then see where that leaves us with this cache question.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-10 23:17 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell)
> Here's an interesting rule of thumb: A 400-row query is only 5x more expensive than a single-row query.

I think this is worth re-stating, particularly in the context of message fetching (with the caveat that my measurements were on Stream--I can fairly quickly find a similar number for Message).

It's really important that our bulk-key caching strategy takes into account that what we're mostly trying to avoid is DB round trips. If we get a cache miss and still have to incur a round trip, then at least for that request, we probably wasted resources.

What I didn't bring up before, and which is slightly off topic, is that I think we should consider this in our backfill strategy as well.  It's probably fine to be a little more aggressive about getting more DB rows per round trip.  I know there's some nuance here, since maybe rendering is the bottleneck, or whatever, but hopefully it's at least food for thought.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-11 01:52 UTC

Currently, on the deletion of the related `modified_user` or `modified_stream`, the `RealmAuditLog` is deleted because we have `ON DELETE CASCADE` on both of them. In response to [this comment](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/26065/files/3ad0e770f0a6d58bf644effc1f5242086990e13f#r1259032571) on the PR that adds `modified_user_group` to `RealmAuditLog`, we want to determine if `ON DELETE CASCADE` is appropriate for any of these `modified_*` fields.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-11 01:57 UTC

This also came up [here](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/101-design/topic/Support.20user.20group.20deactivation/near/1594079) when discussing deactivation vs. deletion. If we want to support a proper implementation of deletion, `CASCADE` almost certainly won't be an option.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-11 02:11 UTC

We might want to use [`PROTECT`](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.2/ref/models/fields/#django.db.models.PROTECT) instead for these fields. It is possible for us to prepare the audit logs that hold a reference to the to-be-deleted row, and remove that reference by nulling it or pointing it to a dummy row.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-07-11 17:50 UTC

I think it's possible that CASCADE is what we want in that there's nothing else to do if one hard-deletes an object, but we should consider this a motivation to change user groups to have a deactivation model.


## select_related() with no args

*2023-07-11 to 2024-03-22 · 80 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/select_related.28.29.20with.20no.20args/with/1607522)*

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-11 10:19 UTC

A good cleanup project for somebody who understands the Django ORM pretty well is to do `git grep '[.]objects.select_related\(\)'` and find all the places where we call `select_related` with no arguments.  When you don't pass in specific tables to `select_related()`, Django tries to pre-fetch all the data that could conceivably be de-referenced from the main objects in the query, and this is usually more aggressive and expensive than we want.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-11 10:19 UTC

For context, I recently eliminated one such use of `select_related()` to make about a 10% speedup for one of our most expensive test modules.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-11 10:20 UTC

When those functions use `select_related()` without any arguments, the bot related fields are not fetched as they are nullable. I think a bunch of the differences are for if they're covariant, invariant, or contra-variant.  Most immutable types are covariant, and most mutable types are invariant.  Ref [relevant mypy docs](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/generics.html#variance-of-generic-types).

Well, I think the modern upstream Python community worldview is the opposite: that you not randomly convert iterable things to lists without a good reason, because the code is just as easy to read/write with lists as with iterators, and the iterator version has these utility benefits around memory usage and deferring computation you may not do (E.g. if your loop over query results has a `break`, a bunch of work can be skipped).

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-07-12 16:53 UTC

`collections.abc` long predates `typing` and mypy. `typing` just reused the same names for the same concepts. (The `typing` ones are deprecated in Python 3.9, in which the `collection.abc` ones gain generic subscripting functionality like the `typing` ones; we can switch after we drop 3.8 support.)

Your point about `Iterable` and consumption is important, and I’ve made it before (#18315, [docs](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/testing/mypy.html#read-only-types)): `Iterable` should only be used for values that are iterated once.

The main reason to prefer `Sequence`/`Mapping`/`AbstractSet` over `List`/`Dict`/`Set` is that it lets mypy help you guard against accidental mutation. This is especially important for function parameters with mutable default values, and our linters [require](https://github.com/astral-sh/ruff/issues/572) the immutable types to be used for this case. But it’s helpful in general to be able to trust that arguments won’t be mutated without auditing lots of code.

Another case that sometimes comes up is that if `B` is a subtype of `A`, then `Sequence[B]` can be coerced to `Sequence[A]`, while `List[B]` cannot be coerced to `List[A]`. (See [invariance vs. covariance](https://mypy.readthedocs.io/en/stable/common_issues.html#invariance-vs-covariance).)

**Steve Howell** · 2023-07-18 09:34 UTC

In #26271 I fix a problem where we have duplicate caches for user-based display recipients.  The first time anybody fetches messages that are sent to Alice as a DM, then we write basically identical cache entries that are keyed on user_id in one cache and then recipient_id in the other cache.  This is obviously a somewhat silly thing to do, so I fix it.  The long commit message for the last commit elaborates a bit on the implications, but the obvious benefit is that my change halves the number of cache entries, cache lookups, and cache writes related to message fetching.

I did a fairly substantial re-write of `bulk_fetch_display_recipients`, which you authored in full, and which has remained basically unmodified up until my changes.

~~~ py
 41 def simple_query(*, fields, table, id_field, ids):
 42     if len(ids) == 0:
 43         return []
 44     field_list = ", ".join(fields)
 45
 46     for id in ids:
 47         assert type(id) == int
 48
 49     id_list = ", ".join(str(id) for id in ids)
 50
 51     cursor = connection.cursor()
 52     sql = f"SELECT {field_list} FROM {table} WHERE {id_field} in ({id_list})"
 53     cursor.execute(sql)
 54     desc = cursor.description
 55     rows = [dict(zip((col[0] for col in desc), row)) for row in cursor.fetchall()]
 56     cursor.close()

*2023-07-25 to 2023-09-12 · 175 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/New.20has_request_variables.20API/with/1615890)*

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-25 20:34 UTC

I'm looking into `cattrs` to rework the validation system introducing an alternative to the current `REQ` design.
Previous discussions: #**development help>overloaded REQ**

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-25 20:34 UTC

I did some study on FastAPI on how we might incorporate `cattrs` into our `has_request_variables` system.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-25 20:34 UTC

FastAPI used to rely on setting [`Query`](https://fastapi.tiangolo.com/tutorial/query-params-str-validations/#alternative-old-query-as-the-default-value) as the default value if you want to do additional validations:
```python
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(q: str | None = Query(default=None, max_length=50)):
  ...
```
which is quite similar to `REQ`. It relies on setting the defaults of the parameters and inspecting them internally with the decorator too.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-25 20:35 UTC

In later versions, `Annotated` is preferred, with `Query` added as the metadata:
```python
@app.get("/items/")
async def read_items(q: Annotated[str | None, Query(max_length=50)] = None):
  ...
```

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-25 20:35 UTC

The latter use is advocated. I'm citing from their explanations of the benefits of `Annotated`:

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-25 20:35 UTC

> ## Advantages of Annotated¶
>  Using Annotated is recommended instead of the default value in function parameters, it is better for multiple reasons. 🤓
>  The default value of the function parameter is the actual default value, that's more intuitive with Python in general. 😌

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-25 20:35 UTC

Applicable. With `REQ` we are hacking the defaults by making REQ return `Any`. It can be less overhead if we just use type annotations and the defaults for the actual default values of the request parameters. `Annotated` does sound like an esoteric typing feature, but it is standard and more adapted.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-25 20:35 UTC

>  You could call that same function in other places without FastAPI, and it would work as expected. If there's a required parameter (without a default value), your editor will let you know with an error, Python will also complain if you run it without passing the required parameter.

>  When you don't use Annotated and instead use the (old) default value style, if you call that function without FastAPI in other place, you have to remember to pass the arguments to the function for it to work correctly, otherwise the values will be different from what you expect (e.g. QueryInfo or something similar instead of str). And your editor won't complain, and Python won't complain running that function, only when the operations inside error out.

> Because Annotated can have more than one metadata annotation, you could now even use the same function with other tools, like Typer. 🚀

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-25 20:35 UTC

Not quite applicable. I think we rarely call the view functions and prefer to run it through the middleware with a test client. Outside testing, we decouple reusable functions into `zerver.actions` or `zerver.lib`. It is more relatable to FastAPI probably because they have a more decorator-centric design hooking up the infrastructure.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-25 20:36 UTC

I think the main takeaway from this is that if gather enough information from the type annotation of the request parameters. hijacking the defaults will no longer be necessary. Even `REQ` itself and `Annotated` will no longer be not necessary for typical request parameters.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-25 20:36 UTC

We can switch to a `REQ`-less design, and only use `Annotated` when necessary.

  config_data: Mapping[str, str] = REQ(default={}, json_validator=check_dict(value_validator=check_string))

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-25 20:36 UTC

we can write

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-26 16:53 UTC

This is what a view in the latest iteration looks like:
```python
    @attrs.define
    class Dolor:
        num: int = attrs.field(validator=non_negative)

    def narrow_validator(
        instance: Any, attribute: Any, value: Sequence[Sequence[str]]
    ) -> None:
        for l in [text for lst in value for text in lst]:
            assert len(l) <= 2, "Too long"

    last_narrow = None
    # Reusable Annotated type
    JSON: TypeAlias = Annotated[T, Metadata(from_json=True)]

    @view
    def func(
        request: Request,
        dolor: Annotated[
            Dolor, Metadata(intentionally_undocumented=True, from_json=True)
        ] = Dolor(num=0),
        lorem: int = REQ(validator=non_negative),
        lpsum: Annotated[int, Metadata(intentionally_undocumented=True)] = REQ(
            validator=non_negative, default=0
        ),
        narrow: JSON[Sequence[Sequence[str]]] = REQ(
            validator=narrow_validator, default=[[]]
        ),
        other_param: int = 0,
    ) -> int:
        nonlocal last_narrow
        last_narrow = narrow
        return lorem + lpsum + dolor.num
```

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-26 16:57 UTC

To address the issues @Anders Kaseorg raised, we combine the use of `REQ` as the default, and `Metadata` in `Annotated`.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-26 17:07 UTC

- The annotated type is the indisputable source of parsing logic. The `cattrs` converter should *always* know how this type should be parsed, either through its built-in structuring functions or additional hooks we defined for our custom classes.
- `Metadata` never carries information about the type of the parameter. It should only describe things like "intentionally undocumented", "path only" or "this parameter should be parsed from JSON". 
- `validator` is a required parameter for `REQ`, so we can discourage the use of it as much as possible. In this case, the original default is passed as an argument to `REQ`. `REQ` is only there for type-checking the validator. For reusability and error handling, the validator should match the format `attrs` uses.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-26 17:10 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> You’re skipping some important subtle details. Consider, for example, the difference between `param: Optional[str] = REQ(default=None)` and `param: Optional[str] = REQ(json_validator=check_none_or(check_string))`, which have very incompatible input formats.
So these two parameters will be distinguishable:
`param: Optional[str] = None`
`param: Annotated[Optional[str], FromJSON()]` or, with a type alias, `param: JSON[Optional[str]]`

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-26 17:19 UTC

Note that nothing stops us from keep using composable validators, but dedicatedly written validators can take advantage of the type information given that we only run the validators after successfully parsing the value:
```python
# Before
alert_words: List[str] = REQ(json_validator=check_list(check_capped_string(100)))

#After
alert_words: JSON[List[str]] = REQ(validator=check_list(check_capped_string(100)))
# or
def check_alert_words(instance: Any, attribute: attrs.Attribute[List[str]], value[List[str]]) -> None:
    validate = check_capped_string(100)
    # No need to check_list
    for alert_word in value:
        validate(instance, attribute, alert_word)
alert_words: JSON[List[str]] = REQ(validator=check_alert_words)
```
```python
# Before
narrow: Sequence[Sequence[str]] = REQ(json_validator=check_list(check_list(check_string, length=2)), default=[])

# After
narrow: JSON[Sequence[Sequence[str]]] = REQ(validator=check_list(check_list(check_string, length=2)), default=[])
# or
def narrow_validator(
        instance: Any, attribute: Any, value: Sequence[Sequence[str]]
) -> None:
    for lst in value:
        assert len(lst) <= 2, "Too long"
narrow: JSON[Sequence[Sequence[str]]] = REQ(validator=narrow_validator, default=[])
```

```python
# Before
service_payload_url: Optional[str] = REQ(json_validator=check_url, default=None)

# After
service_payload_url: JSON[Optional[str]] = REQ(validator=check_url, default=None)
```
Note the main difference from the original validator system is that now the validators are only responsible for runtime checks. We don't get type information from them.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-26 17:23 UTC

Another thing to address here is that `cattrs` might coerce other types to `str` when they have already been handled by `orjson`.
For example, {"val": 1} can be structured as 
```python
@attrs.define
class Foo
    val: str
```
The [solution](https://github.com/python-attrs/cattrs/issues/278#issue-1276829148) to this will be to register hooks overriding this behavior for primitive types.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-26 21:39 UTC

Here is an alternative that doesn't require us to mix `REQ` with the regular defaults. For types that require validation, we define a `NewType` with a structuring hook registered.

```python
    # View
    NonNegInt = NewType("NonNegInt", int)

    def non_neg_int(value: object, typ: Type[NonNegInt]) -> int:
        v = c.structure(value, int)
        assert v >= 0, "No negative int"
        return v

    c.register_structure_hook(NonNegInt, non_neg_int)

    @view
    def func(
        request: Request,
        lorem: NonNegInt,
        lpsum: List[NonNegInt] = [],
        other_param: int = 0,
    ) -> int:
        return lorem + sum(lpsum)

    # Testing
    assert func(Request({"lorem": 12, "lpsum": [1, 2]})) == 15
    with assert_fail(Exception, log_err=True):
        func(Request({"lorem": 12, "lpsum": [1, -52]}))
    test_view(func)
```

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-26 22:26 UTC

Which is not necessarily negative because we are not compromising type safety here.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-07-30 07:29 UTC

Implementation notes from the commit messages:

We define two converters: `zulip_converter` and `json_converter`.
`json_converter` is dedicated for structuring and unstructuring JSON
serialized/deserialized data with some additional hooks. For example,
`json_converter` does not attempt to convert an `int` into a `str`, while
`zulip_converter` may.

This also introduces the `NewType` style structure functions to handle
primitive types that require extra validation, like URLs. To use, define
a type with `NewType`, and a validator function of the type Validator. The
function is expected to raise an error if the validation fails.
The validator function needs to be decorated with `newtype_validator` to
become usable with the converters.

For error handling, we define our own `format_exception` function to
customize how exceptions should be turned into error messages, making
sure that everything is properly translated. We re-raise exceptions that
are not explicitly handled to avoid silencing actual programming
errors, and use very specific conditions to determine if the error is
actually a validation error.

The goal of `endpoint` is to replicate most features supported by
`has_request_variables`, and improve on top of it. There are some
unresolved issues that we don't plan to work on currently. For example,
`endpoint` does not support `ignored_parameters_supported` for 400
responses, and it does not run validators on path-only arguments.

Unlike `has_request_variables`, `endpoint` supports error handling by aggregating
all the validation errors together by customizing cattrs' error
formater.

Most features supported by `has_request_variables` are supported by
endpoint in various ways.
For `REQ`:
- `whence` is supported by using `Metadata(whence="whence")`
- `default` can be just set by using the function parameter default
- `json_validator`/`str_validator` are now converters' responsibilities
  Any validation logic should be implemented as a structure hook on
  `json_converter` or `zulip_converter`. `register_hook_for_converters`,
  `newtype_validator`, `forbid_extra_keys`, and attrs classes are worth
  looking at when implementing validation.
- `converter`s are superseded by cattrs.
- `json_validator`'s JSON parsing can be enabled with
  `Metadata(convert_from_json=True)`.
- `argument_type` can be specified with `Metadata(argument_type_is_body=True)`
- `intentionally_undocumented`/`documentation_pending` can be specified with
  `Metadata(documentation_status=DocumentationStatus.INTENTIONALL_UNDOCUMENTED)`,
  and etc.
- `aliases` are not supported because it is not widely used
- `path_only` can be specified with `Metadata(path_only=True)`

To define a function, use a syntax like this with `Annotated` if there is
any metadata you want to associate with a parameter:
```python
@endpoint
def view(
    request: HttpRequest,
    user_profile: UserProfile,
    foo: int,
    bar: Annotated[int, Metadata(path_only=True)],
    baz: Annotated[int, Metadata(convert_from_json=True)],
    other: Annotated[
        int,
        Metadata(
            whence="lorem",
            convert_from_json=True,
            documentation_status=DocumentationStatus.INTENTIONALLY_UNDOCUMENTED
        )
    ] = 10,
) -> HttpResponse:
    ....
```

There are also some shorthands for the commonly used annotated types,
which are encouraged when applicable for better readability:
```python
JSON = Annotated[T, Metadata(convert_from_json=True)]
WebhookPayload = Annotated[T, Metadata(convert_from_json=True, argument_type_is_body=True)]
PathOnly = Annotated[T, Metadata(path_only=True)]
```

Then the view function above can be rewritten as:
```python
@endpoint
def view(
    request: HttpRequest,
    user_profile: UserProfile,
    foo: int,
    bar: PathOnly[int],
    baz: JSON[int],
    other: Annotated[
        int,
        Metadata(
            whence="lorem",
            convert_from_json=True,
            documentation_status=DocumentationStatus.INTENTIONALLY_UNDOCUMENTED
        )
    ] = 10,
) -> HttpResponse:
    ....
```

There are some intentional restrictions:
- A single parameter cannot have more than one `Metadata`
- Path-only parameters cannot have default values
- `argument_type_is_body` is incompatible with whence
- Unions are not supported out-of-the-box. Only Optionals are supported
  as of now. Hooks need to be implemented to support such types.
- Argument of names "request", "user_profile", "args", and "kwargs" are
  ignored by `endpoint`.
- Nesting endpoint decorators together is currently an undefined
  behavior. However, nesting endpoint inside a has_request_variables
  decorated function is fine (very common with the
  `authenticated_rest_api_view` views).
- positional-only arguments are not supported by `endpoint`.

endpoint's handling of `ignored_parameters_unsupported` is mostly
identical to that of `has_request_variables`. Similarly, we simply ported
the code that integrates `has_request_variables` with openapi to `endpoint`
so that it is supported as well. In the future, we can enhance these
features by further improving the endpoint decorator.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-08-05 02:53 UTC

I have been working to resolve some issues I found when migrating `message_flags` to use the new decorator.
To update, there are a few things to address in the current implementation:
- The handling of `Union` - It is implemented [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/26365/commits/0048e5ce8b4f462c40bd64aea278bd5eee4810b6) at the time of writing. This is a generic way of handling unions. If registered, the converter will iterate through the possible types and return the one that can be successfully converted to.
- Integration of `attrs` class with OpenAPI - We need some extra tweaks to make classes decorated with `@attrs.define` (or similarly, `@dataclass`). This will mostly affect `has_request_variables` view functions that use `check_dict` or `check_dict_only`.
- Error handling - I'm still revising the error handling mechanism of converter errors. The custom converters and validators are allowed to raise arbitrary exceptions, but all known validation errors should be handled by the `zerver.lib.converters.format_exception` function. Otherwise, the exception will be re-raised.
- Calling `@endpoint`-decorated view functions directly - we do that a lot with `get_messages_backend` in the test cases. Because now `REQ` doesn't occupy the defaults of the function, when we call such functions with only the `HttpRequest` object, mypy rejects that for missing required arguments. We can use a util function that calls the view ignoring its parameter signature, or define `NotSpecified: Any = _NotSpecified()` as a placeholder for missing arguments.

One of the major goals here is letting us migrate all our untyped dicts to typed dataclasses. Currently our dict validators have no way to connect to the type system and so we have `Dict[str, Any]` flying around everywhere.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-08-09 00:30 UTC

Delegating this all to a third-party library means less code to maintain, better ecosystem integration, less documentation to write, and reduced temptation to cut safety corners for expedient kludges or by accident.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-08-09 00:34 UTC

Pydantic in particular is battle-tested for our problem domain, since it’s the base of FastAPI. It also has some interesting features like JSON schema generation that might help us do some kind of static checks against our hand-written OpenAPI spec in the future.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-08-09 04:33 UTC

An example would be that we can find more OpenAPI spec inconsistencies using just the type information. Parameters validated with `check_dict` and `check_dict_only` are assumed to be consistent with schemas of `type: object`, but it will be possible to do the validation with Pydantic.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-08-09 17:11 UTC

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-08-11 07:34 UTC

Some notes on reimplementing this with Pydantic.
- In Pydantic, using `TypeAdapter`, value parsing can be done with either `TypeAdapter(type).validate_json` or `TypeAdapter(type).validate_python`. `validate_json` assumes that the input is JSON encoded and is claimed to have [some performance advantages](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/api/pydantic_core/#pydantic_core._pydantic_core.SchemaValidator.validate_json). However, it didn't work for me when the [`Json` wrapper](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/usage/types/json/) is used. A design that uses `validate_python` all the time, marking `Json` when needed would work. Alternatively, we can also use our own annotation variable like before to switch `validate_json` on and off. I feel like that `Json` is intended to be just like a variant of `str` or `bytes`, which describes a nested JSON-encoded field.
- `TypeAdapter` doesn't support `extra="forbid"` by design (which can replace `check_dict_only`), because [`config` is unused](https://docs.pydantic.dev/dev-v2/errors/usage_errors/#type-adapter-config-unused) when `TypeAdapter` is used with `dataclass`, `BaseModel` or `TypedDict`. This means that we might need to override the config by defining `__pydantic_config__ = ConfigDict(strict=True)` on the class.
- To match Pydantic's coercing behavior with our validator system, we need to use [strict mode](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/usage/strict_mode/). It can be enabled per class, per `Annotated`, or per `TypeAdapter(...).validate_python`. I'm inclined to enable it per `validate_python` call that we controlled at only one place in the view function decorator. Because we want to just enable it for all JSON input given that's what json_validators like `check_int` and `check_float` behave.
- Error handling works extremely well for me. We just need to map the [error types](https://docs.pydantic.dev/latest/errors/validation_errors/) to translated messages and do special handling whenever necessary. All error information is well contained within Pydantic.

>>> TypeAdapter(Json[Json[Json[str]]]).validate_python(r'"\"\\\"foo\\\"\""')

```

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-08-12 04:51 UTC

For view functions, `pydantic.Json` will rarely be needed, as we don't need to encode JSON inside query parameters of a URL encoded form payload anymore.

Metadata for each parameter will still be extracted from the view function signature. This includes type information, default values, etc. We construct a Pydantic model combining all the parameters together, instead of using a `TypeAdapter` for each parameter. The same model can be used to validate our OpenAPI schema definitions under `requestBody`.

Upon the arrival of an incoming request, we do only one pass of JSON parsing on `request.body` via Pydantic by calling `.model_validate_json` on the model generated from the view function signature.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-08-12 04:53 UTC

Basically the same as the `argument_type_is_body` behavior, just that we build a Pydantic model from multiple parameters instead.

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-08-12 05:03 UTC

I imagine that if we can switch to `application/json` globally by first checking if the request's content type is `application/json`.
If so, we
1. disallow `argument_type_is_body` to avoid ambiguous parsing behaviors (some views will need to be adjusted for this)
1. remove the `Json` wrapper so that each parameter doesn't require separate JSON parsing
1. use the model construction mechanism described above to parse the body as a whole using the Pydantic model.

Otherwise, we fallback to the `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` behavior for backwards-compatibility.

I think we need to clarify the interaction between `Annotated` and `Optional`.
In the following examples, what should we allow and prohibit?
```python
def func(
    a: Annotated[Optional[str], ApiParamConfig(...)],
    # Enforced by mypy via "no implicit optional"
    b: Optional[Annotated[str, ApiParamConfig(...)]] = None,
    # These two are equivalent in runtime prior to py3.11: https://github.com/python/cpython/issues/90353
    c: Optional[Annotated[Optional[str], ApiParamConfig(...)]] = None,
    d: Annotated[Optional[str], ApiParamConfig(...)]] = None,

    # JSON encoded, but None is only possible when the default value is used
    # because a user cannot provide a Python None value via query parameters.
    e: Optional[Annotated[Json[int], ApiParamConfig(...)]] = None,
    f: Annotated[Optional[Json[int]], ApiParamConfig(...)] = None,
    # JSON encoded, null accepted
    g: Annotated[Json[Optional[int]], ApiParamConfig(...)] = None,
    h: Optional[Annotated[Json[Optional[int]], ApiParamConfig(...)]] = None,
): ...
```

**Zixuan James Li** · 2023-08-16 21:57 UTC

At the moment, we cannot differentiate these two variants in runtime.
So there is no way to only allow the saner second option below:
```python

    d: Annotated[Optional[str], ApiParamConfig(...)]] = None,
```

Because otherwise, it becomes unclear where the config object should come from. So it would be clearer to expect the parameter type is annotated without nesting whenever `ApiParamConfig` is needed.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-09-08 15:59 UTC

The benefits of the new request parameter parsing system are several:
* Using more standard tooling internals means when we want to do something fancy, we don't have to do all the work of writing tooling for it with tests.
* For endpoints with more complex signatures/validation, we're now able to parse parameters directly to nice Python structures like dataclasses that we can then pass around to `actions` functions, rather than the poorly-typed dictionaries that the `check_dict` validator would give us; this makes it a lot easier to write type-safe code.
* We get to take advantage of more battle-tested third-party code for validating that our OpenAPI docs actually match the implementation for what parameters various endpoints accept. Ultimately it'll be less custom code (that is security-sensitive!) for us to maintain.
* As you can see, the actual API for using this stuff is generally more readable than the custom `has_request_variables` system.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-09-08 16:00 UTC

We don't add new endpoints particularly often, and it's pretty easy to adjust an endpoint that's been converted by just looking at surrounding code, but if you're stuck on anything before the documentation updates are out, post here and we'll help you out.

For the rename operation:

```
ALTER INDEX [ IF EXISTS ] name RENAME TO new_name
```

[from the docs](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/sql-alterindex.html):
> The `RENAME` form changes the name of the index. If the index is associated with a table constraint (either `UNIQUE`, `PRIMARY KEY`, or `EXCLUDE`), the constraint is renamed as well. There is no effect on the stored data.
>  **Renaming an index acquires a SHARE UPDATE EXCLUSIVE lock.**

We can't do the `RENAME` operation concurrently. But since it doesn't affect stored data, we can do this operation without concurrency? 

The table-lock will be for a very short period of time; but again that "short period" can be problematic in the case of `UserMessage` table.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2023-08-21 19:02 UTC

@Abhijeet Bodas suggested:

The gist is that, in a normal Django TestCase (which ZulipTestCase subclasses), every test runs inside a transaction, which is rolled back at the end of the test so as to reset the DB state.
However, tests which subclass [TransactionTestCase](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.2/topics/testing/tools/#transactiontestcase) do not run inside a transaction.

Abhijeet Bodas: So if we're going to write a new test here, [TransactionTestCase](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/4.2/topics/testing/tools/#transactiontestcase) might be useful (although I'm not sure if we should be writing a new test).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-08-22 01:27 UTC

@Prakhar Pratyush generally we need to disable/delete tests in `test_migrations` when adding future migrations; @Zixuan James Li has worked with those tests the most recently, and may have more to add. We should do something to improve its internal documentation about this fact, but structurally, those tests are only guaranteed to pass until the next migration is merged, which is fine, since they're only needed during the development process of a migration, not its post-development lifetime, as we rarely do future changes to them unless forced to do so.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-10-31 17:34 UTC

The cost on the multi-column one is 12M and the cost on the single-column one is 8.8M.  Of course, cost is only loosely correlated to actual runtime.

My guess is that the query planner gives a higher cost to the multi-column one because the recheck condition has to recheck "more fields," even if at the low level those bitfields checks may actually be combined.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-10-31 17:51 UTC

So I think the only admissible arguments here for this decision ("one-clause" vs "multi-clause") are:
1. Is one form more fragile and more likely to accidentally stop using the desired index?
2. Is one form easier to understand in the code?
3. Is one form easier to understand in the raw SQL?

For (1), I don't think either has an advantage.  Both forms are vulnerable to "what if another bitfield is OR'd in":
```postgres-console
zulip=> explain select count(*) from zerver_usermessage where ((flags & 8) <> 0 OR (flags & 16) <> 0 OR (flags & 32) <> 0 OR (flags & 64) <> 0 OR (flags & 128) <> 0) AND (user_profile_id < 5000) AND (mod(message_id, 7) = 0);
                                                                                                                         QUERY PLAN
-------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Finalize Aggregate  (cost=13511194.18..13511194.19 rows=1 width=8)
   ->  Gather  (cost=13511193.96..13511194.17 rows=2 width=8)
         Workers Planned: 2
         ->  Partial Aggregate  (cost=13510193.96..13510193.97 rows=1 width=8)
               ->  Parallel Seq Scan on zerver_usermessage  (cost=0.00..13509040.50 rows=461385 width=0)
                     Filter: ((user_profile_id < 5000) AND (mod(message_id, 7) = 0) AND (((flags & '8'::bigint) <> 0) OR ((flags & '16'::bigint) <> 0) OR ((flags & '32'::bigint) <> 0) OR ((flags & '64'::bigint) <> 0) OR ((flags & '128'::bigint) <> 0)))
 JIT:
   Functions: 7
   Options: Inlining true, Optimization true, Expressions true, Deforming true
(9 rows)
```
```postgres-console
zulip=> explain select count(*) from zerver_usermessage where (flags & 248) <> 0 AND (user_profile_id < 5000) AND (mod(message_id, 7) = 0);
                                                       QUERY PLAN
------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
 Finalize Aggregate  (cost=9050622.53..9050622.54 rows=1 width=8)
   ->  Gather  (cost=9050622.31..9050622.52 rows=2 width=8)
         Workers Planned: 2
         ->  Partial Aggregate  (cost=9049622.31..9049622.32 rows=1 width=8)
               ->  Parallel Seq Scan on zerver_usermessage  (cost=0.00..9048474.62 rows=459078 width=0)
                     Filter: ((user_profile_id < 5000) AND ((flags & '248'::bigint) <> 0) AND (mod(message_id, 7) = 0))
 JIT:
   Functions: 7
   Options: Inlining true, Optimization true, Expressions true, Deforming true
(9 rows)
```

Theoretically the multi-clause form is more vulnerable if the clauses are separated in some way that the query planner can't handle, but I don't view this as a likely risk -- we only apply combinations of flags, in adjacent code lines, when we have an index, so we're not in danger of accidentally dropping or moving half of the clause.  And neither form is going to handle *combining* different types of limits (e.g. an index on mentioned AND starred) without extra work -- the single-clause form would need custom code to unify the bitfields into one value for the one clause, and the multi-clause form would need custom code to place them in the same OR clause.

For (2), code legibility, I don't think either is more or less understandable.

For (3), SQL legibility, I think that broken-out has a bit more comprehensibility to me, since I don't have to do a mental binary expansion of the value.  But that has such a tiny weight, since IMHO this is really not a common investigation to do.

Finally, there's a small finger on the scale for "what form are the existing indexes," in that we ideally wouldn't like to churn the existing indexes for consistency.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-31 18:58 UTC

The mentioned index is our only multi-bitfield index, so I think there's no "what form are the existing indexes" decision to make -- we're replacing the one `AND` of two single-bit checks with either an `AND` of 4 or a single mask.

## ✔ stringifying Model objects

*2023-08-11 to 2023-08-11 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/.E2.9C.94.20stringifying.20Model.20objects/with/1623408)*

**Steve Howell** · 2023-08-11 02:22 UTC

We might want to think about stringifying some of our major Model objects in a somewhat more lightweight way, even if it's slightly inconvenient at times.  I think it's generally a bad practice to hit the database or cache to make a string out of a Model object, since sometimes the entire reason you're having to do it is that something went wrong in the first place and you're in a debugging situation where `__str__` itself could fail for similar reasons.

I don't feel super strongly here, as there are some pretty obvious trade-offs in both directions. 5b569ab865ce2e8fd0f63dab264f2a93fe31ebc2 is relevant and why I'm bringing this up as food for thought.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-08-11 02:26 UTC

I think my basic proposal is that Model objects should be allowed to custom-include any fields into their string representation from the direct model with arbitrary fancy formatting but you should not be allowed to traverse foreign-key relationships.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-08-11 02:29 UTC

If this doesn't resonate with folks who have operational experience, then I will quickly resolve this topic after any veto.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-08-11 19:30 UTC

I think in practice the stringification only gets used in the management shell, and the direction I'd like to go in is making them more readable.

## django-seal audits

*2023-08-15 to 2025-02-26 · 38 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/django-seal.20audits/with/1625400)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-08-15 14:55 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell)
> @Sahil Batra Have you had a chance to try out seal?

I tried using seal for `UserProfile` objects. I basically updated all the `UserProfile` queries to call `.seal()` and then ran the test suite. There were a few cases where we were accessing the related objects without using `select_related` which were caught using tests.

Most of the test failures were due to using `refresh_from_db`. Basically what happens is that - we get the user using `example_user` which fetches the realm object using `select_related`. And then after performing some operations, `refresh_from_db` is called to test some other cases.

When we call `refresh_from_db`, the fetched foreign keys are cleared and then if code accesses `realm` field from the user object, seal gives a warning (for current testing I have elevated it to raise errors in tests for ease of testing). I am not sure how to handle these now.

```python
def access_user_by_id(
    user_profile: UserProfile,
    target_user_id: int,
    *,
    allow_deactivated: bool = False,
    allow_bots: bool = False,
    for_admin: bool,
) -> UserProfile:
    """Master function for accessing another user by ID in API code;
    verifies the user ID is in the same realm, and if requested checks
    for administrative privileges, with flags for various special
    cases.
    """
    try:
        import time

        st = time.time()
        target = get_user_profile_by_id_in_realm(target_user_id, user_profile.realm)
        end = time.time()
    except UserProfile.DoesNotExist:
        raise JsonableError(_("No such user"))

    print(end - st)
    return access_user_common(target, user_profile, allow_deactivated, allow_bots, for_admin)

```

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-03-22 17:39 UTC

I think the `is_user_active` denormalization is expensive in terms of complexity to maintain, so if the queries are efficient without doing it, I don't think there's any reason to do it.

I think the motivation for doing `is_user_active` in `Subscription` was precisely to make fetching the subscribers data structure of which is in which stream somewhat more efficient. Since I think we don't expect it to be common for users to be directly members of 20+ groups in organizations with thousands of streams, it is probably not a necessary optimization (and of course something we can add later). Role groups, in particular, we can probably optimize by just having the client impute their membership from the `role` fields on user objects, and even those only put each user in 1-2 groups.

So I'd skip that extra complexity for now, and just do a join, ideally having the join happen in the database rather than post-Python post-processing.

**Steve Howell** · 2023-08-21 16:37 UTC

There's a deep underlying paradigm to our real-time push system
* reader clients register
* writer clients do something
* the multiplexer pushes the events from the writers to the readers

This is every single multi-player game engine in the world. This is Napster.

This should be a solved problem.

The current code organization mostly obscures the underlying universality of what we're doing.

I just want a brutally fast multiplexer that just asks these questions:

* Do I trust the writer?
* Do I trust the reader?
* What does the writer want to send?
* Who does the writer want to talk to?
* What do the readers want to receive?

Splitting the backend into more processes has costs, mainly for RAM usage on low-RAM virtual servers which has been a steady stream of headaches for us. It also requires API changes in this case.

If you’re doing this experiment in an effort to understand the architecture, great, but if you’re aiming to aid an incremental migration to Rust, I should note that there are other ways to orchestrate that. The one I was imagining would involve loading a Rust library into the Python process, or flipping things so a Python library is loaded into a Rust process, so that the Rust and Python parts maintain the ability to talk with each other directly.

            """
            DROP TRIGGER zerver_message_date_sent_to_pub_date_trigger ON zerver_message;
            DROP FUNCTION zerver_message_date_sent_to_pub_date_trigger_function();

            ALTER TABLE zerver_message ALTER COLUMN date_sent SET NOT NULL;
            ALTER TABLE zerver_message ALTER COLUMN pub_date DROP NOT NULL;
            """,
            state_operations=[
                # This just tells Django to, after running the above SQL, consider the AlterField below
                # as done. The building of the index actually happened in the previous migration, not here,
                # but nevertheless this seems like the correct place to put this fake AlterField.
                migrations.AlterField(
                    model_name="message",
                    name="date_sent",
                    field=models.DateTimeField(db_index=True, verbose_name="date sent"),
                ),
            ],
        ),
```

...which does mark the `zerver_message_date_sent_3b5b05d8` index that would be created by `db_index=True` as "owned"  by Django.  So having an explicit `AddIndexConcurrently` in the other migration means we're in this weird state where the index is doubly-owned (by the `state_operations`, as well as `AddIndexConcurrently`), and we have to have an explicit index for it in `Meta.indexes` despite it also being marked `db_index=True`.

Reverting cf0eb46afcb22a236211ee2b3e3d23b8ef924eab keeps makemigrations a no-op, but means we don't have the explicit index in `Meta.indexes` in addition to it being listed as `db_index=True`.

Is there something I'm missing about that commit that we should keep?

## update has_message_access?

*2023-09-12 to 2023-09-20 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/update.20has_message_access.3F/with/1638961)*

**Hemant Umre** · 2023-09-12 18:32 UTC

Issue: #23470 PR: #26634

Zulip has an invariant that all unread messages must be in streams the user is subscribed to. Therefore, with issue #23470, we want to notify users about the messages that were ignored by the server when marking them as unread from a narrow like all messages.

To achieve this, we are adding a field called `ignored_because_not_subscribed` in the response of `/messages/flags/narrow` which is a dictionary mapping streams to messages that were ignored by the server (as discussed [here](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/378-api-design/topic/Not.20marked.20unread.20banner/near/1635508)).

Before adding `ignored_because_not_subscribed` to the response, we want to filter the accessible messages to prevent security bugs. The core functions for obtaining accessible messages are `bulk_access_message` and `access_message`, both of which use `has_message_access`. With this [commit](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/commit/c908b518ef15eee4fb768cd015e8e72261d98e93), we have restricted accessing messages from previously subscribed private streams. However, messages from private unsubscribed streams might be present in the narrow, and we want to include them in `ignored_because_not_subscribed` and the notification banner.

I had a discussion about this with @Sahil Batra in dms, and he suggested the following approach:
> One thing that we might do is to update `has_message_access` to take a `for_read` parameter and then return True if `for_read and has_user_message`.
Basically, this would grant permission to access the message if the user previously had access to the message and if the message is needed for read-only purposes.

Can we go with the above approach or any other suggestions?

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-09-13 23:18 UTC

@Hemant Umre I think for the purpose of this API, we can just compute the set of `stream_id` values for the affected messages, and then use `filter_stream_authorization` to see which streams the user has access to -- I don't see any purpose in checking `has_message_access` on each individual message if all we're returning is a set of stream IDs anyway.

**Hemant Umre** · 2023-09-20 11:57 UTC

Sorry for the delayed response. What we want is to also receive notifications for unsubscribed private streams if we had access to their messages previously, as shown in the screenshot below.

[all_messages.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/22/P4I3lOWbH5TAlYXEKe0q9geG/image.png)

If I click "Mark as unread from here" for the "announce" stream, I want to include both the unsubscribed public stream and the unsubscribed private stream in the notification banner.

**Hemant Umre** · 2023-09-20 11:58 UTC

The `filter_stream_authorization` function does not fulfill this requirement since it considers unsubscribed private streams as unauthorized streams.

**Hemant Umre** · 2023-09-20 12:13 UTC

To clarify, we are returning a dictionary where each entry maps a stream ID to a list of affected messages, as discussed [here](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/378-api-design/topic/Not.20marked.20unread.20banner/near/1636298).

[do_clear_mobile_push_notifications_for_ids](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/actions/message_flags.py#L216)

 Currently `do_clear_mobile_push_notifications_for_ids` is used while marking messages as read and editing a message to remove @-personal-mention.

In both the cases we have either "one user" or "one message"; hence the function has an assertion: `assert len(user_profile_ids) == 1 or len(message_ids) == 1`

To be verbose: 
* A user can mark multiple messages as read 
* While editing a message we can remove @-mention of multiple users; so one message multiple users (to remove push notifications for)

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2023-09-22 23:51 UTC

Now, for delete operation; When we delete a topic, we have the case of "multiple users" and "multiple messages".

The db query that the function includes is:
```python
    notifications_to_update = (
        UserMessage.objects.filter(
            message_id__in=message_ids,
            user_profile_id__in=user_profile_ids,
        )
        .extra(
            where=[UserMessage.where_active_push_notification()],
        )
        .values_list("user_profile_id", "message_id")
    
```

This would be expensive and can lead to timeout (quadratic work).

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2023-09-22 23:53 UTC

But even that might be bad (floods the queue) if there's 20k users and 1k messages. The actual index on the usermessage table is really sparse; it's possible that just walking the full index for all usermessages in the organiation is fast enough and this operation will complete, but I'm a bit skeptical, especially given the query plan I expect this to generate which might be quadratic.

This might be a thing that we can't happily do until we add a `UserMessage.realm` column (which we need for sharding) and do a `(realm, user_id, message_id)` partial index.

## queries to get accessible users #10970

*2023-10-05 to 2023-10-10 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/queries.20to.20get.20accessible.20users.20.2310970/with/1656115)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-10-05 17:34 UTC

We would need multiple queries to get users who can be accessed by a guest user, so just wanted to discuss once about how to make sure that the queries do not impact performance.

The queries we would need to do -
1) Query to get subscribers of the streams subscribed by guest.
2) Query to get the participants of group DMs.
3) Query to get the senders of messages for which the guest has `UserMessage` rows.
4) Query to get the users that the guest had sent DMs to but the user has not responed yet, so it is not covered by the above query for `UserMessage` rows. This can happen when guest previously had access to all users but then the setting was changed.

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-10-05 17:34 UTC

For (1), we can do two queries - one to get streams subscribed by the guest and then one to get subscribers of the stream or we can just do one complex query including a subquery.

For(2), we would need to similar queries like we did for streams.

Since we use `Subscription` table for both stream and huddle members, we can actually get the users who are part of the subscribed streams and huddles using the same queries on `Subscription` table.

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-10-05 17:34 UTC

For (3), we would need to query the `UserMessage` rows to get the sender of all the messages for which the guest user has `UserMessage` rows. 

For (4), one way can be to just do a single query like `Message.objects.filter(sender=guest_user, recipient__type=Recipient.PRIVATE).values_list("recipient__type_id")`.

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-10-05 17:36 UTC

Just wanted some suggestions here on how to optimize it. This query will be executed when sending the users data in `page_params` and `/register` response. And may also be needed while doing API checks like, can the guest user send DM to a particular user or can mention a user.

So, any feedback on like whether we would need to write these queries in raw SQL instead of using Django ORM or add any new indexes would be helpful.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-05 17:42 UTC

For (3), I don't think we need `UserMessage`; just this is roughly `Message.objects.filter(recipient=user_profile).values("sender").distinct()`. Longer term I think we're probably going to move to having `Huddle` objects for direct messages and that will let this just use the same query as in (1) -- just getting the distinct subscribers to the users' streams.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-05 17:44 UTC

That (3) query is probably not going to be incredibly cheap for users who've received a lot of DMs; but that's probably not the common case with guests.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-05 17:46 UTC

I guess we should also keep in mind we need to write two functions:
* `can_access_user_for_read(user_id)` would be a single-target-user form that could be a lot cheaper than the "everyone this user can access" query needed for things like presence.

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-10-05 17:46 UTC

(3) is for the senders of message for which the guest has `UserMessage` rows. So it will also include the case where a user sent message to a stream the guest is subscribed to, i.e. guest has a `UserMessage` row for it but the user then unsubscribes from the stream, so not for DMs only.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-05 17:51 UTC

Oh, I see. What do we need those users for? I don't think that can be cheaply computed.

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-10-05 17:53 UTC

We discussed about allowing access to all users from which the guest has received a message. So, the case which I mentioned above like a user who sent a message to a stream but then unsubscribed from the stream, will not be included in other cases.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-05 17:57 UTC

Yeah, I know that's what we were thinking, but if it's not implementable in a performant fashion, I think we can probably cut that.

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-10-06 02:41 UTC

I cannot think of any better way to do this. I am fine with just giving access to only the stream subscribers and the DM and group DM users. Should we discuss this in #**design** first?

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-10-06 17:41 UTC

Yes please post there.

**Sahil Batra** · 2023-10-10 17:22 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> I guess we should also keep in mind we need to write two functions: * `can_access_user_for_read(user_id)` would be a single-target-user form that could be a lot cheaper than the "everyone this user can access" query needed for things like presence.

## APNs auth for multiple apps #27590

*2023-11-07 to 2024-03-21 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/APNs.20auth.20for.20multiple.20apps.20.2327590/with/1677649)*

**Greg Price** · 2023-11-07 21:28 UTC

The existing notifications code assumes that all iOS clients getting notifications through APNs have the same app ID. In particular all such notifications going through the bouncer are assumed to be for the same app ID, `org.zulip.Zulip`, which corresponds to the main Zulip mobile app.

For the new Flutter-based app, we have a separate app ID `com.zulip.flutter` we'll be using through the Flutter app's beta period, so that it can be installed alongside the existing app. In order to get notifications there, then (#F321), we'll need the same servers to be able to send notifications to both `org.zulip.Zulip` and `com.zulip.flutter`.

**Greg Price** · 2023-11-07 21:28 UTC

Yesterday I sent #27590 which does most of what we need here. There's one more piece which I just [realized](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/27590#issuecomment-1800172255) a few minutes ago: in order to support multiple app IDs we'll also need to do something about how we authenticate to APNs.

**Greg Price** · 2023-11-07 21:35 UTC

Currently we [use a certificate](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/usernotifications/setting_up_a_remote_notification_server/establishing_a_certificate-based_connection_to_apns). The certificate is tied to a specific app.

There are two options:

* We could use several certificates. In this approach, we'd set up several `aioapns.APNs` instances, in order to get separate connection pools. The logic when sending notifications would split up the devices by app ID in order to use the separate instances.

* Alternatively we could use [token-based authentication](https://developer.apple.com/documentation/usernotifications/setting_up_a_remote_notification_server/establishing_a_token-based_connection_to_apns). This is the approach that Apple gently recommends when sending notifications to several apps.

  This means we'd sign a little token, in JWT format, and send that in an HTTP header. The token has a timestamp. There's a requirement to sign a fresh token often, but not too often:
  > Refresh your token no more than once every 20 minutes and no less than once every 60 minutes.

  presumably because Apple memoizes checking the token's validity. So that just means we need to memoize the token too, next to the connection, and replace it with a fresh one when it's like 30 minutes or 50 minutes old.

**Greg Price** · 2023-11-07 21:36 UTC

It looks like `aioapns` does have support for the token method, so probably that's the easiest thing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-11-07 21:38 UTC

Yeah, if `aioapns` does most of the work for us, that does sound like an easier strategy.

**Greg Price** · 2023-11-07 21:39 UTC

I'll go try that out on my dev server.

**Greg Price** · 2024-03-21 01:07 UTC

The PR I sent to aioapns as part of #27590 was merged the other day, and there's a release 3.2 that contains my change. So we should be able to take that upgrade and stop pinning to the PR branch.

I don't think there's any rush here, so I'm guessing the most efficient workflow is just that whenever @Anders Kaseorg next does a round of upgrading Python dependencies, this can be part of that.

**Greg Price** · 2024-03-21 01:11 UTC

(The maintainer did add a [follow-up commit](https://github.com/Fatal1ty/aioapns/commit/0447b208bb6b3be1e9ddfd3738b70b64994b1618) with this unfortunate "simplification":
```diff
-        if request.apns_topic is not None:
-            apns_topic = request.apns_topic
-        else:
-            apns_topic = self.apns_topic
+        apns_topic = request.apns_topic or self.apns_topic
```

But we have an invariant that our `apns_topic` values are nonempty strings — they go through `check_app_id` in `zerver/views/push_notifications.py` — so I believe that doesn't cause any live bug for us.)

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-03-21 03:05 UTC
