## datetime imports

*2023-12-05 to 2023-12-05 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/datetime.20imports/with/1695830)*

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-12-05 19:07 UTC

Our import convention for the `datetime` standard library is split in half: we currently use `from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone` (or subsets) in 65 files and `import datetime` in 66 files.

I argue that `from datetime import …` is better here, because `datetime.datetime` is redundant, and all of the examples in the [Python documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/datetime.html) use `from datetime import …`. So I opened #27794. But Tim wants to discuss it here.

Discuss.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-12-05 19:08 UTC

I'm in favor of the more concise form.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2023-12-05 19:08 UTC

Err, I guess that isn't clear.  More concise in when it's used, so `from datetime import datetime, timedelta, timezone`

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-12-05 19:11 UTC

If what Tim is looking for is a more general policy: some Python standard library modules were clearly designed with `from`…`import` in mind, and we should use it for those. Another one that bothers me is `urllib.parse`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-12-05 19:27 UTC

I think for datetime I agree we should do the more brief version where it's used.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-12-05 19:28 UTC

I'm less convinced by `urllib.parse` because function called `parse` is a very plausible name for a function we'd write ourselves somewhere, and it doesn't at all indicate from seeing it that it's related to URLs.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2023-12-05 19:29 UTC

The function is not `parse`. The function is `urllib.parse.urlparse` (although we should actually be using `urllib.parse.urlsplit`).

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-12-05 19:30 UTC

Ahh, OK, yeah I'd be fine with `urlsplit` being imported for use under that name. But `urllib.parse.quote` is an example where just bare `quote` feels bad.

**Tim Abbott** · 2023-12-05 19:30 UTC

But maybe we should just live with that anyway; we don't use that name in that many files.

2. having traces for troubleshooting db, cache, internal processing or other issues.

## Redis ACL support

*2024-01-02 to 2024-01-03 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Redis.20ACL.20support/with/1711815)*

**Old Schepperhand** · 2024-01-02 19:31 UTC

Currently Zulip is using the old way of authenticating and there is also no way to define a username for authentication.

With the introduction of [ACLs in Redis](https://redis.io/docs/management/security/acl/) it would be possible to restrict the required permissions for Zulip and therefore enhance the security of redis.

This could be done by setting an ACL entry for the application user, like
```
user zulip ((ACL-rules)) on >password
```
in the redis.conf and the possibility to configure a redis_user for authentication, plus the support for it in the code.

For compatibility and as fallback (if the username is not configured) an additional ACL entry for the default user should allow old clients to continue working.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-01-02 19:40 UTC

What versions of Redis support ACLs?  We need to support Ubuntu 22.04 and Debian 11, which means Redis 6.0.

**Old Schepperhand** · 2024-01-02 20:56 UTC

Based on the [Docs](https://redis.io/docs/management/security/#authentication), Redis 6 

> **Authentication**
> 
> Redis provides two ways to authenticate clients. The recommended authentication method, introduced in Redis 6, is via Access Control Lists, allowing named users to be created and assigned fine-grained permissions. ....

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-01-02 21:07 UTC

What the advantage to switching to ACLs?  From their [docs](https://redis.io/docs/management/security/acl/#when-acls-are-useful), I don't think any of these apply:
> Before using ACLs, you may want to ask yourself what's the goal you want to accomplish by implementing this layer of protection. Normally there are two main goals that are well served by ACLs: 1. You want to improve security by restricting the access to commands and keys, so that untrusted clients h …

**Old Schepperhand** · 2024-01-02 21:22 UTC

For me this is actually the relevant part.
The app should only be granted the required permissions to do what it needs to, but not able to execute dangerous admin commands.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-01-03 16:02 UTC

That's a reasonable thought for defense-in-depth, but the redis bindings we're using don't allow for arbitrary command execution -- so I don't think it actually accomplishes much.  Any codepath which allows for arbitrary command execution on Redis is going to be a big problem regardless of if it can `FLUSHALL`.  And even `FLUSHALL` is only moderately problematic, since we treat Redis as non-durable storage -- it's only used for rate-limiting and very-short-term auth information.

A similar proposal would be like splitting the `zulip` PostgreSQL user into two, one which can do DDL, and the other which can do queries.  Moderately complicated to do, and there's not a lot of actual protection it affords -- if lower-privileged account can still `DELETE` (which it has to to in usual operation) then there's little difference between its allowed `DELETE FROM zerver_messages` and the disallowed `DROP TABLE zerver_messages`.

The fact that the latter supports this is self-explanatory. I do not know whether other software supports this sch …

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-01 23:25 UTC

Presumably we could just tweak our Markdown processor to treat `onenote:https://` as a valid URL scheme so that this "works"? It seems like probably anyone who has such a URL does intend to use that OneNote feature.

**Tejansh Sachdeva** · 2024-02-24 15:57 UTC

@Tim Abbott Is this issue still open?
If yes, I'd like to work on this. Also, can you suggest some references on how to resolve this issue.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-02-27 02:31 UTC

I think we first need to decide the policy question of whether this is a thing we're willing to merge if we could get it working.

**Alya Abbott** · 2024-08-01 18:17 UTC

Just bumping the question here.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-27 20:41 UTC

I think there is potentially real security exposure to users from clicking OneNote links. But given it'd be opened by the OS, those links could be generated without collaboration from Zulip.

https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/payloads-in-malicious-onenote-samples/

So I don't see a security reason not to do that tweak. Am I missing something?

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-27 21:36 UTC

It looks like that article is about malware inside OneNote files. I'm not sure if the effect of the malware is different if the file is opened in the browser (like I'm guessing the `https://...` part of the link would do) or in the OneNote desktop app.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-27 21:42 UTC

Looks like our current behavior:
https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/7-test-here/topic/Greg/near/1950318

is that we accept a miscellaneous list of schemes including `mailto`, `tel`, and `nntp`. But not `about`, `onenote` (even when the URL *is* a valid URL, unlike the ones this issue is about), or `nonsense`.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-27 21:45 UTC

I agree there isn't a security reason not to permit these. Most people's devices will have no idea what to do to open a `onenote:` link (just like `nntp:`), in which case they're definitely harmless. And if you've configured your browser to open such links in a particular app, it's not Zulip's job to protect you from running across such links.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-27 21:50 UTC

I'd be a bit more reluctant about making them *auto*link, when these "URLs" just appear in plain text rather than in Markdown link syntax.

We could do it but it'd be an ugly hack — we certainly don't want to take an arbitrary scheme-shaped prefix like this, because then something like
```markdown
Take a look at this link:https://example/thing
```

, where the sender just left out a space, would go to the bogus `link:https://example/thing` (which isn't even a valid URL, for the same reason these OneNote links aren't) instead of the intended `https://example/thing`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-27 22:14 UTC

Yeah, that seems like a reasonable plan.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-03-08 21:17 UTC

So reading [the AGPL text[(https://www.gnu.org/licenses/agpl-3.0.en.html):

> A compilation of a covered work with other separate and independent works, which are not by their nature extensions of the covered work, and which are not combined with it such as to form a larger program, in or on a volume of a storage or distribution medium, is called an "aggregate" if the compilation and its resulting copyright are not used to limit the access or legal rights of the compilation's users beyond what the individual works permit. Inclusion of a covered work in an aggregate does not cause this License to apply to the other parts of the aggregate.

It seems like if we were to have an option in Zulip to interface with this postgres extension over SQL, it seems the AGPL intent is not that Zulip as a whole would need to be licensed under the AGPL as well, since even if we distributed this extension with Zulip, since it'd be an aggregate?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-03-08 21:18 UTC

I think it'd be very hard for anyone to argue Zulip was an extension of `pg_bm25` just because we had an option to use it, or even if we used it for full-text search by default.

**Greg Price** · 2024-03-08 23:23 UTC

Yeah, Zulip definitely doesn't seem like "by [its] nature [an] extension[]" of `pg_bm25`.

I'm not sure what "combined with it such as to form a larger program" means, though. Seems like it turns on the meaning of "program".

**Greg Price** · 2024-03-08 23:24 UTC

The usual practice with the GPL would be that the copyleft doesn't reach the Zulip application code, because that interaction is happening over a wire protocol (with SQL) and not by being linked into the same binary or anything like that.

OTOH I think the PostgreSQL server process running on the Zulip server typically *would* be seen as part of the same program, subject to the copyleft, under typical GPL practice.

And in fact probably the whole reason they're going with AGPL instead of GPL or Apache is so that if Amazon were to try to run this in RDS, their whole Postgres process would be subject to the copyleft. (And so they'd instead have to negotiate with the ParadeDB folks a commercial license on the side.)

**Greg Price** · 2024-03-08 23:25 UTC

There's probably no fundamental obstacle to us treating that Postgres process as covered by AGPL (it's probably under a compatible license, though I haven't checked).

So in that case it'd just mean that we have to deal with figuring out what the logistics should be of complying with AGPL's rather fuzzy terms about offering the corresponding source to anyone who connects to the service.

They're thinking about it in a very similar way to MongeDB: They want anyone to be able to build applications on top of their database extension without thinking about licensing, and just want the AGPL to protect them from things like an Amazon RDS style service where the product is in fact their database extension.

The other big piece of infrastructure that makes up the existing search engine is how we maintain the search indexes, and that is `./puppet/zulip/files/postgresql/process_fts_updates`.

Now, Postgres supports automatically updating the search indexes at the time a message is sent. For latency reasons as measured like 10 years ago, we have a more complex architectural thing using triggers of having sending/editing a message add a row to an `fts_update_log` table, and that `process_fts_updates` worker is responsible for actually updating the search index using the content in the message.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-09 23:02 UTC

We likely want any future search index to take advantage of `realm` now being a denormalized column in the table, so probably it's worth adding any new indexes that way; that would eliminate a current bug in Zulip Cloud.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-04-01 23:33 UTC

I had a long in-person chat with @Anders Kaseorg and @Greg Price about the design for this last week, and we came up with the following proposal that I think lets us do everything that we want.

- We create a [NamedUserGroup model](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/3-backend/topic/set.20a.20group.20setting.20to.20multiple.20groups/near/1749761) proposed above. Tracking this as #29554, which is probably the next step for this process.
- We start allowing group-valued settings to have a value that is an anomymous group, that would be stored in the database as a `UserGroup` but never referenced directly in the API; effectively they're just containers with a list of users and a list of subgroups. Opened https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/29557 defining the semantics, and https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/stream/378-api-design/topic/groups.20redesign/near/1772449 has some API design questions.
- In the `input_pull` UI for a setting, if one sets the value to a setting as specifically a single group ID that corresponds to a `NamedUserGroup`, then we would store that `NamedUserGroup` as the value of the group setting. But otherwise, we'd just send the server a `{direct_member_ids: [1, 3, 6], direct_subgroup_ids: [14, 17]}` type object corresponding to the pills.

This approach would let us get all the functionality we want in this thread, and replaces a different messy thing (single-user groups) that we'd previously been imagining we had to build.

I think this part of the #29557 summarizes the benefits of this data/API model over what had been previously proposed:

> One of the big benefits of these setting-value groups being anonymous is we would not have to do any special live-update data synchronization logic to try to send clients details on one of these setting-value user groups only if the user has access to the setting whose value that is -- because we'd …

@Sahil Batra FYI

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-04-02 04:10 UTC

It does seem redundant but I think it is required. The way this ends up in SQL is `UserGroup` is a table and `NamedUserGroup` is a separate table that references it, though Django does a great job of hiding that complexity via creating a single model object unioning the attributes of both tables, which will contain a `realm` field.

But the `NamedUserGroup` table has a unique index on the pair `(realm, name)`, and that index can be most cleanly defined nicely if it has a local `realm` column in the table itself. We'd also use that column for sharding the database by realm long term.

**Greg Price** · 2024-04-02 04:10 UTC

```py
def get_recursive_subgroups(user_group: UserGroup) -> QuerySet[UserGroup]:
    cte = With.recursive(
        lambda cte: UserGroup.objects.filter(id=user_group.id)
        .values(group_id=F("id"))
        .union(
            cte.join(NamedUserGroup, direct_supergroups=cte.col.group_id).values(group_id=F("id"))
        )
    )
    return cte.join(UserGroup, id=cte.col.group_id).with_cte(cte)
```

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-05-29 16:04 UTC

Wanted to discuss about how to update setting from one anonymous group to other.

What we do currently is we call [`access_user_group_for_setting`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/a6d211245341a041f02f0f166dc3756a863ed163/zerver/lib/user_groups.py#L279) to validate the IDs passed in request which then calls [`update_or_create_user_group_for_setting`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/a6d211245341a041f02f0f166dc3756a863ed163/zerver/lib/user_groups.py#L245).

In `update_or_create_user_group_for_setting`, we just update the existing `UserGroup` object with new members and subgroups. So, what happens in such case is that the `UserGroup` is already updated and then we call `do_change_user_group_permission_setting` which now only is only responsible audit log entry and sending event. The task of updating the `UserGroup` object and audit log entry is not done inside an atomic transaction and that can be problematic. So, we might need to update the code to do both the things in a transaction.

One solution could be to just wrap the `access_user_group_for_setting` inside the transaction. Another solution could be if we do not update the `UserGroup` object in  `update_or_create_user_group_for_setting` and instead just validate the IDs there and update the `UserGroup` object in `do_change_user_group_permission_setting`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-29 19:04 UTC

I think best practice would be the option where we do `access_user_group_for_setting` inside the same transaction, since a future version of the code might want to take a lock for the duration of the work anyway.

Ok, I just noticed the view function itself is wrapped inside a transaction and we use `@transaction.atomic(savepoint=False)` for `do_change_user_group_permission_setting`, so that should handle the above mentioned case as expected.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-02-29 00:59 UTC

The problem is that you have both `user_id` and `realm_id` in your `id_args_keys_update` in the `ON CONFLICT` set, while we only have `user_id` as the unique key :
```python3
class UserCount(BaseCount):
    user = models.ForeignKey(UserProfile, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    realm = models.ForeignKey(Realm, on_delete=models.CASCADE)

    class Meta:
        # Handles invalid duplicate UserCount data
        constraints = [
            UniqueConstraint(
                fields=["user", "property", "subgroup", "end_time"],
                condition=Q(subgroup__isnull=False),
                name="unique_user_count",
            ),
            UniqueConstraint(
                fields=["user", "property", "end_time"],
                condition=Q(subgroup__isnull=True),
                name="unique_user_count_null_subgroup",
            ),
        ]
```

And `user` is which is all that's required, since user-ids are globally unique.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-02-29 01:08 UTC

So the fix is that we can't just reuse the same set of `id_args.keys()` for the `ON CONFLICT`, but need to be specific:
- `InstallationCount`: `[]`
- `RealmCount`: `["realm_id"]`
- `UserCount`: `["user_id"]`
- `StreamCount`: `["stream_id"]`
- `RemoteInstallationCount`: `["server_id"]`
- `RemoteRealmCount`: `["server_id", "realm_id"]`

def do_mark_stream_messages_as_read(
    user_profile: UserProfile, stream_recipient_id: int, topic_name: Optional[str] = None
) -> int:
    with transaction.atomic(savepoint=False):
        query = (
            UserMessage.select_for_update_query()

                message__recipient_id=stream_recipient_id,

        if len(message_ids) == 0:

        count = query.update(
            flags=F("flags").bitor(UserMessage.flags.read),
        )

INSERT INTO "analytics_usercount"(property, subgroup, end_time, value, "realm_id", "user_id")
        VALUES ('messages_read::hour', NULL, '2024-02-26T06:00:00+00:00'::timestamptz, 6, 2, 15)

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-03-04 15:44 UTC

The "index predicate" here is ` WHERE subgroup is NULL`, and we are specifying it.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-03-04 15:47 UTC

They key is that this:
```sql
ON CONFLICT (property, end_time, "user_id") WHERE subgroup is NULL
```

...must match a partial index we have, *exactly*.  Since we have:
```python
class UserCount(BaseCount):
    user = models.ForeignKey(UserProfile, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    realm = models.ForeignKey(Realm, on_delete=models.CASCADE)

    class Meta:
        # Handles invalid duplicate UserCount data
        constraints = [
            UniqueConstraint(
                fields=["user", "property", "subgroup", "end_time"],
                condition=Q(subgroup__isnull=False),
                name="unique_user_count",
            ),
            UniqueConstraint(
                fields=["user", "property", "end_time"],
                condition=Q(subgroup__isnull=True),
                name="unique_user_count_null_subgroup",
            ),
        ]
```

The second `UniqueConstraint` there is on `["user", "property", "end_time"]`, with a condition (predicate) of `Q(subgroup__isnull=True)`.  That translates to this index:
```
    "unique_user_count_null_subgroup" UNIQUE, btree (user_id, property, end_time) WHERE subgroup IS NULL
```

So to use that index, we need an `ON CONFLICT` which exactly matches it -- namely:
```sql
ON CONFLICT (user_id, property, end_time) WHERE subgroup IS NULL
```

Regarding [#29521](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/29521) 
Did some testing to identify a reasonable breakpoint.

500 messages:
Using Narrow: 120 ms
Using ids: 100ms

200 messages:
Using Narrow: 100 ms
Using ids: 85ms

50 messages:
Using Narrow: 90 ms
Using ids: 75 ms

20 messages:
Using Narrow: 70ms
Using ids: 56 ms

Using `do_mark_unread_by_narrow` consistently takes approx 100-120ms, whereas `do_mark_unread_by_ids` performs similarly for more than 200 messages. For less than 200 messages it performs slightly better (20-30 ms improvement). 
Seems like 200 messages would be a correct estimate for a breakpoint.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-03-04 15:41 UTC

pgAdmin is not recommended, no.  Zulip does not enable the Django admin panel.  Both of those make it too easy to corrupt your database state by editing values directly instead of using Zulip's APIs.

If you want a visual database inspector, I would recommend finding a SQL client that does that, rather than installing anything on the server, which poses a security risk.  Or get comfortable with SQL and use `./manage.py dbshell` directly.

## modal to introduce inbox and recent view

*2024-03-07 to 2024-03-08 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/modal.20to.20introduce.20inbox.20and.20recent.20view/with/1753740)*

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2024-03-07 16:48 UTC

I'm working on #29073.

**Background**

To improve onboarding experience, we'll show a one-time modal explaining "Inbox" & "Recent conversations" views. (When user visits them for the first time.)

When a user views a modal, we mark it as read by storing a row in the `OnboardingStep` model.
```py
class OnboardingStep(models.Model):
    user = models.ForeignKey(UserProfile, on_delete=CASCADE)
    onboarding_step = models.CharField(max_length=30)
    timestamp = models.DateTimeField(default=timezone_now)
```

**Query**

We don't want to show these two one-time-modal to existing users. We'll have to do a migration creating **two rows per user** (mark them as read) in `OnboardingStep` model.

Should we do some optimization by creating these rows only for users who are not `long_term_idle`? -- or is it fine to create rows for all the users?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-03-08 18:24 UTC

I think it's probably fine to just create them for everyone; it's not actually a lot of storage.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-03-08 18:24 UTC

(And later we'll get to delete the ones for the existing onboarding hotspots once those are removed from the app)

in `zerver/models/sessions.py` : 
```
# custom session model
class RealmSession(AbstractBaseSession):
    user = models.ForeignKey(UserProfile, null=True, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    realm = models.ForeignKey(Realm, null=True, on_delete=models.CASCADE)

    class Meta:
        models.Index(
            fields=("realm", "user"),
            name="zerver_realmsession_realm_user_idx",
        ),

    @classmethod
    def get_session_store_class(cls):
        return RealmSessionStore


class LeaklessCachedDbSessionStore(CachedDbSessionStore):
    """Caching session object which does not leak into the cache.

    django.contrib.sessions.backends.cached_db does write-through to
    the cache and the backing database.  If the database is in a
    transaction, this may leak not-yet-committed changes to the cache,
    which can lead to inconsistent state.  This class wraps changes to
    the session in assertions which enforce that the database cannot
    be in a transaction before writing.

    """

    @override
    def save(self, must_create: bool = False) -> None:
        assert not get_connection().in_atomic_block
        super().save(must_create)

    @override
    def delete(self, session_key: Optional[str] = None) -> None:
        assert not get_connection().in_atomic_block
        super().delete(session_key)


class RealmSessionStore(LeaklessCachedDbSessionStore):

    cache_key_prefix = "sessions_realm_session_store"

    @classmethod
    def get_model_class(cls):
        return RealmSession

    def create_model_instance(self, data):

        obj = super().create_model_instance(data)
        try:
            user_id = int(data.get("user_id"))
            realm_id = int(data.get("realm_id"))

        except (ValueError, TypeError):
            realm_id = None
            user_id = None

        obj.realm_id = realm_id
        obj.user_id = user_id

        return obj

```

1. I chose to put `realm` first in the index fields, it should be faster, it narrows down search results by realm first then by user (No. realms < No. users), Also if for some reason we want to filter by user only then i will add a separate index for user.

Maybe @Tim Abbott will confirm whether my thoughts here align with his. But  I think we're fine with the behavior changing from `anonymous session (usually) don't get written to db` to `anonymous sessions get written to db (because we start storing some custom fields in them)`. I would leave out any ``checking if a `session_key` has already been created`` and just put whatever we want in the session. We can tweak that later anyway if we're unhappy with it.

What we **don't** want to change is Django's internal decision-making on when it chooses to save an anonymous session. That's what I thought you were considering trying to change when you asked about  `Do we even want to have anonymous sesssions saved in the db?`.

We're not making an explicit call on whether session is saved to db. We just set a custom field in `request.session`. How Django implements that internally, we don't care.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-10-22 00:35 UTC

Correct, what I'd like to do is make a minimal transition that fixes the performance problem that this issue is about without changing anything about how anonymous sessions are stored.

We only care about storing the new metadata for logged-in sessions. If it happens that when an anonymous session is stored, we can store the new metadata for those too without saving an extra anonymous sessions to the database, great, but that's not a goal of this transition.

(replying to Tim Abbott)

Now, that's a clear and really understandable Answer !

**Sandeepa Nadahalli** · 2024-03-18 12:17 UTC

Hi, Zulip noob here and I'm trying to do some customisations on the client side.
Question:
Can I use userprofile.uuid for identifying a user uniquely?

In lib>export.py, it's in the excluded list.

```
# We exclude these fields for the following reasons:
# * api_key is a secret.
# * password is a secret.
# * uuid is unlikely to be useful if the domain changes.
EXCLUDED_USER_PROFILE_FIELDS = ["api_key", "password", "uuid"]
```
I did not understand the comment about uuid. What happens to the uuid if/when the domain changes?
Please help.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-03-18 17:52 UTC

@Sandeepa Nadahalli can you give a bit more context on what you're trying to do?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-03-18 17:53 UTC

The UUID is not sent to clients because its purpose is mainly to prevent a class of bug with the data import/export tools. It is immutable and so it can serve as a unique ID for a user; but the `id` field has the same property unless you import/export the organization (which usually renumbers users).

@Tim Abbott Thanks a lot for your answer. I will use the id itself. And I don't plan to import/export the org. 
I am trying to extend the Zulip client with some custom functionality where I need to map users with accounts from some other server.

Yeah, pulling the SA stuff into its own package feels almost cleaner.  Or I think all three of those could fit into `zerver.lib.narrow` reasonably:
```python3
def topic_match_sa(topic_name: str) -> ColumnElement[Boolean]:
    # _sa is short for SQLAlchemy, which we use mostly for
    # queries that search messages
    topic_cond = func.upper(column("subject", Text)) == func.upper(literal(topic_name))
    return topic_cond


def get_resolved_topic_condition_sa() -> ColumnElement[Boolean]:
    resolved_topic_cond = column("subject", Text).startswith(RESOLVED_TOPIC_PREFIX)
    return resolved_topic_cond


def topic_column_sa() -> ColumnElement[Text]:
    return column("subject", Text)
```

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-24 01:27 UTC

Are those checks from that `apns1` library's import time, or from us invoking it at our import time?

Either way, it'd be good to get them out of import time. If we can't move them out of runtime entirely (in favor of development-time, as a form of test), they should happen lazily when they first become relevant. Or else explicitly, as part of the code called from a "main" function of a process that is going to need them.

**Greg Price** · 2024-09-24 01:34 UTC

(One language-design choice which Dart made and I appreciate is that there *is* no such thing as code that runs at import time. If you write something like `final thing = someComputation();` at top level in a source file, what that compiles to is that `thing` gets lazily initialized — so that `someComputation` gets called — the first time you access it, and then memoized for future accesses.

I think the designers of Dart had experienced seeing big sprawling codebases with lots of libraries by lots of different people where different parts of the codebase let on-startup execution slip in here and there because it feels like the easiest way to deal with some small problem they have, and it adds up to a mess that takes longer and longer to start up.)

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-04-03 04:35 UTC

So we have two 0501 migrations in `main`; `0501_delete_dangling_usermessages.py` and `0501_mark_introduce_zulip_view_modals_as_read.py`.  They merge in `0502`:
[Screenshot-2024-04-03-at-12.06.11AM.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/ef/usfyk3XjGZoKyUQ0gAbwGBi9/Screenshot-2024-04-03-at-12.06.11AM.png)

The former exists in `8.x` as well as `main` -- but with a different history:
```
$ git show upstream/8.x:zerver/migrations/0501_delete_dangling_usermessages.py | rg -A1 dependencies
    dependencies = [
        ("zerver", "0496_alter_scheduledmessage_read_by_sender"),

## Availability of Zulip service

*2024-04-05 to 2024-04-09 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Availability.20of.20Zulip.20service/with/1775659)*

**Jinendra Khabiya** · 2024-04-05 12:16 UTC

Had a few questions around availability of scalability of Zulip service. From the docs and code, I could understand that we can shard the tornado server per realm or at a user level as well. 

1. Is it possible to have multiple tornado servers for a single realm/user combination to ensure higher availability for a single realm/user? 
2. And also, is it possible to run multiple replicas of Django server and other components for a single realm to achieve higher availability? (Basically, is Django server stateless and requests can be served from any of the available instances?)

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-04-05 14:31 UTC

Tornado servers maintain state in-memory, so a user can only be served by a single Tornado process.  Multiple Tornado servers are for scaling, not for HA.

The Django service itself is stateless, but it relies on shared state via PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ, Memcached, and Redis.  So in practice having multiple nginx + uwsgi (Django) servers actually likely *decreases* availability if you still have single PostgreSQL, RabbitMQ, Memcached and Redis servers on another host(s)

**Jinendra Khabiya** · 2024-04-08 06:45 UTC

Got it. Thank you for response, Alex. Wondering if anyone in the community has tried to scale out Django servers with a sharded tornado server, that can help us achieve a higher availability.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-04-09 02:27 UTC

Zulip Cloud runs a more complicated sharded deployment.  You're welcome to drop an email to sales@zulip.com to set up some time to talk about your HA needs and how they can best be addressed.


## Add CUSTOM_EMAIL_SENT event to prevent duplicate email

*2024-04-06 to 2024-04-12 · 3 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Add.20CUSTOM_EMAIL_SENT.20event.20to.20prevent.20duplicate.20email/with/1776436)*

**andrew wang** · 2024-04-06 22:06 UTC

Greetings, everyone
I have submitted [PR](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/29617) for [Issue#19520](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/19529). I will describe the issue and my implementation to get your feedback.
Tim's comments on adding CUSTOM_EMAIL_SENT to prevent duplicate emails are summarized below.

- Create a `RealmAuditLog` entry when custom emails are sent to a given user; we can number it as `CUSTOM_EMAIL_SENT = 800` in `AbtractRealmAuditLog.`  With the full ID (email template's hash code) for the custom email included in the `extra_data` key. 
- We can have the `send_custom_email` function exclude users with a RealmAuditLog entry for the current email's ID. We will want to do this exclusion carefully to ensure that logic like the `--marketing` option, which is designed to only email an address once even if they have multiple accounts for their email address, will avoid sending the email if any UserProfile with that `delivery_email` has such a RealmAuditLog entry.


The current implementation of the send_custom_email function (distinct_email = True) in the pseudo-code below:
send_custom_email(List<UserProfile> users, String email_template):

1. if there are any users with duplicate email addresses, remove them. So the users are changed to users_distinct_emails
2. send email(email_template) to users_distinct_emails.

My PR changed send_custom_email's logic in the pseudo-code:

(notice: we have a unique constraint on UserProfile(realm, delivery_email).
1. if there are any users with duplicate email addresses, remove them. So the users are changed to users_distinct_emails
2. keep a map of {user : [user with the same email]}
3. for user in users_distinct_emails:
           
```python
        find in the past week's RealmAuditLog by (user realm_id, user id, and email_template's hash)
        if no CUSTOM_SENT_EVENT found:
               send an email to the user
               create a CUSTOM_SENT_EVENT for ALL users in [user with the same email]
```
          
With the change, as shown in the unit tests, the behavior is now described below.

- If Aaron and Hamlet are called in send_custom_email, the server crashes after sending Aaron an email. Later, an email will be sent to Hamlet only when the API is called again with the same arguments. 

- if hamlet_mit(mit realm), hamelet(example realm) , both with same email hamlet@zulip.com, are called in send_custom_email, only one email is sent to hamlet@zulip.com.

- if later, aaron(mit realm, aaron@zulip.com) and hamlet are called in send_custom_email again, only one email is sent to aaron@zulip.com.

Do you think the logic is correct to avoid resending the same email to the same address? I'm trying to do an end-to-end test by manually simulating a server failure. I am looking at the document and code to determine the test case. Please let me know what you think. 
Thanks!

**andrew wang** · 2024-04-08 21:54 UTC

If we have concerns about query performance because the RealmAuditLog table can accumulate a lot of data, I have an alternate proposal that uses a new table and the changes are more isolated also.

create CustomEmailLog table with columns (email_address, email_template_digest, sent_time, month_mod_2). The primary key is (email_address, email_template_digest). sent_time is the time the email is sent. It's sufficient for us to keep at most 2-month email sent logs, so month_mod_2 is the month%2 value. We use month_mod_2 as the partition key. Every month, we truncate a partition to maintain the CustomEmalLog table size.  We can maintain query performance while keeping the table size under control

What do you think of this approach? 
Thanks!

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-04-12 00:31 UTC

I think a separate table is unnecessary; we don't send a large number of these custom emails (the average user gets <5 a year, and I don't anticipate that changing).

context : [session migration in my PR](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/29668/files/19aa7f49d972be0f4c901341daffef4e8b38e17a#diff-225a03cc89f5381a1460d330fc27d4f43ab84e37468450ac80fc68a43997b869)

We want to copy all data from `django_session` to `zerver_realmsession` as performantly as possible.

For testing i've filled `50k` rows in `django_session` (which has 3 columns) with dump but  similar to real data. 

query used : 
```sql
INSERT INTO zerver_realmsession (SELECT * FROM django_session);
```

There is an obvious difference in execution time between with and without indexes :

- With Index (default)        `700 : 900 ms`
- After Dropping indexes  `300 : 500 ms`


**My current doubt is whether that approach of (dropping, filling data then create back the indexes) is possible/reliable especially because this would affect a production db,  for example what about other queries trying to use these indexes in the same time in which those indexes are deleted.** ?

Generally you just add the new indexes before you delete the old ones, so there's always a working index.

This is a new table you're inserting into, which isn't used before.  We can just make the indexes after copying the data in.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-04-15 19:34 UTC

That's going to cause some problems for Zulip Cloud, but it's going to be faster for everyone else, who stop / migrate / start the service.

`populate_db` calls `maybe_enqueue_audit_log_upload` six times:

- from `do_create_realm(string_id="zulip", …)`
- from `do_change_user_role(iago, UserProfile.ROLE_REALM_ADMINISTRATOR, acting_user=None)`
- from `do_change_user_role(desdemona, UserProfile.ROLE_REALM_OWNER, acting_user=None)`
- from `do_change_user_role(shiva, UserProfile.ROLE_MODERATOR, acting_user=None)`
- from `do_change_user_role(polonius, UserProfile.ROLE_GUEST, acting_user=None)`
- from `do_create_realm(string_id="analytics", …)`

There’s no deduplication. Also the `deferred_work` worker races with `initialize_push_notifications` to start two concurrent uploads, of which the second fails.

## extra markup on quoted fences

*2024-04-19 to 2024-05-01 · 19 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/extra.20markup.20on.20quoted.20fences/with/1784077)*

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-04-19 14:28 UTC

In working on the rendered Markdown refactor in #29756, [I found that](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/29756#discussion_r1571439356) quoted messages containing only a single fenced item--a code block, a KaTeX block, or a spoiler--receive additional markup around them: a containing `<p>`, which the browser appears to error handle with `<p></p>` inside the `<blockquote>` element. That's lamentable, but a `<br>` tag also gets inserted, which introduces additional space beneath the quoted fenced item.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-04-19 14:29 UTC

Here's the raw HTML response returned by the API for the quote of a standalone code block message:

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-04-19 14:29 UTC

```
<p><span class="user-mention silent" data-user-id="8">Cordelia, Lear's daughter</span> <a href="#narrow/stream/9-devel/topic/single-line.20messages/near/129">said</a>:</p>\n<blockquote>\n<p><div class="codehilite"><pre><span></span><code>I am a single-line code block.\n</code></pre></div><br>\n</p>\n</blockquote>`
```

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-04-19 14:31 UTC

I can also quote that code block to show the effect I'm trying to describe:

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-04-19 14:31 UTC

(replying to Karl Stolley)
> ``` <p><span class="user-mention silent" data-user-id="8">Cordelia, Lear's daughter</span> <a href="#narrow/stream/9-devel/topic/single-line.20messages/near/129">said</a>:</p>\n<blockquote>\n<p><div class="codehilite"><pre><span></span><code>I am a single-line code block.\n</code></pre></div><br>\n< …

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-04-19 14:33 UTC

You can see the error-corrected markup in the browser inspector like this:

[Screenshot-2024-04-19-at-10.32.24AM.png](https://chat.zulip.org/user_uploads/2/e2/JhTa7xOPbBBArkotRSKGX6J-/Screenshot-2024-04-19-at-10.32.24AM.png)

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-04-19 14:35 UTC

I've spent some time looking at `fenced_code.py`, but I'm still not certain as to where this treatment of (presumably) new lines is introducing the extra markup seen here.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-04-19 16:41 UTC

The `fenced_code.py` nesting algorithm is extremely buggy. In this case, what’s happening is that the inner code block is converted to HTML, that HTML result is replaced with a placeholder `␂wzxhzdk:0␃` to be replaced later, and then the outer code block is re-processed as Markdown, at which time `␂wzxhzdk:0␃` looks like a sufficiently cromulent paragraph to deserve its own `<p>` tags.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-04-19 16:47 UTC

Wow, that's weird. But I appreciate the explanation. At least the empty paragraphs (or at least how the browser corrects them to that) don't occupy any vertical space, but it's the break tag that actually holds the box open

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-04-19 16:51 UTC

This [related upstream issue](https://github.com/Python-Markdown/markdown/issues/53) has been open for eleven years.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-04-19 16:52 UTC

Python-Markdown is not a good library.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-04-19 16:53 UTC

That's disappointing. But I guess at least this isn't something we're introducing ourselves

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-04-19 17:02 UTC

It’s still our fault that we’re initiating that re-processing; the whole `process_contents=True` thing is our invention.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-04-19 17:41 UTC

Ultimately I don't think there's something worth doing here beyond replacing the library; there's lots of messy but not important quirks like this that come with the Python-Markdown architecture that are not worth solving individually.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-04-19 17:53 UTC

Ultimately even if we fix new markup generated by the current processor, our CSS still needs to handle the old messages, at least until we can work out a migration to process all previous messages.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-04-19 17:55 UTC

Sure. Fortunately there's nothing amiss with the CSS here...it's that `<br>` tag goofing things up. Once that's gone, margin-collapsing, etc. will take over and things will display correctly (as when quoting a Markdown-only message that itself has been quoted)

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-04-19 17:58 UTC

We can potentially try to get rid of those in `rendered_markdown.ts` while we're editing the HTML for spoilers anyway, if it feels worth it to you.

**Karl Stolley** · 2024-04-19 18:02 UTC

That could be worth a fixup at some point, so I've made a note of it, but since it doesn't really impact the information-density project (it just looks weird when it happens), it's probably not worth the effort for now.

**Greg Price** · 2024-05-01 23:03 UTC

Fascinating — thanks @Karl Stolley for looking into this, and @Anders Kaseorg for the diagnosis!

This symptom has been visible since forever, but as far as I'm aware nobody had previously dug into the cause of it.

I've filed #F641 for eventually papering over this in the Flutter app, just as we intend to eventually do in web. (It's milestoned "post-launch", reflecting that this isn't a priority.)

## groups deactivation

*2024-05-15 to 2024-06-25 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/groups.20deactivation/with/1800414)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-05-15 18:10 UTC

As discussed in #**design>Support user group deactivation**, we want to allow deactivating user groups.

It was discussed there that we should add a `deactivated` field. I just wanted to confirm whether we should add the field in `NamedUserGroup` or `UserGroup` model. I guess `NamedUserGroup` model is fine since we would allow only to deactivate named user groups.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-05-28 22:47 UTC

Yeah, `NamedUserGroup` is correct.

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-06-20 18:37 UTC

As discussed in #**design>Support user group deactivation**, we do not allow deactivating groups which are used as subgroups or used for setting. I have implemented this in #30504 [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/30504/commits/b1e194d693ece52c68823a1964a73532eff532eb#diff-5fe2fd467528b9af1b4b0d2f9aecb6c73bae3a73c4491339dcb26b81996e051aR118).

I wanted to discuss about how to handle race conditions here.

For the subgroups part , we would want to make sure that a group being deactivated does not race with that group being used as a subgroup. I think this is handled well currenlty, as we use `select_for_update` when accessing the group for deletion and when fetching groups to be used as subgroups and if both requests come together one of them will fail.

For settings, we do not use `select_for_update` when fetching group rows to be used for settings. Just wanted to confirm that we can do so and that would be enough to handle the race conditions.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-25 23:10 UTC

I think that should be sufficient; then the operations of "Use group X for setting Y" and "Deactivate group X" must be serialized with respect to each other, and whichever operation happens second would presumably fail.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-05-30 05:12 UTC

So, I have observed it frequently over the years that sometimes czo initial load times are very high like 2 ~ 5 minutes where it is just processing the initial `GET` request on `https://chat.zulip.org/` while something like GitHub loads instantly.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-06 23:40 UTC

We don't know the original hostname/URL at import time, so probably cleanest would be for that sort of rewriting to happen at export time, if it's required. But I don't think that should usually be required; the Markdown processor is responsible for doing that step:
```
def rewrite_local_links_to_relative(db_data: Optional[DbData], link: str) -> str:                                                                                            
    """If the link points to a local destination (e.g. #narrow/...),                                                                                                         
    generate a relative link that will open it in the current window.                                                                                                        
    """                                                                                                                                                                      
                                                                                                                                                                             
    if db_data:                                                                                                                                                              
        realm_url_prefix = db_data.realm_url + "/"                                                                                                                           
        if link.startswith((realm_url_prefix + "#", realm_url_prefix + "user_uploads/")):                                                                                    
            return link[len(realm_url_prefix) :]                                                                                                                             
                                                                                                                                                                             
    return link                                                                                                                                                              
```

such that the HTML in messages we have in the database will be relative links if to the current server.

```
SELECT message_id, flags
FROM zerver_usermessage
JOIN zerver_message ON zerver_usermessage.message_id = zerver_message.id
WHERE user_profile_id = 33 
AND EXISTS (
    SELECT 1 
    FROM zerver_usertopic 
    WHERE zerver_usertopic.user_profile_id = 33 
    AND zerver_usertopic.visibility_policy = 3 
AND upper(zerver_usertopic.topic_name) = upper(zerver_message.subject)
    AND zerver_usertopic.recipient_id = zerver_message.recipient_id
) 
ORDER BY message_id DESC
LIMIT 50;

The query plan from a data base with ~no data in it is fundamentally useless to know how it will perform when there is significant data.  Essentially, there is low constant overhead to using an index, so full table scans always win out on tables with a tiny number of rows.

**Bedo Khaled** · 2024-07-18 23:24 UTC

I have updated news, I have read this research paper[Exploring The State of Rate Limiting in IPv6](https://essay.utwente.nl/96014/1/van%20Heijningen_BA_EEMCS.pdf), with a date of `July 7, 2023`.

I will summarize some key points from that research:

1. Scarcity of academic papers about this topic, it's under-researched.

2. The open-source space clearly knows a little about the impact that IPv6 can have on rate limiting. As is shown by us not being able to find a single open-source web server that does anything more than per-IP rate limiting for IPv6 by default.

3. As per public `NGINX` documentation, default rate limiting behaviour by default on IPv6 is per-IP. However the key variable in `limit_req_zone` can be modified to allow blocking for `/64`, or larger, Zulip does use `NGINIX` and I assume you choose to put the rate-limiting implementation on `Zulip` backend zerver instead of `NGINX` to have more customization and control I guess ? rather than just a configuration, right ?

4. rate limit should at least be done per `/64` block, this is how arguably the industry leader `Cloudflare` implements it. This is reasonable, as per `RFC` spec a minimum of a /64 block should be assigned per end user.

5. Making this limit higher, like `/48` might cause some issues for real users, as it was found that many of the same `/48` blocks are used by hundreds if not thousands of end users. On top of that, while `per-/48` blocking is too strict, it is also useless against an attacker who is motivated enough to acquire an `ASN` number. Which gives them access to a `/32` or more in many RIR regions. Effectively giving them `2^16` usable addresses `per-/48` rate limiting.


6. Given difficulty to obtain a new IPv6 prefix to use, whether that is through an ISP or through a RIR via an `ASN`. We think the best approach to prevent abuse is to monitor for either `/56`, `/48` or `/32` blocks that suddenly have a large spike in requests, and then permanently block that range. Thus requiring the attacker to obtain a new IPv6 address range. System administrators can decide the whitelist of block the range based on previous traffic data, associated ASN, request rate and types of requests to determine if this is an attack or benign user traffic/growth. This should stop most attackers who does not have access to a botnet, that, combined with blocking `per-/64` seems to be most reasonable.
This approach does have the flaw of if an attacker knows about this implementation, he can just simply scale up his `DDoS` attack slowly, thus not showing any suspicion.

So what's making it `insufficient` ? What are its current issues ?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-08-19 14:47 UTC

A DDOS can commonly be hundreds of thousands of requests *per second*.  Zulip Cloud runs 40 Django workers at once.  For a DDOS with 100k requests per second, each request would have to be serviced by a Django process in 0.4ms.

Django cannot even *process a request* that fast, much less make a request to a separate service, receive a reply, and send one back.  That's to say nothing of the time overheads in getting the request through uwsgi and nginx as well, which each provide their own overhead and potential bottlenecks.

Tools to mitigate DDOS attacks also want to be at the *top* of your stack, closest to the traffic, and not all of the way down in the application.  Otherwise, you've giving them access to consume resources of your entire stack, potentially hitting bottlenecks in *those* even before the requests get to the application.  For instance, if nginx were the bottleneck, it doesn't matter how many 429's Django returns -- nobody else is going to get through to Django to get their legitimate requests through.

In short, it's the wrong tool for the job.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2025-09-03 20:06 UTC

The idea behind /64 rate limiting isn’t that it’s a secret. The idea is that it’s somewhat more difficult for an attacker to get addresses on a large number of /64 subnets.

Also, the goal of rate limiting is to prevent a large number of requests from overwhelming our server. We’re intentionally open about this, and we even provide a `retry_after` value to be helpful. When clients reduce their number of requests to avoid getting rate limited, that is a good thing, not a bad thing.

We don’t use django-honeypot. (I assume it can be configured in a variety of ways to make it harder to automatically bypass, but I’m not familiar with it.)

In general, security by obscurity is not helpful. A sufficiently motivated attacker can always figure out what you’re doing.

## message type database index

*2024-06-21 to 2024-06-24 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/message.20type.20database.20index/with/1834087)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-21 23:49 UTC

In https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/30142/commits/9a59c53670008fbfc539d3a981d8034620794589#r1649500646, we're looking at adding an additional use for the `message.type` database column originally defined in #**api design>message type parameter, #24960**. I'll post there for discussion about whether this is a good use for the field. But for here, I'd like to ask the question of what sort of database index on `message.type` is most appropriate.

#30142 proposes a `(realm, type)` index. Since I think we are very unlikely to want to do a query filtering on just those messages that are of the NORMAL/default type, I was thinking we could make it a much smaller index by doing a `WHERE type != NORMAL` filter on the index. Thoughts?

@Prakhar Pratyush FYI.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-06-22 00:54 UTC

Yeah, that index is pretty much useless, stats-wise, if we include `NORMAL` in it.

Is PostgreSQL smart enough to use the partial index if we query for `type = 17` when the index is over `type != 1`?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-06-22 04:13 UTC

Not sure, but if it doesn’t, we could also try querying for `type != 1 AND type = 17`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-06-24 19:05 UTC

So #29794 is a report of problems where our `puppet` logic for deciding how much memory to allocate to Zulip servers is getting the server's total, not the amount allocated to the container, and thus producing bad results. I posted this on the thread:

> One idea would be a `zulip.conf` setting to override the memory detected for the server -- so you can say "treat this server as having only 8GB of RAM for calculating how much to use for your services". I don't think we want a direct setting to change the default process count; there's already one to adjust `uwsgi_processes` directly though, and manually set that plus `queue_worker_multoprocess` is probably the best workaround.

But I also wonder if the problem is deeper than that; for Docker, our container doesn't even contain the postgres/memcached services, and so the logic around how to allocate memory that we have in `puppet` is probably basically nonsensical in that context?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-06-28 21:51 UTC

## Json in @typed_endpoint

*2024-06-29 to 2024-07-05 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Json.20in.20.40typed_endpoint/with/1841921)*

**Bedo Khaled** · 2024-06-29 19:27 UTC

I looked at serveral PRs migrating from `@has_request_variables` to `@typed_endpoint` but still not sure when `Pydantic.Json[]` should be imposed on the parameter ?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-01 23:24 UTC

@Kenneth R probably can give his thinking on the topic to start.

**Kenneth R** · 2024-07-02 08:48 UTC

@Bedo Khaled We use `Json` for parameters that are expected to be `Json` encoded. You can look at the `.yaml` file to see which parameters require `Application/Json`. When using `REQ` we were using  `json_validator` to parse and validate the data.

**Kenneth R** · 2024-07-02 08:49 UTC

Pydantic's `Json` parses the encoded Json string and validates it against the type mentioned.

**Kenneth R** · 2024-07-02 08:53 UTC

We generally use `Json` in REST Apis to ensure uniformity as each language implements `Arrays/ Objects/ Hashmaps/` differently, in order for seamless cross language communication we encode the data into a `Json string`.

**Kenneth R** · 2024-07-02 08:55 UTC

When converting endpoints what you should be looking for is if the existing endpoint uses `json_validator`. If you're still unsure, you can check the `.yaml` file for that endpoint.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-31 02:26 UTC

> Now, In tests where we make POST requests to this view and receive error responses that results in rolling back the entire test transaction.

This doesn’t match my understanding of how any of the forms of Django’s transactions work.

```python
with transaction.atomic():
    cursor.execute(query1)
    try:
        with transaction.atomic():
            cursor.execute(query2)
            raise Exception
    except Exception:
        # here query1 is visible but not query2
        pass

with transaction.atomic():
    cursor.execute(query1)
    with transaction.atomic(durable=True):
        # Django disallows that and raises RuntimeError, although it
        # has an exemption if the outer transaction is the one from
        # TestCase, in which case this works like the above
        pass

with transaction.atomic():
    cursor.execute(query1)
    try:
        with transaction.atomic(savepoint=False):
            cursor.execute(query2)
            raise Exception
    except Exception:
        # here both query1 and query2 are visible
        pass
```

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-31 02:41 UTC

Oh, my understanding is wrong.

> `# here both query1 and query2 are visible`

Actually, Django (≥ 1.7) puts the connection in an error state where all queries raise `TransactionManagementError`, until the actual rollback happens at the end of the outer atomic block.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-31 03:06 UTC

That makes me a little less concerned about playing `savepoint=False` games in production; a production-only `TransactionManagementError` is bad but not arbitrarily bad, I guess.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-01 00:17 UTC

Hmm, I suspect the correct answer here is that we should be using `transaction.atomic(durable=True)`, not `savepoint=False` for those outer view-function transactions, which we don't expect to be composed inside another production transaction.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-01 00:19 UTC

We likely only want to use `savepoint=False` on the small number of lower-level `actions` methods that are sometimes called inside another transaction intentionally.

I think there's been a bit of cargo-culting of `savepoint=False`, and we might want to take the time to audit all the uses of that and add comments noting where they're called inside another transaction as comments, and switch those where that is not a thing to use `durable=True` instead.

## Modernized typing syntax

*2024-07-14 to 2024-07-16 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Modernized.20typing.20syntax/with/1888790)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-07-14 06:06 UTC

I merged #30840, which modernizing the Python 3 typing syntax that we use. You may find your changes fail tests when rebasing them; in theory the linter fixers should work. But mostly the changes are pretty straightforward:
- `List` => `list`
- `Union[foo, bar]` => `foo | bar`
- `Optional[foo]` => `foo` | None`

**Zixuan James Li** · 2024-07-14 17:50 UTC

Does it mean that we can also start using Python 3.10+ features like pattern matching?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-14 17:57 UTC

That’s been allowed since #29458; you don’t need to wait for a mass migration of old code to start writing better new code.

**Bedo Khaled** · 2024-07-16 22:04 UTC

Can someone explain what are the benefits of migrating to that modern Python 3 typing syntax ?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-07-16 22:06 UTC

Having to do fewer iterations of "gaaah, forgot to add `Dict` to the `from typing import ...` line"

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-16 22:07 UTC

Fewer imports from `typing` (`list` is a builtin); fewer brackets to balance; less confusion about [what `Optional` means](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/testing/mypy.html#use-optional-and-none-correctly); alignment with the upstream direction.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-07-16 22:08 UTC

See also the rationales for [PEP 585](https://peps.python.org/pep-0585/) and [PEP 604](https://peps.python.org/pep-0604/).

## local performance vs cloud performance

*2024-07-31 to 2024-08-01 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/local.20performance.20vs.20cloud.20performance/with/1907204)*

**Bedo Khaled** · 2024-07-31 04:34 UTC

When testing the execution time for some endpoint on my machine and it takes `1 min` for example, does it take the same amount in production when that endpoint runs in zulip remote server ? taking into account the conditions are similar (same number of users, same number of streams, etc..) ?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-07-31 18:46 UTC

If you have the same database contents and the same deployment settings and the same memory and the same CPU and the same network, then potentially.

I'm also not clear if by "local" you mean "using `./tools/run-dev`" in which case the answer is even more likely no, since there are several debugging layers which slow down performance (e.g. enabling hot-reload).

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-07-31 18:47 UTC

Oh, and "same database contents" also has to include that the server has the same query plans because it has generated the same statistics from them.

Your question kinda boils down to "what can impact performance" which is ... a very broad question. :)

**Bedo Khaled** · 2024-08-01 14:22 UTC

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> I'm also not clear if by "local" you mean "using `./tools/run-dev`"
Yes, that's what I meant

**Bedo Khaled** · 2024-08-01 14:23 UTC

Generaly a remote cloud server for Zulip should have more CPU power than a normal end-user PC, right?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-08-01 14:24 UTC

It's possible to [run Zulip on a single-processor machine with 2GB of RAM](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/production/requirements.html).

I suspect your development machine is bigger than that.

**Bedo Khaled** · 2024-08-01 14:25 UTC

It's definitely yes

**Bedo Khaled** · 2024-08-01 14:26 UTC

So in short it's not a yes/no question, it depends on many variable things

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-08-01 14:28 UTC

That's pretty much all of profiling and performance analysis, yup. :)

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-01 17:23 UTC

That said, the development environment IS a pretty good simulation of relative performance. On average, if a change makes something 3x faster in development than it was before, it will often be in the range of 2-4x faster in production. It very much depends on the production configuration, especially for things dependant on round-trip-time count, where it might really matter on how far the Zulip server is from its database on the network.

## Converting slack text link format

*2024-08-09 to 2024-08-12 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Converting.20slack.20text.20link.20format/with/1915166)*

**Pieter K** · 2024-08-09 12:39 UTC

I think we want to convert link like the second example here into `[foo](https://foo.com)` instead of `https://foo.com|foo` no?



```python
# This is at data_import/slack_message_conversion.py

def convert_link_format(text: str) -> tuple[str, bool]:
    """
    1. Converts '<https://foo.com>' to 'https://foo.com'
    2. Converts '<https://foo.com|foo>' to 'https://foo.com|foo'
    """
    has_link = False
    for match in re.finditer(LINK_REGEX, text, re.VERBOSE):
        converted_text = match.group(0).replace(">", "").replace("<", "")
        has_link = True
        text = text.replace(match.group(0), converted_text)
    return text, has_link
```

## Slack text reformatting edge cases

*2024-08-13 to 2024-11-19 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Slack.20text.20reformatting.20edge.20cases/with/1919202)*

**Pieter K** · 2024-08-13 09:52 UTC

I was refactoring `webhook/slack_incoming.py` to use some of the Slack reformatting functions we have over at   `data_import/slack_message_conversion.py` as part of #31311. It looks like there are some cases that the regex over at `data_import/slack_message_conversion.py` cannot handle:

* **Formatted strings containing emojis**, e.g., `*1️⃣ Use the '/task' command*`
* **Formatted strings separated by exactly one white space,** e.g., `*foo* *bar*`. This likely happens because the `*foo*` match includes the white space right after it, so  when trying to match for the `*bar*` string, the first capture group in `SLACK_BOLD_REGEX`**>** (`(^|[ -(]|[+-/]|[:-?]|\{|\[|\_|\||\^|~)`) fail to detect anything. 
* **Formatted strings after a new line**. We don't have to worry about this in Slack export because new lines will be in the form of "\n". However, processed Slack text (think of `render_block` & `render_attachment` in `slack_incoming.py`) that needs reformatting will have newlines without using "\n".

- Formatted string with containing whitespace immediately after * or _ or ~. e.g `* bold*`

An array of dictionaries containing data on all direct message and group direct message conversations that the user has received (or sent) messages in, organized by conversation. This da …

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-15 00:31 UTC

`get_recent_private_conversations` in `zerver/lib/message.py` is the function computing that; it has a couple downsides: It's expensive, and it returns potentially incomplete data basically for performance reasons.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-15 00:33 UTC

So I think we would want a `last_message_id` field. There's basically two costs to adding such a thing:
- It needs to be updated whenever we send a message, which adds extra work to a hot code path that we want to be really fast. The work itself is trivial, though, since the newly sent message will always be the new latest, so it's just a write.
- We need to check if it needs to be updated when DMs are deleted. This is probably pretty cheap, since it'd be a direct index lookup to get the correct value each time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-15 00:38 UTC

I feel fairly confident we want a `group_size` field; it's static for a given group, cheap to store, and will just make it easy for any logic that cares about the size of the group to be simple. This probably would not be exposed to the API. 

So maybe the first PR to do would be to add that, with a backfill migration to calculate it from `Subscription` for all the existing `DirectMessageGroup` objects.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-15 00:53 UTC

I'm a little of the feeling that if we're doing `last_message_id`, we might as well calculate `first_message_id` and `total_messages`, since it's likely to be fairly cheap and the same code paths would need to think about updating it and could do so in the same database query:
- Sending a message.
- Deleting messages.
- Message retention policy deletes.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-15 00:53 UTC

But I think it could be reasonable to defer a PR to calculate those until after we've migrated the `Recipient `data structures, so we only need to do a single pass through the `Message` table to backfill it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-15 00:54 UTC

Whereas `group_size` is likely to be directly relevant to doing the data structure transition: Any code that currently tries to distinguish 1:1 DMs from group DMs will want that.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-08-15 02:34 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> * The work itself is trivial, though, since the newly sent message will always be the new latest, so it's just a write.

Not necessarily -- two messages in the same DirectMessageGroup could race.  We may need to lock the DirectMesageGroup before inserting the Message row.

## thumbnailing invalid images

*2024-08-29 to 2024-08-29 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/thumbnailing.20invalid.20images/with/1933316)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-08-29 19:36 UTC

Our design spec for thumbnailing included setting the content-type to `application/octet-stream` in the case that content-type claimed to be an image but we failed to parse its headers as such.

We currently leave the content-type unchanged in these cases.  Should we change to overriding the content-type to `application/octet-stream`?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-29 19:45 UTC

I'm not sure what the full implications of that are, but probably? I wonder if it's worth checking how other image-processing systems like GitHub handle that kind of case.

The trade-off would be, I suppose, is what happens with an image that `libvips` can't parse but your browser can?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-29 19:45 UTC

If we keep it marked as an image content-type, even though it won't be thumbnailed, a user could still click on it and view in their browser?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-08-29 19:48 UTC

Yeah.  Keeping it as-is is mostly a trade-off if we think we know better than browsers.  If we override it, then users may have a slightly better experience (a file download) than a weird broken image link of some sort.  But we might also force a download on a weird format corner case that libvips doesn't handle, but browsers do.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-29 19:49 UTC

There's probably always going to be some weird formats with that property.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-08-29 19:50 UTC

Yeah.  I expect that browsers will be faster to pick up support for weird edge cases, and perhaps be more forgiving at handling bad data?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-08-29 19:50 UTC

So maybe leaving the images as the type we were told they were is best?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-08-29 20:48 UTC

Yeah I think we can leave this as-is pending future evidence that we're doing it wrong.

## slack conversion storage

*2024-09-11 to 2024-09-12 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/slack.20conversion.20storage/with/1940416)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-11 21:12 UTC

We're attempting to make conversions from Slack and other systems be more self-service, without having to use command-line tools to perform the import.

Uploaded Slack exports (which are .zip files containing .json files) can be moderately large (100s of MB), and other systems (which may include attachments) are even larger.  We need someplace to store these files as they're uploaded, until a backend worker process can process the import.

The natural place is in a directory under`~/uploads/files/` or `s3://the-uploads-bucket` depending on the storage backend.  This is mildly complicated by the fact that we need to write automated purging tools for wherever they end up, since for servers with open realm creation, the only thing necessary to perform this upload is a validated email address, and we don't want unused zipfiles to just take up space forever.

My default is going to use `conversion/<PreregistrationRealm.id>/`; Mattermost and RocketChat can have the whole directory for their data, and slack can save it as `slack.zip`.  Modulo that we'll need to solve how to support filename encoding for Mattermost/RocketChat, since S3 can't store arbitrary filenames.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-11 22:04 UTC

That seems plausible. I think we use a top-level directory `avatars` bucket, not the main uploads bucket, for data exports, which is most parallel? And maybe `import` would be a better name than `conversion`; not sure.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-11 22:31 UTC

The exports are stored there because they want to be world-readable.  As discussed previously elsewhere (I'm on mobile and can't find it at the moment, but see #21725), this is a misfeature, and also not a property we care about for uploads.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-11 22:31 UTC

Import is a better name, yeah, because we want to potentially also use this for self-hosted migrations.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-11 23:01 UTC

Yeah, doing it in the uploads bucket seems good. Since that currently has integer realm IDs as its top-level directory structure, it should be fairly cleanly separated.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-12 15:03 UTC

Hm -- we may want `s3://bucket-name/import/1234/convert/slack.zip` because the output of the Slack conversion is going to be a *Zulip* import, which also needs somewhere to live.  Hence perhaps wanting to use `s3://bucket-name/import/1234/realm.json` (and adjacent files) for that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-12 23:04 UTC

I guess I'm not sure how much we'll want to be using tar archives rather than individual files for this, but that concept seems reasonable.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-12 23:17 UTC

Mmm, true.  Storing the tarball is likely more efficient and easier in terms of not having to worry about filename character support.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-22 22:14 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-23 04:42 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-23 04:44 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-23 04:44 UTC

**Shubham Padia** · 2024-09-23 06:02 UTC

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-09-26 03:18 UTC

I saw `litellm` and `openai` in the provision dependencies when trying to provision the development setup via Nix, and was wondering when they were added. Then I found this thread.

One thing to note is that one of the projects I discovered 2 years ago when exploring this, [paper-qa](https://github.com/Future-House/paper-qa), had improved so much that their agentic RAG system is now more accurate than humans at answering questions with citations from scientific sources. The paper describing their result can be found [here](https://arxiv.org/pdf/2409.13740).

Though specifically for text summarization, a non-agentic solution is sufficient. There is a [benchmark](https://paperswithcode.com/sota/text-summarization-on-gigaword) using the ROUGE metric.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-04-02 00:31 UTC

Cool, thanks for sharing.

**Rein Zustand** · 2025-04-07 21:00 UTC

I checked the paper summarizer prompt used in PaperQA2:
> "Summarize the excerpt below to help answer a question.\n\nExcerpt from {citation}\n\n----\n\n{text}\n\n----\n\nQuestion: {question}\n\nDo not directly answer the question, instead summarize to give evidence to help answer the question. Stay detailed; report specific numbers, equations, or direct quotes (marked with quotation marks). Reply \"Not applicable\" if the excerpt is irrelevant. At the end of your response, provide an integer score from 1-10 on a newline indicating relevance to question. Do not explain your score.\n\nRelevant Information Summary ({summary_length}):"

It appears that they summarize a content with the objective of the summary being to help answer the specific question that a user has. This makes more sense and is more accurate than a general directionless summary, but is more expensive. Because the LLM needs to resummarize for every questions the user asks.

Regarding with the cost, just now, I tried indexing the entire Zulip documentation in HTML format, and it costed 1-2 USD (though I bet it would be much cheaper in Markdown, but the new PaperQA2 doesn't support Markdown yet). Asking a question costed me 11 cents, which is very expensive. But for an extremely long discussion thread, ~11 cents should be worth it.

Note: the model being used here is GPT-4o-2024-11-20.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-04-07 22:11 UTC

I think one definitely wants to use a considerably cheaper model than 11 cents per summary.

**Rein Zustand** · 2025-04-08 02:27 UTC

According to this [interview](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=umFbsCqG734&t=4242s), they intentionally optimize for accuracy at the expense of high cost & latency. Something that Perplexity and Elicit wouldn't do because they need to scale to lots of customers and to provide the answer faster.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-04-08 18:45 UTC

Yeah, the big challenge for us is that latency is important, and often we want to be summarizing dozens of messages to get much value out of it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-04-08 18:45 UTC

Certainly you want dozens to maybe a few hundred sentences; messages isn't really the right way to size, since they vary a great deal in length.

**Rein Zustand** · 2025-04-08 20:46 UTC

I think it should be much less than 11 cents if the question asked is about the entire discussion thread of only a single topic, because it is definitely much smaller than the entire Zulip documentation.

The longest single file of the documentation is docs/production/authentication-methods.md. `wc -w` gives 6734 words, or about ~600 sentences. In PaperQA2, the file is indexed with text-embedding-3-small.

GPT-4o's default rate limit is 30k tokens per minute. The context window length is 128k.

For a topic that has ~500 sentences, the number of tokens is well within the context window.
BUt I think even with the 128k context window, just feeding the entire conversation into the LLM memory will most likely contain bad hallucination. And so, indexing for RAG is probably still necessary.

**Rein Zustand** · 2025-04-20 12:27 UTC

Update: PaperQA2 is probably overkill, so I went through other existing solutions, e.g. in this [Pinecone article](https://www.pinecone.io/learn/advanced-rag-techniques/). There are Adaptive RAG, SELF-RAG, Corrective RAG, RAG Fusion -- each backed by an arXiv paper. They have even been implemented in [LangChain tutorials](https://langchain-ai.github.io/langgraph/tutorials/#rag). But none are targeted specifically on documents that are basically multi-turn chat logs.

Fortunately, I have found the go-to benchmark for this problem:  https://github.com/ibm/mt-rag-benchmark. [Preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.03468).
> Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) has recently become a very popular task for Large Language Models (LLMs). Evaluating them on multi-turn RAG conversations, where the system is asked to generate a response to a question in the context of a preceding conversation is an important and often overlooked task with several additional challenges. We present MTRAG: an end-to-end human-generated multi-turn RAG benchmark that reflects several real-world properties across diverse dimensions for evaluating the full RAG pipeline. MTRAG contains 110 conversations averaging 7.7 turns each across four domains for a total of 842 tasks. ...

**Rein Zustand** · 2025-04-20 13:07 UTC

Looks like the MTRAG benchmark is similar but not quite relevant for documents that are chat logs. It's just meant for multiple turns RAG questioning benchmark.
