*2024-09-25 to 2024-09-30 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Tighten.20access.20while.20sending.20events/with/1948620)*

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2024-09-25 10:46 UTC

Regarding [#29380 (comment)](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/29380#issuecomment-2010731437):

> Carefully reviewing all the code around live-update events for messages. I suspect that for example, the "I did an emoji reaction on message ID x" event is sent to all users with a `UserMessage` for the message, without filtering for being still subscribed. We likely will need to create a shared helper for doing the `send_event` calculations for this purpose that gets called from `notify_reaction_update` and friends.

Just to confirm: Do we no longer plan to live update reactions in "Reactions" view for messages which are in unsubscribed channels ? (Message was initially in a subscribed stream)

I think, it's fine to NOT live-update in this case? The only exception would be usermessages with `historical` flag because:
> To ensure that reactions do live-update for any user who has actually participated in reacting to a message, we add a
"historical" UserMessage row for any user who reacts to message, subscribing them to future notifications, even if they are not
 subscribed to the stream.

Also, 
> I think the correct logic would be to just use `subscriber_ids_with_stream_history_access`?

`subscriber_ids_with_stream_history_access` returns an empty  `set` for channels with protected history. So, we can't just use `subscriber_ids_with_stream_history_access`.

**Prakhar Pratyush** · 2024-09-25 11:19 UTC

* `submessage` is buggy. In a public channel, users don't receive the live updates if the poll / todo was sent before they joined. -- Fixing it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-25 17:20 UTC

We don't currently have a goal of doing live-update systematically for content in channels you're not subscribed to; in some ways that's no different from looking at a channel that you've never been subscriber to, and one can't really manage that without sending live updates for every public channel on the server regardless of subscriptions.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-25 17:22 UTC

But if we see an easy way to send live-updates for messages that a user received while they were subscribed, and the user still has access to the message, it'd be nice to do that.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-25 17:23 UTC

I just wouldn't want to make these basic operations significantly slower to do an expensive access-control check involving a lot of extra database queries in non-protected history channels for this sort of live-update detail.

I think we want to do if and only if the user still has current access to the message in question. (Guest users are not guaranteed to have access to messages in public channels, for example).

Basically we can treat the `UserMessage` row (historical or no) as a hint that the user is significantly more likely than other users to have the message cached in their browser or otherwise the message be relevant to them.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-25 14:25 UTC

The `--settings` command-line flag is not specific to `create-realm` -- it's for overriding the `/etc/zulip/setting.py` file with a different path, which is rather not what you're looking for.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-25 14:27 UTC

We don't have a command-line way to adjust the settings on a realm.  It's not hard to do via `./manage.py shell`, but if you're trying to automate it, you may need to write your own small management command to do so.

I think we'd also take a patch to `create_realm` to call `do_set_realm_property` with some set of user-supplied arguments.  I think the complicated part there is doing the right type coercion for a generic property.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-25 14:28 UTC

I guess we have `Realm.property_types`?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-09-25 14:29 UTC

One fix would be to add all of those properties as automatically-generated optional command-line flags, but that'd make the help pretty unwieldly.

**Mikke Schirén** · 2024-09-25 14:48 UTC

Ah ok, I understand, I will look into it in more details. Thanks.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-09-25 20:02 UTC

I don't think the help being unwieldy is a big deal; it's not like this command gets use for much else.

**Mikke Schirén** · 2024-09-26 09:39 UTC

def maybe_get_user_profile_by_api_key(api_key: str) -> UserProfile | None:                              
    try:                                                                                                
        return UserProfile.objects.select_related(                                                      
            "realm",                                                                                    
            "realm__can_access_all_users_group",

        return None

```

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-10-01 18:38 UTC

The current proposed implementation has a migration to populate it from the `RealmAuditLog` table, and then delete the relevant audit logs. I think it'd be better to skip that deletion step, and still write audit log entries when data exports happen? **Prakhar Pratyush** · 2024-10-01 19:06 UTC

The thought behind creating that AudiLog was:
```py
        RealmAuditLog.objects.create(
            acting_user=export_row.acting_user,
            realm=export_row.realm,
            event_type=AuditLogEventType.REALM_EXPORTED,
            event_time=timezone_now(),
            extra_data={"realm_export_id": export_row.id},
        )
```

For new exports, we can simply use `realm_export_id` present to get details like "export_path", "date_started" etc from `RealmExport` table.

As we are doing migration for the older data, I thought, there is no point to store redundant data. 

But yeah deleting this data will give incorrect results if we, in future, use `RealmAuditLog` for some analytical data or something + other reasons mentioned above. So NOT deleting makes sense.

## logfiles

*2024-10-04 to 2024-10-04 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/logfiles/with/1955329)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-10-04 18:46 UTC

I'm attempting to add tusd log rotation, and I'm in the weeds of some of our weirder log decisions.

All of the files which we write to from Python use `logging.handlers.WatchedFileHandler` which means that logrotate can move the old logfile aside and make a new one, and Django will do the right thing, close the old filehandle, and switch over to the fresh empty one.

supervisord handles stdout/stderr from processes, and can write them to files.  It also has its own log rotation code, but that only does rotation on filesize, not days, and doesn't do compression.

We can disable log rotation from supervisord, and have supervisor write the files, and logrotate rotate them.  But this requires using `copytruncate` in logrotate, which does have potential race conditions which can cause small amounts of log loss during rotation.  But if we want to log stdout/stderr from a process, this is the best we're going to get under supervisor.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-10-04 18:47 UTC

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-10-04 18:48 UTC

And then there are the ones where we have *both* Python logs and STDOUT logs.  For instance:
```
$ rg deliver_scheduled_messages.log

757:DELIVER_SCHEDULED_MESSAGES_LOG_PATH = zulip_path("/var/log/zulip/deliver_scheduled_messages.log")

puppet/zulip/templates/supervisor/zulip-once.conf.template.erb

```

**Alex Vandiver** · 2024-10-04 18:51 UTC

So we're writing STDOUT of the process to `/var/log/zulip/events_deliver_scheduled_messages.log`, rotated by supervisord, and a specific logger in Python is writing to `/var/log/zulip/deliver_scheduled_messages.log` (note the lack of `events_`) which is rotated by logrotate.

The most salient difference here is that the supervisord-written logs contain fatal errors.  Those are, of course, *also* in `/var/log/zulip/errors.log` from the Python logger.

So which logs should we be keeping?  The ones which combine all of the output from the process (from supervisor) all in one place, or the dedicated logger (from python) which only has that worker's specific events in it?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-10-04 19:14 UTC

I think the places where we should use dedicated logs is where a given code path is run from multiple places, like `send_email.log`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-10-04 19:15 UTC

I think `deliver_scheduled_messages.log` has no clear reason to exist, and we should probably remove that Python logger.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-10-04 19:16 UTC

The only thing from a UX standpoint that's annoying about `events_*.log` is that they get all squished together into `events.log` in the single-queue-worker model, and it's annoying that when working with a user there isn't a consitent file to ask them to inspect.

## NUL Byte crash:
When importing Slack messages containing NUL byte string (`0\u000`), our importer will complain because it's a forbidden string format in SQL.

I was able to replicate this error with the older version of Zulip (not using #31311). Opened [#31930](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/31930) to track this. If we're going to sanitize converted messages, what other forbidden strings we should watch out for?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-10-16 20:57 UTC

Probably we should just drop the null bytes. I suspect it reflects a Slack bug that they're possibly present there. Would be good to do that across our third-party import tools.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-10-16 20:58 UTC

This function is the complete set of preprocessing rules on `content` before we send a message:
```
def normalize_body(body: str) -> str:                                                                   
    body = body.rstrip().lstrip("\n")                                                                   
    if len(body) == 0:                                                                                  
        raise JsonableError(_("Message must not be empty"))                                             
    if "\x00" in body:                                                                                  
        raise JsonableError(_("Message must not contain null bytes"))                                   
    return truncate_content(body, settings.MAX_MESSAGE_LENGTH, "\n[message truncated]")                 
```

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-10-16 20:58 UTC

So I think the import tools will want to enforce those invariants.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-10-16 21:04 UTC

We don't want to reject messages in the import tool, since there's not an easy answer for what the user can do, so we should just drop them instead. Probably it makes sense to add a parallel function `normalize_body_for_import` next to that one and have the data importer code paths use that.

The current approach is in the following order:

further code won't execute, and on retry the same files will be refetched from db and retry the deletion from storage then bulk delete from db.

again, since the db deletion fails (which would be in its own transaction) the same files wil be fetched on retry, then we will try to delete them from storage first (which is fine, as per doc you can attempt to delete already deleted/non-existing files) then bulk delete them from db

If we, in a transaction, set the `deleted` flag first, we can prevent those failure modes. The standard name for this sort of pattern in system design is "two-phase commit"  if you want to read about it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-27 23:06 UTC

**Bedo Khaled** · 2025-03-18 00:00 UTC

Yes I  read about it,  2pc involves two phases:

1. **Prepare Phase**: The coordinator (transaction manager) asks all participants (databases or services) if they are ready to commit. Each participant performs its work and votes "Yes" (ready to commit) or "No" (not ready to commit).
  
2. **Commit Phase**: If all participants vote "Yes," the coordinator sends a "Commit" message, and all participants finalize the transaction. If any participant votes "No," the coordinator sends an "Abort" message, and all participants roll back the transaction.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-03-18 02:10 UTC

Maybe 2-phase commit as a term is most associated with distributed systems, which is not relevant. But conceptually the process is the design I proposed and you've for some reason been resisting implementing:
- Mark `Attachment` objects in the Zulip for deletion. (This is like a Prepare phase)
- Actually delete the files in S3.
- Delete the `Attachment` objects in the database. (This is like the Commit phase)

The key thing being that if an error (or other failure, like a system losing power or network) inside any of these steps, it is easy for the system to recover.

## Default can_administer_channel_group for imported realms

*2024-11-19 to 2024-11-19 · 6 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Default.20can_administer_channel_group.20for.20imported.20realms/with/1983634)*

**Shubham Padia** · 2024-11-19 01:56 UTC

For Make channel management permissions configurable #31959, what should be the default value for the setting for new channels created while doing an import or populating db? 

The current specification is to have it as the stream creator, and while we have creator_id available in some cases, it can also be [none](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/ffa7e0ac08fd890a885490869d27aff46798b30d/zerver/lib/import_realm.py#L1286). Should it be nobody in that case (same value as legacy channels) so that admins can configure it later however they want to?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-19 03:53 UTC

Hmm. New channels created during import should probably have the NOBODY group -- basically just the organization-level administration permission would apply?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-19 03:54 UTC

I think we want it to be channel creator only if you're making a new channel, not for the backfill. Nothing in the previous UI set an expectation that whoever created a channel has special permanent permissions, so digging up that user to give them permissions on an existing channel would be incorrect.

**Shubham Padia** · 2024-11-19 03:54 UTC

Got it, thanks!

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-19 03:55 UTC

Alternatively I suppose we could set whatever role can administer previous, the administrators group, on each individual channel? That would be equivalent mechanically. But I think it would probably be a worse model -- it would set the expectation that this was the mechanism through which administrators can administer channels, and that's not accurate.

**Shubham Padia** · 2024-11-19 03:56 UTC

Yeah, nobody seems better since org admins can always administer a channel.

## Handling users being unsubscribed to a channel for a while

*2024-11-27 to 2025-01-06 · 24 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Handling.20users.20being.20unsubscribed.20to.20a.20channel.20for.20a.20while/with/1989211)*

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-11-27 11:48 UTC

When user unsubscribes to a channel, we stop creating user messages for them. This means that when user subscribes to that channel again, views that require a user message to include messages won't have messages that we send while the user was unsubscribed.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-11-27 11:50 UTC

To fix it we can create user messages for the messages that were send while the user was unsubscribed. Does that sound like the right fix?

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-28 00:59 UTC

Good question. I think in every case, that can't be correct, because that would grant unexpected access to private channels with protected history.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-28 00:59 UTC

And just trying to exclude that case creates the oddity of what the correct way to handle switching a channel type away from protected history.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-28 01:02 UTC

A next idea might be to maintain on the `Subscription` object a field indicating the last message ID for which which we know all messages after that ID in the channel have `UserMessage` objects attached to them. (Could be backfilled from `RealmAuditLog` rows. I am not sure if that's a thing we can easily maintain correctly, though; the annoying corner case is "what if someone moves messages into a channel you're subscribed to from one you're not?". 

It might be that we create `UserMessage` rows in that case and everything is fine, but I'm not sure and we'll want to check it. If not, I guess we could at least have moving messages for which you don't have a UserMessage row into a channel mutate that property.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-28 01:03 UTC

Still pretty half-baked as a design direction, but maybe enough for you to look at options around it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-28 01:05 UTC

We should keep in mind that probably the thing we want to do longer-term, which might obviate this technical direction, is to start maintaining `Topic` and `UserTopic` objects with basic metadata around ranges of message IDs that the user has access to, and syncing that data to clients to support the Recent view on mobile.

Such data structures would likely allow us to efficiently answer questions of whether we need to contact the server to fetch message data or have a sufficient cache locally, along with doing like 5 other things we want.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-11-28 01:05 UTC

(So I'm somewhat reluctant to go deep into a rabbit hole here if we find that it is not easy to do something correct with this more specialized functionality.)

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-11-29 08:08 UTC

Oh yeah! Just creating user messages for the messages in between won't work. I am not too sure about other approach of tracking a last message id for user messages as well since it has complexing to it.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-11-29 08:08 UTC

What do think about changing how all messages data is populated?

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-11-29 08:11 UTC

We will include all history till first user messages entry for each public stream and only user message entry for streams with protected history. I think that would work for our use case of making all messages data a contiguous block of message history.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-11-29 08:11 UTC

I am not sure about if it would be an expensive query to compute every time a user loads Zulip.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-02 20:22 UTC

The thing that's annoying about that is that if you subscribe/unsubscribe from a channel, suddenly the synced/cached data structure becomes invalid.

(I think what you're proposing is somewhat similar to doing a union of the `channels:subscribed` query with the existing `UserMessage` one for these, and probably would be more expensive, but possibly only moderately).

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-02 20:25 UTC

I do think that aside from the messy problem of how this interacts with one's channel subscriptions being dynamic and all the races that would come with trying to work around that, it'd be a simpler model. But that issue is a significant concern. 

In theory. one could try to cure it with a `channel:{channel_id}` query with the appropriate message ID ranges, but then you're kinda in a messy state during the window while waiting for that to complete. And adding 100 people to a channel all at once would start to create a thundering herd effect, etc.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-12-12 12:30 UTC

I feel like this is the correct way to move forward here to allow for a completely expected user experience. Here is a more specific version of the idea which still doesn't address the thundering herd effect, which I guess is less of an issue if most the messages being requested are cached.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-12-12 12:35 UTC

So, we change the query to fill `all_messages_data` to this union:
* messages in `channels:subscribed with history accessible`
* messages with user messages in `channels:private with history protected`
* Direct messages

Not sure if we should keep any upper limit based on user messages.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-12-12 12:36 UTC

We will ofcouse have to update data when user subscribes / unsubscribes as you mentioned.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-12-12 12:37 UTC

This looks like is important to do before we merge #32150 otherwise users will often run into missing message without realizing it most of the time.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-13 02:38 UTC

I agree #32150 is blocked until we can solve this.

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> A next idea might be to maintain on the `Subscription` object a field indicating the last message ID for which which we know all messages after that ID in the channel have `UserMessage` objects attached to them. (Could be backfilled from `RealmAuditLog` rows. I am not sure if that's a thing we can e …

Hmm, why do you think that approach would be better than this strategy?

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-12-13 03:14 UTC

Only because we will have to deal with moving messages to fix bugs in this space.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-13 22:45 UTC

I think it's likely not that complicated, especially compared to what we already have.

The more robust answer would probably be to build a more extensive `UserTopic` model that could store that class of information on a per-topic basis, and also would be what we need for a recent view API.

**Tim Abbott** · 2024-12-13 22:45 UTC

I'm starting to think maybe we need to design that system and then we can see whether problems like this one can make use of it.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2024-12-16 02:14 UTC

Yeah, maybe it's time we started working towards supporting a `UserTopic` model.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-06 20:00 UTC

Well, we already have a `UserTopic` model, it's just sparse/implicit. But yes, moving towards a dense model `Topic` and then possibly a denser model for `UserTopic` (taking care to avoid creating performance issues with sending messages for soft-deactivated users) is likely the direction we'll be going. Probably a pretty big project.


## report message feature (#20047)

*2024-12-04 to 2025-07-04 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/report.20message.20feature.20.28.2320047.29/with/1992783)*

**Pieter K** · 2024-12-04 14:29 UTC

I've broken down the implementation plan into several steps, starting from the backend changes:

#### Backend:
1. **Add realm-level setting: `abuse_report_channel` and its API**.
PR: #32566.
A new realm setting similar to `signup_announcements_stream` but it's a channel for the new abuse report feature.

2. **Add `/messages/{message_id}/report` API.**
The main endpoint to report a message. It'll probably accept `message_id`, string `reason`, and string`detail`.

3. **Add message report backend.**
If `abuse_report_channel` is not empty, calling a `POST` request to the `/messages/{message_id}/report` API will make the notification bot send an abuse report to the specified message. 

#### Frontend:
4. **Add `abuse_report_channel` UI.**
A new setting in the **Organizational Setting** menu for the user to interact with the `abuse_report_channel` realm setting.

5. **Add message report button & UI.**
A new option in the three-dot message menu, something like "**report**" and a new pop-up menu for abuse detail & reason. This will be the main way the `/messages/{message_id}/report` API is called.

*2024-12-20 to 2026-06-23 · 41 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/updating.20group.20permission.20settings/with/2011298)*

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-12-20 16:35 UTC

There is a bug when updating group permission settings when the following conditions are met -
- Setting was originally set to an anonymous group
- There is exactly one group as subgroup and one user as member in the anonymous group
- User belonging to that anonymous group is deactivated.
- And then the setting is being updated to anonymous group and not a single named group.

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-12-20 16:35 UTC

The bug is when comparing the old value passed in the request to the actual previous setting value.

The setting value that client has is on object like `{direct_subgroups: [group_id], direct_members: []}` because the setting is set to an anonymous group but users list is empty as the user is not active.  This is then pased as "old" value to the server and is parsed as integer `group_id` because we consider an anonymous group obejct only containing one subgroup as a named user group.

But when computing the current actual setting value we know that it is set to anonymous group and it is not parsed to integer keeping the users list empty in the object and thus the comparison made when checking the "old" value passed in the API and the actual current setting value is between `group_id` and `{direct_subgroups: [group_id], direct_members: []}` and it raises error of passing invalid old value.

I am not sure how to fix this.

Either we can just consider `group_id` and `{direct_subgroups: [group_id], direct_members: []}` same when checking the values. Or we can just not parse the "old" value sent in the API request and just expect client to pass the exact value, i.e if setting is set to a named group it should always be passed as an integer and object otherwise.

                setting_value.old, setting_name

**Sahil Batra** · 2024-12-20 16:40 UTC

And these are the used [functions](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/5e8070222ea041e278745c8943249a86836129d8/zerver/lib/user_groups.py#L999)
```py
def parse_group_setting_value(
    setting_value: int | AnonymousSettingGroupDict,
    setting_name: str,
) -> int | AnonymousSettingGroupDict:
    if isinstance(setting_value, int):
        return setting_value

    if len(setting_value.direct_members) == 0 and len(setting_value.direct_subgroups) == 1:
        return setting_value.direct_subgroups[0]

    return setting_value


def are_both_group_setting_values_equal(
    first_setting_value: int | AnonymousSettingGroupDict,
    second_setting_value: int | AnonymousSettingGroupDict,
) -> bool:
    if isinstance(first_setting_value, int) and isinstance(second_setting_value, int):
        return first_setting_value == second_setting_value

    if isinstance(first_setting_value, AnonymousSettingGroupDict) and isinstance(
        second_setting_value, AnonymousSettingGroupDict
    ):
        return set(first_setting_value.direct_members) == set(
            second_setting_value.direct_members
        ) and set(first_setting_value.direct_subgroups) == set(
            second_setting_value.direct_subgroups
        )

    return False


def validate_group_setting_value_change(
    current_setting_api_value: int | AnonymousSettingGroupDict,
    new_setting_value: int | AnonymousSettingGroupDict,
    expected_current_setting_value: int | AnonymousSettingGroupDict | None,
) -> bool:
    if expected_current_setting_value is not None and not are_both_group_setting_values_equal(
        expected_current_setting_value,
        current_setting_api_value,
    ):
        # This check is here to help prevent races, by refusing to
        # change a setting where the client (and thus the UI presented
        # to user) showed a different existing state.
        raise PreviousSettingValueMismatchedError

    return not are_both_group_setting_values_equal(current_setting_api_value, new_setting_value)

```

I started reading #33371 to do integration review. My concern is that currently the PR blocks actions such as `Delete user` via the support panel and CLI if the checks in `check_group_permission_updates_for_deactivating_user` can't be passed.

I worry that this will make processing of `Please delete my account` support requests too onerous. It's unclear what the support person is supposed to do if the user-to-delete is involved in a problematic anonymous group.

My proposal is to tweak the pull request to be more generous about replacing the problematic group permission with a sensible default value. That'd be the `Owners` group for the permissions that don't support `Nobody`.  My old WIP PR #34605 for group deactivation, which had to tackle a very similar problem, implemented a `replacement_group_name` concept for  `GroupPermissionSetting`. Specifically, every `GroupPermissionSetting` specifying what the fallback group should be. It addresses three cases:
1. Most permissions can just have the `Nobody` group as the fallback.
2. A few, such as `can_manage_all_groups` would make the realm dysfunctional if set to `Nobody`; but `Owners` is a sensible fallback for them.
3. Some permissions  can only be set to system groups. These aren't an issue at all and don't even need a fallback value.

Example:
```
        can_manage_all_groups=GroupPermissionSetting(
            allow_nobody_group=False,
            allow_everyone_group=False,
            default_group_name=SystemGroups.OWNERS,
            # This setting can't be set to NOBODY without making the realm dysfunctional.
            replacement_group_name=SystemGroups.OWNERS,
        ),
```

The approach was discussed around #**backend>force-deactivate a group@2217109**  and seemed to be accepted.

*2024-12-27 to 2025-01-02 · 88 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/lint-zulip-message-html/with/2018550)*

**Steve Howell** · 2024-12-27 18:54 UTC

https://github.com/showell/lint-zulip-message-html

I'm happy to answer any questions or get suggestions for how to improve it.  It's under the MIT license.

**Sylwester Cyba** · 2024-12-27 19:33 UTC

So first thing to ask. Any real world usage example? A screenshot maybe?

When people don't see how something work they are not interested to try it. Your project is going to be popular after giving some examples. Some Markdown in /docs folder with code snippets or whatever.

**Steve Howell** · 2024-12-27 19:42 UTC

@Sylwester Cyba Just to be clear, I haven't made any progress on a WYSIWIG editor.  For context, the challenge with supporting WYSIWIG editors (especially third party ones that already exist) is that they will tend to want to send HTML over the wire instead of Zulip markdown or even ordinary markdown.  I'm just trying to remove one barrier to entry.  If a WYSIWIG editor is going to send arbitrary HTML to the Zulip server, then that's a show-stopper until we have some way to validate that the HTML is both secure and sensible in the context of the Zulip UI.  It's highly unlikely that we can use a WYSIWIG editor right out of the box, but a well-written one probably allows you some control over what you send over the wire.  But we'd still need to validate the incoming HTML.

**Steve Howell** · 2024-12-27 19:45 UTC

And even if we have full control over the client-side code (thus mitigating hostile attacks), we still want basic validation to help with automated testing and paranoid checks. (Even if we serve up the client code, there are still avenues for hostile attacks.)

**Steve Howell** · 2024-12-27 19:49 UTC

The two main use cases for markdown are these:
* Some people like to compose in markdown. (But clearly some folks don't.)
* Markdown is safe to send over the wire.

For now I am only addressing the latter point (i.e. making it so we could theoretically send HMTL instead) but not the former point.

**Neil Pilgrim (neiljp)** · 2024-12-28 21:07 UTC

@Steve Howell This could also dovetail, in the opposite direction, with the equivalent of work done in the new flutter client to examine test cases of which message output (as HTML) to support and be able to render successfully/distinctly.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-12-28 23:32 UTC

We’re going to want something that operates like I described above.

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> The sanitizer should operate by parsing the HTML to a tidy AST and then serializing back to HTML, so there’s no room for syntax we didn’t consider to sneak through.

By an AST, I mean a strongly-typed data structure that’s only capable of storing things that belong in Zulip messages. This is [what zulip-flutter has been building](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-flutter/blob/main/lib/model/content.dart)—it’s made of specific structures like `ParagraphNode`, `EmphasisNode`, `GlobalTimeNode`, and `SpoilerNode` that extend sealed classes (the Dart way of doing tagged unions), not a generic structure like `Element` storing arbitrary tags and attributes along with pinky promises that we’ve filtered out everything bad we could think of. [Parse, don’t validate](https://lexi-lambda.github.io/blog/2019/11/05/parse-don-t-validate/).

A validation-based approach will never satisfy our security requirements, because even if we manage to write it correctly during initial implementation, we won’t be able to train every contributor who extends our content model in the future on the discipline required to maintain the hidden nonlocal invariants that must be upheld.

I think at some point, once zulip-flutter’s parser is stable and relatively complete (which seems to be pretty close), we’ll want to extract it to a library that we can use in the backend and web frontend. Perhaps this involves porting it to Rust for performance and embeddability; some architectural investigation is needed. **Steve Howell** · 2024-12-29 01:53 UTC

I don't really believe in the "Parse, don't validate" theory.  You **always** have to validate.  If the Flutter teams comes up with the most pristine AST and the most elegant over-the-wire encoding, then the server still needs to validate the AST.  It's just that simple.

So then there 's the first question.  What's the easiest encoding to validate?  Probably JSON.  But XML and HTML are not far behind.  For any tree-like structure, which is what we're always dealing with (:tree: :tree: everywhere), you have to recursively descend nodes and deal with escaping issues.  JSON is probably the best way to work around escaping issues, but we have `lxml`.

At the end of the day, you have an encoding, and you have an implicit AST, and then you recursively walk the AST to find garbage that you need to reject.

So I think it comes down to practicality for what you send over the wire.  HTML is easy to parse, it's extremely well understood, and you can extend it with pseudo-custom tags to give you an escape hatch for things like huge blobs of katex or not-yet-pretty-printed code snippets inside of `~~~` fences that we just let the server run through `pygments`.

It seems there are a few fundamental questions for how you convey semantically what the user tried to express on the client:

* How much do you actually translate client-side before telling the server? (Maybe in an XML/HTML-centric world, you just send blobs of raw katex in custom tags to the server and let the server deal with it.)
* How do you encode the AST?

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2024-12-29 06:35 UTC

“Parse, don’t validate” doesn’t mean that there isn’t a wire encoding with an untyped tree structure, or that we don’t walk the tree, or that we should accept invalid input. What it means is that, *when* we walk the untyped tree, we do it *once*, and we do it in order to *convert it to a strongly typed structure* (or an error), rather than merely making a mental note that we claim it’s okay. That way, we get static type checking that verifies that (a) any input we successfully parsed has all the fields we expect with the types we expect (else the parser wouldn’t type-check), and (b) any time we access the structure, we only use the fields we expect with the types we expect (else the access wouldn’t type-check).

Obviously there are other ways to cause (a) and (b) to be true (“just program it good!” or “just write hundreds of unit tests without missing any edge cases!”), but there aren’t other ways to *statically verify* that (a) and (b) are true, so that we can easily maintain these invariants over time across thousands of contributions by hundreds of new contributors reviewed by a busy core team with a limited attention budget. Static typing has proved to have enormous benefits for projects of our size, and there’s nothing to be gained in exchange by giving it up.

If we go with a JSON wire format, this strongly typed parsing would be automated by Pydantic, Zod, or Serde. If we go with an HTML/XML wire format, we can do it manually, or maybe with something like pydantic-xml or Serde XML (I haven’t tried those yet).

- A legacy parser that converts legacy HTML to the content AST model

- A serializer that converts the content AST model to the new wire format

**Greg Price** · 2024-12-30 20:42 UTC

(replying to Anders Kaseorg)
> “Parse, don’t validate” doesn’t mean that there isn’t a wire encoding with an untyped tree structure, or that we don’t walk the tree, or that we should accept invalid input. What it means is that, *when* we walk the untyped tree, we do it *once*, and we do it in order to *convert it to a strongly ty …

To expand on this with an example: in valid Zulip content HTML as expressed by zulip-flutter's parser, if you have a `div` element with `class="message_inline_image message_inline_video"`, it [must have](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-flutter/blob/3ff70964ed0d4485b9553292181c160dbb3c1e3f/lib/model/content.dart#L1274-L1304)
* one child, an `a` with no/empty `class`;
* with one child, a `video` with no/empty `class`;
* and that video must have a `src` attribute.

That all gets parsed into an [`InlineVideoNode`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-flutter/blob/3ff70964ed0d4485b9553292181c160dbb3c1e3f/lib/model/content.dart#L430-L445) object with a field `final String srcUrl`.

Then as a result, when code elsewhere in the app consumes one of those objects, it doesn't have to reach down an HTML tree looking for an `a` and a `video` and a `src` attribute on the latter. It just knows, statically, that that object has a `srcUrl` which is a string, and [reads that](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-flutter/blob/3ff70964ed0d4485b9553292181c160dbb3c1e3f/lib/widgets/content.dart#L669-L678).

**Greg Price** · 2024-12-30 20:55 UTC

In the validator/linter discussed in this thread, it looks like `message_inline_image message_inline_video` is one of a [handful of possible values](https://github.com/showell/lint-zulip-message-html/blob/d0b98b01ca3dfc2c5c5985fd7123de3b32a7304f/zulip_message_rules/rules.py#L161) the `class` on a `div` element can have. That's a good start.

But then IIUC the list of children of that `div.message_inline_image.message_inline_video` can be just zero or more of [any nodes](https://github.com/showell/lint-zulip-message-html/blob/d0b98b01ca3dfc2c5c5985fd7123de3b32a7304f/html_validator/validator.py#L58-L76) that would be accepted at all in any place in the tree. Fundamentally the validator has just one type of node it looks for, and puts some light constraints on which nodes can be parents of which.

In order to get the kind of strong typing we need in order to really process the content, we need a lot more structure, which you can see in the shape of the parser.

**Greg Price** · 2024-12-30 20:56 UTC

Specifically the shape of the parser basically mirrors the shape of the tree as expressed in the ContentNode subclasses.

**Greg Price** · 2024-12-30 21:01 UTC

(replying to Steve Howell)
> (replying to Anders Kaseorg) ```quote We’re building the first two pieces in zulip-flutter (by necessity, because it doesn’t use HTML for rendering). ... ``` Does this mean that the Flutter team essentially has to re-implement a browser widget?

No, the job is a lot narrower than what a browser has to do. A browser has to handle arbitrary HTML and CSS (not to mention JavaScript), which have an enormous number of features and can get extremely complicated in all sorts of ways. Our rendering of Zulip message content only has to handle the structures that are part of Zulip's content HTML.

You can find the relevant code in zulip-flutter in `lib/widgets/content.dart`, starting from the [`MessageContent`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip-flutter/blob/3ff70964ed0d4485b9553292181c160dbb3c1e3f/lib/widgets/content.dart#L276-L280) class.

) -> None:

    prop = event["property"]
    value = event["value"]

        "id",
        "type",
        "op",
        "property",
        "value",
        "name",
        "stream_id",
        "first_message_id",

    elif prop == "invite_only":

    elif prop == "message_retention_days":

    elif prop == "name":

    elif prop == "stream_post_policy":

    elif prop in Stream.stream_permission_group_settings:

    elif prop == "is_recently_active":

    else:

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2025-01-01 02:18 UTC

The idea that bare `Dict` has no `Any` is a misunderstanding. Mypy rejects bare `Dict` in strict mode, and otherwise interprets it as `Dict[Any, Any]`. Also `typing.Dict` is obsolete, but the same applies to its replacement, `dict`. Our class names should use `PascalCase`, and should not redundantly use the word “type” unless you’re declaring the type of a type.

The Zulip linters would tell you most of this. You said you don’t have a working development environment; you should fix that, as this project is going to require one. The next step will be to adjust the `send_event` functions and their callers to use the new models, in order to get verification that they match the actual server code. All analogies aside, the diff that I'm working on follows very simple logic if you understand the concept of incrementalism.  Right now we have a successful strategy to safeguard against a certain class of bugs.  It's based on `data_types.py`, which I know you hate.  We can preserve the same strategy with much prettier code based on `pydantic`, which I know you like.

And then when we get that merged, we find all of a sudden that we're in `pydantic` space instead of `data_types.py` space.

And then every deeper problem becomes easier to solve in `pydantic` space vs. `data_types.py` space, just as much as it's easier for a native English speaker to solve deep problems expressed in English vs. Chinese. Or vice versa. (Apparently I can't avoid analogies.)

It's basic incrementalism.

Using defaults for discriminators like `type` and `op` seems to be fine.

```python
from typing import Annotated, Literal
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field, TypeAdapter

class FooEvent(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["foo"] = "foo"

class BarCreateEvent(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["bar"] = "bar"
    op: Literal["create"] = "create"

class BarDeleteEvent(BaseModel):
    type: Literal["bar"] = "bar"
    op: Literal["delete"] = "delete"

BarEvent = Annotated[BarCreateEvent | BarDeleteEvent, Field(discriminator="op")]

Event = Annotated[FooEvent | BarEvent, Field(discriminator="type")]

event1 = BarDeleteEvent()
print(f"{event1=}")

event2 = TypeAdapter[Event](Event).validate_python({"type": "bar", "op": "delete"})
print(f"{event2=}")
```

(replying to Pieter K)
> Since Django will run the migrations in order of the number in the migration file prefix, -


This turned out to be incorrect, we just want to make sure the set of migration files matches. [Django doc](https://docs.djangoproject.com/en/5.1/topics/migrations/):
> Don’t worry - the numbers are just there for developers’ reference, Django just cares that each migration has a different name. **Steve Howell** · 2025-07-15 01:24 UTC

@Bedo Khaled I did a quick skim of the PR and everything looks pretty sane.  I would refine the tests bit to assert that the query count is O(1).  Use `self.assert_database_query_count(...)` to enforce that the query count is low, and try to make it so that the test would fail if your change wasn't in place (by setting up the test data with lots of things).

A good way to structure any optimization PR is to do this:

- add a prep commit that just tests for correctness, and have `assert_database_query_count` report the valid-but-too-big-query-count with a comment
- in the second commit, do the actual optimization in real code, and then have the second commit fix the test by decreasing the query count in the assert and changing the comment from "sorry" to "don't mess this up"

It's worth the effort here to retroactively rebase commits to make it look like you did this in the first place.  Believe me that I've done this myself before, so I'm not asking you to do the impossible.  It's a bit of extra work, but it's a senior-programmer kinda thing.

@Harsh Bansal If you really want to get your head into the submessages architecture after the drag/drop project, then I encourage you to do so.  The essential problem with storing polls and todo lists in the database is that you have races.  The submessages architecture avoids races insofar as the order of the submessages that you receive is basically irrelevant insofar as the widgets are designed to just apply submessages in any order.

Having said that, I think Tim would be nearly ecstatic to move to a better architecture.  I think it's a non-trivial exercise to eliminate races, but it's not rocket science; it just needs some thought.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-01-12 14:56 UTC

**Steve Howell** · 2025-01-12 14:57 UTC

As long as the third user eventually gets both submessages (in any order), then the third user has the same view of the world (and lunch) that we have.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-01-12 15:03 UTC

If, on the other hand, we just have a single database row for the lunch poll, then there is danger of your connection being slow, and I nominate pizza before you, and then you nominate pizza on a stale copy of the poll, and we lose the info that I like pizza. :pizza: 

It's not an impossible problem to solve, to reiterate.  It just requires some thought.

**Apoorva Pendse** · 2025-01-12 16:16 UTC

(replying to Harsh Bansal)
> If I have slow connection, still I'm sending a request to increment one vote on the backend.

I think it's only as slow as both your and his request start executing at different points of time, but your req isn't as slow to read the updates made by committing his increment operation.

**Apoorva Pendse** · 2025-01-12 16:19 UTC

Better explanation:
Your request reads the current state of the poll (let's say pizza has 3 votes) and begins to prepare an update. Meanwhile, another request (mine) completes first, incrementing the pizza votes to 4 and committing that change to the database. However, your request is still working with the outdated (stale) state where pizza had only 3 votes

## S3 uploads without metadata?

*2025-01-13 to 2026-01-07 · 12 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/S3.20uploads.20without.20metadata.3F/with/2039545)*

**Mate Solymosi** · 2025-01-13 15:20 UTC

Hi everyone! – new user here so this was my best guess for the most suitable channel to post this in :fingers_crossed: 

I've run into an issue with S3 storage for public images (avatars, etc.) on our *self-hosted* instance using an S3-compatible object storage provider based on [OpenStack Swift](https://docs.openstack.org/swift/latest/s3_compat.html). Uploads would work just fine, but then fetching any of the images directly using their public URL would fail with an error.

I've tracked the problem down to the underscores (`_`) used in the S3 metadata keys such as `avatar_version` and `user_profile_id` – these metadata fields would get saved in the storage but then the reverse proxy of our S3 provider chokes on them when serving the images. I've reported this to the provider but their reply basically boiled down to *"tough luck, maybe don't use underscores"* :shrug: 

Since we already maintain a slightly modified fork of Zulip, my question is: would anything break if I just patched `zerver/lib/upload/s3.py` (as well as any migrations that upload things directly to S3 without reusing the methods in `s3.py`) not to write any metadata to S3?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-01-13 15:31 UTC

That metadata is necessary when exporting content from Zulip.  If you're OK with never being able to do that, you can probably drop those metadata fields.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-01-13 15:33 UTC

This looks like https://bugs.launchpad.net/swift/+bug/2093413 ?

**Mate Solymosi** · 2025-01-13 15:42 UTC

Yup, I'm 99.9% certain that the *customer* they are mentioning in that thread is us... even the timestamps line up perfectly with my support request to the provider :laughter_tears: – anyways, it looks like they can't easily change things on their end so I'll either have to patch Zulip to use `-` or find another S3 provider.

Thanks for the help!

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-13 19:40 UTC

I suppose the discussion suggests we should think about moving to dashes for that metadata the next time we're doing a migration that walks every upload in S3.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-01-13 19:46 UTC

I guess.  It kind feels like an abstraction implementation leaking, because nothing in S3's API says "metadata becomes headers" and headers getting `_` filtered out is a kludge that *some* servers do because of a service interface written in 1993.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-13 20:21 UTC

Well https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/UsingMetadata.html#UserMetadata does seem to specify that the metadata for S3 objects is sent over the wire as HTTP headers. **Tim Abbott** · 2025-01-31 19:04 UTC

One of the most important things to understand when thinking about performance is that attention is a limited resource, and it's easy to spend it in the wrong places. It is very important to use efficient data structures and algorithms when working with variable-size collections of things that can be large, even if you don't expect them to be in normal use. 

But when you have a fixed collection of ~10 elements, in a function that's not called in a material loop and only in code paths that do a dozen database queries that are quite a bit more expensive, it cannot be a material contributor to the runtime of any part of the program. I'd certainly type out a set if I were writing the code myself.

But if one wants improve the performance of Zulip, details like this one don't matter. What matter are usually things like good API design, avoiding [accidentally quadratic code](https://www.tumblr.com/accidentallyquadratic) and using a constant number of well-indexed database queries that don't fetch excessive data (like fetching entire 1KB `Message` objects just to get their 8-byte IDs`). And after that, rewriting the hottest parts of the server in Rust.

I don't think the conversation is a bad one to have, just because you all can learn from it. But the actual specific case probably isn't worth spending attention on.

## Excluding users from getting events

*2025-02-06 to 2025-02-06 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Excluding.20users.20from.20getting.20events/with/2081521)*

**Shubham Padia** · 2025-02-06 17:49 UTC

In [actions/streams.py](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/205cfc0f850823d0ca37bfc629a27853b49e8a9d/zerver/actions/streams.py#L520), at multiple places, we exclude realm admins from getting create stream event for a stream they already have access to.

Getting realm admins is a single query for all streams.

But now we might want to exclude users with metadata access from those events too which might increase our query count. And it will involve multiple queries for every stream.

**Shubham Padia** · 2025-02-06 17:49 UTC

What is our policy on sending redundant events? Should we exclude users with metadata access in these cases or not.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-06 18:27 UTC

Redundant events should be avoided. It's OK to need an extra query for that.

Probably most clients will do fine with them, in the sense that typically event processing will do things like "if it's a new channel, store it in a dictionary by ID". But it would make the system more confusing.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-06 18:28 UTC

Conceptually, this code likely needs to ask "who newly has metadata access because of this change?". One way to do it that is likely correct is to refactor a bit to first figure out why has metadata access before the change, and then check again after and compare. But you might be able to do something more efficient in most cases, so I would not necessarily recommend doing that algorithm specifically.


## migrating to dataclasses

*2025-02-11 to 2026-05-01 · 29 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/migrating.20to.20dataclasses/with/2085283)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-11 00:41 UTC

I'm starting a thread about a GSoC project idea of working through the `zulip/zulip` server codebase and converting all the uses of `dict[str, Any]` into dataclasses (and in rare cases, some other data structure). I think it's a good fit for GSoC, because it's largely a single self-similar sweep, but also not urgent enough that it's likely to be worth having a core team member drive it. The work is basically an iterative process along the lines of the following:

- Find a `dict[str, Any]` using `git grep 'dict\[str, Any\]'` or your favorite other code search technique. As of this writing, there's about 850 references to this, with another 50 for `dict[str, str]`. But don't let this overstate of these are a single type being referenced in dozens of places. For this example, we'll use the one in `zerver/lib/onboarding_steps.py`.
- Read the surrounding code path, and observe that it's the type returned by `OnboardingStep.to_dict()` for that model class.
- Come up with a good name for it. In this case, something like `APIOnboardingStep` is probably a good choice, since it's the format used to represent an Onboardingstep in the Zulip API. We may come up with a better naming convention for these.
- Write a commit refactoring to add a `dataclass` for that thing and pass that around, submit it for review, and log it in this thread.

In my GSoC proposal, I mapped out the following division which we could potentially adopt as the standard:
- **Event Payloads & API Boundaries (e.g., `send_event_on_commit`)**: Use `TypedDict`. It natively satisfies `Mapping[str, Any]`, matches external API schemas, and avoids the runtime overhead of calling `dataclasses.asdict()` at serialization boundaries.
-    **Internal Core Logic & State**: Use `@dataclass` (ideally with `slots=True`). This provides the best IDE support, memory efficiency, and clear data contracts for internal operations.

For structures that need to be serialized to or from JSON, such as event payloads, the correct answer is *neither* `TypedDict` nor `dataclass`. We want to use Pydantic models for these.

This will allow us to declare a real type for `send_event_on_commit` and get a static guarantee that it accurately describes all our events. (The fact that we have no such reliable guarantee about the current `event_schema.py` system is what has been holding back the remainder of the TypeScript migration.)

```python
def by_channels(self, query: Select, operand: str, maybe_negate: ConditionTransform) -> Select:
        self.check_not_both_channel_and_dm_narrow(maybe_negate, is_channel_narrow=True)

        if operand == "all":
            if self.user_profile is None:
                recipient_queryset = get_web_public_streams_queryset(self.realm)
            else:
                recipient_queryset = get_content_accessible_streams_queryset(self.user_profile)

```
This will return a queryset of streams, which will include all the streams that the user has access to, including subscribed private channels with protected and shared history.



```python
def fetch_messages(
    *,
    narrow: list[NarrowParameter] | None,
    user_profile: UserProfile | None,
    realm: Realm,
    is_web_public_query: bool,
    anchor: int | None,
    include_anchor: bool,
    num_before: int,
    num_after: int,
    client_requested_message_ids: list[int] | None = None,
) -> FetchedMessages:
    include_history = ok_to_include_history(narrow, user_profile, is_web_public_query)
    if include_history:
        # The initial query in this case doesn't use `zerver_usermessage`,
        # and isn't yet limited to messages the user is entitled to see!
        #
        # This is OK only because we've made sure this is a narrow that
        # will cause us to limit the query appropriately elsewhere.
        # See `ok_to_include_history` for details.
        #
        # Note that is_web_public_query=True goes here, since
        # include_history is semantically correct for is_web_public_query.
        need_user_message = False
    else:
        need_user_message = True
    # get_base_query_for_search and ok_to_include_history are responsible for ensuring
    # that we only include messages the user has access to.
    query: SelectBase
    query, inner_msg_id_col = get_base_query_for_search(
        realm_id=realm.id,
        user_profile=user_profile,
        need_user_message=need_user_message,
    )

    if need_user_message:
        query = query.add_columns(column("flags", Integer))

    query, is_search = add_narrow_conditions(
        user_profile=user_profile,
        inner_msg_id_col=inner_msg_id_col,
        query=query,
        narrow=narrow,
        realm=realm,
        is_web_public_query=is_web_public_query,
    )
```

For `channels:all`, this `ok_to_include_history(narrow, user_profile, is_web_public_query)` should return true, right? Just like we do for `channels:public`.
If we return false, then we won't be able to access the contents of the channels with shared history.

And if this `ok_to_include_history(narrow, user_profile, is_web_public_query)` returns true, then all the content of the channels with protected history will also be shown, irrespective of whether the user was subscribed to that channel when that message was sent or not, **which is definitely wrong**.

**Kumar Aniket** · 2025-03-25 11:22 UTC

**Kumar Aniket** · 2025-03-25 11:27 UTC

Oh, and there is a slight modification with how you defined `get_content_accessible_streams_queryset` in your commit (847eba4ec47403a7089760199ba6a3e878418cc7).

```python
def get_content_accessible_streams_queryset(
    user_profile: UserProfile
) -> QuerySet[Stream]:
    realm = user_profile.realm
    user_recursive_group_ids = set(
        get_recursive_membership_groups(user_profile).values_list("id", flat=True))

    private_stream_query_Set = get_subscribed_streams_queryset(user_profile)
    public_streams_query_set = get_public_streams_queryset(realm)
    second_query_set = Stream.objects.filter(
        Q(realm=realm,
        invite_only=True,
        history_public_to_subscribers=True
        ) & (
        Q(can_add_subscribers_group_id__in=user_recursive_group_ids) | Q(can_subscribe_group_id__in=user_recursive_group_ids))
    )

    return public_streams_query_set.union(second_query_set,private_stream_query_Set)

def get_subscribed_streams_queryset(user_profile: UserProfile) ->  QuerySet[Stream]:
    subscribed_stream_ids = get_subscribed_stream_ids_for_user(user_profile)

    return Stream.objects.filter(
        realm=user_profile.realm,
        id__in=subscribed_stream_ids,
    )

```

This ensures that all the subscribed channels are included which was missing in your commit.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-02-25 06:47 UTC

I think there's a question of whether we want to move to shipping Python itself via `uv` for this release. I think Python 3.13 is significantly faster than 3.10 for some workloads; I would not be surprised if that were significant for Zulip CPU usage. And it could be kinda nice for us to be able to backport changes taking advantage of new typing features from `main` to 10.x.

I'm not sure there's much risk associated with doing it, since it'd just be changing which one of the Python versions we currently support are used on which end user systems, or I'd say we definitely shouldn't try this late in the release cycle. But I'd certainly want the change to happen before this week's beta if we are going to do that, so that we get natural production testing from folks upgrading to `10.0-beta1`.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-02-26 14:56 UTC

I don't agree that "cost too many python loops per realm" is really ... a thing?  For loops don't really get tired. :)  And we have other places we've certainly iterated over every realm.; the overhead of a loop iteration is not high.

I think the better argument is that there are a large number of realms with no edited messages, or no significant messages at all, so we'll do a lot of extra *database queries* which amount to no-ops for those realms.  Unlike Python loop iterations, database queries do have significant cost.

And if we run into a runtime error, we're already going to be in the state where either we have entire realms which don't have any changes, or entire tables.  Neither is clearly worse in my mind -- the latter actually seems much easier to resume from, because you'll have higher confidence you've ruled out entire *types* of problems once that table's migration has completed.

I believe the only API requests that the mobile apps make which are influenced by that logic are /api/send-message, and /api/set-typing-status . That basically stems from the conceptual point above: those are the requests that are made from the compose box, based on a topic the user made up and entered there, whereas other requests involving a topic take the topic from some existing message or messages.

Fun fact: When you get [more than 12 joins](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/runtime-config-query.html#GUC-GEQO-THRESHOLD), PostgreSQL resorts to using someone's PhD thesis, which is to [use a genetic algorithm](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/geqo-intro2.html) to perform a [semi-random semi-directed search through the search space of potential join orders](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/geqo-pg-intro.html).

That means we're hitting that in the `MissedMessageEmailAddress` case above, and may even have non-deterministic query plans.  Fun!

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-02-26 18:38 UTC

Ah, looks like the [most-recent change that wasn't a copyright bump or lint fix](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/commits/master/src/backend/optimizer/geqo/geqo_main.c) (...back in 2009) was when they [fixed it to be deterministic](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/commit/f5bc74192d2ffb32952a06c62b3458d28ff7f98f), at least!  I missed that from the last time I was looking at this.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-02-26 18:39 UTC

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> I think it's a natural consequence of having `assert_database_query_count` but no `assert_is_not_an_insane_query`. I don't have a specific solution to propose, I just feel like there's a pattern here that bears looking at.

It is certainly feasible to have an `assert_is_not_insane_query` test helper.  It wouldn't be perfect, but there are obvious heuristics like counting the length of the query, the number of commas, the number of ANDs, the number of JOINs, etc.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-02-27 08:03 UTC

(replying to Alex Vandiver)
> I think that's called the slow query log. :)

The slow query log is a super important tool.  It should be monitored both manually and automatically.  Both in dev and production.  The automated way to monitor the slow query log is to report any queries above a certain threshold and exempt known queries that are acceptable to be slow.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-02-27 08:05 UTC

If you have an automated tool to watch the slow query log, you not only detect slow queries, but you occasionally get alerted about general slowness in the system that might not be due to the queries themselves.  I know I'm not saying anything that people don't already know, but I think it's worth emphasizing how much leverage you get from looking at it.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-02-27 08:32 UTC

**testing**: I have considered the idea in the past of making the backend tests more automatically strict about checking query counts and query sanity in general.  Our current strategy is opt-in, i.e. you need to explicitly add calls to `assert_query_count` to tests.  I think it should be opt-out.  I think the test system should enforce some reasonable limit on query counts for every single test, and then you just need an opt-out mechanism for tests that are legitimately generating a bunch of queries.  And likewise for inspecting the queries themselves.  This could be a combination of simple home-grown tooling and something like django-seal.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-02-27 15:02 UTC

The smiley face on my comment about the slow query log is because we use it heavily already -- for instance, it found the query under discussion here.

> The automated way to monitor the slow query log is to report any queries above a certain threshold and exempt known queries that are acceptable to be slow.

The more canonical automated way is to use [`pg_stat_statements`](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/current/pgstatstatements.html) or something built on top of it, like [POWA](https://powa.readthedocs.io/en/latest/index.html) (see #**backend>PoWA**).

## Data structure for migration_status.json

*2025-03-14 to 2025-03-20 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Data.20structure.20for.20migration_status.2Ejson/with/2123078)*

**Pieter K** · 2025-03-14 08:19 UTC

Since #33042, `migration_status.json` is now written by parsing the output of Django's `showmigration` command. But as @Tim Abbott [commented](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/33042#discussion_r1929424242), it's probably better to write our own version of `showmigration`.

Currently `migration_status.json` looks like this:
```json
{
    "migrations_by_app": {
        "analytics": [
            "[X] 0001_squashed_0021_alter_fillstate_id (21 squashed migrations)"
        ],
        "auth": [
            "[X] 0001_initial",
            "[X] 0002_alter_permission_name_max_length",
            "[X] 0003_alter_user_email_max_length",
        ],
        "confirmation": [
            "[X] 0001_squashed_0014_confirmation_confirmatio_content_80155a_idx (14 squashed migrations)",
            "[X] 0015_alter_confirmation_object_id"
        ],
       // rest of installed apps
    },
    "zulip_version": "10.0-dev+git"
}
```
Where the prefixes stand for:
- `[X]` for applied migration
- `[-]` for applied but not recorded in DB
- `[ ]` for unapplied

[`showmigrations` source code](https://github.com/django/django/blob/8c118c0e00846091c261b97dbed9a5b89ceb79bf/django/core/management/commands/showmigrations.py#L113)

Since we're writing our own function, do we prefer a different data structure for this? Maybe something like a list of tuple
```json
{
    "migrations_by_app": {
        "analytics": [
           ["applied", "0001_squashed_0021_alter_fillstate_id (21 squashed migrations)"],
           ["not applied", "0002_foo_bar"],
        ],
       // rest of installed apps
    },
    "zulip_version": "10.0-dev+git"
}
```
I guess one argument for keeping the data structure as-is, is that we can reuse the existing fixtures and tests for the new function.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-03-14 21:32 UTC

I think probably it's best to not change the format unnecessarily.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-03-14 21:32 UTC

Just because it will make output more confusing for folks comparing the output.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-03-14 21:33 UTC

I am not sure there's anything wrong with the current format from a practical standpoint?

**Pieter K** · 2025-03-17 07:16 UTC

Ok! thanks for confirming

**Pieter K** · 2025-03-18 12:19 UTC

## general chat and database indexes

*2025-03-15 to 2025-06-19 · 137 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/general.20chat.20and.20database.20indexes/with/2124180)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-03-15 00:41 UTC

So we've discovered a problem with using `""` in the database as the topic for "general chat", which is that this is also the value that's stored as the null/not present topic value for direct messages.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-03-15 00:42 UTC

This is problematic not in any business logic sense, but because the database's statistics incorrectly think that "general chat" is a really common topic, and so operations like moving messages to/from that topic can have very bad query plans.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-03-15 00:44 UTC

My current thinking is the best solution for this involves denormalizing the bit for whether a message is a channel message or a DM into the `Message` table, so that we can do things like creating an index on just channel messages with `""` as the topic.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-03-15 00:45 UTC

(Or reworking all of our indexes on topic to have that property)

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-03-15 00:46 UTC

There's a question of how we want to do that. Today, we have a `recipient` table, with 3 types: 1:1 DM, Channel, and DM (values are 1/2/3). But we have plans discussed in #**general>Renaming Huddle to DirectMessageGroup** and elsewhere for merging 1:1 DM and DM in the `recipient` table, and probably after that it'd be natural to just convert it into a boolean field.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-03-15 00:47 UTC

So we might want to think about just having an `is_channel_message` boolean field, rather than copying the structure of the recipient type field?

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-03-15 00:52 UTC

Not sure what to call the field. I'll use `is_channel` for the following. I think what this migration would involve is something like the following series of commits:
- First, adding the nullable `is_channel` boolean, and make sending a message set it.
- Then, a standard `Message` table backfill that just populates it from `recipient__type == Recipient.CHANNEL`. 
- Then, we make the field NOT NULL.
- Then, we add the new indexes; basically copies of all current indexes with `topic` in their fields, with `WHERE is_channel` added to the conditions. 
- Then, we modify code paths that search filter messages by topic to include `where is_channel` in the queries. This likely is largely an audit of code inside and using the `zerver.lib.topic` module.
- Then we over time can carefully remove the old indexes, probably using testing in Zulip Cloud what happens if we disable them temporarily to confirm nothing breaks.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-03-15 00:54 UTC

I think that order is good:
- We avoid doing a bunch of churn on the indexes by building them after the field is populated.
- We avoid adding `is_channel` to queries before we've added the indexes that could result in that being expensive if the query planner doesn't decide to filter it at the end (we know that there should be no messages with a non-`""` topic in DMs, but the query planner doesn't know).
- We avoid most risk of breaking things that are already fast by removing the old indexes only at the end.

## Proposal to Refactor corporate/models.py

*2025-04-04 to 2025-04-08 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Proposal.20to.20Refactor.20corporate.2Fmodels.2Epy/with/2145315)*

**Ethan** · 2025-04-04 17:35 UTC

Hi everyone, I am a computer science student at Iowa State University. As a part of my software architecture course I did an analysis of the Domain-Driven Design of Zulip. 

During my analysis I found some concerns with corporate/models.py. It serves as a bit of a monolith for:
- Customer management (Customer, ZulipSponsorshipRequest)
- Stripe interactions (Session, PaymentIntent, Invoice, Event)
- Plan management (CustomerPlan, CustomerPlanOffer)
- License tracking (LicenseLedger)

I propose to split this file into a models package instead. Inside of the package we can handle each domain event separately. This refactor would offer improved readability and maintainability, as well as ensuring safety from future domain overlap issues.

I would love to hear feedback on if this proposal seems to make sense for Zulip!

Thanks for reading - Ethan

**Sahil Batra** · 2025-04-09 09:20 UTC

I think I found something.

My guess is that problem is in the last loop `for user_id, stream_ids in user_streams.items()` in `send_peer_subscriber_events`.

Only one user is being unsubscribed in the tests so `user_streams` is a dict like `{user_id: set(unsubscribed stream ids)}` and we are using `stream_id` variable to get the `peer_user_ids`.
But `stream_id` is not defined in the scope of that loop, so I guess its value will be the last `stream_id` value in the previous loop.
So `stream_id` value may not be the stream ID which the guest user is subscribed to and thus `peer_user_ids` will not include the guest user.

```py
def send_peer_subscriber_events(
    op: str,
    realm: Realm,
    stream_dict: dict[int, Stream],
    altered_user_dict: dict[int, set[int]],
    subscriber_peer_info: SubscriberPeerInfo,
) -> None:
    # Send peer_add/peer_remove events to other users who are tracking the
    # subscribers lists of streams in their browser; everyone for
    # public streams and only existing subscribers for private streams.

    assert op in ["peer_add", "peer_remove"]

    private_stream_ids = [
        stream_id for stream_id in altered_user_dict if stream_dict[stream_id].invite_only
    ]
    private_peer_dict = subscriber_peer_info.private_peer_dict

    for stream_id in private_stream_ids:
        altered_user_ids = altered_user_dict[stream_id]
        peer_user_ids = private_peer_dict[stream_id] - altered_user_ids

        if peer_user_ids and altered_user_ids:
            event = dict(
                type="subscription",
                op=op,
                stream_ids=[stream_id],
                user_ids=sorted(altered_user_ids),
            )
            send_event_on_commit(realm, event, peer_user_ids)

    public_stream_ids = [
        stream_id
        for stream_id in altered_user_dict
        if not stream_dict[stream_id].invite_only and not stream_dict[stream_id].is_in_zephyr_realm
    ]

    web_public_stream_ids = [
        stream_id for stream_id in public_stream_ids if stream_dict[stream_id].is_web_public
    ]

    subscriber_dict = subscriber_peer_info.subscribed_ids

    if public_stream_ids:
        user_streams: dict[int, set[int]] = defaultdict(set)

        non_guest_user_ids = set(active_non_guest_user_ids(realm.id))

        if web_public_stream_ids:
            web_public_peer_ids = set(active_user_ids(realm.id))

        for stream_id in public_stream_ids:
            altered_user_ids = altered_user_dict[stream_id]

            if stream_id in web_public_stream_ids:
                peer_user_ids = web_public_peer_ids - altered_user_ids
            else:
                peer_user_ids = (non_guest_user_ids | subscriber_dict[stream_id]) - altered_user_ids

            if peer_user_ids and altered_user_ids:
                if len(altered_user_ids) == 1:
                    # If we only have one user, we will try to
                    # find other streams they have (un)subscribed to
                    # (where it's just them).  This optimization
                    # typically works when a single user is subscribed
                    # to multiple default public streams during
                    # new-user registration.
                    #
                    # This optimization depends on all public streams
                    # having the same peers for any single user, which
                    # isn't the case for private streams.
                    [altered_user_id] = altered_user_ids
                    user_streams[altered_user_id].add(stream_id)
                else:
                    event = dict(
                        type="subscription",
                        op=op,
                        stream_ids=[stream_id],
                        user_ids=sorted(altered_user_ids),
                    )
                    send_event_on_commit(realm, event, peer_user_ids)

        for user_id, stream_ids in user_streams.items():
            if stream_id in web_public_stream_ids:
                peer_user_ids = web_public_peer_ids - altered_user_ids
            else:
                peer_user_ids = (non_guest_user_ids | subscriber_dict[stream_id]) - altered_user_ids

            event = dict(
                type="subscription",
                op=op,
                stream_ids=sorted(stream_ids),
                user_ids=[user_id],
            )
            send_event_on_commit(realm, event, peer_user_ids)
```

## Proposal to optimize check_send_message in zerver/actions/

*2025-04-25 to 2025-04-28 · 16 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Proposal.20to.20optimize.20check_send_message.20in.20zerver.2Factions.2F/with/2161493)*

**Ethan** · 2025-04-25 17:24 UTC

Hi everyone, I am an Iowa State University Software Engineering student. As a part of a class assignment my team and I investigated the runtime architecture of Zulip.

We did a runtime analysis of some backend transactions in [message_send.py](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/bf95e9bcae36a60a7f6d4c623d2c6947efaed3dc/zerver/actions/message_send.py#L1435):

Averaging these times across all runs, we found the following effective times:
* [send_message_backend](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/bf95e9bcae36a60a7f6d4c623d2c6947efaed3dc/zerver/views/message_send.py#L131) - 0.992 milliseconds
  
* [check_send_message](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/bf95e9bcae36a60a7f6d4c623d2c6947efaed3dc/zerver/actions/message_send.py#L1417) - 2.739 milliseconds
  
* [check_message](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/bf95e9bcae36a60a7f6d4c623d2c6947efaed3dc/zerver/actions/message_send.py#L1705) 4.867 milliseconds
  

* [do_send_messages](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/bf95e9bcae36a60a7f6d4c623d2c6947efaed3dc/zerver/actions/message_send.py#L857) 10.350 milliseconds

One thing that stuck out was that ** [check_send_message](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/bf95e9bcae36a60a7f6d4c623d2c6947efaed3dc/zerver/actions/message_send.py#L1417) had a much larger runtime than [send_message_backend](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/bf95e9bcae36a60a7f6d4c623d2c6947efaed3dc/zerver/views/message_send.py#L131)**

This saying "legacy build" caught my attention: addressee = Addressee.legacy_build(blah blah blah)

After investigating, I think that the [get_user_profiles()](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/lib/addressee.py) method in addressee.py may be slowing us down. It iterates through each email, doing an individual database query:  base_get_user_queryset().get(email__iexact=email.strip(), realm=realm). 

Database queries are time intensive, and the cost is one query per recipient. By switching to Django’s batch database lookup we can go from N queries down to just one query, which should improve things. 

I would create a function designed for when there are a large number of user profiles to get from the database. Instead of going through each email in emails, calling get_user, then adding the return to the profiles list, we can instead query all of the profiles at once, then convert to list.
