## ✔ Camo user-agent

*2025-10-16 to 2025-10-29 · 25 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/.E2.9C.94.20Camo.20user-agent/with/2278626)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-10-16 14:37 UTC

go-camo advertizes its user-agent as just `go-camo`.  This is insufficient for Wikipedia's [User-Agent Policy](https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Wikimedia_Foundation_User-Agent_Policy), which they [began enforcing harder in August](https://phabricator.wikimedia.org/T400119).

The regex we're hitting is a user-agent which [begins with `go-`](https://gerrit.wikimedia.org/g/operations/puppet/+/6ce137a8ff9be745b2321aa6f2cc52cef51fb6fc/modules/profile/templates/cache/haproxy/tls_terminator.cfg.erb#290).  We can satisfy their requirements by adding [either an email address or a website](https://gerrit.wikimedia.org/g/operations/puppet/+/6ce137a8ff9be745b2321aa6f2cc52cef51fb6fc/modules/profile/templates/cache/haproxy/tls_terminator.cfg.erb#297).

go-camo 2.7.0 (released 2025-10-01) lets us set the user-agent.  Should we set it to:
- `go-camo (for https://zulip.com/)`
- `go-camo (for https://zulip.example.com/)` (i.e. using `EXTERNAL_HOST`)
- `go-camo (admin@example.com)` (i.e. using `ZULIP_ADMINISTRATOR`)
- Any of the above, but with `go-camo/2.7.0` instead of `go-camo`
- Any of the above, but with `Zulip-Server` instead of `go-camo`
- Any of the above, but with `Zulip-Server/11.2` instead of `go-camo`

However, including `bot` is helpful, [per](https://foundation.wikimedia.org/wiki/Policy:Wikimedia_Foundation_User-Agent_Policy):

## S3 access through smokescreen

*2025-10-28 to 2025-10-28 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/S3.20access.20through.20smokescreen/with/2286702)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-10-28 18:31 UTC

In 4f93b4b6e4a4a9a0346aa58e18e68ff9586504cb we introduced `S3_SKIP_PROXY` and defaulted it to True.  This was kinda in order to let S3 access IMDS (due to https://github.com/boto/botocore/issues/2644) but also had the side effect of having S3 downloads and uploads not go through an extra proxy.  This seems like a possible performance benefit.

Upstream has proposed a solution to the botocore issue, using `NO_PROXY` to bypass Smokescreen for the IMDS IPs.  As long as we set the environment at just the right time, and unset it after, the IMDS auth layer can pick up that setting and get access to the IMDS endpoints.

We have two mostly-orthogonal questions:
1. Do we remove the config variable?
2. Do we change the default behaviour back to going through the proxy?  Or something like only go through the proxy if it's not smokescreen?

I'm tempted to say "yes" and "no."  But I have no idea if folks have custom outgoing proxies that they required S3 traffic to go through.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-10-28 18:41 UTC

I don't think I understand the trade-offs properly to make a recommendation. I do know that some organizations have custom proxies for reaching the public Internet; what I don't know is whether any of those organizations would use that same proxy to reach their storage solution.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-10-28 20:44 UTC

Yeah.

I guess the safest thing is to not remove the config variable, and (for performance, so we don't bounce all S3 requests through Smokescreen) continue to default it to on.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-10-28 20:45 UTC

Yeah, that seems potentially OK to me? Again, I'm not sure I follow the question fully.


## helm charts #DZ506

*2025-10-31 to 2025-10-31 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/helm.20charts.20.23DZ506/with/2289365)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-10-31 20:46 UTC

So, #DZ506 talks about how bitnami images went away on September 29th.

Having learned a bit about helm charts recently, I thought I'd spell out what I understand to be the state.

Helm charts are publicly-distributed descriptions of pieces of infra which can be installed in a Kubernetes cluster.  They pull in Docker images, and set up various other pieces of networking or monitoring, and/or run other commands to help with the docker image configuration.

Helm charts depend on other helm charts.  There's version pinning, etc.  A chart can effectively pass config options down into the sub-charts it depends on.

Bitnami is pretty much the only game in town for well-built charts of open-source stuff.  The *charts* have not gone away -- merely the *custom docker images* that they rely on.  Specifically, they now only provide a `latest` image, making it impossible to pin a dependency version (unless you pay for their catalog).  While the charts technically support swapping in arbitrary Docker images, the charts are generally not designed to work with the stock Docker Hub images (e.g. https://hub.docker.com/_/redis).

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-10-31 20:48 UTC

The suggestion in https://github.com/zulip/docker-zulip/issues/506#issuecomment-3459247441 (which is 100% generated by AI) is to continue to use the bitnami *charts*, but point them at the stock upstream *images*.  This apparently works for memcached and postgresql (with some fiddling -- I have some findings relevant to #DZ470), but does not work for Redis or RabbitMQ.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-10-31 20:51 UTC

[This comment](https://github.com/zulip/docker-zulip/issues/506#issuecomment-3223302295)   suggests moving to the `groundhog2k` user's charts, which appear to be the only other at-all-common public charts for the open-source dependencies we have.  That user has a [fork](https://github.com/zulip/docker-zulip/compare/main...greenhost:docker-zulip:main) whose diff to switch to those charts looks reasonable.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-10-31 20:52 UTC

I don't really see any way forward for the helm chart except using groundhog2k's charts as dependencies.  We certainly don't have the bandwidth to maintain other charts.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-10-31 22:11 UTC

Yeah, that sounds like the right answer. 

I feel like this is one of those situations that makes me wonder to what extent the model of having separate containers for each service is the right model, vs. just having an omnibus image that contains all the services.

## Follow-up: URI → URL settings backward-compatibility

*2025-11-10 to 2025-11-11 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Follow-up.3A.20URI.20.E2.86.92.20URL.20settings.20backward-compatibility/with/2296237)*

**Marcela Martins** · 2025-11-10 14:11 UTC

Hi everyone!
I’m continuing the work from [#23380](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/23380) (“Stop using the deprecated *uri* terminology in favor of *url*”).

The first PR ([#30367](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/30367)) already replaced simple *URI → URL* occurrences (comments, local vars, docstrings, and `/user_uploads` API). Now, I’m planning the next step: handling configuration settings that require backward-compatibility.

My proposal is to add new names in `computed_settings.py`, e.g. `AUTH_LDAP_SERVER_URL`, `REALM_MOBILE_REMAP_URLS`, `DEFAULT_AVATAR_URL`, `DEFAULT_LOGO_URL`, and `CAMO_URL` ,each with a fallback to the corresponding legacy `*_URI(S)` name, so if only the old one is defined, it still works. Then I’ll update the codebase to read these values through `computed_settings` instead of directly from `settings.py`, and add tests to ensure both old and new names work (with the new one taking precedence). Since the `realm.uri` references have already been migrated in recent commits, this PR will focus only on the server settings part. `EXTERNAL_URI_SCHEME` will remain unchanged, as previously discussed.

Does this plan for backwards-compatibility (new variable + fallback) look good to the backend team before I start implementing it? Thanks!

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-11-10 14:13 UTC

(replying to Marcela Martins)
> Then I’ll update the codebase to read these values through `computed_settings` instead of directly from `settings.py`

This part doesn't make any sense, since `settings.py` folds together `default_settings.py`, `configured_settings.py`, and `computed_settings.py`.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-11-10 14:13 UTC

And `computed_settings` necessarily already has access to the default and configured values, otherwise there'd be no way to compute anything

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-11-10 14:16 UTC

You will need to add the new names to `default_settings.py`, and do the fallback-setting in `computed_settings`.  The server code should use the new names, and pull them from `settings` as usual.

**Marcela Martins** · 2025-11-10 14:21 UTC

Thanks, Alex! That really helps clarify things and sorry for the earlier confusion, I’m new to the project.

Just to confirm my understanding:
-  I’ll add the new `*_URL(S)` variables in `default_settings.py` (with the same default values as their `*_URI(S)` counterparts).

-  Then I’ll handle the backwards-compatible fallbacks in `computed_settings.py`, so that if only the old setting is defined it still works, but `*_URL(S)` takes precedence.

-  The rest of the codebase will continue pulling these values from `settings` as usual, with no import changes.

Does that plan sound right to you?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-11-10 15:03 UTC

Broadly, yes.

**Lauryn Menard** · 2025-11-11 14:48 UTC

I'd recommend doing these changes as a separate PR from #36416.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-11 20:47 UTC

That sounds very reasonable to me; combining multiple complex transitions usually ends poorly.

I think we should do several things differently.
- We already have a cron job, `analytics/management/commands/update_analytics_counts.py`, that handles the main connection to the bouncer. I think we could have `send_server_data_to_push_bouncer` be updated to support sending the metadata via the `ZULIP_SERVICES_URL` interface, without new parallel infrastructure. 
- Rather than the queue approach, saving a change to `want_advertise_in_communities_directory=True` should probably just call `send_server_data_to_push_bouncer` synchronously, so that we can show an error and reject the change if it doesn't actually work?
- That `RemoteRealm` comment is out of date. When we renamed things around the `ZULIP_SERVICES` scheme, the idea was to be able to support servers subscribed to other services than mobile push notifications. This directory listing should qualify as a very reasonable feature. So we should use `RemoteRealm` for at least the `realm_name`, `realm_url`, and `org_type` fields.
- That leaves `realm_text_description` and `realm_icon_url` to manage. The description is easy, and we could just add as a nullable field on `RemoteRealm` that only gets sent when uploading.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-11 20:45 UTC

The one other thing here on the Zulip Cloud side is whether we block the feature on having a moderation process where we approve listings. It might be that we want the flow to be something like this:
- The server-side handler for the upload checks if the metadata that the directory has differs from what the self-hosted system has. If so, it sends a request to update it.
- The server-side handler for that request stores the metadata in a one table, and triggers a notification for Kandra Labs staff to review the new entry. I think this realistically involves a separate table. A good way to do this might be for `RemoteRealm` always has what the self-hosted server last sent for listing, and we have a separate `RemoteCommunityDirectoryEntry` table that has the approved/published values. Since various `RemoteRealm` fields can be edited freely by the self-hosted system, I think it's better for the published values table to be the new one. This architecture also gives us the flexibility to just have a panel for reviewing the differences between the tables, rather than handling one-by-one, if that becomes preferable over time.
- Only once approved via say the support panel does it go live.

Since we can add such a thing without changing the client/server API, it's not strictly required to do in advance, but I think we might just want to build it that way from the beginning.

## Parse client in request bodies (PR #36056)

*2025-11-15 to 2025-11-26 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Parse.20client.20in.20request.20bodies.20.28PR.20.2336056.29/with/2300840)*

**thedance** · 2025-11-15 10:19 UTC

As suggested by Tim [here](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/36056#discussion_r2512552989), I'm opening this channel to discuss PR #36056, in particular the approach taken in commit `d622a71215c`.

The `generate_all_emails()` view sends a PATCH request with `client=internal` in the URL-encoded body, but `parse_client()` in the middleware wasn't extracting this parameter. I think the cause is Django only populates
request.POST for POST requests, leaving it empty for PATCH/PUT/DELETE regardless of content type.

This commit extends `typed_endpoint` decorator with request body processing (adapted from the existing `process_as_post` decorator logic) to populate request.POST for PATCH/PUT/DELETE requests before parameter
extraction. This ensures middleware `parse_client()` function can access body parameters consistently across all HTTP methods.

The functionality works, but I want to ensure we're not creating technical debt or unexpected side effects elsewhere in the codebase.

Thoughts on this approach?

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-20 01:40 UTC

The easiest answer is definitely to not change production request-parsing code in order to support a somewhat hacky developer tool. I don't think I quite understand why you felt the need to do that.

**thedance** · 2025-11-20 20:32 UTC

Currently, the rest_dispatch function already coerces PUT/PATCH/DELETE requests into having POST-like semantics using the same logic. However, since this is done after the middleware, parse_client (which is executed in the middleware) cannot benefit from that and doesn't parse the client correctly for these requests. To address this, I use the same logic as in rest_dispatch but before parse_client.
That said, I understand this could be risky. I'm going to give it another spin and try to find a better alternative, but if you have any suggestions, I'm eager to hear them.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-20 21:36 UTC

Ahh, OK, can you link to the code that does this in the middleware?

**thedance** · 2025-11-21 07:33 UTC

Currently the system populates request.POST for PATCH/PUT/DELETE here (after the middleware) : https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/e9e49a897321185575f281dc09042c897d43a7e5/zerver/lib/rest.py#L211. Parse client is in the middleware here: https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/e9e49a897321185575f281dc09042c897d43a7e5/zerver/middleware.py#L247

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-25 00:54 UTC

I'm not sure I'll have time to evaluate whether that's safe. I would prefer to not try to change this. But if you think it fixes a production-facing issue to do so, I can ask some others to look at the question. But I'd want a clear explanation of what issue it improves for the actual production codebase.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-11-25 00:54 UTC

It's just not worth making hard-to-analyze changes that only help a hacky developer tool of ours...

**thedance** · 2025-11-26 22:26 UTC

Understood and fair enough. I understand that it's not worth risking production.
I could do a workaround and in the patch call specify the client in HTTP_USER_AGENT instead of encoding it in the request form. This way the development view would work, although I'm not sure if it's a bit of a hacky solution. What do you think? ## Cleanup investigation summary for zerver/filters.py.

*2025-11-20 to 2025-11-21 · 10 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Cleanup.20investigation.20summary.20for.20zerver.2Ffilters.2Epy.2E/with/2307193)*

**Raj Vishwakarma** · 2025-11-20 23:47 UTC

Hi all — I’m looking into the “clean up `zerver/filters.py` using Django’s modern `SafeExceptionReporterFilter` features” [issue](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/36706). Quick summary of what I’ve found so far :

**Findings:**
* Django (3.1+) now auto-cleanses sensitive data using `hidden_settings`, `cleansed_substitute`, and built-in filtering of settings, POST, COOKIES, and META.
  
* A good amount of what `ZulipExceptionReporterFilter` currently does is duplicate behavior Django already handles.
  
* We still have a few Zulip-specific fields that Django doesn’t filter (e.g. `realm_counts`, `installation_counts`).
  
**Proposed plan:**

1. Use Django’s default `SafeExceptionReporterFilter` for most filtering.
  
2. Keep only minimal Zulip-specific overrides (masking a few POST/META keys Django doesn’t know about).
  
3. Add one override to **completely disable including Django settings in error emails**, since that’s a stated goal.
  
4. Update tests to confirm:
  
  * all sensitive POST fields are masked
    
  * META values are sanitized
    
  * **no settings appear** in the error email payload
    

Before I start implementing this, does this direction sound good?

Hmm. In general our pattern is that `acting_user=None` means the action is being done by a system job, like LDAP sync, that doesn't associate with a user account. 

In this code path, I think it is probably less problematic to have `acting_user=None` translate into the sender (who is almost certainly a system bot) being treated as the acting user. But given the bug here was that a caller did not correctly make the correct choice to pass `acting_user`, I think we're not really accomplishing our goals here if we paper over the fact that this is an independent parameter in the `internal_prep/send` code paths that should often be the user triggering the notification, not the system bot.

(A situation where we want the system bot to be the acting user is, for example, sending a notification about a newly created channel to a private channel the acting user can't access).

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-12-01 18:49 UTC

@Sahil Batra what are your thoughts on this detail?

**Sahil Batra** · 2025-12-02 13:29 UTC

I think using sender as `acting_user` would be fine in most cases, but yeah might be helpful to just explicitly pass it from everywhere to avoid situations where we want user triggering the action to be `acting_user`.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-12-02 18:27 UTC

Yeah, I think I find it most helpful for it to be explicit in the callers, since then when you're reading the caller, you can see "Oh, that looks wrong!" rather than needing to know how the internal plumbing will work. And that's what we'd have needed to catch these bugs. Probably that means it should be a mandatory kwarg.

**Shubham Padia** · 2025-12-03 08:04 UTC

Okay, in that case, this might need multiple passes based on some criteria to divide the work. The number of places to put acting_user is a lot, will keep this as a task to do between feedbacks on my existing work.

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-12-03 19:13 UTC

Yeah it's usually best to do one reasonably sized helper function code path per PR for this sort of refactor, once something gets too big it's hard for everyone to manage, and I think it should be very doable to just add the parameter as optional and then work through the steps to make it mandatory individually..

## do_delete_user new behavior details

*2025-12-03 to 2025-12-05 · 14 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/do_delete_user.20new.20behavior.20details/with/2316936)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2025-12-03 20:49 UTC

In https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/35477 we're finalizing a rework of the `do_delete_user` and `do_delete_user_preserving_messages` to be more deliberate about what they do with the associated objects in other tables which have a foreign key to `UserProfile`. The old implementation ends up deleting rows that should be preserved (#**backend>misuse of on_delete=CASCADE@2186305** ).

The two questions that popped in review are:
1. 1:1 DMs. When deleting `user`, should `do_delete_user` delete only the messages **sent** by `user`, or should DM messages **to** `user` be deleted as well? I think I'm aligned with what @Tim Abbott stated in the [comment](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/35477#discussion_r2520406029) - messages sent **to** the user should be preserved. It seems more natural to think of them as belonging to the sender, not just the recipient.

2. A few `RealmAuditLog` types carry important information about the `modified_user` in `extra_data`. Mainly the `USER_EMAIL_CHANGED, USER_FULL_NAME_CHANGED, USER_SETTING_CHANGED` events - `extra_data` of these logs contains the old and new values. So that information needs to be scrubbed. The [question](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/35477#discussion_r2520416556) is whether we should entirely `.delete()` these logs or preserve them, just scrubbing the `extra_data` field.
The latter option feels superior - these logs may still prove useful for some sorts of debugging / investigations in the future and without the personal information in `extra_data` they should be harmless from the perspective of privacy of the deleted user.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-12-03 21:30 UTC

I think I agree with those.  It might slant too much toward "scrubbing," but in the DMs case, I could see the argument for replacing messages *from* the user with a tombstone message which we display differently somehow which says "(message from now-deleted user)".  That way the conversation is *slightly* more comprehensible.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-12-03 21:35 UTC

Not deleting messages *to* makes more sense when you have a 3-person DM, too

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2025-12-04 19:00 UTC

**Alex Vandiver** · 2025-12-04 19:10 UTC

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-12-04 22:17 UTC

*2025-12-04 to 2026-01-23 · 102 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/.E2.9C.94.20make.20ZulipMarkdown.20thread-safe/with/2317889)*

**Bedo Khaled** · 2025-12-04 21:50 UTC

See my [comment](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/36213#discussion_r2582984665) for background

But during **concurrent** message sending requests,  [_md_engine.convert()](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/lib/markdown/__init__.py#L2717), used by the markdown parser, is not thread-safe.

As a result, concurrent requests (each with its own thread spawned by `unsafe_timeout(...)`) try to modify "the same data" resulting in 400 status code "Unable to render message" 

**Traceback**:
```shell
2025-12-02 22:22:03.770 ERR  [] Exception in Markdown parser; input (sanitized) was: 'xxxxxxxxxx'
 (message unknown)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/srv/zulip/zerver/lib/markdown/__init__.py", line 2717, in do_convert
    rendering_result.rendered_content = unsafe_timeout(5, lambda: _md_engine.convert(content))
  File "/srv/zulip/zerver/lib/timeout.py", line 98, in unsafe_timeout
    raise thread.exc_info[1].with_traceback(thread.exc_info[2])
  File "/srv/zulip/zerver/lib/timeout.py", line 59, in run
    self.result = func()
  File "/srv/zulip/zerver/lib/markdown/__init__.py", line 2717, in <lambda>
    rendering_result.rendered_content = unsafe_timeout(5, lambda: _md_engine.convert(content))
  File "/srv/zulip/.venv/lib/python3.10/site-packages/markdown/core.py", line 361, in convert
    newRoot = treeprocessor.run(root)
  File "/srv/zulip/.venv/lib/python3.10/site-packages/markdown/treeprocessors.py", line 391, in run
    self.ancestors.pop()
IndexError: pop from empty list
```
"the same data" in this case is the `self.ancestors` list

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2025-12-14 20:49 UTC

Because of the way `unsafe_timeout` works (read the code, it’s horrifying), it might fail to stop a job that’s in the middle of some uninterruptible operation. It needs to return control to the caller anyway, so the job needs to be on a different thread.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-12-23 13:28 UTC

(replying to Tim Abbott)
> Yeah, it's mostly about caching linkifier construction. Maybe the ahorasick thing for alert words is also relevant?

Pop an aspirin and look at [maybe_update_markdown_engines](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/main/zerver/lib/markdown/__init__.py#L2578]) to see how the linkifier cache complicates things.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-12-23 13:29 UTC

Without totally solving the problem (nor committing to some kind of aho-corasick thing right away), it seems like you could isolate the problem.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-12-23 13:35 UTC

You could have every render event just call something like `make_md_engine` to build a markdown engine on the fly (i.e no global at that level), and for most realms, it would only incur the 50-microsecond cost that @Anders Kaseorg measured.  That's obviously a small cost to pay for thread safety modulo the linkifier complications.

And that function would then still need a line like this:

~~~py
linkifiers = build_linkifier_data(linkifiers_key)
~~~

In a world where `build_linkifier_data` was cheap, there would be no cache, and everything would be thread-safe.  In today's world, that function would still access some kind of global cache, but at least it would be a more narrow window of global yuckiness.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-12-23 13:48 UTC

I think an important consideration here (correct me if I am wrong) is that the linkifier data itself is *tiny* storage-wise.  So the purpose of the cache isn't to save storage somehow between multiple threads; it really is just about avoiding regex compilation.

Also, if some admin does change the underlying linkifier data through the UI, that's a pretty rare event. And then there's no real "race" (I use that word in a very narrow context) to make sure  that the next few messages immediately respect the linkifier changes, because most authors of those messages wouldn't even know about the linkifiers in the first place nor have some message already drafted.

So the whole weird business of having to go update the markdown engines after a change could be done more lazily, I think.  I'm being kind of hand-wavy about that, but my main points are above.  The data itself is tiny and the changes are **very rare** compared to message traffic.

**Steve Howell** · 2025-12-23 14:43 UTC

Here's where the regex compilation happens now, and ~~this seems very easy to upstream by having `LinkifierDict` hold an actual regex instead of a pattern~~ (see later for possibly better place to fix the code).

~~~ py
# Given a regular expression pattern, linkifies groups that match it
# using the provided format string to construct the URL.
class LinkifierPattern(CompiledInlineProcessor):
    """Applied a given linkifier to the input"""

    def __init__(
        self,
        source_pattern: str,
        url_template: str,
        zmd: "ZulipMarkdown",
    ) -> None:
        # Do not write errors to stderr (this still raises exceptions)
        options = re2.Options()
        options.log_errors = False

        compiled_re2 = re2.compile(prepare_linkifier_pattern(source_pattern), options=options)

        self.prepared_url_template = uri_template.URITemplate(url_template)

        super().__init__(compiled_re2, zmd)
~~~

**Steve Howell** · 2025-12-23 16:47 UTC

**Executive summary**:

1. Extract a three-line helper to prepare the linkifier regexes.
2. Wrap the helper with functools.lru_cache (as we do in other places already).
3. Rip out the md_engine and linkifier_data globals.

Save on overall global storage, make the parser threadsafe, and pay about 50 microseconds per call for the benefits. :slight_smile:

```python
def do_change_realm_subdomain(
    realm: Realm,
    new_subdomain: str,
    *,
    acting_user: UserProfile | None,
    add_deactivated_redirect: bool = True,
) -> None:
...
    old_subdomain = realm.subdomain
    old_url = realm.url
    # If the realm had been a demo organization scheduled for

    realm.demo_organization_scheduled_deletion_date = None
    realm.string_id = new_subdomain
    with transaction.atomic(durable=True):
        realm.save(update_fields=["string_id", "demo_organization_scheduled_deletion_date"])
        RealmAuditLog.objects.create(
            realm=realm,
            event_type=AuditLogEventType.REALM_SUBDOMAIN_CHANGED,
            event_time=timezone_now(),
            acting_user=acting_user,
            # Old RealmAuditLog entries for this used "old_subdomain" and
            # "new_subdomain" keys to store this data.
            extra_data={
                RealmAuditLog.OLD_VALUE: old_subdomain,
                RealmAuditLog.NEW_VALUE: new_subdomain,
            },
        )
```

*2025-12-15 to 2026-02-15 · 13 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/YouTube.20link.20previews.20.2331891/with/2327278)*

**Ritesh Tiwari** · 2025-12-15 18:03 UTC

Hi! I'm interested in working on #31891 (YouTube link previews broken due to bot detection).

  I've analyzed the codebase and found:
  - `pyoembed` in `zerver/lib/url_preview/oembed.py` doesn't use Zulip's custom user-agent during autodiscovery
  - This causes YouTube's bot detection to block the discovery request

  I'm considering two approaches:
  1. **Quick fix:** Directly use YouTube's oEmbed endpoint, bypassing autodiscovery
  2. **Full solution:** Custom implementation using oembed.com/providers.json with proper headers


 Which approach would be preferred? Happy to discuss further!

**Tim Abbott** · 2025-12-15 19:44 UTC

What make you think using our custom user-agent would fix this?

**Ritesh Tiwari** · 2025-12-16 05:22 UTC

You're right to question that. After deeper investigation:

  1. pyoembed has no dedicated YouTube provider - it uses autodiscovery
  2. Autodiscovery fetches the YouTube HTML page via `requests.get()` with
     default headers
  3. Even if user-agent was the issue, pyoembed doesn't allow injecting
     custom headers

  So the user-agent point was incorrect. The actual fix would be to
  **bypass pyoembed's autodiscovery entirely** by:
  - Using a hardcoded YouTube oEmbed endpoint
    (https://www.youtube.com/oembed?url=...)
  - Making the request with Zulip's PreviewSession

 This avoids fetching YouTube's HTML page altogether, which is what triggers the bot detection (likely  IP-based for cloud servers).

 Does this analysis align with your understanding? Happy to dig deeper if I'm still missing something.

**Anders Kaseorg** · 2025-12-17 00:42 UTC

We should replace pyoembed with a maintained library like [micawber](https://github.com/coleifer/micawber) or the new [meta-oxide](https://github.com/yfedoseev/meta_oxide).

**Ritesh Tiwari** · 2025-12-17 06:29 UTC

Thanks Anders! Did some digging on both:

  micawber looks promising - it's actively maintained (last release was
  Dec 6, 2024), supports custom user-agents, and has bootstrap_oembed() 
  which pulls from oembed.com's provider list (1000+ providers including 
  YouTube).

  The tricky part is that micawber uses urllib under the hood, not requests. 
  Since Zulip routes outgoing requests through smokescreen via OutgoingSession 
  (which extends requests.Session), we'd need to work around that.

  A few ways to handle this:
  - Subclass micawber's Provider and override fetch() to use PreviewSession
  - Build a simple oEmbed client from scratch using PreviewSession + the 
    oembed.com providers.json file
  - Patch micawber's urllib calls to go through requests

  I'm leaning toward the custom client approach since it's probably cleaner 
  than wrapping micawber, but open to suggestions.

## DirectMessageGroup migration

*2026-01-07 to 2026-04-05 · 122 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/DirectMessageGroup.20migration/with/2346049)*

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-07 01:34 UTC

I think we're now getting close to the point where we can seriously consider integrating #25713 / #**general>Renaming Huddle to DirectMessageGroup**, and I'd like to have a conversation about release engineering of this. 

As a reminder, the benefits of this transition are:
- More readable and consistent code for fetching messages, likely resulting in better query plans.
- Better performance for `POST /register` code paths around fetching "all your DM conversations". 
- It'll be easy to add settings/configuration for "direct messages" that apply to both 1:1 DMs and groups.

The main downsides are transition cost and a more dense `DirectMessageGroup` database table, as well as additional database queries when sending a direct message and thus creating a `DirectMessageGroup`. 

@Mohammad Reza Kianifar @Alex Vandiver FYI.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-07 01:34 UTC

As I understand it, the state of affairs of that:
- We've already integrated a ton of refactoring changes that implemented code paths for using `DIRECT_MESSAGE_GROUP` objects for 1:1 DMs, if there is already a DirectMessageGroup for the pair of users involved. These code paths are disabled through two mechanisms.
- The first mechanism is that we only use a `DirectMessageGroup` if one already exists for that pair of users.
- One is that the `PREFER_DIRECT_MESSAGE_GROUP` setting controls whether those are created. It's currently always `False` outside tests.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-07 01:38 UTC

So the remaining steps for the transition are:
- #35769, which switches `PREFER_DIRECT_MESSAGE_GROUP` to True, among other things. I'm hoping to write a few more messages detailing its exact behavior and risks before I head out for the day.
- #35795, which is a migration that loops through transitioning existing 1:1 DM pairs to use DirectMessageGroup. I've not reviewed this one at all yet.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-07 01:40 UTC

The goal of this thread is to make sure we have a clearly documented plan for how to go about doing this integration in large installations like Zulip Cloud where the migration may take hours to run. 

For example, one could easily imagine arranging #35795 to handle one Realm at a time atomically.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-07 01:57 UTC

Yeah. I think the simplest story would be this:
- If there is a `DirectMessageGroup` between that pair of users, then that gets used, and it is assumed that we've arranged this only happens if the `Recipient.PERSONAL` object for both users is empty. 
- If there is no `DirectMessageGroup` between that pair of users, then the `Recipient.PERSONAL` objects are authoritative.

And then our migration would aim to cut over an entire realm at a time, by creating the DirectMessageGroup objects and moving the `Message.recipient` values atomically.

**Steve Howell** · 2026-01-07 02:45 UTC

The way to do this type of migration without race concerns:
* record a cutoff id
* start writing to the new schema and old schema while still reading from the old schema
* slowly convert all the old schemas before the cutoff id to the new schema
* change the code so that it still writes to both the new schema and old schema but reads from the new schema
* remove the code that writes to to the old schema
* slowly remove all the old-schema records

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-01-07 02:50 UTC

Yes, that style of migration is a valid solution -- but not one that I think would be reasonable to manage or worth the trouble here.  I expect that the merge-reads-from-both-schemas approach will be easier to manage operationally.

**Steve Howell** · 2026-01-07 02:54 UTC

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-03-04 03:26 UTC

This is actually not a tiny bug.

The problem is that we can't actually use the `PREFER_DIRECT_MESSAGE_GROUP` as a binary flag, because it will roll out incrementally across processes during a rolling restart.

The code needs to:
1. merge in direct message groups with personal recipients in narrows if they exist
2. send to direct message groups if they exist
3. send to personal recipients if they do not
4. never create direct message groups for 2-person DMs

We deploy that state, which is safe to do in a rolling manner, since there are no 2-person direct message groups yet.

We then do a rolling restart of the same code with PREFER_DIRECT_MESSAGE_GROUP=True, which makes the code:
1. merge in direct message groups with personal recipients in narrows if they exist
2. create 2-person direct message groups if necessary, and always sends to them

...and then start the migration, which will rewrite existing personal recipient pairs into their 2-person direct message groups, making those groups if they don't exist.

----

As currently written, the behaviour with PREFER_DIRECT_MESSAGE_GROUP=False is:
1. narrows with message groups only show personal recipients
2. send to personal recipients always
3. never create direct message groups for 2-person DMs

...which is correct if you're looking for `PREFER_DIRECT_MESSAGE_GROUP=False` to mean "no behaviour change from the previous commit" which is not actually what we want.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-03-04 04:18 UTC

Combined with, in `narrow.py`:
```python
        # Direct message with another person
        if other_participant:
            # We need bidirectional direct messages with another person.
            # But Recipient.PERSONAL objects only encode the person who
            # received the message, and not the other participant in
            # the thread (the sender), we need to do a somewhat
            # complex query to get messages between these two users
            # with either of them as the sender.
            self_recipient_id = self.user_profile.recipient_id
            other_recipient_id = other_participant.recipient_id

            # Include messages from both PERSONAL and DM group recipients.
            # This handles the migration period where messages may exist
            # with either recipient type.
            group_recipient = tuple()
            if recipient and recipient.type == Recipient.DIRECT_MESSAGE_GROUP:
                group_recipient = (
                    (column("recipient_id", Integer) == recipient.id,)
                )
            cond = and_(
                column("flags", Integer).op("&")(UserMessage.flags.is_private.mask) != 0,
                column("realm_id", Integer) == self.realm.id,
                or_(
                    and_(
                        column("sender_id", Integer) == other_participant.id,
                        column("recipient_id", Integer) == self_recipient_id,
                    ),
                    and_(
                        column("sender_id", Integer) == self.user_profile.id,
                        column("recipient_id", Integer) == other_recipient_id,
                    ),
                    *group_recipient,
                ),
            )

            return query.where(maybe_negate(cond))
```

I am working in this PR #37662 , trying to add a new search filter topic-contains: that matches topics containing a substring (case-insensitive)

For this query, I'm using ILIKE with wildcards on both sides (%pattern%). My understanding is that standard B-tree indexes cannot be used in this case, requiring a sequential scan of matching rows. And, as mentioned in a previous PR, this could become a performance issue.

* Scope the search to a specific channel .However, this would also limit the usefulness of the operator.
* pg_trgm (trigram indexes) could help with pattern matching queries like this, though the index size may be considerably larger.
* tsvector for full-text search. But would provide word-based matching instead of substring matching.

## Help with issue #19655

*2026-01-26 to 2026-02-03 · 9 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Help.20with.20issue.20.2319655/with/2363477)*

**Janhavi Kulkarni** · 2026-01-26 14:36 UTC

Hello,
I wanted to work on this issue #19655 and wanted to confirm my understanding of the current behaviour and clear a few doubts.

From reading the code paths, messages sent via the email gateway are posted with the email gateway bot as the sender. While stream access checks special-case the channel email address creator, wildcard mention permissions (@all, @everyone, @stream, etc.) are checked against the message sender in check_message(). As a result, when an email-originated message contains a wildcard mention, the permission check is evaluated using the email gateway bot, which does not have permission to use wildcard mentions, and the message is rejected, even if the original human sender would normally be allowed to use them when posting directly in Zulip.

Based on this, it seems that wildcard mentions are currently effectively disallowed for all messages sent via the email gateway, and the error in this issue is a consequence of that behavior.

Given the earlier discussion about potentially rendering wildcard mentions silently instead of raising an error, I wanted to clarify the intended scope:

Is this issue primarily about fixing the behavior of messages sent via the email gateway? Or is the intent to revisit the behavior more generally, so that unauthorized wildcard mentions do not result in a hard error regardless of how the message is sent?
If both are in scope, should a fix here focus on the email gateway case for now, while aligning with a broader change in how Zulip handles unauthorized wildcard mentions overall?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-01-27 04:23 UTC

> From reading the code paths, [snip two paragraphs...]

That's a very long way of re-expressing the one summary sentence at the top of the issue.  Please read our [guide to using AI for communication](https://zulip.readthedocs.io/en/latest/contributing/contributing.html#using-ai-for-communication), particularly around conciseness.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-01-27 04:26 UTC

There is no broader behaviour here to revisit -- we only get the exception logged because it's going through the internal-message-sending codepath.  Normal messages from end-users that don't have permission don't generate this error in the logs.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-01-27 04:27 UTC

The ideal fix should cause incoming email messages containing `@all` to be sent to their intended destinations with no wildcard behaviour and no errors logged.  No other behaviour should be changed.

**Janhavi Kulkarni** · 2026-01-27 17:29 UTC

Thanks for the clarification and apologies for the lengthy message earlier. I’ll make sure to keep things concise going forward.

**Janhavi Kulkarni** · 2026-02-03 18:00 UTC

Hello,

I was wondering if i can apply this logic to @topic too since it follows the same path of being logged as an error and TopicWildcardNotAllowedError happening against same threshold <=15. **Alex Vandiver** · 2026-02-03 18:34 UTC

In general, folks writing email messages are not intending to do wildcard mentions -- it's accidental based on content which happens to be in the message.

## Make "new login" notifications less spammy

*2026-01-27 to 2026-01-30 · 11 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Make.20.22new.20login.22.20notifications.20less.20spammy/with/2364381)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2026-01-27 16:53 UTC

I'm investigating our options for an initial version of solving #5854. 

As @Greg Price [proposed](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/5854#issuecomment-926152671) in that discussion, we could do something like this:
> The most straightforward thing to do would be to leave behind a long-lived cookie even when you log out. If that cookie is still present when you log in, then we'd say no email is necessary.

I'm starting this thread to discuss whether we want to do this and  the possible design for this.

1. What should be the trigger for setting and refreshing the cookie? Doing it when you log out specifically would mean most users don't really get the cookie. So e.g. it wouldn't be usable for some kind of `Known devices list` feature we might consider in the future. And users who lose their logged-in state via their session expiring would have their device considered not-trusted upon logging back in, even using the same browser.
Other options would be:
- Set/refresh the cookie upon login.  Downside: It'll expire eventually and the device/browser will just suddenly become not-trusted again.
- Set/refresh upon every `/` load (or some variant of this type of trigger). This keeps the cookie fresh for as long as the user keeps using Zulip on this device regularly.

2. What should be the validity time of the cookie? Something like 2x the session validity time might be reasonable?

3. Do we want a database table `KnownDevices` to go with it? It could be a record tracking some last-seen info about the device:
```
id: int,
cookie_value: str,  # perhaps just a UUID generated randomly for the device
user_agent: str, # the last user agent we've seen from this device
ip_address: str, # last IP address seen from this device, or list[str] - list of all IP addresses seen
...
```

**Karl Stolley** · 2026-01-27 16:54 UTC

If I'm understanding this situation correctly, perhaps this is akin to other services (I'm thinking particularly of banks) that have a checkbox with *Trust this device* or *Remember this device*? Would such an approach be useful here? That takes the guesswork out of setting long-lived cookies, at any rate.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2026-01-27 17:04 UTC

I think it's somewhat akin to it, but not quite, because, at least in  my experience,  in the case of a bank the difference between a `trusted device` vs `not trusted device` is much greater. That is, a login attempt from a `not trusted device` will trigger additional protections, such as requiring 2FA. While a `trusted device` can be logged in from with just username+password, bypassing 2FA.

Since what we're discussing here is just about `don't send an email notification for "trusted" devices` (a relatively small deal), rather than about skipping an entire authentication step like 2FA (a big deal!), I think it's probably reasonable to let this be a heuristic that happens silently, without explicitly prompting the user?

(perhaps it's more accurate to phrase this as a `known device` rather than `trusted device` specifically for what we're discussing here, to make this distinction clearer)

**Karl Stolley** · 2026-01-27 17:42 UTC

Yeah, `known device` sounds much more accurate in terms of what is on the line, and what’s being promised in terms of security (little)

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-30 01:08 UTC

Yeah, "known device" is better terminology here, since this is not about 2FA.

I guess what would be the use case for the database table? From my standpoint, the existing `Session` database table is the thing for logged-in devices.

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2026-01-30 03:16 UTC

It might not be super useful i suppose - it would be a more long-lived list of devices that we've recently seen using your account, including those that might be logged out.

Google does expose this information at least - https://support.google.com/accounts/answer/3067630
> Devices or sessions where you’re signed out will have a “Signed out” indication.

I imagine the main use case is being able to see if any suspicious devices are on the list, even if they already signed out.

If we do the table, we don't need to immediately implement the UI, it could still be useful for internal auditing by server admins. Though maybe not that useful, because the information it'll provide will overlap with `auth.log` and `server.log`, if the log files are kept around for reasonably long.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-01-30 17:59 UTC

@Alex Vandiver thoughts on the approach here?

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-01-30 19:52 UTC

I think my gut would be to skip the table for now -- I don't think we can manage the "places where you have logged-out sessions" in any coherent way (can you remove things from it?  do you get a new entry every time you move IPs? etc)

Far more useful would be "currently logged in sessions" which we don't even have yet (ref #29668)

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-01-30 19:53 UTC

I think there are potential privacy concerns with having long-lived user-tracking cookies which persist even if the user's session expires.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-01-30 19:56 UTC

We also want this to not be trivially fakable by an attacker manually setting a cookie before doing their Evil Login.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-01-30 19:58 UTC

Which means that the server needs to sign something.  We ideally need the cookie name or contents to be keyed specifically to one user-id.

**Pieter K** · 2026-02-05 11:34 UTC

It seems like if we import .txt file with content_type=None, it will not be accessible in the imported realm:
```
2026-02-05 08:09:25.521 INFO [zr] 127.0.0.1       GET     200   5ms (db: 2ms/2q) /user_uploads/8/90/jbPCTP_QrXSYMoYpjdtSIDLH/text-file.txt (64@mtrmst via Mozilla)
Traceback (most recent call last):
  File "/usr/lib/python3.12/wsgiref/handlers.py", line 137, in run
    self.result = application(self.environ, self.start_response)
                  ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
  File "/home/pieter123/zulip/.venv/lib/python3.12/site-packages/django/core/handlers/wsgi.py", line 133, in __call__

  File "/usr/lib/python3.12/wsgiref/handlers.py", line 238, in start_response

  File "/usr/lib/python3.12/wsgiref/headers.py", line 39, in __init__
    self._convert_string_type(v)
  File "/usr/lib/python3.12/wsgiref/headers.py", line 45, in _convert_string_type
    raise AssertionError("Header names/values must be"

```
During import, `import_uploads` doesn't check upload files' content_type if it's not s3_uploads and in `fix_attachments_data` it only does `guess_type` if the file is one of `THUMBNAIL_ACCEPT_IMAGE_TYPES`. So, in this case, import doesn't do anything to non image file's content type if it's None.

I tried adding a quick patch that fills missing attachments' content_type using `guess_type` during import, and it still doesn't fix this specific issue, the exact same error would still popup.

I think this is because the server expects this exact kind of content_type for .txt file:
```
     "content_type": "text/plain; charset=\"ascii\"",
```
The Zulip exporter generates this for .txt files. Whereas, if one were to use`guesss_type` for .txt file, it'll return `text/plain`.

Not sure if this is also the case for other file types or not. And currently, both the Mattermost and Slack importer generate this kind of output for message attachments.

I haven't done any investigation downstream from import.

**Nithyaraj Mudhaliyar** · 2026-02-12 07:16 UTC

@Tim Abbott Following up on your [suggestion](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/36789#issuecomment-3666599480) regarding **Issue #21859 (Linkify Custom URL Protocols)**:

I researched the behavior using Babelmark and confirmed that while standard Markdown requires `<brackets>` for custom schemes, users of tools like **Obsidian** and **Zotero** frequently paste bare URLs (`obsidian://...`, `zotero://...`), which standard parsers treat as plain text.

I have implemented a fix locally that bridges this gap:

1.  **Protocol Whitelist:** I added `obsidian` to the backend link regex and the `html_safelisted_schemes` sanitizer list. This allows these links to render correctly as clickable links in both the live preview and sent messages.
2.  **Test Infrastructure Fix:** While writing regression tests, I discovered a bug in `zerver/tests/test_markdown.py`. The `linkify_tests` helper was forcibly prepending `http://` to any URL that didn't start with `http` or contain `@`. I generalized this to respect URLs that already contain a valid scheme (e.g. `://`).

All backend tests are passing with these changes.

Does this "high-utility allowlist" approach sound good for a PR? It immediately solves the friction for users of these tools (as requested in #21859 and related threads) without opening the door to all custom schemes.

## Convert Slack `rich_text` blocks.

*2026-02-26 to 2026-03-04 · 4 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Convert.20Slack.20.60rich_text.60.20blocks.2E/with/2392071)*

**Pieter K** · 2026-02-26 18:27 UTC

Opening this to discuss the follow up for #37483. @Tim Abbott's comment:
> Can you chart a chat.zulip.org thread about your views on the options for the `rich_text` blocks that this is still not supporting? Include a recommendation on what you think we should as next steps.

The `rich_text` blocks handle these text formatting, each has its own `rich_text` block type:
- bold, italic, underline, strike through
- linked text (markdown link)
- channel mention, wild card mention, user mention
- code block and inline codes
- lists

The logic to convert basic text formatting is probably going to be simpler than the regex based functions we have now. The part that's probably going to be a little tricky is adding the logic that handles `rich_text` mention blocks since each `render_block` call site works with a different set of data (The webhook integration calls Slack API) but the code for that has to be baked into `render_block` instead of its own separate function (like `convert_slack_user_and_channel_mentions`).

Once we start processing `rich_text`, it will probably replace `convert_to_zulip_markdown` since we can't convert only some of a message's `rich_text` blocks and somehow stitch the rest from the `message["text"]` field without messy regex. So the initial version probably needs to handle all `rich_text` block types above.

Opened #38146 to start this. (It already has fixtures of the various `rich_text` blocks)

## chardet dependency

*2026-03-06 to 2026-03-06 · 2 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/chardet.20dependency/with/2400545)*

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-03-06 14:14 UTC

We started using chardet in #35334.  It is apparently [LGPL licensed](https://github.com/chardet/chardet/blob/6.0.0/LICENSE).  Or, well, was?  Until it was [rewritten (?) by AI in 7.0](https://github.com/chardet/chardet/releases/tag/7.0.0) and reliscensed under MIT license, and it's a [whole thing](https://github.com/chardet/chardet/issues/327).  simonw has a [blog post summary](https://simonwillison.net/2026/Mar/5/chardet/) of it.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-03-06 17:58 UTC

LGPL license is fine for a Zulip dependency, since we're not modifying the library itself. 

But the story is one I've been expecting to see some version of since I've experienced what is possible with Claude Code. I think we'll see a lot more stories like this. There are two outcomes of the new capability of AI-assisted rewrites that I see as credibly plausible:
- Copyleft as a strategy for protecting the openness of smaller projects is greatly weakened. (I don't think this is relevant to GCC or Linux, since the cost to get a quality debugged, optimized version with Claude Code style tools seems prohibitive).
- Open core business models. If your concept is to have a small set of features that are proprietary within an otherwise OSS project, it may not be hard for a competitor to use AI to implement just the proprietary features, especially if they and their test suite is source-available.

*2026-03-25 to 2026-03-27 · 19 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/oauth.20url.20namespace/with/2417892)*

see also #**backend>SCIM test fails when making Zulip an OAuth provider.**

**Steve Howell** · 2026-03-25 14:03 UTC

When Rohitt and I did the original oauth spikes back in 2020, we just had our oauth client use the same url namespace (e.g. "/api/v1/messages") as regular API clients use.  In other words, in our minds, our oauth client was pretty much the same as every other API client with the **only** difference being what we put in the HTTP header to get ourselves authorized.

**Steve Howell** · 2026-03-25 14:04 UTC

This decision was totally driven by expediency.  It would have been no effort at all to use a different prefix in our client's code, but it would have required some changes on the Django side.  I don't think the Django changes would have necessarily been difficult; we just didn't see any reason to make them.

**Steve Howell** · 2026-03-25 14:05 UTC

For due diligence, I am asking if @Apoorva Pendse should re-visit that decision in his current efforts.  I think the advantages for using the same URL paths are pretty obvious.  It's less work now, and it also arguably means there are fewer things to think about in the future.

**Steve Howell** · 2026-03-25 14:06 UTC

But I can also see advantages to requiring different URL prefixes from oauth clients. For an example, if oauth clients send to different URLs, then you can automatically spot them in the logs without doing any additional work.  Having said that, if that's the only problem you want to solve (spotting oauth clients in the logs), then there are probably easier solutions.

**Steve Howell** · 2026-03-25 14:07 UTC

So this is more of an open-ended question: do folks see any drawbacks with us continuing to piggyback off of the "/api/v1/..." namespace for oauth clients?

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-03-25 18:20 UTC

How does one check authentication for OAuth clients -- is it via an HTTP header or something else? 

I think if it's something where the routing of "Which authentication method is used?" is trivial, using the same URLs is ideal.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-03-25 18:23 UTC

I see #**backend>SCIM test fails when making Zulip an OAuth provider.** kinda answers that.

**Steve Howell** · 2026-03-25 21:24 UTC

Yes, the server checks authorization/authentication for OAuth clients by looking at encoded bearer token in the HTTP Authorization header.  We delegate the check to the django-oauth-toolkit library, and the library looks up a database table to match the incoming token to the user.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-03-25 21:50 UTC

Yeah so I think it should be fine, `Authorization` header parsing can very naturally check multiple possible types for the header. And it's definitely way easier for client implementations to not have an additional URL scheme.

**Steve Howell** · 2026-03-26 12:00 UTC

I actually don't agree with the premise that it's way easier for clients to not have an additional URL scheme, having played with this myself as the client.

As a client, you have to funnel all your requests through helper functions to put the token into the correct HTTP header, so in the same function it's just as easy to put "/oauth" as the prefix as "/api/v1".

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-03-26 19:54 UTC

Is it common for other products to use a separate URL namespace for this, though? At the very least, it seems easier to talk about both in conversations and documentation if API clients all use the same URL for a given endpoint.

**Steve Howell** · 2026-03-26 22:21 UTC

I have no idea what other products do.  I'm just giving you my report that it wouldn't matter to me as a client author whether the prefix was "/api/v1" (which is a little strange to begin with for a 13-year-old product) or "/oath/foo", because I have to create a helper to effectively use the API under an oauth regime anyway.  I don't see how it would be different for any other developer.

I do think that you're right about the documentation issue to a certain degree, which is why I still think the default answer is to use the same prefix, unless there are some operational reasons (or just other reasons that we haven't thought of) to use a different namespace for the URL paths.

The Zulip precedent here is that we already have parallel path namespaces--"/json" and "/api/v1".  But that's just a data point to consider.  The differences between how official clients and API clients talk to the server are more than the differences between how API clients and OAuth clients talk to the server.  I'm working under the V1 assumption that an OAuth token gives you identical privileges to what an API token gives you.  That's not necessarily a safe assumption in V2, when clients can start specifying that they only grant certain kinds of access to Zulip with their OAuth token.  I honestly don't know either way how that affects the central question here, which is why I ask.

I defer to the people more involved here while still reporting my own personal experiences from 2020.  (I also have a vested interest in this for my own 2026 client--see #**off topic>Angry Cat Zulip Client** for more context there.)

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-03-26 23:07 UTC

I think we can go with keeping the same URL scheme. OAuth scopes will be great, but I think are an orthogonal axis here.

**Steve Howell** · 2026-03-26 23:40 UTC

I've never been upset with /json vs. /api/v1 for kinda the same reason that I don't think it really matters from the client's perspective whether you use /api/v1/... vs. /oath/foo/...

Having said that, I would actually encourage some deliberation here.  These decisions tend to last FOREVER.  We have /api/v1 and "v1" is completely meaningless at this point.

If there are any reasons to diverge the oauth paths from the api-token paths, I encourage everybody to speak now or forever hold your peace.  Because this decision is effectively impossible to reverse (even though I lean toward it being the right one).

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-03-26 23:48 UTC

v1 isn't meaningless. It reflects that we've not yet made a major breaking change, like changing how responses are encoded, that would require a bump in the API's major version number.

But yes I agree this is the kind of decision that is annoying to change later!

**Steve Howell** · 2026-03-27 00:47 UTC

Using "api/v1" doesn't provide me with any guarantee of meaningful consistency in the results. ## Ubuntu 26.04 (beta) provision

*2026-04-01 to 2026-04-22 · 7 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Ubuntu.2026.2E04.20.28beta.29.20provision/with/2424420)*

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2026-04-01 17:48 UTC

I tried to get provision working on Ubuntu 26.04 since the beta for that is out. It wasn't too painful. Here are some notes that will be helpful when updating the script when the release is out (used Claude to help with it):

  Key platform changes

  - GCC 15 defaults to -std=gnu23, where () in function declarations means "no arguments" (C23). This breaks
   K&R-style code. Workaround: build with CFLAGS="-std=gnu17".
  - Python 3.14: ast.Constant.s attribute removed. django-bitfield 2.2.0 (latest on PyPI) fails to install.
  Fixed in git tag 2.3.0 but not yet published to PyPI.
  - PostgreSQL 18: index_beginscan gained a 6th parameter (IndexScanInstrumentation *). PGroonga >= 4.0.4
  required.

  Package availability

  - Groonga/PGroonga: no resolute packages published yet. Noble packages are incompatible (e.g.,
  libmsgpackc2 dependency doesn't exist on resolute).
  - libcrypt-dev must be explicitly installed — the -lcrypt linker symlink is no longer provided by default.
   Needed for uwsgi.
  - libheif and libde265 PPAs are not needed — resolute ships up-to-date versions.

  Node.js / corepack

  - corepack enable installs shims to /usr/bin/ instead of /usr/local/bin/ on resolute. Fix: corepack enable
   --install-directory /usr/local/bin.

## Previews using GitHub apps.

*2026-04-12 to 2026-04-21 · 5 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Previews.20using.20GitHub.20apps.2E/with/2432041)*

**Apoorva Pendse** · 2026-04-12 16:25 UTC

Previous discussion: #**feedback>github issue titles**.

Useful links:
- [Available REST API endpoints for app installation access tokens](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/authentication/endpoints-available-for-github-app-installation-access-tokens?apiVersion=2026-03-10#issues)
- [Using an installation access token to authenticate as an app installation](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/generating-an-installation-access-token-for-a-github-app)
- [Generating a user access token for a GitHub App](https://docs.github.com/en/apps/creating-github-apps/authenticating-with-a-github-app/generating-a-user-access-token-for-a-github-app#about-user-access-tokens)


Since we prefer using GitHub app installation over PATs, I'd like to hear opinions on which path should we be taking here:
Using app installation access tokens VS user access tokens associated with a GH app.

Using installation access tokens means we'd have Realm level installation tokens for apps that are installed in a GitHub org and user level app installation tokens in case the user links some repo owned by a "user" account, instead of an "org" account.

Installation access tokens have this problem where even if the Realm admins install the app in their org(s), we don't know whether the Zulip user asking for the preview is part of the org on GH, because we might lack info about their GH identity.

Skipping that check would pose the same the risk as using a global PAT created by some privileged GH user, which #36434 does.

We'd need to map a Zulip user to their GH user account and identify whether they are part of the org for `/org/repo/pull` links.

The other way is to generate and maintain user access tokens associated with the GitHub app.
From the docs:

>A user access token is a type of OAuth token. Unlike a traditional OAuth token, the user access token does not use scopes. Instead, it uses fine-grained permissions. A user access token only has permissions that both the user and the app have. For example, if the app was granted permission to write the contents of a repository, but the user can only read the contents, then the user access token can only read the contents.

So the app must be installed in the user's or org's account that owns the repo and the requesting user must have access to that repo.
Every Zulip user who wants to see previews must go through the OAuth flow.
The advantage is we'd just need to maintain a single token in [`third_party_api_state`](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/blob/2fa36d66dd31d4c462fd4d8d104343c2cf221219/zerver/models/users.py#L690).

I'd vote for using user access tokens.

**Sarthak** · 2026-04-12 18:44 UTC

User access tokens seem preferable here, since installation tokens authenticate the app rather than the requesting user and would require us to re-implement org/repo access checks. User access tokens let GitHub enforce authorization automatically, ensuring previews only work when the Zulip user actually has repository access.

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-04-13 18:54 UTC

If one is using user access tokens, how would caching work? Or would we be expecting to just fetch from GitHub the information live on-hover, with no ability to cache, since we're relying on GitHub itself to do the ACLs?

**Apoorva Pendse** · 2026-04-21 17:34 UTC

Hmm, we can probably do something better for the public repos.

We can cache the visibility status of a repo for a longer time, and serve directly for the public ones, with a smaller timeout for the cached issues/PRs than the visibility status cache.

That'd help to avoid forcing everyone on the realm to go through the OAuth flow, especially where most links point to something public, and also make it possible to stick within rate limits for public links.

We have to setup a PAT on the server for the second benefit:
> Making a conditional request does not count against your primary rate limit if a `304` response is returned and the request was made while correctly authorized with an `Authorization` header

[source](https://docs.github.com/en/rest/using-the-rest-api/best-practices-for-using-the-rest-api)

**Tim Abbott** · 2026-04-21 17:55 UTC

Yeah, caching public repo data seems nice, though maybe even then we do need a fairly short TTL (5-30 minutes range?), since the metadata we're showing can change.

## New status for exported RealmExport rows

*2026-05-04 to 2026-05-04 · 2 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/New.20status.20for.20exported.20RealmExport.20rows/with/2449762)*

**Mateusz Mandera** · 2026-05-04 16:34 UTC

In #38862 we're fixing a bug introduced by 25a61f52cccbb5717814c062eee17e69bd6801ac, where exported `RealmExport` rows have their recorded `export_path` overwritten to `None`. 
In #**production help>Cloud import version mismatch@2415881**  we saw that an imported `RealmExport` row with `status=SUCCEEDED` and `export_path=None` crashes the `get_realm_exports_serialized` endpoint, which doesn't expect such a state.

So #38862 is adding a new status ``NOT_INCLUDED_IN_EXPORT`` for `RealmExport` rows that get their `export_path` stripped away during an export. 

Do we also want a migration to find any `RealmExport.objects.filter(status=SUCCEEDED, export_path=None)` rows and update their status to the new `NOT_INCLUDED_IN_EXPORT`? This would fix any pre-existing rows like this that may have been created since 25a61f52cccbb5717814c062eee17e69bd6801ac, such as #**production help>Cloud import version mismatch@2415881**  (probably very rare).

I guess the only concern is wrongfully setting this status for `RealmExport` rows which might have  the ``status=SUCCEEDED, export_path=None`` state for a different reason than 25a61f52cccbb5717814c062eee17e69bd6801ac. But In principle such rows shouldn't exist, and I don't think we're aware of any other way they could be created.

**Alex Vandiver** · 2026-05-04 18:18 UTC

I think since we're convinced there's no codepath that gets to that pair of states otherwise, it's a reasonable migration to add

Message sending is a performance-critical code path so I'd favor the CTE approach with good tests. We do many messier things to optimize that code path already.


## do_delete_user_core: scrubbing scope

*2026-05-24 to 2026-09-11 · 13 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/do_delete_user_core.3A.20scrubbing.20scope/with/2467188)*

**Agnish Bauri** · 2026-05-24 19:40 UTC

@Mateusz Mandera [asked](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/39347#issuecomment-4529189817) for #backend input on two open questions from #39347 (per-user PII scrubbing in `do_delete_user_core`).

## 1. `UserActivity` / `UserActivityInterval` retention on user deletion

These tables are documented (model docstring) as kept for org-level endpoint-usage analytics. Today `do_delete_user_core` leaves them in place. The question is whether that's the right behavior for an explicit deletion:

- **Keep**: preserves the analytics signal; downside is that a deleted user's per-endpoint access pattern is still inferable.
- **Delete**: cleaner privacy stance; loses the deleted user's contribution to org-level stats.

Either way, I believe the decision should be documented in a comment in `do_delete_user_core` so future contributors don't second-guess it.

## 2. `RealmAuditLog` `extra_data` scrubbing scope

Currently `do_delete_user_core` scrubs `extra_data` for three event types: `USER_EMAIL_CHANGED`, `USER_FULL_NAME_CHANGED`, `USER_SETTING_CHANGED`.

@Mateusz Mandera flagged `USER_MUTED` / `USER_UNMUTED` as additional candidates. Their `extra_data` carries `muted_user_id`, which is sensitive behavior data about who the deleted user was muting.

Questions for the channel:

- Add `USER_MUTED` / `USER_UNMUTED` to the scrubbing list? (Seems clearly yes from a PII standpoint, but flagging in case there's a reason to preserve.)
- Are there other `AuditLogEventType` values whose `extra_data` could carry the deleted user's PII that we should also include? A systematic audit of all event types would be useful if anyone has done that recently.

#39347 has the full audit. The ongoing [PR1](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/39393) is scope-limited to the seven "definite PII" tables and is unaffected by either question above.

## Link previews in compose preview

*2026-06-18 to 2026-06-19 · 8 messages · [open in Zulip](https://chat.zulip.org/#narrow/channel/3-backend/topic/Link.20previews.20in.20compose.20preview/with/2481904)*

**Aadyot Nandan S** · 2026-06-18 22:46 UTC

Working on [#19465](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/issues/19465) (PR [#38630](https://github.com/zulip/zulip/pull/38630)). When an org has link previews on, the compose preview (eye icon) shows everything except the link-preview cards, so it isn't an accurate picture of the message that will be sent. The goal is to show link-preview embeds in the compose preview, same as they appear on the sent message.

The current PR gets there by warming the embed cache from the render endpoint (on background threads) and then having the client poll until the embed appears. @Aman (amanagr) 's feedback was to drop both and instead reuse the existing `embed_links` queue, and push an event to live-update the preview when the fetch finishes. I agree that's the better shape, but how exactly to do it needs some discussion, posting here to settle the implementation design before I rewrite it.

---

**Aadyot Nandan S** · 2026-06-18 22:46 UTC

## How sent messages get their embeds today

Rendering collects the links worth previewing, and the send path drops a job on the `embed_links` queue. A single worker pulls the job, fetches each link's preview data (slow - a few seconds, sometimes two HTTP round trips), re-renders the message with the embeds, and pushes an update out to everyone who received it, who then see the cards appear. The fetched data also gets cached, keyed just on the URL.

A compose preview can't reuse that directly, for three reasons:

- The whole flow is built around a saved message, identified by its message ID: the worker looks the message up by that ID, re-renders it, and notifies its recipients. A draft has no message ID - it isn't saved and hasn't been sent to anyone - so there's nothing to look up and no recipients to notify.
- The update is private: it should reach only the composer, not the eventual recipients.
- The draft keeps changing as the user edits, so whether a finished preview is still current has to be judged on the client, not by comparing against a stored message.

---

**Aadyot Nandan S** · 2026-06-18 22:47 UTC

## Two options

Both keep the fetch on the `embed_links` queue and notify the composer with an event instead of polling; they differ only in what the worker does once the fetch finishes.

### Option A - worker renders the preview and pushes the HTML

The worker fetches the data, builds an unsaved message stub, re-renders, and emits an event carrying the rendered HTML, which the client swaps into the preview box. It's a single hop with the lowest latency, and it closely mirrors what the `embed_links` worker already does for sent messages (fetch > re-render > push), so it's close to consistent with existing behavior; pushing rendered HTML over the event bus isn't novel either, since `update_message` already does it.

The trade-off is that the worker renders the content as it was when the job was enqueued, so by the time the HTML arrives the user has likely typed more, and the client has to confirm the snapshot still matches the current draft and discard it otherwise - which can surface as a brief stale or empty state. It's not incorrect, and it settles once editing stops, but while editing continues the worker is often rendering something that gets thrown away, and each preview puts a full markdown render plus a mention-data DB query on the single shared worker, on top of the fetch.

---

**Aadyot Nandan S** · 2026-06-18 22:47 UTC

### Option B - worker only fetches; the client re-renders

The worker fetches the data and writes it into the shared cache, but doesn't render anything itself. Once the cache is warm it emits a lightweight "embeds ready" event to the composer - no HTML, just a signal - and the client responds by making one more `/render` call for the draft as it currently stands. That render comes back almost immediately, since the data it needs is now cached, and the client swaps the result in just as it handles any normal preview render. Because the worker only ever fetches, all message rendering stays in the one `/render` endpoint - no rendering logic duplicated into the worker that has to be kept consistent with it - and the event carries no draft content.

The key difference from A is that the re-render runs against whatever the draft contains at that moment, not a snapshot from when the job was enqueued, so it can't show a stale preview: either the embed is cached and appears, or it isn't ready yet and the preview is simply left unchanged.

The cost is the extra round trip - A's event delivers the finished HTML, whereas B's only tells the client to ask again, so there's one more request before the embed appears (cheap, but real) - plus a bit more client-side handling than A's single swap.

I lean slightly toward B - the can't-go-stale behavior and the lighter worker seem worth more than A's small latency edge - but it's close.

---

**Aadyot Nandan S** · 2026-06-18 22:48 UTC

## Open questions

These apply regardless of A or B:

1. **Share the `embed_links` queue, or give previews their own?** The queue handles only sent and edited messages today, served by a single worker, so a slow compose-preview fetch sitting ahead of a real one would delay the embed cards that appear under sent messages (it wouldn't affect sending or the feed itself, just when those cards show up). A per-URL cap and skipping in-flight duplicates help, but a dedicated preview queue would isolate it cleanly - a slow compose preview could then only delay other previews - and it's cheap, since the fetch and the URL cache are shared either way. This is independent of the A/B choice (a dedicated queue would still run A or B).     
                                                                                                                                                                                                             @Aman (amanagr)  did "reuse the queue" mean literally enqueue onto `embed_links`, or just reuse its fetching code and the shared cache (which would still allow a separate preview queue)?
2. **A vs. B** - any preference?
3. **Which links get previewed, and how many?** The preview currently fetches only the first 2 links sorted alphabetically, whereas the sent message previews all of them in document order (up to its own limit of 24 per message). So the preview can show fewer cards, in a different order, than the real message. The cap was just to bound how many fetches one preview fires off, and the alphabetical sort only to make the choice deterministic - neither matches the send path. Should the preview instead mirror the send path's behavior (same links, same order), perhaps with a higher or no preview-specific cap?

4. **What should the user see when a preview can't be fetched?** A link with no embed just renders as normal link text (today's behavior), so the fallback isn't broken - the only choice is whether to leave it as the plain link, or add a small "no preview available" hint. Any preference, or is silently showing the plain link fine?

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2026-06-19 02:19 UTC

I just want us to reuse the existing mechanism we have for rendering the preview after a message is sent. I don't see a reason to differ here. If we want to make changes in that logic, it will be for the both of them.

**Aman (amanagr)** · 2026-06-19 02:21 UTC

Also, it is not a good idea to paste so much AI-generated content for discussion; you only need to use it for your own reference and understanding.

**Aadyot Nandan S** · 2026-06-19 09:37 UTC

Got it. Sorry about that, will keep future discussions to the point and use the background information for my understanding. I'll update the PR to reuse the current mechanism
